name: American Energy
title: The Energy Election: Voters Chose Clean Energy and Lower Costs
description:
The result: energy costs exploded – and that drove costs up for everything else.
How Trump’s dirty energy agenda backfired Energy costs were a defining issue of the midterms up and down the ballot.
Voters rejected Trump’s attacks on clean energy Republicans have relentlessly attacked clean energy, but voters didn’t buy it.
Voters chose clean energy and climate action Voters made it clear they’re fed up with Trump and his allies’ corrupt, dirty energy agenda.
Voters chose candidates who will protect people and the planet In addition to their frustration with high energy costs, voters also brought their climate concerns to the ballot box.
text:
Trump’s energy agenda has been an economic disaster for voters and a political disaster for Republicans. In 2024, they promised to cut energy costs in half. Instead, they gutted cheap, reliable clean energy. They doubled down on oil, coal, gas and dirty data centers to enrich themselves and their donors. The result: energy costs exploded – and that drove costs up for everything else. While families struggled with rising bills, Republicans gave data centers tax breaks. To top it all off, Trump started a war in Iran that skyrocketed gas prices. But in the midterm election, voters rejected Trump’s soaring costs and corruption fueled by his dirty energy agenda.

Fed-up voters elected Democrats who ran on lowering costs and investing in clean energy. They flipped the House, Senate, governorships and state houses across the country, even in the reddest districts. Voters trust these newly elected leaders to put the people’s interests and wallets first – not Big Oil and Big Tech’s profits.

How Trump’s dirty energy agenda backfired

Energy costs were a defining issue of the midterms up and down the ballot.

Utility bills have spiked by as much as 18% nationwide since Trump took office. Between utility bills, gas prices, tariffs, and war, Trump’s agenda has cost the average family an extra $2,000 and counting.

Americans made it clear: they can’t afford their energy bills. Leading national outlets, state newspapers, and politicians took notice. LCV Victory Fund named Energy Bill Voters as the election force to be reckoned with. Heading into the final weeks of the midterms, two energy cost topics ranked among voters’ top three issues. 2026 was the energy election.

Voters saw who raised their bills, and they acted. Trump and Republicans’ failed energy policy flipped former Trump voters to Democrats. It also gave Democrats a clear advantage in critical battleground races. All of the worst-of-the-worst congressional candidates named in the LCV Victory Fund’s Dirty Dozen were defeated. And the State Dirty Dozen was a clean sweep as well.

Voters rejected Trump’s attacks on clean energy

Republicans have relentlessly attacked clean energy, but voters didn’t buy it.

Clean energy is the fastest, cheapest way to increase energy supply and bring down costs. But Trump has made blocking clean energy a cornerstone of his agenda.

Trump’s so-called “Big Beautiful Bill” slashed clean energy tax credits and renewable energy projects. Even before Republicans voted to pass it last year, voters were unhappy with its clean energy cuts. Voters voiced their disapproval in the 2025 elections in New Jersey, Virginia, and Georgia. Climate champions won in landslides by running against GOP clean energy cuts.

This year, voters still weren’t buying Trump’s anti-clean-energy agenda. Our own election-eve polling conducted by Hart Research found that:

Voters hold Republicans responsible for high energy bills. They have strongly rejected and are ready to move past Trump’s approach to energy.

Nearly two thirds (64%) say Trump has made things worse for consumers on energy prices; 59% say this of Republicans in Congress, the highest rates we recorded across six surveys over the past year.

Fully 78% say oil, gas, and utility companies have benefited more than consumers from Trump’s and the GOP’s energy policies, and a majority believe that Trump and his family (63%) and Republicans in Congress (67%) have personally profited from them.

Nearly six in 10 (58%) want our energy policies to be different from Trump’s going forward. Voters are ready to move on.

Clean energy cuts were a major midterm weakness for House Republicans, LCV Victory Fund found. Sure enough, Republicans who ran against clean energy lost up and down the ballot. At least 24 congressional Republicans who voted against clean energy lost their seats.

For example, in Arizona’s 6th district, JoAnna Mendoza defeated Dirty Dozen candidate Rep. Juan Ciscomani. Ciscomani voted for the Big Beautiful Ugly Bill, and voted to repeal a $4.5 billion program that helps families lower energy bills. Arizonans face some of the steepest electricity increases in the country, with electricity prices up 18% since January 2025.

Voters supported the candidate who wants to lower prices, not raise them. A 20-year Navy veteran, JoAnna Mendoza has served her community at several nonprofits, including the Arizona Center for Economic Progress where she championed clean energy as a climate and economic solution. Mendoza has said earlier clean energy investments “would have diversified our energy. We probably wouldn’t be looking at high gas prices, electricity bills right now if we had done this many, many years ago.”

Voters rejected Trump’s coal obsession

While blocking clean energy progress, the Trump administration props up expensive dirty energy. Trump has forced aging, polluting coal plants to remain open long past their retirement dates. As families’ energy bills rose as a result, this became a campaign issue.

One infamous example: Trump ordered the J.H. Campbell Coal plant to stay open, which cost Michiganders hundreds of millions of dollars and kept the health of nearby communities at risk. Michigan’s attorney general said that Trump’s orders to keep the plant open have cost customers about $259 million as of spring 2026. The plant sits in Michigan’s 4th District, represented by Rep. Bill Huizenga. But Huizenga refused to act. He also voted for the Big Ugly Bill and its clean energy cuts.

Angry voters responded at the ballot box, electing State Sen. Sean McCann to replace Dirty Dozen candidate Huizenga. McCann ran on lowering energy costs, saying, “We can create good-paying energy jobs and lower utility rates.” As chair of the Energy and Environment Committee in the Michigan Senate, McCann fought to transition the state away from dirty energy and investigate the coal power plants that were kept open despite their high costs and pollution. Voters chose McCann to bring the same fight to rein in polluters and champion clean energy to Congress.

Voters rejected corporate corruption

Fossil fuels’ “freaking fortune”

Voters are sick of corruption, including Republicans’ close ties to Big Oil and Gas. Oil and gas companies – big donors to Trump and Republicans – saw profits jump 142% from the war in Iran. They also got $190B in tax breaks and other handouts from his budget bill.

Trump made as much as $21 million this year alone through investments in oil and gas companies. Nine days before the election, Trump’s glee at oil industry profits made headlines as he gloated, “We’re making a freaking fortune.”

Voters across the country, however, were not so pleased with all this corruption. A Fox News poll from Oct. 9-12 found 60% of voters “extremely concerned” about government corruption. That beat inflation (58%) and gas prices (50%).

Big Tech’s dirty data centers

Big Oil and Gas weren’t the only corporate cronies on voters’ minds. Big Tech was too. Republicans gave data center developers $83 billion in tax breaks. With LCV Victory Fund’s breakout ad program focused on data centers, voters connected the dots. At least 10 of the Republicans who voted for those tax breaks lost their race.

Concerned about Big Tech’s impact on energy demand, air and water quality, and utility costs, voters pushed back through ballot measures as well. In 10 states, voters backed restrictions on data centers or rejected data center development measures in over 40 local ballot contests.

Anti-corruption candidates won

In races across the country, candidates ran, and won, on ending the corruption that makes life more expensive for working Americans.

For example, take the Senate race in Ohio – a state Trump won by 11 points in 2024. On Election Day, Sherrod Brown won against Republican incumbent and Dirty Dozen candidate Sen. Jon Husted. Husted was dogged by a scandal centered on FirstEnergy’s $1.3 billion HB 6 bailout, called out by LCV Victory Fund as “the largest public corruption scandal in state history.” Husted also won the title of “the face of data centers.” He couldn’t win with voters, however, who saw that his corrupt corporate ties would not bring their bills down.

The Senate race in Texas is another example. The state House impeached state attorney general and U.S. Senate candidate Ken Paxton on charges including bribery. He was also tied to the Republican tax law’s “massive handouts to Big Oil.” As LCV Victory Fund’s ad said, “Ken Paxton is for sale, not for Texas.” Texas voters instead chose James Talarico, who ran on lower costs for communities.

Voters chose clean energy and climate action

Voters made it clear they’re fed up with Trump and his allies’ corrupt, dirty energy agenda. Instead, they trust Democrats to lower energy prices and improve energy policy. Even in red states and districts, Democrats pitched clean energy as homegrown power and good jobs, and won. Our polling showed that, when asked in an open-ended question what changes they would make, the top response (34%) was more reliance on and investment in renewable energy.

Georgia has seen some of the largest utility bill increases in the country. Last year, the state’s elected Public Service Commission passed back-to-back rate hikes. But midterm voters elected Peter Hubbard and Sheila Edwards, giving Democrats a majority on the commission for the first time since the 1990s. Both promised to take on big utilities and data centers and lower costs with clean energy. Edwards won despite more than $2.5 million spent to support her opponent Josh Tolbert, who was backed by state utility interests.

Voters chose candidates who will protect people and the planet

In addition to their frustration with high energy costs, voters also brought their climate concerns to the ballot box. Voters worried about clean water and air, extreme weather, and the future of their homes and health.

For example, in Florida’s 14th District, extreme weather has driven up home insurance costs. Tampa Bay residents also worried about Medicare, Medicaid, and the price of fuel and groceries. Florida voters chose Rep. Kathy Castor, who made climate a priority and fought for lowering costs. She defeated Mike Beltran, who had a record of bailing out the insurance industry while it drove up rates for homeowners.

Meanwhile in Iowa’s Senate race, a water crisis linked to rising cancer rates was front and center. Senatorial candidate U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson voted against clean water protections and took money from corporations that are contaminating Iowa’s water. She lost to Josh Turek, who is a champion for effective environmental protection. In Iowa’s state legislature, Rep. Turek has fought for clean air and water, extreme weather resiliency, and lower utility bills to benefit the working and rural families of his district. Now he’ll bring the same fight for all Iowans to Congress.

What comes next: lower bills, cleaner power

After Republicans won the presidency and Congress in 2024, they blocked cleaner, cheaper energy, started a war in Iran, and gave tax breaks to data centers. Families have paid the price. But they pushed back at the ballot box in 2025 and again this year. Now, voters have elected climate champions nationwide to deliver real solutions and lower energy bills.

In January, Democrats will lead in the House and Senate. With the majority, they’ll have more power to push back against the Trump administration and fight for solutions. For example, 120 House Democrats cosponsored the Energy Relief Act earlier this year. It would ramp up clean energy like wind and solar, hold data centers accountable, and expand heating for low-income families. Republicans have blocked it from moving forward. But in the new Congress, the shoe will be on the other foot. The new pro-clean energy, pro-climate majority will have the chance to move bills like this forward.

Voters made this happen, but the work is not done. We must all stay in the fight for a clean energy future. A few next steps to take:

title: As Diesel Prices Rise, Electric School Buses Are Helping Districts Keep Costs Low
description:
But for school districts across the U.S. that rely on diesel-burning school buses, the financial strain of high diesel prices is direct and immediate – and strains already scarce school budgets.
In rural Fleming County, Kentucky, the school district expects to save around $600,000 per year, thanks to its electric school buses, and is using those savings to give teachers a raise.
Electric school bus charging can also be managed to take advantage of off-peak rates, and in some cases, allow vehicles to send energy back to the grid.
Shawnee Public Schools in Shawnee, Oklahoma, saved roughly $40,900 in fuel costs during the 2024-2025 school year after adding eight electric school buses to its central Oklahoma fleet.

text:
Over the past few decades, diesel and gasoline prices have fluctuated, spiking in times of geopolitical turmoil. Since the war on Iran began in early 2026, costs spiked to historic highs, with diesel prices in the U.S. up 70% from February and unleaded gas up 45%. Most people don’t fill up their cars with diesel at the pump, so the economic shock hits home with rising prices of everyday goods that are transported by medium- and heavy-duty fleets. But for school districts across the U.S. that rely on diesel-burning school buses, the financial strain of high diesel prices is direct and immediate – and strains already scarce school budgets.

This fall, diesel prices surpassed $6 a gallon for the first time in history — and have stayed there for months on end, with the average national cost of diesel rising from $3.75 a gallon in September 2025 to $6.29 in September 2026. As a result, the national average cost to fuel a diesel-burning school bus at those prices rose from $7,924 per year in 2025 to $13,292 in 2026.

“This was already a tight budget year without skyrocketing diesel prices,” said Richmond Public Schools Superintendent Jason Kamras when speaking with the Times-Dispatch. Amherst County, another Viriginia school district, estimated that they spent about $78,000 on diesel in August. That was roughly $37,000 more than the monthly charge for December 2025.

In Jefferson County, Colorado, the district’s transportation director says soaring diesel prices have already cost the district $100,000 more than during the same quarter the year before.

When diesel costs cause the price of goods and services to ramp up, businesses pass along increased prices to consumers. But school budgets don’t work that way. As Peter Manella, public policy liaison for the National Association for Pupil Transportation, explained to Colorado Public Radio, schools “have to look at, do we take the team to the football game, or do we let mom and dad do that? Do we have field trips to museums and to the state capital and other places that we go?”

For districts looking for cleaner air, lower emissions and cost savings, electric school buses have proven to be a promising alternative, especially as diesel costs rise. Districts are already seeing cost savings from making the switch, even before the recent spike in diesel prices.

“What I can save in diesel and maintenance, I can almost hire a teacher, or an instructional aide, or give some other benefit to my teachers. The cost savings are going to let me better support my kids,” said Keith Kimbrough, principal at Martinsville ISD in unincorporated Martinsville, Texas, according to the Texas Tribune. In rural Fleming County, Kentucky, the school district expects to save around $600,000 per year, thanks to its electric school buses, and is using those savings to give teachers a raise.

Electricity costs rose on average between September 2025 and September 2026, too, but much less dramatically than diesel prices. The average nationwide cost to fuel an electric school bus rose from $3,481 per year in September 2025 to $3,860 in 2026. The cost to fuel an electric bus rose 10.8%, versus a 67.7% increase for diesel buses. When electricity costs rise, they generally do so at more gradual rates, which allows for time to prepare, unlike volatile shocks to gas and diesel that can upend school budgets in months.

Electric school bus charging can also be managed to take advantage of off-peak rates, and in some cases, allow vehicles to send energy back to the grid. This allows school districts to earn electricity credits to offset utility bills, therefore sending more money back to school budgets.

Shawnee Public Schools in Shawnee, Oklahoma, saved roughly $40,900 in fuel costs during the 2024-2025 school year after adding eight electric school buses to its central Oklahoma fleet. This summer, the district connected with the local utility to send power back to the grid through vehicle-to-grid technology to save the district even more money. That makes for valuable reinvestments in school supplies, teacher salaries and building upgrades.

“We saved so much money just running the electric bus,” said John Wiles, transportation director for Shawnee Public Schools. “Now that we’re going to the [vehicle-to-grid], we’re going to save even more money.”

text:
Officials gathered in the city of Woodruff on Nov. 13 to celebrate the opening of BMW Plant Woodruff, the first high-voltage battery assembly plant in North America. The small Upstate city now plays a key role in the production of BMW's first all-electric vehicle made in the United States.

BMW's $700 million Woodruff facility was first announced in October 2022. Now, the plant is open and creating sixth-generation high-voltage batteries to power electric vehicles.

"From the very first conversation, I knew this partnership was different," said Woodruff mayor Kenneth Gist at the plant opening. "BMW and the city of Woodruff want the same thing – success in business, success in our community and success in building the next generation of BMW electric vehicles to be the best in the world. Today that dream is right in front of us."

The new Woodruff plant will work hand in hand with BMW's Plant Spartanburg, located just 15 miles away. The high-voltage batteries produced at Plant Woodruff will be transported to Plant Spartanburg and used to assemble the BMW iX5.

The iX5 is a new all-electric BMW SUV model. Made at Plant Spartanburg, it will be the first fully electric BMW assembled in the United States, the company announced in July.

The new one-million-square-foot plant includes a virtual reality training center, a complex production line, a quality testing hub, and more. Every high-voltage battery produced inside the facility has over 90 characteristics verified before reaching end-of-line testing, in alignment with BMW's zero-defect principle, according to company officials.

"BMW continues to deliver on its commitments to South Carolina," said Gov. Henry McMaster. "Just a few years ago, I stood on this site with BMW leadership to break ground on this facility. Today, we are seeing that investment come to life and marking another milestone in BMW's commitment to South Carolina."

There are already 300 employees working in Plant Woodruff, according to BMW. The company said they cannot yet speak to future employment growth.

The Plant Woodruff property, which sits along SC-101, is the former home of the S.J. Workman Peach Farm. At the Nov. 13 opening, BMW distributed pins featuring peaches to pay tribute to the property's history.

"We are honored to be a part of that story, and we will do our very best to carry that legacy forward," said BMW Plant Spartanburg CEO Robert Engelhorn. "While this land has changed dramatically, its purpose has not changed as much. For generations, it was a place where people worked, where families built lives and where someone believed in the future of Woodruff. Today, that continues in a new way."

BMW's economic impact on South Carolina

In 1992, BMW Group announced that its first plant outside Germany would be built in South Carolina. Plant Spartanburg opened in 1994, helping transform the Upstate's economy.

At that time, BMW said it would invest $600 million in the plant and employ 2,000 associates by the year 2000. Today, more than three decades later, Plant Spartanburg employs more than 11,000 people and produces 1,500 vehicles per day.

In 2026, Plant Spartanburg created $36.1 billion in annual economic output in South Carolina, according to a University of South Carolina Darla Moore School of Business study led by research economist Joey Von Nessen. However, even more astounding than BMW's economic output is their jobs multiplier rate of 4.2, Von Nessen said at a BMW stakeholder event on Nov. 10.

This means that for every 10 jobs created by Plant Spartanburg, an additional 32 jobs are created elsewhere in South Carolina. For comparison, the jobs multiplier is about 1.7 for the average company. In total, Plant Spartanburg has created around 55,327 jobs in South Carolina.

"It is such an outlier compared to what we see for the average industry...and that's really exciting because when we look at Plant Woodruff, in the future we look at future expansions and future investments in South Carolina."

title: Texas Has A Power Grid Unlike Any Other State, And AI Is Exposing Its Biggest Weakness
description:
The interconnection requests for data centers could see electricity demand overtaking realistic supply, and this has exposed Texas' power generation limitations and ineffective demand forecasting.
The bill will require AI data center developers to share the cost of infrastructure upgrades needed to enable the delivery of power to their facilities.
The bill also introduced clear guidelines that could mandate the shutdown of data centers during emergencies like Winter Storm Uri.
Abbott ordered a comprehensive audit of interconnection requests at ERCOT in response to soaring requests from AI data center developers.
This will place interconnection requests under more comprehensive scrutiny than what the Batch Zero study could have provided.
text:
As the world continues to adopt AI at an incredible rate, its computing needs are demanding more data centers to be built, which in turn demands more electricity. The need for more data centers is skyrocketing, and Texas is becoming a hotspot for AI mostly thanks to power availability and low operating costs. As plans for new data centers continue to increase in numbers, the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) is getting requests for interconnections that the grid cannot supply. The Texas grid experienced an all-time high demand of about 91.1 gigawatts on July 22, 2026, and current project proposals (of which data centers account for about 90% of the power requested) total more than five times that July peak.

Texas is unique in terms of its energy generation, being almost entirely isolated from other states. A lot of its power generation comes from renewable sources, with Texas having the largest number of wind turbines in the United States. The state's limited power import capability was a significant factor in the largest controlled outage in U.S. history during Winter Storm Uri in 2021. The interconnection requests for data centers could see electricity demand overtaking realistic supply, and this has exposed Texas' power generation limitations and ineffective demand forecasting. This has forced it to consider interconnection requests from data center developers with increased scrutiny.

ERCOT introduced a batch screening process called Batch Zero for these proposals because of how long it was taking to perform the due diligence for each request. Not all proposed data centers are viable, with many lacking funding and support. A targeted senate bill and recent action by Gov. Greg Abbott have sought to realign interconnection requests with what the grid can support, and saw the introduction of legislation to support a stable grid infrastructure.

Texas lawmakers introduced Senate Bill 6 (SB 6), which was signed into law by Gov. Abbott on June 20, 2025. The bill will require AI data center developers to share the cost of infrastructure upgrades needed to enable the delivery of power to their facilities. The cost of these upgrades had in the past been passed to ratepayers, who saw it play out on their power bills. The bill also introduced clear guidelines that could mandate the shutdown of data centers during emergencies like Winter Storm Uri.

After SB 6 took effect, Gov. Abbott ordered a comprehensive audit of interconnection requests at ERCOT in response to soaring requests from AI data center developers. This will place interconnection requests under more comprehensive scrutiny than what the Batch Zero study could have provided. As a result of the audit, ERCOT delayed the Batch Zero process, with new approvals for large data centers on hold until the audit is complete.

The audit mandated by Gov. Abbott will have a significant impact on the timelines and feasibility of some of the data center developments impacted by it, but will go a long way toward ensuring that Texas maintains a stable electricity supply.

title: Permitting Bill Could Enable Trump Administration's New Public Lands Sell-Off Plan
description:
If enacted into law, BAAJA would make it harder for the public to learn about, or stop, the sale of public lands.
Public lands should be protected, not privatized.
Selling public lands is highly unpopular among the American public.
Just this week, a new veterans’ initiative to defend public lands was unveiled.
The strategic plan also indicates Interior’s vision for projects on public lands that are not sold off: oil-and-gas drilling, mining, and AI data centers.
text:
—

The release of the Trump Administration’s official strategic plan for the Department of the Interior this week revealed its intention to “decrease the size of the federal estate” by offering public lands for sale. Under current law, such a plan would be difficult to implement – but the Bipartisan Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) now before the Senate includes rollbacks that would make it easier for Trump’s Interior Department to accomplish this goal. If enacted into law, BAAJA would make it harder for the public to learn about, or stop, the sale of public lands.

In response, Drew Caputo, Vice President of Litigation for Lands, Wildlife and Oceans at Earthjustice released the following statement:

“Our public lands belong to every American, but the Trump administration wants to sell them to the highest bidder. Public lands should be protected, not privatized. Unfortunately, the permitting bill now before the Senate would make it much easier for the Trump administration to proceed with its plans to sell off America’s natural bounty. Senators should just say no to this terrible idea.”

Background

BAAJA, the permitting bill now before the Senate, would greatly erode protections under the National Environmental Policy Act, seriously impairing the public’s ability to challenge the Trump administration’s proposed land sales. Selling public lands is highly unpopular among the American public. An effort by Senate Republicans led by Sen. Mike Lee, a cosponsor of BAAJA, to include public lands selloffs in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act was defeated last year, following significant pushback from Americans across the political spectrum.

Interior’s land sell-off plan has already sparked opposition from conservation groups and even Republican U.S. Senators from Montana, who said they weren’t consulted. A story about conservationists’ opposition that appeared in Source New Mexico noted that Sen. Martin Heinrich, also a cosponsor of BAAJA, reacted to Interior’s announcement by saying: “Public lands belong in public hands.” There is broad support for this idea. Just this week, a new veterans’ initiative to defend public lands was unveiled.

The Interior Department’s strategic plan offers few clues as to how much land could be sold. While the plan suggests lands would be offered for purchase by states, localities, and Tribes, there is nothing guaranteeing they would not be immediately sold to developers in turn – as many states are legally bound to generate revenue from lands, which could force them into land sales. The strategic plan also indicates Interior’s vision for projects on public lands that are not sold off: oil-and-gas drilling, mining, and AI data centers. BAAJA would also make it difficult to reverse these kinds of projects once they have won approval by federal agencies.

The fate of public lands may have played a factor in last week’s midterm elections; according to an analysis from the Center for Western Priorities, “85 percent of voters across Mountain West states see issues involving public lands, waters, and wildlife as a motivating factor in supporting an elected official.”

Earthjustice, the nation’s premier nonprofit environmental law organization, is in court now with dozens of lawsuits seeking to prevent federal lands from being destroyed by mining, logging, or drilling.

title: BMW opens first North America high-voltage battery plant in Upstate - GoUpstate
description:
Officials gathered in the city of Woodruff on Nov. 13 to celebrate the opening of BMW Plant Woodruff, the first high-voltage battery assembly plant in North America.
The new Woodruff plant will work hand in hand with BMW's Plant Spartanburg, located just 15 miles away.
The high-voltage batteries produced at Plant Woodruff will be transported to Plant Spartanburg and used to assemble the BMW iX5.
"We are honored to be a part of that story, and we will do our very best to carry that legacy forward," said BMW Plant Spartanburg CEO Robert Engelhorn.
Today, more than three decades later, Plant Spartanburg employs more than 11,000 people and produces 1,500 vehicles per day.
text:
Officials gathered in the city of Woodruff on Nov. 13 to celebrate the opening of BMW Plant Woodruff, the first high-voltage battery assembly plant in North America. The small Upstate city now plays a key role in the production of BMW's first all-electric vehicle made in the United States.

BMW's $700 million Woodruff facility was first announced in October 2022. Now, the plant is open and creating sixth-generation high-voltage batteries to power electric vehicles.

"From the very first conversation, I knew this partnership was different," said Woodruff mayor Kenneth Gist at the plant opening. "BMW and the city of Woodruff want the same thing – success in business, success in our community and success in building the next generation of BMW electric vehicles to be the best in the world. Today that dream is right in front of us."

The new Woodruff plant will work hand in hand with BMW's Plant Spartanburg, located just 15 miles away. The high-voltage batteries produced at Plant Woodruff will be transported to Plant Spartanburg and used to assemble the BMW iX5.

The iX5 is a new all-electric BMW SUV model. Made at Plant Spartanburg, it will be the first fully electric BMW assembled in the United States, the company announced in July.

The new one-million-square-foot plant includes a virtual reality training center, a complex production line, a quality testing hub, and more. Every high-voltage battery produced inside the facility has over 90 characteristics verified before reaching end-of-line testing, in alignment with BMW's zero-defect principle, according to company officials.

"BMW continues to deliver on its commitments to South Carolina," said Gov. Henry McMaster. "Just a few years ago, I stood on this site with BMW leadership to break ground on this facility. Today, we are seeing that investment come to life and marking another milestone in BMW’s commitment to South Carolina."

There are already 300 employees working in Plant Woodruff, according to BMW. The company said they cannot yet speak to future employment growth.

The Plant Woodruff property, which sits along SC-101, is the former home of the S.J. Workman Peach Farm. At the Nov. 13 opening, BMW distributed pins featuring peaches to pay tribute to the property's history.

"We are honored to be a part of that story, and we will do our very best to carry that legacy forward," said BMW Plant Spartanburg CEO Robert Engelhorn. "While this land has changed dramatically, its purpose has not changed as much. For generations, it was a place where people worked, where families built lives and where someone believed in the future of Woodruff. Today, that continues in a new way."

BMW's economic impact on South Carolina

In 1992, BMW Group announced that its first plant outside Germany would be built in South Carolina. Plant Spartanburg opened in 1994, helping transform the Upstate's economy.

At that time, BMW said it would invest $600 million in the plant and employ 2,000 associates by the year 2000. Today, more than three decades later, Plant Spartanburg employs more than 11,000 people and produces 1,500 vehicles per day.

In 2026, Plant Spartanburg created $36.1 billion in annual economic output in South Carolina, according to a University of South Carolina Darla Moore School of Business study led by research economist Joey Von Nessen. However, even more astounding than BMW's economic output is their jobs multiplier rate of 4.2, Von Nessen said at a BMW stakeholder event on Nov. 10.

This means that for every 10 jobs created by Plant Spartanburg, an additional 32 jobs are created elsewhere in South Carolina. For comparison, the jobs multiplier is about 1.7 for the average company. In total, Plant Spartanburg has created around 55,327 jobs in South Carolina.

"It is such an outlier compared to what we see for the average industry...and that's really exciting because when we look at Plant Woodruff, in the future we look at future expansions and future investments in South Carolina."

title: At COP31, Governor Newsom announces $81 million to fund climate-smart agriculture ...
description:
Backed by the climate bond voters approved Funding for these climate-smart agriculture projects comes from Proposition 4, the $10 billion climate bond approved by California voters in 2024.
Economic contribution: In 2025 alone, California agriculture generated $64.7 billion in sales, accounting for 11% of total U.S. agricultural sales and exported $26.1 billion in goods.
Supporting climate-smart agriculture $1.1 billion: Governor Newsom’s 2021 California Comeback Plan committed $1.1 billion over two years to help agriculture adapt to climate change.
Farm to School: Championed by First Partner Jennifer Siebel Newsom, the program connects California agriculture with school nutrition.
Ongoing support: Governor Newsom signed SB 172 in July 2026, permanently establishing Farm to School in state law.
text:
ANTALYA, TÜRKIYE – As Donald Trump pulls back federal support for farmers and his reckless Iran war drives up the cost of diesel and fertilizer, Governor Gavin Newsom today announced $81 million for climate-smart agriculture projects across 55 counties, showing the world at COP31 that California is delivering results. The funding builds on state programs that are already cutting pollution and saving water through thousands of on-farm projects, and will help more farmers improve soil health and prepare for drought.

Through the California Department of Food and Agriculture’s (CDFA) Healthy Soils Program and State Water Efficiency and Enhancement Program, local partners will help farmers access funding, apply for projects, and put climate-smart practices to work on farms across the state.

alifornia voters recognized the importance of investing in climate resilience when they approved the Climate Bond in 2024,” said CDFA Secretary Karen Ross. “These funds help ensure that farmers and ranchers have the tools, technical assistance, and regional support needed to adopt practices that improve water efficiency, increase soil health, and support long-term sustainability.”

California’s climate-smart agriculture results

Since 2014, SWEEP has supported over 1,300 on-farm projects to improve irrigation water and energy use efficiency. SWEEP projects have resulted in:

1 million metric tons of CO2e reduced through the program.

1.5 million acre-feet of water conserved.

Since 2017, the Healthy Soils Program (HSP) has funded more than 2,300 on-farm projects across California.

1.6 million metric tons of CO2e reduced through HSP.

Emissions reductions equal to removing about 370,000 cars from the road for a year.

Together, the two programs have reduced emissions equivalent to removing 610,000 cars from the road, impacted nearly 390,000 acres, and provided over $320 million in grants to producers for climate-smart agriculture.

Backed by the climate bond voters approved

Funding for these climate-smart agriculture projects comes from Proposition 4, the $10 billion climate bond approved by California voters in 2024. The bond includes $300 million for climate-smart agriculture, including $65 million to improve soil health and store more carbon in the ground and $40 million for SWEEP, which helps farmers save water and energy.

Additional information about HSP and SWEEP, including future producer funding opportunities and contact information for the block grant recipients, will be available at cdfa.ca.gov/oars as awards are executed and agreements begin. The list of awardees and their service areas can be found here. These awards are tentative until CDFA receives approval through the bond accountability process.

Climate-smart agriculture and sustainable food systems

Home to one of the world’s five Mediterranean-climate regions, California is the nation’s leading producer of milk and specialty crops. Its agricultural reach is substantial:

400-plus commodities: California produces over 400 commodities and supplies nearly half of the country’s vegetables, over three-quarters of the nation’s fruits and nuts.

Milk production: The state produces about 20 percent of the nation’s milk.

Economic contribution: In 2025 alone, California agriculture generated $64.7 billion in sales, accounting for 11% of total U.S. agricultural sales and exported $26.1 billion in goods.

California’s agricultural story is one of constant adaptation, responding to climate pressures — like drought, flooding, rising temperatures, and new pest pressures — while continuing to grow food for the world under some of the strongest environmental and labor standards anywhere.

Governor Newsom has made agricultural resilience part of California’s climate strategy.

Supporting climate-smart agriculture

$1.1 billion: Governor Newsom’s 2021 California Comeback Plan committed $1.1 billion over two years to help agriculture adapt to climate change.

Water resilience: In 2023, the Newsom administration announced nearly $300 million for groundwater sustainability, irrigation efficiency, and carbon-sequestration projects.

Farmland protection: In October 2025, the Newsom administration approved more than $128 million to protect over 40,000 acres, including projects that will return 11,316 acres to California Native American tribes.

Connecting farms, schools, and healthy meals

Universal school meals: California provides school meals at no cost to students under legislation Governor Newsom signed in 2021. Nearly 3.5 billion meals had been served by June 2026.

Farm to School: Championed by First Partner Jennifer Siebel Newsom, the program connects California agriculture with school nutrition. Since 2021, the state has committed $120 million, with $86 million awarded to 375 projects that reach 49% of California’s students. The 2026-2027 state budget makes grant funding permanent at $24.6 million a year.

Ongoing support: Governor Newsom signed SB 172 in July 2026, permanently establishing Farm to School in state law.

California at COP31

COP31 is the 31st Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, an annual global climate conference that brings together world leaders, scientists, businesses, non-governmental organizations, and civil society to advance action on climate change. Held in Antalya, Türkiye, from November 9–20, 2026, the conference is hosted by Türkiye, with Australia leading the negotiations. This year’s focus is on implementation: turning climate commitments into concrete, measurable results.

As a founding member of the Under2 Coalition and the U.S. Climate Alliance, and with Governor Newsom serving as co-chair of America Is All In, California is demonstrating how states and regions can sustain international cooperation, accelerate clean energy, and deliver climate solutions that lower costs, create jobs, and strengthen resilience, even as the federal government retreats.

California’s delegation includes Governor Gavin Newsom; First Partner Jennifer Siebel Newsom; California Natural Resources Agency Secretary Wade Crowfoot; California Department of Food and Agriculture Secretary Karen Ross; California Public Utilities Commission President John Reynolds; California Air Resources Board Chair Lauren Sanchez; and Governor’s Office of Land Use and Climate Innovation Director Samuel Assefa.

name: Clean Energy
title: How we can double electrification by 2050 - Pembina Institute
description:
This three-part blog series "Electric Ambition" explores how we can double electrification, supply and energy efficiency/productivity.
We must also double our energy productivity.
Most people have heard of energy efficiency: using less energy to deliver the same output.
We need to recognize that building demand for electricity is as important as building electricity supply.
How can the construction industry—from manufacturing and supply chains, to design/build and ongoing operations and maintenance—effectively coordinate retrofits that integrate energy efficiency, productivity and electrification?
text:
Canada has a vision to create a fully electrified, net-zero economy by 2050. This three-part blog series "Electric Ambition" explores how we can double electrification, supply and energy efficiency/productivity.

At the heart of Canada’s national strategy for an electrified economy is a commitment to doubling our electricity supply by 2050 and meet growing demand. This ambitious goal is an effort to enhance energy security and make life more affordable for Canadian households and businesses.

But energy supply is only part of the equation. We must also double our energy productivity.

What is energy productivity? Most people have heard of energy efficiency: using less energy to deliver the same output. Energy productivity takes efficiency a step further by increasing economic output or value without changing the amount of energy used, making full use of existing resources. This comes in part from increasing energy efficiency, but also by reducing energy losses in the utility system and implementing demand flexibility—shifting when energy is used so we can do more with grid assets (infrastructure that supports an electricity grid, whether it be a power line or a solar panel).

Increasing energy productivity also means growing the economic and social value of each unit of energy used. For example, using energy productively allows Canadians to benefit from improved energy security and be prepared for a rapidly changing and increasingly volatile future. It would also allow us to spend less on energy and direct more resources towards other societal needs.

Buildings as productive grid infrastructure

Buildings—the places where we live, work, and park—are the logical places to start. Residential, commercial and institutional buildings account for 30% of energy use across the economy; over 70% of existing buildings will be in use in 2050. And we already have the equipment, design and construction know-how and operating practices to significantly improve energy use in buildings.

The Pembina Institute’s research and convening platform, the Reframed Initiative, shows that early and deeper retrofit action is increasingly needed to mitigate risk and capture an array of benefits. For building owners and occupants, this means lower utility and operating costs, mitigate rising insurance and financing costs, reduce impact of hotter summers and extreme weather events, increase comfort brings fewer tenant complaints and less risk of reputational damage as well as better management of deferred maintenance backlogs. For our communities, this means local economic development and jobs, greater energy reliability and security as wasted energy is made available for high value use, and lower emissions.

Making full use of the energy going into buildings

Buildings are the end point for much of the energy we use, making them a logical starting point to reconsider how we use the energy that goes into them. We first need to reduce and optimize building energy use, and we can start by increasing focus on integrated long-term building plans, where retrofits can be conducted all at once or overtime. Building owners can introduce high impact but less invasive tools like controls and load management for quick energy-saving wins that deliver immediate value. They can also prioritize the building envelopes (the barrier between a building’s interior and exterior) to reduce energy demands and use the replacement of major equipment, either planned in the building's long-term plans, at the equipment's end of useful life, or as a result of unforeseen breakdowns.

The federal government also has an important role to play: it can set building codes and equipment standards, support retrofit planning and phased implementation, and enable financing and insurance to recognize the full value of retrofits.

Buildings as electricity grid infrastructure

Beyond reducing energy use by the buildings, on-site electricity generation, such as solar panels and battery energy storage systems, and tools to manage when electricity is used, such as automating controls to manage space and water heating/cooling or managed electric vehicle charging, make buildings a component of the energy system. This can help mitigate peak demands and reduce the need for costly centralized grid resources. This type of local power generation also keeps both people and dollars in their communities.

On top of efficiency measures, technologies like managed electric vehicle charging and smart controls turn buildings into scalable tools that let utilities balance loads effectively, shifting demand away from peak hours and fully utilizing any saved energy to power other system and customer needs. This means utilities can serve more customers with the same amount of energy supply, and they can build fewer power plants.

Much of the energy used in our buildings goes to space and water heating, typically using conventional fuels like natural gas, oil, or propane. But we can now use heat pumps for both heating and cooling, using far less energy than conventional systems while making buildings more comfortable, more affordable to operate and more resilient during extreme weather. Efficient electric systems, such as high-performance motors, lighting and building system controls, can also reduce energy waste on average by 15 to 30%. For buildings with significant deferred maintenance, such systems can reduce energy waste by upwards of 75%.

How will we measure success?

We need to recognize that building demand for electricity is as important as building electricity supply. The following proposals would be demonstrations of real progress:

A national retrofit program is established for multi-family residential buildings funded by governments, with clear responsibilities at each level of government, timelines for creating building plans and implementation phases, and a strategy for public/private capital.

Full adoption of the upper tiers of both the National Building Code for single family residential buildings and National Energy Code for Buildings for commercial and multifamily building, along with advances in energy efficient equipment standards for emerging technologies.

Build a durable retrofit market. Value-driven retrofit market can attract private and institutional capital by monetizing the full range of benefits of better-performing building deliver.

Where to from here?: Demand is as important as supply

Doubling energy efficiency in buildings and the related energy productivity for the energy system is a massive undertaking, with many questions remaining, including:

How can we balance the up-front costs of retrofits with the long-term cost savings?

How can we consistently value, and monetize, the non-energy benefits including protection from extreme weather and health?

How can federal, provincial and local governments work together towards common goals?

How can the construction industry—from manufacturing and supply chains, to design/build and ongoing operations and maintenance—effectively coordinate retrofits that integrate energy efficiency, productivity and electrification?

title: World is now in 'age of electricity', energy agency chief says | Cop31 | The Guardian
description:

“One staggering number [is that] in the last 10 years, the world has added about 5,000 gigawatts of electricity.

text:
The world has left behind the age of coal, oil and gas and is now firmly in “the age of electricity”, the world’s leading energy economist has said.

Fatih Birol, the executive director of the International Energy Agency (IEA), said more than twice as much electricity generation would be added to the global economy in the next decade than in the last, as countries scramble to secure their energy supplies against fossil fuel price volatility and supply shocks, such as the Iran war.

Transport is being electrified at an unprecedented rate: outside China, sales of electric cars have risen by 60% in the last nine months, the IEA has found. The growth of AI datacentres is also spurring electricity generation, as is the rapid growth in air conditioning, according to Birol, as heatwaves grow more intense and more frequent under rising global temperatures.

“We will still use oil and gas, but the dominant source of energy is becoming electricity,” Birol told the Guardian in an interview at the Cop31 UN climate summit in Turkey. “One staggering number [is that] in the last 10 years, the world has added about 5,000 gigawatts of electricity. And we expect, in a very conservative way, in the next 10 years, about 12,000 gigawatts, more than two times more than what we had in the last 10 years.”

Governments from 185 countries are meeting this week and next in Antalya for the annual talks, where the turn to electrification in place of fossil fuels is one of the key topics. A resolution to derive 35% of final energy worldwide from electricity by 2035 is on the table, which if it succeeds, could be one of the most important ways of achieving the needed decarbonisation of economies by mid-century.

Electricity now fulfils about a quarter of most energy needs while three-quarters of final energy worldwide is supplied by fossil fuels, mostly for transport, heating and industrial uses. Global electricity was increasingly generated by renewable sources and that process would speed up even faster over the next decades, Birol said.

The more our lives can be powered by clean energy the better, say experts, not least because, as a result of the inefficiency of fossil fuels, most of the rest of our energy is wasted as heat, so when these activities are electrified, only about half of the energy needs to be replaced.

Most countries back the electrification goal, according to Birol. He has worked closely with the Turkish and Australian governments, which are jointly presiding over this year’s summit. “It will be an unmistakable signal to the markets and investors that governments see that the future of energy is in electricity,” he said. “This will make the age of electricity even earlier and cheaper. It might be one of the most consequential decisions coming from Cops in the last several years.”

But even if the resolution was not adopted – some governments, including Saudi Arabia and Russia, are said to be opposed, and owing to the convention by which consensus is needed to pass decisions, a small number of countries can hold the rest to ransom – the “staggering” progress would continue, Birol said.

“The reason is there are three major drivers for electrification: one is AI and datacentres; second is the electrification transportation sector; and third, the most important one in terms of volume, is air conditioning. Air conditioners are growing explosively,” he said.

In the US, about 90% of households have access to air conditioning, but in India it is fewer than 20%, and in Nigeria about 5%. “With the increasing effects of climate change, and if they have more money, [people] buy air conditioners,” said Birol. “These things are happening, and electrification is not bad. It is good for energy security, because it is your own electricity [generated within a country rather than imported, as fossil fuels often are], good for the competitiveness of countries, and good for climate change.”

He added: “Global energy demand is growing strongly, but global electricity demand is growing three times faster than total energy demand. And it is impossible to stop it. The one and only issue is making electricity affordable for people.”

Birol placed the blame for the UK’s high electricity prices firmly on gas. “There is always a debate about this in the UK, but in fact the single most important reason why UK electricity prices may be on the high side is reliance on imported gas. Gas prices went up, so did the electricity prices, full stop. And the solution is not importing more gas, but building more [renewable] electricity at home,” he said.

The transformation is happening fast. “Five years ago, only 5% of all the cars sold was electric. And this year, we expect it is about one-third of all the cars sold is electric, and electric trucks are coming. This is going to displace a significant amount of oil,” he said.

text:
Swiss-headquartered YES-EU has signed a preliminary agreement to acquire the former Maserati factory in Grugliasco, near Turin, Italy, with plans to establish electric bus and minibus production alongside battery pack assembly, energy storage systems and battery lifecycle services, targeting the start of operations in 2028.

The agreement, signed on 12 November 2026 and reported by Italian news agency Adnkronos, concerns the former automotive manufacturing site at Corso Allamano 46, covering approximately 230,000 square metres. The industrial project envisages the adaptation of existing facilities during 2027, followed by the commissioning of the first production lines in 2028. Employment at the site could reach up to 150 people once operations are fully established.

YES-EU’s participation in Italian public procurement procedures is well documented: in the Consip framework agreement for 600 electric buses, published in September 2026, YES-EU Italy appeared among the ranked suppliers with CRRC vehicles. YES-EU Italy also participated in the ATM Milan tender for 110 electric buses, where it ranked third behind KMobility/Karsan and BYD Europe. The contract was awarded to KMobility/Karsan. In Bari, YES-EU was among the five bidders for the supply of 42 articulated electric buses for the city’s bus rapid transit system, a procedure also won by KMobility with Karsan vehicles.

YES-EU’s Italian operations are headed by Fabrizio Simoni, the group’s General Manager Italy, who previously headed Quantron Italy, the Italian subsidiary of the German zero-emission commercial vehicle manufacturer.

YES-EU plans electric bus production and battery operations

According to Adnkronos, the Grugliasco facility is intended to accommodate several activities covering electric mobility and energy storage. These include the production of electric buses and minibuses for the Italian and wider European markets, battery pack operations, battery energy storage systems (BESS), technical assistance and recycling.

The industrial programme is being developed with the support of Italiano & Partners, which is assisting YES-EU with the acquisition process, the industrial plan and discussions with banks and public institutions.

In brief

Where does YES-EU plan to manufacture electric buses in Italy?

At the former Maserati factory in Grugliasco, near Turin, covering approximately 230,000 square metres.

When is production expected to begin?

Facility adaptation is planned for 2027, with the first production lines scheduled to start in 2028.

Which electric bus manufacturers does YES-EU work with?

YES-EU has distributed Yutong buses and markets CRRC-manufactured vehicles under its own brand.

What battery activities are planned at the Italian factory?

Battery packs, BESS, technical assistance and recycling are included in the announced industrial project.

The announcement does not specify which bus models will be manufactured at Grugliasco, whether vehicle production will involve complete manufacturing or assembly of imported components, or which stages of battery production will take place locally. The announced battery activities concern packs, storage systems, servicing and recycling; battery cell manufacturing has not been explicitly identified among the planned operations.

The timetable provided by Adnkronos identifies 2027 as the year for facility adaptation and 2028 as the planned start of the first lines. The projected workforce of up to 150 employees refers to operations at full capacity, without a disclosed employment schedule for the intervening years.

YES-EU’s existing bus business focusing on CRRC

YES-EU is already active in the European electric bus market as a vehicle importer, distributor and service provider, with operations particularly established in the Nordic countries. Its commercial activities have included the distribution of buses manufactured by Chinese manufacturers Yutong and CRRC, alongside charging infrastructure, vehicle maintenance and high-voltage battery services.

The group’s Finnish business continues to identify itself as an importer, seller and service provider for Yutong electric buses. YES-EU has also developed a range of vehicles marketed under its own brand and manufactured by CRRC Electric Vehicle in China.

The planned Italian facility also forms part of YES-EU’s announced activities in battery servicing and energy storage. On 2 October 2026, the group announced a strategic partnership with NING Service, CATL’s official aftermarket service brand, alongside the launch of a battery service centre in the Oslo area of Norway.

According to the company’s October press release, the YES-EU NING Service Center covers more than 10,000 square metres and is dedicated to battery lifecycle management, technician training and certified repairs. YES-EU states that its cooperation with CATL dates back to 2018, when it became the battery manufacturer’s first service partner in Europe.

The service network covers warranty and out-of-warranty interventions on high-voltage batteries, including diagnostics, component-level and module-level repairs, replacement parts and battery lifecycle support. Its activities extend beyond electric buses to electric trucks, passenger vehicles, marine applications and stationary energy storage systems.

If a federal agency finalizes a harmful action, the record of public comments provides a basis for bringing them into court. Read more.

Throughout each of the public comment periods we alert you to, Earthjustice’s attorneys are researching and writing in-depth, technical comments to submit — detailing how the regulation could and should be stronger to protect the environment, our communities, and our planet.

We need you to join us — your specific experiences, knowledge, and voice are crucial to add to the Administrative Record through the comment periods.

Many of us may have never heard of the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) and the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), but laws like these require our government to ask the public to weigh in before agencies adopt or change regulations.

Regulations essentially describe how federal agencies will carry out laws — including decisions that could undermine science, or weaken safeguards on public health.

Public comments are collected at various points throughout the federal government’s rulemaking process, including when a regulation is proposed and finalized. (Learn about the rulemaking process.) These comments become part of the official, legal public record — the “Administrative Record.”

text:
Honda has confirmed that the next-generation CR-V will arrive next year and be sold exclusively as a hybrid. It will bolster the brand's efforts to compete with the Toyota RAV4, which is also sold solely as a hybrid in the U.S. The compact crossover will also be the first Honda to launch with its latest-generation two-motor hybrid system.

The Japanese marque has teased the new CR-V with a single image showing the updated badge. Dealers who were recently shown the next-gen CR-V at a retailer meeting in Las Vegas said the new model will include thin LED headlights, a full-width LED light signature at the rear, and "muscular rear haunches," Auto News reports. While we will have to wait a little longer to see the new CR-V in person, Honda has already published several important details about its platform and powertrain.

Underpinning the SUV will be Honda's all-new mid-size architecture that was announced 12 months ago. A new structure and engineering methods have allowed Honda to save 198 lbs (90 kg) from its current hybrid platform, and Honda wants more than 60% of parts to be shared between the models built on it, which should help cut costs.

The platform has been developed to be more rigid in some areas and less rigid in others than the current architecture, allowing for more flex during cornering to "realize an unprecedented level of driving stability and a sporty and pleasant driving experience." The platform will also incorporate Honda's new Motion Management System to control posture and the same advanced pitch control technology as the Accord and Prelude.

Honda's new hybrid system also promises to be an improvement on the outgoing system. Known simply as the Honda Hybrid, this powertrain will drive 15 next-generation hybrid models launching by March 31, 2030. The hybrid will include a new 2.0-liter Atkinson-cycle four-cylinder with direct injection and a pair of updated electric motors. The manufacturer claims the next-gen Honda Hybrid system will cost 30% less to produce than the current hybrids and improve fuel economy by over 10%. The new CR-V will also be equipped with Honda's latest electric all-wheel-drive system.

"With a 100% hybrid powertrain, the next-generation Honda CR-V will further expand the appeal of America's most popular SUV as demand for hybrid-electric vehicles reaches record levels," Luis Guerra, assistant vice president of Honda National Auto Sales, said in a statement. The current CR-V is on track to surpass 400,000 sales for the third consecutive year.

Honda has confirmed the new CR-V will be built at its factories in Ohio, Indiana, and Canada. Its new Honda Hybrid powertrain will also be manufactured at the Honda Transmission Plant in Ohio, while the new four-cylinder engine will be built at the Anna Engine Plant, Honda's largest auto engine plant anywhere.

Deputy Premier and Minister of Health

President, University of Toronto

text:
Two research projects at the University have received awards of nearly $1 million each from the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE). Both projects will receive funding over four years and will generate training opportunities for both undergraduate and graduate students at UNR, who will work with leading scientists in their discipline.

The awards are part of DOE's Established Program to Stimulate Competitive Research (DOE EPSCoR), which supports partnerships between universities in eligible states and DOE national laboratories to advance fundamental, early-stage energy research. The program aims to strengthen research capabilities in participating states while providing students with hands-on research and training opportunities alongside national laboratory scientists.

Krista Carlson, an associate professor in Materials Science and Engineering in the College of Engineering, has received a $1,000,000 award to improve mercury detection and capture. Mercury is released into an off-gas stream when radioactive and hazardous waste at the Hanford Site in Washington State is converted to glass for safe, permanent disposal. Carlson’s project will investigate sorbents which can capture mercury to reduce disposal toxicity. The team also includes co-investigators Professor Dev Chidambaram, from Materials Science and Engineering, and Professor Mae Gustin and Research Professor Sarrah Dunham-Cheatham from the College of Agriculture, Biotechnology & Natural Resources.

“The sorbent selected for Hanford’s off-gas system is no longer being manufactured by the supplier, so alternatives must be identified,” Carlson said. “Another challenge is effectively identifying and capturing all the different forms of mercury that could be present. Mercury detection and abatement from the off-gas directly supports DOE EM mission of waste remediation in a way that protects workers, the public, and the environment.”

Hiroshi Sawada, an associate professor in the Department of Physics in the College of Science, has received a $989,916 award to develop advanced diagnostic tools and establish a new experimental platform using an X-ray free-electron laser at the Matter in Extreme Conditions (MEC) instrument of the Linac Coherent Light Source (LCLS), located at SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory in California. Sawada uses powerful lasers to explore high-density plasmas, used in fusion experiments. The diagnostic tools developed by Sawada and his collaborators will improve understanding of these technologies.

“This new capability will allow us to explore the behavior of high-density plasmas under conditions that have been difficult to probe,” Sawada said. “Experiments combining long- and short-pulse lasers have been conducted at single-shot facilities, but measuring conditions inside dense plasmas remains challenging, particularly under high-intensity laser irradiation, which generates strong radiation backgrounds that can interfere with measurements.”

“DOE EPSCoR investments like these strengthen Nevada’s research capacity by connecting our faculty and students with the expertise and resources of the nation’s leading laboratories,” Senior Vice President for Research and Innovation, Mridul Gautam, said. “These awards give our researchers the opportunity to tackle complex energy challenges while building expertise and training the next generation of scientists and engineers here in Nevada.”

text:
The 2026 U.S. midterm election delivered historic results that have changed the landscape of Ceres’ policy work. A new generation of leaders who support clean energy is heading to Congress, governor’s offices, and state legislatures on promises to bring down prices and make the economy more affordable.

The policies that take shape in the coming years will define the next chapter of American-made clean energy.

During our recent webinar, The Post-Election Playbook: Opportunities to Advance Clean Economy Policy, the Ceres policy team analyzed what the results mean for the private sector, as well as for bipartisan solutions that lower electricity costs by modernizing the grid and expanding homegrown clean energy and domestic manufacturing.

Watch the recording

There are incredible opportunities in Congress and in the states to build a cleaner, more resilient, and affordable economy.

Here are five key takeaways:

1/ A moment of clean economy opportunity

With new leaders on Capitol Hill and in statehouses nationwide, there is an opening to advance a policy agenda centered on expanding clean energy and modernizing our aging power grid. Wind, solar, and energy storage are the fastest and most affordable ways to meet increased power demand and address rising electricity prices. We expect renewed momentum at the state and federal levels to open the door to more clean energy investment, good jobs, and lower bills.

2/ Policy progress will come from the affordability lens

Affordability was the top policy issue in the election. Our work over the next two years will be focused on helping policymakers deliver. In the near term, Congress can make it easier to build clean energy and transmission projects, while states can modernize their existing infrastructure and expand cost-saving efficiency programs. Looking towards the future, we see an opportunity to develop a more durable framework for long-term clean energy and clean transportation incentives to both keep costs down and reduce pollution.

3/ Stars aligning in the states

The states offer an opportunity for responsible businesses to make a big impact next year. Legislatures will have new pro-clean energy majorities across the country, from Arizona to Pennsylvania to North Carolina. New utility regulators are taking over, , including in Georgia, where voters sent new members to the Public Service Commission. Ceres has laid out commonsense, bipartisan policy options for states in Powering Affordability: A Business-Backed Playbook for a Modern Clean Energy System. With business and sustainability leaders helping to chart the path, states can deliver a new vision for energy policy.

4/ Building bipartisan support

Despite new majorities for Democrats in Congress and statehouses, the reality is that bipartisan solutions are durable solutions. Without consensus, it’s all too easy for clean energy policy to change with the winds of each presidential administration. We are committed to rebuilding the coalition of bipartisan support in Congress needed to secure durable policy outcomes for a clean economy. Companies can tell a powerful story to policymakers about how clean energy investment can benefit their districts and states, including through new local jobs, reliable and affordable power, and lower costs.

5/ Urgency on permitting and transmission reform

The Bipartisan Affordability and Jobs Act would get critical clean energy projects built faster, strengthen reliability, and deliver lower-cost power to the people and industries that need it. While the bill is not perfect, we are confident that constructive amendments will improve its substance and its prospects in the short term. The window to pass it before the current Congress adjourns in December is closing, and the business voice is vital. Policymakers need to hear directly from business leaders to pass the bill so we can spend the next two years ensuring strong implementation and working on the next round of policies to lower prices and expand reliable, American-made clean energy.

The road ahead

So, what’s next? Ceres spent the past two years laying the groundwork for this moment, and we are ready to act. We’re heading to Capitol Hill on December 10 for an advocacy day focused on clean economy priorities for the next Congress, and we'll return in March for LEAD on a Clean Economy, our annual advocacy event.

In the states, we’re bringing together companies and policymakers in Georgia in December to discuss electricity load growth and sustainability. We’re also partnering with Siemens and Advanced Energy United in December for a similar event in Pennsylvania, with speakers from the governor’s office and the state legislature.

This work is stronger with a big tent. We hope you’ll join us and be part of it as we build an affordable, clean economy.

title: UN chief says 'immediate and drastic' emissions cuts needed to avert climate change catastrophe
authors: Suzan Fraser, Associated Press, Tammy Webber, Seth Borenstein, Anton L. Delgado
description:

text:
ANTALYA, Turkey (AP) — The world must immediately and drastically cut fossil fuel emissions to avert the most catastrophic effects of climate change, United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said Friday at his final climate summit, urging the world to "follow the science" and face hard facts.

"You cannot build peace on a burning planet," Guterres told reporters, stressing that climate change is central to the U.N.'s work because it contributes to geopolitical instability by driving hunger and displacement, pushing countries into debt and fueling competition for land and water.

READ MORE: At UN climate talks, 5 nations back plan to double rooftop solar panels by 2030

"You cannot eradicate poverty when climate disasters keep throwing people back into it," he added. "You cannot promise young people a better future while destroying the natural systems on which that future depends. And you cannot speak seriously about justice when those who did least to cause this crisis suffer first and worst."

World leaders meeting in Turkey for the annual U.N. climate talks are trying to reach consensus on concrete actions to address climate change — which is fueling more intense and deadly heat waves, droughts, floods and other disasters — and help countries at greatest risk, including island nations that also are losing land to rising seas.

Electrification goals emerge as point of contention

Achieving reductions in emissions is setting up a point of contention at the climate talks, especially around electrification. A goal introduced this year would increase the share of electricity in total global energy consumption from roughly 21% to 35% by 2035, preferably from renewable energy such as solar and wind.

But it does not require that electricity be generated by renewable sources — something Guterres said is essential — meaning coal and other fossil fuels could be used, at least initially. Climate TRACE, which tracks global emissions via satellites, found that prioritizing clean energy would cut global emissions 14% compared to 7% if fossil fuels also are used for electrification.

READ MORE: Democrats plan to challenge Trump's fossil fuel agenda and push clean energy to lower bills

International Energy Agency Executive Director Fatih Birol said it's more important that as many countries as possible sign on to the pledge, which works best without a clean energy requirement.

But environmental groups say that electrification will only have a real impact if fossil fuels are omitted.

"Electrification must end fossil fuel dependence, not be an end in itself," said Jasmin Duregger, from Greenpeace's Global Gas Campaign.

Vulnerable nations seek more compensation as warming takes a toll

Leaders from countries ravaged by climate change — mostly poorer, vulnerable countries that contributed little to the problem — also are calling for more money to deal with climate disasters and adapt to a warming world. Leaders of small island nations, who say climate change is a life-or-death matter for their people because rising seas are engulfing their lands, have been the most vocal at this year's summit, COP31, saying a U.N. fund created for compensating vulnerable nations must be urgently strengthened.

Guterres said wealthier countries that have contributed most to climate change "must deliver the finance they have promised" at past summits — but also contribute much more.

"Let us be clear about the scale of the gap," he said. "Even tripling adaptation finance would meet less than 30 percent of what is needed."

Progress stalls, top-emitting countries skip summit

Progress is difficult without the cooperation of all nations, "particularly the biggest emitters," Guterres said.

A report released Thursday by the independent Climate Action Tracker found that progress in slowing global warming has essentially stalled for the past five years. That means the world is sure to overshoot the goal set in the 2015 Paris Agreement of limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial temperatures.

Climate change is caused primarily by greenhouse gases emitted by burning gas, oil and coal, and countries have established plans to reduce those emissions. But even if they fulfill all their promises — a big if — the globe will end the century 2.6 degrees Celsius (4.7 degrees Fahrenheit) warmer than pre-industrial times, the report said.

"Our responsibility is to keep it as small as possible, for as short a time as possible and bring temperatures back below 1.5 degrees as quickly as we can," by cutting emissions about 6% per year for several years, Guterres said, calling the overshoot "a recipe for catastrophe."

READ MORE: COP31 climate summit begins after disastrous year of extreme weather

But some of the top-polluting countries stayed away from this year's summit, most notably the United States — the world's second-largest polluter after China and the largest historical polluter.

It's the second year in a row the U.S. skipped the summit, after President Donald Trump withdrew the U.S. from climate negotiations.

"Facts are facts," Guterres said. "No country can protect itself from climate change alone. We share one planet, and whether we like it or not, we share one fate."

Webber reported from Fenton, Michigan; Borenstein from Kensington, Maryland; and Delgado from Bangkok.

Automotive affordability is not just determined by vehicle sticker prices but also the state of household budgets.
