text:
Ahead of a midterm election cycle where the price of gas was a major concern in exit polls, the Eno Center for Transportation hosted a conversation focused on automotive affordability as a part of the Transportation Affordability Webinar Series. The webinar featured panelists Corey Cantor from the Zero Emission Transportation Association, Abbie Olson from Atlas Public Policy, Zohaib Rahim from Cox Automotive, and Matthew Vining from Atlas Public Policy.

Consumers are facing increasing gas prices because of the War in Iran, but automotive affordability extends beyond the pump and is a combined package of vehicle affordability, maintenance costs, insurance costs, and of course fueling costs. During the webinar, the panelists discussed how increasing average vehicle costs and gas prices have impacted consumers. They also discussed how the US market and policymakers can promote more affordable and fuel-efficient vehicle options and discussed the intersection of international competitiveness and vehicle affordability.

What is the State of Automotive Affordability?

Rahim began the conversation providing perspective on the overall economic outlook for automotive consumers. Automotive affordability is not just determined by vehicle sticker prices but also the state of household budgets. Personal expenses have grown faster than personal incomes. Last quarter, the economy grew at a 3.4% annualized rate, the fastest in 2026, and new vehicle sales are on pace to hit 16 million this year. However, Rahim attributed this to wealthier households and highlighted negative consumer health based on consumer sentiment and the labor market. Growth in car sales is being driven by the wealthiest consumers including older households, with buyers 65 and older making up 27% of new vehicle purchases.

For most consumers, higher gas prices are placing increased pressure on consumers, and tax rebates from earlier in the year are no longer giving households an extra boost. To adapt to these pressures, consumers are choosing to purchase older vehicle models or hold onto to their vehicles for longer. While these decisions have enabled households with tighter budgets to remain in the market, they may produce higher costs later with higher repair bills or longer loans.

Cantor described overall trends in vehicle costs and changes to the electric vehicle market. According to Edmonds, new car prices have increased by 46% from 2015 to 2025, with Kelly Blue Book finding that average new vehicles are now $50,000. While research from IEA indicates that electric vehicles are still more expensive than their comparable vehicle types, the top five selling EVs are under $50,000. Corey attributed the overall price increases in vehicles not only to the introduction of more electric and hybrid options but also to the increase in vehicle size. In 2008, sales of new sedans were 50% of the market; that figure has declined to only 17% last year. In contrast, SUVs went from 25% to 60% of sales in this period. Over this period, pickups remained around 20% of sales.

Since 2020, US EVs sales have accelerated from 300,000 to 1.6 million in 2024. With the expiration of the EV tax credit in 2025, there was a decline in electric vehicle sales, so the industry is in a transitional phase as it works to provide more affordable vehicles. In South America and Southeast Asia there has been notable growth in electric vehicle sales with the increase in fossil fuel prices.

Used Electric Vehicle Market as a Pathway to Affordability

Olson and Vining opened the webinar by providing an overview of their research on the used electric vehicle market. They emphasized that a significant percentage of households are purchasing vehicles off the used market—regardless of drivetrain—and that the used market is 2.5 times the size of the new vehicle market, making it a critical point for vehicle affordability. From 2022 to 2025 the average price for used vehicles has dropped to around $25,000 for both EVs and internal combustion vehicles, with the average used EV price around 36K in 2025. Vining found that in Colorado from 2020-2024 the used EV market sales share grew four times. The median price point for these sales was just under 30K, and the sales were concentrated amongst early models and certain counties. It takes around 7 years or 90,000 miles for EVs to depreciate to deeper affordability around $20,000.

Olson also found 4X growth in used EV sales from 2019-2025 in Tennessee. She found that 60% of EV borrows had incomes over $100,000 in comparison to 37% of gas vehicle borrowers. Olson and Vining emphasized that while used EVs provide a more affordable option than a new vehicle, making them accessible to lower income groups may require a policy intervention providing access to upfront capital.

Vining and Olson highlighted that as the EV market continues to mature, the number of electric vehicles on the used market will also continue to grow. Vining highlighted that last quarter a high of 127,000 used EVs were sold on the used market. Olson emphasized that the battery capacity of two to three-year old electric vehicle batteries have around 90% of their capacity and most electric vehicles have an eight year or up to 80,000-mile warranties that transfer with ownership. Vining and Olson highlighted additional findings that across comparable vehicle types over seven years, the electric option can save consumers $10,000 in Colorado, $8,0000 in California, and $10,000 in Washington.

International Conflict Impacting Fuel Affordability and Consumer Decisions

When asked about international tensions are impacting the affordability of driving, Rahim shared that since the start of the conflict in Iran, the national average for regular gas prices has moved from $2.94 a gallon to $4.27, a 45% increase, and peaked at $4.50 in May. This was also the first October since 1990 with gas prices above $4. For the average household, energy prices are also $1,000 higher than before the conflict and overall prices rose 0.5% last quarter, adding to budgetary pressure. Diesel prices are about two thirds higher than before the war, making the cost of shipping goods, including vehicles, higher. Rahim shared that compact vehicle, EV, and hybrid sales have increased, indicating that consumers may be looking for better fuel efficiency.

Cantor added that in previous high fuel price periods such as during Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, interest in cleaner vehicles has grown, but drivers first instinct is to hold their vehicles before potentially purchasing a new vehicle. Given that average prices are $50,000 for new vehicles and used vehicle prices also become elevated in a high-cost environment, those purchasing EVs or hybrids were likely already considering the purchase of a new vehicle but as fueling prices remain high people will likely continue to pursue affordable EVs and hybrids. He highlighted movement within the EV markets towards models closer to the $32,000 and $40,000 price range and that Toyota, which has been an affordable option for many households, is making many of their base-trims hybrids. He did emphasize that households also consider brand value, size, and family needs in addition to sticker price when purchasing vehicles.

Vehicle Affordability and International Competition

Rahim shared that globally affordable electric vehicle and hybrid options have been key drivers of growth within respective new vehicle markets. From the consumer perspective, has been demand for affordable vehicle options from Asian brands, and international brands selling affordable vehicles in the US markets has been important for consumers. For companies, the ability to service affordable vehicles in different regional markets will be crucial. Cantor shared that even if Chinese vehicles continue to be banned from US markets, US companies will still be competing with Chinese, Japanese, and Korean manufacturers in the international market. He emphasized the importance of bringing down costs in order to both deliver consumer affordability and better compete.

Cantor highlighted the importance of battery prices in making EVs affordability, as batteries drive 30 to 50% of the value of an electric vehicle. He cited a decrease from $1,400 to $108 per kWh from 2010 to 2025. He emphasized that there is still room for battery costs to come down, potentially further unlocking more affordable EV options. Vining seconded Cantor’s views that a continued reduction in the costs of batteries will make EVs are more viable option for a wider more of consumers. Vining also emphasized the importance of onshoring more of the battery supply chain to reduce import costs. Even with the removal of the 30D tax credit and setbacks in the EV market, there has been continued interest at the federal level and in the private sector on batteries, including access to critical minerals and scaling battery production. Battery chemistry and production improvements present opportunities for cost reductions. According to Cantor, on the internal combustion side, these types of cost improvements have already been made, so future cost efficiencies for internal combustion vehicles will more likely be found through a shift back to sedans.

Policy Changes and Affordability

The panelists also discussed how federal policy actions can impact vehicle affordability. Rahim said that the reduction in fuel efficiency standards through the CAFE program will have minor cost savings for consumers in the short term and highlighted that automakers will continue to plan for future product cycles with more fuel-efficient vehicles. Reducing fuel economy standards also presents a longer-term trade off to drivers, as a potentially cheaper but less fuel-efficient vehicle will be more costly from a fueling perspective. Fuel economy can also affect resale values, with higher miles per gallon vehicles outperforming the overall market. Cantor highlighted a cost benefit analysis showing that the increase in fuel prices will far outweigh savings from having less stringent fuel economy standards in place. Cantor also fluctuating fuel economy standards can have negative ramifications on US performance in the international market due to the cost of policy instability and concern about the US falling behind international fuel economy trends. Cantor emphasized the importance of automakers have a robust electric vehicle portfolio both for international competition and meeting future CAFE standards.

In terms of surface transportation reauthorization, Olson recommended that EV fees which are included in BUILD America 250 are capped or indexed to the gas tax to ensure that they are comparable to want gas drivers are paying in fuel taxes. She also suggested allowing installments to promote affordability and raised concerns that a registration fee will disproportionately impact lower income households that tend to drive less on average. Vining said there is agreement that the existing funding structure for the Highway Trust Fund is not fair nor sufficient and encouraged further exploration of fees based upon vehicles miles traveled.

At the state level, Cantor, Vining, and Olson highlighted several state level incentive programs including in California, Colorado, Delaware, Oregon, Rhode Island, New Jersey, and Maryland providing tax credits for vehicle purchases. These programs can particularly support affordability when offered at the point of purchase rather than waiting for a tax rebate. Cantor also highlighted programs in Massachusetts and Colorado to help rideshare drivers access EVs. Going into a new Congress, these state level programs can provide lawmakers with key insights into increasing affordable options for drivers on the margins of new or used vehicle purchases.

NYSERDA’s Bulk Energy Storage Programme employs an Index Storage Credit (ISC) incentive, as established in the New York State Public Service Commission 2024 Energy Storage Order, modelled in part after the Renewable Energy Certificate and Offshore Wind Renewable Energy Credit utilised in other NYSERDA programmes.
Through its clean energy siting resources, the siting team empowers communities with the tools and knowledge to make informed decisions and manage responsible clean energy development in host communities.
The announcement builds on awards recently announced by NYSERDA through its first Bulk Energy Storage solicitation.

text:
Adding more bulk energy storage to New York’s grid will lower costs, optimise the generation and transmission of power, enhance energy grid infrastructure, and ensure the reliability and resilience of the State’s electricity system – all of which support the Governor’s Clean, Highly Affordable, Reliable Grid Expansion (CHARGE) agenda.

“Today’s Bulk Energy Storage solicitation is another example of Governor Hochul’s commitment to meeting New York’s growing clean energy demand by putting affordability and reliability front and centre” said NYSERDA President and CEO Doreen M. Harris. “Energy storage reserves power when it is less expensive so that we can limit reliance on the most expensive power during peak hours – reducing the strain on our grid and delivering real cost savings to New Yorkers.”

Administered by NYSERDA through its Bulk Energy Storage Programme, this competitive solicitation is open to a range of eligible energy storage technologies and seeks to achieve timely progress towards procuring three gigawatts of bulk energy storage over at least three annual solicitations in support of the state’s broader goal of deploying six gigawatts of energy storage by 2030.

Any NYSERDA-supported energy storage project is contractually required to meet updated storage safety codes, which are among the most stringent in the nation, and reflect the work and recommendations of the New York State Inter-Agency Fire Safety Working Group convened by Governor Hochul in 2023. These safety codes ensure that first responders have the necessary training, facilities are sited safely, and that all sites have comprehensive emergency response plans.

Entities interested in responding to this solicitation must first complete “Step One,” which is an initial qualifying step for proposers to demonstrate programme eligibility. Step One Eligibility Applications are due to NYSERDA by 3:00 p.m. ET on Thursday, December 15th, 2026. If NYSERDA deems proposals eligible, proposers will be invited to submit a “Step Two” bid proposal for project evaluation.

NYSERDA’s Bulk Energy Storage Programme employs an Index Storage Credit (ISC) incentive, as established in the New York State Public Service Commission 2024 Energy Storage Order, modelled in part after the Renewable Energy Certificate and Offshore Wind Renewable Energy Credit utilised in other NYSERDA programmes.

NYSERDA supports robust safety measures for all projects and, as a result, will not pay for ISCs until the awarded and contracted projects are permitted, installed and operating and have passed their peer review process and quality assurance inspection – both key milestones to ensure that all projects are designed and constructed with New York’s best-in-class safety standards. Project proposals must include plans to comply with the State’s comprehensive safety and security requirements, and to comply with the Bulk Energy Storage Programme Manual requirements.

Also, associated with this solicitation, NY Green Bank (NYGB), a division of NYSERDA and a specialised investment fund dedicated to bridging financial gaps in clean energy and renewable infrastructure markets in New York State, is prepared to support project developers and investors with a range of financing options in order to advance energy storage. Entities interested in applying for this financing can submit an application to NYGB RFP No. 1.

NYSERDA’s siting team also works closely with local governments to provide tailored education, technical assistance, and model local laws. Through its clean energy siting resources, the siting team empowers communities with the tools and knowledge to make informed decisions and manage responsible clean energy development in host communities.

“Battery storage can help lower costs for consumers by making better use of the existing electric grid, reducing wasted renewable energy, providing extra power when demand is highest and potentially eliminating the need for costly new transmission lines” added Secretary of State Walter Mosley. “Adding more bulk energy storage to New York’s grid will lower costs and enhance energy grid infrastructure and that’s why we applaud the Governor’s ongoing commitment to protecting New York’s energy consumers, while moving us closer to the state’s energy goals.”

New York’s 6 GW Energy Storage Roadmap, created to support the state’s target of 6 gigawatts deployed by 2030, recommended deployment of an incremental 4,700 megawatts consisting of 3,000 megawatts bulk, 200 megawatts of new residential-scale energy storage and 1,500 megawatts of new commercial and community-scale energy. Additionally, at least 35 percent of off-site retail and bulk energy storage projects supported by NYSERDA are planned to be sited in downstate New York, where they are most likely to benefit disadvantaged communities and reduce peaker plant emissions.

The announcement builds on awards recently announced by NYSERDA through its first Bulk Energy Storage solicitation. The eight contracted bulk energy storage projects, which range geographically from New York City and Long Island to Hudson Valley and Western New York, will add 950 megawatts of new energy storage capacity once operational.

The Clean, Highly Affordable, Reliable Grid Expansion (CHARGE) agenda is a comprehensive plan to keep the lights on and costs down for New Yorkers while achieving a reliable, zero-emission grid. The five-pronged strategy focuses on driving down consumer costs, holding energy companies accountable, building clean energy at scale, modernising the state's aging grid, and growing a clean economy with family-sustaining jobs. Through bold initiatives like the Ratepayer Protection Plan, historic transmission buildouts, and a new 8.4-gigawatt "Nuclear Backbone," the CHARGE agenda ensures an affordable, resilient, and self-sufficient energy future that prioritises everyday ratepayers while building a cleaner, more sustainable New York.

title: Florida Conservation Groups Urge Senators Scott and Moody to Reject Permitting Bill ...
description:
For Florida, protecting clean water and protecting endangered wildlife are inseparable.
“The Endangered Species Act has prevented the extinction of more than 99 percent of the species it protects.
“Restoring America’s Everglades requires a sustained commitment to clean water, sound science, and accountability,” said Eve Samples, Executive Director, Friends of the Everglades.
Florida’s clean water, endangered wildlife, and natural heritage are too important to put at risk.
### The Endangered Species Coalition(opens in new tab) is a national coalition of 480 member organizations and 540,000+ activists working together to protect and recover at-risk threatened and endangered species and to defend the Endangered Species Act and other wildlife laws and policies.
text:
Contact: Marilu C. Flores, marilu@endangered.org

Kelcey Innes, Save the Manatee Club, media@savethemanatee.org

TALLAHASSEE, FL, November 13, 2026 — The Endangered Species Coalition, Save the Manatee Club, and Florida coalition partners are raising serious concerns following the U.S. Senate’s advancement of the misleadingly titled permitting overhaul bill, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (S. 5653), warning that the legislation would weaken longstanding protections for Florida’s endangered wildlife, clean water, wetlands, and coastal ecosystems. These changes will weaken review standards for activities that threaten Florida’s environment, economy, public health, and way of life, particularly poorly regulated data center development and offshore oil drilling.

On November 9, Florida Senators Rick Scott and Ashley Moody both voted to advance the legislation in a 73–25 procedural vote. Florida organizations are calling on both senators to reject passage of the bill, particularly provisions that would undermine the Endangered Species Act (ESA) and other bedrock environmental laws such as the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) and the Clean Water Act (CWA).

From the Everglades and Florida Bay to the Indian River Lagoon, Biscayne Bay, and the Gulf Coast, Florida’s natural heritage depends on healthy waterways and science-based protections. These ecosystems provide essential habitat for endangered and threatened wildlife, including Florida manatees, sea turtles, American crocodiles, wood storks, and other vulnerable species. They also support fisheries, tourism, recreation, and local economies across the state.

For Florida, protecting clean water and protecting endangered wildlife are inseparable.

The legislation would make concerning changes to the ESA, NEPA, and CWA, such as restricting the scientific data that federal agencies may consider to develop protections for imperiled species, narrowing the scope of projects that need environmental review, shortening consultation timelines, and limiting state authority to review certain water pollution impacts of federally permitted projects. The bill would also restrict opportunities for communities to challenge certain harmful permitting decisions.

These changes are particularly concerning in Florida, where harmful algal blooms, declining seagrass habitat, polluted runoff, erosion, and unsustainable development already place significant pressure on fragile freshwater and coastal ecosystems.

“Florida’s wildlife and waterways are part of what makes this state extraordinary, and protecting them should never be a partisan issue,” said Marilu Cristina Flores, Communications & Digital Lead at the Endangered Species Coalition. “The Endangered Species Act has prevented the extinction of more than 99 percent of the species it protects. Weakening these protections while also undermining safeguards for clean water puts decades of conservation progress at risk. Senators Scott and Moody have an opportunity to stand up for Florida’s natural heritage and ensure that economic development does not come at the expense of the wildlife and healthy ecosystems future generations deserve.”

Florida’s manatees offer a clear example of the connection between water quality and imperiled species recovery. Manatees depend on healthy seagrass beds and aquatic vegetation for food, yet water pollution-driven seagrass losses present devastating challenges for the species. For example, in 2020–2022, over 1,200 manatees tragically died, largely from starvation, due to pollution-driven seagrass loss in the Indian River Lagoon. Further weakening federal water quality safeguards could compound the threats facing these beloved marine mammals. Highly concerningly, the redefinition of “best scientific and commercial data available” contained in S. 5653 could tie agencies’ hands in considering important scientific literature to avoid further seagrass losses or prevent manatees from being killed or injured by boats.

“Manatees cannot recover without clean water and healthy aquatic habitats,” said Elizabeth Neville, Director of Environmental Law and Policy, Save the Manatee Club. “Floridians have witnessed firsthand the consequences of declining water quality and disappearing seagrass beds. Furthermore, as 96% of adult manatees bear scars from watercraft collisions—preventable accidents that kill and injure hundreds of manatees per year—it is essential that government agencies remain capable of addressing manatees’ most consequential threats. Our elected leaders must show leadership for Florida and maintain protections for manatees and their aquatic ecosystems, which are the waters that Floridians depend on for our lives and livelihoods.”

Manatees and Florida’s waterways are also threatened by unsustainable data center development. Presently, there are 24 planned data center projects that pose severe harm to springs, rivers, and other water resources that comprise manatee habitat —including a proposed data center in Citrus County, home of Crystal River National Wildlife Refuge, an essential habitat for manatees. Provisions of this bill explicitly support data center development while materially degrading permitting standards essential to prevent catastrophic harm to Florida’s communities and environment. If this passes, Florida stands to suffer disproportionately from such poorly regulated facilities.

The Everglades, one of the world’s most extraordinary wetland ecosystems, is also at stake. Decades of public investment and bipartisan cooperation have supported efforts to restore natural water flows, improve water quality, and recover wildlife habitat. Conservation leaders warn that weakening water quality protections and environmental oversight could threaten the long-term success of these restoration efforts.

“Restoring America’s Everglades requires a sustained commitment to clean water, sound science, and accountability,” said Eve Samples, Executive Director, Friends of the Everglades. “Florida and the federal government have invested decades and significant resources in restoring this remarkable ecosystem. Any changes to federal permitting laws must protect that progress, maintain strong water quality standards, and ensure that restoration efforts deliver lasting benefits for wildlife, communities, and Florida’s economy.”

Florida’s beaches and coastal waters are also critical to the survival of threatened and endangered sea turtles. The state’s beaches provide internationally important nesting habitat, while its seagrass beds, estuaries, and nearshore ecosystems support sea turtles throughout their lives. Weakened wildlife consultation requirements and reduced oversight of development in sensitive coastal areas could place additional pressure on these vulnerable species.

“Florida is home to some of the most important sea turtle nesting beaches in the world,” said Stacey Gallagher, Policy Coordinator, Sea Turtle Conservancy. “The recovery of these species depends on strong protections for nesting beaches, coastal habitat, and water quality. We cannot afford to undermine the science-based safeguards that have helped sea turtles survive while development and environmental pressures continue to grow along our coastlines.”

In South Florida, Biscayne Bay and surrounding waterways already face serious water quality challenges from stormwater runoff, wastewater pollution, and urban development. Conservation organizations are particularly concerned that narrowing Clean Water Act protections would limit the ability of states and communities to prevent additional pollution and hold harmful projects accountable.

“Clean water is fundamental to the health, safety, and prosperity of Florida’s coastal communities,” said Rachel Silverstein, CEO and Waterkeeper, Miami Waterkeeper. “At a time when waterways like Biscayne Bay are already struggling with pollution, weakening the Clean Water Act moves us in the wrong direction. Communities need strong, enforceable safeguards that prevent pollution before it reaches our waters, not fewer opportunities to protect the places where we swim, fish, and live.”

Beyond South Florida, the legislation could affect coastal and marine ecosystems across the Gulf, from estuaries and wetlands to seagrass meadows, barrier islands, and offshore waters that support wildlife, coastal communities, and local economies.

“The Gulf coast depends on healthy, connected ecosystems from our coastal wetlands to our open Gulf waters,” said Christian Wagley, Coastal Organizer, Healthy Gulf. “These habitats support endangered species, sustain fisheries, protect communities from storms, and drive the regional economy. Weakening the bedrock environmental laws and locking in flawed decisions to expand offshore drilling would put both wildlife and the people who depend on these resources at greater risk.”

The Bureau of Ocean Energy Management has proposed opening up Florida’s coastal waters to offshore drilling, in violation of President Trump’s 2020 moratorium. The legislation would cement those decisions for years to come, potentially locking in offshore oil lease sales and leases sold through those sales, and leaving future administrations with virtually no way to undo them – even if those decisions are rushed or legally flawed. The Florida Congressional delegation has unanimously opposed expansion of offshore drilling to Florida’s waters.

While the legislation’s supporters argue that permitting changes will lower energy costs and accelerate infrastructure development, independent estimates have indicated the bill would save households only a few dollars per month in 2040, fourteen years from now, due to provisions in the bill unrelated to rollbacks to wildlife and habitat protections. Conservation organizations emphasize that these goals do not require sacrificing the nation’s most effective wildlife protection laws or weakening safeguards for clean water. Furthermore, the preventable expenses that Florida faces from unsustainable activities, such as oil spills and flooding from poorly-executed coastal development, seriously bring into question the net-benefit of this sweeping legislation.

“Florida’s senators should recognize that the costs of weakened environmental protections are not abstract,” Flores added. “They are felt in polluted waterways, fish kills, algal blooms, disappearing habitat, struggling wildlife populations, and communities that depend on healthy natural resources. We can build needed infrastructure and support affordable energy without compromising the protections that safeguard Florida’s future.”

The Endangered Species Coalition and Florida conservation partners urge Senators Scott and Moody and the Florida delegation in the House of Representatives to oppose the legislation in its current form and work to remove provisions that weaken the ESA, NEPA, and CWA. Any final legislation must preserve strong science-based protections, meaningful water quality safeguards, and public accountability.

Florida’s clean water, endangered wildlife, and natural heritage are too important to put at risk.

text:
ANTALYA – The world must immediately and drastically cut fossil fuel emissions to avert the most catastrophic effects of climate change, United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said Friday at his final climate summit, urging the world to “follow the science” and face hard facts.

“You cannot build peace on a burning planet," Guterres told reporters, stressing that climate change is central to the U.N.'s work because it contributes to geopolitical instability by driving hunger and displacement, pushing countries into debt and fueling competition for land and water.

“You cannot eradicate poverty when climate disasters keep throwing people back into it,” he added. “You cannot promise young people a better future while destroying the natural systems on which that future depends. And you cannot speak seriously about justice when those who did least to cause this crisis suffer first and worst.”

World leaders meeting in Turkey for the annual U.N. climate talks are trying to reach consensus on concrete actions to address climate change — which is fueling more intense and deadly heat waves, droughts, floods and other disasters — and help countries at greatest risk, including island nations that also are losing land to rising seas.

Electrification goals emerge as point of contention

Achieving reductions in emissions is setting up a point of contention at the climate talks, especially around electrification. A goal introduced this year would increase the share of electricity in total global energy consumption from roughly 21% to 35% by 2035, preferably from renewable energy such as solar and wind.

But it does not require that electricity be generated by renewable sources — something Guterres said is essential — meaning coal and other fossil fuels could be used, at least initially. Climate TRACE, which tracks global emissions via satellites, found that prioritizing clean energy would cut global emissions 14% compared to 7% if fossil fuels also are used for electrification.

International Energy Agency Executive Director Fatih Birol said it's more important that as many countries as possible sign on to the pledge, which works best without a clean energy requirement.

But environmental groups say that electrification will only have a real impact if fossil fuels are omitted.

“Electrification must end fossil fuel dependence, not be an end in itself,” said Jasmin Duregger, from Greenpeace's Global Gas Campaign.

Vulnerable nations seek more compensation as warming takes a toll

Leaders from countries ravaged by climate change — mostly poorer, vulnerable countries that contributed little to the problem — also are calling for more money to deal with climate disasters and adapt to a warming world. Leaders of small island nations, who say climate change is a life-or-death matter for their people because rising seas are engulfing their lands, have been the most vocal at this year’s summit, COP31, saying a U.N. fund created for compensating vulnerable nations must be urgently strengthened.

Guterres said wealthier countries that have contributed most to climate change “must deliver the finance they have promised” at past summits — but also contribute much more.

“Let us be clear about the scale of the gap,” he said. “Even tripling adaptation finance would meet less than 30 percent of what is needed.”

Progress stalls, top-emitting countries skip summit

Progress is difficult without the cooperation of all nations, “particularly the biggest emitters,” Guterres said.

A report released Thursday by the independent Climate Action Tracker found that progress in slowing global warming has essentially stalled for the past five years. That means the world is sure to overshoot the goal set in the 2015 Paris Agreement of limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial temperatures.

Climate change is caused primarily by greenhouse gases emitted by burning gas, oil and coal, and countries have established plans to reduce those emissions. But even if they fulfill all their promises — a big if — the globe will end the century 2.6 degrees Celsius (4.7 degrees Fahrenheit) warmer than pre-industrial times, the report said.

“Our responsibility is to keep it as small as possible, for as short a time as possible and bring temperatures back below 1.5 degrees as quickly as we can,” by cutting emissions about 6% per year for several years, Guterres said, calling the overshoot “a recipe for catastrophe.”

But some of the top-polluting countries stayed away from this year's summit, most notably the United States — the world’s second-largest polluter after China and the largest historical polluter.

It's the second year in a row the U.S. skipped the summit, after President Donald Trump withdrew the U.S. from climate negotiations.

“Facts are facts,” Guterres said. “No country can protect itself from climate change alone. We share one planet, and whether we like it or not, we share one fate.”

___

Webber reported from Fenton, Michigan; Borenstein from Kensington, Maryland; and Delgado from Bangkok.

text:
(TNS) — Within one week, Sacramento Regional Transit received millions in grant funds for a little less than two dozen zero-emission buses and took a step closer to requesting an exemption to California’s ZE bus requirements.

The California State Transportation Agency announced Thursday it awarded RT $57.7 million to purchase 21 fuel-cell electric buses, which use hydrogen to generate electricity onboard, and pay for other zero-emission improvements.

The grant funds were awarded through the eighth cycle of the Transit Innercity Rail Program, which handed out $549.4 million to 19 projects. About 54 applications were submitted for the program, asking for nearly $4.08 billion combined.

Where the grant will go

RT’s grant award will go to its Northern Sacramento and Yolo Zero-Emission Transit Project, which includes the fuel cell buses. The funding will also help develop hydrogen fueling infrastructure and improve the agency’s bus maintenance facility in McClellan Park. So far, the transit agency has received a total of $87.6 million for the project through a combination of state, regional and local funds.

The grants will also be used to install bicycle parking, heat-resilient bus shelters and transit signal priority technology at 30 intersections. A workforce development program will be created in partnership with American River College.

The project will be carried out in phases through 2030.

Regional Transit plans to use the 21 buses to augment Route 138, increasing daily trips between Davis and Sacramento to 23 and reducing time between buses from 60 minutes to 30 minutes during peak hours, according to grant documents. The buses will also allow RT to offer 15-minute weekday service on Routes 30 and 81, which will also help with getting people to train services like Capitol Corridor and Caltrain.

The agency does not currently have fueling infrastructure for hydrogen fuel-cell buses or charging infrastructure for a large number of battery-electric buses, RT spokesperson Jessica Gonzalez said. Part of the improvements to the McClellan Park facility will include a 25,000 gallon liquid hydrogen storage system.

“This project is about more than introducing 21 hydrogen fuel cell buses,” Gonzalez said. “It is an investment in the infrastructure, technology and workforce needed to support the future of public transportation. It will also provide more frequent service on important regional connections.”

About 9% of RT’s fleet are zero-emission vehicles, Gonzalez said.

Applying for the exemption

A few days before RT was awarded the grant, its board of directors authorized the agency to seek exemptions from a California Air Resources Board requirement related to zero-emission buses.

As of this year, CARB requires 50% of the agency’s new bus purchases be zero-emission. By 2040, all transit agencies will be required to use only zero-emission buses — meaning battery electric or fuel-cell electric.

However, Sacramento Regional Transit made two decisions earlier this year that complicated the agency’s ability to meet that goal.

Due to “current operational, infrastructure, funding and technology considerations,” RT decided to reallocate $76.8 million that was initially awarded for a similar zero-emission project with 29 fuel-cell buses, Gonzalez said in September. Instead, the money is going toward purchasing natural gas buses and rehabilitating the McClellan Park complex, though without the low-emission infrastructure. The agency’s board of directors in July approved an amendment to the 2026-27 budget to allow the switch.

The board also approved the purchase of another 49 compressed natural gas buses in August, on the condition it receives the CARB exemption.

The board approval on Monday allows RT to apply for exemptions this year and “as necessary” in 2027 and 2028, according to a board document.

RT is seeking exemptions due to “its inability to offset the incremental costs of purchasing ZEBs and associated infrastructure,” according to the board document. It is one of the conditions outlined by CARB. Also, RT does not have the equipment to fuel the hydrogen fuel-cell buses and “no existing shared hydrogen fueling station in the region can accommodate SacRT’s transit fleet.”

RT is not alone. The Sacramento Area Council of Governments is speaking with multiple transit agencies in its six-county jurisdiction about their transition to zero-emission bus fleets, spokesperson Mia Lopez said. SACOG may be applying for a regional exemption nearer to 2029, but has not yet made a decision.

If RT’s was not pursuing an exemption, it would have to purchase about 40 zero-emission buses this fiscal year, costing an additional $50 million, according to agency estimates using CARB’s cost benchmarks.

According to the board document, RT still aims to have a 100% zero-emission fleet by 2040.

text:
Fermi America held its third-quarter earnings call with investors on Thursday morning. Lee McIntire, Fermi CEO since August, began by noting recent significant changes in the power market.

“Power got more scarce. State-by-state moratoriums tightened up access to electrons, and in Texas, ERCOT, for example, froze new large-load connections, which are powering AI data centers. Land got harder to find. Community angst about the spread of data centers, concerns about water, noise, light, and the natural environment have taken many sites off the table,” McIntire said in prepared remarks. “Permits are harder to come by. Texas, for example, paused new air permits before the election. And the elections last week added more uncertainty.”

McIntire said these changes are driving demand and bringing investment-grade hyperscalers to Fermi’s door. Fermi announced both new agreements with one such hyperscaler and the termination of its agreement with TensorWave, which had been announced in August.

Fermi is developing agreements with the undisclosed investment-grade hyperscaler to include a $200 million prepayment agreement for 600 megawatts, a $15 million early construction and site development agreement, and a $90 million structural steel and building materials purchase agreement. The parties continue working toward a definitive long-term lease.

McIntire said Fermi has invested over $1.6 billion on the site. According to the investor call presentation, Fermi’s land now includes around 8,400 acres acquired, under lease, or under option. In March, the company said the Project Matador site was expanding to around 7,570 acres from the 5,769 acres initially planned.

Chief Commercial Officer Anna Bofa said Fermi is targeting initial power availability late in the second quarter or early in the third quarter of 2027. “If the opportunities we’re pursuing today convert into definitive agreements, they could absorb our planned 2.2 gigawatts of capacity,” Bofa said.

Public meetings and comment periods

The Panhandle Groundwater Conservation District Board of Directors meets Thursday at 9 a.m. in its office at 201 W Third Street in White Deer to discuss, among other things, the district’s comments on the environmental impact statement for the Project Matador’s combined license application. The board will also discuss and potentially take action on the City of Amarillo’s transport of groundwater outside the district and compliance with district rules.

Fermi’s environmental impact statement was posted in October and can be found on the Nuclear Regulatory Commission’s website. Public comment is open through Nov. 23. Comments can be submitted to FermiAmericaEnvironmental@nrc.gov or mailed to:

Office of Nuclear Material Safety and Safeguards, Mail Stop: TWFN-5-A85, U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission, Washington, DC 20555-0001, ATTN: Guidance and Publication Branch.

Editor’s note: Fermi is an Amarillo Tribune advertiser.

title: From the United Nations climate summit, Governor Newsom declares to the world that ...
description:
The meeting builds on the California–Australia climate partnership signed in 2023.
California’s climate leadership Since Governor Newsom took office in 2019, California has added more than 39,000 megawatts of utility-scale clean energy to serve the California grid.
Last year, clean energy met 100% of the state’s electricity needs for at least part of the day on 279 separate days.
California’s clean energy workforce grew by nearly 7,300 workers in 2024, outpacing job growth in the rest of the state’s economy by more than three times.
Brazil (2025): California signed a memorandum of understanding with the Brazilian federal government to scale up cooperation on climate, clean energy, cutting pollution, and job-creating climate opportunities.
text:
ANTALYA, TÜRKIYE – Alongside state and regional leaders at a United Nations press conference at COP31, Governor Gavin Newsom today declared to the world that America’s climate fight is far from over and that California, the world’s fourth-largest economy, is proof that we don’t have to choose between a growing economy and a healthy planet.

The Governor’s message to international partners was clear: American climate leadership is bigger than any one president, and California will keep delivering while Donald Trump does the fossil fuel industry’s bidding. In his remarks, the Governor traced California’s climate leadership to 1967, when Republican Governor Ronald Reagan created the California Air Resources Board, and made the case that the state has moved past setting goals to delivering results at scale.

The Governor also called out the industry at the heart of the crisis. While families pay the price for climate-driven disasters and volatile global oil markets, fossil fuel companies keep cashing in and stalling the solutions already at hand.

“The polluted heart of this climate crisis is Big Oil. The climate crisis is not complicated; it’s a fossil fuel crisis. It’s the burning of oil, gas, and coal. They’ve been lying to us; they’ve been deceitful. They have delayed the implementation and the application of the solutions that are already at hand, and they need to be called out, and they need to be held accountable,” said Governor Newsom. “Same group of Big Oil companies that just last quarter generated $100 billion of profit at your expense. That needs to be clearly called out. If we’re going to be serious about addressing the issue of this climate crisis, it’s about the polluters, and we need to advance strategies of accountability in that context.”

Asked whether California’s climate commitments will last beyond his administration, the Governor pointed to decades of bipartisan leadership and the expertise of the state’s energy and climate agencies: “It was a Republican governor when we were the 8th largest economy in the world that in 2006 established our cap-and-trade program, and all the big polluters said it would wreck the economy. Well, you’ve seen the evidence. Quite the contrary. I believe it’s built into the DNA of our state.”

The Governor closed with a message for California’s partners around the world: “I’m here to remind you that California is a stable partner in these endeavors. And that’s why I’m honored to be back here at COP, despite the fact that my federal government is once again a footnote in these conversations”

Watch the Governor’s remarks at the UNFCCC press conference

A b-roll package of the Governor’s Day 2 COP31 engagements can be downloaded here.

Working with Australia on oceans, resilience and clean energy

Governor Newsom and First Partner Jennifer Siebel Newsom began their day with a bilateral meeting with Australia’s Minister for Climate Change and Energy, Chris Bowen, who is leading this year’s COP31 negotiations. They discussed sea-level rise, global financing for climate resilience, ocean health, sustainable and regenerative farming, and growing the share of electricity that comes from clean energy instead of fossil fuels. California Air Resources Board Chair Lauren Sanchez also joined the meeting.

The meeting builds on the California–Australia climate partnership signed in 2023. Input from the California Air Resources Board helped inform Australia’s first-ever vehicle carbon emissions standards, and the California Public Utilities Commission and California ISO have advised Australia on electricity market reform. The partnership has also supported research exchanges on critical minerals, grid innovation and energy storage. In September, California and the Australian state of Queensland signed a new partnership on agricultural innovation and climate resilience.

Women’s leadership is essential to a resilient future

First Partner Jennifer Siebel Newsom joined New Mexico Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham and Gina McCarthy, Chair of America Is All In, for “Trailblazers, Changemakers & Innovators: Women Climate Leaders,” a U.S. Climate Alliance-hosted panel exploring how women’s experiences and leadership are shaping climate solutions and building more resilient communities.

“When women have seats at the tables of power,” the First Partner said, “they prioritize solutions that are ultimately better for our communities and Mother Nature.”

Drawing on her early career with Conservation International, the First Partner reflected on how her experiences working alongside communities around the world shaped her commitment to environmental protection and continue to inform her work in California. She highlighted California’s leadership as the nation’s top agricultural producer and its investments in incentivizing climate-smart agriculture, demonstrating how the state is advancing solutions at home while sharing innovations and partnering globally to accelerate climate progress.

The First Partner also underscored that climate action requires collective action, and that women must have a meaningful role in shaping the solutions. Ensuring women have equal economic opportunity and the resources to lead and innovate is not only a matter of equity, but essential to building stronger economies and more climate-resilient communities.

California at COP31

COP31 is the 31st Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, an annual global climate conference that brings together world leaders, scientists, businesses, non-governmental organizations, and civil society to advance action on climate change. Held in Antalya, Türkiye, from November 9–20, 2026, the conference is hosted by Türkiye, with Australia leading the negotiations. This year’s focus is on implementation: turning climate commitments into concrete, measurable results.

As a founding member of the Under2 Coalition and the U.S. Climate Alliance and as co-chair of America Is All In, California is demonstrating how states and regions can sustain international cooperation, accelerate clean energy, and deliver climate solutions that lower costs, create jobs, and strengthen resilience, even as the federal government retreats.

California’s delegation includes Governor Gavin Newsom; First Partner Jennifer Siebel Newsom; California Natural Resources Agency Secretary Wade Crowfoot; California Department of Food and Agriculture Secretary Karen Ross; California Public Utilities Commission President John Reynolds; California Air Resources Board Chair Lauren Sanchez; and Governor’s Office of Land Use and Climate Innovation Director Samuel Assefa.

California’s climate leadership

Since Governor Newsom took office in 2019, California has added more than 39,000 megawatts of utility-scale clean energy to serve the California grid. That’s helped make the grid more reliable and pushed the state further along its path in the clean energy transition.

The most recent numbers, from the end of 2024, show real progress: 67% of retail electricity sales in the state already come from clean energy. Last year, clean energy met 100% of the state’s electricity needs for at least part of the day on 279 separate days.

Solar and battery storage have been a key part of that progress, and are changing how California keeps the lights on. Since 2019, battery resources serving California grew from fewer than 700 megawatts to more than 23,000 megawatts — an increase of more than 3,100%. Batteries store solar power when it is abundant and deliver it after sunset. That reduces how often the state needs to run natural gas plants, which cuts air pollution and supports a more cost-effective electricity system.

California’s approach is also where the money is heading. Global investors are now putting roughly two dollars into clean-energy technology for every dollar that goes into fossil fuels. California is leading that shift while Donald Trump watches from the sidelines.

For California, that means investing in the good-paying jobs of the future. The Golden State is the 4th-largest economy in the world and leads the nation in total clean energy jobs, with 552,300 workers employed across clean energy technologies, nearly twice as many as the second-ranked state, Texas, according to a 2025 report from E2. California’s clean energy workforce grew by nearly 7,300 workers in 2024, outpacing job growth in the rest of the state’s economy by more than three times.

California’s global climate network

California has long been a key player on the international stage, from taking joint action on climate change to identifying new pathways and partnerships for sustained economic growth. During the Newsom administration alone, California has formed over 70 international partnerships that lay critical groundwork for our continued economic success, while prioritizing workers and businesses that benefit from these new opportunities.

Golden State and global partnerships

Portugal (2026): California and Portugal signed a memorandum of understanding to cooperate on low-carbon, clean energy development; climate change adaptation and mitigation, including extreme heat resilience; zero-emission mobility and transportation; emergency response and management; wildfire management and prevention; the sustainable blue ocean economy; and trade, investment and economic development.

United Kingdom (2026): California and the United Kingdom signed a memorandum of understanding to tackle climate change and promote sustainable development together. The memorandum of understanding builds on an already strong history of cooperation, and focuses on areas for collaboration including clean energy technologies, climate resilience, decarbonizing transportation, and protecting the natural environment.

Chile (2025): California and Chile signed a memorandum of understanding regarding exchanging information, developing best practices, and cooperating on methane emissions reduction. Methane is a highly potent greenhouse gas, and the partnership between California and Chile opens up new opportunities for both partners to cooperate on methane reduction in waste, agriculture, and energy sectors.

Colombia (2025): California and Colombia signed a partnership to advance joint efforts on forest conservation, methane reduction, climate resilience, and clean energy development. The memorandum of understanding deepens coordination on protecting the Amazon, strengthening biodiversity, and expanding nature-based climate solutions that support sustainable and equitable economic growth.

Nigeria (2025): California signed a memorandum of understanding with Nigeria on sustainable urban transportation, green ports, low-carbon transportation fuels, climate adaptation, methane detection and abatement policies, greenhouse gas emissions and air quality, and academic exchange and university partnerships. The partnership will build upon our shared commitment to sustainable growth, accelerate the transition to zero-emission transportation, and expand opportunities for the next generation.

Brazil (2025): California signed a memorandum of understanding with the Brazilian federal government to scale up cooperation on climate, clean energy, cutting pollution, and job-creating climate opportunities. This new partnership, announced in September 2025, will advance market-based carbon pricing programs, expand clean transportation, including zero-emission vehicles and low-carbon fuels, and strengthen air quality management through enhanced monitoring and regulatory controls. The partnership also focuses on conserving 30% of lands and coastal waters by 2030, including nature-based solutions and biodiversity protection. In 2025, California also advanced a partnership with the State of Pará to strengthen cooperation on wildfire prevention and response — enhancing forest monitoring, identifying areas most at risk, and sharing research and expertise to improve firefighting and emergency management.

Kenya (2025): California signed a partnership focused on cutting pollution and supporting trade. The partnership advances medium- and long-term low-carbon development, policy research, development, and innovation in sustainable land use and urban planning that reduces long commutes and urban sprawl, while promoting integrated land use and transport systems.

Noord-Holland (2024): California and Noord-Holland signed a Letter of Intent advancing next-generation air mobility — from drones to zero-emission aircraft. Joint innovation missions are producing pilot projects that inform California’s Advanced Air Mobility Implementation Plan and readiness for major global events.

Australia (2023): California signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with Australia that helped inform the country’s first-ever vehicle carbon emissions standards through input from the California Air Resources Board. The California Public Utilities Commission and California ISO have also advised Australia on electricity market reform to better align incentives for renewable energy.

British Columbia (2023): California and British Columbia signed a memorandum of understanding on mutual wildfire assistance that is delivering results. British Columbia sent incident management experts to support California’s Palisades Fire in 2025, while CAL FIRE deployed personnel during British Columbia’s 2025 fire season. These exchanges established a lasting framework for cross-border wildfire support.

China (2023): California signed five Memoranda of Understanding (MOUs) with China’s National Development and Reform Commission, the provinces of Guangdong and Jiangsu, and the municipalities of Beijing and Shanghai to advance cooperation in cutting greenhouse gas emissions, transitioning away from fossil fuels, and developing clean energy.

Denmark (2021): California and Denmark signed a memorandum of understanding to collaborate on groundwater mapping, leak detection, and water efficiency, which has modernized California’s data systems and informed key state programs, like the Airborne Electromagnetic Survey. Danish technologies and expertise have helped strengthen drought and water-supply resilience statewide.

Mexico (Baja California & Sonora): California signed Memoranda of Understanding (MOUs) with the Mexican states of Baja California and Sonora to advance zero-emission freight corridors, clean ports, and battery manufacturing — strengthening North American supply chains and workforce readiness. Joint forums have already produced new research collaborations and training programs advancing clean-tech.

text:
WHITE SANDS MISSILE RANGE, N.M. (Nov 13, 2026) — White Sands Missile Range held a groundbreaking ceremony Nov. 10 for a $27 million energy and water microgrid at Stallion Base Camp, located on the northern part of the range.

Funded through the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, the microgrid project is part of the range’s enduring commitment to strengthening installation energy and water resiliency while reducing risks to missions posed by utility disruptions.

"This project is about mission assurance," said Col. Michael Lueckeman, White Sands Missile Range garrison commander. "It is about guaranteeing that White Sands Missile Range can continue to execute some of the nation's most important testing, regardless of what happens to the commercial power grid. This project will provide the ability to operate independently from the commercial grid for up to 14 continuous days while maintaining electrical power and water distribution to critical facilities across the complex."

Funded through the Energy Resiliency Conservation Investment Program, the project will install a 600-kilowatt photovoltaic carport, a 700-kilowatt generator, a 600-kilowatt battery system, new electrical distribution lines, fiber connectivity, and security infrastructure. When complete, the microgrid will provide critical facilities at Stallion Base Camp with 14 days of energy and potable water during an extended power outage.

Lueckeman emphasized that the microgrid helps guarantee testing continuity.

"Whether the mission involves directed energy systems, counter-UAS technologies, long-range precision fires, missile testing, or hypersonic capabilities—reliable power is a foundational requirement," Lueckeman said. "This investment ensures that critical test data is collected, test schedules remain intact, and operational readiness is maintained."

The project also directly supports the secretary of war's vision under Project Fortress to build installations that are more resilient, self-sufficient, and capable of operating through disruption.

Craig Collins, WSMR installation energy manager, said the project will enable the installation to meet the U.S. Army’s requirement of 14-day energy and water independence. The Army has set a service-wide goal of sustaining water and power on installations for up to two weeks without depending on civilian supplies.

The Army established the 14-day requirement after studying past power outages and water shortages, matching those patterns to critical mission requirements.

"When complete, we won’t have to worry about power outages affecting our energy needs or water supply," Collins said.

"This microgrid represents how we will fight and win tomorrow," said Lt. Col. Brian Williams, commander of the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Albuquerque District. "By integrating clean solar and tactical storage, we directly support Installation Management Command’s resiliency objectives. We are reducing operating costs while hardening installations against physical, cyber, and grid disruption."

In 2025, WSMR held a ribbon-cutting for a microgrid that provides backup power to four groundwater wells on the southern range. That microgrid is equipped with a solar photovoltaic array, a natural gas generator, and a lithium-ion battery system to energize local water wells during an extended power outage.

These microgrids will ensure White Sands Missile Range can continue critical missions without a disruption to energy and potable water needs on the northern part of the range. The projects demonstrate WSMR’s continued efforts to nest future construction with Army Directive 2020-23 and the Installation Management Command Energy and Water Initiatives.

"At White Sands, we don't have the luxury of hoping critical infrastructure works when we need it," Lueckeman said. "Our job is to ensure it works every time. This project helps guarantee exactly that."

title: Dow, X-energy Receive Construction Permit for Advanced Nuclear Project in Texas
description:
The approval marks the first advanced nuclear facility authorized for construction at a U.S. industrial site, the first NRC construction permit for a high-temperature gas-cooled reactor in more than 50 years, and the first-ever NRC approval for a pebble-bed core design.
This project is supported by the U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE) Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program, which aims to accelerate commercial deployment of advanced nuclear reactor technologies in the United States.
Each Xe-100 reactor is designed to produce 80 megawatts of electricity or 200 megawatts of thermal energy.
The project demonstrates how advanced nuclear reactors could support energy-intensive manufacturing operations by providing both electricity and process heat directly where they are needed.
“This milestone marks a significant step forward for the Department of Energy’s Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program and our efforts to bring next-generation nuclear technologies to market,” said Principal Deputy Assistant Secretary for Nuclear Energy Mike Goff.
text:
The U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) approved(link is external) a construction permit on November 9 for Dow and X-energy’s proposed Long Mott Generating Station at Dow’s Seadrift Operations site in Texas.

The approval marks the first advanced nuclear facility authorized for construction at a U.S. industrial site, the first NRC construction permit for a high-temperature gas-cooled reactor in more than 50 years, and the first-ever NRC approval for a pebble-bed core design.

This project is supported by the U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE) Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program, which aims to accelerate commercial deployment of advanced nuclear reactor technologies in the United States.

Nuclear Power for American Industry

The proposed Long Mott Generating Station would deploy four X-energy Xe-100 small modular reactors to provide reliable electricity and high-temperature steam to Dow’s Seadrift manufacturing operations.

Each Xe-100 reactor is designed to produce 80 megawatts of electricity or 200 megawatts of thermal energy. Together, the four reactors could provide up to 320 megawatts of electricity while supporting the site’s industrial steam needs for 60 years.

The project demonstrates how advanced nuclear reactors could support energy-intensive manufacturing operations by providing both electricity and process heat directly where they are needed.

“This milestone marks a significant step forward for the Department of Energy’s Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program and our efforts to bring next-generation nuclear technologies to market,” said Principal Deputy Assistant Secretary for Nuclear Energy Mike Goff. “The NRC’s approval demonstrates meaningful progress toward deploying advanced reactors that can deliver reliable power and industrial heat, strengthen American energy leadership and expand the role of nuclear energy in meeting our nation’s growing energy demands.”

Meet the Next Generation

X-energy’s Xe-100 is a high-temperature gas-cooled reactor that uses TRISO-X fuel, a form of tri-structural isotropic (TRISO) coated particle fuel that uses high-assay, low-enriched uranium (HALEU), and is designed to retain radioactive materials under extreme conditions beyond any credible accident scenario.

The Xe-100 combines the robust characteristics of TRISO fuel with advanced safety features for a flexible design that enables a dramatically smaller footprint than conventional light-water reactors.

DOE has supported decades of research and development on high-temperature gas-cooled reactors and TRISO fuel technologies, helping establish the technical foundation for today's advanced reactor designs.

TRISO-X, a wholly owned subsidiary of X-energy, completed vertical construction in September 2026(link is external) on its TX-1 fuel fabrication facility in Oak Ridge, Tennessee, to produce TRISO-X fuel “pebbles” for the Xe-100. The facility is the first commercial-scale HALEU fuel fabrication facility in the United States to receive NRC approval, and the first new U.S. fuel facility licensed in over 50 years.

What’s Next?

The construction permit allows X-energy and Dow to advance the project toward construction readiness, including finalizing the Xe-100 design, strengthening the supply chain for long-lead components, and preparing an operating license application for NRC review.

If completed, Long Mott Generating Station would demonstrate a new application for advanced nuclear energy in the United States, providing dependable electricity and industrial steam directly to a major manufacturing facility that helps nuclear technology expand beyond conventional power, and into the industries powering our country forward.

The project is targeting initial energy delivery in the early 2030s.

name: Detroit and Evs
title: More Power, Better MPG? Edison Motors Plans Hybrid Test Trucks
description:
Beyond ditching traditional differentials paired to electric motors, Edison is utilizing a highly modular battery architecture for its upcoming production rollout.
Three Validation Trucks Before Production With its latest fourth-generation (V4) design nearing completion, Edison plans three validation trucks: a mechanical truck for logging operations, a customer hybrid and an internal hybrid test truck.
A capital injection of that size would fund a pilot run of ten production trucks out of their new facility in Donald, British Columbia.
If successful, Edison Motors would deliver on the broken promises of companies hundreds or even thousands of times its size.
In every way that matters, Edison Motors plans to be the anti Tesla.
text:
Nine years ago, two British Columbians were among the first in Canada to pre-order a Tesla Semi. When this predictably went nowhere, the two decided they could provide a more viable product on their own. Better still, they bet that they could do it without telling right to repair folks to take a hike. Four years later, the duo founded Edison Motors, and in 2026, the group is sharing what a year of rapid scaling and hybrid truck innovation looks like at its annual investor day.

Breaking Down the Hardware

At their recent annual investor day in Donald, British Columbia, Chace Barber, Eric Little, and the rest of the Edison Motors crew pulled back the curtain on how far they’ve come since the company began in what amounted to a backyard tent. Now situated in a freshly-built warehouse, the Edison group has a small fleet of pickups and semis on display, including diesel-electric hybrids and the conventional mechanical-diesel Big D. For the gearheads in Edison’s audience, the annual investor day wasn’t just about business dealings. It was a showcase of serious prototype trucking hardware that isn’t locked behind a billion-dollar research facility.

Beyond ditching traditional differentials paired to electric motors, Edison is utilizing a highly modular battery architecture for its upcoming production rollout. With chassis capable of carrying anywhere from two to six battery packs, the architecture has the capability to handle shorter-haul trips as well as jobs further afield—all without locking owner/operators into overkill one-size-fits-all packs that cut into cargo capacity. Among the standout machines is “Big D,” a mechanical diesel winch tractor, not a hybrid, featuring a 605-horsepower Cummins X-15, an Eaton 18-speed manual transmission, and a heavy-duty Tulsa 40-ton winch that’d make the owner/operators the group was most inspired by feel proud. Because navigating Transport Canada’s electronic stability control (ESC) testing requirements for a tractor setup can take over a year, Edison cleverly registered the truck in Alberta as a winch tractor/bed truck to expedite regulatory compliance.

Alongside their heavy-duty commercial rigs, Edison has also been fulfilling customized specialty builds, such as a heavy-duty LC79 Land Cruiser hybrid delivered to an undisclosed military client, and an EREV-swapped Ram truck that was once a bare-bones 2WD 5.9 Magnum rig, functioning as a technological demonstrator. Meanwhile, Edison’s latest generation of hybrid semis has drifted away from single-motor differentials towards more efficient and powerful dual-motor-per-axle layouts. On both fronts Edison appears closer than ever to full-scale production, and they already have clients lined up.

Three Validation Trucks Before Production

With its latest fourth-generation (V4) design nearing completion, Edison plans three validation trucks: a mechanical truck for logging operations, a customer hybrid and an internal hybrid test truck. At the investor event, the team said design work should be complete within roughly a month, followed by parts ordering and builds to work out remaining issues. These are planned validation trucks, not an already launched production fleet. The team is also targeting a U.S.-based Regulation A funding round of $20 million to $40 million to help get production off the ground.

A capital injection of that size would fund a pilot run of ten production trucks out of their new facility in Donald, British Columbia. From there, the goal is to field production orders from a larger pool of clients ranging from over-the-road truckers to logging operations, and possibly even a handful of intermodal specialists. Edison’s goal is for its fleet of semis to fill the very same roles that modern diesels do, with the aim of reducing fuel use and maintenance through its hybrid powertrains. More power and better MPG are the promise, not a demonstrated outcome for the planned V4 fleet: Edison did not present measured comparative MPG results at this event.

If successful, Edison Motors would deliver on the broken promises of companies hundreds or even thousands of times its size. In doing so, it would prove the future of trucking doesn’t need to rely on fragile, impossible to repair technology or massive corporate campuses. In every way that matters, Edison Motors plans to be the anti Tesla.

Better MPG Depends on the Job

How much fuel could a diesel-electric truck save? Edison’s FAQ estimates savings of 5–10% for highway work and fuel-use reductions of 70–100% in logging or city applications. Those are the company’s estimates, not independently verified test results. The FAQ does not provide a test methodology or a defined comparison baseline for those figures, and it does not establish a measured MPG rating for the planned V4 trucks. A percentage reduction in fuel consumed also is not the same percentage increase in MPG.

The distinction between comparing a hybrid with a conventional diesel and comparing two generations of Edison hardware matters, too. In Edison’s generator-engine discussion, the company says the fuel-economy benefit depends on the job and does not expect a noticeable change versus its previous generator setup. The higher engine output discussed there is generator-engine power, not a directly interchangeable measure of power at the wheels.

That leaves a promising idea with testing still to do, not a blanket promise that every operator will get the same savings. Route, load and duty cycle will determine how useful the hybrid system is. For the upcoming validation trucks, measured fuel use under comparable working conditions is the number that will matter.

A Right to Repair Warrior

For the everyday pickup truck driver, Edison’s ambitions stretch far beyond the commercial trucking sector. That 5.9-liter Magnum Dodge Ram test mule isn’t just a fun shop project, it’s the rolling billboard for the company’s ability to match the same trends as billion-dollar OEMs. At the present, Detroit titans like Ram and Ford are pivoting hard back to hybrids and extended-range electric vehicles after the pure-EV venture ran into insurmountable hurdles.

Future flagships such as the Ram 1500 REV, formerly called Ramcharger, and Ford F-150 Lightning EREV pursue the same extended-range electric concept. Ford projects more than 700 miles of range for its next-generation Lightning; these are manufacturer targets, not independently verified real-world results. Yet, while those modern rigs are rolling supercomputers wrapped in massive price tags and locked behind proprietary software, Edison is taking a strictly right-to-repair approach to the exact same concept. All of this testing feeds into Edison’s planned incomplete rolling chassis, allowing a chosen truck body to be paired with a diesel-electric powertrain. The company says testing must establish efficiency, reliability and power before the product is ready.

Rather than competing directly with Detroit by selling a complete new pickup, Edison is developing a rolling-chassis alternative for existing truck bodies. That does not mean bypassing dealers: its official pickup-chassis plan calls for dealer installation and service. Market timing remains unconfirmed.

The Roadmap Ahead

While bringing its diesel-electric rolling chassis to market remains a longer-term goal, the Edison team is already laying the groundwork to translate their heavy-duty engineering down to the consumer level. Design work has officially kicked off on the pickup-sized incomplete chassis, with the stated goal of having a fully realized prototype to reveal by next year’s investor day.

text:
The most important legal development from the midterm elections happened in Texas. Nope, I’m not talking about the election of James Talarico, or the Democrats’ newfound power to block Donald Trump’s judicial appointments. That stuff matters, of course, but the single biggest change to what happens in the courts over the next two years probably comes down to Democrat Nathan Johnson, the new attorney general for the state of Texas.
