The Texas AG’s office has been ground zero for many of the most destructive legal battles Republicans have fought and largely won over the past generation. The outgoing Texas AG is the guy who lost to Talarico for the Senate, Ken Paxton. Paxton has been suing abortion providers who send mifepristone (the “abortion pill”) to his state. He has attacked trans people, immigrants, and the environment. He tried to single-handedly block Joe Biden’s agenda from ever being enacted in Texas, and has generally been a despicable menace who uses the law to promote bigotry. Paxton has been at the post since 2015. Before him, the Texas AG was Greg Abbott (the Texas governor who just lost to Gina Hinojosa). Before him, John Cornyn held the role; he’s the outgoing Republican senator whom Paxton beat in the primary. Cornyn replaced Democrat Dan Morales as AG in 1999. Republicans have literally controlled this post this whole century.

What makes the person who occupies this post particularly influential is that the Texas attorney general is always backed up by the Texas solicitor general, who has the job of arguing the AG’s cases in court. The Texas AG, rather than the governor, is also the one who appoints the SG. Past Texas solicitors general include Johnathan Mitchell—who is the guy who had the bright idea to set bounty hunters on abortion providers—and… Senator Ted Cruz.

All of this matters because a disproportionate number of this Supreme Court’s worst, most corrosive cases originate in Texas. That’s because of a quirk in Texas’s judicial structure that allows for easy and flagrant judge-shopping. In other states, the initial judge presiding over a federal lawsuit is chosen by lottery from among the available judges in the district where the lawsuit is filed. In Texas, the presiding judge is whoever happens to run the courthouse in the place where the case is filed. That means that the Texas AG can pick the judge who will rule on any given case by filing the case in the right mailbox. For the past few years, the judge of choice for culture-war issues has been the “emperor of Amarillo,” the reactionary misogynist Matthew Kacsmaryk. For the past 20 years, the judge of choice for immigration issues has been reactionary bigot Reed O’Connor.

Sometimes, a case might end there, with a favorable ruling from one of these handpicked judges. But if the losing party appeals—and, the Texas AG and SG are often counting on this—they can defend their case in front of the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals. The Fifth Circuit is the most conservative appellate court in the country, by some margin. It is full of people openly auditioning for Supreme Court appointments, and in the Trump era that audition has devolved into judges’ ruling in the most insane way possible. Fifth Circuit judges like James C. Ho, Stuart Kyle Duncan, and Andy Oldham are truly some of the worst people the system has to offer.

From there, once the next inevitable appeal arrives, it’s a straight shot to the Supreme Court, where whatever legal monstrosity the Texas AG cooked up is often enshrined into national law by the six Republican justices. What starts in Texas rarely stays there.

This is why replacing the Texas AG with a Democrat is so important. It stops a bunch of lawsuits before they even start. It greatly diminishes the evil the people on the Fifth Circuit can do. It deprives the conservatives on the Supreme Court of some of the cases they need if they want to change the law. Other Republican attorneys general who survived the blue tsunami will surely try to pick up the slack for Texas, but because other states lack the unique judge-shopping structure available in Texas, those surviving AGs are unlikely to be as effective as the Texas AG has been. Moreover, as Ian Millhiser points out, the attorney general offices in other states (like Louisiana and Mississippi, which are the other two states in the Fifth Circuit) are fundamentally smaller than Texas and don’t have as much money. “[T]hey will likely only have the resources to bring a fraction of the number of partisan lawsuits filed by Paxton.”

You don’t have to take our words for it. Just listen to conservative legal commentator Josh Blackman bemoaning the loss of the position in a post-election article in Reason:

I would suspect that all of the conservative strategic litigation cases brought by Attorney General Paxton will be dismissed. Indeed, it is conceivable that the new Texas Attorney General would not defend the Texas Ten Commandments Law if cert is granted.… The Texas Attorney General will also not bring original jurisdiction actions before the Supreme Court of Texas. Going forward, all of the strategic forums in Texas will be severely underutilized.

To de-jargonize some of the gobbledygook: “original jurisdiction actions” refer to cases where Texas sues some other state for, say, “election fraud”; “strategic forums” refer to the judge-shopping Texas AGs traditionally do; and “strategic litigation” is whatever antidemocratic cultural nonsense people like Josh Blackman can think up next. As Sean Rankin, head of the Democratic Attorneys General Association, put it in an interview with Politico, “We took the head of the snake.”

With that head gone, the Texas AG will no longer be the force for pure evil that it has been. There’s a lot of bad stuff the office will cease to do. The other side of the coin is the good stuff the AG can do. Nathan Johnson has already said he will end the out-of-state prosecutions of abortion providers and restore a “respect for the rule of law,” which was something that was severely lacking under his predecessor. But I will dare to hope for a little more than a mere restoration of respect. Texas is the corporate home of a number of companies that haven’t been regulated or investigated at the state level during this century, among them: ExxonMobile, McKesson Pharmaceuticals, AT&T, Oracle… and the entire Elon Musk cinematic universe, including Tesla, SpaceX, and Twitter.

That’s right, Nathan Johnson is poised to become Elon Musk’s worst nightmare: a Democrat with jurisdiction. Musk and his companies fled California after Tesla was sued for civil rights violations there. Do we think he stopped allegedly violating workers’ civil rights when he got to Texas? I don’t think so, and I bet Johnson doesn’t think so either. The judge-shopping door swings both ways, and all Johnson needs is one favorable district court judge in, say, Austin, and he can haul Musk before a jury of his new neighbors.

Think about all the work New York Attorney General Tish James (who won a third term last week) has done trying to hold the Trump crime family accountable. Think about all the work Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison has done trying to hold police accountable. Think about all the work California Attorney General Rob Bonta (who just won a second term) has done trying to hold ICE accountable. Now think about the fact that we added new Democratic AGs in Georgia, Iowa, Ohio, and Kansas (defeating Republican Kris Kobach, who would have been the worst AG in the country if Ken Paxton did not exist).

description:
The Ministry of Heavy Industries (MHI) has received 22 bids for establishing 10 GWh of Advanced Chemistry Cell (ACC) battery manufacturing capacity in India, specifically earmarked for Grid-Scale Stationary Storage (GSSS) applications.
The 10 GWh capacity forms part of the broader target of establishing 50 GWh of domestic ACC manufacturing capacity under the national programme.
10 GWh Capacity Dedicated to Stationary Storage Unlike battery manufacturing capacity primarily intended for electric mobility, the 10 GWh allocation is specifically earmarked for Grid-Scale Stationary Storage applications.

The latest tender for 10 GWh of grid-scale stationary storage capacity represents a targeted step towards developing India's domestic battery manufacturing ecosystem for renewable energy integration.
text:
The Ministry of Heavy Industries (MHI) has received 22 bids for establishing 10 GWh of Advanced Chemistry Cell (ACC) battery manufacturing capacity in India, specifically earmarked for Grid-Scale Stationary Storage (GSSS) applications. The bidding is part of the government's Production Linked Incentive (PLI) Scheme for the National Programme on Advanced Chemistry Cell Battery Storage.

The technical bids were opened on 11 November 2026 at the Ministry of Heavy Industries in the presence of participating bidders. The ministry announced the development on 12 November 2026, following the closure of the bidding process on 10 November.

The 10 GWh capacity forms part of the broader target of establishing 50 GWh of domestic ACC manufacturing capacity under the national programme. The tender was floated on the Central Public Procurement Portal on 15 July 2026, with a pre-bid conference held on 29 July.

22 Companies Participate in ACC Manufacturing Tender

The list of bidders includes companies from the solar, power, battery and energy infrastructure sectors. ACME Solar Holdings, Amara Raja Advanced Cell Technologies, Avaada Electro, Exide Energy Solutions, Reliance Industries, JSW Neo Energy, Vikram Solar and Waaree Energy Storage Solutions are among the participants.

Other bidders include Fujiyama Power Systems, GK Energy, Godawari New Energy, Megha Engineering and Infrastructures, Renew Photovoltaics, Shirdi Sai Electricals, Sun Drops Energia and Utex New Energy.

The selection process is being conducted through a two-stage Quality and Cost Based Selection (QCBS) mechanism. The opening of technical bids marks the next stage of the tender process. The ministry has not yet announced the final allocation of manufacturing capacity among the bidders.

10 GWh Capacity Dedicated to Stationary Storage

Unlike battery manufacturing capacity primarily intended for electric mobility, the 10 GWh allocation is specifically earmarked for Grid-Scale Stationary Storage applications.

This is significant as India's expanding renewable energy capacity is increasing the need for storage solutions that can manage fluctuations in solar and wind generation. Grid-scale battery storage can absorb electricity during periods of surplus generation and discharge it when renewable output declines or electricity demand rises.

The proposed manufacturing capacity could therefore support the development of domestic battery supply chains for utility-scale Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS).

However, the actual impact will depend on the successful selection of manufacturers, project execution and the commissioning of the proposed facilities.

₹18,100 Crore PLI Scheme Targets 50 GWh ACC Capacity

The Union Cabinet approved the PLI Scheme for the National Programme on Advanced Chemistry Cell Battery Storage in May 2021, with a total budgetary outlay of ₹18,100 crore.

The programme aims to establish 50 GWh of domestic ACC manufacturing capacity by attracting domestic and international companies and reducing dependence on imported battery technologies and components.

The latest tender for 10 GWh of grid-scale stationary storage capacity represents a targeted step towards developing India's domestic battery manufacturing ecosystem for renewable energy integration.

With 22 companies participating, the next stage will be to determine how much capacity is ultimately awarded and how quickly the selected manufacturers can establish production facilities.

text:
Electric vehicles make up a sliver of the world's cars, but they're already putting a dent in global oil demand.

Transport & Environment estimated that battery-electric cars save 1.2 million barrels of oil a day despite accounting for just 4.2% of vehicles worldwide.

Here's what to know

In 2021, battery-electric cars displaced about 215,000 barrels of oil per day. That figure has since grown more than fivefold, according to a T&E analysis cited by CleanTechnica.

In 2021, battery-electric models accounted for 6.6% of new-car purchases worldwide. T&E said that share has surged to a quarter of all purchases.

No other strategy cuts oil demand, shores up energy security, and lowers pollution as effectively as electric vehicles, it said. Battery-electric cars save the equivalent of 1.2% of the oil consumed worldwide.

More background

T&E reported that battery-electric models make up about 1% of the world's trucks and a majority of new truck purchases in some countries. It put the electric share of the global bus fleet at 5%.

Daily oil consumption would be up to 320,000 barrels higher without electric buses and trucks, T&E estimated.

Nearly half the oil consumed worldwide goes to road transportation.

T&E warned that oil demand could spiral out of control as more cars and trucks hit the road unless EV adoption keeps pace.

What's being done?

At the 2021 COP26 summit in Glasgow, 24 countries and a group of major automakers agreed to stop selling gas- and diesel-powered vehicles no later than 2040, per CleanTechnica.

The analysis tracked the growth of electric transportation over the five years following that commitment.

By 2034, battery-electric cars could cut daily oil use by about 5.8 million barrels if current policies hold, T&E projected.

Global energy markets have weathered two crises since the Glasgow pledge, and T&E called for faster EV adoption to help ward off future oil shocks.

It estimated that the battery-electric fleet in use prevents over 200 million metric tons of carbon dioxide-equivalent emissions each year.

Antony Froggatt, a senior director at T&E, connected the trend to energy security as well as climate goals. "Five years after Glasgow, EVs stand as one of the clearest victories in global climate history," he said, per CleanTechnica.

Where can I learn more?

Electric vehicles are cutting oil use as they claim a growing share of new-car sales.

• Worldwide, gas-only cars now account for less than half of new vehicle sales.

• In Europe, EVs have overtaken gas and diesel vehicles while U.S. adoption lags.

• China's EV market share reached a record 65% in August as combustion-engine sales collapsed.

• The U.S. EV share fell to 6% after tax credits ended; Europe reached 23%.

• In Norway, EVs accounted for 96% of new-car sales.

text:
Insider Brief

May Mobility plans to deploy more than 10,000 autonomous Volkswagen ID. Buzz vehicles through 2031, with U.S. road testing scheduled for early 2027 and initial production deliveries targeted for 2028.

The company is working with ECARX and Charlton Intelligence.ai to integrate its autonomous driving technology and support vehicle deployment, targeting cost savings of at least 50% compared with its current-generation vehicle.

May Mobility has completed more than 600,000 commercial autonomous rides across 1.1 million miles in the United States and Japan, with existing U.S. operations and a planned Uber robotaxi launch in Arlington, Texas, in 2027.

May Mobility plans to deploy more than 10,000 autonomous Volkswagen ID. Buzz vehicles through 2031 as it expands its robotaxi operations with fleet partners worldwide.

According to the Ann Arbor, Michigan, company, U.S. road testing is scheduled to begin in early 2027, with the first production vehicles targeted for delivery in 2028. The electric vehicles will be adapted to work with May Mobility’s autonomous driving system.

May Mobility indicated it will collaborate with automotive technology company ECARX to integrate its autonomous driving kit into a version of the ID. Buzz designed for self-driving operations. Charlton Intelligence.ai has also joined the partnership to help deploy the vehicles.

The companies are targeting total cost savings of 50% or more compared with its current-generation autonomous vehicle through their supply chain collaboration, according to May Mobility,

“Scaling autonomous ride-hail depends heavily on the vehicle platform, and the Volkswagen ID. Buzz gives us one well suited for it,” May Mobility founder and CEO Edwin Olson. “We think riders will love the ID. Buzz running on May Mobility’s autonomous driving system, and the vehicle will be built on economics that can scale with the robotaxi market.”

The ID. Buzz is an all-electric vehicle based on Volkswagen’s original bus design. May Mobility cited its multiple entry doors and spacious interior as features suited to passenger service, and the company plans to deploy the ID. Buzz through fleet operator partnerships, building on its existing autonomous ride-hailing operations.

Expanding Autonomous Ride-Hailing

May Mobility’s autonomous driving system uses a predictive world model to assess road conditions and evaluate possible driving decisions. The technology simulates driving scenarios up to 10 seconds into the future before selecting a course of action.

May Mobility reported completing more than 600,000 commercial autonomous rides covering 1.1 million miles in the United States and Japan. It also reported three deployments operating without onboard safety drivers.

The company currently provides commercial services in three U.S. locations, including through Lyft in Atlanta and autonomous ride services in Eden Prairie and Grand Rapids, Minnesota. May Mobility is also planning a 2027 commercial launch with Uber in Arlington, Texas. In Japan, the company began a six-month on-demand autonomous vehicle pilot with NTT Mobility in Nagoya in September.

May Mobility said it will release additional details on the ID. Buzz specifications, testing and deployment plans at a future date.

title: Climate could force more than 200 bn from homes: UN migration chief - Star City News
description: Climate change could force more than 200 billion people from their homes even as countries spend billions on securing their borders, the head of the UN's migration body said Friday.
text:
Climate change could force more than 200 billion people from their homes even as countries spend billions on securing their borders, the head of the UN's migration body said Friday.
Amy Pope, director general of the International Organization for Migration (IOM), made the warning in an interview with AFP at the United Nations climate conference in the Turkish resort of Antalya.
"Over 200 billion people are currently living in extremely climate-vulnerable communities who are at risk of displacement," she said.

"If we don't act now, we anticipate that those movements will increase significantly."
In 2025, storms, drought, forest fires, extreme temperatures or flooding forced nearly 30 million people to flee their homes, according to IOM data.
"What we don't see, though, is the kind of policy or investment that's needed to address those drivers of migration," said Pope.
"And, of course, the tension is that we know that countries are spending billions of dollars on border security."
Some of the very countries that stayed away from the climate conference were the same expressing concern about migration, said Pope. Yet the two issues were connected, she said.
"It is critical that governments not put these different issues into silos," she argued.
- 'Cost-effective' measures not funded -
"We often are asked to help support governments as they address irregular migration when it happens," she said.
"We know how expensive that can be, we know how many lives can be lost."
What would make more sense, she argued, would be to help communities threatened by climate change to find ways of mitigating its effects.
That was "a much more humane but also cost-effective way of responding to those challenges", she said.
"We're talking about adaptation measures that are estimated to cost about $310 million or so," she added.
And yet, so far, there had been about $30 million in funding, and that was "nowhere close to what it needs to be".
Pope regretted the absence of so many heads of state from the COP31 talks.
"We encourage all states to be engaged, to be driving solutions, to ensure that they have a comprehensive approach," she said.
"We would love to see them all at the table."

title: California governor Gavin Newsom endorses global fossil fuel phaseout - The Guardian
description:
The leader of the world’s fourth biggest economy, California governor Gavin Newsom, has explicitly endorsed a global phase out of the fossil fuels that drive climate breakdown.

text:
The leader of the world’s fourth biggest economy, California governor Gavin Newsom, has explicitly endorsed a global phase out of the fossil fuels that drive climate breakdown.

Newsom told the Guardian that California is “100%” behind the efforts of the so-called Santa Marta coalition, a group of more than 50 countries that includes many of the world’s largest economies, to transition away from oil, gas and coal toward solar, wind, batteries and other non-carbon energy sources.

Speaking at the Cop31 UN climate summit on Thursday, Newsom said: “When you have a product that is obviously superior, which clean energy is for the climate and the economy, why wouldn’t you make that shift as quickly as possible?”

As the head of America’s most populous and economically powerful state, Newsom is the most prominent US politician at Cop31, a process the administration of US president Donald Trump continues to boycott.

Newsom, a Democrat, is widely expected to run for president in 2028. His statement raises the possibility that the US, the world’s biggest economy and largest historical emitter of planet-warming gases, could join the Santa Marta coalition if he wins the presidency two years from now.

More than 80 countries wanted last year’s COP30 to begin to develop a global “roadmap” to phase out fossil fuels. A handful of petrostates led by Saudi Arabia blocked that effort, relying on the disputed notion that decisions at UN climate summits can only be made by consensus. Undaunted, countries favoring a roadmap met in April in Santa Marta, Colombia, to begin designing a phase out on their own.

“Love it,” Newsom said of the challenge that this Santa Marta “coalition of the willing” is posing to the US and other states intent on keeping the world burning fossil fuels.

The coalition is in effect no longer allowing petrostates to employ procedural tricks and endless talk to prevent what scientists say is imperative: rapidly phasing out fossil fuels. Instead, this critical mass of countries, which includes Germany, France, Brazil and The Netherlands – with additional countries, perhaps including the UK, expected to join later in Cop31 – is proceeding on its own with roadmaps to transition away from fossil fuels, hoping that its example and economic power will lead others to follow suit.

“You don’t ask drug dealers to vote for Prohibition, and you won’t get petro-states to agree to phase out fossil fuels,” said Mohamed Nasheed, the former president of The Maldives, who once convened a cabinet meeting underwater to dramatize the plight of low-lying island nations like his. “Countries wishing to phase out fossil fuels should just go ahead and do it,” Nasheed told the Guardian.

Newsom’s statement could add momentum to a CopP31 summit that has been widely expected to yield modest progress at best. The governor’s comments follow two political earthquakes that also raised hopes of a new era in global climate politics. First came the surprising re-election of president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva of Brazil in October, then the crushing rebuke of Trump and his Republican Congress in the US midterm elections in early November.

What makes the Santa Marta coalition’s vision more than a pipe dream is the coalition’s economic might. Collectively, the 80-plus countries that wanted a phase out roadmap at Cop30 amount to the biggest economic superpower on earth.

If the coalition can begin implementing a credible transition away from fossil fuels, it “would send an unmistakable message that the age of oil, gas and coal is ending, and the smart money is shifting,” Mohamed Adow, director of the nonprofit Power Shift Africa, said in an interview. Governments and financial markets around the world would be put on notice that staying invested in fossil fuels will be an increasingly risky proposition that could leave them holding trillions of dollars of stranded assets.

Thus far, Germany, the world’s third biggest economy, has committed to phasing out fossil fuels by 2045. France, the world’s sixth biggest economy, and The Netherlands, the 18th biggest, have released phase out roadmaps as well.

California’s clean energy track record aligns with the one policy goal that, analysts say, Cop31’s final agreement might endorse: a commitment to obtain 35% of the world’s energy from electricity by 2035. California’s economy has run on 100% clean electricity nine out of every 10 days during much of 2026, with batteries emerging as “a game changer”, as Newsom described it. As the costs of clean energy continue to fall, Newsom expects more counties to follow California’s example because “the markets are moving in our direction”.

The midterms also brought to power scores of climate champions at the state and local level. In Texas, the US’s second largest state economy after California, the new governor is Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who shunned contributions from the fossil fuel industry that has long dominated her state. In all, 29 states will have Democratic governors who, among other things, could block datacenters.

Humanity is in “a final battle against the evil forces” trying to keep the world burning fossil fuels, said Johan Rockstrom, the director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impacts Research. As the Nepal glacier disaster and 50,000 extreme heat deaths in Europe this summer illustrate, climate breakdown is already wreaking terrible damage. Nevertheless, Rockstrom added, “89% of citizens across the world trust science [and] want action. We are a majority power that can have confidence we have a collective global community that really wants this to succeed--and that it isn’t too late.”

The AA rating provides independent recognition of CS PowerTech's manufacturing platform and its focus on building a scaled, globally competitive, and resilient domestic solar supply chain. CS PowerTech is one of only three manufacturers, out of 22 evaluated, to receive a rating of AA or higher. The report assessed manufacturers based on their U.S. production output and capital expenditure.

Rusty Schmit, President of CS PowerTech Inc., added, "We're building a U.S. manufacturing platform designed to compete for the long term, and this AA rating is an important recognition of our progress. Our strategy is straightforward: invest in advanced, reliable technology and build the domestic manufacturing capabilities our customers need. I'm proud of what our team has accomplished in Texas and Indiana and eager to build on our momentum."

The recognition comes at an important time for the U.S. solar industry, as customers, developers, financial institutions, and other stakeholders increasingly look beyond manufacturing capacity alone, placing greater emphasis on the quality, resilience, and long-term credibility of their manufacturing partners.

Over the past 25 years, Canadian Solar has successfully delivered nearly 180 GW of premium-quality solar photovoltaic modules to customers across the world. text:
Market snapshot: Ola Electric Mobility Limited is advancing its vertical integration strategy by pairing in-house Lithium Iron Phosphate (LFP) cell chemistry with its modular Gen 4 vehicle platform. The company expects 20% cost savings from making its own batteries (as stated in the source alert; not independently verified), aiming to lower bill-of-materials costs across its upcoming product line starting in the fourth quarter.

Data Snapshot

Ministry of Heavy Industries approved revised Advanced Chemistry Cell PLI scheme timelines for Ola Cell Technologies, unlocking up to ₹7,240 crore in cumulative incentives over five years.

Ola Cell Technologies installed battery cell manufacturing capacity is expanding toward 6 GWh at its Gigafactory.

In Q1 FY27, Ola Electric reported consolidated revenue from operations of ₹455 crore and narrowed its net loss to ₹336 crore.

What's Changed

Secured MHI approval for a full 5-year ACC PLI window through CY2031, providing recurring quarterly incentive disbursements.

Transitioned cell manufacturing strategy from external pack sourcing to indigenous 4680 NMC and 46100 LFP cell platforms.

Narrowed quarterly operational net loss to ₹336 crore in Q1 FY27 supported by lower manufacturing overheads.

Key Takeaways

In-house battery manufacturing directly targets the EV component cost structure, as battery packs represent a major share of total vehicle bill-of-materials.

Deploying LFP cell chemistry on the modular Gen 4 platform provides structural flexibility across two-wheelers and energy storage units.

Government PLI scheme alignment secures financial backing for Gigafactory scale-up, strengthening unit economics as production ramps up.

SAHI Perspective

Ola Electric's pivot toward indigenous cell integration represents a pivotal step in EV supply chain independence. If material cost reductions materialize as planned through the Gen 4 platform transition, the company can improve gross margins while expanding vehicle accessibility across broader price bands.

Market Implications

Successful internal cell deployment enhances long-term margin profiles for electric two-wheeler manufacturers. Additionally, in-house cell capabilities allow cross-application into stationary battery energy storage systems, widening revenue opportunities beyond automotive mobility.

Trading Signals

Market Bias: Bullish

Directional optimism is supported by MHI approval unlocking up to ₹7,240 crore in cumulative PLI incentives and Gigafactory expansion to 6 GWh, paving the way for in-house cell cost efficiencies.

Overweight: Electric Two-Wheeler OEMs, Advanced Battery Storage & Cell Manufacturers

Trigger Factors:

Commercial deployment timeline of Gen 4 vehicles integrated with homegrown LFP cells in Q4

Quarterly PLI incentive disbursement cash flows from the Ministry of Heavy Industries

Achieving 6 GWh installed cell capacity at the Tamil Nadu Gigafactory

Time Horizon: Medium-term (3-12 months)

Industry Context

Battery packs account for 30% to 50% of total electric two-wheeler manufacturing costs in India. Transitioning to LFP chemistry offers higher thermal stability, longer cycle life, and lower material cost relative to NMC chemistry, driving industry-wide adoptability for mass-market EV offerings.

Key Risks to Watch

Potential yield stabilization delays during high-volume Gigafactory cell scaling

Raw material price volatility in cathode active materials like lithium and synthetic graphite

Execution risks in seamlessly transitioning existing vehicle assembly lines to the Gen 4 platform

Recent Developments

Ministry of Heavy Industries approved revised ACC PLI timelines for Ola Cell Technologies, securing up to ₹7,240 crore in cumulative incentives. Ola Electric also launched its S1Z mass-market scooter featuring indigenous LFP cell technology and unveiled its expanded Shakti energy storage portfolio.

Closing Insight

Mastering cell manufacturing is the ultimate differentiator in electric mobility. As Ola Electric combines indigenous LFP chemistry with its Gen 4 platform, execution speed and manufacturing yield will dictate whether cost savings translate into sustainable operating profitability.

text:
Will the U.S. Welcome Kei-Class EVs?

Fair Use [17 U.S.C. § 107] AI-imagined Kei-class electric truck designed as more city-friendly logistics vehicle.

By EVWorld.com AI Editorial Team

Safety Rules Keep Micro-EVs on the Sidelines

As electric propulsion reshapes global transportation, Japan's ultra-compact Kei-class vehicles may seem like an ideal fit for congested American cities and zero-emission last-mile delivery services. Yet despite growing enthusiasm for imported mini-trucks and micro-vans, the chances of regulators broadly opening U.S. roads to new electric Kei vehicles remain limited.

Federal Safety Rules Create a Major Barrier

The primary obstacle lies within the federal vehicle safety framework administered by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA). Four-wheeled vehicles must either comply with comprehensive Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards (FMVSS), including extensive crash-testing requirements, or qualify under the Low-Speed Vehicle (LSV) category.

LSVs are exempt from many crashworthiness requirements but are restricted to a maximum speed of 25 mph and are generally limited to streets posted at 35 mph or less.

Manufacturers Have Few Options

For automakers hoping to bring modern electric Kei vans and micro-trucks to the U.S. market, the most practical route is to deliberately limit vehicle performance to comply with LSV regulations. Toyota is pursuing this strategy with its upcoming Scion KEI-01 commercial utility vehicle, which is electronically governed to a top speed of 25 mph.

While this approach enables legal operation in certain environments, it also limits broader utility and consumer appeal.

No Appetite for a New Vehicle Category

Some advocates have proposed creating an intermediate vehicle classification, often described as a Low-Speed Electric Vehicle (LSEV) category, allowing speeds up to 45 mph while avoiding the full cost of FMVSS compliance.

However, federal regulators have shown little interest in establishing such a category. Safety agencies remain concerned about crash compatibility between lightweight micro-vehicles and the larger SUVs and pickup trucks that dominate American roads.

In mixed-traffic environments, regulators fear that allowing small vehicles to travel at higher speeds could create substantial safety and liability concerns.

States Hold Significant Authority

Even if federal policy were relaxed, state governments retain considerable control over vehicle registration and road access. Several states, including Texas, Vermont, and Alaska, permit registration of qualifying imported Kei vehicles for local road use.

Others, including New York, Georgia, Maine, and New Jersey, continue to prohibit or restrict registration, citing safety concerns and regulatory inconsistencies.

This patchwork of state laws further complicates nationwide adoption of Kei-class EVs.

The Road Ahead for Kei-Class EVs

While compact electric vehicles offer potential environmental and congestion-reduction benefits, climate goals alone are unlikely to override decades of U.S. vehicle safety policy. Unless manufacturers can engineer Kei-class EVs to satisfy federal crash requirements or identify profitable applications within low-speed fleet, campus, and municipal environments, widespread adoption will remain elusive.

For now, Kei-class EVs occupy a regulatory gray area: admired for their efficiency and practicality, yet constrained by a transportation system designed around much larger vehicles.

text:
The Town of Pittsboro Board of Zoning Appeals voted to approve a special exception on Thursday night clearing the way for a natural-gas-fired power plant built specifically to feed a data center campus, over the objections of residents who packed the meeting to voice concerns about noise and living next to the project. The vote split 3-2, with three members signing off on the exception alongside conditions and commitments while two members voted no.

The decision, reached after a hearing that ran from 6 p.m. to 10 p.m. and included a lengthy stretch of community public comment, covers a data center campus site that has been in the works since 2025, according to Fox 59. That outlet reports the broader property spans 625 acres and currently permits both a data center campus and other industrial uses, with the special exception itself requested for a 265-acre area within that campus. A separate account of the application's own figures, published by The Republican Newspaper, lists the total land area as approximately 625 acres and the special-exception area as approximately 264 acres — a discrepancy the available records do not resolve.

Board members held a question-and-answer portion during Thursday's meeting as part of their review, Fox 59's report indicates. Residents who spoke out described concerns ranging from noise disruption to broader environmental worries, with several saying outright that they were uncomfortable with the idea of living next to the campus.

What the Application Actually Proposes

According to application materials described by The Republican Newspaper, the project is framed as a way to construct and operate an onsite natural-gas-fired electric power generation facility meant to serve the reliability and phased generation needs of the already-approved data center campus. The same materials state that the facility uses no process water and requires no groundwater, a detail the applicant appears to have emphasized to address environmental questions.

The gas plant proposal builds on groundwork laid last year, when a 2025 Pittsboro Town Council meeting approved rezoning former farmland to make room for the data center campus itself, per Fox 59's reporting. That earlier rezoning decision is distinct from Thursday's special-exception vote, which dealt specifically with the power-generation facility rather than the data center buildings.

Part of a Broader Indiana Pattern

Pittsboro's gas-plant fight is not happening in isolation. The Indiana University Environmental Resilience Institute projects that data-center electricity demand statewide will jump from about 1 terawatt-hour in 2025 to more than 6.5 terawatt-hours by 2030, and the institute notes that utilities across the state are largely proposing new natural-gas-fired power plants to keep pace. The Indianapolis Star has similarly reported that some Indiana utilities are planning new gas plants and battery storage buildouts specifically to meet the rush of incoming data centers.

The noise concerns raised by Pittsboro residents echo a pattern the Environmental Resilience Institute has tracked elsewhere in the state, where communities near data-center projects have raised concerns about noise from cooling systems, backup diesel generators, heating, and ventilation equipment. As of July 2026, 11 Indiana counties had already passed ordinances establishing planning, design, and reporting requirements specifically for data centers, the institute's fact sheet notes.

Similar Fights Playing Out Elsewhere

Pittsboro's split vote mirrors contentious outcomes in other states grappling with the same energy question. In Davidson County, North Carolina, commissioners approved Duke Energy's rezoning request for a liquefied natural gas storage facility by a similarly narrow 4-3 vote, as reported by Carolina Public Press. That same outlet noted that North Carolina's Utilities Commission had blocked a separate Duke gas-plant proposal in Richmond County in September, calling the permit application premature while regulators reviewed the utility's broader resource plan.

Not every community has gone along with similar requests. In Iowa, Linn County supervisors unanimously rejected Alliant Energy's rezoning request for a proposed natural-gas plant after nearly four hours of public comment, according to Inside Climate News. Within Indiana itself, Inside INdiana Business has reported that the Pittsboro Town Council's original rezoning of the 626-acre data center site passed unanimously after a 4-1 recommendation from the Advisory Plan Commission, and that a separate 391-acre data-center site in northern Morgan County also won unanimous rezoning approval from county commissioners.

text:
The U.S. National Science Foundation recently stated that lithium, gallium, and rare earth minerals are essential for manufacturing smartphones, computers, semiconductors, microchips, rechargeable batteries, artificial joints, MRI scanners, sensors, and guidance systems.

However, global supplies of these essential minerals are vulnerable to disruption, and the U.S. will require approximately 6,000 additional mining engineers over the next decade.

To address this, the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) has announced several initiatives to increase the number of graduates and credentialed professionals in mining and related supply chain fields.

In October, the DOE's Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation selected 16 universities to receive $16 million through a planning prize, as part of the broader $100 million PROSPECT initiative.

This program aims to restore American energy leadership, support economic growth, rebuild domestic supply chains, and reduce reliance on foreign sources for critical minerals.

Selected institutions include leading universities such as Colorado School of Mines, Missouri University of Science and Technology, University of Arizona, University of Kentucky, and Virginia Tech.

These universities will help expand the skilled workforce needed to produce, process, recover, and recycle critical minerals in the United States while creating quality jobs.

The U.S. will require approximately 6,000 additional mining engineers over the next decade.

Tennessee State University (TSU) recently launched a mining engineering minor, with the potential to become a full major to meet national demand and strengthen supply chain security.

Curt Coccodrilli, DOE Assistant Secretary for Hydrocarbons and Geothermal Energy, visited TSU to review the program, its use of $800,000 in funding, and future plans.

Coccodrilli helps set the strategic direction for U.S. fossil and geothermal energy policy and programs

According to TSU News Service, Coccodrilli praised the program's strong start, noting 15 or 16 students enrolled, a growing internship pipeline, and industry partnerships.

He also highlighted the potential for the program to become a major, as federal support bridges research and commercialization and strengthens domestic supply chains.

The program was established with an $800,000 DOE grant, and the minor launched in fall 2025, making it the only mining engineering program in the southern region and at a historically Black college or university.

According to TSU News Service, the U.S. Department of Energy's recent campus visit included a roundtable with university leadership, engineering faculty, industry partners, and students, followed by a tour of engineering labs.

Discussions focused on federal support, faculty development, scholarships, and internship pipelines connecting students to public and private sector jobs.

Tyler Sanders, a mechanical engineering student at TSU, shared on LinkedIn that the most impactful aspect of the visit was seeing student leaders present their vision alongside university leadership and industry partners from Luck Stone, Rogers Group, and Crucible Tennessee Mines.

This collaboration highlights the importance of investing in HBCU STEM talent for critical minerals and supply chain security.

Sanders noted the program's strong momentum and ongoing discussions about elevating the minor to a full major.

Surveys by Career Communications Group’s USBE magazine show the Department of Energy consistently ranks among the top government and nonprofit supporters of HBCU engineering schools, as recognized by engineering deans and the Advancing Minorities' Interest in Engineering (AMIE) alliance.

The DOE and its national laboratories, including Oak Ridge, Sandia, and Idaho National Laboratories, partner directly with HBCU engineering faculty and students on nuclear science, grid resilience, and clean-tech workforce development.

The DOE also provides targeted funding through programs like the National Energy Technology Laboratory University Training and Research Program to enhance HBCU research competitiveness in energy engineering.

text:
Divert Inc., a circular infrastructure company protecting the value of food, on Nov. 10 announced the opening of its new Integrated Diversion & Energy Facility in Lexington, North Carolina. The new facility transforms unsold food that can no longer be donated into renewable natural gas (RNG) to help power communities and fertilizer to support regional agriculture. The facility also recovers food-bound water to run its own operations and captures data to help customers prevent future waste.

Divert’s Lexington facility is expected to service over 2,500 retail grocery locations and 20 retail distribution centers across the region by the close of 2026. Additionally, the company will responsibly process unsold food, food byproducts, and residuals from food manufacturers and other businesses across the Southeast.

“The success of Divert’s Circularity Platform is driven by our employees and rooted in our customer base” said Ryan Begin, CEO and co-founder of Divert. “The strong customer relationships we have built over the past twenty years are what allow us to invest in regional infrastructure, including our new facility here in Lexington.”

Harris Teeter is among the anchor customers served by Divert’s Lexington Integrated Diversion & Energy Facility, which will support all of the retailer’s locations.

“At Harris Teeter, our purpose is to enrich lives, one meal, one family, one associate, and one community at a time,” said Danna Robinson, Director of Corporate Affairs & Customer Relations for Harris Teeter. “We believe food serves its highest purpose when it is feeding people. When food can no longer be donated, our partnership with Divert helps us find a productive use for it, reducing waste and protecting the value of food across the communities we serve.”

In addition to Harris Teeter, the facility will also serve select locations for Publix, UNFI, and other customers across the region.

At full capacity, the Lexington facility will be capable of processing up to 120,000 tons of unsold, non-donatable food annually from food retailers, distribution centers, warehouses, and manufacturing locations. Renewable natural gas, which is injected directly into local pipeline infrastructure, is already being produced at the Divert facility from unsold food in the area. The facility will also be capable of producing Divert® Food-Derived Fertilizers, including OMRI-listed organic options for use in organic food production. Divert’s technology also provides customers with actionable data to help prevent wasted food and increase donations before unsold food reaches the facility.

“This facility will reduce food waste and create renewable natural gas, helping our state power its future,” said Governor Josh Stein. “North Carolina is a leader in innovation and the clean energy economy, and I am pleased to welcome Divert, Inc. to be part of our thriving business and energy ecosystem.”

“North Carolina represents the fourth largest food and beverage industry in the United States and ranks eighth nationally in agricultural production,” added Begin. “This makes Lexington an ideal location for advancing circularity in our food system, and this facility will allow us to serve more businesses, keep more food out of landfills, and recover valuable resources that can be put back to productive use.”

Divert’s Lexington facility is part of the company’s vertically integrated Circularity Platform, through which Divert develops, owns, and operates regional infrastructure to prevent wasted food and recover valuable resources from food that can no longer be donated. The model combines data and technology to help customers prevent waste, facilitates edible food recovery to support local hunger relief, and transforms remaining unsold food into renewable energy, fertilizer and reclaimed water.

The Lexington facility is the latest addition to Divert’s growing national infrastructure, following the opening of its Integrated Diversion & Energy Facility in Longview, Washington, earlier this year.

Divert is a portfolio company of Ara Partners, a global private equity, infrastructure and energy firm focused on decarbonizing the industrial economy.

text:
Texas A&M will limit micromobility vehicle usage on most campus sidewalks effective Jan. 1 as part of a new safety plan, as first reported by KBTX on Nov. 12. The decision comes following warnings from the A&M University System Board of Regents after it discussed usage at a Sept. 3 meeting in which concerns for pedestrian safety were raised.

At the meeting, Chief Operating Officer Peter Lange reported that incidents involving micromobility vehicles had increased by 37%, with 52 incidents being reported and nearly half of them resulting in injury, according to a report by The Battalion on Sept. 30.

According to KBTX, the plan will restrict micromobility usage on certain campus sidewalks from 7 a.m. to 6 p.m. during weekdays, with an exception of sidewalks that run along the edges of campus. The restrictions may also apply when special events or campus activities are held.

Restrictions do not just apply to where the vehicles can go, but also how they are used. Under the new plan, micromobility vehicle users will be restricted to a 20 mph speed limit and one person per vehicle, along with other policies restricting the usage of handheld devices and noise canceling headphones, according to reporting by KBTX

The university is expected to release a public statement on Monday, Nov. 16, with details of the plan, including a map of approved paths and limited “slow zone” sidewalks, according to Lange. More information will follow as updates are received.

text:
NEW ORLEANS, LA — The New Orleans City Council's Climate Change and Sustainability Committee will convene Monday, November 16, at 10 a.m., to open a new docket to expand access to affordable solar energy and strengthen the city's electric grid. The meeting will include a series of presentations from energy industry leaders and advocates on the importance of transmission planning.

Expanding Access to Solar Energy Through Plug-In Solar Devices

The Committee will vote on a resolution to establish a formal regulatory proceeding to evaluate the use, safety, and regulation of small portable solar generation devices, commonly known as plug-in solar or balcony solar.

These devices allow residents to generate electricity using small solar panels that connect directly to a standard household outlet. Unlike traditional rooftop solar systems, plug-in solar devices are more affordable, easy to install, and generally do not require professional installation. This resolution examines how plug-in solar systems could be safely incorporated into New Orleans' electric grid, potentially opening new opportunities for residents to lower their electricity costs and participate in the city's clean energy transition.

At least 30 states have approved or are considering policies governing these devices, including 10 states that have already authorized their use.

Industry Leaders Discuss Transmission Planning and Grid Reliability

The Committee is also hosting a Transmission Education Day, bringing together utility representatives, regional grid operators, renewable energy developers, and nonprofit organizations to discuss the role of electric transmission infrastructure in meeting New Orleans' long-term energy needs.

Presentations will feature representatives from Entergy New Orleans, GridLab, the Midcontinent Independent System Operator (MISO), and EDP Renewables North America, who will offer perspectives on regional transmission planning, grid challenges in MISO South, and the infrastructure needed to support an evolving energy system.

The meeting will conclude with a panel discussion featuring the Alliance for Affordable Energy, the Union of Concerned Scientists, and Entergy New Orleans, focusing on the importance of coordinated transmission planning to support an affordable, reliable, resilient, and sustainable electric grid.

text:
The Dutch Entrepreneurial Development Bank (FMO) has committed USD 50 million to the Decarbonization of Textile, Apparel & Footwear Suppliers Fund (D-TAFS), a financing vehicle designed to reduce greenhouse gas emissions across textile supply chains. The fund, managed by Social Investment Managers & Advisors (SIMA), targets USD 400 million in total commitments, with a first close expected at USD 225 million.

D-TAFS brings together development finance institutions, private investors and global apparel brands to channel capital to suppliers seeking to lower emissions in regions where textile production is concentrated. FMO said its investment will focus on energy as a key driver of decarbonizing textile manufacturing, including renewable power and energy-efficiency solutions.

Background: emissions challenge in textile supply chains

The textile, apparel and footwear (TAF) industry accounts for an estimated 8% to 10% of global greenhouse gas emissions, according to FMO. While large brands are increasingly seeking to reduce supply chain emissions, FMO said many small and medium-sized suppliers struggle to access financing for the investments needed to cut their environmental footprint.

FMO linked the financing gap to the scale and complexity of decarbonization projects, which can be difficult to fund through conventional lending channels. D-TAFS is designed to address that barrier with tailored financing support for suppliers.

How D-TAFS is structured and funded

D-TAFS is managed by SIMA and supports investments intended to reduce emissions along textile supply chains. FMO said the fund will connect leading European and global apparel brands with textile, apparel and footwear suppliers across key manufacturing hubs in Asia, Africa, the Middle East and North Africa, and Latin America.

FMO also noted that Inditex, the Spanish owner of Zara, Pull&Bear and other brands, has committed USD 50 million to the fund. This brand participation is intended to support decarbonization efforts upstream, where energy and production equipment decisions are often made.

Renewable energy as the focus of FMO’s investment

According to FMO, reducing emissions across the TAF supply chain requires access to renewable energy, energy-efficient technologies and storage solutions. The bank said its D-TAFS financing will support distributed energy developers and energy service companies (ESCOs) that provide clean and efficient energy solutions to textile manufacturers in emerging markets.

FMO’s stated emphasis reflects the operational role that energy plays in textile production, including power generation and heat-related processes. By financing energy providers and related services, the fund aims to enable suppliers to implement projects that can reduce emissions at the factory level.

FMO’s Director of Energy, Marnix Monfort, said renewable energy has an important role in decarbonizing textile manufacturing and that FMO is supporting energy developers and service providers that bring clean and efficient solutions to manufacturers. He added that the initiative builds on FMO’s “long-standing partnership” with SIMA to scale such solutions across the sector.

Support beyond capital: moving projects from pipeline to delivery

Alongside financing, FMO said SIMA pairs loans with support and follow-up to help turn a pipeline of decarbonization projects into realized savings and impact. D-TAFS fund manager Jeremy Levin said availability of capital alone does not get projects built, noting that suppliers may need help sizing and structuring loans, convincing internal decision makers to invest, and ensuring projects are implemented and commissioned properly.

Levin said SIMA provides that support to complement the financing, with a process aimed at improving the likelihood that planned investments deliver operational results.

Expected reach and implementation footprint

FMO said D-TAFS will direct financing to reduce emissions in the regions where much of the industry’s production takes place, including Asia, Africa, the Middle East and North Africa, and Latin America. The fund is expected to work through energy developers and ESCOs serving textile, apparel and footwear manufacturers, with solutions aimed at reducing emissions linked to production activities.

Why this development matters for the sector

The announcement situates decarbonization finance within broader trends in sustainable development and climate action, focusing on how industrial suppliers can access the investment needed to adopt cleaner energy and technologies. For NGOs, civil society organizations and development professionals, it also highlights how blended structures—combining development finance, private investment and brand commitments—can be used to address barriers that smaller suppliers face when seeking climate-related financing.

Key Details

Initiative/Programme: Decarbonization of Textile, Apparel & Footwear Suppliers Fund (D-TAFS)

Lead organization: Social Investment Managers & Advisors (SIMA) (fund manager); FMO (USD 50 million commitment)

Partners: Inditex (committed USD 50 million); development finance institutions, private investors and global apparel brands (as described by FMO)

Funding amount: USD 50 million committed by FMO; fund target USD 400 million; first close expected at USD 225 million

Geographic focus: Asia, Africa, the Middle East and North Africa, and Latin America

Target groups: Textile, apparel and footwear suppliers seeking to reduce emissions; distributed energy developers and energy service companies (ESCOs) providing renewable energy, efficiency and storage solutions

Duration or timeline: Not specified in the provided source

Expected reach/outcomes: Financing to reduce emissions across textile supply chains by supporting renewable energy and energy-efficiency investments (expected realized savings and impact referenced, but no quantified targets were provided)

Why This Matters

D-TAFS reflects a growing approach to industrial decarbonization: aligning brand supply-chain pressure with financing mechanisms that can reach smaller suppliers. For NGOs and development professionals, the structure—development finance plus private capital and operational support—signals where climate-focused funding may be directed next, particularly toward energy-related investments that can help manufacturing sites cut emissions.

The emphasis on renewable energy access, energy-efficiency technologies and storage also points to a practical area for program learning and potential partnerships, including technical assistance that helps projects move from identification to implementation. Finally, by targeting the geographic regions where textile production is concentrated, the initiative may offer lessons for how to support supplier-led climate action across multiple manufacturing hubs rather than only in higher-capacity markets.

text:
The EU-funded MACBETH project has published a specification for multipoint Megawatt Charging System (MCS) hubs for electric trucks. The Charging Interface Initiative (CharIN) led the work and authored the document with VTT Technical Research Centre of Finland.

The document, Deliverable D4.1, is a shared reference framework for site layouts, power architectures and technical requirements that will guide the project's pilots in Belgium and Sweden. VTT coordinates MACBETH, a Horizon Europe project that ends in January 2029.

D4.1 describes two reference site layouts. In a drive-through design, trucks enter, charge and leave in a forward-only flow without reversing. The second layout adds a dedicated waiting area, a buffer zone where vehicles queue until a charger is free, and is designed to improve traffic management at high utilization.

In a shared power cabinet concept, one central conversion system distributes power dynamically across several charge points based on vehicle demand, priorities and grid limits. A modular multi-cabinet concept instead grows capacity by adding independent cabinets, and is designed to offer redundancy and step-by-step scalability for smaller or early-stage sites.

Vehicle-to-charger communication is based on ISO 15118-20 with its MCS profile, using a 10BASE-T1S physical layer. The security baseline is mutual EV-EVSE authentication and TLS 1.3. The specification also includes a charger uptime target above 97%, heating for winter conditions and cooling to sustain megawatt power. Site energy management can throttle charger output during power peaks.

D4.1 maps the hub concepts against more than 40 ISO, IEC and EN standards and identifies four areas that existing standards do not yet fully address. These are power sharing and arbitration between simultaneous MCS sessions, automated and robotic MCS connections, guidance for mixed CCS and MCS sites, and site-level effects such as cumulative noise and waste heat.

"Through MACBETH, we are combining research and industry expertise complemented by CharIN's standardization leadership to ensure that Megawatt Charging can be deployed at scale across Europe and deliver real value for electric heavy-duty transport," said Yancho Todorov, Senior Scientist at VTT and Coordinator of the MACBETH project.

title: 'Electrify everything' hits the global stage | Canary Media
description:
But if the power that supplies all those electric vehicles, heat pumps, and furnaces comes from fossil fuels, will electrification still make a dent in global emissions?
For one, electrification is a necessary step to ditching fossil fuels.
Electric-powered machines are also way more energy efficient than fossil-fueled options, as energy and climate policy expert Jan Rosenow has explained.
A lot of energy gets wasted when you burn fossil fuels, particularly in small localized applications like a boiler that heats up a home.
It lets countries reduce their reliance on imported fossil fuels.
text:
This analysis and news roundup come from the Canary Media Weekly newsletter. Sign up to get it every Friday.

World leaders — well, some of them — gathered in Turkey this week for COP31, the annual climate conference, for discussions focused on how we power our world. Specifically, conference organizers proposed that attendees join in on a goal of meeting 35% of the world’s final energy demand with electricity by 2035, up from just over 20% today.

Achieving that target demands participation from across the global economy. Everyday drivers and shippers will need to replace gasoline- and diesel-powered cars and trucks with plug-in alternatives. Manufacturers will need to swap in industrial heat pumps and electric boilers. Steel and ironmakers must embrace electric arc furnaces and other cleaner technologies.

But if the power that supplies all those electric vehicles, heat pumps, and furnaces comes from fossil fuels, will electrification still make a dent in global emissions? Yes, and there are a few reasons why.

For one, electrification is a necessary step to ditching fossil fuels. And it can take a long time to make the switch, whether it’s your home’s heating or an industrial-scale system providing steam to a factory. Getting more homes and processes electrified now means a larger portion of the world’s energy demand will be cleaned up as soon as more renewables arrive on the grid.

Electric-powered machines are also way more energy efficient than fossil-fueled options, as energy and climate policy expert Jan Rosenow has explained. A lot of energy gets wasted when you burn fossil fuels, particularly in small localized applications like a boiler that heats up a home. But you can get the same result with less fuel — and fewer carbon emissions — if you burn natural gas at a big power plant and then use that electricity to power a heat pump.

Electrification has a benefit beyond emissions, too — one that has has become especially pertinent as the war in the Middle East has sent global oil and gas prices through the roof. It lets countries reduce their reliance on imported fossil fuels.

In Europe and Asia, people have responded by buying electric stoves and cars to curb their reliance on imported oil and natural gas. And the EU, learning both from the Iran war and the ongoing struggle in Ukraine, announced plans in July to ramp up electricity’s share of energy use to 46% by 2040.

Whatever comes out of this year’s COP meeting, expect these climate, efficiency, and security benefits to keep nudging countries toward ever-greater levels of electrification.

More big energy stories

What’s next for the permitting bill?

The Senate’s bipartisan permitting bill passed its first big test this week as legislators voted 73-25 to formally take up the proposal. The bill as written would speed up permitting timelines for transmission, clean energy, and fossil fuel projects, but it’s likely to undergo a lot of edits before it becomes law.

Monday’s vote was the Senate’s first since Election Day, when it became clear Democrats would have resounding majorities in both houses of Congress next year. Many Democratic senators voted against advancing the permitting bill, with some saying they could use their newfound power to beef up the legislation’s clean energy benefits — and address concerns that the bill is too generous to fossil fuel interests.

Democrats and Republicans will have a chance to address any qualms via amendments, which Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) said the chamber will likely vote on next week before deciding whether to send the legislation to the House. It’ll face a challenge there from Democrats who say they didn’t have enough input in the bill’s creation, though House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) says his party will guarantee its passage.

One step forward, one step back for SMRs

Small modular nuclear reactors’ murky future is no clearer this week as the industry notched one win and one setback.

On a bright note for the industry, the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission approved X-energy and Dow Chemical’s plans to build four Xe-100 advanced reactors in Texas, reports Brian Martucci. The NRC OK’d the application in a record 18 months, following its approval of two other small reactor projects from Kairos Power and TerraPower.

Up in Canada, the news was a bit more drab. Ontario Power Generation said Tuesday that its SMR, poised to be the first in North America, won’t be online by its 2030 target, nor will it stay within its budget, Dan McCarthy reports. That’s especially problematic given that the project uses the same technology behind most of the world’s existing nuclear fleet — and a design that developers in the U.S. are eyeing themselves.

Clean energy news to know this week

Manufacturing meltdown: Offshore wind manufacturing once seemed destined to rise in the U.S., buoyed by a raft of projects and Inflation Reduction Act incentives — but that promise has since sunk thanks to the Trump administration’s attacks. (Canary Media)

Winter heating woes: The average U.S. household will see heating costs rise 7% this winter compared to last, while heating oil users could pay as much as 70% more than last season. (New York Times)

Unlocking a cleaner pickup: The failure of Tesla’s Cybertruck provides yet another lesson for automakers looking to figure out how to make electric pickup trucks popular in the U.S. market. (Grist)

From prison to solar: A Chicago halfway house has trained more than 100 formerly incarcerated people for solar installation and other clean energy jobs, bolstered by Illinois laws that aim to strengthen the industry’s workforce. (Canary Media)

Batteries gallop on: New research from Ford indicates its 2021 Mustang Mach-E’s batteries have retained more than 90% of their original capacity after five years on the road. (Axios)

text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, U.S. Rep. Kathy Castor (FL-14), Jay Obernolte (CA-23) and Doris Matsui (CA-07) introduced the Optimizing Networks for Distributed Energy Management and New Demand (ON-DEMAND) Act to help lower electric bills and meet growing energy demand. The legislation supports wider adoption of virtual power plants by directing the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) to adopt standards, strengthen consumer protections and provide technical assistance to utilities, regulators and grid operators.

“My neighbors need relief from sky-high electric bills, and we should be putting every practical solution to work to lower their costs,” said Rep. Castor. “Our ON-DEMAND Act would help communities use rooftop solar, batteries, and smart appliances more safely and effectively, with strong protections for consumers. As demand for electricity grows, we must make our grid more reliable and ensure the benefits of innovation reach the people paying the bills.”

“As electricity demand continues to grow, innovative solutions like virtual power plants can help strengthen our electric grid and lower energy costs for American families,” said Congressman Obernolte. “The ON-DEMAND Act will help remove barriers to the adoption of this technology, allowing consumers to make better use of existing energy resources while improving grid reliability and reducing costs.”

“Families in Sacramento and across the country are paying too much for electricity, and we need to do more to bring those costs down,” said Congresswoman Matsui. “The ON-DEMAND Act will help lower utility bills by making smarter use of the energy resources we already have, including home batteries and smart appliances, to meet growing electricity demand without driving up costs. This is a practical solution that puts money back in Americans’ pockets while building a cleaner, more reliable energy grid.”

Virtual power plants coordinate devices across homes and businesses, such as batteries, smart thermostats, water heaters and rooftop solar systems, to help balance electricity supply and demand. For example, water heating could be shifted to a less busy time or battery power can be deployed during peak demand.

View the full bill text HERE and section-by-section HERE.

“Amid an unprecedented rise in energy demand, some of the most promising solutions are the distributed resources already in our homes and communities — rooftop solar, smart thermostats, and EV chargers — and the Virtual Power Plants (VPPs) that help them work together. From lowering bills for families to keeping the lights on, VPPs support a more flexible, affordable, and resilient electric grid. Advanced Energy United is proud to support the ON-DEMAND Act. We applaud the work of Representatives Castor, Matsui, and Obernolte to bring this bill to fruition and believe it will help unlock the benefits of VPPs for all Americans." – Dylan Reed, Managing Director at Advanced Energy United.

“Energy security and economic growth depend on a resilient and efficient electric power system. Virtual power plants provide a proven, scalable way to deliver reliable, affordable power amid growing grid constraints,” said NEMA Senior Vice President of Government Affairs, Will Hupman. “By directing the Department of Energy to pursue open, stakeholder-driven processes for VPP standards development and other objectives, the ON-DEMAND Act promises to eliminate hurdles to VPP deployment and scaling, ushering in a new era of grid flexibility.”

“The ON-DEMAND Act represents an important step toward modernizing America's electric grid and ensuring we can meet growing electricity demand affordably and reliably,” said John Pappas, Government Affairs Director for Siemens USA. “By addressing barriers to the deployment of virtual power plants, this legislation will help utilities unlock the full potential of distributed energy resources, improve grid flexibility, and make more efficient use of existing infrastructure. Establishing consistent standards and expanding technical assistance will help accelerate the adoption of innovative grid technologies and build a smarter, more resilient, and more affordable energy system.”

"Leveraging customer-focused energy independent solutions like distributed power plants is essential to creating a more cost-effective, resilient and clean grid for all, particularly amidst the surging demand for electricity. The ON-DEMAND Act will help accelerate the customer-led revolution that's tackling these challenges head-on." – Mary Powell, CEO, Sunrun

"Schneider Electric applauds the introduction of the ON-DEMAND Act and its support for the flexible energy resources needed to build a more resilient, reliable, and affordable grid. As electricity demand grows, flexibility will be essential to balancing supply and demand, improving grid performance, and empowering consumers. Virtual power plants are one important way to unlock that flexibility at scale, and we welcome policies that help accelerate their adoption." – Ruben Llanes, CEO, Digital Grid, Schneider Electric

Endorsing organizations include Advanced Energy United, Deploy Action, Electricity Consumers Resource Council, Environmental Defense Fund, GridWise Alliance, Information Technology Industry Council, National Association of State Energy Officials, National Electrical Manufacturers Association, Rewiring America, Schneider Electric, Siemens USA, Sierra Club, and Sunrun.

The company has plans to expand its business model beyond the commercial EV world, and has raised a new pot of money to do so.

“Harbinger exists to challenge what industry has learned to accept, and reinvent the critical systems the world depends on,” said co-founder and CEO John Harris (read our 2026 interview). “By rethinking critical systems from first principles, we aim to unlock better performance, greater reliability, safer operations, and more room to grow. Electrification is at the core of everything we do, and increasingly, electrification is at the core of industry, defense, mobility and AI. Harbinger’s role is not simply to give customers another option. It is to reset expectations for what critical systems should deliver.”

text:
Written by Marine Log Staff

The Woodlands, Texas -based Arena Energy LLC reports that its wholly owned subsidiary, Elkhorn Offshore LLC, has reached financial close on a $480 million loan from the U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE) Office of Energy Dominance Financing (EDF) supporting Project Elkhorn, an energy-infrastructure reinvestment project in the Gulf of America.

Arena says that the financing will be used to retool, refurbish, repower, and expand capacity across offshore platforms in the Southern Eugene Island area off the coast of Louisiana, extending their use and enabling critical infrastructure upgrades.

Project Elkhorn will return idled platforms to service and expand production and water-handling capacity at active facilities. The project also includes the development of new natural gas pipeline infrastructure to connect future wells into existing pipelines, improving midstream connectivity across the field. Together, these investments are expected to add approximately 125 million barrels of additional oil and 250 billion cubic feet of natural gas production over the life of the project. This increase in domestic production will lead to an estimated $1.6 billion in additional royalties collected by the federal government,.

The closing follows completion of the technical, legal, environmental, and financial due diligence required under DOE’s loan program.

“Project Elkhorn will increase oil production by up to 38,600 barrels per day and create thousands of jobs.” said U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright. “Project Elkhorn will increase oil production by up to 38,600 barrels per day and create thousands of jobs. By providing financing for projects like Project Elkhorn, the Energy Department is expanding domestic production and strengthening our energy security to power American prosperity for decades to come.”

“Arena was founded on the belief that the mature fields of the Gulf Shelf still hold vast potential, and Project Elkhorn is a critical part of that strategy,” said Mike Minarovic, CEO and founder of Arena Energy, LLC. “The Southern Eugene Island area is one of the most prolific oil-producing regions in American history, and its infrastructure still has decades of productive life ahead. What it needed was long-term capital to match the opportunity. This financing from the Department of Energy delivers that capital and lets us put existing infrastructure back to work, develop proved reserves, and keep producing some of the most reliable barrels in the world right here at home – with American workers, on American leases, for American refineries.”

Arena will execute the project with its long-standing affiliated partners White Fleet Drilling and Rosefield Pipeline.
