text:
Connecting Africa’s energy resources to industrial opportunities

Africa has abundant solar, wind, hydropower and geothermal resources, alongside critical minerals essential to the global clean energy transition. Participants highlighted the opportunity to leverage these assets to develop domestic mineral processing capabilities, manufacture clean technologies and build competitive industrial value chains across the continent.

Since 2023, at least 13 African countries have introduced mineral export restrictions to encourage domestic processing and greater value capture.

Advancing green industrial value chains can also support the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), the African Union’s Agenda 2063 and deeper partnerships with Europe and other international partners.

The discussion also highlighted the potential of carbon markets under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement to complement public and private investment. Africa is well-positioned to generate high-integrity emissions reductions through renewable energy deployment and industrial decarbonization, using carbon finance to accelerate clean energy investment and industrial development.

Strengthening Africa-Europe cooperation

Co-chaired by Damilola Ogunbiyi, CEO and Special Representative of the UN Secretary-General for Sustainable Energy for All, and Mattias Frumerie, Sweden’s Climate Ambassador and Head of Delegation to UNFCCC, the roundtable brought together ministers, development finance institutions, international organizations and private sector representatives.

Discussions focused on two fundamental questions: What clean energy and grid investments should countries prioritize to accelerate productive use and industrial value addition? And which clean industrial value chains should Africa and Europe develop together?

Participants highlighted existing frameworks that can be better aligned to accelerate implementation. These include Mission 300, which aims to connect 300 million Africans to electricity by 2030, as well as continental initiatives such as the African Single Electricity Market, Continental Power System Master Plan and African Energy Efficiency Strategy, which provide additional foundations for regional energy integration.

On the European side, participants also discussed the Africa-EU Green Energy Initiative, delivered through the Global Gateway Investment Package, which aims to add 50 gigawatts of renewable energy capacity and provide electricity access to 100 million Africans by 2030.

Participants emphasized that the success of these initiatives depends on addressing Africa’s underlying energy infrastructure and reliability challenges. Without sufficient clean energy generation, transmission and distribution, industrial investment and local value addition will remain constrained.

The roundtable also highlighted the importance of international and South-South cooperation. Africa brings renewable energy resources, critical minerals, growing markets and industrial opportunities, while European partners can contribute capital, technology, engineering expertise and access to markets.

Building on collaborative platforms, including the Africa Green Industrialization Initiative, SEforALL’s Green Industrialization Hub and the Africa-Europe Foundation’s Strategy Group on Green Industrialization, the meeting reinforced the importance of aligning existing frameworks and partnerships behind mutually beneficial industrial agendas.

title: Why even a fraction of a degree can escalate climate change impacts | NCPR News
description:
A decade ago, countries agreed to limit climate warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit).
Globally, average temperatures are already close to 1.5 degrees Celsius warmer than they were before the Industrial Revolution.
"The crucial point is that every fraction of a degree matters," says Tim Lenton, climate professor at the University of Exeter.
The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change found that beyond 2 degrees Celsius of warming, 99% of corals would be lost.
At the ongoing climate negotiations in Turkey, countries are not expected to make major new commitments to cut climate emissions.
text:
Countries have gathered at the annual climate change negotiations at the COP31 summit in Turkey to discuss how to achieve a goal that is increasingly unachievable. A decade ago, countries agreed to limit climate warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit). Now, that goal is out of reach.

Globally, average temperatures are already close to 1.5 degrees Celsius warmer than they were before the Industrial Revolution. Heat-trapping emissions from burning fossil fuels are still rising in the atmosphere, and most countries are not on track to meet their climate pledges to cut emissions by transitioning to cleaner energy.

The best-case scenario for the planet is now 1.7 or 1.8 degrees Celsius of warming (roughly 3 degrees Fahrenheit), according to a recent United Nations study. If fossil fuel emissions stay on their current path, the world would be around 2.8 degrees Celsius (5 degrees Fahrenheit) hotter by the end of the century.

While the difference between 1.5 and 2 degrees Celsius may seem tiny, scientific research shows those increments can produce dramatically different outcomes for the planet. More warming raises the risk of extreme weather globally and could lead to the collapse of some of the planet's most sensitive ecosystems.

"The crucial point is that every fraction of a degree matters," says Tim Lenton, climate professor at the University of Exeter. "Every fraction of a degree that we avoid is really able to do a huge amount of limiting harm."

Coral reefs already close to the edge

Corals are architects of an entire ecosystem. As they grow, they create the framework that supports vast numbers of other species, making reefs biodiversity hotspots. They're also vital to hundreds of millions of people who depend on them for food and livelihoods.

Corals are also highly vulnerable to heat. Prolonged marine heat waves cause corals to bleach, turning them white, which can eventually kill corals. Since the late 1990s, there have been four global bleaching events. With a historically strong El Niño now raising water temperatures, scientists say the fifth global bleaching event is likely unfolding.

Even before the previous bleaching event from 2023 to 2025, researchers found that 44% of coral species globally are at risk of extinction.

"These are incredibly worrying statistics, but they also emphasize that time matters," says David Obura, director of the coral research organization CORDIO East Africa, who worked on the study published last month in the journal Nature. "Every ten years, every five years counts."

Given their susceptibility to heat, the survival of most coral reefs depends on the difference between 1.5 and 2 degrees of warming. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change found that beyond 2 degrees Celsius of warming, 99% of corals would be lost.

"At 2 degrees of warming, we anticipate most corals just won't survive, not in functional ways to build a reef ecosystem," Obura says. "So you might still find some of the species, but many of them may be so rare or so compromised that they will have gone extinct by then."

With the dire forecasts for the future of coral, conservation groups and coastal communities are working to make reefs as healthy as possible in many areas so they can better withstand climate change. That includes restoring corals, reducing water pollution and even breeding more heat-tolerant corals.

"Most people around the world don't have the luxury of giving up on degraded ecosystems, because that's where they live," Obura says. "That's all they have. So we have to work out how to make them function again."

Millions more exposed to extreme heat

The goal of 1.5 degrees Celsius is an average temperature, measured across the planet. What it masks is the increasingly extreme heat events that are raising the average.

Researchers have found that for every tenth of a degree of warming, an additional 140 million people are exposed to dangerous levels of heat.

Heat waves are already causing heavy death tolls, like in Europe, where an estimated 50,000 people died of heat-related causes this past summer. Heat is particularly dangerous for those with chronic health conditions, as well as for people who are elderly or pregnant. The real toll of heat waves is often hidden, since many heat-related deaths are undercounted.

"You could think of it a bit like a tipping point for the human organism or body," Lenton says. "At some point, our physiology kind of reaches a tipping point and the worst tipping point is death."

Powerful storms

Every degree of climate change also affects the intensity of storms. Warmer air can produce heavier downpours because it holds 7% more water vapor for every degree. Rainstorms are already getting more intense in most of the U.S.

Scientific research also shows higher levels of warming could lead to other risky tipping points, like the collapse of Antarctic glaciers. If they destabilize, the melt would add vast volumes of water to the ocean, raising sea levels globally.

"We're never exactly sure where the tipping point is until we cross it, but we can be 100% confident that, for most of them, more warming is a bigger likelihood of crossing them," Lenton says. "Less warming is controlling that risk and that's why we should fight for every fraction of a degree that we can stave off."

At the ongoing climate negotiations in Turkey, countries are not expected to make major new commitments to cut climate emissions. Discussions are focusing on a new goal for electrification, meaning more cars and homes would run on electricity instead of fossil fuels. That would help reduce overall emissions, since a growing share of the world's electricity comes from cleaner sources, like solar and wind.

The DOE-funded center provides complimentary technical assessments to eligible small and medium-sized manufacturers and commercial building operators. Working with faculty and students, the center evaluates energy use and industrial operations to identify opportunities for reducing costs, improving productivity and minimizing waste.

DOE officials met with ITAC leadership, students and workforce development representatives, toured the MSU Civil Infrastructure Laboratory and learned how the program, which has operated at MSU since 2021, connects technical assistance for businesses with hands-on engineering education and workforce preparation.

The center is led by Kristen Cetin, Red Cedar Distinguished Professor in MSU's Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering. The program serves two interconnected purposes: helping businesses improve their operations while preparing students to meet the evolving technical demands of industry.

According to Cetin, MSU ITAC has worked with 150 manufacturers and trained 110 students over the past five years. ITAC collaborates with Michigan Technological University and Henry Ford College.

“MSU’s Industrial Training and Assessment Center demonstrates the academic excellence, spirit of collaboration and forward-thinking approach that the Department of Energy seeks to foster through its partnerships with American universities,” said Assistant Secretary of Energy Audrey Robertson. “By delivering practical assistance to Michigan manufacturers, this program helps businesses reduce costs and improve productivity while equipping students with the skills and hands-on experience they need to succeed in America’s energy and manufacturing industries.”

Connecting engineering education with industry

Following an assessment conducted by ITAC faculty and students, participating businesses receive recommendations outlining potential improvements, estimated savings and implementation costs.

Cetin reports that 50% of MSU ITAC’s recommendations are implemented by manufacturers. Nationwide, DOE reports that ITAC assessments identify an average of $144,000 in potential annual savings per facility.

"Our goal is to give students opportunities to work through the same challenges they will encounter in industry," Cetin said. "By working directly with manufacturers, they learn how to evaluate complex systems, communicate with clients and translate technical findings into practical recommendations. At the same time, we're helping businesses identify opportunities to improve their operations."

During the laboratory tour, students demonstrated how engineering tools can be used to evaluate building performance and identify opportunities for energy savings.

Using an infrared thermal imaging camera, students showed DOE officials how temperature differences can help identify areas that may require further investigation, including potential insulation deficiencies or other building envelope issues.

Students also explained blower-door testing, which uses a fan to create a pressure difference between the inside and outside of a building. By measuring the airflow needed to maintain that pressure difference, engineers can evaluate air leakage and identify opportunities to improve building efficiency.

Preparing students for careers in energy and manufacturing

As part of its work with industry, ITAC gives students opportunities to apply classroom knowledge to real-world engineering challenges.

"Collecting data is an important part of the assessment process, but students also have to understand what those measurements mean," said Annick Anctil, ITAC assistant director. "They learn to connect technical findings with the practical needs of a facility and develop recommendations that businesses can use to make informed decisions."

Working alongside faculty and technical professionals, students assess industrial operations, analyze data and develop recommendations for participating businesses. Direct interaction with clients also strengthens their communication, presentation and project management skills.

For Aanchal Gupta, a doctoral candidate in civil and environmental engineering and lead student with the center, the experience has helped connect her academic studies with the operational challenges facing manufacturers.

Originally from Nepal, Gupta worked in energy efficiency and industrial energy auditing before joining MSU. She said discovering the center's work encouraged her to pursue opportunities to build on that experience.

Through ITAC, Gupta has gained firsthand experience with industrial systems while strengthening her communication and problem-solving skills.

"We see things, and it clicks," Gupta said, describing how visiting facilities helps bring concepts discussed in the classroom into focus.

She added that the experience has strengthened her confidence when communicating with industry professionals and understanding their operational needs.

Casey Maxwell, a fourth-year student studying environmental engineering, described a similar connection between classroom instruction and practical experience.

Maxwell completed the program's training before beginning work as an energy analyst with ITAC. Her responsibilities include examining how energy is used in manufacturing facilities and identifying opportunities to improve efficiency.

"The hands-on portion is really nice because I can see what I'm learning about in class and apply that to real-world scenarios," Maxwell said.

Maxwell said she has also applied the skills gained through ITAC in other internships.

Expanding workforce training opportunities

The visit also included discussions about the broader Career ITAC program, which connects MSU and the Workforce Development Institute with organizations providing technical training and workforce development opportunities.

Through the initiative, MSU and the Workforce Development Institute provide field management and technical advisory support to participating organizations, helping expand access to training and resources across the manufacturing workforce.

“We're working to bring MSU's technical expertise to the building trades,” said Walter Lodes, director of apprenticeship at the Workforce Development Institute. “For organizations unfamiliar with registered apprenticeships, we can help them understand how to establish a program, find training providers and develop the necessary standards. That's what we're here for.”

The national Industrial Training and Assessment Centers program traces its origins to 1976, when it was established under the U.S. Department of Commerce. It moved to DOE in 1978 and has since expanded into a network of more than 50 centers at universities, community colleges, trade schools and union training programs.

text:
Environment and Climate Change Canada intends to support 12 projects from the international climate finance program, for a total of up to $116 million, that aim to strengthen the policy, regulatory, and institutional foundations needed to accelerate climate action on adaptation and mitigation in emerging and developing economies. Seven of the projects, which total over half of the funding, will address climate adaptation and resilience as either a primary or significant secondary objective.

This group of projects is expected to increase access to clean and reliable energy, reduce emissions from industrial activities, enhance food security and resilience for vulnerable populations, improve livelihoods, and strengthen capacity in developing countries to adapt to climate change and pursue sustainable economic growth.

Climate Risk and Early Warning Systems

Up to $10 million over five years, starting in 2026–2027, for the Climate Risk and Early Warning Systems initiative. This initiative helps the world’s most climate-vulnerable countries strengthen early warning systems that save lives, protect livelihoods, and build resilience to climate change.

Energy Sector Management Assistance Program

Up to $15 million over five years, starting in 2026–2027, for the Energy Sector Management Assistance Program at the World Bank. This program helps developing countries deploy clean energy solutions and improve the climate resilience of their energy sectors.

Clean Energy Transitions Programme

Up to $10 million over five years, starting in 2026–2027, for the Clean Energy Transitions Programme at the International Energy Agency. This program supports emerging and developing countries in accelerating clean energy transitions.

Climate and Clean Air Coalition

Up to $10 million over four years, starting in 2026–2027, for the Climate and Clean Air Coalition. Led by the United Nations Environment Programme, this project helps developing countries to reduce emissions of methane and other short-lived climate pollutants.

International Methane Emissions Observatory

Up to $5 million over four years, starting in 2026–2027, for the International Methane Emissions Observatory. Led by the United Nations Environment Programme, this project provides reliable methane emissions data and analysis to support climate action and accelerate global methane reduction.

NDC (Nationally Determined Contributions) Partnership

Up to $6 million over three years, starting in 2027–2028, for the NDC (Nationally Determined Contributions) Partnership. The NDC Partnership works to accelerate the implementation of the Paris Agreement by strengthening the capacity for and collaboration around country-owned climate and development action.

Adaptation Capacity Through Implementation and Transformative Ecosystem Building

Up to $12 million over four years, starting in 2027–2028, for the Adaptation Capacity Through Implementation and Transformative Ecosystem Building project. Led by the Canadian non-profit NovaSphere, this project enables developing countries to advance climate-resilient development and translate climate priorities into effective implementation.

Climate Finance Access Network

Up to $11 million over four years, starting in 2027–2028, for the Climate Finance Access Network (CFAN) at the Rocky Mountain Institute (RMI). CFAN aims to improve Small Island Developing States’ access to climate finance by building local capacity, improving project pipelines, and mobilizing public and private investment.

Ocean Risk and Resilience Action Alliance Project

Up to $14 million over four years, starting in 2027–2028, for the Ocean Risk and Resilience Action Alliance (ORRAA). ORRAA connects more than 140 member organizations, including investors and governments, to create new finance tools, influence environmental policies, and make ocean protection a mainstream part of global investing.

Powering Past Coal Alliance Secretariat

Up to $5 million over four years, starting in 2027–2028, for the Powering Past Coal Alliance (PPCA) Secretariat. The PPCA, co-chaired by Canada and the United Kingdom, works to accelerate the phase-out of unabated coal-fired electricity and advance energy transitions by helping governments plan, finance, and implement coal-to-clean energy projects.

Southeast Asia Energy Transition Partnership

Up to $6 million over four years, starting in 2027–2028, for the Southeast Asia Energy Transition Partnership. This multi-donor technical assistance facility helps countries in Southeast Asia move to cleaner and more reliable energy systems with a focus on electrification and coal phase-out.

National Adaptation Plan Global Network

Up to $12 million over four years, starting in 2027–2028, for the National Adaptation Plan Global Network. Led by the International Institute for Sustainable Development, this multi-donor initiative helps developing countries strengthen their climate adaptation planning and implementation.

description:

text:
Sign up for TPR Today, Texas Public Radio's newsletter that brings our top stories to your inbox each morning.

An environmental organization says it has documented significant releases of pollution from a natural gas facility near Laredo.

Earthworks says the emissions of methane and other possible hazardous chemicals were captured using a specialized infrared camera at the facility on Monday, Nov. 9, at Howard Energy Spears natural gas facility near Encinal. The facility is primarily owned by Howard Energy Partners, based in San Antonio. They are one of the largest privately held midstream infrastructure companies in the country.

Andrew Klooster is the senior thermographer at Earthworks who took the images of the emissions from the ground. He uses a specially designed Optical Gas Imaging, or OGI camera.

“It allows us to visualize certain pollutants that are invisible to the naked eye, and in particular, the pollutants that we're looking for when we are training our OGI camera on an oil and gas facility, are methane, which is the primary component in natural gas, but is also a major greenhouse gas that's released directly into the atmosphere, and then other volatile organic compounds, like benzene, toluene, which are often co-pollutants with, methane and are harmful to human health.”

Klooster says the information Earthworks gathered has been handed over to The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality.

“It's something that needs to be investigated further, but it's always concerning when you see these sorts of emissions because, again, they're harmful to the environment, potentially harmful to human health,” Klooster added.

Earthworks says satellite imaging shows previous emissions from the plant eight times since 2025.

Tanager-1 is a space satellite deployed in 2024 that is specifically designed to detect and track methane and CO2 super-emitters with state-of-the-art imaging capability.

The Tanager-1 satellite documented pollution from space emitting from this facility each of the five times it was observed in 2025 and again twice in August and once in September of 2026.

Edgar Villaseñor is advocacy campaign manager at the Rio Grande International Study Center in Laredo. ​RGISC has formed partnerships and alliances with a diversity of groups to improve the environmental health of the area.

Villaseñor says he believes the oil and gas industry in the area doesn’t follow the rules.

“What concerns me the most is that there's not enough oversight on them. So even though they have rules to follow and they're supposed to follow certain procedures, there's nobody really overseeing these facilities," he told TPR.

Villaseñor says the TCEQ has not been much help.

“I would like to see them be a legit regulation agency because as of right now, it feels like they're very industry-in-favor-of-industry. And so it doesn't make sense to have this agency that's supposed to take care of our quality of life, and they're not doing much. I really want them to hold these industries more accountable.”

Earthworks believes the emissions captured on Nov. 9 may be considered a so-called super-emitter event, which the Environmental Protection Agency defines as having an emissions rate of 100 kilograms per hour or greater. Evidence of the recent emissions from the Spears facility has been turned over to TCEQ.

Howard Energy Partners did not respond to TPR's request for comment.

Fermi Inc.’s Chief Nuclear Construction Officer Mesut Uzman has left the company, and the startup pushed back the timeline for four large reactors at the center of its Texas AI campus, according to a quarterly filing Thursday.

The setbacks were disclosed the same day Fermi said it had terminated its first binding customer deal and landed a $200 million commitment from a prospective hyperscaler tenant for its massive data center project in Carson County. The company didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment on the departure and the delays.

Fermi fired its co-founder and chief executive officer, Toby Neugebauer, in April, in part over struggles to line up an anchor tenant for its 17-gigawatt megacampus Project Matador. A growing backlash against data centers in Texas and across the US is becoming another risk factor, Fermi said Thursday.

Uzman left on Oct. 12, Fermi said. The company hired him last year to lead the nuclear part of Project Matador, because of his work delivering reactors in China and the United Arab Emirates.

Fermi now plans to commission one Westinghouse reactor a year from 2034 to 2037. In its last quarterly filing, it said it was targeting 2033 through 2036, while its original plan called for the first unit in 2032.

Fermi plans to power the campus largely with its own private grid, combining on-site natural gas generation, solar and batteries with four nuclear reactors in the longer term, supplemented by some electricity from the local utility.

“The implementation of moratoria and new requirements and restrictions could increase costs, delay or reduce planned data center infrastructure investments, limit the size and location of data centers, cause tenants to shift planned development to other jurisdictions, or otherwise constrain the deployment or expansion of data center infrastructure by our tenants,” the company said in the filing.

text:
The forecast and the turn in coal

Energy Innovation, a nonprofit research group, sees a small step down in US carbon emissions from energy use in 2026. The team pegs the decline at around 70 million metric tons from 2025, or about 2%, which would land total emissions near 4,850 million metric tons.

That call blends federal energy figures available through July with near-term projections for the remaining months. It also marks a pivot from last year, when higher coal burn pushed emissions up after two straight years of declines, according to the US Energy Information Administration.

Fuel shifts behind the numbers

Coal is doing the heavy lifting on the downside. From January through July, federal data show US coal consumption ran 10% below the same stretch in 2025. Within industry, coke plants cut coal use by 4.8% and sectors like cement and chemicals trimmed by 4% over that period.

Natural gas demand is holding close to 2025 levels in power and industry, while Americans are using slightly less gasoline and diesel as oil market shocks have lifted the cost of driving. Robbie Orvis, who leads modeling and analysis at Energy Innovation, noted that an especially cold winter in 2025 pushed natural gas prices up and coal use higher for heating, while cheaper gas this year created an incentive to move away from coal.

Other researchers see the same arc. Glen Peters at Oslo's Center for International Climate Research, a leader of the Global Carbon Budget, said US coal use has fallen each year since 2014 except in 2021 and 2025. The Global Carbon Budget released Nov. 10 projected US coal use will be 6.7% below 2025.

Shifts in energy trends often create quiet opportunities for patient, informed investors. We're hosting our first ever investor livestream on 11/17 to show you how to use ChatGPT and Claude to invest like a pro, hosted by Briefs Finance CEO Jaspreet Singh. Save your seat.

Policy pushes and the power mix

Even with federal moves intended to bolster coal, coal's footprint is shrinking. The Trump administration has issued emergency orders to keep some retiring coal plants running, loosened pollution controls, and steered hundreds of millions in federal funding toward modernizing existing coal stations and constructing new ones. Yet, as Orvis put it, "Coal remains uneconomic in spite of the different policies that have been put in place by this administration."

The emissions math in power underscores why coal's decline matters. Coal and natural gas each account for about 750 million metric tons of CO2 from the US power sector, even though coal produces roughly one third of the electricity that gas does.

Renewables keep climbing.

What it means for your portfolio

In plain English: a modest emissions dip in 2026 is being driven mainly by a retreat in coal use, flatlined gas demand, slightly lower gasoline and diesel consumption, and ongoing renewable buildouts. For investors, that mix ripples across coal exposure, gas-linked cash flows, and clean energy developers' pipelines. The bottom line is anchored by specific numbers - a 70 million metric ton decline, about 2%, to roughly 4,850 million metric tons - based on year to date data and short-run forecasts.

description:
DockChain uses a distributed charging model, under which a single power module can distribute power sequentially to multiple EVs, as opposed to an all-in-one model, which features a separate DC charger at every parking bay.
A distributed charging model can reduce the number of chargers and the amount of electrical infrastructure required, potentially accelerating deployment.
The new project will focus on developing custom hardware, firmware and software to improve DockChain’s control over starting, stopping and restarting charging sessions.
The project will also investigate how the technology could support bidirectional charging and vehicle-to-grid (V2G) services in the future.
Some EVs need another attempt to start; others can be reluctant to restart charging after power flow is paused for grid or priority reasons.
text:
Go Eve, a joint University College Dublin (UCD) and Imperial College London spin-off company, has secured £750,000 in funding from Innovate UK and private investors for an 18-month project to develop the next version of DockChain, its patented distributed DC fast charging technology.

DockChain uses a distributed charging model, under which a single power module can distribute power sequentially to multiple EVs, as opposed to an all-in-one model, which features a separate DC charger at every parking bay. A distributed charging model can reduce the number of chargers and the amount of electrical infrastructure required, potentially accelerating deployment.

The new project will focus on developing custom hardware, firmware and software to improve DockChain’s control over starting, stopping and restarting charging sessions. Existing DockChain units will be upgradeable to incorporate the new technology.

The project will also investigate how the technology could support bidirectional charging and vehicle-to-grid (V2G) services in the future.

Go Eve’s engineering team in Wolverhampton, England, will lead development and testing, with the aim of delivering a production-ready version of DockChain to its manufacturing partners in 2027.

Go Eve is inviting fleet operators to discuss potential trial sites, particularly those where vehicles share limited charging capacity, have different departure times and charging priorities, or remain parked long enough to offer V2G revenue opportunities.

“The ability to make better use of existing chargers, parking bays and available grid capacity will be increasingly important in managing the EV transition,” said John Goodbody, co-founder and Marketing Director of Go Eve. “We’ve already shown that fleets can serve more bays without multiplying the number of fast chargers. That’s where DockChain delivers immediate cost and deployment benefits. Working with fleets has also taught us that vehicles don’t always behave as expected at the charging connector. Some EVs need another attempt to start; others can be reluctant to restart charging after power flow is paused for grid or priority reasons. This project addresses those practical issues so we can make DockChain more reliable and flexible.”

text:
General Motors GM is strengthening its renewable energy strategy with a $550 million investment in two solar projects in Michigan. Developed by NorthStar Clean Energy, the facilities have a combined capacity of 300 megawatts and are expected to generate enough renewable energy credits to offset the annual electricity consumption of three GM assembly plants. The move could improve long-term energy cost visibility, support manufacturing operations and advance the automaker's emissions reduction goals.

GM's Solar Projects to Secure Long-Term Renewable Energy Supply

The Branch Solar facility in Branch County and Lake Iris Solar project in St. Clair County represent GM's largest clean energy project to date. The two facilities are expected to generate renewable energy credits equivalent to 539,000 megawatt-hours of electricity annually. GM will be the primary customer, accounting for 92% of their combined capacity, with the credits intended to offset electricity-related emissions at Factory ZERO, Flint Assembly and Lansing Delta Township Assembly, per Detroit News.

GM will not directly receive electricity from these facilities. Instead, it will purchase renewable energy credits through a virtual power purchase agreement. Securing long-term renewable energy at predictable costs could help the automaker limit exposure to fuel-market volatility and manage a significant operating expense. This becomes increasingly relevant as electrification, battery production and AI-related energy requirements raise the importance of reliable and cost-effective power supplies.

General Motors' Solar Projects Support Emissions Goals

The projects build on GM's progress in securing renewable electricity for its operations. In 2025, the automaker secured enough renewable energy to match 100% of its electricity consumption across its U.S. facilities. GM has also reduced its Scope 1 and 2 operational emissions by 52% since 2018. The latest projects could further support these efforts by generating renewable energy credits for its Michigan manufacturing operations.

Beyond its environmental benefits, the projects are expected to generate economic value for local communities. Their development created more than 550 full-time local construction jobs. The Branch project also helped Bethel Township secure a $1 million Renewables Ready Communities Award for local infrastructure improvements. Meanwhile, Lake Iris plans to incorporate pollinator habitats, potentially supporting local biodiversity and reducing long-term site maintenance requirements.

Overall, GM's solar investments could strengthen energy cost visibility and support its manufacturing and sustainability priorities. However, as the arrangement relies on renewable energy credits rather than direct electricity supply, its benefits will primarily come through emissions accounting and greater energy price predictability rather than a direct reduction in the electricity consumed by its plants.

Competitive Landscape

GM's move follows similar renewable energy initiatives by its automotive peers. Ford F partnered with DTE Energy in August 2022 to secure 650 megawatts of renewable energy capacity in Michigan through the MIGreenPower program. The agreement is expected to help Ford avoid up to 600,000 metric tons of CO2 emissions annually. While the automaker initially targeted 2025 to achieve the equivalent of 100% carbon-free electricity for its Michigan manufacturing operations, the timeline has since shifted to the end of 2027.

Similarly, Stellantis N.V. STLA entered into a 400-megawatt solar agreement with DTE Energy in December 2022. However, its Silver Creek Solar project, representing 200 megawatts of capacity, is now expected to begin commercial operations by September 2028. The initiative is expected to reduce annual carbon emissions by more than 670,000 metric tons.

Delivered by Innovate UK on behalf of the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade, the competition is designed to support UK businesses and researchers to develop new battery technologies.

The competition focused on sourcing and processing battery materials, recycling valuable materials, strengthening UK manufacturing and reducing reliance on overseas supply chains.

Battery recycling

Lithium Battery Recyclers Ltd has been awarded more than £1.2 million to lead project Reclaim, to develop a new UK process for recycling end-of-life electric vehicle batteries.

The process, developed by the University of Leicester, uses a tiny quantity of vegetable oil in water to separate valuable battery materials, including graphite, without acid leaching or hazardous chemicals.

The project will scale up the technology at a pilot facility in Widnes, Cheshire, and test the recovered materials for reuse in new batteries.

It aims to reduce the energy needed for recycling and keep valuable battery materials in the UK to support domestic manufacturing.

Reducing waste

Hyperbat, now part of Unipart Manufacturing Group, has received more than £2.4 million to lead a project aimed at reducing the number of electric vehicles written off because their batteries are damaged or no longer working as expected.

At present, it can be difficult to assess whether these batteries are safe to repair or reuse. This can lead to unnecessary vehicle write-offs, higher insurance costs and valuable materials being lost.

Working with partners including Coventry University, EMR, RevoTech and The Green Part Specialist, the project will develop a clear process for checking each battery and deciding whether it can be repaired, reused in a vehicle, given a second life for energy storage or safely recycled. The work could keep batteries in use for longer, reduce waste and create skilled jobs in the UK.

Feasibility studies

The competition has also awarded just over £6.2 million to 15 shorter feasibility studies exploring new ideas across the battery supply chain. Running for between six and 12 months, these projects will test whether early-stage technologies could improve how batteries are made, used, reused and recycled, helping the most promising ideas move towards further development and commercial use.

Superdielectrics Group and Sytronix have been awarded almost £500,000 to test a new type of battery that could help data centres manage the rapid changes in electricity demand created by artificial intelligence. The water-based battery is designed to store and release power quickly, helping data centres run more AI servers without placing additional strain on local electricity networks.

The project will build on an existing battery pack and test how it responds to the changing power needs of AI systems. If successful, the technology could help data centres make better use of their existing grid connections and expand without requiring immediate upgrades to local power supplies. It could also provide a safer alternative to conventional lithium-ion batteries and reduce reliance on imported battery materials.

Investment in Skills

The Battery Innovation Programme has also awarded £3.6 million to three regional skills initiatives that will accelerate the development of the UK’s battery manufacturing workforce and strengthen national capability across the battery value chain.

The investment will support the delivery of industry-focused nationally accredited training programmes across England, equipping learners with the skills needed to secure careers in one of the UK’s fastest-growing advanced manufacturing sectors and helping businesses access the talent required to meet increasing demand.

In Somerset, University Centre Somerset will deliver Level 2 and Level 3 battery manufacturing training to support workforce development for the emerging South West battery cluster, including opportunities linked to the Agratas Gigafactory near Bridgwater.

In Birmingham, University College Birmingham will expand its successful Battery Manufacturing Skills Pathway beyond Levels 2 and 3 by introducing higher-level provision at Levels 4 and 5. This will strengthen regional skills capability and provide advanced technical training aligned with the needs of battery manufacturers and the wider electrification supply chain.

And in the North East, Newcastle University and New College Durham will build on their collaboration with AESC by expanding battery manufacturing training to Levels 4 and 5. The initiative will support a highly skilled regional workforce and reinforce the North East’s position as a leading UK battery manufacturing cluster.

Dr Valentina Gentili, Director of the Battery Innovation Programme, said: “As global demand for batteries continues to grow, it is increasingly important that the UK focuses on the areas where it can deliver the greatest impact and strategic value. The projects supported through this competition demonstrate the breadth of innovation taking place across the UK battery sector.

“By investing in new technologies, strengthening supply chains and supporting business growth, we are helping to build the capabilities, expertise and partnerships that will further strengthen UK sovereign capability and position the UK as a leader in battery innovation.”

Minister for Reindustrialisation Blair McDougall, said: “This funding will give Britain’s battery manufacturing industry the support they need to power the industries of the future and keep our country at the cutting edge of innovation.

“Through our Modern Industrial Strategy we’re doubling down on Britain’s high-growth sectors like advanced manufacturing, and I want to congratulate all the winners on their success and their role in reinforcing Britain’s leadership in this fast-growing industry.”

text:
Overview

• The plant would open in an industrial building on Dunn and Weeks roads on the east side of Fayetteville.

• The Fayetteville City Council voted unanimously to offer the company a grant of $54,600 to pick the city.

• The Cumberland County Board of Commissioners is scheduled to consider another $54,600 grant for the company on Monday.

Fayetteville is competing with a community in Georgia for an electric motor factory that promises to hire 104 people and pay them an average of $65,000 a year.

That compares to Cumberland County’s average annual wage of $49,382, according to a legal advertisement about the project.

The Fayetteville City Council voted unanimously November 9 to offer the company a $54,600 grant to come here. The Cumberland County Board of Commissioners is scheduled to consider a similar grant, also worth $54,600, at its meeting on Monday.

The vote will follow a public hearing on the topic. Members of the public who want to speak at the hearing may sign up online or call 910-678-7771.

The state is considering grants for workforce development, said Robert Patton, the executive vice president of the Fayetteville Cumberland Economic Development Corp., at the council meeting. The state requires the grants from the city and county to match its grants, he said.

The city and county said in legal ads to notify the public of public hearings for the grants that the local governments “will recover the cost and the public will benefit through future property and business taxes, stimulation of the economy, promotion of business, and the creation of new jobs.”

The factory, which Patton said would be run by an American company, would be set up in a recently constructed, 54,600-square-foot industrial building for lease on Weeks Road at Dunn Road, on the east side of the city. It’s on property the city annexed in 2022 for industrial development. Grant-Murray Real Estate has the listing.

Photos show a vast space in a metal building. It’s next to an Amazon depot on Dunn Road, and near the NVR Inc. factory that makes trusses and other components for site-built homes.

The property is 8.65 acres, according to county land records, and the land and building are valued at $2.6 million. The owner is NC Fayetteville Dunn LLC of Greenville, South Carolina.

The name of the electric motor company has not been made public. Instead, it’s being referred to by a code name, Project Vermilion. Merriam-Webster defines vermilion as a vivid-red orange color, and as a bright red pigment.

If the company opens its factory in Fayetteville, it will spend $5.1 million to buy real and personal property, generate more than $157,000 in property taxes over 10 years, and add $9.7 million of annual payroll income to the area, Patton said.

Local officials did not say where in Georgia the company is considering locating.

A series of local and state incentives totaling about $815,000 helped convince SteelFab in September to proceed with a $22 million expansion of its Fayetteville facility, a project that is projected to add 42 jobs.

In July, global drone manufacturer Skyeton, armed with $743,000 in local and state incentives, picked Fayetteville to build its first manufacturing facility in North America.

Plant to Make Brushless Electric Motors

The Project Vermilion factory would make brushless electric motors, Patton said. Depending on their size and design, brushless motors are used in many types of consumer, commercial, medical, aerospace, and industrial products, according to Stepperonline, an electric motors vendor. These include aerial drones, home appliances, medical devices, robotics, and electric cars.

“Brushless” describes the internal design of the motors.

Simple electric motors use a component called a brush to transfer electric current through the motor to spin its output shaft, according to Renesas Electronics Corp.. A motor’s brushes constantly contact the spinning shaft.

Brushless motors spin the shaft without physical contact between the shaft and the electricity source.

Brushless motors are more complicated and expensive to make than brushed motors, but brushless motors are also more efficient, use less electricity, are better at producing torque, and their operating speed can be more precisely controlled, Renesas said.

Senior reporter Paul Woolverton can be reached at pwoolverton@cityviewnc.com.

text:
I’ve been at a conference all week which has given me some Substack time! So this is my third post this week (!), and probably the last for a bit :-)

So, the midterms are over, and the Democrats have taken decisive control of both the House and Senate.

This video covers in about 5 minutes what the administration has done in the days since, particularly in going after Democrats, the press and nonprofits.

I also highligh some important science and environment actions that slipped under the radar.

Subtitles are available and all actions are on TrumpActionTracker. Written version below.

*********************

The midterms are over, and the Democrats have won a huge victory with decisive control of both the House and the Senate. So in this video I want to look at what the administration has done in the days since. Separately, I also want to cover some key actions undermining the environment and health that have slipped under the radar.

Post midterms

I’ll start with the response to losing where the administration has reached for levers that bypass congress.

On the 6th of November, it emerged the White House is weighing an executive order that would brand certain nonprofits as having ties to terrorism and strip their tax-exempt status. Which organisations is not clear, but it builds directly on the administration’s existing campaign against nonprofits it dislikes. The reporting on an earlier tax crackdown this year named likely targets including the Open Society Foundations, George Soros’s network that funds pro-democracy and human-rights groups worldwide, and the Southern Poverty Law Center, which tracks and sues hate groups.

On the 7th, Trump ordered the Justice Department to investigate Democrats for, in his words, threatening people with impeachment, which he called a criminal act. Trump gave no evidence, and threatening impeachment is not a crime.

The same day, the Justice Department moved to join a lawsuit against Planned Parenthood in Texas, seeking to claw back Medicaid payments and impose penalties that Planned Parenthood says could close its Texas clinics. This came days after a Democrat was elected Texas attorney general, so adding the federal government to the suit keeps the case going whatever the new state attorney general wants.

And on the 8th November, prosecutors told a judge they were considering treating the New York Times as a conspirator in the criminal case against former FBI director James Comey, over an alleged leak of national security information. Naming a newspaper as a co-conspirator is a direct move against freedom of the press.

The press pressure went further. In a separate leak investigation, the Justice Department demanded 18 months of journalists’ private LinkedIn messages, including the identity of everyone they had contacted, which could have exposed hundreds of unrelated confidential sources, and it got a court order stopping LinkedIn from telling them. However On the 10th of November a unanimous federal appeals court threw the demand out as far too broad and a threat to the First Amendment.

The threats against Democrats also escalated. Also on the 10th, Attorney General Todd Blanche warned newly elected Democrats that promising to investigate Trump officials could itself be criminal. He singled out Senator Elissa Slotkin from Michigan over comments discouraging students from working for the administration, which Trump called a criminal act, though Blanche named no actual crime. It follows an earlier, failed attempt to indict Slotkin and five other Democrats over a video reminding soldiers they can refuse unlawful orders.

And there are signs that the administration is already trying to cover its tracks. Whistleblowers allege that the Interior Department has been destroying records of Trump’s Washington building projects ahead of oversight by the incoming Democratic Congress. The department categorically denies it. If the allegation holds up, it means evidence is being destroyed before a Democratic Congress can subpoena it.

Sources

White House weighs an order branding nonprofits terrorism-linked to strip tax status, days after the Democrats’ win (Independent)

Trump orders the DOJ to investigate Democrats over impeachment “threats”, no evidence (Reuters)

AG Blanche warns elected Democrats that promised oversight could be criminal; singles out Sen. Slotkin (Democracy Docket)

DOJ joins the Texas Planned Parenthood suit, days after a Democrat wins the state AG race (Reuters)

Prosecutors weigh treating the New York Times as a conspirator in the Comey leak case (New York Times)

Appeals court rejects DOJ demand for 18 months of journalists’ LinkedIn messages as a First Amendment threat (Politico)

Whistleblowers allege Interior is destroying records of Trump’s building projects; the department denies it (CNN)

Science

Now to science.

At the end of October, a New York Times investigation set out how much federal research capacity has already been lost. National Institutes of Health (NIH) – the world’s largest funders of health research – has had its staffing reduced by a fifth, the National Science Foundation by a third, Pentagon labs by about 14%. More than 2,000 biomedical research grants have been delayed or cancelled, across cancer, Alzheimer’s, defence and more.

Meanwhile, an Environmental Defense Fund analysis found the administration has kept dozens of coal plants running past their retirement dates, handing $950 million to 24 of them and exempting 70 from regulatory limits on toxic pollution.

Then, an analysis for the Natural Resources Defense Council counted more than 500 separate actions from this administration that weakened the protections that keep known carcinogens out of our air, water and workplaces, including changes to the scientific processes that decide how dangerous a substance is.

On the 2nd of November, the Justice Department’s research arm said it would fund studies into violence committed by people treated for gender dysphoria. It follows a health department report arguing that people who support gender-affirming care are more likely to support political violence. There is no credible evidence that transgender people are more likely to commit violence, including mass violence, than anyone else. Research doesn’t support a trans-to-violence link. If anything, the robust finding runs the other way: trans people are disproportionately victims of violence.

Finally, some news on conflicts of interest. On the 5th November, the New York Times reported that four of the eight people RFK Junior has appointed to the US Preventive Services Task Force, the panel that decides which screenings and preventive care get recommended, own stock in companies affected by its decisions. All four were given waivers to serve anyway despite the conflict of interest.

How LG Energy Solution Michigan Is Expanding Its Battery Ecosystem Through ESS LG Energy Solution Michigan is expanding its manufacturing operations to increase ESS battery production and support energy storage projects across the region.

Creating Jobs and Strengthening Michigan’s Battery Workforce LG Energy Solution Michigan’s continued growth is expanding employment across its operations.

Why LG Energy Solution Michigan’s Long-Term Growth Matters LG Energy Solution Michigan’s operations bring together battery manufacturing, energy storage, workforce development, and community engagement across the state.
text:
LG Energy Solution has invested more than USD 5 billion in Michigan since 2010, expanding battery manufacturing across Holland and Lansing while maintaining R&D operations in Troy.

The company expects its Michigan workforce to exceed 3,300 by the end of 2026, while expanding ESS production and supporting energy storage projects and community initiatives across the state.

LG Energy Solution, then part of LG Chem, began building its manufacturing presence in Michigan when it broke ground on its Holland battery plant in 2010. The plant started production in 2012 as America’s first electric vehicle (EV) battery plant, supplying batteries to automakers including General Motors, Stellantis and Ford. Today, the company operates manufacturing facilities in Holland and Lansing and maintains its North American Regional Group and a research and development (R&D) facility in Troy. With more than USD 5 billion invested in the state since 2010, LG Energy Solution Michigan has strengthened the state’s battery manufacturing base, supported job creation and workforce development, and contributed to local communities.

LG Energy Solution’s Michigan Manufacturing Growth Since 2010

In 2022, LG Energy Solution Michigan announced plans to invest USD 1.7 billion in the expansion of its Holland site, increasing production capacity for EV and energy storage system (ESS) batteries. In May 2025, the company took full ownership of the Lansing facility, which was originally developed through a joint venture with General Motors.

As its Michigan operations expanded, LG Energy Solution also broadened local battery production. The Holland plant began mass production of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries for ESS in June 2025, while the Lansing facility started LFP battery cell production in August 2026.

Lansing also produces nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) cells for EVs. By producing both LFP and NMC cells, the facility will support both energy storage and automotive applications. At the facility’s grand opening, Michigan Governor Gretchen Whitmer highlighted LG Energy Solution’s longstanding ties to the state, noting that the company “has called Michigan home for more than 20 years.”

The Michigan Economic Development Corporation (MEDC), Michigan’s lead economic development agency, recently highlighted LG Energy Solution’s economic and workforce contributions in an article examining the long-term impact of its investment in Holland. The article cites an analysis by the W.E. Upjohn Institute for Employment Research, which found that every USD 1 in incentive cost associated with the 2022 Holland expansion is expected to generate USD 2.23 in benefits for Michigan residents and the Holland community.

How LG Energy Solution Michigan Is Expanding Its Battery Ecosystem Through ESS

LG Energy Solution Michigan is expanding its manufacturing operations to increase ESS battery production and support energy storage projects across the region.

LG Energy Solution Vertech, the company’s U.S. energy storage division, connects its local manufacturing base with complete ESS solutions for utility and grid-scale applications. In May 2026, LG Energy Solution Vertech entered into a supply agreement with DTE Energy as part of the utility company’s USD 1.6 billion investment in Michigan battery storage. The agreement will support eight projects across the state, providing 1.5 GW of power capacity and 6 GWh of energy storage capacity. Battery systems will be delivered over a two-year period. Battery cells for these projects will be produced at LG Energy Solution facilities in Michigan and elsewhere in the U.S. and Canada.

According to DTE Energy, the investment is expected to generate approximately USD 2.3 billion in total economic impact, while contributing to local employment and improving grid reliability in Michigan. Together, LG Energy Solution’s battery manufacturing operations and LG Energy Solution Vertech’s system integration capabilities help strengthen Michigan’s manufacturing base and energy infrastructure.

Creating Jobs and Strengthening Michigan’s Battery Workforce

LG Energy Solution Michigan’s continued growth is expanding employment across its operations. By the end of 2026, the company expects its total Michigan workforce to exceed 3,300, making it one of the state’s top 50 employers. As of August 2026, the Lansing facility employed about 900 team members, with employment expected to reach 1,700 at full capacity.

LG Energy Solution Michigan also works with regional partners to develop and retain local talent. West Michigan Works!, the region’s workforce development agency, has supported the company’s recruitment and retention efforts by participating in hiring events and providing workforce development resources. LG Energy Solution Michigan has also expanded its recruitment of military veterans for production, technical, and leadership roles.

“Our growth in Michigan is about more than expanding our manufacturing capabilities—it’s about investing in the people who make our success possible,” said Anthony O’Donovan, Operations Director at LG Energy Solution Michigan. “As the battery industry evolves, we’re focused on developing local talent, creating opportunities for employees, and building a workforce to drive the next generation of energy technology. Michigan has been central to our story from the beginning, and we’re committed to this partnership for years to come.”

How LG Energy Solution Michigan Supports Local Communities Year-Round

Beyond manufacturing and employment, LG Energy Solution Michigan maintains an active presence in local communities. The company has served as the title sponsor of LG Energy Solution’s Holland on Ice since 2023 and has supported the U.S. Marine Corps Reserve’s Toys for Tots program since 2019. Its Lansing site has also organized a food drive in support of the Greater Lansing Food Bank.

Its community initiatives also include sponsoring the Tulip Time Festival’s Fun Run, serving as the main sponsor of Community Impact Day 2025, and supporting more than 10 youth sports teams.

Together, these efforts demonstrate LG Energy Solution Michigan’s commitment to local traditions, charitable programs, youth activities, and cultural events, strengthening its relationships with the communities where employees live and work.

Why LG Energy Solution Michigan’s Long-Term Growth Matters

LG Energy Solution Michigan’s operations bring together battery manufacturing, energy storage, workforce development, and community engagement across the state. As its Holland and Lansing operations continue to grow, the company’s investments are supporting jobs and local talent while strengthening Michigan’s battery manufacturing base and energy infrastructure.

text:
The U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE) Advanced Research Projects Agency-Energy (ARPA-E) has selected eight projects that could receive up to a combined $30 million to accelerate development of geothermal technologies. The funding announced November 12 is through the Stimulate Utilization of Plentiful Energy in Rocks through High-temperature Original Technologies (SUPERHOT) program. The projects will develop innovative approaches to harness superhot geothermal resources at temperatures above 375C and pressures above 22 megapascals to expand access to reliable baseload power.

“SUPERHOT pursues exponential, not incremental, progress by pushing the boundaries of innovation to fundamentally change how we tap into geothermal energy,” said ARPA-E Director Conner Prochaska. “The Energy Department is investing in technologies that could unlock America’s vast untapped energy potential and increase geothermal well productivity to deliver affordable, reliable, and secure power to American families and businesses.”

The U.S. holds at least 15,000 GW of potential geothermal power beneath its surface, yet existing technologies currently generate less than 4 GW of utility-scale power. Building on ARPA-E’s work to advance Enhanced Geothermal Systems (EGS) and Advanced Geothermal Systems (AGS), SUPERHOT aims to more than triple the output of individual geothermal wells by overcoming challenges in well construction and heat transfer. These advancements could help meet growing U.S. energy demand by delivering 10–20 GW of baseload power at less than $30 per megawatt-hour by 2040.

Selected projects include those led by the University of Oklahoma (Norman, OK); Oak Ridge National Laboratory (Oak Ridge, TN); Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (Livermore, CA); XGS Energy (Houston, TX); Pacific Northwest National Laboratory (Richland, WA); the University of Southern California (Los Angeles, CA); Los Alamos National Laboratory (Los Alamos, NM); and Blade Energy Partners, Ltd. (Houston, TX).

Learn more about the selected projects here and the SUPERHOT program here.

VinFast VF 8

VinFast

While most electric vehicle (EV) battery warranties come with strict mileage restrictions, VinFast is taking a distinctly different approach. Its 10-year, unlimited-mileage battery warranty offers American drivers one less thing to calculate as the odometer ticks upward.

IRVINE, Calif. , Nov. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Consider two drivers purchasing identical electric vehicles on the same day. One covers a modest 10,000 miles annually, while the other logs 25,000 miles between long commutes, family obligations, and weekend getaways. Four years in, both vehicles remain reliably on the road—yet only one driver still enjoys battery warranty coverage.



Under a typical eight-year or 100,000-mile battery warranty, the high-mileage driver has already reached the coverage ceiling. Meanwhile, the lower-mileage driver retains protection for another four years before the time limit expires.

It highlights a subtle paradox in vehicle ownership: the more heavily you rely on your EV, the sooner you risk losing coverage on its most critical component.

Decoding the Fine Print

America's reliance on driving is clear, though yearly mileage varies significantly. Federal Highway Administration data indicates that the average U.S. motor vehicle logged approximately 11,071 miles in 2024 1 . However, lengthy commutes, frequent interstate travel, and active lifestyles push that figure much higher for millions of households.

High mileage typically indicates a dependable vehicle doing its job, but standard warranty structures present a catch. Most automotive warranties operate on dual limits—years and mileage—expiring whichever threshold is crossed first.

While an eight-year/100,000-mile policy sounds generous on paper, its real-world lifespan hinges entirely on driving habits:

The irony is clear: those who utilize their vehicles the most receive the shortest window of protection.

Granted, an expired warranty does not mean a battery is nearing the end of its operational life. Industry research demonstrates that modern EV batteries are engineered to perform well past their warranty windows, often outlasting the vehicle itself. Nevertheless, physical durability and financial peace of mind are distinct. Even with high-end battery design, having a long-term safety net against unexpected issues provides vital reassurance.

Removing the Mileage Ceiling

VinFast offers an alternate path for American EV buyers. Available on its VF 8 and VF 9 electric SUVs, VinFast's 10-year battery warranty eliminates the mileage limit entirely under standard personal use. Complementing this is a new-vehicle limited warranty of up to 10 years or 125,000 miles (subject to standard terms and conditions).

Under this model, logging 25,000 miles a year—accumulating 250,000 miles over a decade—will never prematurely void the battery warranty, simply because no ceiling exists. Long-distance commuters no longer need to track the odometer with concern, and frequent road-trippers can travel without worrying that extra miles are quietly eroding their coverage.

Beyond the Battery

This warranty framework forms part of a broader ownership package designed to streamline EV adoption. Alongside its comprehensive vehicle and battery protection, VinFast provides:

By combining long-term financial protection with practical convenience, VinFast aligns its warranty coverage with the reality of how Americans actually drive: without limits.

text:
As the President doubles down on authoritarianism and white nationalism, the waning days of the 119th Congress are a dangerous time. This month’s US election was a cry for help from voters struggling to make ends meet and a warning to billionaires and corrupt politicians who have tried to rig the system for their own benefit.

Few special interests have reaped more financial rewards than Big Oil in the first two years of the Trump administration. With regulatory rollbacks, assaults on clean energy, illegal US military incursions in Venezuela and Iran, and tens of billions of dollars in handouts, the 119th Congress—in lockstep with the Trump administration—has already been a boon for the fossil fuel industry. The election came on the heels of eye-popping profit reports by major oil and gas corporations—and the results were a sharp rejection of these profiteers, who President Trump gushed are “making a freaking fortune” at everyone else’s expense.

I’m hopeful that the incoming Congress will fulfill its responsibilities to advance climate progress, accelerate the transition to clean energy, and hold big polluters accountable for climate deception and damages. Look for a series of blogs from me and other leaders at Union of Concerned Scientists on priorities for the 120th Congress in the next several weeks.

In the meantime, between now and early January, corporate accountability advocates must remain vigilant and mobilize to ensure that the Big Oil tiger—ExxonMobil’s chosen mascot—doesn’t feast on this lame duck Congress.

Here are three priorities to prevent any more giveaways to big polluters by the 119th Congress:

1) No immunity for Big Oil

Among the clear messages US voters sent in the 2026 election: no one should be above the law, including Big Oil. As the clock ticks down on this session of Congress, fossil fuel interests are desperately pushing for legislation that would grant them immunity from laws or lawsuits that could hold them accountable for their role in the climate crisis.

This lobbying blitz is especially audacious after a record-breaking, deadly Triple Danger Season from May to October 2026. Climate extremes were compounded by the Trump administration’s rollbacks of systems that keep people safe—and by the affordability crisis forcing working families to make tough choices between paying for essentials like food and medicine and cooling their homes. In California, as my colleague Jeremy Martin has written, consumers face even higher gasoline prices as oil companies take advantage of supply constraints and market consolidation to charge consumers unfair monopoly prices.

Members of Congress should expect and repel a push to pass the sweeping liability waiver proposed by Ted Cruz in the Senate and his soon-to-be Senate colleague, Harriet Hageman, in the House—and ensure that none of its provisions slip into other bills considered during the lame-duck session. Not only would this bill (modeled on the 2005 gun industry liability waiver) grant the fossil fuel industry immunity from legal and financial liability for climate deception and damages, it also attempts to legislate away source attribution science—a robust field that enables us to trace how much emissions from the largest fossil fuel producers contribute to climate harms and damages.

A new poll from Boston University found little support for giving oil and gas companies immunity from liability for climate deception and damages: for example, 83% agreed that oil and gas companies should be subject to the same laws as other industries.

2) Don’t settle for a permitting deal championed by Big Oil and the Koch network

As my colleague David Watkins wrote, the Senate Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) sponsored by Senators Capito, Whitehouse, Lee, and Heinrich—also known as the Senate permitting deal—is warped in favor of fossil fuel interests and would harm people, communities, and the environment if enacted.

Full-throated support for the bill by the fossil fuel industry and its allies is a flashing red warning light:

A coalition of groups—many backed by the Koch family—urged the Senate to pass the bill to “protect property rights, promote energy abundance, and restore America’s ability to build.”

Along with a liability waiver, permitting reform is a top 2026 priority for Big Oil’s chief lobbying arm, the American Petroleum Institute (API). API made no secret of its intention to use permitting reform as a vehicle to gut regulations under the National Environmental Policy Act and the Clean Water Act. (They inexplicably took to Washington DC earlier this week with a “BAAJA on the Hill” taco truck to push their support for the bill.)

Now, President Trump has weighed in on his social media platform, promoting touting that the bill will “ensure that we can build Pipelines, Mines, and Power Plants faster than ever before.”

The Senate is expected to vote on a revised version of BAAJA as soon as next week. While an amendment released over the weekend improves the provisions to speed up transmission line deployment and tempers the lock-in of fossil fuel project permitting, it fails to address the fundamental imbalance of the legislation in favor of fossil fuels. Without further significant amendment, BAAJA would be the most significant legislative reversal in environmental and community protections in decades.

3) Protect free speech on public health and safety issues

Congress is also negotiating a deal to reauthorize the Pipeline and Hazardous Material Safety Administration’s pipeline safety programs—an opportunity to improve the safety of hazardous liquid and gas pipelines that run through communities’ backyards, schools, parks, and waterways across the country.

In negotiating final text of the bill, Congress must keep out language from the House versions of the legislation—HR 9338 and HR 5301—that would broadly expose climate and Indigenous rights activists to criminalization for First Amendment-protected free speech, assembly, and the press, while redirecting attention away from the pipeline industry’s own problematic safety record.

Pipeline safety matters. Congress should focus on real pipeline safety issues like mitigating corrosion and equipment failure, rather than chilling free speech and discouraging people from speaking out about the public health and safety risks that oil and gas pipelines pose to communities. The dangers communities and pipeline workers face come from pipeline builders and operators, not from protesters.

As we gear up to demand that the 120th Congress restores science-informed public policymaking; investigates Big Oil’s corruption, disinformation, and inflated profits; reorients the nation toward a fair, fast phaseout of fossil fuels; and makes polluters pay their fair share, we must not take our eyes off the dangers that could come in a lame duck Congress.

text:
World Fusion Energy Group: The report was released in conjunction with the third meeting of the IAEA’s World Fusion Energy Group (WFEG), which was held on November 12 at the IAEA headquarters in Vienna, Austria.

The WFEG seeks to bring together governments, corporations, academia, and other relevant sectors to form a global fusion community by focusing on accelerating the research, development, demonstration, and deployment of fusion energy. The group states on its website that it hopes “to expedite the transition of fusion energy from development stages to commercial viability, ensuring that fusion becomes a bedrock of the world’s clean energy future.”

This year’s WFEG meeting featured high-level technical sessions on such topics as advancements and trends in fusion enabling technologies, evolving models of international collaboration and public–private partnerships, different financing approaches in all aspects of fusion development, and diverse perspectives on fusion programs presented by panelists from several countries.

A look inside the Outlook: World Fusion Outlook includes the findings of a study by EUROfusion—the organization that coordinates fusion research for the European Commission—that explores different fusion deployment scenarios, focusing on various factors that influence fusion deployment and scale-up, such as technology availability, capital costs, deployment rates, and integration of renewable energy. The study concludes that by 2100, depending on these factors, fusion energy could supply anywhere from just a very small percentage of global electricity generation or as much as 20 percent.

Also in the report is an article contributed by the London-based FusionX Group describes the raising of about $22 billion in committed capital by the fusion private sector—with more than 90 percent of that amount raised within the past five years. However, for fusion energy to reach the commercialization stage, FusionX Group says, an additional $80 billion in private capital is estimated to be required over the next 20 years. The article suggests that the required financing could best be achieved through industrial consolidation, as well as new sources and forms of investment.

Six overall trends are examined in the report as shapers of fusion’s future:

Increasing investment.

Increasing industrial activity and improving manufacturing capacity and supply chains.

The progression of fusion blueprints to actual power plants.

Research progress by experimental facilities around the world.

The adaptation and development of regulatory frameworks for fusion facilities.

The growth in the number of fusion facilities (operating, under construction, or planned).

These trends are examined by highlighting certain statistics. For example, the trend of increasing investment is highlighted by the record $4.5 billion in new fusion funding that was recorded between July 2025 and July 2026, while the trend of increasing industrial activity and improving manufacturing capacity and supply chains is highlighted by the spending of more than $530 million by private fusion firms on suppliers in 2025.

The present and the future: According to the report, “Dozens of fusion plant concepts are currently at various stages of development in Canada, China, the European Union (EU), France, Germany, Israel, Japan, the Republic of Korea, New Zealand, the Russian Federation, Sweden, the United Kingdom (UK) and the United States of America (USA), with target completion dates ranging from the 2030s to the 2050s. These concepts are being developed by individual governments, private companies, and public–private partnerships.”

The report goes on to describe 26 fusion power plants that are currently in planning stages, including seven private projects and one public project slated for electricity generation by the early 2030s; eight private projects and one public project scheduled for electricity generation by the late 2030s; one private project and one public project by the 2040s; one public project by the 2050s; and four private projects and two public projects with no operation dates yet specified.

It also details the growth in the number of operating, under-construction, or planned fusion facilities around the world, from 134 in 2022 to 174 in 2026. “Publicly funded facilities remain the majority in 2026, although the number of private facilities has tripled since 2021. Of the 111 public facilities worldwide, 85 are operating (77%), compared with 13 of the 63 private facilities (21%),” according to the report.

text:
A new study found that small, dam-less micro-hydropower systems could generate up to 22.6 megawatts of electricity across the Tribe’s 83-square-mile Qualla Boundary in western North Carolina.

As per the team from the Department of Energy’s Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) and the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians (EBCI), this power is enough for 5,000 homes.

Based in Cherokee, North Carolina, the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians is a federally recognized Native American tribe. Its members descend from the Cherokee people who stayed in their ancestral Appalachian homelands during the forced Trail of Tears removals of the 1830s.
