At present, steep terrain in the Blue Ridge Mountains complicates power line maintenance, causing frequent blackouts and forcing residents to use diesel generators.

“This project is assisting in assessing our full range of options to harness the energy available in natural Earth systems and contribute to long-term environmental and economic sustainability,” said Mike LaVoie, director of EBCI Natural Resources.

3D mapping and modeling

About 15,000 EBCI members live across the Blue Ridge Mountains. Conventional power lines are hard to build and maintain on such uneven terrain. Hence, this leaves remote pockets vulnerable to severe weather and frequent, prolonged blackouts. Many isolated families have had little choice but to depend on noisy, expensive diesel generators for days at a time.

The Oconaluftee River basin runs straight through the Qualla Boundary with fast-moving, well-fed streams. But the Tribe has long rejected hydropower dams, which slice up river systems and block the movement of fish and other aquatic wildlife.

More from Energy

See All

To find a middle ground, ORNL ecologist Evin Carter teamed up with the Tribe’s Natural Resources Department to explore “hidden hydro.” Using satellite imagery, machine learning, and LiDAR mapping, the research team built a detailed 3D model of the landscape and analyzed more than 1,500 stream sites.

The strategy targeted existing obstacles. Tracking native brook trout, researchers mapped 1,533 barriers, such as aging dams and road culverts, that block fish migration. Removing these obstacles and installing fish-friendly micro-hydropower devices achieves two goals at once. It reconnects fragmented waterways and generates steady, local power.

Serving remote communities

Researchers evaluated two fish-friendly hydropower options for the area. Compact micro-turbines generate over 1 kilowatt to power single homes or small businesses, while larger vortex generators produce up to 100 kilowatts for offices, health centers, or groups of houses.

Out of 533 viable locations identified in the study, 366 sites could produce at least 2 kilowatts, easily supporting individual households. Researchers even discovered several high-elevation spots above 3,900 feet capable of generating more than 100 kilowatts each.

The implications go beyond North Carolina. Carter noted that the Qualla Boundary acts as a microcosm of Southern Appalachia, capturing everything from high mountain forests to developed valley towns. What works here could serve as a blueprint for remote mountain communities across the entire region.

Next, researchers and biologists will head into the field to survey brook trout populations and test water flows at the most promising locations, paving the way for the first pilot installations.

title: Faced with new frequency requirements, renewable energy generators in Peru are ...
description:
This shift is occurring within a context of stricter frequency regulation requirements and new economic conditions for compliance , following the implementation of technical procedure PR-21 in August 2026.
Until now, energy storage for these purposes had been primarily used in conventional power plants.
From conventional power plants to new solar projects Energy storage for primary frequency regulation is not new in Peru.
According to COES data, in 2026 Peru had 63 solar power plants with approved pre-operational studies, totaling 13,778.2 MW of projected capacity.
The integration of energy storage into these installations is increasingly becoming part of developers' technical assessments.
text:
The integration of batteries is gaining traction in the assessments of large renewable energy generators in Peru, not only for new photovoltaic projects but also for plants already in operation. This shift is occurring within a context of stricter frequency regulation requirements and new economic conditions for compliance , following the implementation of technical procedure PR-21 in August 2026.

“Large IPPs are already considering BESS systems for primary and secondary frequency regulation for their current projects in operation and all those that will come into operation,” said Jorge Alvarado , Sales Manager BESS & PV Inverters at Sungrow, during Future Energy Summit (FES) Peru 2026 .

Until now, energy storage for these purposes had been primarily used in conventional power plants. However, the elimination of the exemption for solar, wind, and tidal installations over 10 MW, scheduled for 2025, extended the obligations to a segment that was previously not required to contribute to primary energy regulation reserves.

For the renewables achieved, a 24-month adjustment period was established from the approval of the corresponding technical procedures, while certain power plants with contracts from RER auctions retain a temporary exemption until their expiration.

This does not imply an obligation to install BESS systems. Generators can evaluate different alternatives to meet the requirements, but each has consequences for operation and energy availability.

From conventional power plants to new solar projects

Energy storage for primary frequency regulation is not new in Peru. In 2023, ENGIE put Chilca-BESS into operation, associated with its thermoelectric complex, while Kallpa had previously made progress with a similar solution.

Electroperú's annual report for 2024 already recorded five BESS systems intended for this service within the National Interconnected Electric System (SEIN).

The current difference lies in the extension of obligations to variable renewables , which must review their operating strategies and consider whether storage can be economically advantageous compared to other solutions.

The size of the potential market is also linked to the expansion of photovoltaics. According to COES data, in 2026 Peru had 63 solar power plants with approved pre-operational studies, totaling 13,778.2 MW of projected capacity.

Utility-scale photovoltaic projects, especially those exceeding 100 MW, represent a significant portion of the commercial opportunities. The integration of energy storage into these installations is increasingly becoming part of developers' technical assessments.

“We could be talking about a ratio of 100 MW of photovoltaic generation power and a system between 20 and 30 MWh,” Alvarado specified.

These figures represent commercially evaluated sizing references and not a capacity required by regulation. The amount of energy stored will depend on the power required, the duration of service, and the operational characteristics of each project.

What needs to be resolved to expand the BESS business?

Business decisions are also taking place amidst regulatory adjustments. The new PR-21, in effect since August 2026, modified the methodology for evaluating compliance with primary regulations and the scheme of charges for non-compliance, incorporating economic signals linked to the marginal costs of electricity.

On the other hand, Peru has yet to implement provisions to expand the scope of complementary services, while the new PR-22, linked to secondary frequency regulation, is scheduled to come into effect on January 1, 2027.

“While in terms of investment it is a small step, in legislative terms it is a giant leap,” said Alvarado, who also warned that there are still pending issues to take full advantage of the benefits that batteries can offer to the electrical system.

The challenge for developers will be to determine to what extent the incorporation of storage allows them to meet technical obligations without compromising the profitability of their power plants.

For now, the statements gathered during FES Peru show that large generators are already incorporating this alternative into their assessments, although they do not yet allow us to establish how many of those decisions will become concrete investments.

text:
SAN FRANCISCO — Terawatt Infrastructure, a full-stack charging infrastructure platform for autonomous and electric fleets, today announced four new purpose-built charging depots supporting leading customers in key U.S. markets.

The new sites in South San Francisco, Nashville, Miami, and Dallas together deliver 22 megawatts (MW) of dedicated charging capacity, enough to charge more than 3,000 vehicles per day.

Terawatt has overseen development and construction on these charging depots, including entitlements, utility interconnection, and site design. It will also manage all ongoing charger operations and maintenance, leveraging its proprietary Charge Management Software (CMS) and energy management tools alongside its 24/7 operations and maintenance system.

These sites join Terawatt's network of nearly 30 depots in active construction or development across 16 U.S. markets.

"We are bringing to life the necessary infrastructure buildout for commercial electric fleets to operate reliably at scale," said Neha Palmer, CEO and co-founder of Terawatt. "We're excited to have new sites up and running across the country, with more on the way in 2027. Our vision of an electrified economy for a cleaner, safer planet is closer to reality than ever before."

These new sites join Terawatt's network of nearly 30 charging depots in active construction or development across 16 markets throughout the U.S., expanding the company's footprint in California and underscoring the rapid growth of EVs to new metropolitan markets throughout the central and southern regions–with many more sites in planning stages:

South San Francisco, California — Located near San Francisco International Airport, this 6.6 MW site supports one fleet's Bay Area operations. Terawatt completed the buildout ahead of schedule and reduced costs by six figures through innovative site-energization methods and close collaboration with Pacific Gas & Electric Company (PG&E).

Nashville, Tennessee — Located near Nashville International Airport, this 4.5 MW site supports local fleet operations.

Miami, Florida — Located in the Design District/Wynwood area and opening this quarter, this 3.5 MW site will support Miami operations for a commercial fleet operator.

Dallas, Texas — Located near Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport, this 7 MW site supports a commercial fleet operator and will go live this quarter.

With the nation's largest portfolio of purpose-built commercial fleet charging depots, Terawatt continues to increase its operational footprint in top U.S. metropolitan markets.

Unlike powered land models that leave site construction to the operator, Terawatt delivers turnkey, fully built-out depots. Fleets that partner early with Terawatt gain access to strategic sites within high-barrier urban cores, securing an operational and cost advantage as commercial electrification accelerates.

About Terawatt Infrastructure

Terawatt is the leading full-stack infrastructure platform powering AV and EV fleets. Serving the largest industry fleet operators, including Waymo and Flexdrive by Lyft, Terawatt acquires, develops, and operates purpose-built depots for autonomous vehicles, heavy-duty logistics, and commercial electric fleets, delivering faster site deployment, a lower cost-per-mile, and commercial-scale operational reliability.

With the nation's largest network of purpose-built charging sites — including nearly 30 sites in active construction or development across 16 markets — Terawatt is accelerating the transition to electrified transportation.

Terawatt's network has delivered more than 93 million miles of clean driving range for commercial EV and AV fleets and has safely dispensed more than 30 million kWh of clean electricity.

text:
TOP NEWS

Introducing Healthy Home: A New Interactive, Online Experience:

The American Lung Association’s Healthy Home is a new interactive educational tool that guides users through a virtual home, room by room, to identify potential indoor air quality hazards and “hot sports.” Participants can explore one of three housing types: single-family homes, multi-unit housing, or manufactured homes. In addition, users have free access to personalized education and support from health experts through our Lung HelpLine and Lung Health Navigator program, as well as a customizable Indoor Air Quality Action Plan and other educational resources.

Learn more at www.Lung.org/healthy-home. Also, read our blog, “10 Simple Steps for Healthier Air at Home.”

November is Lung Cancer Awareness Month

Help us raise awareness about lung cancer and support people impacted by the disease:

Meet our Lung Force Heroes.

Learn more about lung cancer screening.

Ask Congress to support the Clinical Trial Modernization Act, to reduce barriers that prevent people from participating in clinical trials.

Learn more at Lung.org/lcam.

Open Enrollment is Underway for Marketplace and Medicare Healthcare Coverage

Open enrollment is now underway for both Medicare and Affordable Care Act (ACA) Marketplace health coverage. Medicare Open Enrollment runs through December 7, while enrollment for Affordable Care Act Marketplace coverage is open through January 15, 2027. This is an important opportunity to review your healthcare options and make sure your coverage continues to meet your needs.

Medicare Open Enrollment. Medicare beneficiaries can switch health plan and/or Part D prescription drug plan during the annual enrollment period. In 2027, annual out-of-pocket prescription drug costs are capped at $2,400. Individuals with higher medication expenses may also benefit from the Medicare Prescription Payment Plan, which allows costs to be spread throughout the year. More information is available at Lung.org/Medicare.

ACA Marketplace Open Enrollment. Enrollment for affordable, comprehensive health coverage through the ACA Marketplace starts November 1 and continues through January 15 in most states. Individuals renewing coverage should verify that their personal information, payment details and plan selections are up to date. More information on Marketplace options is available at Lung.org/OpenEnrollment.

Lung Association Continues to Invest in High-Impact Research

The American Lung Association recently announced an additional $21 million investment, which includes $11million in direct research funding, to support 120 promising research projects in 2026–2027. As President and CEO Harold Wimmer emphasized, “We are proud to continue to invest in high-quality research with the potential to improve lung health for everyone.” Meet the new class of scientists making a difference: Lung.org/research-team

YOUR HEALTH

Pulmonary Hypertension Awareness Month

Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a rare lung disease that can be difficult to diagnose, often delaying vital treatment. This month, take a few minutes to learn more about how to live well with PAH.

Start with Pulmonary Hypertension Basics to learn about diagnosis, treatment and support options.

Read Jenna's story to learn how she is navigating life with PAH.

ADVOCACY

FDA Approves Marketing for 24 New Flavored Nicotine Pouches, Putting Kids at Risk

Last month, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) authorized the marketing of 24 new nicotine pouch products. The authorizations were issued as part of FDA's nicotine pouch pilot program. The Lung Association voiced our strong disagreement with this decision.

EPA Proposed Rollback of Methane Would Worsen Air Pollution and Health

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) recently proposed a rollback of the 2024 methane pollution limits designed to limit hazardous emissions from the oil and gas industry. The proposal would weaken critical methane protections, increase air pollution and harm health, particularly for communities near oil and gas sites. “If finalized, this proposal would help polluting industries avoid cleanup and harm the communities who bear the brunt of dirtier air and a warming planet," said Lung Association President & CEO Harold Wimmer in a statement.

Act Now: Join the Lung Association in urging EPA to uphold the 2024 Methane Rule.

EACH BREATH BLOG

How an Unexpected Lung Cancer Diagnosis Led to a Radon Awareness Mission

Cary, who lived a healthy lifestyle, was shocked when she received a stage 4 lung cancer diagnosis. While chemotherapy and a targeted therapy gave her hope and precious time, she was determined to understand what had caused her disease. She soon learned that environmental exposures, including radon—the second leading cause of lung cancer—may have been a contributing factor, and testing revealed high levels of radon in her home. title: OPG says Darlington SMR won't meet 2030 start date or cost target - Power Engineering
description:
More broadly, the trouble raises questions about the certainty of first-of-a-kind SMR projects, particularly as utilities and governments look to advanced nuclear technology to meet rising electricity demand.
SMRs are intended to benefit from standardized designs, modular construction and repeatable manufacturing, unlike conventional nuclear megaprojects.
Deployment delays are of concern because Darlington is intended to demonstrate a pathway to commercial deployment for GEVH’s BWRX-300 reactor technology.
The BWRX-300 is the 10th evolution of GE’s boiling water reactor design.
RELATED: OPG awards manufacturing contracts for Pickering, Darlington nuclear projects
text:
One of the most closely watched small modular reactor projects in North America is facing delays and cost overruns, raising questions about the economics of next-generation nuclear power.

Ontario Power Generation said Unit 1 of its Darlington New Nuclear Project (DNNP) is no longer expected to meet its October 2030 commercial operation target or be completed within its estimated cost of C$7.7 billion($5.5 billion U.S.), which includes systems and services to be shared with future units at the site.

Wholly owned by Ontario’s government, OPG is one of the largest electricity generators on the continent. Its portfolio includes nuclear, hydroelectric, natural gas and energy storage facilities.

The update was announced in OPG’s Nov. 10 third-quarter financial report and deals a setback to one of the most closely watched advanced nuclear developments.

OPG hasn’t shared a revised cost estimate or completion date for its flagship SMR project, but expects to substantially complete its assessment by mid-2027.

The company’s disclosure attributed the setback to ongoing engineering by reactor technology supplier GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy (GEVH) on its first-of-a-kind design, which OPG said is affecting construction execution and supply chain performance.

More broadly, the trouble raises questions about the certainty of first-of-a-kind SMR projects, particularly as utilities and governments look to advanced nuclear technology to meet rising electricity demand.

SMRs are intended to benefit from standardized designs, modular construction and repeatable manufacturing, unlike conventional nuclear megaprojects.

OPG said it is working with GEVH to wrap up outstanding engineering work, which will inform a broader reassessment of construction and procurement assumptions, design maturity, market conditions including inflation and geopolitical risk, and the effectiveness of recovery measures.

RELATED: Ontario to build “fleet of SMRs” at Darlington nuclear site

“We have made meaningful progress in building the G7’s first small modular reactor, and critical work continues every day on site,” said OPG President and CEO Nicolle Butcher in the announcement. “At the same time, we have identified risks that will impact Unit 1’s schedule and budget.”

Construction is still moving forward. OPG has installed a 2.1-million-pound basemat, which the company called the first nuclear foundation laid in Canada in more than 30 years. It also has completed the first turbine building foundation pour and finished assembling a tunnel boring machine that will excavate and line the plant’s condense cooling water tunnel. Tunnelling is expected to begin in the fourth quarter of 2026.

Deployment delays are of concern because Darlington is intended to demonstrate a pathway to commercial deployment for GEVH’s BWRX-300 reactor technology.

The BWRX-300 is the 10th evolution of GE’s boiling water reactor design. The 300 MW water-cooled reactor design is based on the company’s Economic Simplified Boiling-Water Reactor (ESBWR), which is already licensed by the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC).

GEVH previously shared that the company took the basic ESBWR design and simplified it, including several design safety features which are new to boiling water reactor technology. The safety relief valves, deemed the most likely cause of a loss of coolant accident (LOCA), were eliminated in the design.

The isolation condenser system (ICS) provides overpressure protection in accordance with ASME BPV code, section III, class 1 equipment (Status Report – BWRX-300 – GE Hitachi and Hitachi GE Nuclear Energy). In order to accommodate this change, the design pressure has been raised by 20% from previous boiling water reactors. GEVH has also implemented integral isolation valves, which close to stop the loss of coolant in an accident scenario.

RELATED: OPG awards manufacturing contracts for Pickering, Darlington nuclear projects

title: Elbert County's Eastern Plains Ranch could include Colorado's largest data center
description:
KIOWA, Colo. — More than 100 Elbert County residents attended a county planning commission meeting Nov. 4 about a proposal to develop a massive ranch that could include Colorado’s largest data center.
If approved, the industrial portion would include a 540-megawatt data center, on-site natural gas and renewable energy generation, battery storage and biochar and regenerative agriculture.
Some oppose the construction of a data center, while others welcome the economic investment and potential tax revenue it could bring to the community.
Colorado Plains Ranch, LLC's ownership has not been verified.
On Nov. 5, the Elbert County Planning Commission voted 6–2 to recommend approval of the Colorado Plains Ranch Planned Unit Development.
text:
KIOWA, Colo. — More than 100 Elbert County residents attended a county planning commission meeting Nov. 4 about a proposal to develop a massive ranch that could include Colorado’s largest data center.

Developers are seeking to rezone Colorado Plains Ranch — a 5,672-acre parcel of land in eastern Elbert County — to allow development for a mix of businesses and industrial uses. If approved, the industrial portion would include a 540-megawatt data center, on-site natural gas and renewable energy generation, battery storage and biochar and regenerative agriculture. The project developer, Colorado Plains Project, LLC, selected the location because it is relatively isolated from established communities, surrounded by open land with easy access to Interstate 70 and the State Highway 86 corridor, and close to existing natural gas and electric transmission infrastructure.

Locals are divided over the proposed rezoning of the ranchland. Some oppose the construction of a data center, while others welcome the economic investment and potential tax revenue it could bring to the community. Still others say they are only now learning about the project and want to slow the approval process.

Leon Vick, a cattle rancher whose cow-calf operation sits on the Big Sandy River in Hugo, is concerned about the scarcity of water in eastern Colorado and opposes the development of a new data center. Large data centers are notorious for their substantial water needs, using up to 5 million gallons a day to cool the servers and equipment that store and process data.

“Our wells are already starting to dry up. If they continue to do these kinds of projects, the ranches in eastern Colorado will not exist,” Vick said. “We have land for probably 200 head of cows … We have water for 70 head of cows at the same time. If they continue to use our water, it will get harder for us to operate.”

Bill Rigler, a spokesperson for the Colorado Plains Ranch project, said the proposed data center would use “less water than an Olympic-sized swimming pool,” or approximately 500,000 gallons in total, through a closed-loop cooling system.

According to Gregor Henze, a professor of civil, environmental and architectural engineering at the University of Colorado Boulder, closed-loop cooling systems continuously circulate the same fluid through sealed pipes, pulling heat away from servers and releasing it into the outdoor air through large dry coolers.

Colorado Plains Ranch, LLC has applied for groundwater rights from the Laramie-Fox Hills aquifer — which sits directly beneath the property — for agricultural, domestic, commercial and industrial uses. The maximum water that the Colorado Plains Ranch can use annually under Elbert County’s 300-year rule is 187 acre-feet annually, according to the project proposal. Final approval is still pending.

Even if the developers’ application is approved, they say the water used by the data center would not come from the Laramie-Fox Hills aquifer, according to Bruce Lytle, a water consultant with Moore Engineering. Instead, the deionized water, or water from which minerals and dissolved salts have been removed, would come from an industrial facility offsite, Lytle said.

Henze said dry closed-loop cooling uses very little water but requires more electricity, especially during hot weather when cooling demand is highest. Potential impacts could include high energy use, fan noise and, in rare cases, cooling fluid leakage.

According to the Colorado Plains Ranch website, projected tax revenues will support critical community infrastructure and services in Elbert County annually, including more than $10 million for the Road and Bridge Authority, $15 million for the Agate and Big Sandy fire districts, $46 million for the Agate and Big Sandy school districts, $10 million for public safety and more than $20 million for the county's General Fund.

“This could be a model for what data centers could look like in terms of generating their own power using a fraction of the water of these legacy systems,” Rigler said. “This project alone will generate more than $79 million each year in new property tax revenues. I mean, it’s an enormous investment back into this community.”

Christina Nowak of Agate, a community of fewer than 700 residents in eastern Elbert County, is an EMS paramedic who supports the development. She said rural EMS services in her community face significant challenges because they cover enormous distances with limited personnel and funding.

“A heart attack in Agate is just as deadly as a heart attack in Denver. Our lives are not worth less just because we live farther apart,” Nowak said. “A strong tax base can help build a future where EMS response doesn’t depend on a handful of exhausted individuals.”

A resident from Elizabeth, Laura Putzier, voiced opposition to the data center due to the health risks that come with it. “It’s reasonable to assume that fossil fuels will power new data centers,” she said. According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, natural gas and coal together generated about 58% of U.S. electricity in 2025. Coal-fired power generation in the U.S. also increased by 13% that year, marking a resurgence in carbon emissions after several years of decline. An EIA report pointed to growing electricity demand from data centers and increased reliance on coal as contributing factors to the rise in carbon emissions.

“Air, water and land pollution emitted by all types of fossil fuel power plants creates high health costs as pollutants lead to higher asthma rates and heart and lung disease,” Putzier said. “We’re hearing that this is an agricultural project. I beg to differ.”

Other residents questioned whether the county has adequate regulations to oversee the project. Gary Davis, whose land borders Colorado Plains Ranch to the west, urged the Elbert County Board of Commissioners to place a moratorium on the data center portion of the project and take time to establish strict guidelines for data centers and their developers.

Tim Craft of Craft Companies, LLC is listed as the company's contact in the project’s draft plan. Colorado Plains Ranch, LLC's ownership has not been verified.

On Nov. 5, the Elbert County Planning Commission voted 6–2 to recommend approval of the Colorado Plains Ranch Planned Unit Development. The Board of County Commissioners is scheduled to hold a hearing and make a final decision on the proposed rezoning and development Nov. 18 at 1 p.m.

description:

text:
A £28.6m investment in 27 UK projects will support efforts to develop more efficient battery recycling methods, improve electric vehicle battery recovery and explore new energy storage technologies.

The funding, awarded through the Battery Innovation Programme, will also support specialist manufacturing training and technologies intended to strengthen the UK’s capabilities across the battery supply chain.

Innovate UK is delivering the competition on behalf of the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade. Its focus spans several areas of the industry, including raw material processing, recycling, manufacturing and reducing dependence on international suppliers.

Dr Valentina Gentili, Director of the Battery Innovation Programme, explained: “As global demand for batteries continues to grow, it is increasingly important that the UK focuses on the areas where it can deliver the greatest impact and strategic value.

“The projects supported through this competition demonstrate the breadth of innovation taking place across the UK battery sector.

“By investing in new technologies, strengthening supply chains and supporting business growth, we are helping to build the capabilities, expertise and partnerships that will further strengthen UK sovereign capability and position the UK as a leader in battery innovation.”

Finding new uses for end-of-life batteries

Keeping valuable materials in circulation is a central theme of the funded projects, with two major awards targeting challenges associated with electric vehicle batteries.

Lithium Battery Recyclers Ltd has secured more than £1.2m for Project Reclaim, which will take a recycling technique developed by the University of Leicester towards pilot-scale operation.

Rather than using conventional acid leaching or hazardous chemicals, the process employs a small quantity of vegetable oil mixed with water to separate materials such as graphite from discarded batteries.

A pilot facility in Widnes, Cheshire, will be used to scale up the approach and establish whether the recovered materials are suitable for manufacturing new batteries.

The project aims to lower the energy requirements associated with recycling while retaining valuable resources within the UK.

A separate project led by Hyperbat, now part of Unipart Manufacturing Group, is addressing another problem: what happens when an EV battery is damaged or stops performing as expected.

The company has received more than £2.4m to develop a consistent assessment process that can determine whether individual batteries are suitable for repair, reuse, repurposing for energy storage or recycling.

Without a reliable way to establish battery condition and safety, potentially recoverable vehicles can be written off, contributing to higher insurance costs and the loss of materials that could have been used again.

The project aims to provide a clearer route for determining the future of these batteries, potentially extending their useful lives and reducing unnecessary waste.

Battery storage for growing AI demand

The programme is also supporting research into how battery technology could help manage the electricity requirements of expanding digital infrastructure.

Superdielectrics Group and Sytronix have received almost £500,000 to investigate a water-based battery designed to respond rapidly to changes in electricity demand at data centres.

The technology is intended to store and release electricity quickly, helping facilities meet the fluctuating power requirements of AI servers.

The project will build on an existing battery pack and assess its performance under changing demand conditions.

If successful, the approach could help data centres increase their capacity while making better use of existing electricity grid connections, potentially avoiding the immediate need for local network upgrades.

It could also provide a safer alternative to conventional lithium-ion batteries and reduce reliance on imported materials.

Feasibility studies explore future technologies

The Superdielectrics project is one of 15 feasibility studies sharing just over £6.2m to examine potential improvements throughout the battery supply chain.

Each study will run for between six and 12 months, allowing researchers and businesses to investigate whether early-stage technologies could offer practical improvements to battery production, use, reuse or recycling.

The intention is to establish which concepts have sufficient potential to progress towards further development and eventual commercial application.

Building the skills needed for battery manufacturing

Technology development is only part of the investment. A further £3.6m has been allocated to three regional initiatives to prepare workers for roles in the battery manufacturing industry.

The projects will deliver nationally accredited, industry-focused training across England, covering different qualification levels to meet workforce requirements.

University Centre Somerset will provide Level 2 and 3 battery manufacturing courses for the South West battery cluster.

Meanwhile, University College Birmingham in the West Midlands and a partnership involving Newcastle University and New College Durham in the North East will expand training opportunities at Levels 4 and 5.

The initiatives are intended to help learners access careers in battery manufacturing while giving businesses the specialist skills needed to support activity across the sector.

By funding projects ranging from experimental recycling techniques to workforce training, the Battery Innovation Programme is addressing several different requirements of the UK’s battery industry, from recovering materials already in circulation to developing the technologies and skills needed for future manufacturing.

title: Data Centers Cannot Absorb Every Lost Clean Energy Job
description:
Clean Energy Employment Reverses After Four Years of Growth E2 found clean energy employment fell in 35 states.
"America's clean energy jobs boom didn't just slow in 2025," said Michael Timberlake, E2's director of research.
Energy efficiency, the largest clean energy segment, lost about 21,400 workers.
One Small Data Center Category Grew Within energy efficiency, DOE tracks jobs tied to certified data center equipment.
No national dataset yet shows whether clean energy workers are making the move.
text:
Delegates at the COP31 climate talks in Antalya, Türkiye, devoted the conference's second day to electricity, as the host country promoted a pledge to raise power's share of global final energy use from just over 20% to 35% by 2035. Goals like that depend on electricians and line workers, and in the United States those trades are losing work in one corner of the energy economy while being recruited hard in another.

U.S. clean energy employment fell by 36,949 jobs in 2025 to about 3.52 million, the first decline since the pandemic, according to an analysis of federal energy employment data released Sept. 22 by E2, a national nonpartisan business group that advocates for clean energy policy. This year, construction firms working on data centers have been reporting some of the tightest labor conditions in their industry. The two trends can look like a handoff, with workers leaving one part of the energy economy and finding work in another. The available data do not show that happening.

Data center projects draw on a different mix of trades, often in other parts of the country and on their own schedules. Utilities and manufacturers planning their own projects are left hiring into a market that is shedding workers and short of them at the same time.

Clean Energy Employment Reverses After Four Years of Growth

E2 found clean energy employment fell in 35 states. California lost almost 21,000 jobs, and Florida led all states with a gain of about 3,800. "America's clean energy jobs boom didn't just slow in 2025," said Michael Timberlake, E2's director of research. "It went into reverse."

Energy employment overall slipped too. The Department of Energy's (DOE) 2026 U.S. Energy and Employment Report, which E2's analysis draws on, put the drop in total energy employment at about 86,000 jobs, or 1%, leaving roughly 8.4 million workers. Energy efficiency, the largest clean energy segment, lost about 21,400 workers. DOE said several 2025 policy changes likely shifted workers' time, and in some cases jobs, away from efficiency work, so not all of that drop represents lost jobs.

One Small Data Center Category Grew

Within energy efficiency, DOE tracks jobs tied to certified data center equipment. That category added about 1,100 workers in 2025 and has grown by about 3,300, or 33%, since 2022. DOE linked the gain in part to data center construction, which it said grew more than 30% in 2025.

The category covers only a sliver of data center work. Most of the electricians and equipment installers on these sites fall outside it. Neither DOE nor E2 tracks individual workers, so the reports cannot show whether anyone who left a clean energy job ended up on a data center site.

Contractors Are Competing for the Same Crews

In a survey released Sept. 3 by the Associated General Contractors of America (AGC) and NCCER, a construction training and credentialing organization, 28% of 1,830 respondents said they had done data center work in the previous 12 months. Among those firms, 58% reported more competition for skilled workers and 49% reported more wage pressure.

"The need for people to work on new data centers is keeping labor conditions tight" even as "demand for many other types of projects remains relatively soft," said Ken Simonson, AGC's chief economist.

Across all respondents, 42% said worker shortages had delayed projects, and half said available candidates lacked the skills, certificates or licenses the work requires. Project owners are absorbing some of that, because a thin pool of qualified contractors shifts schedule exposure onto the project owner.

Indeed's Hiring Lab reported in July that data center postings had more than doubled over two years, to about 6 of every 1,000 U.S. listings, while total postings fell about 12%. Roughly a quarter of the data center openings were for installation and maintenance workers, and those hourly roles advertised median pay about 42% higher than similar jobs elsewhere. A posting shows an employer is recruiting, and it does not show whether the job was filled.

Electrification Goals Lean on the Same Trades

Employers outside the United States report the same shortage. In its most recent World Energy Employment report, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said more than half of the roughly 700 companies, unions and training institutions it surveyed reported critical hiring bottlenecks. Electricians, pipefitters, line workers and plant operators were among the hardest roles to fill. In advanced economies, the agency counted 2.4 energy workers nearing retirement for every new entrant under 25, and 1.4 for every new entrant in grid-related jobs.

Grids were part of the same COP31 discussion. About 2,500 gigawatts of generation and other energy projects worldwide are waiting for grid connections, said Dario Liguti, director of the energy division at the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe (UNECE), at the talks.

"Two things," he said. "Increase the quantity of the grid and increase its quality." Building those connections takes many of the same crews that U.S. data center developers are trying to hire.

Geography and Credentials Decide Who Can Move

In the United States, data center hiring clusters in a few places. Data center roles made up a growing share of postings in Columbus, Ohio; Jackson, Mississippi; and Reno, Nevada, and about 8% of this year's postings in the Washington, D.C., area, according to Indeed. E2's biggest losses were in California. For a solar installer laid off in the Central Valley, an electrician opening outside Columbus means a move of some 2,000 miles.

Licensing is another hurdle. An electrician licensed in one state may need another state's license, plus experience with critical power equipment, before joining a data center crew. A worker from an electric vehicle plant brings manufacturing experience that could suit an equipment supplier without qualifying for a construction role. Companies trying to close that gap are building training pipelines before projects break ground, often with apprenticeship programs and community colleges tied to specific openings.

Construction Crews and Operating Staff Are Different Hires

A data center needs a large construction workforce during the build and a much smaller operating staff once it opens. The people who keep equipment running after commissioning come from a separate labor pool, and that maintenance workforce is growing more slowly than the equipment it services. Construction workers can build a career moving from project to project, though each job lasts only as long as the build.

No national dataset yet shows whether clean energy workers are making the move. DOE publishes its energy employment report each year, and the next edition will show whether the data center equipment category keeps growing while the rest of efficiency shrinks. Simonson's comment points to another open question. If data center work slows, those crews would be looking for jobs in a construction market that AGC describes as soft elsewhere.

text:

For dealers, hybrids now represent about 30% of all Honda brand sales. Honda set back-to-back hybrid sales records in 2024 and 2025 and is on track for another record year in 2026, and it says hybrid and SUV consideration are at all-time highs.

text:
Electric vehicles make up a sliver of the world's cars, but they're already putting a dent in global oil demand.

Transport & Environment estimated that battery-electric cars save 1.2 million barrels of oil a day despite accounting for just 4.2% of vehicles worldwide.

Here's what to know

In 2021, battery-electric cars displaced about 215,000 barrels of oil per day. That figure has since grown more than fivefold, according to a T&E analysis cited by CleanTechnica.

In 2021, battery-electric models accounted for 6.6% of new-car purchases worldwide. T&E said that share has surged to a quarter of all purchases.

No other strategy cuts oil demand, shores up energy security, and lowers pollution as effectively as electric vehicles, it said. Battery-electric cars save the equivalent of 1.2% of the oil consumed worldwide.

More background

T&E reported that battery-electric models make up about 1% of the world's trucks and a majority of new truck purchases in some countries. It put the electric share of the global bus fleet at 5%.

Daily oil consumption would be up to 320,000 barrels higher without electric buses and trucks, T&E estimated.

Nearly half the oil consumed worldwide goes to road transportation.

T&E warned that oil demand could spiral out of control as more cars and trucks hit the road unless EV adoption keeps pace.

What's being done?

At the 2021 COP26 summit in Glasgow, 24 countries and a group of major automakers agreed to stop selling gas- and diesel-powered vehicles no later than 2040, per CleanTechnica.

The analysis tracked the growth of electric transportation over the five years following that commitment.

By 2034, battery-electric cars could cut daily oil use by about 5.8 million barrels if current policies hold, T&E projected.

Global energy markets have weathered two crises since the Glasgow pledge, and T&E called for faster EV adoption to help ward off future oil shocks.

It estimated that the battery-electric fleet in use prevents over 200 million metric tons of carbon dioxide-equivalent emissions each year.

Antony Froggatt, a senior director at T&E, connected the trend to energy security as well as climate goals. "Five years after Glasgow, EVs stand as one of the clearest victories in global climate history," he said, per CleanTechnica.

Where can I learn more?

Electric vehicles are cutting oil use as they claim a growing share of new-car sales.

• Worldwide, gas-only cars now account for less than half of new vehicle sales.

• In Europe, EVs have overtaken gas and diesel vehicles while U.S. adoption lags.

• China's EV market share reached a record 65% in August as combustion-engine sales collapsed.

• The U.S. EV share fell to 6% after tax credits ended; Europe reached 23%.

• In Norway, EVs accounted for 96% of new-car sales.

In an iconic photo from the 1930s, ironworkers eat lunch, perched on the steel beam of a skyscraper. The photo documents the critical role these tradesmen played in building city skylines.

And now, ironworkers are also essential for building another kind of tall tower – wind turbines.

Noah Mihaly, a union ironworker for White Construction, is helping build the Coles Wind Farm in Illinois.

Mihaly: “It’s almost entirely ironworkers that are preparing the engine rooms, preparing the blades … and then putting together all the pieces, as well as constructing the foundations.”

Given their vital role in building wind farms, ironworkers are in high demand as the clean energy industry expands.

So to recruit and prepare more people for these jobs, Illinois established a workforce training program under the state’s Climate and Equitable Jobs Act.

Called the Climate Works Pre-Apprenticeship Program, it provides people from underserved areas with free training and help applying to apprenticeships.

Mihaly: “The pre-apprenticeship program was my jumpstart. It was the main reason I was able to get into the ironworker’s union.”

And Mihaly says he finds the job rewarding.

Mihaly: “I just like the idea that I’m able to help put together renewable energy.”

text:
This year Prof. Mike McGehee has been selected as the 128th Distinguished Research Lecturer, one of the highest honors bestowed by the faculty of CU Boulder upon a faculty member.

Harnessing Sunlight and Mentoring Startup Founders to Address Climate Change

Michael McGehee

Wednesday November 18, 2026

4:00 - 5:00 PM

Chancellors Hall and Auditorium, CASE

More Information

Register Now

While the selection for this honor is made based on the scholarship, research, and creative achievement of the nominee, of which McGehee has an immense track record, Mike has chosen to use the lecture as an opportunity to reflect and discuss something a little harder to quantify, the sense of innovation and entrepreneurship that has been cultivated in his group over the years. In the last 25 years graduates of the McGehee group have founded 22 companies, now worth more than an estimated $6 B combined.

The McGehee group was established with a single mission statement: to use materials science to prevent climate change. While, like most inspiring calls to action, this may seem simple on the face of it, it has proven to be a rich space for investigation and advancement. Research has covered a wide range of challenges, from materials engineering for more efficient and affordable solar cells, to regulating the temperature in buildings by controlling how much light passes through windows. The technical advances are only part of what Mike is talking about this year as he thinks about his group's research.

“It has been amazing to see how effective my students have been at addressing pain points for renewable energy and electrification in unique ways” explains McGehee. The companies that members of his team have gone on to build are making impacts across a wide range of challenges. Advancing technologies in everything from solar cells (Swift Solar, Tandem PV, Alion Energy, PLANT PV, Photara) and thermal storage materials (Antora Energy), through circuits that connect batteries in electric vehicles (CelLink) and battery materials (Molten Industries), to energy efficient windows (Tynt Technology), flexible OLED displays (Sinovia) and microLED displays for augmented reality eyewear (Raxium), to name but a few. This breadth of exploration can be traced to the development of problem-solving approaches that can be leveraged to work on many different problems. In many cases the graduates have gone on to tackle problems quite unrelated to the ones they addressed in their studies. This is enabled more by an attitude that fosters an agility to identify critical problems and work to solve them rather than simply seeking deep knowledge in one specific topic. To learn more about this we checked in with some of McGehee Group alumni below. To find out more about McGehee’s approach to research and innovation, make a plan to join us at the lecture on November 18, 2026.

CelLink, which was founded in 2011, are building some of the key fundamental building blocks of an electrified future. The technologies developed by CelLink are improving how electric vehicles and clean energy hardware are wired by replacing bulky, traditional copper wire systems with flat flexible circuits. This results in significant improvements in efficiency by reducing weight and size needs, integrating modern controls, and streamlining manufacturing. We caught up with Kevin Coakley, the first student in the McGehee group who graduated in 2004 and co-founded CelLink in 2011. “My career as an entrepreneur was hugely influence by my early experience in Mike’s group,” Kevin share with us. “From the day I joined the group, we needed to build an OLED and OPV lab on a tight budget and work together to invent and discover new device structures. It was a perfect training ground for a career in entrepreneurship and innovation.”

Craig Peters, who graduated from the McGehee group in 2011, was CEO of Raxium when they were acquired by Google in 2022. “Working with Mike was the foundation for my subsequent entrepreneurial ventures in deep tech” explains Peters. Raxium pioneered ultra-high-density MicroLED displays, addressing the core materials, hardware, performance, and manufacturing limitations for displays that were holding back consumer-grade augmented reality (AR) and mixed reality (MR) devices. “Mike provides freedom to explore, test, fail, and reinvent, while being there when you need him. He also has a strong sense for what problems are worth going after, how to get to the essence of these problems, and how to arrive at a set of simple questions and tasks that are actionable. This training establishes a perfect springboard into entrepreneurism in hard tech” said Craig. “A typical materials-based company can take 10-15 years to bring a new optoelectronic material to mass production. So going after the right problem is critical. You then need to break the problem down into critical questions, prioritize them and systematically try to address them. On top of this, you need to build and manage high performance teams and provide them with a similar ability to explore, test, fail, and pivot when needed. So much of this ties back to the environment and lessons Mike provides his students.”

Molten Industries, founded in 2021, is scaling a new technology that uses renewable electricity to convert methane or natural gas into clean hydrogen and battery-grade graphite, a critical material for lithium-ion batteries. Co-Founders Kevin Bush and Caleb Boyd graduated from the McGehee group in 2018 and 2020, respectively, where they worked in collaboration with researchers at the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (now The National Laboratory of the Rockies). “Mike consistently pointed us towards solving big-picture problems and answering bottleneck questions in research, an attitude that is equally important in building successful companies. Seeing the stories of other successful founders in the McGehee group made me think ‘I can do this too,’ and the network and camaraderie with those founders has been an invaluable asset to my own journey as a startup founder.”

Antalya, 13 November 2026 – African banks, businesses, and households are driving a surge in private climate finance, according to a new report which finds that private investment across the continent has more than tripled since 2019/20.

The third edition of the Landscape of Climate Finance in Africa, published by Climate Policy Initiative (CPI), FSD Africa, the government of Norway and the UK government, reveals that private climate investment reached USD 26.5 billion a year in 2023/24, with more than three-quarters (76%) coming from domestic sources.

African banks and businesses are leading the change. Commercial financial institutions accounted for almost half of the increase in private climate finance between 2021/22 and 2023/24, with corporate investment also rising substantially. The report links the rise to stronger climate engagement among African banks, growing regulatory attention to climate risk, and falling global costs for solar, wind and battery storage.

Meanwhile, household climate investment more than doubled to USD 5.1 billion a year, 19% of private climate finance, and accounted for over a fifth of the increase. Small-scale solar drove more than 90% of that growth, with household spending on solar PV rising nearly fivefold to USD 3.3 billion a year, highlighting the growing role of African households, alongside businesses and financial institutions in funding the continent’s clean energy transition.

The findings point to a significant shift in Africa’s climate finance landscape, which has traditionally been dominated by international public finance. But despite the growth in private investment, Africa still has the lowest proportion of private climate finance of any region in the world, at just 36% of total flows. International public finance remains the backbone, providing almost two-thirds of flows, and is increasingly catalytic: private finance mobilized by multilateral and bilateral development finance more than doubled since 2021/22, to USD 8.2 billion. Yet, the growth is uneven, international public climate finance to low-income African countries fell by 11%, even as funding to middle-income countries rose by 33%.

The report finds that closing the gap is not just a matter of increasing the volume of private finance but of building financial systems that can originate, prepare and finance climate investments at scale and tailored to each country. That means building the capacity of African financial institutions to originate and finance climate investments and keeping consumer finance channels such as pay-as-you-go models and local bank lending available and affordable, particularly in local currency. It also points to clear policy frameworks and risk-sharing mechanisms, such as those that have supported renewable energy, as models for other sectors.

Barbara Buchner, CEO of Climate Policy Initiative, said: “Africa’s climate finance has grown significantly, driven in large part by homegrown private investment. But the challenge is not only volume. African banks, insurers and pension funds manage around USD 3.2 trillion in assets, yet many projects are too small and fragmented for these investors to reach. Clear, predictable policy frameworks and investment vehicles can help bridge this gap, as parts of the renewable energy sector have shown.”

Mark Napier, CEO of FSD Africa said: “The trends in the report are consistent with the global picture: climate finance in Africa is increasingly being driven by the private sector. It shows that if we build well-functioning, sustainable financial markets we can unlock investment not just in clean energy but in other sectors of the green economy such as agriculture, housing and transport, creating vibrant markets that deliver jobs and basic services as well as climate benefits.”

Other key findings include:

Climate finance more than doubled to USD 74 billion annually in 2023/24 but remains far below the estimated USD 300–USD 572 billion needed each year for mitigation alone.

is still the bulk of Africa’s climate funding, accounting for almost two-thirds of flows. However, international public climate finance to low-income African countries fell by 11%, even as funding to middle-income countries rose by 33%.

Investment is concentrated in a handful of countries and sectors. Energy attracted USD 32.3 billion annually, while agriculture, forestry and other land use received just USD 6.5 billion. Middle-income countries received more than 80% of energy finance, while low-income countries saw slower.

Climate adaptation remains underfunded, accounting for just 21% of climate finance, down from 28% in 2021/22, despite growing climate risks.

The report calls for greater efforts to unlock African institutional investment and direct finance towards underserved countries and sectors, while maintaining vital international public funding.

text:
Last week, Democrats won historic majorities in the House and Senate, receiving an extraordinary mandate to take on the bad actors they campaigned against: President Donald Trump, the Republican Party, data centers, and Big Tech. This week, in their first major action since then, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and 21 other Democratic senators voted to fast-track a Republican bill that would eviscerate America’s bedrock environmental laws in order to, in Trump’s words, “codify our America First Energy Agenda” of building “Pipelines, Mines, and Power Plants faster than ever before” so that America remains “Number One” in data center construction.

So what can explain this almost unimaginable betrayal—and can it be stopped?

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, which the Senate is expected to vote on next week, has been framed as a compromise to make it easier to build both clean energy and fossil fuel infrastructure. It was developed behind closed doors by Senate Republicans and two Democrats, Sheldon Whitehouse and Martin Heinrich. But there was a fundamental mismatch in this secretive drafting process. The fossil fuel industry has been all in for permitting reform—indeed, it has long been the top priority of the American Petroleum Institute, the lobbying arm and political face of major oil and gas corporations. So Big Oil was involved in BAAJA’s drafting.

Whitehouse and Heinrich, by contrast, kept Democrats’ traditional allies in the dark—not just environmental groups, which are uniformly opposed to the legislation, but tribal organizations (many of which released a joint statement condemning BAAJA provisions that “fundamentally undermine Tribal sovereignty” and “threaten sacred sites and cultural resources”); racial justice organizations like NAACP (which warned that BAAJA “directly threatens the health, safety, and future of Black and frontline communities”); and anti-ICE groups like Detention Watch Network (which condemned how BAAJA will “pave a path for detention expansion by making immigration detention facilities easier to build and much harder to stop”).

The upshot is that the staff of two Democratic senatorial offices were alone at the negotiating table, while Republicans had the full lobbying, analyzing, and bill-drafting capacity of the entire fossil fuel industry. So of course the Democrats got rolled. And BAAJA reflects this asymmetry in the severe lopsidedness of its ostensible “compromise.”

The positive pitch from BAAJA’s Democratic-leaning cheerleaders, like Democratic strategist Adam Jentleson’s Searchlight Institute, is that the legislation will be a huge boon to Democrats’ affordability and climate goals by lowering energy costs and supercharging the build-out of renewables. These claims are dubious at best. It’s essentially impossible to confidently model the full climate effects of a legislative package like BAAJA, but current analyses include predictions out of Purdue University that BAAJA will actually increase both “domestic energy-related greenhouse gas emissions” and “domestic mortality attributable to air pollution from fossil fuels.” The most optimistic modeling, from Rhodium Group, predicts a range: from BAAJA having zero effect on greenhouse gas emissions to a best-case scenario of reducing U.S. emissions by a negligible 4 percent by 2040. Rhodium’s modeling on affordability is similarly laughable, with a best-case scenario reduction of energy bills by $4–$7 a month by 2040.

So that’s what Democrats stand to gain from supporting this Republican bill. What are they giving up? From an environmental perspective, the costs are almost unimaginable. BAAJA severely weakens the Clean Water Act, robbing states and tribes of their ability to protect water quality and require adequate safeguards for activities that pollute or destroy water resources. It practically nullifies the Endangered Species Act by delegating its core responsibilities to the states, most of which either oppose the act’s wildlife protections or lack the expertise and resources to adequately fulfill these obligations. And it essentially repeals the National Environmental Policy Act, the bedrock environmental law that gives the public a voice in decisions that impact the environment, by prohibiting the enforcement of NEPA violations. These three legal frameworks are responsible for most the improvements in water quality, green space, and wildlife recovery in our country over the last half-century.

And that’s just the beginning. Other provisions of BAAJA go to even greater lengths to radically lock in fossil fuel development far into the future. The “disparate treatment” section of the bill effectively makes the permitting decisions of the Trump administration permanent. In the words of David Bookbinder, an environmental lawyer who has worked for both the left-leaning Sierra Club and the libertarian Niskanen Center, “The result of making these energy permitting policies permanent is that future administrations will be unable to effectively reduce GHG emissions.” BAAJA also guarantees not just the construction of fossil fuel projects but also their “operation at full capacity,” permanently blocking any future administration from regulating energy infrastructure.

If you’re thinking this legislative assault on the environment sounds like it was pulled straight out of Project 2025, well, you’re right—and the authors of Project 2025 are strong supporters of the bill. BAAJA is also the top legislative priority of API, ExxonMobil, Chevron, Shell, BP, ConocoPhillips, and other fossil fuel giants. So no wonder climate advocates have been sounding the alarm—and not just progressive leaders like Bill McKibben, but moderate climate advocates like Jody Freeman, John Podesta, and Al Gore, who recently warned that “now is not the time to give the Trump administration freer rein to double down on fossil fuels—which is what President Trump would surely do.” This point is crucial: Trump will be implementing BAAJA if it passes, and he very clearly has no intention of allowing the “supercharge clean energy” side of the bargain to move forward. Indeed, just this week Trump reiterated that he is not going to approve any wind turbines, even if Democrats submit to his desire to “codify our America First Energy Agenda” by passing BAAJA.

Of course, Big Oil companies aren’t the only villains that want to see this Republican legislation pass. Big Tech is also all in, from Marc Andreessen’s tech venture firm to ITI, the trade association for OpenAI, Nvidia, Meta, Amazon, Google, and other tech giants, which praised BAAJA as “essential to America’s ability to build, compete, and lead—especially in the AI era.” Advocates of BAAJA, including Trump, have tried to obscure this support by pointing to provisions in the legislation that would require data center developers to pay for the grid and transmission upgrades their projects require. But Americans have made overwhelmingly clear—not least through the massive victories they just handed to Democrats who pledged to support data center bans and moratoriums—that they don’t just want AI data centers to help pay for some of their own costs. More than anything, they want the ability to say “no” to these monstrosities coming into their communities. They want to be able to decide their own futures, rather than having Big Tech billionaires make those decisions for them.

BAAJA is a direct response to this democratic backlash. AI corporations want to cut the public out of these decision-making processes, and BAAJA is laser-focused on overcoming the two most important roadblocks the public can use to check the explosion of Big Tech’s data center build-out: permitting and easy access to fossil gas. (Abigail Dillen, the president of Earthjustice, recently explained exactly how BAAJA enables “the dirtiest version of the data center build-out to move even faster.”)

The antidemocratic betrayal here really cannot be overstated. Democrats just won their biggest congressional majorities in 50 years—to say nothing of victories in places like Texas, where Democrats swept every single statewide office and flipped the state House—in large part by promising to respond to the massive voter backlash against the AI industry’s out-of-control expansion of hyperscale data centers. Just a week later, Democrats’ Senate leadership team—not just Schumer but incoming Majority Whip Brian Schatz and DSCC chair Kirsten Gillibrand—joined Trump and the GOP to pass a catastrophic giveaway to the Big Tech billionaires who spent hundreds of millions of dollars trying to defeat their incoming colleagues, directly rebuking the massive voter mandate their party just received to stand up to those billionaires.

And that, maybe more than anything, helps explain the timing of this push. It’s not just that BAAJA was developed without hearings or any of the other review procedures that a bill of this magnitude would normally go through. It’s that Democrats like Whitehouse, Heinrich, Schumer, and Schatz are trying to ram this Project 2025 atrocity through a GOP-controlled lame-duck session weeks before Democrats take control. BAAJA advocates have argued that the legislation needs to move now because Trump would never sign a bill passed by a Democratic Congress, but that’s an absurd claim. We have no idea how Trump will respond to the Democratic majority. There are myriad ways he could be brought to the table on a clean transmission bill—name the legislation after him, insert some shady Trump Organization business opportunity in the text, send in Zohran Mamdani to sell it ...

The reason top Senate Democrats are working to pass BAAJA now, before their majority is seated, is that this rotten handout to Big Oil and Big Tech—and massive “screw you” to the voters who just gave Democrats their majority—would never pass in a Democratic Congress. BAAJA is a radical MAGA bill that takes a sledgehammer to America’s most important environmental laws, permanently locks us into an expansion of fossil fuels, disempowers local communities’ ability to decide their own futures, and opens the door to a radical expansion of methane-powered hyperscale data centers. It needs to pass now because it is fundamentally a Republican bill.

BAAJA is on a fast track through the Senate, with a final vote only days away. But we must not accept this as a done deal. The Congressional Progressive Caucus, which represents more than 100 members of Congress, just announced its opposition to the legislation. So did the Democratic attorneys general from California, Colorado, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New York, Oregon, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, and Washington, D.C., who sent a letter asking Senate leadership to halt the upcoming votes on BAAJA in order to “protect our natural resources, historic and tribal sites, and state regulatory prerogatives.” And it’s not just elected officials who can weigh in. Everyone can make a difference by calling and emailing their representatives and senators and looking out for further mobilization opportunities. If all else fails, at the very least, we must make sure that Democrats understand that their voters are paying attention to who is selling out our futures to Big Oil and Big Tech—and that 2028 is not so far away.

text:
The Ugliest Stocks in the Market Just Got a Very Expensive Vote of Confidence

X-Energy XE reported a 118% increase in third-quarter revenue and grant income as engineering activity expanded, while executives highlighted a construction permit for a proposed advanced nuclear project at Dow’s manufacturing site in Texas.

The permit, issued by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission to Dow subsidiary Long Mott Energy, allows construction of the project at Seadrift but does not represent a decision to build it. CEO Clay Sell said Dow is expected to consider a preliminary investment decision in 2027, with full-scale nuclear construction following a final investment decision.

MarketBeat Week in Review – 06/29 - 07/03

X-Energy reported $66.3 million in total revenue and grant income for the third quarter of 2026, consisting of $51.5 million in services revenue and $14.8 million in grant income tied to the Dow demonstration reactor. Operating expenses rose 139% from a year earlier to $169.9 million.

Dow project moves through regulatory review

Sell said the NRC issued the construction permit more than a month ahead of schedule. He described it as the first NRC construction permit for a high-temperature gas-cooled reactor in nearly 60 years and the first approval for a pebble bed gas reactor.

Xcel Energy Stock Offers Stability as Electricity Demand Builds

Although Long Mott Energy was the permit applicant and recipient, X-Energy led the reactor licensing work on its behalf, Sell said. The company is continuing engineering, procurement and development work while preparing an operating license application.

Sell said Dow’s preliminary decision will depend on its own formal review process, including assessments of engineering, cost targets and operating and maintenance assumptions. X-Energy’s reactor design will not be complete before that preliminary decision, he said, but the company intends to finish it before construction begins.

The CEO said the first project is expected to come online in the early 2030s. X-Energy anticipates an operating license review of about 18 months and may file the application roughly two years before commissioning.

Sell said the company expects to reuse engineering and safety analysis from the Dow project in subsequent applications. The Dow permit took 17 months from docketing to issuance; Sell said unofficial guidance from the NRC indicated an objective of bringing subsequent reviews into a range of six to 12 months. He identified supply-chain readiness, rather than regulatory approval, as a major opportunity to shorten future project schedules.

AEP partnership expands project pipeline

In October, X-Energy announced a joint development agreement with American Electric Power and Amazon for a proposed 12-unit Xe-100 project in Sullivan County, Indiana. The project would provide approximately 960 megawatts of generating capacity and would redevelop a former coal-fueled generation site, using existing infrastructure and its PJM grid connection.

The early work includes site characterization, feasibility studies and preparation for a future construction permit application. Sell said the parties are defining the information needed to make decisions about the project’s next stages.

X-Energy is also advancing the initial phase of front-end engineering for its project with Energy Northwest in Washington state, another deployment opportunity supported by Amazon. Fluor and the Cascade Nuclear Partners consortium are working on elements of the plant design, Sell said.

Across a pipeline of 144 reactors, the company has up to 40 Xe-100 reactors associated with identified project plans and development partnerships involving Dow, Energy Northwest, AEP and Centrica, according to Sell. In the United Kingdom, the Xe-100 design was accepted into the Generic Design Assessment process in September, beginning a regulatory evaluation ahead of any site-specific approvals.

Fuel manufacturing and testing advance

Vertical construction of TX-1, X-Energy’s first commercial-scale fuel facility at its Oak Ridge, Tennessee, campus, was completed on schedule, Sell said. Interior construction and equipment installation are next, alongside work on a graphite matrix powder facility that will support fuel pebble production.

The company is also advancing designs for a second planned fuel facility, TX-2, and a dedicated research and development center. Sell said X-Energy’s TRISO-X business intends to pursue fuel customers beyond the company’s own reactor fleet.

At the X-Energy Technology Advancement Center in Frederick, Maryland, the company is expanding capabilities to test and manufacture reactor components. Sell said initial testing is underway on graphite and other components, while a planned helium test loop will be used to validate mechanical systems over the next couple of years. He said the facility’s work is not a significant input to Dow’s next investment decision.

Expenses and cash use increase

CFO Daniel Gross said third-quarter operating expenses included $93.6 million in direct costs and $76 million in selling, general and administrative expenses. The latter included $22 million in noncash equity-based compensation and costs associated with design and site preparation for TX-2.

Net cash used in operating activities increased to $51.2 million from $30.8 million a year earlier. Capital expenditures totaled $71.8 million, including spending on construction projects such as TX-1; the Department of Energy reimbursed $27.8 million in cash during the quarter, Gross said.

X-Energy ended September with approximately $1.8 billion in cash and investments and no outstanding debt. Gross said the Department of Energy had reimbursed the company $618 million under the Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program as of Sept. 30.

Sell also said TRISO-X President Joel Duling plans to retire from his full-time role but will remain a part-time senior adviser. The company is searching for a successor and expects to provide an update in the coming months.

About X-Energy XE

X-energy is an advanced nuclear technology company developing small modular reactors and nuclear fuel. Its flagship design, the Xe-100, is a high-temperature, gas-cooled reactor intended to provide electricity and industrial process heat. The company's reactor design uses pebble-shaped fuel containing TRISO-X particles, which are engineered to retain radioactive materials at high temperatures. Founded in 2009, X-energy has worked with government and commercial partners to advance its reactor and fuel technologies.

text:
Supports clean energy

Newly elected Democrats should make clean energy a top priority, not just to fight climate change but to lower energy bills for Americans. Solar and wind are now among the cheapest sources of new electricity, and unlike fossil fuels, they aren't subject to volatile fuel prices.

Expanding renewable energy, modernizing the electric grid and investing in battery storage can increase electricity supplies, reduce dependence on expensive natural gas and protect consumers from unpredictable price spikes. Clean energy also creates jobs and strengthens our energy independence.
