ONLY 99¢

Democrats should champion policies that accelerate solar and wind development, remove barriers to clean energy projects and ensure savings reach consumers. Americans shouldn't have to choose between affordable electricity and a healthier climate. Clean energy offers a path to both, and Democrats should lead the way.

Andrea Christgau, Keller

Worried about water shortages

Most Americans acknowledge the link between climate change and disastrous weather events (although maybe not the role of human agency). This consensus is probably due to the extensive news coverage extreme weather events receive. Even a relatively localized one may make national news.

Water shortages don’t get the same sort of in-our-faces coverage as, for example, tornadoes do, but they, too, are linked to climate change and threaten outcomes at least as catastrophic. Given a warming planet and population growth, water shortages are going to happen. Period. If left unchecked, “catastrophic,” even “cataclysmic,” hardly begins to cover it.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Conservation is imperative. Find me the person who says otherwise. Still, there are those who ignore facts, who argue in favor of the expanding the capabilities of artificial intelligence, and who support the construction of data centers, water hogs that they are.

Those people say the U.S. economy generally and the stock market specifically will take a hit if data centers are not built and China will surpass us in AI technology.

Be that as it may, those things are survivable. A world, a region, a cornfield without enough water is not. Period.

Joan Ravkind Susman, North Dallas

Texans should be appalled

This is (still) not what democracy looks like

Lost in all the “blue wave” talk is the fact that Texas representation to the Texas Senate and U.S. House still fails to accurately reflect the people of Texas.

Yes, Texas Democrats were able to withstand the 2025 gerrymandering by the GOP Legislature in four out of five targeted districts. But let’s not miss the fact that the GOP has claimed 24 of the 38 Texas U.S. House seats, despite a majority of voters choosing Democrats. This was achieved — and solidified — by the legacy gerrymandering executed by the Texas Legislature prior to 2025.

And while only half of Texas Senate seats were contested this year, the fact that 19 of the 31 seats remain in the hands of the GOP is evidence of how their strategic selection of Texas voters will permit them disproportionate power and control in the next (and future) legislative sessions. This includes the ability to maintain these undemocratic districts moving forward.

All Texans should be appalled at this.

John Quinn, Allen

Working together

Re: “Party’s leaders can look higher — Talarico, Hinojosa could build political organizations; GOP must chart new path,” by Gromer Jeffers Jr., Monday Metro column.

Jeffers states Speaker Dustin Burrows and his allies could help determine the strength of the GOP’s resistance to state Rep. Senfronia Thompson, the incoming House speaker, and the Democrats. What happened to working together for the good of Texans? This is exactly the kind of partisan attitude that will never allow the Texas Legislature to pass any meaningful legislation.

Maxwell Kashiwa, Far North Dallas

A gag reflex?

Re: “Voters reject billions in bonds, tax measures — Officials face pressure to scale back projects and better justify costs,” Nov. 5 Metro & Business story.

Dallas County residents voted overwhelmingly for the blue team yet still voted against a tax proposition to raise $100 million to bolster homeless services. The selfishness and surprising lack of compassion for those living among us without shelter or health services from the very same electorate that has railed against the Trump administration for being mean and cruel to illegal immigrants is very discouraging. It leads me to ask was the midterm election a blue wave, or just an emotional gag reflex against all things Trump?

John Riggs, Highland Park

New leadership needed

I want to voice my support for the newly elected Democrats who do not support House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries or Sen. Chuck Schumer. We need new leadership who will hold the president accountable and take bold action to begin repairing the damage his criminal administration has wrought.

Robert Lavery, Grand Prairie

To serve the people

Politics in the era of President Donald Trump has disillusioned many of us. Until last week’s election, the darkness of hate and its manifestations from Washington to Austin often seemed insurmountable.

However, and as in the past, we, the people, had enough, and we voiced our views with our votes. Regardless of our motivations, hope for the future of Texas and America was restored last week.

And yes, there is much to be done to repair the damage imposed by the current administrations, but our newly elected leaders can embrace their responsibilities with a different interpretation of governance: to serve the people. It’s a better day.

Bill Lively, North Dallas

Thoughtful and eloquent

Sunday’s Opinion pages were spot on. Thoughtful and eloquent describes them well. And, I’m not a Democrat. Your analysis of the stupidity, arrogance and ennui of the Republican Party was displayed in column after column. Well done.

text:
The global electric vehicle market is becoming increasingly competitive, with Tesla (NASDAQ: TSLA) and BYD (OTC: BYDDY) emerging as two of the industry's dominant players. However, despite their market leadership, both companies face significant financial challenges that could shape investment returns heading into 2027.

BYD has established itself as a global manufacturing powerhouse, generating more revenue than Tesla through its vertically integrated automotive and battery businesses. Tesla, meanwhile, continues to command a premium valuation based on its technological leadership and ambitions in autonomous driving.

While both companies offer substantial long-term growth potential, BYD's negative free cash flow and Tesla's elevated valuation raise important questions about which stock offers the more attractive investment opportunity.

The case for BYD

China-based BYD has established itself as one of the world's largest electric vehicle manufacturers, leveraging a vertically integrated business model spanning automobile manufacturing, battery production, electronics, and energy storage. By producing many of its own critical components, including battery cells, BYD maintains greater control over manufacturing costs and supply chains. The company is also rapidly expanding internationally, reducing its reliance on China's increasingly competitive automotive market.

Over the 12 months ended September 30, 2026, BYD generated approximately $120.6 billion in revenue and $4.7 billion in net income. Although its trailing revenue growth has been sluggish, its latest quarterly results showed signs of improvement, with revenue increasing 13.6% and net income climbing 28.1% year over year. Strong overseas sales helped offset weaker domestic demand, highlighting the growing importance of international markets to its long-term expansion.

However, BYD's aggressive growth strategy comes at a substantial financial cost. The company ended 2025 with a debt-to-equity ratio of approximately 0.7 and a current ratio near 0.8, indicating relatively limited short-term liquidity. Free cash flow was negative by roughly $14 billion, as heavy capital expenditures significantly exceeded operating cash generation.

The case for Tesla

Tesla (NASDAQ: TSLA) has built a global electric vehicle business around direct-to-consumer sales, proprietary software, and an extensive charging network. Beyond automobiles, Tesla is increasingly investing in autonomous driving, robotics, and energy storage as future sources of growth.

Over the 12 months ended September 30, 2026, Tesla generated approximately $103.6 billion in revenue, up 8.3% year over year, and $3.2 billion in net income. However, profitability remains under pressure. Third-quarter revenue was essentially flat compared with the prior year, while net income declined 43%, reflecting rising operating expenses and substantial investments in artificial intelligence and new technologies.

Tesla's balance sheet provides an important advantage over BYD. The company ended 2025 with a debt-to-equity ratio near 0.1 and a current ratio of approximately 2.2, indicating relatively modest leverage and substantial short-term liquidity. It also generated $6.2 billion in free cash flow, compared with BYD's significant cash outflows. By September 2026, Tesla's cash and short-term investments had climbed to $45.4 billion, providing considerable financial flexibility to fund its ambitious growth initiatives.

Risk profile comparison

BYD faces mounting pressure from intense price competition in China's electric vehicle market, which threatens profit margins even as sales volumes expand. Its aggressive international expansion also introduces regulatory and geopolitical risks, particularly as tariffs and trade restrictions complicate access to major Western markets. Meanwhile, substantial capital expenditures and relatively limited short-term liquidity could strain its balance sheet if demand weakens or overseas expansion fails to deliver expected returns.

Tesla faces a different set of challenges. Increasing competition from Chinese automakers threatens its market share and pricing power, while the expiration of U.S. federal EV purchase incentives could weigh on domestic demand. The company's growing emphasis on autonomous driving and robotics also introduces considerable execution and regulatory risks, particularly as it works to commercialize its Cybercab platform.

Valuation comparison

BYD looks cheaper due to its lower P/S ratio, which measures price against sales over the past twelve months, and its lower Forward P/E.

MetricBYDTeslaForward P/E14.7x232.3xP/S ratio0.7x14.9x

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

Which stock would I buy for 2027?

While EV adoption continues to expand globally, affordability is becoming a critical competitive advantage, particularly as government incentives decline and manufacturers compete more aggressively on pricing.

Against this backdrop, BYD looks like the better buy. Its vertically integrated manufacturing model, extensive lineup of affordable electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles, and growing international footprint position it to capture demand across a broader range of consumer budgets. Although its negative free cash flow and exposure to China's intensely competitive automotive market remain concerns, its valuation offers a substantial margin for uncertainty. At just 14.7 times forward earnings and 0.7 times sales, BYD trades at a fraction of Tesla's 232.3 times earnings and 14.9 times sales.

Tesla maintains a stronger balance sheet and considerable upside potential from autonomous driving, robotics, and energy storage. However, its valuation already reflects extraordinary expectations for these businesses, many of which have yet to demonstrate profitability at scale. With consumer demand increasingly favoring affordability and global competition intensifying, I favor BYD's manufacturing advantages, broader product lineup, and significantly more attractive valuation heading into 2027.

text:
COLORADO SPRINGS, Colo., Nov. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Centu…









VinFast VF 8

VinFast

While most electric vehicle (EV) battery warranties come with strict mileage restrictions, VinFast is taking a distinctly different approach. Its 10-year, unlimited-mileage battery warranty offers American drivers one less thing to calculate as the odometer ticks upward.

IRVINE, Calif. , Nov. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Consider two drivers purchasing identical electric vehicles on the same day. One covers a modest 10,000 miles annually, while the other logs 25,000 miles between long commutes, family obligations, and weekend getaways. Four years in, both vehicles remain reliably on the road—yet only one driver still enjoys battery warranty coverage.



Under a typical eight-year or 100,000-mile battery warranty, the high-mileage driver has already reached the coverage ceiling. Meanwhile, the lower-mileage driver retains protection for another four years before the time limit expires.

It highlights a subtle paradox in vehicle ownership: the more heavily you rely on your EV, the sooner you risk losing coverage on its most critical component.

Decoding the Fine Print

America's reliance on driving is clear, though yearly mileage varies significantly. Federal Highway Administration data indicates that the average U.S. motor vehicle logged approximately 11,071 miles in 2024 1 . However, lengthy commutes, frequent interstate travel, and active lifestyles push that figure much higher for millions of households.

High mileage typically indicates a dependable vehicle doing its job, but standard warranty structures present a catch. Most automotive warranties operate on dual limits—years and mileage—expiring whichever threshold is crossed first.

While an eight-year/100,000-mile policy sounds generous on paper, its real-world lifespan hinges entirely on driving habits:

The irony is clear: those who utilize their vehicles the most receive the shortest window of protection.

Granted, an expired warranty does not mean a battery is nearing the end of its operational life. Industry research demonstrates that modern EV batteries are engineered to perform well past their warranty windows, often outlasting the vehicle itself. Nevertheless, physical durability and financial peace of mind are distinct. Even with high-end battery design, having a long-term safety net against unexpected issues provides vital reassurance.

Removing the Mileage Ceiling

VinFast offers an alternate path for American EV buyers. Available on its VF 8 and VF 9 electric SUVs, VinFast's 10-year battery warranty eliminates the mileage limit entirely under standard personal use. Complementing this is a new-vehicle limited warranty of up to 10 years or 125,000 miles (subject to standard terms and conditions).

Under this model, logging 25,000 miles a year—accumulating 250,000 miles over a decade—will never prematurely void the battery warranty, simply because no ceiling exists. Long-distance commuters no longer need to track the odometer with concern, and frequent road-trippers can travel without worrying that extra miles are quietly eroding their coverage.

Beyond the Battery

This warranty framework forms part of a broader ownership package designed to streamline EV adoption. Alongside its comprehensive vehicle and battery protection, VinFast provides:

By combining long-term financial protection with practical convenience, VinFast aligns its warranty coverage with the reality of how Americans actually drive: without limits.

About VinFast

description:

There is a massive dependency on China for many necessary items, such as consumer goods, pharmaceutical inputs, and rare earth metals.

text:
Executive Summary

The U.S. was a production giant in the twentieth century, whose industrial capacity exceeded that of every other participant in World War II. Despite this power, the nation decided to offshore much of its manufacturing might. As a result, China now leads the U.S. in manufacturing output. There is a massive dependency on China for many necessary items, such as consumer goods, pharmaceutical inputs, and rare earth metals. The downstream effect of this is an inability to react to conflicts across the globe for fear of upsetting China and being cut off from goods on which there is such a dependence. The U.S. needs to reindustrialize.

There are barriers to reviving domestic manufacturing. The National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) has put up roadblocks to any industrial buildout, with permitting processes that take years to complete, and environmental remedies that are egregious. California’s High-Speed Rail project, first approved by voters in 2008, has yet to lay any operational track. NEPA has done considerably more harm than good for the outlook of the environment, delaying clean energy projects by years while environmental impact statements are prepared.

There is a solution to these maladies. The interstate compact, a tool originating from the earliest days of the U.S., may provide the answer to reindustrializing quickly and efficiently. States can enter into operational agreements that allow cooperation over certain issues. Compacts were further empowered by a 2015 law, the Fixing America’s Surface Transportation (FAST) Act. In a provision titled FAST-41, the “consent of Congress is given for 3 or more contiguous States to enter into an interstate compact establishing regional infrastructure development agencies to facilitate authorization and review of covered projects, under State law or in the exercise of delegated permitting authority described under section 41006, that will advance infrastructure development, production, and generation within the States that are parties to the compact.”

Effectively, three or more contiguous states have congressional consent to set up interstate compacts to deal with facets of reindustrialization, superseding any federal regulations in the permitting process, so long as the interstate compact deals with advancing infrastructure development, production, and generation. This blanket consent is a solution for state-level policymakers and manufacturing companies who want to turn the tide against the consequences of offshoring U.S. industrial might.

text:
World Economic Forum, public.affairs@weforum.org

A new World Economic Forum report highlights technologies that could deliver cleaner, more secure energy and expand equitable access to reliable power.

Several of the technologies are moving closer to deployment, including batteries made from abundant materials, industrial thermal storage and software that allows households and electric vehicles to support power grids.

Released alongside COP31, the report identifies actions governments, businesses and investors can take to accelerate adoption across homes, factories and power grids.

Read the report here.

Geneva, Switzerland/Antalya, Türkiye, 13 November 2026 – As world leaders gather at COP31 to advance global climate action, the World Economic Forum today released Top 10 Emerging Technologies for Planetary Health: Energy Edition, highlighting innovations that could help transform the future of energy.

Produced in collaboration with Frontiers, the report examines 10 technologies that could make energy cleaner, more reliable and more secure by 2030. It comes amid volatile energy prices, concentrated supply chains and rising demand for electric vehicles, data centres and extreme heat, while storms, droughts and heatwaves place further strain on power grids. The urgency is underscored by the breach of seven of the nine planetary boundaries, according to the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research.

“Energy is not abstract. It determines if families can keep their homes cool during a heatwave, whether businesses can stay open and whether children grow up with clean air,” said Sebastian Buckup, Managing Director, World Economic Forum. “That means clean energy alone is not enough. A technology that is expensive and relies on limited resources will not scale, and one that doesn’t scale won’t change anything for the people who need it.”

The 10 technologies are:

Calcined-clay limestone cement (LC3): Cement, the glue in concrete, is produced by baking limestone and clay at extreme heat, which releases large amounts of carbon dioxide. LC3 processes limestone and clay differently and reduces the need for high-temperature processing, lowering emissions from the construction of roads, bridges, homes and other infrastructure.

Virtual power plants and grids: Software links home batteries, electric cars and smart thermostats so they work together as a coordinated energy system. During periods of peak demand, this could reduce pressure on the grid and limit reliance on carbon-intensive backup generation.

Abundant materials batteries: Using widely available materials such as sodium, zinc and iron instead of lithium and cobalt, whose supplies are concentrated in fewer countries, these batteries can offer better performance in cold conditions, greater fire resistance and longer-duration storage, helping keep homes and businesses powered when sunlight or wind is limited.

Thermal energy storage (heat batteries): Heat batteries can absorb surplus or low-cost renewable energy, including wind and solar, and store it as heat in simple materials such as sand or brick. Factories can then use that heat instead of burning gas or coal, potentially reducing emissions and reliance on imported fuels.

Perovskite-silicon tandem solar cells: These solar panels add a second light-catching layer on top of silicon, enabling them to convert more sunlight into electricity. This could allow homes, businesses and solar farms to generate more power from the same roof area or patch of land.

Advanced subsea HVDC interconnectors: Undersea high-voltage direct current (HVDC) power cables carry electricity between countries, helping transfer surplus renewable power such as wind and solar power to where it is needed. They could improve energy security and help reduce exposure to price volatility when weather conditions vary between regions.

Modular nuclear reactors: These are smaller nuclear reactors built in factories and assembled on site, rather than custom-built over many years. They could provide a continuous supply of low-carbon electricity to cities, data centres and remote communities, potentially reducing reliance on gas or diesel.

Building-integrated photovoltaics: Solar cells are built into roofs, walls and windows, allowing buildings to generate electricity. This could enable cities to produce clean power close to where it is used, without requiring additional land for separate solar installations.

Floating offshore wind: Wind turbines sit on floating platforms anchored like ships, so they can be placed far out at sea where the winds are strongest. This could open up a new source of clean power for coastal regions and islands.

Next-generation lithium batteries: These batteries store more energy at lower weight, with some replacing flammable liquids with solid materials. They could extend electric vehicle range, reduce drone weight and improve battery safety.

These technologies deliver the greatest impact when deployed together. For example, subsea cables are more valuable when batteries can store the electricity they carry, while heat batteries can absorb surplus power only when a smart grid can direct that power to them. Together, they could make energy systems more resilient by addressing three interconnected challenges: generating enough power, moving it where it is needed and storing it until demand rises.

Decisions in the coming years will determine whether these technologies deliver benefits at scale. Governments can accelerate adoption through clear standards and purchasing rules, opening electricity markets to household batteries and thermal storage, and investing in infrastructure for wind farms and power cables. These measures can give businesses the confidence to expand manufacturing, build equipment that works across systems and source critical materials from more places.

“Many of the energy solutions we need already exist in labs. The challenge is getting them into homes, factories, and power grids fast enough to matter,” said Frederick Fenter, Chief Executive Editor of Frontiers. “Open science speeds this up by letting engineers, business leaders and governments build on shared research. This report puts trusted evidence in the hands of those deciding how to strengthen energy security while reducing harm to the climate.”

The report uses a multi-stage process, beginning with an AI-enabled discovery tool that screened and ranked 80 technologies against criteria including readiness, deployment potential and planetary impact. An advisory committee of experts from 10 countries then assessed a shortlist and helped shape the final selection. The process was designed to identify technologies with the potential to move beyond the laboratory and deliver broad, real-world benefits.

title: Solar PAC got revenge on clean energy's enemies in Congress - Canary Media
description:
Before this election cycle, it was hard to identify any politician who feared the solar industry.
The super PAC, funded and led by solar entrepreneurs and investors, emerged during the midterm primaries with pledges to spend millions of dollars on attack ads against politicians who undermined clean energy policy.
The last two sessions of Congress delivered historic highs followed by historic lows for the clean energy industry, emphasizing the value of not just passing policy but also making it stick.
That’s where ITC’s retributive style has the most to offer, and its well-publicized results will still be on file if a future Congress has a chance to revisit laws that help the clean energy industry thrive.
Election season never really stops, however, and the 2028 presidential primary will offer high-impact opportunities to push candidates to support clean energy, or hound them for past attacks against it.
text:
Before this election cycle, it was hard to identify any politician who feared the solar industry. The Invest in Tomorrow Coalition PAC set out to change that, and now has a roster of wins to back up its threats.

The super PAC, funded and led by solar entrepreneurs and investors, emerged during the midterm primaries with pledges to spend millions of dollars on attack ads against politicians who undermined clean energy policy. ITC got the outcomes it wanted in all six primaries it targeted. Its ads didn’t mention renewables, but instead used messages that tested well with voters — for instance blasting archconservative members of Congress for not being MAGA enough.

In the general election, ITC engaged in 17 congressional races, many of them in districts that President Donald Trump won by double digits, said Tom Matzzie, who chairs the PAC. ITC saw its desired outcome in 13 of those races, counting the apparent, though not totally final, loss by Republican Lauren Boebert in Colorado’s 4th District. ITC’s targets won election in four cases: Arizona’s 2nd District, Florida’s 13th, Florida’s 27th, and New York’s 21st.

“We definitely sent a message that we can make an impact no matter where you are,” Matzzie said. Of the Republicans who signed a letter in May 2025 calling to ​“fully repeal” the Inflation Reduction Act, 40% won’t be returning to their jobs in Congress.

The PAC lost its perfect hit rate, but after spending $17 million across the election cycle, it’s on track for 19 wins out of 23 races, or 83% success.

ITC wasn’t solely responsible for all Republican losses. The group exploited a political environment that had soured on unified GOP control of Washington, amid rising costs, an open-ended war in Iran that disrupted the global energy trade, novel and highly lucrative forms of corruption, and masked federal operatives attacking immigrants and citizens alike in the streets of American cities.

But the group demonstrated a knack for homing in on its targets’ weaknesses and amplifying them to voters who might not have gotten the message otherwise. The PAC also frequently trolled the candidates to get under their skin. After the election, the group issued press statements calling Brandon Herrera, who lost in Texas’ 23rd, ​“one of the most despicable candidates we’ve ever seen run for office,” and saying of the incumbent in New Jersey’s 2nd, ​“Jeff Van Drew always looked out for Jeff Van Drew, and now he can do it full time.”

In several races, ITC’s targets ended up corroborating the group’s effectiveness, by giving interviews venting about how the PAC was making reelection harder for them. Boebert recently guest-hosted ​“The Matt Gaetz Show” — a conservative talk show — and spent some of that time in the spotlight criticizing the solar PAC for obscuring its true policy aim behind ads on other topics.

To maximize its impact, the PAC deliberately chose races where promising Democratic candidates weren’t getting much outside funding. It became the biggest spender in Indiana’s 5th District, dropping more money on ads than either candidate’s campaign mustered. After the Republican lost, the group released a braggadocious statement to the press: ​“Tell Victoria Spartz. We want her to know it was us.”

While that assertion would be tough to prove, the PAC’s founders previously told Canary Media that their goal is to establish narrative influence: If members of Congress believe that voting to strip incentives from the solar industry will cost them in their next election, they may think twice about it next time. Now that nearly all the PAC’s targets, many of whom hail from the ultraconservative House Freedom Caucus, have indeed lost their jobs, the threat is credible.

The last two sessions of Congress delivered historic highs followed by historic lows for the clean energy industry, emphasizing the value of not just passing policy but also making it stick. That’s where ITC’s retributive style has the most to offer, and its well-publicized results will still be on file if a future Congress has a chance to revisit laws that help the clean energy industry thrive.

“Our overall hope is we can come to a place of peace with politicians of both parties and move forward,” Matzzie said. ​“I’d much rather our industry was boring.”

For the next few years, at least, the diminished Freedom Caucus won’t have the sway it exerted over the last two years, when Republicans had a threadbare majority. Battles over energy policy will now unfold within a pro-clean-energy Democratic caucus.

Election season never really stops, however, and the 2028 presidential primary will offer high-impact opportunities to push candidates to support clean energy, or hound them for past attacks against it.

description: Electric vehicles are increasingly likely to be included in the domestic production tax credit introduced to protect and nurture strategic industries at…
text:
Electric vehicles are increasingly likely to be included in the domestic production tax credit introduced to protect and nurture strategic industries at home. The government initially left EVs out of the eligible items, but as the National Assembly debates the amendment, lawmakers are moving to add them.
As of the 13th, four amendments to the Act on Restriction on Special Cases Concerning Taxation that would include EVs in the domestic production tax credit have been introduced, according to political circles. Lawmakers from both the ruling and opposition parties have signed on. More than 50 lawmakers are listed as sponsors. A National Assembly official said, "There is no disagreement between the parties about including EVs among the eligible items."
An electric-vehicle charging station at a building in Seoul./Courtesy of News1
The domestic production tax credit cuts taxes when key processes are carried out in Korea and domestic spending accounts for a certain share of eligible production costs. Unlike the existing investment tax credit, it ties credits to domestic production or sales performance, focusing on strengthening Korea's industrial supply chains and production base.
In the tax reform plan the government released in August, six sectors were designated for support: solar power, wind power, secondary batteries, semiconductors, key materials, and AI robot parts. EVs, which had been expected to make the list, were left out. The government cited indirect EV support through tax benefits for secondary batteries and concerns about overlapping support with current purchase subsidies.
Since then, several bills have been introduced in the National Assembly to include EVs among eligible items. Among the amendments to the Act on Restriction on Special Cases Concerning Taxation now before the Assembly, four would add a domestic production tax credit for EVs: bills by Yoon Young-seok (People Power Party), Ahn Sang-hoon (People Power Party), Lee Un-ju (Democratic), and a joint bill by Yoon Hu-duk (Democratic) and Yoon Han-hong (People Power Party). These bills were placed on the tax subcommittee's agenda this month and are under discussion.
A National Assembly official involved in codifying the EV domestic production tax credit said, "Both parties agree on including EVs," adding, "We expect a decision soon."
What remains are the details, because each bill proposes slightly different support methods. The amendment led by Democratic lawmaker Lee Un-ju would include not only domestic sales but also exports as eligible. It would also calculate the credit based on 4 million won per vehicle.
The bill by Yoon Hu-duk and Yoon Han-hong, introduced across party lines, sets the credit cap at 100% of the cumulative investment in business-use tangible assets directly used in production. The government's plan set the cap at 50%, so the bill would expand the limit.
The bill by People Power Party lawmaker Yoon Young-seok would apply a higher credit rate than the base rate to production activities outside the Seoul metropolitan area. Yoon said, "We need to encourage relocating production bases to the regions and spurring new investment," adding, "This is expected to create quality local jobs, promote clustering of related industries, strengthen regional industrial ecosystems, and help narrow the competitiveness gap between the capital area and the rest of the country."

Industry Minister Melanie Joly speaks to the media following discussions over the sale of the Stellantis Brampton assembly plant, in Toronto on Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026.

Industry Minister Melanie Joly speaks to the media following discussions over the sale of the Stellantis Brampton assembly plant, in Toronto on Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026.

TORONTO (AP) — Canada threatened Thursday to sue automaker Stellantis and recover hundreds of millions of dollars in government funding after the company shifted planned vehicle production to the United States during President Donald Trump’s trade war and agreed to sell its idled assembly plant in Brampton, Ontario.

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said Ottawa had issued Stellantis a formal notice alleging breaches of its funding agreement, giving the automaker 30 days to address the violations or face legal action.

“We sent a notice of default and, basically, they have 30 days or else. Of course, we’ll sue them,” Joly told reporters in Toronto.



Joly said Stellantis violated the agreement by abandoning production at Brampton without identifying a replacement vehicle.

Trump’s tariffs have put pressure on Canada’s auto industry, which is deeply integrated with U.S. manufacturing. Trump has repeatedly pushed automakers to move production south of the border.

Stellantis, the world’s fourth-largest carmaker , abandoned plans to build the Jeep Compass at its Brampton plant and shifted production to Illinois, leaving more than 2,000 Canadian workers without jobs.

Canada committed up to 529 million Canadian dollars (US$380 million) in 2022 to help Stellantis retool its Brampton and Windsor plants for electric vehicle production.

“Stellantis is on the hook for hundreds of millions of dollars,” Joly said.

A message left for a spokesperson for Stellantis was not immediately returned.

Stellantis announced Monday it had agreed to sell the Brampton plant to Canadian armored vehicle manufacturer Roshel. The company offered to repay government funding received for the Brampton project but declined to disclose the amount.

Prime Minister Mark Carney accused Stellantis of betraying Canadian workers, calling the sale a partial solution that failed to fulfill the company’s obligations.

Joly said federal and Ontario officials plan to meet with Stellantis’ global chief executive.

Unifor President Lana Payne said a meeting Thursday involving Stellantis, the union and both governments failed to produce a resolution.

“The time to stop that was last week, the week before and the week before that,” Payne said. “Now we’re going to a different situation. We can’t stop the sale. The sale has occurred, so we would have to reverse it, which is doubly difficult, obviously.”

Autos are Canada’s second-largest export and Carney has noted the sector employs 125,000 Canadians directly and almost another 500,000 in related industries.

title: Multnomah County Office of Sustainability works to secure 'FAIR' energy rates
description:

Among its many features, the law kickstarted a process to reform how rates are set for Oregon’s privately owned energy utilities, including the three energy utilities that serve Multnomah County: Pacific Power, Portland General Electric and NW Natural.
The Office of Sustainability supported this critical law both in its development and throughout the legislative process.
How rates were set before the FAIR Energy Act and Performance-Based Ratemaking The Oregon Public Utility Commission regulates Oregon energy utilities with an eye toward safety, reliability and price fairness.
Prior to the FAIR Energy Act, utilities could essentially ask for a rate increase whenever they wished.
text:
Energy costs have been in the news a lot lately, as electricity demand from data centers skyrockets both in Oregon and across the country, and the rates consumers pay for electricity and natural gas climb ever higher.

During the last year, Multnomah County’s Office of Sustainability team has been hard at work to support a more affordable energy future for our community while maintaining high quality service and strengthening the focus on the priorities of often-overlooked communities. Affordability, programs and protections that benefit low-income community members and a just energy transition have long been prioritized in the office’s advocacy to the Oregon Public Utility Commission(link is external) (PUC), the state agency that regulates utilities.

To further strengthen their advocacy, the Office of Sustainability has been working with a coalition that includes the Oregon Citizens Utility Board and several environmental justice organizations like the Oregon Just Transition Alliance, Community Energy Project, and Verde. The coalition has also brought in environmental advocates like the NW Energy Coalition and the Green Energy Institute, and many others.

Consumer and energy justice advocates scored major wins in the 2025 Oregon legislative session, buoyed by the passage of the FAIR Energy Act (House Bill 3179) — a response to the drastic and consistent rise in energy bills that community members had begun experiencing in 2020. Among its many features, the law kickstarted a process to reform how rates are set for Oregon’s privately owned energy utilities, including the three energy utilities that serve Multnomah County: Pacific Power, Portland General Electric and NW Natural. The Office of Sustainability supported this critical law both in its development and throughout the legislative process.

Passage of Senate Bill 688 (SB 688) on Performance-Based Regulation was another hallmark success from the 2025 legislative session. SB 688 builds on PUC’s existing authority to regulate the six privately owned energy utilities in Oregon by supporting the establishment of a framework that rewards utilities for outcomes communities value — like reducing disconnections or investing in community-based energy projects — while disincentivizing outcomes they don’t want, such as lower system reliability or worse customer service.

Together, these two 2025 laws started a process to implement their vision of a system that motivates utilities to contain costs while maintaining service quality and prioritizing outcomes Oregonians want to see.

The ensuing work included multiple rule-making processes at the PUC. The Office of Sustainability staff have focused on Docket No. AR 676(link is external): the process of transitioning to a different way for the six privately owned energy utilities in the state to set rates, with more tools for cost-containment, along with more incentives for utilities to maintain high-quality service and prioritize outcomes valued by communities.

How rates were set before the FAIR Energy Act and Performance-Based Ratemaking

The Oregon Public Utility Commission regulates Oregon energy utilities with an eye toward safety, reliability and price fairness. The utility companies are subject to regulation because they are monopolies or the only provider of gas or electricity in their service territory.

Before the FAIR Energy Act and Performance-Based Ratemaking were passed, the process for rate setting started with the utilities submitting a request for a rate revision to the PUC. They typically requested an increase, often seeking to recover the costs of doing business (like the costs of business supplies or wages for their employees) and to begin recovering new investments in infrastructure like transmission, distribution or energy generation assets. These investments are important to utilities, not just because they are critical to their ability to provide service but because they are generally the only cost category for which the utility gets to make a profit, rather than simply recover costs.

The submitting utility’s filing included the percentage change they desired, as well as evidence for why the PUC should grant it. Their submission triggered a “General Rate Case,” or a process that functions like a court proceeding, complete with parties, witnesses, evidence, discovery, settlement conferences, legal briefs and hearings.

Other stakeholders, like the Citizens Utility Board, PUC staff, and environmental or environmental-justice advocacy intervenors, would review the utility’s filing line by line, making challenges to portions of the utility’s proposal, while also presenting their own evidence for a different outcome.

The PUC has three commissioners who are the decision-makers at the agency and are tasked with setting “just and reasonable” rates. They are appointed by the Governor and confirmed by the Oregon Senate. This three-commissioner panel decides how much the utility can increase rates, as well as whether to approve other utility requests, based on the record developed through the rate case process.

However, the PUC commissioners cannot unilaterally decide to deny a proposal to raise rates simply because rates are too high and they don’t want to raise them. When the utility can show that it spent money to serve customers in ways that meet the legal applicable standards, the PUC must allow the utility to recover reasonable costs and also make a reasonable profit.

How the FAIR Energy Act and Performance-Based Ratemaking change rate setting

The Office of Sustainability and coalition partners have been working to make sure the implementation of the FAIR Energy Act and Performance-Based Ratemaking delivers tangible benefits for community members.

One of the main tools the FAIR Energy Act provides to support cost containment is Multiyear Rate Plans (MRPs). Prior to the FAIR Energy Act, utilities could essentially ask for a rate increase whenever they wished. They also had access to many additional mechanisms that allowed them to pass their costs, dollar for dollar, onto community members’ utility bills. Now, in contrast, MRPs put the utilities on a five-year budget for most of their costs. This budget is indexed to inflation and adjusted for factors like growth and expected efficiency improvements.

While MRPs have great potential to help utilities contain their costs more effectively, that outcome is not a given — the devil is in the details. One example of the many factors that can either weaken or strengthen the cost-containment value of MRPs is the number of expenses that must be “under the budget.” The more utility cost categories (e.g., equipment, technology, labor, programs, etc.) are included in the budget, the stronger the MRP’s cost-containing effect can be. MRPs essentially ask the utility to manage costs of expenditures under those categories and stay under the budget. While some costs may rise faster than inflation, others won’t, so the utility will need to stay within its budget — perhaps by prioritizing certain investments — while avoiding the reduction or degradation of their service. Conversely, the MRP’s cost containment effect is weakened if the utility is allowed to recover more categories of spending outside of the budget.

Requiring utilities to stay within a budget may push them to deprioritize things we value as a community, such as high quality customer service. As a result, this process intends to establish incentives that help ensure utilities don’t sacrifice the quality or safety of their service when containing costs, and that utilities have a greater stake in reducing disconnections, using their existing infrastructure more efficiently, and prioritizing clean, community-based infrastructure.

The shared goal of the Office of Sustainability and its myriad collaborators throughout this process has been to make sure the design details of the MRP mechanism support cost containment, high-quality and affordable service, and the incentive for utilities to better prioritize important goals like reducing disconnections and emissions.

Oregonians are fortunate to have excellent staff in the PUC who have genuinely and thoughtfully organized a process grounded in principles(link is external) that include mitigating the impacts of rate changes on customers, and goals like affordable and high-value service, efficient clean energy development and emissions reductions, distributional equity, and resilience. As a result, the Office of Sustainability is optimistic about the chances this implementation process will deliver on the combined vision of the two 2025 laws that set this journey in motion. We are similarly fortunate that the PUC commissioners have supported their staff’s vision and are genuinely interested in delivering the vision of the two laws.

Conclusion

We have learned a ton and dedicated a lot of time to this process over the last year, filing more than a dozen letters with the PUC and participating in hours of workshops and meetings. Yet there is a significant amount of work ahead to make sure that Oregon’s FAIR Energy Act and Performance-Based Ratemaking laws deliver on their promise. For the Office of Sustainability, our focus has, and will continue to be, energy justice and making sure that we transition to a clean energy system in which everyone in our state can afford to use the clean energy that they need to live and thrive.

title: Transforming Canada's buildings sector for a net-zero and resilient future
description:
To continue making progress toward Canada’s emissions reduction goals, it is essential to cut buildings sector emissions.
Canada’s residential buildings account for 47% of buildings sector emissions in Canada (excluding electricity).
Canada's green buildings industry already employs about 460,000 workers, and the transition of the buildings sector will create hundreds of thousands of new jobs.
Shape the buildings sector of the future The third priority of the CGBS is to shape the buildings sector of the future.
They are seeking funding for self-determined green buildings activities including increasing capacity, expertise, services, and economic and long-term career opportunities in the green buildings sector.
text:
Ministerial foreword

Buildings play a central role in the lives of Canadians. They are where we work, where we play, where we gather, where we shelter, and where we raise our family. How we build and manage our buildings is critical to the health and vitality of the nation. This is particularly true at this critical time. Housing, energy affordability and climate action form the intersection where Canadians’ most pressing concerns meet.

The Canada Green Buildings Strategy (CGBS) gets to the heart of these issues. The CGBS sets out the Government’s vision and next steps for greener, more energy efficient and affordable homes and buildings. It outlines how the Government is acting to drive down monthly energy bills, to help Canadians reduce their carbon emissions, and ensure that the homes and workplaces of Canadians are protected against the increasingly harmful effects of climate change—all while creating good-paying, sustainable jobs. Transitioning buildings to clean energy sources and reducing overall energy consumption will address not just climate risks but also the physical and financial well-being of all Canadians.

Buildings are the third largest emitting sector, after oil and gas and transportation. And importantly, it is a challenging sector to decarbonize because we must all do it, together. To succeed, close collaboration is needed between the federal government, provinces, municipalities, indigenous groups, businesses, financial institutions, and industry. There are 16 million homes and half a million other buildings standing in Canada today and most of these are expected to still be standing in 2050. Each home and building owner has a role to play in this sector to upgrade and retrofit these spaces to significantly reduce emissions in that time. The scale of this renewal requires annual investments, a rapid increase in the pace of retrofits and changing the way we build. This includes the hundreds of thousands of new residential and commercial buildings that need to be built annually to respond to the housing challenge and stay current with our rapidly growing clean economy. These new homes and buildings must be built with net-zero emissions in sight if we are to avoid having to retrofit them before 2050.

At the same time, our buildings must be made stronger to withstand the impacts of climate change. This includes the ability to withstand extreme weather events such as floods, wildfires and hurricanes, as well as changes in temperature and precipitation. Disasters that are more frequent and intense, temperatures are getting warmer and parts of the country are facing drought while others are seeing an increase in precipitation. All are due to climate change. Old buildings must be updated, and new homes built to withstand the changing climate. The most expensive home is the one that has to be built twice.

The CGBS complements Canada’s National Adaptation Strategy which lays out an agreed-upon framework to reduce the risk of climate-related disasters, improve health outcomes, protect nature and biodiversity, build and maintain climate resilient infrastructure, and support a strong economy and workers. Building strong resilient communities means managing the risks to our health, well-being, and livelihoods.

And critically, both existing and new buildings must also be affordable to construct and to operate. Canadian households spend an average of $2,200 a year on home energy costs. These costs are significantly higher in homes that heat with oil and in older homes that have poor insulation, ventilation, and heating/cooling systems. By transitioning buildings to clean energy sources and decreasing overall energy consumption, we can effectively tackle not only climate risks but also make homes healthier and reduce energy costs for Canadians.

The time to act is now.

Actions to make our buildings green and resilient help to reduce the amount of energy used so energy bills can be lower, year after year. We can add insulation and other energy efficiency measures to our homes and buildings to reduce energy consumption, improve or replace windows, doors, and ventilation systems and we can choose to move away from fossil fuel burning equipment to heat our homes. New buildings can be built to high energy efficiency and performance standards - if all levels of government look ahead and adopt higher tiers of the model building codes and increase the use of low-carbon construction materials, maximizing material efficiency and performance-based design. Low-carbon building materials sourced from within Canada not only support the domestic market and help cut carbon pollution (PDF) (including emissions from transportation and shipping of materials from international suppliers), but also leverages Canadian manufacturing ingenuity, stimulates market competitiveness, and creates sustainable jobs. We can take the opportunity to increase buildings' climate resilience through waterproofing, flood protection, supporting efficient space cooling, or installing batteries connected to solar photovoltaic systems. Energy efficiency measures can keep homes warmer in the winter and cooler in the summer, providing safer and healthier living conditions as the climate continues to change.

Crucially, the construction and improvement of better buildings will generate demand for more contractors, electricians, and other skilled workers, leading to sustainable, well-paying employment opportunities for Canadians over the long term. Taking action on climate change and working to mitigate climate-related risks can also unlock new economic prospects and quality jobs for Canadians.

Canadians have said loud and clear that they want a green solution to the housing crisis—one that keeps costs down, one that minimizes pollution, and one that protects their homes from the damaging effects of a changing climate. The CGBS responds to that call with a vision and next steps for how to green our homes and buildings to make them more livable and affordable. Acting quickly in collaboration with Provinces, Territories, Indigenous and Municipal partners, the financial sector, buildings industry and other businesses will help spur innovations and avoid locking in the high cost of burning fossil fuels on Canadians’ pocketbooks and the planet.

The CGBS puts forward a vision to enable this approach and pursue the priorities about which Canadians care most.

Signed by:

Jonathan Wilkinson

Minister of Energy and Natural Resources

Sean Fraser

Minister of Housing, Infrastructure and Communities

Steven Guilbeault

Minister of Environment and Climate Change

Overview

The CGBS comes at a critical time. To reach our climate goals, reduce monthly bills and increase the supply of Canada’s housing stock, we need to accelerate the retrofit of approximately 11 million buildings and construct millions of new greener buildings in the coming decades. A renewal of Canada’s buildings sector is underway, one that has the potential to create hundreds of thousands of sustainable jobs and prosperity for all regions of Canada, while lowering monthly bills for homeowners, tenants, and businesses.

The buildings sector has an important role to play when it comes to reducing greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and improving resiliency to climate hazards, such as floods, wildfires and hurricanes. The Canadian Net-Zero Emissions Accountability Act enshrines in legislation the Government of Canada’s commitment to reduce GHG emissions by 40-45% below 2005 levels by 2030 and to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050. Buildings account for 18% of Canada’s emissions, when including electricity-related emissions, and is the third largest emitting sector after the oil and gas sector and the transportation sector. Almost all buildings’ operating emissions (>96%) come from space and water heating from the use of equipment that runs on fossil fuels, such as natural gas furnaces and boilers, while further emissions are embodied in construction materials used in buildings, such as concrete, steel, aluminum and wood.

The technology already exists to reduce emissions efficiently and effectively from heating equipment in buildings. Electrification is the most cost-effective and efficient approach to decarbonizing buildings in most parts of Canada. Ultimately, moving away from the use of fossil fuel heating equipment, towards alternatives such as heat pumps, is an essential step to reducing the operational emissions from buildings. It is necessary to work with provinces and territories, communities and Indigenous Peoples to initiate a phased approach to transition away from fossil fuels for space and water heating. Starting with a focus on the most expensive, high emitting fuel – heating oil – can support a stepped approach to pursuing buildings decarbonization with affordability in mind.

In addition to combating climate change, green building retrofits and building green from the start can help make buildings more livable, improve air quality and significantly reduce overall costs, including by reducing monthly energy bills and avoiding the costly impacts of extreme weather. As Canada accelerates its investments in housing, as outlined in Canada’s Housing Plan, it is important to ensure homes are affordable to maintain and operate. It is critical that the green buildings sector renewal leaves nobody behind.

Beyond climate and affordability considerations, this renewal also presents an enormous economic opportunity. From the need to draw on skilled trades and supply low carbon construction materials, to the growth of clean technology businesses and innovative building designs, Canada is uniquely positioned to lead globally while becoming more prosperous locally. Each region of Canada is presented with unique circumstances for this transition, based on its geography, natural resources, and local markets and expertise. The CGBS seeks to seize each of these opportunities over the next critical decade and beyond.

The CGBS aims to decarbonize and improve the resiliency of Canada’s buildings stock, while supporting affordability, job creation and economic growth. The CGBS centers around three priorities:

Accelerate retrofits

Build green and affordable from the start

Shape the buildings sector of the future

These priorities were shaped by an extensive engagement process with buildings sector industry partners, Indigenous partners, municipalities, provinces, territories and the Canadian public. The published What We Heard Report summarizes the online submissions, written responses to the CGBS discussion paper, Ministerial roundtables, and multi-lateral conferences held over the last two years to inform the CGBS.

Importantly, we are not starting from zero. The federal government has invested heavily in support of buildings sector decarbonization goals since 2016 which has provided a foundation of knowledge and awareness across the sector for more ambitious decarbonization. The buildings sector is already taking action to advance priorities, and the Government of Canada will help to accelerate them with a series of initiatives and investments, including with nearly $1 billion in new, targeted federal investments announced in Budget 2024, as well as other measures, across three categories of buildings:

Residential buildings, where we live - through flagship programs like the Canada Greener Homes Grant and Loan programs, which have received over 590,000 applications for grants and 78,000 applications for loans since their launch in 2021, to help homeowners retrofit their homes to be more energy efficient - and programs focused on affordability with the Oil to Heat Pump Affordability Program and the Canada Greener Affordable Housing Program. As announced in Budget 2024, we are moving forward with the next phase of home retrofit programming with $800M in new funding for the Canada Greener Homes Affordability Program, while cracking down on renovictions as part of a proposed new Canadian Renters’ Bill of Rights. We will continue developing a national approach to home energy labelling, which will empower prospective home buyers with information about the energy efficiency of their new home, with the support of energy auditors.

Commercial / institutional buildings, as well as community buildings, where we work, study and play, with initiatives like theDeep Retrofit Accelerator Initiative to accelerate the development of deep retrofit projects, adoption of the highest energy performance standards, and private and public sector partnerships with the Canada Infrastructure Bank. As announced in Budget 2024, we are expanding our work with an investment of $73.5M – with programs such as the ENERGY STAR® Portfolio Manager® platform – to support the implementation of local initiatives including benchmarking, labelling and disclosure policies, and better, more ambitious building performance standards to further reduce emissions and lower energy bills.

Federally owned buildings: As the country’s largest building asset owner and procurer of construction materials, the Government of Canada is helping decarbonize and improve the resiliency of Canada’s buildings sector through its Greening Government Strategy (GGS) and Greening Government Fund. Through the GGS, the Government of Canada’s is reducing environmental impacts associated with federal building operations and construction projects, while enhancing the climate resiliency of federal assets, services, and operations. Moreover, by implementing a ‘buy clean’ policy approach through the GGS, the Government of Canada is promoting the adoption of construction materials with low embodied carbon and that are renewable such as wood, reclaimed or recycled materials, and low-emission concrete and steel.

New federal actions will make further strides towards these priorities:

Greening the buildings sector remains a substantial and complex undertaking. Buildings have long lifecycles and therefore reducing emissions, while also improving resilience to climate change, requires important investments that often need multi-year planning. The Federal government, provinces, territories, Indigenous communities, and municipalities must work together, alongside home and building owners, to maximize the impact of our collective actions, while simultaneously ensuring that residential buildings are constructed at the pace and scale required to tackle the housing crisis. New construction needs to be high performance – adopting the highest viable tier of the National Energy Code for Buildings (for larger buildings) and of the National Building Code (for residential homes and small buildings) – and consider embodied carbon (in construction materials).

Alongside governments, the private sector has an important role to play in providing capital, expertise, and leadership to transform Canada’s buildings. Financial institutions are now starting to recognize their role in this space and must continue to build momentum and deploy capital.

Strategies like maximizing utilization, reusing, refurbishing, and repurposing already built space provide a cost-effective way to help decarbonize Canada’s buildings stock by extending the lifespan of existing buildings and avoiding the energy-intensive process of creating new materials. Deep retrofits – that involve upgrades to multiple building systems and equipment (such as replacing roofs; adding, upgrading, or rearranging windows; adding or increasing insulation; replacing or improving building envelope or cladding) – can achieve maximum energy savings and GHG emissions reductions.

Furthermore, climate resilience considerations – including locating, planning, designing, managing, adapting, operating and maintaining buildings infrastructure – and current and projected climate change impacts must be kept in mind.

Accelerated ambition and coordination is needed across all levels of government to ensure design and delivery of initiatives that work in concert towards the CGBS strategic priorities – both today and as we collectively continue to advance towards net-zero in 2050.

Canada’s buildings landscape

Canada’s buildings stock

The buildings footprint in Canada is vast: there are over 16 million buildings are used for residential purposes, including single-family detached and semi-detached homes, multi-unit apartments, and other residential buildings;

over 564,000 are commercial and institutional buildings, such as businesses and facilities, hospitals and long-term care homes, community and cultural buildings, schools and university campuses; and

over 34,000 buildings are owned and managed by the Government of Canada, including offices, research laboratories, warehouses, storage facilities, Department of Defence owned infrastructure, and more.

The vast majority of these buildings are expected to still be standing in 2050 and will require upgrades and retrofitting. In addition, Canada needs millions more homes to be built now and in the decades to come to address housing needs. By 2050, the number of households in Canada may increase by up to 25% of what it is today.

Emissions profile and trajectory

Although Canada is making progress in reducing economy-wide emissions towards its 2030 greenhouse gas reduction target, the built environment is still the third largest source of emissions in Canada (see Figure 1), with annual GHG emissions accounting for 89 megatonnes (Mt) in 2022 – around 13% of direct emissions (see Figure 2) (PDF). This number rises to 18% if we account for emissions from generating the electricity that buildings use. To continue making progress toward Canada’s emissions reduction goals, it is essential to cut buildings sector emissions.

Figure 1. Breakdown of Canada’s greenhouse gas emissions by economic sector (2022)

Figure 2. Operational emissions from residential & commercial building sectors in Canada (2021)

Over 96% of direct operational buildings emissions come from space and water heating (PDF), the majority of which is due to equipment that runs on fossil fuels (see Figure 4). Electrification of space and water heating will be an essential component of decarbonizing the buildings sector, with other clean fuels also playing a role where major barriers to electrification remain (for example, access to clean electricity).

Canada’s residential buildings account for 47% of buildings sector emissions in Canada (excluding electricity). Approximately 54% of all homes use fossil fuels for space heating and 44% use electric-powered equipment. The residential buildings stock is aging and many will require retrofits to be energy efficient. Twenty percent of all homes (~3 million) are more than 80 years old, and about 50% are more than 60 years old. About 2 million homes (12%) have been built in every decade since 1980.

Figure 3: Buildings Emissions Focus – Comparison of GHG emissions from buildings (per capita), (excluding electricity) 2020

Commercial and institutional buildings together make up the remaining 52% of our country’s building sector emissions. For commercial and institutional buildings, approximately 30% use electricity as their only energy source. The remaining 70% use some fossil fuel in addition to electricity, the most prominent being natural gas (present in 60% of all commercial and institutional buildings). Canada’s commercial and institutional buildings stock is also aging and uses a lot of energy. Approximately forty percent (40%) of commercial and institutional buildings in Canada were built more than 50 years ago.

On top of operational emissions, the emissions embedded in construction material supply chains for retrofits and new buildings are significant. Clean Energy Canada estimates that the production, transport and demolition of construction materials used in public infrastructure accounts for approximately 8 million tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions annually (PDF). If private construction is considered, this figure increases to approximately 28 million tonnes, which is equivalent to around half of Canada’s electricity generation emissions or four percent of Canada’s total emissions in 2021.

Emission reductions in the buildings sector are not presently on track to make reductions in line with Canada’s 2030 or 2050 emission targets, despite progress stemming from current policies. With most of Canada’s existing buildings likely to remain in use for decades to come and the need for millions of new homes to be constructed, seizing opportunities to improve energy efficiency and resiliency, and reduce emissions is a critical goal for the sector.

Adapting to a changing climate

Canada’s climate is changing. Higher temperatures, shifting rainfall patterns, extreme weather events including floods and wildfires, and rising sea levels are just some of the changes already affecting many aspects of our lives (see Figure 5). Climate change impacts to the building sector are already significant and projected to rise. In 2023, severe weather caused $3.1 billion in insured damages nationally, leading to direct costs to homeowners in the repair and maintenance in the aftermath of a climate-related event, as well as ongoing indirect costs, including rapidly increasing insurance premiums. With climate change impacts becoming more frequent and intense, the provision of affordable, equitable and resilient solutions for our buildings and homes is critical for the health of Canadians and the economy.

Taking proactive adaptation action is ultimately a cost-effective solution to address both climate risks and affordability. Constructing new homes and buildings and retrofitting existing ones to increase climate resilience can help to avoid damages and long-term costs. For example, a recent study demonstrates that each dollar ($1) invested in wind protection results in $6 of avoided damage to Canadian homes (PDF). Similarly, a previous benefit-cost analysis (PDF) concluded that the use of impact-resistant asphalt roof shingles could save up to 8 times what they cost and even greater savings in areas that experience frequent hailstorms.
