Volume 2, issue 3

All new! ENERGY STAR score for supermarkets and food stores in Canada

NRCan training opportunities for the all-new ENERGY STAR score for supermarkets and food stores in Canada

Hard-boiled facts about energy use in the Canadian retail food and beverage sector: You can’t manage what you don’t measure

Other grocers have done it, and you can too: Reap great savings from energy efficiency and benchmarking

New publications now available from Natural Resources Canada

Impressive results for New Brunswick’s Horizon Health Network with ENERGY STAR Portfolio Manager

Kingston General Hospital soars to energy efficiency heights

Calendar of events and other important dates

Let us know what you think

All new! ENERGY STAR score for supermarkets and food stores in Canada

In the U.S., over 2,300 supermarkets that have achieved a score of 75 or more using ENERGY STAR Portfolio Manager have earned the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s (U.S. EPA) ENERGY STAR label. The U.S. EPA reports that stores that have met this goal consistently use 35 percent less energy compared to other buildings of the same size and function.

Although the ENERGY STAR label for buildings is not available in Canada, Canadian supermarkets and food stores can also achieve the same level of energy savings.

Supermarkets and grocery stores are always hungry for opportunities to remain competitive on the expense side of the ledger. Food stores are among the most energy-intensive commercial buildings. Keeping overhead costs down – including energy – is always a primary concern. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency estimates that $1 in energy savings is equivalent to $59 in increased sales. It is clearfix that managing energy wisely can provide food retailers with a real competitive advantage!Footnote 1

The good news is that Natural Resources Canada (NRCan) has just made managing energy in the food retail sector that much easier, with an all-new 1-100 Canadian ENERGY STAR score for supermarkets and other food establishments that is now available.

With the addition of this 1-100 ENERGY STAR score, food retailers will be able to implement or enhance an energy benchmarking routine using the ENERGY STAR Portfolio Manager tool. Portfolio Manager is the only tool in Canada that provides a comparison metric based on statistically validated data. The score will apply to supermarkets, grocery and beverage stores, food sales, and convenience stores with or without gas stations.

What is Portfolio Manager?

Portfolio Manager is a free, interactive energy management tool that helps you track and assess energy and water consumption across your entire portfolio of buildings in a secure online environment.

Energy benchmarking is a key starting point that is often overlooked for effective energy management and decision-making. It is key to deciding what to do next because it helps to establish baselines and set goals. For instance, benchmarking against the industry can provide key insights into the competitive use of energy. The data that you will receive from using the tool will help you answer challenging questions such as:

In the summer of 2013, NRCan launched ENERGY STAR Portfolio Manager in Canada. At the time of the launch, ENERGY STAR scores were available for K-12 schools and commercial offices. In May 2014, NRCan launched a new 1-100 ENERGY STAR score for hospitals, and will continue to add other building types over time. Buildings that are not eligible to receive a score can also benefit from energy use intensity calculations.

You can incorporate Portfolio Manager as a tool to support your sustainability plans and use the results to build a solid business case that can positively impact your store’s profitability and public image.

Hard-boiled facts about energy use in the Canadian retail food and beverage sector: You can’t manage what you don’t measure

It’s no secret that there is fierce competition in Canada’s food and beverage retail sector. Increasingly, energy efficiency is recognized as a solid approach to increase profits and improve a store’s bottom line. Supermarkets, grocery and other food retail stores that have an established energy management program are aligned to put their stores in a more price-competitive position. Being aware of your store’s energy consumption and managing it wisely enables you to concentrate on sales while doing something positive for the environment.

Let’s take a look at the typical energy use breakdown in a Canadian supermarket.

According to NRCan’s Canmet ENERGY division, supermarkets use more energy per unit area than most commercial buildings. A large supermarket will consume 5,000 megawatt hours (MWh) of electricity per year, and there are over 5,000 such large supermarkets in Canada. Together, this represents electricity consumption of around 25 terawatt hours (TWh) per year, or the output of about three large power plants.Footnote 2

Refrigeration systems typically account for around 50 percent of a supermarket’s energy costs and lighting around 25 percent – in terms of energy consumed these figures would be slightly lower. This translates into $150,000 per year in energy costs for refrigeration in a large supermarket. To put this into context, energy costs are equivalent to roughly 1 percent of supermarket sales. This is very significant, considering that the average net profit margin for a supermarket is also approximately 1 percent. That means that, all other things being equal, a 10-percent reduction in energy costs increases profits by about 10 percent!Footnote 3

What is the potential for savings in Canada?

Food and beverage stores can make a significant contribution towards the energy efficiency of the Canadian building sector. The 2009 Survey of Commercial and Institutional Energy Use (PDF, 3,67 MB) provides insight into the size of this sector. The opportunity to showcase leadership in this sector is great. In Canada, food and beverage stores may be broken down as follows:

In the U.S., over 2,300 supermarkets that have achieved a score of 75 or more using ENERGY STAR Portfolio Manager have earned the U.S. EPA ENERGY STAR label. The U.S. EPA reports that stores that have met this goal consistently use 35 percent less energy compared to other buildings of the same size and function.

Although the ENERGY STAR label for buildings is not available in Canada, Canadian supermarkets and food stores can also achieve the same level of energy savings.

There is no doubt that grocers face many challenges: there are varying requirements to keep food items cool, frozen or heated. Customers want uniform levels of lighting and don't want to be uncomfortable in a store that is either too warm or too cold. Energy demands are intense, and the cost of providing this energy strongly influences a store’s profitability.

By investing in efficient energy use, you can reduce your operating costs, buffer your supermarket from future energy cost increases, lower your environmental impact, and increase your long-term profitability. Make energy efficiency part of your thinking. Consider improving the efficiency of your operations through energy benchmarking using NRCan’s ENERGY STAR Portfolio Manager or improve the energy awareness of your staff through NRCan’s Dollars to $ense workshops.

Other grocers have done it, and you can too: Reap great savings from energy efficiency and benchmarking

The release of NRCan’s new 1-100 ENERGY STAR score for food and beverage stores will provide a powerful tool that Canadian food retailers can use to maximize the energy savings potential in their stores. There are many supermarkets and grocery stores that are already profiting from sound energy management and improving both their bottom line and corporate profile.

The distinction of most supermarkets is that they are large facilities, and utility costs represent a much bigger slice of the overhead in comparison to other retail ventures – this is particularly due to refrigeration. In an industry where profit margins are small, and the competition fierce, the U.S. EPA reports that even $1 in energy savings can translate into $59 in increased salesFootnote 6. In addition to demonstrating sound fiscal responsibility and increasing the bottom line, these savings also attract the over 60 percent of consumers who have explicitly stated that they wish to make their purchases from companies that are environmentally responsibleFootnote 7. Here are some examples of food stores that are benefitting from a vision and commitment to sound energy management.

The U.S. EPA reports that even $1 in energy savings can translate into $59 in increased sales

Food Lion, an American supermarket chain has consistently delivered on its commitment to energy efficiency by receiving the ENERGY STAR Partner of the Year Sustained Excellence Award for ten consecutive years. They have taken a proactive approach that focuses on both equipment upgrades and in-house education. This has resulted in over 85 percent of Food Lion’s stores receiving the ENERGY STAR label and a 30-percent increase in efficiency across the board since 2000.

Another American retailer, Lowes Foods, through retrofitting and benchmarking five of its stores, saved enough energy to power 444 homes for one year and cut carbon dioxide emissions by nearly 10,000 tonnes per year.

Canadian grocers are also realizing energy management successes. In Saint-Pascal de Kamouraska, the IGA supermarket (a subsidiary of Sobey’s Québec), became the first LEED-certified supermarket in Canada. The store consumes 43 percent less energy compared to Canadian standards for similar buildings, is self-sufficient for heating, and water consumption has been reduced by 47 percent.

In 2014, the family-run independent store Kudrinko’s in Westport, Ontario received the “Greatness in Green, Outstanding Independent Award” from Progressive Grocer for its environmental efforts. Kudrinko’s competed against entries throughout North America. In addition to monitoring and tracking its energy use and refrigerant losses, Kudrinko’s implemented many energy-saving measures such as replacing inefficient equipment, increasing building envelope insulation, installing energy efficient lighting and many other retrofits before receiving the award.

Combining sound energy management best practices with a reduction in their environmental impact is the strategy the food retail industry is adopting on both sides of the border. NRCan is dedicated to enabling Canadian grocery stores to use energy more responsibly through energy benchmarking with Portfolio Manager. For more information on how to get started visit our Energy Benchmarking Roadmap, or, better yet, register for one of the upcoming webinars on the new 1-100 ENERGY STAR scores for supermarkets and food stores by visiting our energy benchmarking training resources page.

Energy Management Best Practices Guide: For Commercial and Institutional Buildings (PDF, 1,47 MB)

Energy management best practices provide a solid framework for any energy management strategy – a framework that not only includes traditional technology-based energy performance solutions but also incorporates organizational and behavioural aspects of energy use. This latest guide from NRCan focuses on how energy management best practices can improve your organization’s energy performance to produce a more sustainable building with an extended life cycle.

Case study: Four Centres at Red Deer College (PDF, 832 KB)

The Four Centres building added nearly 16,000 square metres of new and renovated space to the main campus of Red Deer College in 2009. Numerous energy-saving design elements have made the Four Centres about 61 per cent more efficient than the Model National Energy Code of Canada for Buildings (1997).

Impressive results for New Brunswick’s Horizon Health Network with ENERGY STAR Portfolio Manager

“ENERGY STAR Portfolio Manager offers an excellent way to showcase energy improvements with its scores and visuals that speak volumes,” says Kate Butler, Project Manager at FaciliCorpNB, an organization that manages shared services for New Brunswick’s health care system. “The tool tells a story about energy performance and provides a case for energy efficiency improvements.”

At the beginning of June 2014, FaciliCorpNB approached the Horizon Health Network proposing a facility-wide integration using NRCan’s ENERGY STAR Portfolio Manager. Operating 12 hospitals and more than 100 other medical service facilities, Horizon Health Network delivers health care services to residents of New Brunswick, northern Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island.

Butler, who has managed the integration of Portfolio Manager in New Brunswick’s health care facilities, has seen the impressive results of energy benchmarking in the New Brunswick buildings sector and the potential for the entire health sector as well.

Horizon approved the facility-wide integration, and data will be entered into the tool starting with the larger hospitals including the Saint John Regional Hospital, New Brunswick’s largest health care facility. As Butler explains, once the facilities are in Portfolio Manager, they can compare their performance with peer hospitals within New Brunswick and across Canada. “Everyone can share, enter and access data.” Moreover, the use of the tool ties in well with the province’s Climate Change Action Plan.

To demonstrate the success that can be achieved by strategic planning, Butler highlighted the 1-100 ENERGY STAR score received by the Saint John Regional Hospital: the hospital received an 86, demonstrating top performance. In addition, a smaller health facility improved its score from 18 to 56 through the baseline measures provided by energy benchmarking.

Prior to Portfolio Manager, Excel spreadsheets were used to record energy data, which are easy to import into the tool. Butler said the facilities that have been integrated have found the tool very easy to use. Also, the tool is free, and technical support is readily available.

“Engagement and communication is key in getting facilities on board with Portfolio Manager,” says Butler, noting that awareness and engagement will help keep energy top of mind and engage staff to continually try to improve energy performance.

For more information on how your organization can start to benchmark energy consumption, visit the ENERGY STAR for Buildingsweb page.

Kingston General Hospital soars to energy efficiency heights

The Kingston General Hospital (KGH) boasts more than innovative medical advances. The facility is also making great strides in energy efficiency. Since 2010, $10 million has been earmarked for a host of energy projects that have turned the facility into one of the most energy-efficient acute care hospitals in Canada. That investment has led to savings of over 3.5 million kilowatt hours (kWh) in energy per year and more than 14 percent reduction in the facility’s carbon footprint, states Allan McLuskie, director of facilities.

Long description

Allan McLuskie, director of facilities at Kingston General Hospital, discusses the energy-saving steps the hospital has taken over the past five years.

The projects began in 2010 with the start of a major retrofit to the hospital infrastructure that would reduce energy costs and improve the efficiency of the buildings. The second energy project started in 2013. “These projects combined have netted us over $800,000 in energy and water savings and reduced our carbon footprint by over 14 percent,” notes Allan McLuskie, director of facilities at KGH. The hospital qualified for grants amounting to $500,000 from Ontario’s saveONenergy retrofit program through the local utility – Utilities Kingston.

Upgrades include the replacement of more than 9,500 light fixtures, 250 inefficient windows, air-handling systems and the replacement of 10 oil-fired boilers with high-efficiency gas-fired boilers. Insulation and weather sealing were also improved. Many of the upgrades were focused on the oldest parts of the building – 20 percent of the facility is over 100 years old. McLuskie explains that improving heating, cooling and water systems in such an old building was a challenge as was maintaining patient comfort at all times.

“It’s a combination of replacing old with new and hooking up our existing systems to building automation so we can control them better,” says McLuskie. “Despite our age, we are still able to become one of the most energy-efficient hospitals in the country.”

KGH has also been working on water conservation projects. For example, adding low-flow toilets and other more efficient water fixtures reduced water use by more than 25 percent.

The hospital has been recognized for its efforts by earning a 78 percent energy score on the North American ENERGY STAR Portfolio Manager, which charts energy and water use by acute care hospitals in North America. “We have jumped 25 percent from where we were five years ago,” added Gary Greene, KHG manager of plant operations and maintenance.

“The hospital will continue looking for energy efficiency opportunities and with incentives that help reduce the capital cost of projects, KGH will be able to save even more on energy costs,” notes Greene. McLuskie adds, “The money saved is now available to be spent where it matters — on patient care.”

title: The Impact of Permitting Reform on State-level Residential Electricity Prices and Bills
description:
We quantify the impacts of BAAJA provisions against a current policy baseline without BAAJA.
We find that key BAAJA provisions reduce average national electricity prices for residential customers by 3-4% in 2035 compared to current policy, depending on future clean technology costs and fossil fuel prices.
Residential electricity prices decline because easier permitting allows lower-cost resources to connect to the grid and enables greater sharing of resources between neighboring regions.
As a result of these effects, average residential household bills decline by $41-66 in 2035 compared to current policy, and savings total $36-56 billion through 2035 across all residential customers.
Nearly all states experience these benefits from key BAAJA provisions: residential electricity prices and bills fall compared to current policy in 46 to 48 states out of the 48 contiguous states we modeled.
text:
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) is actively under consideration after the US Senate voted on Monday, November 9 to begin debate on the bill. If passed in its current form, BAAJA would apply sweeping changes to many federal environmental permitting laws, mandate new transmission planning and cost allocation processes, and require data centers to pay for the costs they impose on the grid.

In this analysis, we model key provisions of BAAJA (excluding manager’s amendment updates) focused on easing barriers to building linear infrastructure (transmission lines and natural gas pipelines), protecting ratepayers from data center costs, and securing federal permit certainty for wind power plants. We quantify the impacts of BAAJA provisions against a current policy baseline without BAAJA. We find that key BAAJA provisions reduce average national electricity prices for residential customers by 3-4% in 2035 compared to current policy, depending on future clean technology costs and fossil fuel prices. Residential electricity prices decline because easier permitting allows lower-cost resources to connect to the grid and enables greater sharing of resources between neighboring regions.

The ratepayer protection provisions also protects residential customers from the costs associated with growing data center demand, which drives the majority of economy-wide demand growth through 2035 in our modeling. As a result of these effects, average residential household bills decline by $41-66 in 2035 compared to current policy, and savings total $36-56 billion through 2035 across all residential customers. Nearly all states experience these benefits from key BAAJA provisions: residential electricity prices and bills fall compared to current policy in 46 to 48 states out of the 48 contiguous states we modeled.

Read the analysis

text:
Dominion Energy customers packed a meeting in North Charleston on Thursday night to weigh in on a proposed $67 billion merger between Dominion and NextEra Energy, raising concerns about whether the deal is fair and what it could mean for electric bills in South Carolina.

Residents gathered to provide feedback to the South Carolina Public Service Commission, with many questioning whether customers are getting enough in return if the merger is approved.

One attendee criticized the bill relief being offered, saying, “I’m sorry, but a $10 credit for a month, that’s not doing nothing for me if my bill is $350.”

BACKGROUND READING | "SC Public Service Commission holds hearing at 6 p.m. on Dominion-NextEra deal."

Under the proposal, the companies have offered South Carolina customers a $10 monthly credit for two years if the merger goes through. Speakers at the meeting questioned what happens after that period and whether there would be protections for families.

“The companies have offered a $10 monthly credit for two years if the merger goes through," One speaker said. "But what happens after those two years? What are protections for the families? South Carolinians need and deserve more than a short-term discount.”

Another point of contention was the difference in benefits offered in other states. Virginia customers would receive $10 monthly bill credits for four years, compared with an average of $10 a month for two years in South Carolina if the merger is approved.

Dominion has said the combined company could buy, build, operate and finance more efficiently, and that customers would not pay for the merger itself.

BACKGROUND READING | "$67B Dominion-NextEra merger draws pushback over rates, pollution and data centers."

A Dominion representative said, “You might wonder, as a customer, am I paying for the merger? And the answer to that question is absolutely not. Customers are not paying one cent for this merger.”

Even so, some residents said they fear the consolidation could still lead to higher costs.

“We cannot keep asking families to carry more," One speaker told the commission. "We’re already seeing higher bills here in South Carolina, which demand separate 2026 rate increases. That increase is not because of this merger.”

Others urged regulators to reject the deal. One speaker said, “You have a choice, an incredibly important one, that will affect all of us, and I hope that that choice will be to deny the petition for this merger.”

Kiana Linen-Stacey, identified as a resident, described the stakes for families struggling to keep up with utility costs.

“If not, my children will not have those lights," she said. "And guess what? I will have a disconnection. And five children don’t care. They don’t want to come home to the cold. They don’t want to come home to no food."

Multiple state and federal approvals are required before the merger can take effect.

The companies anticipate closing in the second half of 2027.

text:
A new agreement: In the third-quarter news release issued alongside the earnings call, the Peak+ program was described as an “integrated customer solution that combines new capacity to support peak demand growth with energy products tailored to customer needs.” In this first agreement, Constellation signed a 20-year, 270-MW agreement “of unit-contingent energy, capacity, and attributes from our existing nuclear fleet set to begin in 2028.”

President and CEO Joe Dominguez said in the earnings call that Peak+ would give “customers another path to get new demand on line efficiently and gives us another path to capture premium value that supports the existing fleet.” One example he provided was potentially pairing a customer with a battery storage provider.

Constellation did not disclose who its first Peak+ customer is.

Uprates updates: During the third quarter of 2026, Constellation signed agreements with three customers for 4,560 MW, which includes 1,165 MW of new nuclear capacity through ongoing and planned uprates that the utility has said will cost $4.3 billion. It is set to invest roughly $1.3 billion in uprates in 2026–2027, with the other $3 billion to fund uprate projects in 2028–2032.

The Department of Energy has committed to a $5 billion conditional loan that would cover up to 80 percent of eligible costs from 2023 to 2035, according to Constellation. This could include potential future investments.

“We have not finished exploring uprates at plants. Design and engineering work continues,” said Dominguez.

Constellation’s nuclear fleet produced 46,677 GWh in the third quarter, up from 46,477 GWh in the third quarter of the previous year. Excluding its two partly owned plants, Salem and South Texas Project, its fleet reported a 97.2 percent capacity factor for the third quarter, higher than the 96.8 percent capacity factor reported for the third quarter of 2025.

Crane update: Dominguez said the restart of the former Three Mile Island-1 in Pennsylvania remains on track for the second half of 2027, which, he added, would be ahead of schedule. The restart project cleared a regulatory hurdle in September when the Nuclear Regulatory Commission issued its final environmental assessment and a finding of no significant impact for Crane, a decision that Dominguez described as “favorable” during the earnings call. Fuel assemblies and transformers are already on site, he added.

Weighing in on midterms: Dominguez referenced the November 3 midterm elections a few times during the earnings call. He said there was a “bit of an overreaction” in the market to the election results—where Democrats flipped the U.S. House and U.S. Senate—and the impact Democratic majorities may have on the data center boom. Much like with nuclear energy expansion, Dominguez said there are bipartisan solutions out there to address the topic of data centers.

“The bottom line is Democrats care deeply about economic growth and they care very deeply about the many labor jobs that go with data center construction,” he said. “Indeed, with labor such a key constituent for Democrats, it's hard to imagine that we are going to halt work.”

Clean public transport. Energy-efficient buildings. Affordable energy.

Those are a few of the things the president of the U.N. climate talks — known as COP31 — asked global leaders, delegates and climate activists to pledge as part of the global electrification plan laid out during the world’s largest annual climate summit.

But environmental and human rights organizations caution that without strong safeguards, the mining boom for the minerals and metals needed to make the power lines, batteries, wind turbines and other energy infrastructure that can make the pledge a reality could have serious environmental and human rights impacts across the globe.

Mining has come at a cost to communities and habitats around the globe: Forests have been felled, water supplies poisoned and Indigenous peoples have lost access to land. Rights groups have urged COP31 officials to focus on how to fairly source the materials needed for the transition.

COP31 sets ambitious electrification goal

Turkey announced that electrification would be one of the main priorities during its copresidency of COP31 with Australia. The “35-by-35” global electrification pledge aims to increase the use of electricity from 21% to 35% by 2035 to reduce planet-warming greenhouse emissions, preferably from renewable energy such as solar and wind.

The pledge builds on commitments made at previous U.N. climate summits: At COP28, countries agreed to work toward tripling renewable energy capacity and transitioning away from fossil fuels. COP29 focused on energy storage, grid modernization and climate finance.

The COP31 presidency said electrification is the next logical step, translating earlier pledges into changes in how energy is consumed.

“This transition brings together renewable energy, strong grids, storage capacity, energy efficiency, clean transport and green industry. Each supports the others,” said COP31 President Murat Kurum, who is also Turkey’s environment minister. “We want people to feel the results of climate talks in daily life: in buildings that use less energy, in clean public transport, in energy they can afford and in new jobs.”

Environmental activists note that the pledge does not require that electricity must come from renewable sources, meaning coal and other fossil fuels could be used. But as countries try to move away from fossil fuels, renewable energy is expected to play a major role.

Experts warn of a mining boom

From Indonesia to Brazil, the boom in demand for the metals and minerals needed to create wind turbines, solar panels, electric vehicle batteries, high-speed railways and other technologies crucial for the renewable energy transition has been underway for some time, according to the International Energy Agency.

Countries are also exploring new ways, like deep-sea mining, to secure their own mineral supplies, especially as the Iran war drives clean energy development.

The 35-by-35 pledge is expected to push demand even higher.

Data released by the Business & Human Rights Resource Centre shows those threats are on the rise. The international nonprofit recorded over 300 human rights allegations linked to transition mineral mining in 2025, up 73% from the previous year.

And experts warn that a boom in mining would likely lead to an increase in abuses.

“If mining is going to ramp up without proper protections in place, I think we can probably expect to see some of these problems ramp up as well,” said Emily Iona Stewart, the head of policy and advocacy at environmental and human rights group Global Witness.

Environmentalists call for guardrails against abuse

Environmental and human rights groups are urging governments to strengthen safeguards across critical material supply chains.

In an open letter to the COP31 presidencies, over 120 international civil society groups laid out conditions they want met for the 35-by-35 target, including protecting ecosystems, having binding human rights and environmental due diligence, and protecting Indigenous peoples.

“The transition must not repeat the harms of the fossil fuel era or replace one dependency with another,” the letter stated.

Experts said better recycling of already-mined materials is also key to reducing the reliance on mining. The IEA estimates that a successful scaleup of recycling could also lower the need for new mining by 25‑40% by 2050.

Yet, most countries don’t have waste management programs or supportive regulations that would enable recycling, according to the IEA.

Rights experts also point out that the official negotiations and main talking points of COP31 do not contain explicit language on critical minerals and mining, leaving the door open for mining abuses to spread.

“If we want to do good by communities, bringing electricity to communities who don’t have it right now is a basic human need and right,” said Aimee Boulanger, executive director of the Initiative for Responsible Mining Assurance. “But we can’t do good by some communities by doing inherent harm against others where the raw materials are extracted.”

The COP31 presidencies — Turkey is the official host while Australia is leading the negotiations — did not respond to requests for comment.

name: EPA
title: What Bill C-39's loosened environmental regulations could mean for Canadians
description:
Hailed as a major advancement by the government, it has also been criticized as a bill that could bulldoze environmental regulations.
What could this new legislation mean for environmental regulations and how could it impact Canadians if passed into law?
However, Bill C-39 reduces the time period for thorough environmental review.
Environmental regulations are not simply environmental protections, they also protect public health.
Media coverage of Bill C-39 tends to focus on pipelines, mines and regulatory processes.
text:
Protests took place in cities across Canada today against a proposed bill that some fear could undermine environmental protections as well as the rights of workers and Indigenous communities.

The Canadian government introduced Bill C-39, the Building Canada Strong Act, in September 2026, with the stated aim of fast-tracking large-scale projects. Hailed as a major advancement by the government, it has also been criticized as a bill that could bulldoze environmental regulations.

The government has said the proposed legislation is aimed at protecting “economic security.” Under the new bill, new “federal economic zones” would be created where projects could be “pre-approved.” This would provide exceptions to habitat and species-at-risk protections and other federal oversight.

What could this new legislation mean for environmental regulations and how could it impact Canadians if passed into law?

Less time for environmental review

In October 2024, the government released a framework for implementing the right to a healthy environment under the Canadian Environmental Protection Act, linking environmental protection directly to human health and well-being. However, Bill C-39 reduces the time period for thorough environmental review.

The government has touted the bill’s shortened timeline for project approval, compressed to a one-year review. This allows for quick decisions to be made, and proponents to know whether a specific project will be able to proceed in a shorter timeframe. While this is viewed as a clear advantage, some are warning that the one-year timeline could still be extended and delayed.

Environmental regulations are not simply environmental protections, they also protect public health. Effective regulations reduce exposure to polluted air, contaminated water, toxic chemicals and climate-related hazards.

They help prevent disease, improve quality of life, reduce health-care costs and protect the well-being of current and future generations. Recent evidence shows that the health and economic benefits of environmental regulation far outweigh the relative costs.

Build first, assess later

Under Bill C-39, the government would be able to permit preliminary construction to begin before the Impact Assessment Agency of Canada completes an assessment. This would be the case if the environment minister considers a project to be in the “public interest.”

Reduced environmental regulations would directly impact the communities within the area of the proposed projects and those downstream. It could mean potential environmental degradation and destruction, as well as weakened habitat protection, before a full assessment can be done.

Many of the proposed “projects of public interest” are in areas of significant ecological importance. Many are situated on or near First Nations territories. Leaders from the Nishnawbe Aski Nation stated they “will not accept this legislation as it stands,” stating they support responsible development but that acceleration of development cannot be at the expense of Indigenous communities.

The government is wrong in assuming the choice is either environmental protection or rapid development. Many jurisdictions have shown that projects can move faster when governments improve co-ordination across departments and agencies.

This could include digitizing permitting, establishing clear timelines, conducting strategic planning earlier and eliminating duplication in approval processes. The evidence suggests that delays often arise from fragmented governance and administrative inefficiencies, not environmental safeguards.

Pay now, worry later

Bill C-39 also introduces changes to the Fisheries Act that make it easier to advance projects that may impact fish or fish habitats. The bill introduces third-party “habitat credits” and fees for minor impacts. Under this model, a third party can engage in habitat restoration and effectively “sell” credits to companies building major projects.

The bill would allow companies that damage fish habitat during construction to buy habitat restoration credits from approved conservation groups instead of doing the restoration work themselves. The goal is to speed up project approvals while still requiring companies to compensate for environmental damage.

Supporters say this could fund larger and more effective habitat restoration projects, reducing red tape without comprising environmental monitoring. Critics worry it could make it easier for companies to damage fish habitats as long as they can afford to pay for credits elsewhere, allowing habitat damage to become simply a cost of doing business.

Media coverage of Bill C-39 tends to focus on pipelines, mines and regulatory processes. However, it’s also about the air Canadians breathe and the water they drink. It is about the fish we catch and the natural spaces that support our health and well-being.

The question is not whether Canada should build new projects or strengthen its economy. It must. The real question is whether it can do so without weakening environmental safeguards that protect communities, ecosystems and future generations.

As governments push to accelerate development, Canadians should pay close attention. The consequences will be felt not only in boardrooms and construction sites. They will be felt in rivers, forests and households across the country for decades to come.

text:
For 12 years, Texas energy and environmental regulators have been influenced by Gov. Greg Abbott’s appointments to lead agencies. That includes the five-member Public Utility Commission, the three-member Texas Commission on Environmental Quality and, more indirectly, the board that oversees ERCOT.

On Jan. 19, that appointment power passes to Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa. But she won’t be able to reshape everything overnight. Some positions are immediately available for her appointments, but others are tied to expiring terms, and many require approval from the Republican-majority Texas Senate.

Public Utility Commission (PUC)

The Texas PUC is arguably Hinojosa’s most consequential appointment opportunity for influencing energy. The governor appoints all five members and designates the chair.

Day one: Hinojosa can name a new chair, replacing Thomas Gleeson. She can also move to replace Commissioner Courtney Hjaltman, whose term expired in 2025.

By late January: The Senate never confirmed Commissioners Patrick Rhode or Morgan Johnson. Hinojosa will need to resubmit their nominations or select replacements within the first 10 days of the legislative session, which begins Jan. 12.

Sept. 1: Terms expire for Commissioner Kathleen Jackson and Rhode, creating additional opportunities to change membership.

Hinojosa would have the opportunity to influence a majority of the five-member commission in her first year. If she also replaces Johnson in January and secures Senate approval, she could influence four of the five seats.

title: STEP begins major procurements; First Light collaborates with U.K. laser facility
description:
STEP procurements: UKFE has launched a procurement program seeking industry partners to develop five of STEP’s key systems.
First Light Fusion: First Light Fusion, which is based in Oxford, England, will collaborate with the CLF to work on the fast ignition physics of its inertial confinement fusion concept.
According to First Light, “CLF scientists will model the generation and transport of energetic electrons produced by the laser and how efficiently their energy can be deposited into dense fusion fuel.
The CLF has world-leading expertise in laser and plasma physics to accelerate this step.
Bringing these two phases together gives us a clear route towards integrated FLARE experiments,” said Jonathan Skidmore, chief scientist at First Light.
text:
STEP procurements: UKFE has launched a procurement program seeking industry partners to develop five of STEP’s key systems.

The program budget allocates up to £115 million (approximately $152,180,000) across the five areas for two-year contracts.

The call seeks partners to design, integrate, manufacture, and operate STEP’s breeder blanket system, fuel cycle system, and plant control system, which collectively cover the systems for harvesting energy from fusion, producing fuel supplies, processing and storing fuel, and monitoring and coordinating plant operations.

UKFE also seeks a partner to develop and operate facilities to test technologies and engineering solutions before deployment and a partner to support the systems engineering and overall plant integration.

First Light Fusion: First Light Fusion, which is based in Oxford, England, will collaborate with the CLF to work on the fast ignition physics of its inertial confinement fusion concept.

First Light has been developing a two-step approach to inertial confinement fusion, first compressing the fuel using magnetic pressure and then igniting it with a high-intensity laser pulse. The collaboration with CLF focuses on making that second step as effective as possible.

According to First Light, “CLF scientists will model the generation and transport of energetic electrons produced by the laser and how efficiently their energy can be deposited into dense fusion fuel. The program will explore approaches including engineered target structures and magnetic fields designed to guide energetic electrons into the ignition region.”

For a fusion energy facility, the target would be surrounded by lithium, which would facilitate heat conversion. According to the company’s website, this is intended to be a high-gain, low-repetition method with a self-sustaining fuel cycle. First Light is developing the fuel system for this approach, which it calls FLARE, and plans to find partners that will utilize the technology it’s developed to build fusion energy facilities.

“We have validated the first half of the FLARE concept using the target itself to create the pressure history needed to assemble fuel at high density, with a relatively simple pulsed power driver. The next phase is to rapidly heat that dense fuel. The CLF has world-leading expertise in laser and plasma physics to accelerate this step. Bringing these two phases together gives us a clear route towards integrated FLARE experiments,” said Jonathan Skidmore, chief scientist at First Light.

text:
BASF has opened a methylene diphenyl diisocyanate (MDI) manufacturing facility at its Verbund site in Geismar, Louisiana. The company, which produces chemicals and materials including MDI, invested approximately $1 billion in the project, its largest wholly owned investment in the United States to date.

The expansion nearly doubles annual MDI production capacity at Geismar to approximately 600,000 metric tons, making BASF the largest MDI producer in North America. MDI is a raw material used to manufacture polyurethanes, which are used in construction, appliances, transportation, automotive, footwear and furniture.

The project was completed in three phases beginning in 2018. BASF commissioned a new MDI synthesis unit in 2020, expanded upstream units in 2021, and completed the final phase with additional upstream units and a splitter. The final phase incorporated advanced digitalization and technology intended to increase production flexibility and strengthen supply reliability and competitiveness. BASF also increased aniline production capacity at Geismar, supporting its integrated production chain and availability for North American customers in agricultural chemicals, rubber, and dyes and pigments.

BASF executives discuss investment and production capacity

“This significant investment reflects our confidence in the continued growth of the polyurethane market and ensures that our customers benefit from a highly reliable, competitive and locally integrated supply source for years to come,” said Ramkumar Dhruva, president of BASF’s Monomer Division, in a November press release. “With this expansion BASF is taking the lead in MDI production in North America.”

“The United States has long been a key market for BASF, and this $1 billion investment is a strong commitment to our customers and to our future here,” said Dr. Markus Kamieth, chairman of the Board of Executive Directors of BASF SE. “With our new world-scale MDI facility in Geismar, we are strengthening our core businesses, driving innovation and bringing more production closer to our customers.”

text:
Congress is considering a national fee for electric vehicles to fund road construction as gas tax revenue declines.

Some EV drivers argue a flat fee is unfair compared to the usage-based gas tax paid by other motorists.

Lawmakers have been hesitant to implement a mileage-based tax due to privacy concerns.

A reader, Edward Robertson of Texas, responded to a story we wrote recently about a $130 national fee for electric car drivers that Congress is considering imposing as soon as December. We took a deeper dive to attempt to answer his questions. If you have questions about anything you read in our coverage, email me at klaing@usatodayco.com and I'll do my best to answer. You can also subscribe to our Cars newsletter here.

Robertson raised two points as he asked us to explore the topic of the proposed national EV fee further. First, he said "states are already imposing their own fixed fees on EVs," noting that he already pays a $200 registration fee for his EV in Texas. Secondly, he added, the proposal calls for "flat fees rather than being use-based fees like the gas tax."

"That means that I have to pay them even if I do not drive the car at all," Roberston wrote. "They should be based on my annual odometer reading at registration (based on my annual inspection documentation) to calculate a gas tax equivalent using a reference mpg figure - say 30 mpg.

"These EV fees are arbitrary, excessive, and unequal," he added. "And to add insult to injury, I already pay taxes on the electricity that is used to 'fuel’ my EV. Furthermore, by driving an EV I am also reducing the amount of pollution emitted. I demand equal treatment."

Why is Congress considering adding an EV fee?

Congress is considering adding an EV fee because lawmakers have struggling to come up with news ways to pay for road construction as receipts from the federal gas tax that has historically funded them dwindle.

The federal government currently collects 18.4 cents per gallon on every U.S. gasoline purchase to help pay for road and transit construction projects, and most states also tack on their own fees. EV drivers don’t pay that tax because their vehicles don’t use gasoline.

Money collected from gas-car drivers through federal fuel taxes goes into the U.S. Department of Transportation’s Highway Trust Fund and is then distributed to states to help pay for road and transit construction projects. As cars have become more fuel-efficient and more drivers have opted for EVs and hybrids, less money per mile driven has been collected, despite increased use of roads. Lawmakers have looked for ways to close that growing gap in federal gas tax revenue.

The federal gas tax hasn't increased since 1993, and it brings in about $40 billion a year at its current level, according to the Tax Policy Center. President Donald Trump and some lawmakers in Congress have recently proposed suspending the federal gas tax as the average price of gas hovers around $4 per gallon, according to the AAA Auto Club.

The federal government typically spends about $60 billion on transportation projects, and infrastructure advocates say that amount is just enough to maintain the nation's roads and transit systems. Most states also levy their own gas taxes to fund local road projects.

Supporters of the proposed fee say it's time for EV drivers to contribute to the fund that helps pay for the upkeep of the roads they use. Rep. Sam Graves, a Republican from Missouri who chairs the U.S. House Transportation Committee, said in a statement that the EV fee "ensures that electric vehicle owners begin paying their fair share for the use of our roads."

Why is Congress not considering a mileage-based fee for road construction?

Mileage fees have been floated by infrastructure supporters as a potential replacement for the gas tax before.

Vehicle miles traveled (VMT) programs tax drivers based on miles they drive on U.S. roads instead of how much gasoline they purchase. Mileage-based road tax proposals have long been controversial in U.S. transportation funding debates because critics question how the government would monitor drivers' traveling habits without infringing on their privacy.

A number of states, such as Oregon, Pennsylvania, Utah, Hawaii, Virginia, and Colorado, have adopted mileage fee programs, but thus far Congress has been unwilling to do so. As gas tax receipts have dwindled, Congress has resorted to transferring money into the Highway Trust Fund to make up for the shortfall rather than raise the fuel levy or adopt a controversial mileage menu.

Supporters of the current proposal note that the EV tax proposal would involve no tracking or reporting from drivers about their travels. EV owners would simply pay the $130 annual fee upon registering their vehicles each year.

What do EV drivers potentially have to pay in state and federal fees?

The national gas tax money only pays for federally funded road construction projects, which are usually related to the upkeep of the interstate highway system.

States have their own roads, which they need to raise money for to maintain and improve. Even for gas car drivers, states usually tack on their own taxes on top of the 18 cents per gallon the federal government charges. The average state gas tax that gets tacked on at the pump is 33.8 cents per gallon, according to US Gas Gauge.

Robertson argued that a mileage-based fee approach would be more fair.

"To be clear, I am fine with paying my fair share of taxes to support road infrastructure development and maintenance, but these fees are arbitrary and unfair," he wrote, nothing that in three years of owning an EV, he has traveled less than 6,000 miles, "but I have paid $600 extra for the Texas EV registration fee."

"Either that, or eliminate the gas tax and charge all passenger vehicles the same flat fees at the state and federal levels," Roberston said of the proposed mileage fee. "As long as I am being treated equally and fairly, then I can deal with that."

A lot of EV supporters agree with him that a national fee targeting plug-in model drivers would be unfair.

Electric vehicle owners save an average of about $8,811 in ownership and maintenance costs over 200,000 miles compared with owners of best-selling gas-powered vehicles in the same class, according to Consumer Reports.

A driver who opts for a new or used EV could save $2,200 annually on gas, according to the U.S. Department of Energy. Hybrid drivers can save $1,500 on gas each year, according to the agency.

EV supporters have argued that additional annual fees increase the cost of owning an electric vehicle.

“Charging a punitive fee on Americans who choose to drive electric vehicles goes against the idea of drivers paying their fair share based on their driving habits, as drivers will pay based on their drivetrain of choice and not their use of public infrastructure," Albert Gore, who is executive director of the Zero Emission Transportation Association, which lobbies in Washington for EV-friendly policies, said in a statement.

An EV fee "would also discourage drivers from choosing vehicles that are among the most American-made cars on the road — and the domestic jobs and supply chain investments these products represent," Gore added.

title: Despite slow start on climate action, Omaha officials say city making progress
description:
The city hasn’t done enough, argued Omaha City Council member Pete Festersen, a Democrat who has represented north-central Omaha, including neighborhoods like Dundee and Benson, since 2009.
“We have raised the bar to where this is one of the most important things we’re working on in the city,” Ewing said.
But the month after the Omaha City Council approved the plan, President Donald Trump took office.
The city passed its climate plan in 2021 and hired Kim Morrow to be its chief sustainability officer the next year.
The projects, which range from composting to wetland cleaning, align with the city’s climate plan.
text:
Christie Abdul-Greene swiped along her iPad on a City of Omaha website describing its roadmap to address climate change.

The city promised to build “climate resilience” and “a more sustainable future” in Omaha. It was serious about bettering the lives of its citizens, according to a quote highlighted on the website from Mayor Jean Stothert.

Two problems: The city passed the plan in 2024 and Stothert left office more than a year ago.

“Gosh,” sighed Abdul-Greene, co-chair of a city task force charged with addressing climate change.

Since passing its climate action and resilience plan in December 2024, the city has been quiet on how it’s preparing for an increasingly volatile environment. The plan’s bold 2050 goal calls for Omaha to reach net zero emissions — meaning the majority of the city’s energy would come from renewable energy or fuels that don’t create greenhouse gases.

City officials say they’re investing in climate-related projects for biking and walking infrastructure, flood management and urban forestry. But in the last two years, they have also lost the city employee supposed to oversee the work while the federal government paused a promised federal grant that may never arrive.

The city hasn’t done enough, argued Omaha City Council member Pete Festersen, a Democrat who has represented north-central Omaha, including neighborhoods like Dundee and Benson, since 2009. The City Council has passed policies, like allowing denser, less car-centric development, but those have been “one-off’s” rather than steps along a designed path, he said.

Meanwhile, neighboring cities like Lincoln seem to have left Omaha in the dust.

“I’m concerned we haven’t made more progress,” Festersen said, “and that it’s not being actively managed or measured.”

The city is moving toward that, Abdul-Greene said.

For the last year, a climate risk and resiliency task force has met to decide where to start among the 10-year plan’s 46 strategies and 173 potential actions. Many of those actions were designed to be initiated within Phase 1 of the plan, which ends next year.

This year, the city hired a consultant to prioritize action steps and target easier wins.

“I’m both frustrated and excited,” said Abdul-Greene, who is the executive director of Keep Omaha Beautiful. “I think there’s a lot of potential. I think the climate is right for us to move forward.”

Mayor John Ewing said he can’t be responsible for what did or didn’t happen prior to his election in May 2025. He does believe the city is on the right track now.

Its current priorities are to figure out how to make City of Omaha buildings run on renewable energy and electrifying its non-emergency vehicles by 2035 as well as create an online hub where citizens can track progress toward goals.

“We have raised the bar to where this is one of the most important things we’re working on in the city,” Ewing said.

Unexpected setbacks contributed to the slow start, said Marco Floreani, also a co-chair of the city’s task force.

The city developed its plan through a federal grant offered by President Joe Biden’s administration. The plan showed Omaha’s greenhouse gas production and identified the city’s risks to a warming climate, including a 12-degree increase in average temperatures by 2100 if global emissions are not reduced, 70 additional days over 95 degrees and more heavy rainstorms.

To curb climate change and protect from its effects, the city set myriad goals, including designing 100 miles of new biking routes and requiring airtight building construction for energy efficiency.

The city hoped to have more federal money available for implementation, Floreani said. But the month after the Omaha City Council approved the plan, President Donald Trump took office. In March, his pick to lead the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency promised to “drive a dagger through the heart of the climate change religion” by “launching the biggest deregulatory action in U.S. history.”

The federal government awarded the City of Omaha a $461,600 grant for solar charging stations for the city’s bikeshare program, weatherization programs and electric vehicle infrastructure and planning, but the city never got the money. The grant has been under review for more than a year, Floreani said. The U.S. Department of Energy did not return a request for comment.

The city also lost its staff member overseeing climate work. Robert Laroco, previously a city planner and project manager for the climate plan, said he left for a job in Sarpy County soon after Trump began his second term. He did not respond to additional questions.

Last year, Ewing restarted work by creating the risk and resilience task force. But the duties still fell to people like Floreani, who’s primarily the mayor’s deputy chief of staff for economic development and development services.

Ewing said the city is preparing to hire someone to implement climate action in the next several months.

Said Abdul-Greene said, “That is absolutely necessary. This is more than a full-time job.”

Omaha was one of the last big American cities to adopt a climate action plan. It passed an environmental chapter to the city’s master plan in 2010, which included similar goals but largely went unimplemented.

Ryan Wishart, an assistant sociology professor at Creighton University and one of many people who helped develop the plan, is frustrated. But he doesn’t blame the city — yet.

He understands the challenges presented by the Trump administration and new local leadership. But with the Ewing administration established, he’s waiting to see what happens this year.

“We’re going to see more clearly what kind of commitments are being made,” he said. “Are they putting in the staff time? Are they putting in the resources to take this seriously? It has been two years, so now it’s time to start seeing what we’re going to do about it.”

Craig Moody has also been disappointed before. But the managing partner at Verdis Group, a local environmental consultant that the city has hired to work on its climate plan, believes this time will be different.

But he said the city still needs someone to oversee implementation.

“Governance is massively critical to successful execution,” he said. “Absent it, you lose accountability, you lose direction.”

Lincoln shows the effect of that kind of hire, Moody said.

The city passed its climate plan in 2021 and hired Kim Morrow to be its chief sustainability officer the next year. This year, a progress report showed the city cut greenhouse gas emissions by 30% compared to 2011. Of the plan’s goals, 76% are either completed or in progress, according to the report.

Morrow said Trump’s election hasn’t affected the city much. While it did lose some funding, most projects have continued normally.

The city added more than five miles of bike lanes and six miles of trails. Along with Lincoln Electric Systems, it spent $600,000 to help residents install energy-efficient heating and cooling systems. The City of Lincoln also restarted a program to offset the costs of adding renewable energy systems, electric vehicle charging stations and other upgrades to commercial, industrial or multifamily properties.

In July, the city received the highest certification from the U.S. Green Building Council. Lincoln is only the 10th city to receive the platinum award from the Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design program.

The plan has helped the city evaluate data centers, too. It denied an application a few years ago because the server hub’s potential draw on resources didn’t align with city environmental goals, Morrow said.

Recently, Morrow also got two full-time employees, one fellow and an intern to keep up with the evolving work.

“Moving forward in this direction has been a priority of the mayor’s from the very beginning,” Morrow said of Lincoln Mayor Leirion Gaylor Baird who, like Ewing, is a Democrat. “The fact that she created my position and put me in her executive office makes a huge difference.”

Once Omaha hires that employee, progress will follow, Abdul-Greene said. And once the city starts posting some wins, the community will see there’s momentum.

The signs may be starting to show.

Its website now lists progress, current priorities and the people leading the effort. After Flatwater Free Press inquired, the attribution on Stothert’s quote on the website was updated to: “Former Omaha Mayor.”

On Oct. 29, the city awarded 12 grants of up to $5,000 each to teenagers and young adults to do climate work. The projects, which range from composting to wetland cleaning, align with the city’s climate plan.

But more importantly, Ewing said, the city is showing the community, particularly environmentally conscious young people, that it’s committed to this issue.

“We have to be responsible and listen to the science that says that our climate is changing and it’s warming, and if we don’t do something to address that,” he said, “then we are going to have a long-term problem.”

Dive Brief:

The Pentagon has a queue of around 400 onshore wind projects awaiting approval, but lacks sufficient staffing to address the issue, said Dale Marks, assistant secretary of defense for energy, installations, and environment, in a Nov. 3 legal filing. with the U.S. District Court for the District of Oregon.

Marks’ comments were part of a Pentagon response in an ongoing lawsuit filed by a coalition of clean energy trade groups, developers, and states against the U.S. Department of Defense. The original complaint, filed May 31, alleged that DOD “stopped fulfilling its statutory mandate to assess wind projects’ impacts on military readiness,” with the process “[grinding] to a halt” after Marks was confirmed. The suit asked the court to vacate DOD’s review freeze policy and order DOD to take action by certain dates.

In the Nov. 3 filing, DOD said it is complying with an August court injunction ordering a stay of what DOD called a “temporary pause” and has “returned to reviewing” permits for wind projects. It opposed a motion from the plaintiffs asking the court to enforce the stay.

Dive Insight:

Since the court stayed the wind review pause, DOD said, the office that issues wind project permits — the Military Aviation and Installation Assurance Siting Clearinghouse — has shifted from a “pause on processing-related activity to active assessment of projects.”

American Clean Power Association Vice President of Policy and Regulatory Affairs Tom Vinson disputed this in an Oct. 20 declaration, based in part on “information that ACP members provided to me.”

“Despite the Court’s clear orders, DOD has not resumed review,” Vinson said. “While it may have reported some administrative activity, none of this activity has resulted in any substantive movement through mitigation review.”

He testified that DOD’s delay has threatened the economics of wind projects awaiting permits as developers continue to incur costs as they wait for DOD to move forward.

Vinson said one project has seen turbine delivery pushed back and noted that “equipment delivered after December 31, 2027, will not qualify for the Advanced Manufacturing Credit, which the developer estimates would otherwise provide a benefit of approximately $200,000 per turbine, or roughly $24 million across the project.”

In the Nov. 3 filing, Marks said none of the teams tasked with reviewing wind energy permits “are sized to manage the dramatic influx of applications received in recent years during a period simultaneously characterized by downward pressures on resourcing (manning, funding, and contractor support).”

Contractors can’t execute inherently governmental functions, Marks wrote, so action on the approximately 400 projects in the queue rests “solely” with eight federal employees across DOD.

“In an average year, the [DOD] would execute 13 mitigation agreements, but more recently, this number has hovered around 30,” Marks said.

title: Plugging Into Low-Carbon Investment: What Corporate Capex Reveals - Sustainalytics
description:
Between 2021 and 2024, electricity distribution and transmission capex rose by only about 14%, while clean generation capex rose by more than half and EV manufacturing capex more than doubled.
At the lagging end, Latin America and Africa/Middle East together receive only about one-tenth of electrification capex globally.
As shown in Figure 3, transmission capex kept pace with clean generation in 2022 but fell behind from 2023 onward.
While historical grid investment falls short, the question now is whether planned spending in the future will close the gap.
Clean investment needs to displace — not just sit alongside — existing fossil-fuel and combustion-engine investment.
text:
Key Insights:

Setting carbon reduction targets is necessary, but targets alone are not always indicators of transition readiness. Capex shows whether they are being funded.

About three-quarters of companies’ low-carbon capex is focused on electrification, the central pathway to COP31’s goal of raising electricity’s share of final energy consumption to 35% by 2035.

Grids are the bottleneck. Between 2021 and 2024, electricity distribution and transmission capex rose by only about 14%, while clean generation capex rose by more than half and EV manufacturing capex more than doubled.

Planned capex points to grids catching up in Europe and North America, but investment remains concentrated.

Over the past decade, low-carbon transition has moved from technological possibility toward economic reality. What remains unresolved is whether investment will shift at a sufficient pace and scale to translate that progress into real-world decarbonization. At the 2026 UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye, the overarching goal remains to shift global focus from climate pledges to implementation of the 2015 Paris Agreement.

Electrification is central to that shift because it links clean power to end use. It is also a key theme at COP31. The COP31 Presidency has proposed a collective goal to raise electricity's share of final energy consumption to 35% by 2035, up from about 20%.1 To reach that goal, companies will need to translate it into their own decarbonization targets. As we highlight in our report, Transition or Illusion?, setting such targets is necessary, but it is not enough. We therefore view capital expenditure (capex) as an important signal of whether those targets are being funded, and electrification is where that test matters most.

Targets Show Ambition, but Capex Shows Action

Disclosure on decarbonization measures has matured through the introduction of various standards and frameworks, including the Task Force on Climate-Related Financial Disclosures (TCFD), International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB), and IFRS S2 Sustainability Disclosures, and has significantly increased companies’ transparency on their climate transition commitments. Corporate climate targets, disclosures, and strategies have increased, but they remain poor differentiators of what companies are actually doing. If companies are not allocating capex to align with their strategies and meet goals, those strategies and goals remain aspirational, rather than actionable. The question for investors has shifted from, “Does the company have a target?” to “Is the company sufficiently funding the transition to achieve the target?”

Capex is a measure of real transition action. It provides insights into which assets are built and which technologies are deployed, and whether they line up with decarbonization targets. It shows true intent and, ultimately, the ability to execute those targets. Unlike traditional metrics (mainly emissions data), which tend to be backward-looking, capex shows what will be built next and is therefore more decision-useful for investors. And when we follow capex, it clearly points to electrification.

Low-Carbon Capex Is Concentrated in Electrification

Electrification is the bridge between building low-carbon capacity and decarbonizing the economy, and it is how COP31’s goal will be reached in which electricity accounts for 35% of final energy consumption by 2035. As transportation, buildings, and eventually industry become more reliant on electricity, investment must extend beyond renewable energy generation to grids and end-use technologies.

Our corporate capex data show that companies are already investing in this direction. Electrification-related activities account for about three-quarters of all low-carbon capex in our Low Carbon Transition Rating (LCTR) data coverage (see Figure 1), with investment flowing not only into low-carbon power generation but also into the network infrastructure and end-use technologies needed to support a more electrified economy.

Figure 1. Top 10 Low-Carbon Activities (% of Low-Carbon Capex), 2021–2028

Source: Morningstar Sustainalytics.

Note: Electrification activities are shown in dark blue. Based on activity-level capex for about 2,400 listed companies in Morningstar Sustainalytics’ capex dataset. 2025–2028 reflects capex plans disclosed by companies, which cover fewer companies than 2021–2024.

We view COP31’s electrification goal as a useful lens for assessing companies’ transition plans, and Figure 1 shows where the capex is going. Electricity transmission and distribution alone account for a large amount of low-carbon capex, well ahead of solar generation, electric vehicle (EV) manufacturing, and other generation capex. Where this money is spent, however, differs sharply by region.

Figure 2. Regional Split of Electrification Capex, 2021–2028

Source: Morningstar Sustainalytics.

Note: Based on activity-level capex for about 2,400 listed companies in Morningstar Sustainalytics’ capex dataset. 2025–2028 reflects capex plans disclosed by companies, which cover fewer companies than 2021–2024.

Three Regions Dominate and Each Funds a Different Part of the System

Regionally, Asia-Pacific, Europe, and the US and Canada each account for about 30% of electrification capex, but they fund different parts of the system. For example, Asia-Pacific accounts for about half of global capex in power supply and EV manufacturing. This is driven largely by China, which met its 2030 wind and solar capacity target in 2024, six years early.2 Europe and North America, meanwhile, lead in electricity transmission, supported in both regions by increasing regulation for utilities. At the lagging end, Latin America and Africa/Middle East together receive only about one-tenth of electrification capex globally. This is a gap that matters for an electrification target set at the global level, as emerging and developing economies are expected to drive nearly 80% of electricity demand growth through to 2030.3

Electrification Needs Supply, Grids and Demand to Grow Together

Electrification is a system: generation, distribution, and demand. Clean generation produces power, the grid carries it, and end users (such as EVs) consume it. Each depends on the others. New solar farms, for example, have limited value without transmission lines to connect them, and EVs cut emissions only if the electricity they use comes from clean energy sources. To reach COP31’s 35% by 2035 target, all three parts of the system must grow together, and the fossil fuel capacity they replace must shrink. The balance between them — more than the absolute amounts — tells us whether electrification is on track.

Our data show that this balance is slipping. Between 2021 and 2024, capex at the demand end (EV manufacturing) more than doubled, and supply capex (clean power generation) rose by more than half, but transmission capex rose by only about 14% (see Figure 3).

Figure 3. Global Electrification Capex in the Power System, 2021–2024 (% change since 2021)

Source: Morningstar Sustainalytics.

Note: Demand = EV manufacturing; supply = clean power generation (solar, wind, hydro, nuclear, geothermal); transmission = electricity transmission and distribution. Based on activity-level capex for about 2,400 listed companies in Morningstar Sustainalytics’ capex dataset.

The Slump in the Middle

The electrification system is being built faster at either end compared to the middle. Grids are the largest single destination for low-carbon capex, yet they are falling behind clean generation. As shown in Figure 3, transmission capex kept pace with clean generation in 2022 but fell behind from 2023 onward. In 2024, transmission dropped below its 2023 peak, while supply kept climbing. This left transmission 14% above its 2021 level against 56% for supply, a gap of 42 percentage points. Our data cover listed companies only, so unlisted state-owned grid investment is not captured, and total grid spending is likely higher. But because electricity supply and transmission are measured across the same companies, the gap between them is a like-for-like signal that grid investment is falling behind.

Because every unit of new renewable generation ultimately depends on network capacity to deliver electricity to consumers, this widening gap between supply and transmission capex provides a simple indicator of whether grid expansion is keeping pace with clean energy deployment. This relative lack of growth in transmission is becoming a bottleneck, as clean power cannot connect to end users fast enough to keep up with demand. This puts the 2035 electrification goal at risk. The challenge is no longer generating demand for electrification technologies or building renewable generation capacity. It is ensuring that grid infrastructure expands rapidly enough to connect the two.

While historical grid investment falls short, the question now is whether planned spending in the future will close the gap. Figure 4 shows how capex is split between supply, grids, and demand, and compares spending between 2021 and 2024 with companies’ planned spending for 2025 to 2028. As plans for future years cover fewer companies, the change is indicative, rather than a forecast.

Figure 4. Electrification Capex by Power System Part and Region, 2021–2024 and 2025–2028 Plans (% of total)

Source: Morningstar Sustainalytics.

Note: Demand = EV manufacturing; supply = clean power generation (solar, wind, hydro, nuclear, geothermal); transmission = electricity transmission and distribution. 2025–2028 reflects capex plans disclosed by companies, which cover fewer companies than 2021–2024. Latin America and Africa/Middle East are included in “All regions” but not shown separately because of their small base. Based on activity-level capex for about 2,400 listed companies in Morningstar Sustainalytics’ capex dataset.

Grid Plans Suggest a Catch-up, but Are Uneven

Planned capex points to grids catching up in some regions, but visibility remains limited. As shown in Figure 4, transmission’s share of electrification capex across all regions rises from 60% in 2021–2024 to 66% in 2025–2028 plans. Regionally, that figure is projected to be about three-quarters in Europe, and in the US and Canada. Asia-Pacific’s plans tilt more toward supply as grid share falls from 46% to 41%. Note, though, that the region’s grid share is understated, as figures for China’s state-owned grid operators (which build most of the country’s network) are not included in our listed-company data.

The rising grid share may also partly reflect which companies disclose their capex plan, rather than a real shift in investment. According to our data, only a small share of companies disclose capex plans for electrification activities in 2027 and 2028, and grid operators are more likely than other companies to publish such long-term plans. A catch-up by grid investment therefore exists on paper, but it is uneven and hard to verify.

What It Takes to Reach COP31’s 35% Electrification Goal

Corporate investment in electrification is real, but it is concentrated rather than broad. To achieve COP31’s 35% electrification target, capital allocation needs to:

Shift into the grid faster. Grid infrastructure already receives the largest share of low-carbon capex, but investment growth is not keeping pace with clean generation or EV manufacturing capex, and without stronger grids, new supply cannot reach users and demand cannot scale.

Expand beyond solar. Solar dominates clean-generation investment, while wind, nuclear and hydro each account for a much smaller share.

Move to replace, not just add. Clean investment needs to displace — not just sit alongside — existing fossil-fuel and combustion-engine investment.

Pick up the pace in lagging regions. Investment remains heavily concentrated in Asia-Pacific, Europe, and North America, while Latin America and Africa/Middle East together account for only around one-tenth of all global electrification capex.

One practical outcome from COP31 would be to encourage more consistent forward-looking capex disclosure. Investors currently have some visibility into near-term spending plans, but little insight into how companies intend to deploy capital beyond the next few years. Disclosure by activity, by year, and in connection with transition plans, building on the capital deployment requirements of IFRS S2, would make it easier to assess whether corporate strategies are aligned with long-term climate goals. Targets will continue to define the ambition. Capex will show whether the 2035 goal is being funded, and whether supply, grids, and demand are growing together.
