text:
It may cost you more to be environmentally cautious.

Under the proposed BUILD America 250 Act, electric vehicle owners would pay a new $130 annual federal fee. The fee would increase by $5 every two years, up to a maximum of $150. Owners of plug-in hybrids would pay $35 a year.

The proposal is part of a five-year, $580 billion highway funding package aimed at renewing federal transportation programs and paying for road repairs and infrastructure projects.

The federal government relies partly on gasoline taxes to fund highway construction and maintenance. Because electric vehicles don't use gasoline, their owners don't pay into that funding stream through fuel taxes. Supporters say EV drivers should help pay for the roads they use, just like drivers of gas-powered vehicles.

The proposal was introduced by House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee Chairman Sam Graves, a Republican from Missouri, and the committee's top Democrat, Rep. Rick Larsen of Washington.

Larsen supports the fee, saying that all drivers should contribute to road maintenance regardless of what they drive.

"I came in in 2001 supporting the user-pays principle, and it's 2026, and I haven't changed my view of that," Larsen told E&E News, a Politico publication, in May.

The proposal would also send 20 percent of the money collected toward the Department of Transportation's mass transit account, Larsen said.

Republican Sen. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia has also backed the idea.

"They use the roads, they should help pay," Capito said, according to the outlet

Meanwhile, Democratic lawmakers and environmental groups argue that making EVS more expensive could discourage consumers from making the switch.

Sen. Ron Wyden, a Democrat from Oregon, accused Republicans of targeting the electric vehicle industry.

"This is another right-wing ideological trophy. They just don't want to have renewable energy in the future, and they think these ideas up pretty regularly," Wyden told E&E News.

Wyden also said the proposal was "off the table" in negotiations over the transportation bill.

Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, a Democrat from Rhode Island, also questioned whether the fees would address the country's highway funding needs.

"Slapping a fee on electric vehicles isn't a solution for the Highway Trust Fund," Whitehouse said in a May statement.

The Natural Resources Defense Council also opposed the proposal, arguing that the fees would add costs for drivers while reducing investments in electric vehicle charging stations.

"This legislation is a punch in the gut to the millions of Americans struggling to pay higher prices at the pump," Shruti Vaidyanathan, the group's director of federal and state transportation advocacy, said of the proposal in a May statement.

"With Americans demanding more affordable transportation options as gasoline tops $4.50 a gallon, this bill would impose an onerous new fee on electric vehicles and plug-in hybrids, while slashing investments in new EV chargers. Congress should be boosting investments in projects that cut costs, cut emissions, create jobs, and build a transportation system that works for all Americans. This bill largely ignores the need to build cleaner, more affordable transportation options," she continued.

The group urged lawmakers to reject the fees and continue investing in electric vehicle infrastructure.

title: A Big Deal: Honda's New 2028 CR-V Loses Gas-Only Power for an All-Hybrid Lineup
description:
Despite the confirmation of the redesigned SUV’s hybrid-only powertrain, other details on the next-generation 2028 Honda CR-V remain scant.
ADVERTISEMENT - CONTINUE READING BELOW Honda has been more specific about its production plans for the 2028 CR-V.
It will build its new Honda Hybrid system at the Honda Transmission Plant in Ohio (TMP-O) with a mix of domestically and globally sourced parts.
The 2028 Honda CR-V arrives next year with more details and pricing to come following its official debut.
ADVERTISEMENT - CONTINUE READING BELOW
text:
The most important aspect is that Honda will only offer customers the 2028 CR-V in hybrid form. Highly likely not by chance, this move follows the path Toyota charted when it introduced an all-hybrid RAV4 lineup for the 2026 model year. Hybrid models already represent more than half of all CR-V sales, and about 30 percent of all Honda models sold are hybrids. In other words, the automaker is rather safely hedging its bets on this move.

ADVERTISEMENT - CONTINUE READING BELOW

Honda says the new 2028 CR-V will be powered by its fifth-generation two-motor hybrid system, the successor to the powertrain used in the existing version of its compact SUV. The CR-V will again use two motors and an Atkinson-cycle four-cylinder engine. However, this time the available all-wheel-drive system has an electric motor driving the rear wheels rather than a mechanical connection as found in the soon to be old AWD CR-V Hybrid.

Engine displacement and power output of the new CR-V’s Honda Hybrid system are unknown, but we figure it will at least match the existing model’s 204 hp and 247 lb-ft of torque. Honda says both the engine’s and the hybrid system’s peak efficiency ranges increase compared to before.

ADVERTISEMENT - CONTINUE READING BELOW

To the point, Honda says it aimed to improve the 2028 CR-V Hybrid’s fuel economy by more than 10 percent. Today’s model yields 43/36/40 mpg city/highway/combined with FWD, and 40/34/37 mpg city/highway/combined with AWD if we look at its EPA mpg ratings. This means a 10 percent increase would bring those figures up to 47/40/44 mpg and 44/37/41, respectively. Our back-of-the-napkin math indicates the new 2028 CR-V’s fuel economy will finally be closer to the hybrid-only Toyota RAV4’s EPA-rated figures of 47/40/43 mpg (FWD) and 46/39/42 mpg (AWD).

As for other changes? Despite the confirmation of the redesigned SUV’s hybrid-only powertrain, other details on the next-generation 2028 Honda CR-V remain scant. Honda confirmed the seventh-generation CR-V will be underpinned by a new platform with the aim of improving rigidity and lightness. A teaser image shows the CR-V logo adopting a new font, suggesting the compact crossover could also deliver edgier styling than we get with today’s conservative model. The paint beneath the badge appears to be a new metallic blue, presumably the seventh-generation SUV’s launch color.

ADVERTISEMENT - CONTINUE READING BELOW

Honda has been more specific about its production plans for the 2028 CR-V. It will build its new Honda Hybrid system at the Honda Transmission Plant in Ohio (TMP-O) with a mix of domestically and globally sourced parts. The CR-V’s Honda Hybrid system will be built alongside powertrains destined for other compact, midsize, and larger vehicles as the company aims to ramp up production capacity by 250 percent. Meanwhile, the Anna Engine Plant in Ohio will be retooled to build Honda’s next-generation Atkinson-cycle four-cylinder engines. Honda will also continue final assembly of CR-V SUVs in the same three North American plants as before: East Liberty Auto Plant in Ohio, the Indiana Auto Plant, and Honda of Canada Mfg. in Alliston, Ontario.

The 2028 Honda CR-V arrives next year with more details and pricing to come following its official debut. In terms of pricing, expect it to start at slightly more than the existing CR-V LX base model, which begins at $33,070. Honda won’t stray too far from that number, however; we logically expect it to remain close to the rival 2027 Toyota RAV4’s starting price of $33,895.

title: A Texas campus that will generate its own electricity without drawing from the public grid sits ...
description:
If you wanted to plug a big new data center into the Texas grid this year, you’d have had a rough time of it.
The Texas campus, SpaceX says, will make its own electricity and won’t pull power from the public grid.
A self-powered campus builds its own generation on site and feeds the buildings directly, so the grid never has to carry that load.
A few sections down, the same update says SpaceX plans to invest up to $24 billion in this project alone.
Brownsville gets the water money Then there’s the water, which I’d argue is what Brownsville residents will feel first.
text:
If you wanted to plug a big new data center into the Texas grid this year, you’d have had a rough time of it. Back in August, Gov. Greg Abbott ordered grid operators to put new data center hookup requests on hold until the facilities could be audited, according to the Texas Tribune.

SpaceX’s Texas plan gets around that in a pretty blunt way. On November 12, the company published an update on its website laying out more than $74 billion in planned investment across two supercompute campuses, one at Starbase in Texas’ Rio Grande Valley and one in Cochise County, Arizona. The Texas campus, SpaceX says, will make its own electricity and won’t pull power from the public grid.

I keep coming back to that line.

Most big data centers buy electricity the same way your house does, just in absurd quantities, which is why utilities and regulators get twitchy when a new one shows up. A self-powered campus builds its own generation on site and feeds the buildings directly, so the grid never has to carry that load. It’s basically a power station and a server farm sharing a fence line.

SpaceX is pitching that as a favor to the neighbors. The company says running off the grid keeps the campus out of a tug-of-war with local homes and businesses over electricity, and that it won’t “shift generation costs onto existing ratepayers.” A local environmental group has already announced a protest over air quality, water use and energy bills, according to the Tribune, so that’s frankly a smart thing to lead with.

How much is Texas actually getting?

That depends on which paragraph you read. Near the top of its update, SpaceX says it plans to invest more than $24 billion in the Rio Grande Valley. A few sections down, the same update says SpaceX plans to invest up to $24 billion in this project alone. That’s a pretty flexible way to describe one number, and since “up to” is the cautious version, I’ll stick with that.

Either way, Texas is the smaller piece of the $74 billion. SpaceX says the Texas project is already behind more than 3,000 construction jobs, with more than 500 permanent ones expected once it’s running.

So where does the electricity come from?

SpaceX’s update is a bit vague on that. It mentions emissions controls designed to meet federal and state air-quality rules, but it doesn’t name a fuel.

The City of Starbase’s public hearing notice fills in the blank. It describes the project as a “gas-fired power plant and super-compute facility,” according to the Tribune, and Starbase commissioners plan to hold a public hearing in December on a possible tax break for it.

For the hardware, you have to go back to an earlier filing. The 956 Report, a local news site, says it obtained a registration SpaceX filed with the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) on September 8 for its Boca Chica Facility. According to the outlet, that registration describes a temporary first phase of 35 gas turbines adding up to about 748 megawatts, and a permanent setup of eight GE Vernova 7E turbines at roughly 708 megawatts. The construction and operation dates just say “TBD.”

None of that is in SpaceX’s November 12 update, so I’d treat it as what was on paper two months ago rather than a final design.

I checked TCEQ’s air permit database, and the registration (number 185303) is still listed as pending. It’s filed under the agency’s standard permit for electric generating units, which is basically a pre-written permit. Instead of a case-by-case review, a company registers under rules that already exist, and the record shows this one was flagged for expedited permitting.

Is 748 megawatts a lot? For one site, that’s power plant territory by pretty much any definition. I can’t tell you how much of that the computers would actually use, since SpaceX hasn’t said how much power the campus will draw.

Brownsville gets the water money

Then there’s the water, which I’d argue is what Brownsville residents will feel first. SpaceX says it’s put up $220 million for new water and wastewater projects in Brownsville and Cameron County, and $40 million of that has already gone to the Brownsville Public Utilities Board.

The reason the city wants it is pretty simple. Brownsville gets roughly three-quarters of its main water supply from two Rio Grande reservoirs, and SpaceX says both have dropped to critically low levels. Three cities near Austin are building a deep intake in Lake Travis for a similar reason, so their supply doesn’t hang on floating barges during a drought.

The Southmost Regional Water Authority has lined up projects that would add about 20 million gallons a day from sources that don’t depend on the river. Eight million gallons a day would come from potable reuse, and 12 million from expanding the region’s brackish groundwater treatment. Potable reuse means taking wastewater the city already treats and cleaning it further until it’s safe to drink. Brackish groundwater is too salty to drink straight but a lot less salty than seawater, so it goes through a desalination plant first.

Don’t read that 20 million gallons as the campus’s water bill, though. It’s new capacity for the region. SpaceX says the city and the utilities board keep full ownership and that it isn’t acquiring water rights. It also says any extra water it uses will be a lot smaller than the capacity these projects add, and that SpaceX and Starbase will keep paying standard rates like everyone else.

SpaceX figures that if Brownsville had borrowed the roughly $220 million the usual way, water customers could’ve ended up paying more than $370 million over 25 years once you count interest.

The money came with a land deal. As part of the agreement, Brownsville de-annexed about 444 acres of empty land out by the port and the city landfill, and the tract went to the City of Starbase. Brownsville also put a 90-day moratorium on new data center applications in place earlier this month, but by then the tract was already outside city limits.

Arizona is getting a very different setup

The second campus is the bigger check. SpaceX wants to build a roughly $50 billion campus in Cochise County, with about 5,500 construction jobs and 1,000 permanent ones, and it’s still seeking approval.

Instead of building its own power plant, SpaceX says it’ll work with local electric cooperatives and lean on renewable investments already in place there. It also claims co-op members could see their power bills drop by as much as 20%. I’d treat that as a ceiling, since SpaceX’s own wording hedges it twice.

Arizona also gets dry cooling. A lot of data centers keep their chips cool by evaporating water, the same basic trick your body uses when you sweat. Dry cooling dumps heat through air and radiators instead, a bit like the radiator in your car. The trade-off is that it usually takes more electricity on a hot day. SpaceX says the Cochise campus won’t pump groundwater for industrial use or drill new wells under the current plan, which seems like a pretty sensible call for the desert.

If you live in Brownsville, that Starbase hearing in December is the next public stop. As of November 12, TCEQ still lists SpaceX’s Boca Chica Facility registration as pending.

text:
Energy Secretary joins 400 young people at Birmingham Clean Energy Jobs Fair

Over 400 young people and jobseekers met with some of the UK’s largest clean energy employers at the third Clean Energy Jobs Fair, held at University College Birmingham today (Thursday, 12 November).

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh and Local Energy and Jobs Minister Martin McCluskey joined young people at the event, as employers such as Octopus and National Grid showcased the jobs and training opportunities being created across the region as Britain builds its clean energy future.

The event comes as the Prime Minister attends COP31 where he welcomed £12 billion investment for two major new UK offshore wind projects believed to be the biggest in UK history, powering millions of homes and supporting thousands of jobs.

Ahead of the upcoming Milburn review, around 400 15 to 18-year-olds from local schools and colleges, as well as 50 who are not in education, employment or training (NEETs), met employers to find work and build careers in the sector.

The government is working with a range of employers to help NEETs into work, such as National Grid’s £5 million fund to upskill them into energy and infrastructure jobs.

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said:

Our clean power drive has already attracted over £110 billion in private investment, bringing new jobs to thousands across the country.

This is the economic opportunity of this century, and I want young people entering the job market today to be able to seize it.

From electricians, engineers, and welders to those working in the technologies of the future, there is a place for everyone in Britain’s clean energy economy.

Backed by record government and private sector investment in fields like renewables and nuclear, the clean energy economy is driving a boom in demand for good industrial jobs across the UK – with 31 priority occupations such as plumbers, electricians, and welders particularly in demand.

For young people, that can mean better-paid careers from the outset, including in jobs AI simply can’t do. Entry-level roles in the majority of clean energy occupations pay 23% more than the same occupations in other sectors.

The West Midlands Clean Energy Jobs Fair is the latest in a series of events across the country, following the first fair, held in the North East in 2025.

The fairs follow the launch of the government’s Clean Energy Jobs Plan, which sets out how the clean energy mission could support thousands of extra clean energy jobs in the West Midlands by 2030.

The West Midlands is already home to major clean energy initiatives including Tyseley Energy Park and seven demonstrator Net Zero Neighbourhoods, as well as innovation and technology centre Energy Systems Catapult and the UK Battery Industrialisation Centre in Coventry.

Richard Parker, Mayor of the West Midlands, said:

Our region’s transition to clean energy has created a fast-growing sector that already employs in excess of 20,000 people.

We expect that figure to more than double over the next decade, thanks to our biggest ever programme of energy upgrades to homes, businesses and public buildings, as well as plans to cement our region as a major battery technology and manufacturing hub.

It’s essential that we train our young people in the skills needed for these jobs of the future. I recently met a young man in Coventry who went from one of our retrofit bootcamps to a well-paid job in a matter of weeks. That’s exactly the kind of opportunity we want to open up for more local people.

Professor Rosa Wells, Deputy Vice-Chancellor (FE College Principal, Apprenticeships & STEM) at University College Birmingham, said:

We are proud to host the Clean Energy Jobs Fair alongside our Green Skills Advisory Panel, bringing government, industry and education together to help people across the West Midlands seize the opportunities of clean energy.

University College Birmingham is committed to developing the skilled workforce this transition demands, working with employers to create clear routes through further and higher education into rewarding careers.

Cordi O’Hara, Executive President at National Grid UK, said:

Choosing a career and deciding what to do next can be daunting for many young people. Events like this make a real difference. Students can talk to apprentices and graduates who were in their shoes not long ago, ask questions and find out what a career in energy actually involves, and whether it might be right for them.

For those who like what they hear, applications for our apprenticeship and graduate programmes open this week. But we know not every young person is in a position to take that step, which is why, through our £5m Power Within Employability Fund, we’re working with specialist partners to reach young people facing greater barriers and help them into work.

Chris O’Shea, Chief Executive of Centrica:

The energy transition is creating real jobs and careers right across Britain. At Centrica, we need the next generation of engineers and skilled people to help build and operate the energy system of the future. These are good, well-paid jobs with a future, and we want young people to understand the opportunities a career in energy can offer. That’s why we’re committed to recruiting 3,500 apprentices by 2030.

Chris Drake, Country HR Manager at Hitachi Energy, said:

The transition to a sustainable energy future depends on attracting talented people from every background and at every stage of their career journey. At Hitachi Energy, we are committed to creating opportunities that are accessible, inclusive, and rewarding, whether someone is entering the workforce for the first time, returning to employment, or seeking a new career in the clean energy sector.

Events such as the Clean Energy Jobs Fair play an important role in connecting people with the skills, training and career pathways that will help deliver the UK’s net-zero ambitions while creating lasting economic opportunity for local communities.

Rachel McCrystal, Social Impact and Sustainability Manager at Daikin UK said:

The clean energy transition will depend on people with the skills to deliver it. That means giving young people a clear view of the careers available, from engineering and installation to training, technical support and commercial roles. This event is an important opportunity to turn a broad ambition into something students can see, understand and consider for their own future.

Guy Newey, CEO of Energy Systems Catapult, said:

Every young person at this fair is a potential founder, innovator or entrepreneur. By joining a UK clean energy firm, or starting their own, they could help deliver cleaner energy, tackle fuel poverty and power growth right across the UK. Day in, day out, we work with entrepreneurs who are building the energy system of the future. I’d love to see more young people join them.

text:
At a gathering of natural gas suppliers and data center developers Thursday in Austin, Texas, the question on everyone's mind was what last week's blue sweep of the state's top offices means for their projects.

"I don't think anybody foresaw the extent of the outcome that we experienced," Brandon Seale, senior adviser at VoltaGrid, said while moderating a panel at the LDC NatGas to Power Forum. "We're used to dealing with different administrations, different states, different jurisdictions. But it feels like something changed last week."

Voters elected candidates who campaigned on reining in data centers. But, as many noted, the public backlash had already become so pronounced that it was outgoing Republican governor Greg Abbott who first caught the industry off guard: in August, with a pause on new approvals for data centers seeking a connection to the state's grid and then in September with a sweeping freeze on permits for data center projects.

Trenton Thornock, founder of Prometheus Hyperscale, said his company had assumed it was shielded from efforts to slow down some development because its projects make their own power on site from natural gas, with no grid connection, and did not expect to find itself caught in the dragnet.

"What surprised us is the way that Governor Abbott directed the TCEQ [the state environmental regulator]," Thornock said. "Now you can't get a wastewater permit, can't get an air permit. Even if you were planning on using fuel cells, that's a big question mark. So we were really surprised."

His Texas projects now have "a big question mark" hanging over them, he said, while the value of his Wyoming site "went way up last week, just by creating scarcity in Texas, which is the biggest market."

Peter Belmonte, principal at Stallion Energy & Environmental, said projects already under way have momentum. "This freight train is going 100 miles an hour," he said. "It's going to be hard to derail things that are already on the books, even with the moratoriums." But if Texas shuts the door, "people will go to Wyoming, they'll go to Louisiana, they'll go to Oklahoma," he said.

Many in the industry have acknowledged that things were moving too fast. "There was already a pause on new permitting, and I think it was needed," said Coby Washburn, vice president of business development at Woodway Energy Infrastructure. "It's been kind of a bit of a wild west."

Still, most of the panelists said they plan to wait and see how things shake out, betting that demand is not going away and that Texas' competitive advantages are hard to beat.

Few places can match Texas for land, gas, renewables, pipelines and support for growth, said Dilanka Seimon, chief commercial officer at gas producer and power generator BKV.

"It's never a good idea to bet against Texas," he said, "and I wouldn't start now."

title: Mercedes-Benz EV Charging Network Reaches 100 Locations - Electric Cars Report
description:
Mercedes-Benz is celebrating a major milestone in North America as its High-Power Charging network reaches 100 locations, with nearly 1,000 charging points installed across the United States and Canada.
The growth of Mercedes-Benz High-Power Charging has accelerated considerably since its first stations opened in late 2023.
By the end of 2024, it had expanded to 19 locations and 188 charging points.
By November 2026, the network had reached 100 locations and 934 active charging points, representing a significant expansion in just three years.
Every Mercedes-Benz High-Power Charging location features chargers capable of delivering up to 400 kW.
text:
Mercedes-Benz is celebrating a major milestone in North America as its High-Power Charging network reaches 100 locations, with nearly 1,000 charging points installed across the United States and Canada.

Launched in November 2023, Mercedes-Benz High-Power Charging (MB HPC) has expanded rapidly over the past three years, growing from just five locations and 32 charging points into a network spanning 28 US states and British Columbia, Canada.

The milestone highlights the growing importance of reliable public fast-charging infrastructure as electric vehicle adoption continues to expand. It also shows how traditional automakers are becoming increasingly involved in building charging networks that serve drivers beyond their own vehicle brands.

According to Mercedes-Benz, more than 245,000 customers have used the network since its launch, completing over one million charging sessions.

The growth of Mercedes-Benz High-Power Charging has accelerated considerably since its first stations opened in late 2023.

The network started with only five locations and 32 charging points. By the end of 2024, it had expanded to 19 locations and 188 charging points. Growth continued throughout 2025, when the number of locations reached 63, supported by 597 charging points.

By November 2026, the network had reached 100 locations and 934 active charging points, representing a significant expansion in just three years.

The infrastructure now has approximately 205 megawatts of installed charging capacity, giving it a stronger presence along major travel routes and at popular shopping destinations.

The expansion is particularly notable because Mercedes-Benz has positioned the network as a premium charging option while making it available to electric vehicles from multiple manufacturers.

Although the majority of locations are in the United States, the network has also expanded into Canada, with British Columbia becoming its first Canadian market.

400-kW Chargers Support Multiple EV Brands

One of the network’s biggest selling points is its charging speed.

Every Mercedes-Benz High-Power Charging location features chargers capable of delivering up to 400 kW. The network primarily uses hardware supplied by Italian charging equipment manufacturer Alpitronic.

However, the actual charging speed depends on the electric vehicle’s battery architecture, temperature, state of charge, and maximum charging capability. Not every EV can take advantage of the full 400-kW output.

Mercedes-Benz has also focused on making its charging infrastructure accessible to drivers of different electric vehicle brands.

The network supports vehicles from 19 automotive manufacturers, including Tesla, Rivian, Ford, Hyundai, BMW, Porsche, Audi, Kia, and Volkswagen.

Connector compatibility is another important part of the strategy. According to the company’s anniversary report, 93% of its Alpitronic charging stalls offer both CCS1 and the North American Charging Standard (NACS) connectors, while the remaining 7% are CCS-only.

This approach allows a wider range of EV drivers to use the network without relying on charging adapters.

As more automakers adopt NACS for their North American electric vehicles, supporting both standards could become an increasingly important advantage for public charging operators.

Mercedes-Benz Focuses on Charging Reliability

Adding more charging stations is only one part of improving the public charging experience. Reliability remains equally important, particularly for drivers traveling long distances.

Mercedes-Benz says its first-time charging success rate has improved from approximately 84% in 2023 to more than 90% in 2026.

This metric measures how often a charging session successfully starts on the first attempt, without requiring drivers to reconnect the cable, restart the charger, or repeat the payment process.

The improvement reflects the company’s focus on making charging more convenient and predictable.

The wider charging industry has also made progress. According to figures presented in Mercedes-Benz’s three-year report, the overall DC fast-charging success rate in the United States and Canada increased from 80% in 2023 to 88% in 2026.

That represents a meaningful improvement, although it also shows that failed charging attempts remain an issue across the industry.

Customer satisfaction rankings provide another indication of the changing competitive landscape. In the 2026 J.D. Power EVX public charging study, Mercedes-Benz, IONNA, and Rivian secured the top positions, ending Tesla’s three-year run as the overall leader.

The results suggest that competition among charging providers is increasingly shifting toward service quality, reliability, and the overall customer experience.

Mercedes-Benz Is Expanding in a Competitive Charging Market

The growth of MB HPC comes at a time when the North American public charging market is becoming increasingly competitive.

Tesla’s Supercharger network remains a major player, while companies such as IONNA and Rivian are expanding their own infrastructure. Automakers and independent charging operators are investing in larger stations, faster hardware, and improved reliability.

Mercedes-Benz is taking a somewhat different approach by combining premium charging locations with high-powered equipment and broad vehicle compatibility.

Its stations are typically positioned along major travel corridors and near shopping centers, where drivers can recharge while taking a break or running errands. Individual locations range from smaller four-stall installations to larger hubs with as many as 20 charging points.

The company’s decision to deploy 400-kW chargers throughout its network also provides additional capacity for future EVs that can accept higher charging power.

There is another interesting development in Mercedes-Benz’s charging strategy. While the company has exited its European high-power charging business, its North American operation continues to expand.

This makes the United States and Canada important markets for Mercedes-Benz’s charging infrastructure ambitions.

text:
A law that eliminated North Carolina’s interim climate target accounted for 17% of Duke Energy earnings per share increase in 2026, according to Duke’s most recent earnings report. But Duke says the difference comes from a different part of the law — and that the effect on earnings will be “neutral” in the long run.

In 2025, the North Carolina General Assembly passed a law that eliminated the state’s 2030 climate goal. That goal had required Duke to reduce planet-warming emissions by 70% from 2005 levels. Sue Sturgis, research and communications manager for the Energy and Policy Institute, said Senate Bill 266 was “a really big deal.”

“It was really the bill this session that was the ‘Duke bill,’” Sturgis said, referring to last year’s legislative session.

The law also changed how Duke Energy recovers the cost from customers for building new power plants, making it less risky for the utility to invest in energy sources like natural gas-fired generators and nuclear reactors. Ratepayer advocates say this also shifts the risk onto the people who buy that electricity, while clean energy advocates worry that this makes cheaper solar farms less appealing to the utility.

Sturgis said the Energy and Policy Institute was curious to see how soon these and other changes would affect Duke’s bottom line. This is the first earnings report showing how much more Duke shareholders earned as a result of the 2025 law. The reference to SB266 appears as two footnotes in the nearly 40-page report.

The report shows the difference between earnings now and this time last year.

title: Ohio GOP circulates bill that would stymie coal plant closures - Canary Media
description:
A draft bill obtained by Canary Media would block coal-fired power plants from closing when the shutdown is required by a settlement agreement.
The administration has repeatedly ordered coal plants to stay open past their planned closure dates because of alleged reliability concerns.
But the grid operator has signaled a desire to keep the power plant online due to the Trump administration’s declaration of a grid emergency.
On one hand, it could limit community groups’ or environmental organizations’ tools for bargaining with coal plant owners in cases involving claims about nuisance problems or violations of regulatory permits.
Canary Media has not heard back from Republican Rep. Adam Mathews, who shared the draft bill with some other lawmakers.
text:
Republican lawmakers in Ohio are circulating a plan to keep coal plants open, even if an owner has a contractual obligation to close a facility. And they hope to pass it fast, before the new Democratic governor-elect, Amy Acton, takes office.

A draft bill obtained by Canary Media would block coal-fired power plants from closing when the shutdown is required by a settlement agreement. It would apply to both past and future contracts between plant owners and private parties to resolve issues in a state court or regulatory proceeding.

“My first thought was, ​‘Why is there a piece of legislation trying to go against the Ohio Constitution?’” said Neil Waggoner, Midwest coordinator for the Sierra Club’s Beyond Coal campaign, referring to a prohibition against retroactive laws. ​“This breaks not just any contract moving forward but also breaks any previous contract.”

The proposal would directly affect the 620-megawatt coal unit at the Cardinal power plant in eastern Ohio, which is slated to close by the end of 2028. In 2015, the Sierra Club and American Electric Power’s Ohio utility, which owned part of the plant at the time, reached a settlement in a regulatory case that included a commitment for the closure and other measures.

Under the draft bill, Buckeye Power, which took on AEP’s obligations for the Cardinal power plant following a 2022 sale, could ignore the terms of the settlement and keep the facility online if requested or ordered by various people or agencies.

In a statement sent to Canary Media, Buckeye Power said that it ​“supports the draft legislation and intends to file testimony in its favor after it is introduced.”

The company added that it views the proposal as ​“a balanced and narrowly tailored solution that helps keep electricity reliable and affordable for Ohio consumers by allowing critical generation resources to remain available until the reliability crisis has passed.”

For years, Ohio lawmakers have made it harder and harder to build renewable energy projects that would bring down electricity costs in the state while reining in greenhouse gas emissions that cause climate change.

Now, instead of reducing those barriers with a genuine all-of-the-above strategy, ​“they’re extending the life of these dirty, expensive coal plants,” said Democratic Rep. Tristan Rader, who is the ranking minority member on the House Energy Committee and opposes the plan. Rader said it’s unclear whether the draft bill will be considered on its own or tacked onto other legislation that is further along so it could pass in the lame-duck session. The session ends on Dec. 31. In January, Acton will move into the governor’s mansion, and Republicans will no longer have a supermajority in the House.

The draft legislation cites grid reliability as justification for the proposal, echoing the Trump administration’s assertions that aging coal plants are needed to prevent power outages. The administration has repeatedly ordered coal plants to stay open past their planned closure dates because of alleged reliability concerns. Critics say those orders are unfounded and unlawful.

Waggoner said the bill’s language seems directly aimed at nullifying Buckeye Power’s obligation under the settlement agreement. Plus, he said, if the concern is about reliability, mechanisms are already in place to determine whether any specific facility must keep operating as a technical matter.

Assessment by the regional grid operator PJM Interconnection is one such mechanism. PJM’s website shows its analysis is still underway for the scheduled deactivation of the 620-megawatt Cardinal unit by Jan. 1, 2029.

But the grid operator has signaled a desire to keep the power plant online due to the Trump administration’s declaration of a grid emergency. On March 6, Michael Bryson, PJM’s senior vice president of operations, wrote to Buckeye Power, urging it to get a voluntary waiver from the Sierra Club or a court declaration that the settlement agreement is invalid.

“As your company is aware,” the letter said, ​“the President and the Secretary of Energy have declared that an emergency exists that poses a threat to the reliability and the ability to serve load, including emergent data centers needed to help fuel the United States’ advancements in artificial intelligence.”

Two weeks later, on March 19, Sarah Parrot, the federal energy advocate at the Public Utilities Commission of Ohio, told Buckeye Power that the commission wouldn’t enforce the agreement, claiming that regulators hadn’t approved the deal. In fact, PUCO greenlit the settlement agreement in March 2016.

How the draft bill would impact future settlements is unclear. On one hand, it could limit community groups’ or environmental organizations’ tools for bargaining with coal plant owners in cases involving claims about nuisance problems or violations of regulatory permits. However, many of those claims would be in federal court, Waggoner noted, and the bill language only applies to state court and regulatory settlements.

Canary Media has not heard back from Republican Rep. Adam Mathews, who shared the draft bill with some other lawmakers.

text:
Coulomb Solutions (CSI), a supplier of electrification components for the North American commercial vehicle market, has announced the launch of a new wholly-owned subsidiary: ReadyGrid, a mobile energy storage company focused on providing power solutions for commercial and industrial applications.

CSI has transferred all its mobile battery energy storage system (BESS) activities to ReadyGrid, including engineering, product development, purchasing, manufacturing, sales, distribution, service and warranty operations. The new organization will bring these activities under one brand.

ReadyGrid has developed a portfolio of mobile energy storage systems with capacities ranging from 233 kWh to 5 MWh. Applications include commercial EV charging, demand response, grid resilience, construction and remote operations and emergency or temporary power. In addition to hardware, the company offers software, telematics and real-time data monitoring.

ReadyGrid’s flagship product is its 2.3 MWh mobile BESS. The system combines energy storage with an integrated 1-megawatt power conversion system. It provides 480-volt AC power and up to 1 megawatt of bidirectional Megawatt Charging System (MCS) capability for charging commercial vehicles and equipment. The system has been evaluated for compliance with applicable UL 9540 requirements.

ReadyGrid systems are designed for frequent transport and repeated deployment. They use commercial vehicle-grade LFP batteries from CATL, and feature integrated thermal management and reinforced system architecture for mobile applications.

“Creating ReadyGrid gives this business the dedicated people, resources and focus to solve our customers’ toughest power challenges and scale rapidly,” said CSI CEO David Mazaika. “We see an enormous and growing need for electrical power that can be deployed wherever and whenever it is needed. We have developed outstanding products, built expertise and, through our partnership with CATL, have access to world-class battery technology and supply.”

A MARTÍNEZ, HOST:

Week 1 of the United Nations' annual climate summit, known as COP31, wraps up this week in the Turkish resort town of Antalya. Nearly 200 nations are represented at the two-week conference to negotiate how to curb climate change. Here's NPR's Hadeel Al-Shalchi reporting from Antalya.

HADEEL AL-SHALCHI, BYLINE: World leaders gathered for their first day of negotiations at COP31 on Wednesday, urging nations to get tougher on global warming. U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres had an urgent plea.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

ANTONIO GUTERRES: We know the truth. Now we must act on it, because climate action is more than a fight over a number or a thermometer. We are in the fight for our lives and our children's future.

AL-SHALCHI: Scientists say that global warming is set to surpass 1.5 degrees Celsius or 2.7 Fahrenheit in a few years. That could trigger the collapse of ice sheets in Greenland and Antarctica. Many leaders blame the war on Iran. The destruction of energy infrastructure has caused massive greenhouse gas emissions. The president of the Marshall Islands, Hilda Heine, said that's not an excuse.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

PRESIDENT HILDA HEINE: We are told there is no money, but the spending on war grows. The greatest security threat we face remains underfunded. I appeal to you, find money for life, not death.

AL-SHALCHI: The European Union President Ursula von der Leyen said this year was a wake-up call.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

URSULA VON DER LEYEN: This summer was the summer of truth. Devastating floods in Nepal, droughts from Sudan to Central America, and in Europe, one of the worst wildfire seasons on record.

AL-SHALCHI: The EU has been successful at cutting emissions, unlike the U.S., which is absent from the summit for a second year in a row. In 2026, President Trump withdrew the U.S. from the Paris Agreement, the legally binding treaty to limit global warming. But Palo Alto Mayor Vicki Venker still showed up to COP31.

VICKI VENKER: America is still embracing climate action, making progress in climate action and committed to climate action.

AL-SHALCHI: Her community is working on projects to significantly cut down greenhouse gas emissions.

VENKER: It would be better and stronger if the federal government were supportive. I hope with our new Congress, we can start turning that ship.

AL-SHALCHI: Venker says, until then, it's people like her who need to keep up the work.

Hadeel Al-Shalchi, NPR News, Antalya.

title: What do the US midterms mean for solar and energy storage? - CRU Group
description:
Electricity affordability concerns and state-level results may support deployment, while data centre opposition could dampen near-term battery energy storage system (BESS) demand.
Data centre opposition could dampen near-term BESS demand because data centres are expected to be an important driver of US battery storage buildout.
According to CRU data, the two states account for nearly 25% of data centres expected to be built by the end of 2027.
CRU’s Energy Storage Technology and Costs Outlook, published before the midterms, forecast that more than one-third of US grid-scale BESS deployed in 2030 would support data centre demand, primarily from inference applications.
State-level support could encourage grid-connected buildout, while data centre deployment in Texas and Georgia could falter.
text:
The article below is an edited version of an Insight originally written by Forrest Levy. Read thefull Insight here or speak to a CRU expert about market intelligence and analysis relevant to your organisation.

The November 2026 US midterms represent a moderate upside for solar and storage, but the policy outlook remains mixed. Electricity affordability concerns and state-level results may support deployment, while data centre opposition could dampen near-term battery energy storage system (BESS) demand.

Why could data centre restrictions and opposition affect battery storage demand?

Data centre opposition could dampen near-term BESS demand because data centres are expected to be an important driver of US battery storage buildout.

Exit polling showed that 56% of voters considered data centres a major or crucial factor in how they voted. Georgia governor-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms called for an immediate statewide freeze on data centres. Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa also called for an immediate moratorium until the state legislature could establish protections. According to CRU data, the two states account for nearly 25% of data centres expected to be built by the end of 2027.

Of 39 data centre-specific referendums on 3 November, 38 voted for some form of moratorium or restriction; many anti-data centre initiatives received more than 70% of the vote.

CRU’s Energy Storage Technology and Costs Outlook, published before the midterms, forecast that more than one-third of US grid-scale BESS deployed in 2030 would support data centre demand, primarily from inference applications. Extended moratoriums could slow data centre BESS buildout and pose a near-term demand risk.

Could rising electricity prices support solar and storage deployment?

Electricity affordability was a key campaign issue and may support solar and storage deployment.

US residential electricity prices rose 13.9% from when President Trump was inaugured to August 2026. In states that flipped a Senate seat, excluding Mississippi and Alaska, the average increase was more than 20%. Although not the only factor, above-average increases were a notable example of cost pressures that hurt incumbents.

What do the midterm results mean for clean energy policy?

The election leaves uncertainty over federal legislation and clean energy tax credits.

The results are likely to embolden Democrats to push for more clean energy support and fewer oil and gas pipelines in the proposed Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), putting the bill at risk. Its passage could speed up permitting for energy projects and transmission lines, potentially lowering costs for solar and storage. However, its passage remains uncertain.

The industry is divided over the potential return of solar and storage tax credits. Many large developers oppose reinstating the original Inflation Reduction Act structure, preferring to compete without ongoing policy support. Smaller developers and many behind-the-meter installers favour an extension amid headwinds including trade actions.

Industry support is stronger for expanding the Section 45X production tax credit. CRU modelling shows that a BESS using US-made components remains significantly more expensive than a comparable system using Chinese components, even when tariffs and tax credits are included. Expanding 45X is one tool policymakers could use to help the industry remain competitive.

How could US state elections influence renewable energy deployment?

State-level results could create a more favourable environment for clean energy deployment. From January 2027, nearly 75% of Americans will live in a state with a Democratic governor; Democratic leaders have historically been more supportive of clean energy development.

New leadership in Texas and Nevada could further bolster buildout. Ohio governor-elect Dr Amy Acton campaigned partly on lowering electricity costs through low-cost renewable energy. In Texas, new state leadership could bolster solar and storage deployment after previous proposals to restrict development.

CRU describes the state-level results as a mild, not transformative, upside. For developers, the key question is whether political shifts lead to concrete policy changes.

What should solar and energy storage market participants watch?

The policy outlook offers no clear message on short- to medium-term solar and storage impacts. State-level support could encourage grid-connected buildout, while data centre deployment in Texas and Georgia could falter. Federal results may create opportunities for manufacturing support and limit further repeals of clean energy tax credits.

CRU identifies price changes, data centre demand and policy updates as key developments for clients to monitor.

text:
Broad coalition of national and local labor organizations representing hundreds of thousands of skilled workers supports legislation projected to create up to 105,600 trades and manufacturing jobs

WASHINGTON — The AFL-CIO has endorsed U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich’s (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), joining a broad coalition of national and local labor organizations representing the skilled workers who build, operate, and maintain America’s energy infrastructure.

The AFL-CIO’s endorsement adds to growing support from across organized labor, including the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers (IBEW), International Association of Iron Workers, International Association of Sheet Metal, Air, Rail, and Transportation Workers (SMART), International Brotherhood of Boilermakers, International Brotherhood of Teamsters,International Union of Operating Engineers (IUOE), Laborers’ International Union of North America (LIUNA), North America’s Building Trades Unions (NABTU), United Association of Plumbers and Pipefitters, Pipeliners Local 798, and the New Mexico Building and Construction Trades Council. These organizations represent the electricians, ironworkers, sheet metal workers, boilermakers, Teamsters, operating engineers, laborers, plumbers, pipefitters, and other skilled tradespeople who will build the next generation of America's energy infrastructure.

The labor support comes as an independent analysis from Employ America estimates that BAAJA will create up to 105,600 trades and manufacturing jobs through 2040 by making it easier to build and maintain new energy infrastructure, including wind, solar, battery storage, and transmission projects.

BAAJA will lower energy costs for working families, provide greater certainty for energy infrastructure projects, and help ensure American workers are on the job building the infrastructure our country needs.

Independent analyses find that BAAJA will:

Create up to 105,600 trades and manufacturing jobs through 2040;

Require data centers to pay for increased grid and energy costs they create, estimated at $55 billion over the next 10 years;

Save $19 billion in residential electricity bills over the next 14 years;

Nearly double the amount of solar and wind that can connect to the grid; and

Avoid 1.5 gigatons of CO2 emissions, the equivalent of taking 39 coal plants offline for a decade.

BAAJA will lower energy costs for working families, provide greater certainty for energy infrastructure projects, and help ensure American workers are on the job building the infrastructure our country needs.

ANN ARBOR, Mich. — May Mobility, a leading developer of autonomous driving technology for commercial ride-hail, today announced its plan to bring the iconic Volkswagen ID. Buzz to global robotaxi platforms, powered by May Mobility's autonomous driving system. May Mobility targets deployment of more than 10,000 autonomous ID. Buzz vehicles through 2031.

The plan includes delivery of Volkswagen ID. Buzz vehicles adapted to May Mobility's autonomous driving kit (ADK) design requirements, creating a production platform well-positioned for scaling autonomous vehicle (AV) fleets, with the first production vehicles targeted for delivery in 2028.

May Mobility will leverage its previously announced alliance with ECARX (Nasdaq: ECX), a leading global automotive intelligence company, to integrate May Mobility's autonomous driving system into the AV-ready version of the ID. Buzz, which May Mobility will deploy with its fleet operator partners.

Development is already underway, with on-road testing in the U.S. beginning in early 2027. May Mobility also said that its supply chain collaboration with ECARX and Charlton Intelligence.ai will support the company's all-in targeted cost savings of 50%+ relative to its current-generation vehicle. Charlton Intelligence.ai has joined the partnership with May Mobility to help deploy the autonomous Volkswagen ID. Buzz.

"Scaling autonomous ride-hail depends heavily on the vehicle platform, and the Volkswagen ID. Buzz gives us one well suited for it," said Dr. Edwin Olson, CEO and Founder of May Mobility. "We think riders will love the ID. Buzz running on May Mobility's autonomous driving system, and the vehicle will be built on economics that can scale with the robotaxi market."

ID. Buzz brings playful vibes to the robotaxi market

The ID. Buzz supports May Mobility's ambition to pair an industry-leading rider experience with its autonomy, giving riders a new reason to choose autonomous ride-hail.

Drawing on the visionary design of the original VW Bus, the ID. Buzz blends high-tech engineering with retro charm. It is an all-electric vehicle well suited for robotaxi deployment, with multiple entry doors for ease of access, generous interior space and a design that will set it apart from other robotaxis.

Proven technology, commercial track record

May Mobility is a pioneer of an asset-light, partnership-first approach to deploying physical AI in robotaxi applications, differentiating itself in an industry traditionally dominated by asset-heavy fleet operators.

May Mobility's autonomous driving system understands the physical world through a predictive world model and reasons through it. Simulating up to 10 seconds into the future, real-time reasoning evaluates multiple driving strategies and executes the one deemed best suited to the current situation.

May Mobility has completed more than 600,000 commercial autonomous rides across 1.1 million miles in the United States and Japan, including three driver-out deployments to date.

May Mobility is one of just a handful of companies to have deployed public driver-out routes across multiple sites in the United States. May Mobility currently operates commercially in three U.S. locations, with Lyft in Atlanta and autonomous ride services in Eden Prairie and Grand Rapids, Minnesota, and targets launching commercial operations with Uber in Arlington, Texas, in 2027.

Additionally, a six-month on-demand AV pilot with NTT Mobility in Nagoya, Japan, launched in September.

Additional details on vehicle specifications, testing, and deployment are expected to be announced in the near future.

About May Mobility

May Mobility develops autonomous vehicle technology for commercial ride-hail and public transportation services. Its patented physical AI system runs on-vehicle, integrating deep learning, a dynamic world model and a real-time reasoning engine to navigate through new and complex situations on the road.

In partnership with Toyota Motor Corporation, NTT, Lyft, Uber and Grab, May Mobility delivers Autonomy-as-a-Service (AaaS) at commercial scale and has completed more than half a million commercial autonomous rides across deployments in the U.S. and Japan.

SAN DIEGO, Nov. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Sempra (NYSE: SRE) today announced the successful close of its previously announced sale of a 45% equity interest in Sempra Infrastructure Partners (SI Partners) to affiliates of KKR, a leading global investment firm, with indirect co-investor Canada Pension Plan Investment Board.

FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE November 12, 2026

CONTACT: EPN Press Office

epn-press@environmentalprotectionnetwork.org

New Post-Election Poll: Voters Want Congress to Protect EPA Safeguards and Hold Polluters Accountable

81% concerned polluters have too much influence over EPA; 70% want Congress to stop safeguards from being weakened; 88% support equal pollution safeguards for AI data centers, including 80% of Republicans

WASHINGTON, D.C. — As the newly elected Congress prepares to take office, a new nationwide post-election poll finds that voters expect lawmakers to protect public health, prevent the weakening of EPA safeguards, and hold polluting industries accountable. The findings point to a broad public expectation that Congress will address corporate influence over EPA decisions and protect families from the health and financial costs of pollution.

Eighty-eight percent of voters agree that AI data centers and their power plants should follow the same federal pollution safeguards as everyone else and that Americans shouldn’t pay for the AI boom with their health. That includes 80% of Republicans, 86% of independents, and 95% of Democrats. More than three-quarters of voters (77%) strongly agree, while just 3% disagree.

“Voters are giving the new Congress a mandate for change: protect the safeguards that keep families healthy and make sure EPA decisions aren’t driven by polluters,” said Michelle Roos, Executive Director of EPN. “When eight in ten voters are worried that polluting companies have too much influence over EPA, Congress needs to take that seriously. People want an EPA that works for them, not one that leaves them paying the price for pollution through higher medical bills and other health costs.”

Voters Want Accountability for Polluters and Action to Protect Public Health

The survey of 1,577 registered voters, conducted November 5–10 by Change Research for the Environmental Protection Network (EPN), also found:

81% are concerned that polluting companies have too much influence over EPA decisions about toxic chemicals and pollution, including 99% of Democrats, 81% of independents and 63% of Republicans.

70% agree that the newly elected Congress should take action to stop EPA safeguards from being weakened under President Trump, including 75% of independents and 40% of Republicans. Among Republicans, more support congressional action (40%) than oppose it (27%), while 32% neither agree nor disagree.

69% are concerned that weakened EPA safeguards under President Trump will mean higher medical bills for their families, including 49% who are very concerned. Concern is especially high among women (76%) and voters ages 18–34 (80%).

The findings underscore a clear expectation for action from the incoming Congress. Support for stopping EPA safeguards from being weakened is nearly unanimous among Democrats (98%) and extends to three-quarters of independents. Broad concern about polluter influence and overwhelming support for equal pollution safeguards for AI data centers also cut across party lines. Together, the results underscore the importance of congressional oversight of federal decisions affecting pollution protections, power generation, and the rapid expansion of AI data centers.

The Health Costs of the AI Boom

The findings come as the Trump administration seeks to accelerate AI data center construction and power generation while pursuing regulatory changes that could weaken pollution safeguards or create new loopholes for the industry.

In September, EPN released The Hidden Health Costs of AI Data Centers, documenting at least 30 federal actions that could increase pollution-related health risks, including changes affecting power plants, on-site generators, permitting, and public review.

“There’s been a lot of attention to whether the AI boom will raise families’ electricity bills, but far less attention to its pollution and health costs,” said Marc Boom, EPN’s Senior Director of Public Affairs. “Powering these facilities can mean more pollution from power plants and on-site generators. The new Congress should scrutinize federal decisions that weaken pollution safeguards or create loopholes for the industry. The public shouldn’t have to choose between technological progress and clean air.”

EPN and leading national health, environmental, and consumer organizations have called for a Data Center Health Protection Pledge to ensure public health receives the same attention as electricity affordability as AI infrastructure expands.

Poll Methodology: Change Research conducted a nationwide online survey of 1,577 registered voters November 5–10, 2026, using Dynamic Online Sampling. Results were weighted by age, gender, race/ethnicity, education, region, and 2024 presidential vote. The reported overall margin of error is ±2.7 percentage points. Subgroup estimates are less precise. Full methodology here.

text:
The following is a transcript of remarks delivered by UN Climate Change Executive Secretary Simon Stiell during the "Caring for Climate" event organized by the Global Compact at COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, on 12 November 2026.

Excellencies,

Colleagues and dear friends,

My thanks to the UN Global Compact and the UN Environment Programme for bringing us here together.

The transition to clean energy is irreversible.

Its speed and scale. Who benefits and how, depends on decisions taken in cabinet rooms, boardrooms and living rooms, around the world.

Governments set policies.

Businesses decide where to invest.

Families weigh what they can afford.

When policy and investment bring down the cost of clean power, more households can make the switch.

In the negotiations here at COP31, countries must agree practical steps to deliver on commitments already made.

And across the real economy, cities, regions and businesses must make clear commitments of their own and back them with investment.

People should feel the benefits in their daily lives.

They should also be able to see what was promised and what was delivered.

That is why transparency matters.

Workers can see what a transition plan means for their jobs.

Investors can see which investments are cutting emissions.

Governments can see which policies are working and where businesses need support.

The UN Climate Change Net-zero Recognition Framework is an important transparency tool and, today, it moves from pilot to implementation.

Through our renewed NAZCA portal, companies, financial institutions, cities, regions and more will be able to share their plans and report on progress.

In essence, the Framework gives us a clearer picture of who is delivering on their net-zero commitments, and NAZCA puts that evidence in everyone’s hands.

Eight initiatives have joined so far, with nearly 80 signatories across 22 countries.

More than half of those signatories say they are willing to share an independently reviewed transition plan.

Nearly a third are willing to share evidence of progress towards their interim targets.

I invite more initiatives to join and their signatories to report through NAZCA.

Show what you committed to, where you invested and what you achieved.

And – please – use today's discussion and this COP to share what would make your investments possible.

The policy, the finance or the purchase order you need may well be in the hands of someone in this room.

I thank you.

When women thrive, communities can weather the storm

First Partner Jennifer Siebel Newsom joined women entrepreneurs from around the world for “Engendering Sustainability,” a panel hosted by The Climate Registry at its USA Climate Pavilion, to discuss women’s empowerment as a cornerstone of climate resilience and a necessary climate adaptation strategy.

The First Partner made the case that gender equality is essential to climate resilience. When women have greater economic security, they have the power to make decisions for the future of their families, their communities, and the environment.

“Women are only receiving 1.1% of venture capital dollars in the United States of America right now,” said First Partner Jennifer Siebel Newsom. “Money and power are what is valued in our society, and money and power aren’t in the hands of women.”

The First Partner also emphasized that women’s leadership is essential to building a more resilient future. When women have a seat at the table, in government, boardrooms and communities, they champion the inclusive policies and investments that build climate resilience. Closing the wage gap, expanding workforce participation and investing in women entrepreneurs, especially in food, land, water and technology, lifts families out of poverty, strengthens economies and helps communities withstand climate-driven instability.

“No woman can reach her full potential if her physical safety, mental health, or healthcare needs are compromised,” the First Partner said. “Strengthening women, the backbone of communities, ensures they will be resilient enough to withstand climate shocks, survive disasters, and lead long-term recovery.”

The First Partner also highlighted the work of California’s Women’s Wealth Advisory Council and the state’s nation-leading Farm to School Program, which sources school meals from local, regenerative and organic farms, cutting supply chain emissions. Through the Healthy School Food Pathway apprenticeship, school food workers, a predominantly female workforce, receive paid, hands-on training in scratch cooking that creates a direct path to higher wages and financial independence.

Laying the groundwork for COP32 in Africa

Governor Newsom congratulated Ethiopia’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and COP32 President-designate, Dr. Gedion Timothewos, on hosting next year’s conference in Addis Ababa, the first COP in sub-Saharan Africa since 2011. They discussed his priorities for the summit and Ethiopia’s remarkably quick adoption of electric vehicles, as well as California’s work to expand battery storage and EV charging.

In 2024, Ethiopia became the first African country to prohibit imports of gasoline and diesel vehicles. EVs now make up about 8% of its vehicle fleet, and more than 95% of its electricity comes from renewable sources, mainly hydropower. Like California, Ethiopia faces severe climate-driven weather, including an El Niño-linked drought affecting about 3.5 million people, and is advancing reforestation through its Green Legacy Initiative.

States and cities showed up

Governor Newsom closed the day at the invitation of UN Secretary-General António Guterres, joining governors and mayors from around the world, including Minnesota Governor Tim Walz and London Mayor Sadiq Khan, to elevate the role of states and cities in global climate action.

Governor Newsom thanked the Secretary-General for his longstanding commitment to climate action and for creating forums where states and cities can share what works. Calling this an era of implementation, he pointed to California’s Cap-and-Invest program as an example of what states can deliver and said the work of turning commitments into results is now underway.

California at COP31

COP31 is the 31st Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, an annual global climate conference that brings together world leaders, scientists, businesses, non-governmental organizations, and civil society to advance action on climate change. Held in Antalya, Türkiye, from November 9–20, 2026, the conference is hosted by Türkiye, with Australia leading the negotiations. This year’s focus is on implementation: turning climate commitments into concrete, measurable results.

As a founding member of the Under2 Coalition and the U.S. Climate Alliance and as co-chair of America Is All In, California is demonstrating how states and regions can sustain international cooperation, accelerate clean energy, and deliver climate solutions that lower costs, create jobs, and strengthen resilience, even as the federal government retreats.

California’s delegation includes Governor Gavin Newsom; First Partner Jennifer Siebel Newsom; California Natural Resources Agency Secretary Wade Crowfoot; California Department of Food and Agriculture Secretary Karen Ross; California Public Utilities Commission President John Reynolds; California Air Resources Board Chair Lauren Sanchez; and Governor’s Office of Land Use and Climate Innovation Director Samuel Assefa.

California’s climate leadership

Since Governor Newsom took office in 2019, California has added more than 39,000 megawatts of utility-scale clean energy to serve the California grid. That’s helped make the grid more reliable and pushed the state further along its path in the clean energy transition.

The most recent numbers, from the end of 2024, show real progress: 67% of retail electricity sales in the state already come from clean energy. Last year, clean energy met 100% of the state’s electricity needs for at least part of the day on 279 separate days.

Solar and battery storage have been a key part of that progress, and are changing how California keeps the lights on. Since 2019, battery resources serving California grew from fewer than 700 megawatts to more than 23,000 megawatts — an increase of more than 3,100%. Batteries store solar power when it is abundant and deliver it after sunset. That reduces how often the state needs to run natural gas plants, which cuts air pollution and supports a more cost-effective electricity system.

California’s approach is also where the money is heading. Global investors are now putting roughly two dollars into clean-energy technology for every dollar that goes into fossil fuels. California is leading that shift while Donald Trump watches from the sidelines.

For California, that means investing in the good-paying jobs of the future. The Golden State is the 4th-largest economy in the world and leads the nation in total clean energy jobs, with 552,300 workers employed across clean energy technologies, nearly twice as many as the second-ranked state, Texas, according to a 2025 report from E2. California’s clean energy workforce grew by nearly 7,300 workers in 2024, outpacing job growth in the rest of the state’s economy by more than three times.

SACRAMENTO – Governor Gavin Newsom and First Partner Jennifer Siebel Newsom opened their first day at COP31 at Türkiye’s International Forestry Training Centre, joining the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), the Under2 Coalition and governors from around the world for a high-level exchange on wildfire resilience. The visit set the tone for California’s week at the UN climate conference: with the Trump administration willfully absent, California is showing up as a reliable partner, sharing what’s working and learning from others confronting the same climate threats.

Home to the world’s largest aerial firefighting fleet and pioneering technologies that detect, track and fight wildfires, California is a globally recognized leader in wildfire prevention and response. The visit brought together leaders confronting the same growing climate threats to exchange expertise, strengthen international cooperation and share innovations that save lives and protect communities. With the Trump administration absent from the summit, California is continuing to engage with international partners on climate resilience.

Operated by Türkiye’s General Directorate of Forestry since 2011, the center is a regional hub for wildfire training, preparing forestry professionals and firefighters in wildfire prevention, suppression, and post-fire restoration. With support from the FAO, it is expanding its international training programs, using advanced simulators that let incident commanders practice fighting fires across shifting weather, terrain, and vegetation.

A b-roll package of the Governor and First Partner’s visit to the International Forestry Training Centre can be downloaded here.

The same fight, half a world away

Governors and regional leaders from across the globe compared notes on what works, from forest management to frontline firefighting, weighing Türkiye’s experience alongside California’s and others’ while recognizing differences in governance, resources, and landscapes. They discussed practices they could adapt at home and opportunities for continued cooperation, including technical exchanges and training.

California brought significant experience to the exchange. Under Governor Newsom, the state has invested more than $5 billion in wildfire and forest resilience, assembled the world’s largest aerial firefighting fleet, and deployed cutting-edge technologies to detect and respond to fires faster. From first-in-the-nation real-time fire mapping to satellite detection and AI-assisted firefighting, California’s innovations are helping reshape how communities prepare for and respond to increasingly destructive wildfires.

Governor Newsom recalled the 2018 Camp Fire, which destroyed the town of Paradise, and noted the experience California and Türkiye share. This summer, Türkiye fought large-scale wildfires that burned nearly 20,000 hectares over the course of a few days in July and September alone, and about 15 million hectares of the country’s forested land remain under threat.

Like California, Türkiye has invested heavily in forest management, firebreaks and clearing while strengthening its firefighting capabilities and crews.

“I feel like I’m home. Everything you are doing is so familiar,” said Governor Newsom to the group, describing California’s investments in forest management and firefighting. Reflecting on the extraordinary natural beauty and growing wildfire risk that California and Türkiye share, he said it is “what brings us all together. This is real. This is humbling, and this is hard work.”

Much like California’s operation, the Antalya, Türkiye, center includes a Forest Fire Fighting Training Simulator, which allows forest engineers and incident commanders to simulate wildfire scenarios under varying weather, vegetation and terrain conditions. Trainees can model fire behavior, deploy resources, evaluate suppression strategies and practice emergency coordination. A UN Food and Agriculture Organization partnership with Türkiye is expanding the center’s international training capabilities, particularly in Central Asia and the Caucasus.

How California is fighting fire

California co-founded the Under2 Coalition in 2015 to bring states and regions together on climate action, and today that partnership is helping governments share lessons on one of the most urgent climate threats they face.

Since 2019, the Newsom administration and the Legislature have invested more than $5 billion in wildfire and forest resilience, and the Governor recently signed legislation to speed up wildfire prevention projects and harden communities against future disasters. Over the past five years, CAL FIRE has added an average of 1,800 full-time and 600 seasonal positions each year, and it will keep hiring firefighters, natural resource professionals, and support staff to meet growing demands.

Real-time intelligence: The first-in-the-nation Fire Integrated Real-Time Intelligence System (FIRIS) has flown more than 2,000 missions since 2019, mapping fires within minutes of ignition.

Forecasting the threat: The state’s Wildfire Forecast & Threat Intelligence Integration Center is a first-of-its-kind hub for wildfire forecasting, weather intelligence and fire threat assessments.

The world’s largest aerial firefighting fleet: California is the first state to own and operate C-130H airtankers for wildfire suppression, with four in service and seven planned.

Early detection from space: CAL FIRE partnered with the Earth Fire Alliance on FireSat, whose first three wildfire detection satellites launched in June to help firefighters spot fires sooner.

Mapping wildfire risk: Statewide 3D LiDAR maps give decision-makers a clear picture of fuel loads and wildfire risk.

California’s global climate network

California has long been a key player on the international stage, from taking joint action on climate change to identifying new pathways and partnerships for sustained economic growth. United Kingdom (2026): California and the United Kingdom signed a memorandum of understanding to tackle climate change and promote sustainable development together.
