title: Marine Carbon Dioxide Removal: Promise, Risks, and the Path Forward - EDFish
description:
What is marine carbon dioxide removal, and how could it contribute to addressing climate change?
John: The buildup of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere is driving global warming, so we need to deeply and rapidly reduce more carbon dioxide from getting into the atmosphere.
That’s where marine carbon dioxide removal could come in.
Governments have been working for years to develop guidelines for marine carbon dioxide removal under these agreements.
Governments adopted assessment frameworks at the LC/LP for three marine carbon dioxide removal approaches.
text:
A conversation with EDF’s Associate Vice President for Oceans Science, Dr. Kristin Kleisner, and EDF’s Vice President for Ocean Climate Innovation, Dr. John Mimikakis

By: Maddie Voorhees, EDF Oceans

Climate change poses escalating risks to people and nature. The ocean is already a powerful climate ally. Protecting its ability to absorb and store carbon, and the ecosystems that support that role, is essential. Deep and rapid emissions reductions remain an essential priority in addressing climate change. But a substantial gap exists between the amount of carbon dioxide that we need to mitigate to prevent worsening impacts from climate change and the world’s current carbon removal capacity. As researchers investigate whether marine carbon dioxide removal, or mCDR, could provide additional climate benefits, important questions remain about its effectiveness, environmental impacts and governance.

Two meetings of global government leaders recently brought these issues into focus: the Convention on Biological Diversity’s (CBD) COP17 and the meetings of the London Convention and London Protocol (LCLP), where governments adopted new frameworks for assessing research related to three mCDR approaches.

We spoke with Dr. Kristin Kleisner, EDF’s Associate Vice President for Oceans Science, and Dr. John Mimikakis, EDF’s Vice President for Ocean Climate Innovation, about EDF’s work to advance ambitious and responsible ocean climate innovation.

What is marine carbon dioxide removal, and how could it contribute to addressing climate change?

John: The buildup of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere is driving global warming, so we need to deeply and rapidly reduce more carbon dioxide from getting into the atmosphere. But recent assessments from the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), and others now show that meeting climate goals also requires removing carbon that’s already in the atmosphere, at a scale far greater than today’s capacity.

That’s where marine carbon dioxide removal could come in. mCDR aims to expand the ocean’s natural ability to remove and store carbon dioxide to remove more from the atmosphere and keep it out. Three approaches illustrate the idea:

Ocean alkalinity enhancement changes seawater chemistry, for example by adding minerals, so it can absorb and store more carbon dioxide.

Ocean fertilization adds nutrients to the ocean to encourage small marine plants like algae that absorb carbon dioxide to grow, taking up additional carbon that could then sink into deeper waters.

Biomass sinking sends plants that absorb carbon dioxide, such as seaweed, into the deep ocean to keep the carbon it contains away from the atmosphere.

However, these methods haven’t yet demonstrated whether they can work, are safe, and make sense when compared to other carbon removal approaches. If research shows they can meet those standards, they could someday help be part of the strategy for combating climate change.

Why were these international discussions important, and what did EDF bring to the conversation?

Kristin: The CBD COP sets global policy for protecting biodiversity, and the London Convention and Protocol (LC/LP) focuses on regulating ocean pollution. Oceans, climate, and biodiversity were featured prominently throughout these discussions, reflecting how closely connected these issues are. Climate change is driving ocean warming, acidification, and marine heatwaves, and a loss of biodiversity weakens the ocean’s ability to cope with these pressures. These gatherings are an opportunity to ensure governments address the climate and biodiversity crises together rather than in isolation.

EDF participates to ensure that conversations on climate action consider implications for biodiversity and the environment, and that conversations on biodiversity and conservation acknowledge the threat of climate change. At CBD COP17, I participated in several panels focused on bringing responsible and ethical research into emerging climate approaches, to understand their potential climate, biodiversity and socio-economic trade-offs. We also worked to build support for an initiative focused on conserving the mesopelagic, or ocean twilight zone, where marine species play a significant role in moving carbon through the ocean so it can be stored away for a long time, helping the ocean act as a climate ally.

John: Kristin and I were in London for the meetings of the LC/LP, two international agreements that protect ocean ecosystems from pollution caused by dumping waste and other materials at sea. Governments have been working for years to develop guidelines for marine carbon dioxide removal under these agreements. Introducing materials into the ocean has the potential to cause harm, even when the goal is to help the climate, so these agreements take a strict, precautionary approach.

EDF joined other non-governmental organizations that engage at the LC/LP to support countries as they wrestled with those questions, bringing scientific evidence, ideas for regulation, and information about developments in the field. That perspective helps policymakers assess whether mCDR could contribute to climate action, and what safeguards would be needed to protect ocean health.

Governments adopted assessment frameworks at the LC/LP for three marine carbon dioxide removal approaches. What do these frameworks do, why does their adoption matter, and what questions remain unresolved?

John: The frameworks give governments a common process for evaluating research on ocean fertilization, ocean alkalinity enhancement, and biomass sinking. They offer guidance to regulators on assessing environmental risks, consulting the public, and requiring monitoring and oversight when permitting mCDR research activities. Their adoption is an important step toward more transparent, consistent governance that helps policymakers make informed decisions about mCDR. Importantly, they are not a green light for deployment. Significant questions remain about whether, when, and under what conditions any of these approaches could or should be deployed.

The ocean already helps regulate our climate. How does EDF’s work to protect the ocean twilight zone connect with mCDR?

Kristin: EDF has been working with partners at Ocean Conservancy, Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI), Marine Conservation Institute, and others to raise awareness of a critically important yet largely unknown part of the ocean, the mesopelagic or ocean twilight zone—which to me embodies the connection between biodiversity conservation and ocean climate regulation.

This is the area of the water column from 200 to 1000m below the surface, where sunlight begins to filter out, transitioning to total darkness. Although it’s cold and mysterious, research over the past few decades has highlighted that it is teeming with life. These animals have evolved in fascinating ways to thrive in this deep-sea environment. However, we have only scratched the surface in understanding what lives there, with an estimate of over one million undescribed species.

These species undertake the largest daily migration of animals on the planet, and this movement contributes to the ocean’s ability to move and store carbon, helping to capture 2-6 gigatons of carbon annually. As we look for new ways to remove additional carbon dioxide through various mCDR approaches, we need to ensure that these methods don’t negatively impact biodiversity and the ecosystem.

How would you describe EDF’s position on mCDR, and the distinction between supporting research and supporting commercial deployment?

John: EDF supports responsible research into mCDR approaches. We don’t assume that deployment will follow. Supporting science to examine their effectiveness and its potential impact is not an endorsement of commercial deployment.

If approaches demonstrate that they can work, are safe for people and nature, and have strong guardrails in place to ensure they remain safe and effective, EDF may consider supporting their deployment.

Kristin: First, I’d note that mCDR is not just one thing. It encompasses several different methods that affect how the ocean works. That means there are different questions about how these approaches change the ocean, whether they are safe for the environment and people, and whether they can meaningfully and affordably help combat climate change.

Our research aims to identify which questions can be answered, what further research is needed, and whether an approach should not advance because the risks or trade-offs are unacceptable.

What role should fishers, Indigenous peoples and coastal communities have in shaping mCDR research and decisions?

Kristin: Communities and rights holders deserve a voice in decisions that affect them. They need accessible information and opportunities to ask questions and raise concerns. Engagement needs to be meaningful and two-way. By operating on a more level field, you can build legitimacy and trust, but of course, engaging just to gain acceptance should not be the goal.

John: Some governance processes are beginning to recognize these voices. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) issued permits for a mCDR research project in federal waters off the coast of Massachusetts (the LOC-NESS project) only after extensive consultations and open public comment periods. The assessment frameworks for mCDR research recently adopted by the London Convention and Protocol also encourage consultations with local communities and Indigenous peoples.

What comes next for EDF, and what would meaningful progress look like?

John: EDF will continue working with governments, scientists, communities, and industry to strengthen the evidence and rules needed for responsible mCDR research. We’ll also be at the United Nations’ global meeting of climate diplomats – the Climate COP – to advance these conversations. Meaningful progress means better understanding which approaches can deliver real climate benefits, which risks can be managed, and which approaches should not move forward—all while protecting the ocean and the people who depend on it.

description:

If all goes according to plan, the Osprey platform will enable solid-state battery developers to continue pursuing sulfide to their hearts’ content.

text:
Support CleanTechnica's work through a Substack subscription, on Patreon, or on Stripe. Help us produce all of the high-quality, original content we publish week after week despite the challenges of content-scraping AI, antisocial media, inflation, and other hurdles.

Federal policy makers orchestrated an EV sales crash in the US last year, only to see electrification stakeholders gradually piece together a comeback focusing on cars that hit the affordability MSRP of $30,000 or less. New, higher-performing solid-state EV batteries are also inching their way towards the market, with the US startup QuantumScape among the innovators contributing some fresh news in recent weeks (for the record, Finland’s Donut Labs is another).

To Be Or Not To Be A Solid-State Battery

As the name indicates, a solid-state battery replaces the liquid electrolyte of a conventional lithium-ion battery with a solid material. If that sounds like a deep electrochemical challenge, its is. Nevertheless, science loves a challenge, and so do electrification stakeholders who are determined to sharpen the contrast between EVs and gasmobiles. Compared to the current generation of EV batteries, solid-state technology meets a higher bar for energy density and other performance benchmarks, while avoiding the use of volatile chemicals (see more solid-state background here)

High tech ceramics have emerged as one of the options, and that is where QuantumScape has set its sights. The company launched in 2010 and it surfaced on the CleanTechnica radar in 2012, when Volkswagen dropped word of its interest in the solid-state forumula.

QS has been focusing its attention on developing a lithium-metal formula for the anode (the part of a battery that collects a charge), by tweaking the separator, which is the part of a battery that serves as a buffer on the electrolyte.

“A solid-state lithium-metal battery…replaces the polymer separator used in conventional lithium-ion batteries with a solid-state separator. The replacement of the separator enables the carbon or silicon anode used in conventional lithium-ion batteries to be replaced with a lithium-metal anode,” QS explains.

To ice the solid-state cake, the QS anode does not make an appearance during the battery manufacturing process. It self-forms as part of the battery’s first charging cycle.

One Step Closer To The EV Battery Of The Future

QS has accumulated a string of investors and affiliations since 2012, capped by a hookup with the legacy firm Corning last year aimed at developing a manufacturing system that accommodates its ceramic separator.

The latest news takes QS farther into all-solid state technology, this time with a focus on the cathode, under the trade name Osprey.

“Osprey pairs the QS proprietary ceramic separator and anode-free lithium-metal design with a solid cathode, creating an all-solid-state cell,” the company explained in a press statement on November 11.

“Osprey builds on the company’s QSE platform, and opens new licensing and co-development options for current QS customers and expanding its offering to developers of sulfide-based all-solid-state batteries,” the company elaborates. The QS blog further explains that Osprey is a “solid-state platform that allows developers of sulfide-based solid-state batteries to incorporate QS technology into their all-solid-state battery (ASSB) development programs.”

Don’t get too excited just yet — the cathode work is still in the early stages of validation — but QS is now confident that its data will stand up under public scrutiny. In addition to safety improvements compared to conventional Li-ion batteries, QS checks a list of additional performance boxes for ASSBs:

“Cycle life: 1,000 full charge cycles with ~80% capacity retention under gold-standard testing conditions

Fast charging: 10% to 80% in five-minutes

Low pressure: Requires only one atmosphere of pressure

Cold-weather performance: Operational to less than -20 °C (-4 °F)

Want more details? Check out the QS blog, where the company takes a deeper dive into the new cathode.

What Is This Sulfide Of Which You Speak?

As for why QS is working the sulfide angle, that’s a good question. “Sulfides can react with lithium metal, which shortens battery life, and they typically need to be held under high pressure to operate, which is impractical for vehicles and many other applications,” QS notes. Despite those challenges, QS also notes the sulfide formula continues to attract widespread interest in the solid-state field, due to its high level of conductivity and ease of processing. If all goes according to plan, the Osprey platform will enable solid-state battery developers to continue pursuing sulfide to their hearts’ content.

“The industry has invested heavily in sulfide-based batteries but keeps hitting the same fundamental limits,” explains QS president and CEO Dr. Siva Sivaram, “As the data shows, Osprey can address these limitations.”

As another indication that sulfide stakeholders are not out chasing rainbows, take a look at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, part of a sprawling network of research facilities under the umbrella of the US Department of Energy. ORNL has just published a new study in the journal Energy Materials under the title, “Operando neutron radiography reveals calendar aging-induced lithium redistribution and back-diffusion in thick-cathode all-solid-state batteries.”

As the title indicates, the researchers deployed a neutron radiation tool to probe the inner workings of lithium batteries while they are in operation, enabling them to deliver a precise map of the degradation process that has bedeviled the sulfide field. They also delivered a roadmap for further work:

“Based on these findings from calendar aging, we envision future formation strategies should be redesigned to minimize sustained potential gradients while stabilizing interphases, for example through optimized composite electronic percolation and catholyte or coating materials and validated with time-resolved neutron imaging to establish transport-informed, durability-first conditioning rules that generalize across cathode loadings and operating temperatures.”

Got all that? The real question is why a federal research institution is still delivering advanced analyses leading to the next generation of EV batteries that outperform conventional batteries while improving EV safety and reducing overall costs. After all, US President Donald Trump and the Republican majority in Congress have expended considerable time and effort to stop, if not reverse, EV sales in the US. In addition to prematurely killing off the $7,500 EV tax credit last fall, the President also tried (and ultimately failed) to claw back funds from the federal NEVI public EV charging station program.

Readers, take a guess at the answer in the discussion thread. One possible explanation is the energy storage angle. While the President’s whackadoodle “American Energy Dominance Policy” dials down solar and wind (especially wind), it supports practically every other domestic energy resource including nuclear, biomass, geothermal, and hydropower alongside fossil fuels, with energy storage also making a substantial appearance.

The electronic war of the future is another factor to consider, with crewless vehicles and “anti-idling” kits serving as a sort of gateway drug that demonstrates the logistical and tactical advantages of battery power, silent running, and a lower heat signature compared to diesel fuel.

description:
It was the climate movement’s unifying slogan for the past decade: “Keep 1.5 Alive.” The tagline referred to the central ambition of the 2015 Paris climate agreement, in which almost every country pledged to try to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius.
Now, just 11 years after the target was set, 1.5 is effectively dead.
Scientists now say that without drastic efforts to reduce greenhouse gases, it is very likely that the planet will warm at least 2.6 degrees Celsius, or 4.7 degrees Fahrenheit, by the end of the century.
At COP31, the United Nations climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, diplomats who spent so long championing the 1.5 degree target lamented the abrupt setback.
“The world has no chance of holding to 1.5 degrees,” said Chris Bowen, Australia’s minister for climate change and energy, who is leading the negotiations.

description:

According to Brookings, despite historic investments flowing into Indian Country after the pandemic, a massive underinvestment in Indigenous communities continues.
The report authors are calling for policy changes that would ensure tribes receive funding, regardless of political winds.

text:
Every year, Kotzebue, a small city in northwest Alaska, has a three-month window to receive all the diesel fuel it will use throughout the following year. It sits on a gravel spit that juts into Kotzebue Sound just north of the Arctic Circle, and is accessible only by air and sea. Ice keeps freight barges from reaching it for most of the year.

The community relies on diesel for 75% of its power, and residents put about 20% of their income toward buying it. That’s more than three times the average energy burden for low-income households nationwide.

“We’re pretty much at the mercy of world markets,” Chad Nordlum, who is the energy project manager for the Native Village of Kotzebue, told Grist. “Right now, with the Iran war going on, the diesel prices are very high and we’re locked in to much higher prices than we’ve had in the past. There’s really nothing the community can do about diesel prices, but what we can do is produce our own energy.”

That’s why Nordlum was so excited about a $20 million grant from the Environmental Protection Agency to support a wind energy project. The funding, announced in 2024, was part of a larger $150 million allocation for tribal infrastructure in Alaska. Nordlum says it would have lowered the community’s reliance on diesel to about 40% to 50% and given the tribe more control over energy and economic decisions.

But the Trump administration canceled the grant in May 2025. More than a year later, the project remains paused.

That cut was among hundreds of millions of dollars the Department of Government Efficiency pulled from Indian Country, and part of a broader pattern of funding rollbacks and underinvestment in Indigenous communities. Two new reports from the Brookings Institution show that the so-called One Big Beautiful Bill Act killed many of the funding streams established by the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act, while DOGE eliminated another $468 million, about half of which was allocated for environmental and natural resources. Another 11% targeted agriculture. Those projects include climate resiliency plans, renewable energy projects, and jobs programs.

According to Brookings, despite historic investments flowing into Indian Country after the pandemic, a massive underinvestment in Indigenous communities continues. Not only is that a violation of the federal government’s trust and treaty obligations to tribes, it is hindering Indigenous efforts to protect the environment and address climate change. The report authors are calling for policy changes that would ensure tribes receive funding, regardless of political winds.

Rob Maxim, who is Mashpee Wampanoag and a fellow at Brookings Metro, said climate and environmental funding is especially crucial for Indigenous communities because they are often the most severely impacted by climate change, especially after years of underinvestment.

“The actions that the Trump administration is taking are particularly significant, but it’s not totally out of trend with previous administrations,” he said. “And what we wanted to show was that actually this underinvestment is kind of the default for the U.S. rather than a blip.”

The true aberration was the unprecedented levels of funding after the pandemic. That funding, which came under the Biden administration, included over $700 million in climate, energy, and infrastructure funding for tribes. It covered projects like development of climate action plans, food systems analysis, and more. For example, the Hopi Tribe was to receive a $25 million grant to install solar panels for 600 homes. That grant, and the entire $7 billion Solar for All program, were cut.

Maxim says that funding for Indigenous communities is a federal obligation based on treaties and other agreements with tribes and should be standard and irrevocable. “The funding that was flowing to Indian Country was not being done on the basis of race or DEI, and it was absolutely not illegal,” he said. “It was aimed at the promotion of tribal sovereignty and the well-being of tribal citizens and tribal communities, and so that is, you know, an obligation that the U.S. government maintains.”

The White House did not respond to a request for comment. The EPA provided a comment several days after this story originally published Nov. 2.

“The Trump EPA is committed to ensuring taxpayer dollars are being used appropriately and has reviewed all funding activities with that lens. Through the agency’s General Assistance Program (GAP) and other granting programs, EPA has awarded more than $351 million in Tribal grants funding since the beginning of the second Trump administration,” the agency said in an email to Grist.

Glencora Haskins, a senior research associate and applied research manager at Brookings Metro, said that the administration had targeted funding to tribes, with “tribal” being the most frequently flagged term. “I think that there was a very surface-level view of what a lot of these programs were doing, rather than any deep interrogation of the types of systemic infrastructure deficits that programs were trying to fix,” Haskins said.

In Native communities throughout Alaska, and around the country, energy and infrastructure needs are especially acute because of increasingly frequent and destructive storms, wildfires, and other climate-driven disasters.

Haskins and Maxim recommend that Congress pass legislation that bars the cancellation of grants and contracts for tribes, and stipulates that all funding for Indigenous nations and communities is in service of trust and treaty obligations even if it is from a program with a different stated purpose. They also call for a statutory requirement that money should flow directly to tribes rather than having them seek reimbursement from the U.S. Treasury.

In Kotzebue, Chad Nordlum hopes the political tide will turn enough to get the funding for the wind project moving. In the meantime, he is working on a smaller solar project that he hopes will help alleviate the community’s energy challenges.

“Our main goals are energy security and economic development for the tribe, which is ultimately being able to invest in our own community, help make the lives of people here a little more sustainable,” Nordlum said. “We want our community to continue on into the future. We have to get a handle on our energy prices and availability.”

text:
Who pays for the roads that bring the world to Myrtle Beach, SC ?

Congress is considering a new annual federal fee on electric vehicle owners as part of a larger transportation funding bill. The proposal (in the BUILD America 250 Act) would start at $130 a year for full EVs and $35 for plug-in hybrids, with small increases in later years. It’s not law yet, but the idea is straightforward: gas-powered vehicles contribute to the federal Highway Trust Fund through the gas tax (unchanged since 1993). Electric vehicles don’t.

LOCAL NEWS AND COMMUNITY SUPPORT PROVIDED BY Jake Lee - Myrtle Beach & Pawleys Island Top Realtor

On the Grand Strand, this conversation lands a little differently than in places like California or the Northeast.

South Carolina has one of the lower EV adoption rates in the country... roughly 0.8% of vehicles compared to a national average around 2.2%. You’re still far more likely to see a traditional family SUV or sedan on Ocean Boulevard or Highway 501 than a fully electric vehicle. Local EV owners remain a relatively small group, and South Carolina already charges its own EV road-use fee (about $60 a year equivalent for battery electrics).

At the same time, our economy runs on roads. Nearly 18 million visitors a year drive into the Grand Strand, supporting billions in local spending and tens of thousands of jobs. Projects that improve connectivity ( including the long-sought Interstate 73 ) depend on strong federal transportation funding. The roads that get visitors here and get residents around town benefit everyone.

MYRTLE BEACH HOMES FOR SALE

So here’s the question for our community: As more visitors (and eventually more locals) switch to electric, how do we keep the roads that power our tourism economy well-funded? A federal fee on the relatively small number of EVs registered here would have a limited direct cost for most Grand Strand households, while contributing to the Highway Trust Fund that helps maintain the infrastructure we all use.

What do you think? Should EV owners contribute a fixed annual amount toward the roads, or is there a better approach?

title: Datacentres are deeply unpopular. Has Sweden made one we can all love? - The Guardian
description:
Conditions for datacentres are pretty good in Sweden as a whole.
The rest of the heat (such as from the liquid cooling) goes directly into the local district heating system in Falun.
Already, district heating systems make use of excess heat from wastewater, sewage and supermarket refrigerators; datacentres are now another source to add to the mix.
Stockholm claims to have the world’s largest district heating system, with more than 3,000 km of pipes, serving close to 90% of the capital.
There are about 50 small-scale datacentres in the region (typically less than 20MW), and about 20 are connected to the district heating.
text:
‘It was pretty cool, when they were building it. It looked like a very large Ikea,” says John Wernvik, of EcoDataCenter. He is giving me a tour of their facility in Falun, Sweden, which could lay claim to being the world’s greenest datacentre – although to many, that is a contradiction in terms.

One difference is immediately visible: this datacentre is made out of wood. Huge panels of cross-laminated timber arrived at the site pre-cut, and were assembled by crane according to instructions, like flatpack furniture. Aesthetically, this section of the datacentre is more like an Ikea before the fit-out, a cavernous, echoey, immaculately clean hangar. The wood is not EcoDataCenter’s only claim to sustainability; it is more than just cosmetic, says Wernvik, the company’s chief external relations and sustainability officer. “Compared with a traditional datacentre built with steel and concrete, we lower the embodied carbon of the full structure by three times.” With a complex the size of a football pitch, that is a lot of wood, but, says Wernvik, “the amount of timber one of our datacentres uses takes the Swedish forest about 10 to 15 minutes to grow back”.

Datacentres have become a dirty word and a political issue in much of the world – especially the US, where opposition to them was said to be a factor in the recent midterm elections – but here in Sweden, not so much.

There is a familiar litany of reasons why datacentres are bad: they are being built without the consent or knowledge of local people; they consume vast amounts of land, electricity and water, with knock-on effects for communities and the environment; they provide no jobs and enrich rapacious tech companies.

What’s remarkable is how little any of those arguments apply in Sweden, especially here in Falun, a former copper-mining town a few hours north of Stockholm. If your abiding image of a datacentre is something like xAI’s Colossus facility in Tennessee, built at lightning speed with little public notice, partly powered by banks of unpermitted, methane gas-burning temporary generators, releasing huge amounts of CO2 and harmful pollutants into the atmosphere and the community, then EcoDataCenter is practically the polar opposite. “I’m biased, but we believe that we build datacentres in a somewhat different way,” says Wernvik.

For starters, the company’s electricity supply is 100% renewable: 75% from hydroelectric power and 25% from wind. Sweden’s power mix as a whole is virtually carbon-free – just 1% of it comes from fossil fuels (in the EU as a whole, the figure is 29%, in the US it is 55%). In rural areas like Falun, there is sometimes too much electricity being generated by nearby hydroelectric, solar and wind, so power-hungry datacentres are actually helpful in balancing the grid.

Conditions for datacentres are pretty good in Sweden as a whole. The cold northern climate means less cooling is required; the energy is not only green, it is cheap and reliable; there is plenty of water and space; and the country is relatively politically stable and well-regulated – as Wernvik puts it, “it’s very hard to develop something in Sweden where there’s not a consensus”.

Energy is still a concern at EcoDataCenter, considering this place has a capacity of 80MW (the equivalent of about 60,000 homes). There are two key measures of datacentre performance. One is carbon usage effectiveness (CUE): the carbon emissions for each kWh of energy consumed. The average for US datacentres is 414gCO2/kWh, the European Union’s is 263gCO2/kWh, EcoDataCenter’s is 1.17gCO2/kWh. Another key measure is power usage effectiveness (PUE); how efficiently the datacentre uses the power going into it. The EU average is 1.36 (where a score of 1 would be 100% efficiency), EcoDataCenter’s is 1.15. The company is bringing down both its CUE and PUE year by year, according to EcoDataCenter’s sustainability report.

The primary use for energy is powering the graphics processing units – the expensive chips that do the computing, mostly made by the US company Nvidia. (Wernvik reminds me that although 70% of their computing power goes towards AI, almost everything online is run through datacentres somewhere, from banking transactions to streaming TV.) The supply must be constant – even a small drop in current for a few milliseconds could be consequential – so there are numerous backup generators on site, but even these are fuelled by hydrotreated vegetable oil (HVO), a biofuel made from waste vegetable oil and animal fat, so also fossil fuel-free.

The other main energy use is cooling; removing the vast amounts of heat the chips generate. This is where controversies have arisen in the US over extracting from the local water supply, but it is less of an issue here, says Wernvik. The Swedish climate means less cooling is required, and there is plenty of water around (they get most of theirs from a nearby lake that was once used for drinking water). On a dreary, rainy day, no water is needed: the air is cold enough already (15C – anything below 20C will do). They simply have to pipe it around the building. On days when it is hot, or there is surplus electricity to use, there are electrically powered chillers on the roofs that cool air using a mist of water before it is circulated around the buildings.

The future, however, lies in liquid cooling – where the heat from the chips is transferred directly to liquid, rather than through the air. The latest generation of chips require this, Wernvik explains, as we walk through a spotlessly clean room containing several fridge-sized racks of chips, arranged in two parallel rows. They take up about the same amount of space as a bus. The noise is deafening (but inaudible outside), the chips themselves are barely visible behind a spaghetti of cables and cooling tubes connected to the backs of the server racks. It is a closed-loop system, so it does not use any external water, he says. “Each rack here is basically 25 saunas that we need to cool away and keep at about 27 degrees for it to not burn up inside,” says Wernvik. “That’s the whole engineering challenge we’re trying to solve.”

These particular Blackwell chips are powering DeepL, the German-based AI translation platform. Some of EcoDataCenter’s clients are confidential; declared ones include US cloud computing company CoreWeave, French AI firm Mistral, and research institutes including the universities of Hull and York. Supporting sovereign European tech is one of their key aims, Wernvik says.

The final part of the energy equation is excess heat, which EcoDataCenter reuses as much as possible. Much of it is used to dry wood pellets – a byproduct of the timber industry. The pellets go into incinerators in populated areas to provide heating. There is one right next door, which is no coincidence. (Admittedly, burning them emits CO2, but given the circular nature of the timber industry, they are arguably carbon-neutral.)

The rest of the heat (such as from the liquid cooling) goes directly into the local district heating system in Falun. Since the 1950s, Sweden has been building district heating networks across the country, where water is heated at large, centralised boilers, rather than in individual homes, then piped around towns and cities in underground pipes, typically at 60C to 80C. Homes and businesses extract the heat via a heat exchanger on their property. Already, district heating systems make use of excess heat from wastewater, sewage and supermarket refrigerators; datacentres are now another source to add to the mix.

There’s another aspect of EcoDataCenter’s operation that stands out. While datacentres are being imposed on many communities from the outside, in Falun it was practically the opposite. The project was initiated by local government, says Wernvik, “so the idea from the beginning was very much based on, how do we integrate a datacentre in the local community in order for it to fit the municipality?” This was in 2010, long before the AI revolution. The municipality (like a local council) decided the project would be better handled by a private company, which led to the formation of EcoDataCenter in 2014. The first part of the Falun site was up and running in 2019. The final phases are still under construction.

Local benefits were built in from the outset: 90% of its suppliers are sourced locally and 60% of its capital expenditure is spent locally, Wernvik says. It invests in local education and training, including sponsoring local sports teams and youth activities.

Local integration is even more evident at EcoDataCenter’s second site, in the industrial city of Borlänge, about a 20-minute drive away. This facility, the first phase of which will open in 2027, has a capacity of 240MW – three times larger than Falun. And the site is enormous: 200,000 sq m. In Borlänge, by contrast, they are building on a brownfield site. Poetically, perhaps, it used to be a paper mill, which closed in 2021. A datacentre is a good replacement: it can plug into the existing industrial infrastructure in much the same way – the power grid, the nearby water supply, the district heating. It will also employ 200 to 300 people, roughly the same number that worked at the paper mill before it closed, says Wernvik. “The discussion that datacentres don’t generate that amount of jobs, that needs to be put in context. There are a lot of different datacentres.”

In Stockholm, the datacentre strategy is different, but no less joined up. Sweden’s capital has become something of a European tech centre in its own right, and demand for datacentres is high. Stockholm Data Parks – a joint initiative by the city council and the city’s energy, power grid and fibre optic companies – was founded in 2014 as “a one-stop shop in order to make it easier to attract datacentre operators,” explains Michael Gullberg, product manager at energy company Stockholm Exergi. They free up suitable land, and again, the emphasis is on sustainability, including clean power (the city hopes to be net zero by 2035) and recycling waste heat. Stockholm claims to have the world’s largest district heating system, with more than 3,000 km of pipes, serving close to 90% of the capital. There are about 50 small-scale datacentres in the region (typically less than 20MW), and about 20 are connected to the district heating. They contribute about 1.5% of the city’s annual heat demand, which might not sound much, “but 110 gigawatt-hours of recovered heat is still a decent amount, because the system is so vast,” says Gullberg.

I visit one such facility in Kista, a suburb north of the city centre that has become Stockholm’s tech hub. It is an unobtrusive shed on an industrial estate, with a capacity of 12MW. Crucially, it is right next door to a district heating plant, so the datacentre basically pipes its heated water over the fence. It’s a win-win, says Sandra Karlsson, senior public affairs manager: “When they need to do district heating, they don’t need to boil the water from six degrees, they get it at 30 degrees from us, so they save a lot of energy.” In return, it takes in cold water from the district heating plant, which it uses for cooling.

This datacentre is run by atNorth, a company that began in Iceland, and now has 13 datacentres running or under construction across Sweden, Iceland, Norway, Denmark and Finland. Conditions are similar to Sweden in all these countries, says atNorth’s CEO, Eyjólfur Magnús Kristinsson: renewable power, reliable grids, district heating, “as well as the crappy weather that we have. We barely can live there as human beings, but datacentres love it.” As with EcoDataCenter, it claims to put sustainability and community engagement to the fore, investing and employing locally, using resources efficiently.

In terms of heat recovery, it’s a bit of a catch-22, Kristinsson points out: larger datacentres must be built in more remote areas, where there is less need for district heating, and vice versa. So they have been thinking of other ways. At its “mega site” in Varde, Denmark, with an initial capacity of 250MW, as well as district heating the plan is to channel excess heat into a 20 ha complex of greenhouses. “That means that Denmark can be self-sufficient with tomatoes during the six months of winter,” says Kristinsson. In turn, that means fewer imported vegetables: “that also saves a lot of carbon footprint, creates local jobs, and increases energy efficiency.” In Rjukan, Norway, Green Mountain’s datacentre channels excess heat to the fish farm next door.

Could other countries replicate this model? Yes and no. For one thing, the AI “hyperscalers” – such as Google, Meta, Amazon Web Services and Microsoft – dwarf Europe in terms of demand. Currently Europe’s datacentre capacity is estimated to be between 15% and 25% of that of the US. In addition, the renewable energy infrastructure in countries like Sweden has taken decades to establish; it is difficult to see the US catching up quickly. Added to which, European countries are relatively strict, both in terms of building and environmental regulations, and in areas like data privacy and protection. Elon Musk would never get away with trucking in some gas generators without permission in Sweden. To many critics, tighter regulation is exactly what the US datacentre landscape is crying out for. In July 2025, the Trump administration announced its AI Action Plan, which dismantled environmental and planning protections and rejected “radical climate dogma” in order to win the AI race.

Having said that, the US is building big in Nordic countries, to service their European users. In Sweden, Meta is building a 723MW facility in Lulea, Canadian-American firm Brookfield is planning a 750MW datacentre in Strängnäs, and Google broke ground on a 150MW plant in Horndal this June. These companies profess to be adopting the Nordic model, including building their own renewable energy supplies, although last month, the Guardian reported that Google had illegally felled 250,000 trees in Muhos, in northern Finland, to clear a site for its datacentre, leaving a barren 330 ha landscape. Google’s Finland country manager, Antti Järvinen, has apologised for the forest clearings but claimed the company had acted “on the best understanding we had of the legislation at the time” and planned to plant trees across 130 hectares there. Contractors building Microsoft’s datacentre in Gävle, Sweden, have been accused of housing their mostly foreign workers in poor conditions and subjecting them to long hours. Microsoft said of its contractors and suppliers, it “set clear requirements on health and safety, working conditions, and the freedom of association and right to collective bargaining” and had “robust processes in place” to ensure contractors’ compliance with Microsoft’s human rights and fair labour policies. The community engagement has not gone so smoothly for Google in Sweden, either. In 2021, a local metal band, also named Horndal, released an album railing against Google’s imminent arrival, called Lake Drinker (sample lyrics: “The digital devil shivers of thirst … First you took our trees / Now you drink our lake”).

Both atNorth and EcoDataCenter avoid importing cheap foreign labour, they say, but Kristinsson acknowledges that opposition to datacentres in the region has been growing, largely fuelled by the backlash in the US: “It’s probably not as strong [here], but Nordics are early adopters of everything that is new. We adopt, also, the same TikTok propaganda that is showing now in the US.”

Wernvik is more measured: “The American companies and the hyperscalers are definitely needed in the ecosystem as well because they possess unique competitiveness and capabilities.”

Could Sweden become a victim of its own success? The prospect of more and more of these gigantic facilities eating up the landscape is pretty dystopian even in a large country like Sweden. Wernvik is not too worried, though: “Our core components into what we sell are land and power. It’s a very linear business in that way. It’s very hard to have exponential growth because we work with physical constraints.” Exactly how many datacentres the world needs is largely a question of demand: how much more AI we require, and how much the benefits offset the harms. That’s really a separate conversation, but at the very least, Sweden’s joined-up, long-term approach to tech, energy and communities shows that there are better and worse ways to build our digital future.

This article was amended on 12 November 2026 because an earlier version said the site covered by the EcoDataCenter in Borlänge is 200 sq km. In fact the figure is 200,000 sq m.

text:
ANTALYA, TÜRKIYE – From COP31, Governor Gavin Newsom today announced the first 14 members of California’s Environmental Youth Advisory Council (Youth Council), affirming that young people have a role not only in inheriting the future, but in building it.

The inaugural cohort selected by the California Environmental Protection Agency brings together young Californians ages 14 to 20 from across the state to share their experiences and ideas, build leadership skills, and make recommendations to inform California’s environmental policies and programs. Through the council, members will learn from state environmental officials and bring forward perspectives on the challenges facing their communities, recognizing that change sparked locally can inspire action across California, the nation, and the world.

“Young people everywhere will inherit the environmental legacy we build today,” said California Secretary for Environmental Protection, Yana Garcia. “The lived experiences and diverse perspectives of the extraordinary Youth Council members are vital to ensuring our state’s environmental policies protect the most vulnerable communities and pave the way for a more resilient future.”

Representing California’s diverse communities

Selected from a highly competitive pool of more than 300 applicants, the inaugural members reflect California’s geographical, cultural, and socioeconomic diversity.

Young people are no strangers to the effects of wildfires, extreme heat, flooding, poor air quality, and other pollution. The Youth Council creates an opportunity to share those experiences directly with California’s environmental officials and contribute ideas for a cleaner, healthier, and more resilient future.

The inaugural cohort members:

Arsenia Briones — San Joaquin County

Abby Costello — San Diego County

Lauren Ferran — Alameda County

Magnus Figueroa — Sonoma County

Max Gomez — San Bernardino County

Christopher Kricorian — Ventura County

Bettina Lee — San Bernardino County

Nicholas Munkhbaatar — Sacramento County

Neha Prabhakar — Stanislaus County

Ceasar Cano Ramos — Fresno County

Sofia Reyes — Orange County

Isabelle Shapiro — Los Angeles County

Amari Sims — Santa Clara County

Precious Zaraspe — Los Angeles County

Building a framework for California’s next generation of environmental leaders

The mission of the California Environmental Protection Agency (CalEPA) is to restore, protect, and enhance the environment, to ensure public health, environmental quality, and economic vitality for all Californians.

CalEPA established the Youth Council to strengthen communication and collaboration between California’s young people and the agency and its boards, departments, and offices. The council combines opportunities to share ideas and make recommendations with hands-on learning and leadership development.

The first official meeting will take place in December. During this inaugural term, the council members will:

Share ideas and recommendations: Offer youth perspectives on environmental policies and programs addressing climate change, air quality, clean water, and waste management.

Advance environmental justice: Elevate the voices of communities most impacted by pollution and health hazards.

Engage their peers: Lead public awareness initiatives to foster civic and environmental engagement among young Californians.

Identify youth priorities: Focus on issues that matter to their generation, including climate action, clean air and water, and community health.

Build leadership skills: Work directly with state environmental officials to learn how policies and programs are developed and implemented.

The cohort will participate in periodic virtual meetings throughout the year, alongside a scheduled annual in-person meeting, to collaborate directly with state decision-makers. After this initial one-year pilot, the program is scheduled to transition to full two-year council terms starting in Fall 2027, with up to 20 council members.

For more information regarding the council’s mission or future application cycles, please visit the official CalEPA Youth Council Page.

Empowering young Californians to lead

Since the beginning of his administration, Governor Newsom has made investing in the next generation of leaders a priority by expanding opportunities for young people to lead, serve their communities, build careers, and help shape the decisions that will define their future.

Through youth commissions and advisory bodies — including the California Teen Tech Council, the California Youth Empowerment Commission, the California Commission on the Status of Women and Girls Youth Advisory Council — young Californians are bringing their experiences and ideas directly to policymakers to help advance solutions on issues that matter to their lives.

California is also connecting young people to paid service and career pathways through the California Conservation Corps and the California Service Corps, including the California Climate Action Corps, College Corps, and Youth Service Corps. These programs put young Californians to work in their communities, provide hands-on training and valuable experience, build leadership and technical skills, and help participants develop the networks they need to launch their careers.

text:
WASHINGTON — The editorial boards of The New York Times and The Washington Post have endorsed U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich’s (D-N.M.) Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), recognizing the legislation as a significant opportunity to lower energy costs, accelerate the development of clean energy, modernize the nation’s energy infrastructure, create good-paying jobs, reduce emissions, and hold data centers accountable.

Today, The New York Times endorsed the legislation, highlighting its potential to deliver lower electricity costs and reduce emissions while advancing long-overdue permitting reform: “The bill’s supporters recognize that it is merely a first step toward a much broader agenda to reduce carbon emissions and lower energy costs. But anyone who cares about climate change should cheer this bill. And a party that just won an election on affordability should not pass up a chance to start delivering immediately.”

In its November 9 editorial, The Washington Post Editorial Board called the legislation “a major step toward historic permitting reform,” writing that making it easier to build energy infrastructure “would greatly boost” wind and solar industries. The board also noted that the legislation is projected to reduce carbon emissions and highlighted the support it has received from climate organizations including the Environmental Defense Fund, Evergreen Action, and Citizens’ Climate Lobby.

The endorsements come as a growing body of independent research and analysis reinforces the legislation’s benefits for American families, workers, and the clean energy industry.

New independent polling shows overwhelming public support for BAAJA, even after voters hear opposition arguments.

A new national poll from Third Way found that 79% of voters support BAAJA, with 66% continuing to support the legislation even after hearing arguments against it. Support cuts across party lines, with voters responding particularly strongly to provisions that lower electricity bills, create jobs, improve critical infrastructure, and ensure data centers pay their fair share.

Independent analyses demonstrate BAAJA will deliver significant savings for American families and hold data centers accountable.

Grid Strategies estimates that BAAJA will require data centers to pay approximately $55 billion in transmission costs over the next decade — $35 billion more than they would pay under current policy — helping protect other electricity customers from shouldering the costs of data center expansion.

Analysis from the Center for Climate and Energy Solutions and Greenline Insights projects that BAAJA could save households $19 billion on electricity bills through 2040.

The Corporate Energy Buyers Association has also outlined how the legislation will help reduce electricity costs for American consumers and businesses.

Independent research shows BAAJA will accelerate clean energy development and significantly reduce emissions.

Columbia University’s Center on Global Energy Policy developed an analysis comparing how BAAJA would affect permitting timelines for different types of energy projects.

The Solar Energy Industries Association estimates that BAAJA would enable solar and wind to supply 37.4% of U.S. electricity generation by 2035, compared to 19.6% under current permitting conditions. Its analysis also projects approximately 20% lower power-sector carbon emissions, 51% less net new gas capacity, and $6 billion in lower cumulative electricity costs between 2028 and 2035.

Rhodium Group has independently analyzed the legislation’s impacts on emissions and the broader U.S. energy system.

The Corporate Energy Buyers Association has also detailed the legislation’s potential to increase clean energy generation and reduce emissions.

BAAJA will create over one hundred thousand good-paying American jobs.

A new analysis from Employ America estimates that BAAJA could create up to 105,600 industrial jobs through 2040. Those jobs would come from building and maintaining new wind, solar, battery, and transmission infrastructure, as well as reducing energy costs for American manufacturers.

The legislation has also been endorsed by a broad coalition of labor, energy, and business stakeholders.

text:
As western powers, such the US and EU, pursue non-adversarial sources of critical minerals, Zambia’s Southern province offers an example of how artisanal and small-scale mining (ASM) can be harnessed. In the process, these western powers can provide additional incentive for ASM miners to formalize their operations in countries like Zambia, which can serve to grow the economic impact of ASM for these resource-rich communities as well as to raise the safety and environmental standards relative to current practice.

Zambia’s Southern province contains the Choma-Kalomo Block, a geological formation that hosts economically significant quantities of pegmatites similar to those in the tungsten, tantalum and tin (3T) mining sector in eastern DRC and Rwanda. These pegmatites often also contain coltan; a mineral composed of tantalum and niobium.

These minerals are primarily mined by ASM operations, yet the sector is not well developed. Tin mining is considered a seasonal opportunity for communities; it provides temporary income during periods with little agricultural work. Artisanal miners visually and gravimetrically separate the tin ore from the waste, which they then sell to middlemen at steep discounts relative to its price in marketplaces. The discount reflects a combination of shortfalls in knowledge and/or capacity: of beneficiation facilities; of knowledge of how to recognize and process coltan and how to price and sell 3T concentrates; and of resources to move minerals to other buyers farther away from the communities in centralized locations.

DFARS EXPECTED TO FORCE NEW SUPPLY CHAINS

Tantalum and tungsten are amongst a handful of minerals covered in the upcoming Defense Federal Acquisition Regulation Supplement (DFARS) that precludes covered minerals being procured from Foreign Entities of Concern (FEOCs). For tantalum, the restriction covers every stage, from mining to producing the finished metal. DFARS has excluded FEOC-sourced minerals since 2024, but exemption waivers had been widely granted, blunting any impact. Starting in January 2027, however, these waivers are expected to be subjected to greater scrutiny and fewer approvals.

Reducing the number of waivers will push more of the US’s demand for these materials into secondary regional markets. If the Pentagon continues its efforts to decouple its supply chains from adversaries, price premiums that have already appeared in tungsten are likely to appear for other metals like tantalum. Given the long development timeline of mines in the US, artisanal miners around the world will have the opportunity to command higher prices for their products if they can demonstrate independence from China.

Tantalum is a metal with a small market but a large strategic footprint. It is irreplaceable in electronics grade capacitors and aviation superalloys. Most of it is mined in Central Africa and then refined in China. There are no pricing benchmarks for tantalum outside of the Shanghai Metal Exchange.

Tungsten on the other hand, has benchmarks in Shanghai and Rotterdam. After Beijing imposed export controls, Chinese exports of ammonium paratungstate (APT), the main tungsten intermediate, fell to zero in October 2025. Western buyers suddenly had to compete for whatever feedstock was left. By March 2026, European APT prices had jumped 30%. This gap with Chinese prices had grown to over $1500 per metric ton unit (mtu) from near parity in 2025. Recent commentaries from the Shanghai Metals Market describe the European premium as persistent despite consistent downward pressure on Chinese APT prices. The product specifications/quality is the same in Rotterdam and Ganzhou. What differs is whether the material pass through an operation that could be influenced by the China government.

ZAMBIA’S ATTEMPTS TO FORMALIZE ASM

Developing a trusted alternative value chain requires supply chain transparency. This implies that at least some degree of formalization of Zambian ASM’s 3T mining will be required. At its “lowest” level, Western sources could retain partners to purchase ore/concentrate from ASM miners. But Zambia, like other countries in mineral resource-rich regions, has enacted several policies to take this further. These policies include providing technical, safety and environmental training, access to finance for general business purposes and equipment (leases), and simplified tax policies. They also encourage the development of cooperatives (collections of individual ASM miners or entities), which can share larger, more sophisticated equipment (for example) washing plants to recover/concentrate gold vs. using mercury) and administrative efficiencies and they call for the development of entities that will purchase minerals directly from ASM miners. Albeit from a very small base, these steps are encouraging more formalization; ASM license applications, for example, rose 57% in 2025 from a year earlier, to 1,068.

In the case of gold, the Zambia government has also taken steps to develop more beneficiation capacity and provide access for ASM production, i.e. to create more value via moving down the value chain to share with ASM miners (or cooperatives). The country recently opened its first refinery, smelting gold, just last month. Ministers have expressed the ambition to broaden refining/processing to more minerals over time.

The imperative to develop non-FEOC supply chains creates powerful economic development opportunities across resource-rich communities in the Global South. Zambia offers an example where this understanding has led to enactment of a set of policies to encourage this development through ASM and thus directly at the local community level. Western demand commitments and support for infrastructure can enable formalization, transparency and value addition can help realize the opportunity.

text:
MICHIGAN (WJRT) - General Motors is embarking on its largest renewable-energy project to date through a new partnership to power its Michigan manufacturing operations.

Company officials announced Thursday that the automaker is serving as the primary customer for two new utility-scale solar facilities in Branch and St. Clair counties.

According to General Motors, the projects, developed by NorthStar Clean Energy, includes a solar generation facility in Branch County and the Lake Iris solar project in St. Clair County. GM secured the energy through a virtual power purchase agreement to support its long-term business needs and bring predictability to its operating expenses.

The developments have already created more than 550 full-time local construction jobs. In Branch County, the project helped Bethel Township secure a $1 million Renewables Ready Communities Award, which local leaders plan to use for road improvements and a township hall expansion.

In St. Clair County, the Lake Iris facility plans to establish a native pollinator habitat across its grounds to support local biodiversity and solar-panel efficiency. GM will support the habitat effort and partner with researchers to study its regional value.

text:
Duke Energy, the electric utility that controls nearly all of North Carolina’s power generation, is pushing forward with a natural gas buildout intended to support a deluge of new data centers.

The utility checked off a crucial step in that process Monday evening, when the Davidson County Board of Commissioners approved a rezoning request from Duke to build a liquified natural gas storage facility along the Yadkin River near Lexington.

The county board split over the zoning change, which passed on a 4-3 vote. A grassroots group, fueled in part by public skepticism of data centers, led opposition to the project in partnership with several environmental advocacy organizations.

One of those organizations, the Southern Coalition for Social Justice, sent the Davidson commissioners a 17-page letter last week arguing that the proposed project conflicts with the county’s land use policies.

Aiswarya Murali, a staff attorney for SCSJ, explained that state statute requires counties to assess whether a rezoning request is consistent with its adopted land development plan.

“Based on our analysis, it is a clear ‘no,’” Murali told Carolina Public Press.

“The land development plan very clearly commits to preserving agricultural land, protecting natural resources, as well as locating industrial development in appropriate places.”

Murali cited air and water pollution, industrial noise, light pollution and burden to neighboring property owners through easements and land acquisitions as potential consequences of the project.

Ultimately, the commissioners narrowly sided with Duke, which assured them of the safety of liquified natural gas and touted the jobs and taxes the facility would bring. Board chair Karen Watford referenced recent power outages in Thomasville as a reason for her aye vote.

“I think about that little old lady down the street, your grandmother on the other side of the county, them losing power for long periods of time and possibly dying because of it,” Watford said.

“I think we need this.”

Commissioner Tripp Kester disagreed.

“The way I look at it is, ‘Is this in the public interest?’” Kester said.

“From everything I’ve heard in the last week … obviously they ain’t interested, and they don’t want it. And I can’t support it.”

Power plants await scrutiny from NC regulators

The rezoning request was for 1,600 acres of land that previously had been designated as a rural agricultural area. Duke Energy has owned the land for decades but hasn’t done much with it other than lease it out to a hunting club.

Now, Duke sees that parcel as a crucial part of a project it's calling the Davie-Davidson Energy Complex. The company is currently seeking approval for two gas-fired power plants in Davie County. In neighboring Davidson County, it wants to build a liquified natural gas storage facility to support those power plants.

Davie and Davidson are bisected by the Yadkin River. Duke plans to connect the power plants and the storage facility with a pipeline which will run under the river. But before any of those proposed facilities can be built, they need to be approved by state regulators.

If recent history is any tell, approval is far from guaranteed.

The North Carolina Utilities Commission, which consists of five appointed members, must give the go-ahead when it votes later this year to finalize Duke’s integrated resource plan. That’s the biennial document that lays out how much new power generation Duke is permitted to build based on projected demand.

In September, the Utilities Commission blocked Duke’s attempt to build a separate gas-powered power plant in Richmond County, calling its permit application “premature” given that the commission was still reviewing the utility’s integrated resource plan.

Duke had tried to circumvent the traditional timeline and get approval for the power plant before its resource plan had been finalized. The company said it did so because any delay in getting new power plants approved could result in higher construction costs and difficulty meeting increased demand from “large-load” users such as data centers.

The Utilities Commission didn’t buy the argument, writing in its order that potentially higher construction costs didn’t necessitate expedited approval of a project that was certain to raise customers’ rates.

The commission also questioned the accuracy of Duke’s projections, which suggested that electricity demand would spike in the coming years. Approval of the Richmond plant would “impose a significant risk that new generation is approved before the need for that generation is determined,” the commission wrote.

Clean energy advocates criticize pivot to natural gas

The Davie-Davidson and Richmond projects are part of a larger push by Duke to increase its power generation through natural gas. It is currently building gas-fired facilities in Catawba County and Person County, which are expected to come online by 2029 and 2030, respectively.

Natural gas is primarily methane, a greenhouse gas. It is generally considered a cleaner energy source compared to other fossil fuels, such as coal, but it isn’t “zero emission.”

According to Shelley Robbins of the Southern Alliance for Clean Energy, the reason for Duke’s shift to natural gas is simple.

“Money, money, money,” Robbins said.

Of course, that is not Duke’s position. The company has told regulators that electricity demand is rising in the era of artificial intelligence, and it is merely trying to keep up.

Duke is statutorily obligated to go carbon-neutral by 2050, but renewable energy sources like wind and solar aren't far along enough to meet the short-term needs. In the interim, it has ramped up development of natural gas facilities and delayed the sunsetting of its coal-fired plants.

New data centers make up most of the increased demand for electricity, but Duke has also been upfront about its efforts to recruit these projects to North Carolina. That makes for a sort of chicken-and-the-egg problem, Robbins said.

Organizations like the Southern Alliance for Clean Energy have criticized Duke for prioritizing its business interests over its customers. Ratepayers are facing a 9.5% increase in their electric bills next year, and that price hike didn’t even account for the potential cost of proposed projects like the ones in Davie and Davidson.

Earlier this year, Duke proposed a “large-load tariff,” which would lock in data centers and other large-load consumers into long-term contracts and require them to pay for any upgrades needed to connect them to the electric grid. The tariff, Duke said, was intended to shield ordinary consumers from having to pay for the energy costs associated with data centers.

However, Robbins pointed out that the proposed tariff doesn’t cover the cost of new power generation, only upgrades to the electric grid.

“These two plants (in Davie County) would not be built but for data centers,” Robbins said.

“The rest of us, we will be paying for data center generation in the form of these large combined cycles.”

Broad coalition of national and local labor organizations representing hundreds of thousands of skilled workers supports legislation projected to create up to 105,600 trades and manufacturing jobs

WASHINGTON — The AFL-CIO has endorsed U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich’s (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), joining a broad coalition of national and local labor organizations representing the skilled workers who build, operate, and maintain America’s energy infrastructure.

The AFL-CIO’s endorsement adds to growing support from across organized labor, including the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers (IBEW), International Association of Iron Workers, International Association of Sheet Metal, Air, Rail, and Transportation Workers (SMART), International Brotherhood of Boilermakers, International Brotherhood of Teamsters,International Union of Operating Engineers (IUOE), Laborers’ International Union of North America (LIUNA), North America’s Building Trades Unions (NABTU), United Association of Plumbers and Pipefitters, Pipeliners Local 798, and the New Mexico Building and Construction Trades Council. These organizations represent the electricians, ironworkers, sheet metal workers, boilermakers, Teamsters, operating engineers, laborers, plumbers, pipefitters, and other skilled tradespeople who will build the next generation of America’s energy infrastructure.

The labor support comes as an independent analysis from Employ America estimates that BAAJA will create up to 105,600 trades and manufacturing jobs through 2040 by making it easier to build and maintain new energy infrastructure, including wind, solar, battery storage, and transmission projects.

BAAJA will lower energy costs for working families, provide greater certainty for energy infrastructure projects, and help ensure American workers are on the job building the infrastructure our country needs.

Independent analyses find that BAAJA will:

Create up to 105,600 trades and manufacturing jobs through 2040;

Require data centers to pay for increased grid and energy costs they create, estimated at $55 billion over the next 10 years;

Save $19 billion in residential electricity bills over the next 14 years;

Nearly double the amount of solar and wind that can connect to the grid; and

Avoid 1.5 gigatons of CO₂ emissions, the equivalent of taking 39 coal plants offline for a decade.

BAAJA will lower energy costs for working families, provide greater certainty for energy infrastructure projects, and help ensure American workers are on the job building the infrastructure our country needs.

text:
In a statement to C&EN, the American Chemical Council (ACC) says it “applaud[s]” the Senate’s move to advance the bill. “We are encouraged by the momentum behind this legislation and ACC will continue working with policymakers to get it passed by Congress this year,” the industry group says.

Other industry groups, including the National Association of Manufacturers, spoke up in favor of the bill when it was first introduced.

Though the vote passed 73–25, Politico reports that some senators will not support the current bill in a final vote without key amendments, such as to the legislation’s proposed changes to the National Historic Preservation Act, which critics say would compromise tribal sovereignty.

With Democrats about to gain significant majorities in both the House and Senate, some analysts believe the party may hold out for a permitting reform deal that’s more favorable to renewable energy and other priorities.

—Alex Music, special to C&EN

FDA actions on color additives set worrying precedent, advocacy groups say

The US Food and Drug Administration said on Nov. 9 that it will revoke authorizations for the use of three chlorine-based solvents in color additives for food, but advocacy groups who pushed for the change worry that the agency’s reasoning could open the door for other carcinogens to remain in food.

Methylene chloride, ethylene dichloride, and trichloroethylene will no longer be permitted in the production of annatto extract, paprika oleoresin, or turmeric oleoresin, which are food color additives derived from plants. The FDA acted in response to a petition from the International Association of Color Manufacturers, which showed that the industry has discontinued the use of the solvents for this purpose.

But a petition from a different set of advocates—the Environmental Defense Fund, Breast Cancer Prevention Partners, Center for Environmental Health, Environmental Working Group, and environmental health consultant Lisa Lefferts—argues that the chlorinated solvents should be banned from the color additives because of their demonstrated cancer-causing properties. According to this reasoning, the ban would fall under the Delaney Clause provision of the Food Additives Amendment of 1958, which prohibits the FDA from approving any additive that is carcinogenic in people or animals; all three solvents have been shown to cause cancer in animal studies.

The FDA instead ruled that any residue of the chlorinated solvents left in the food additives would be an impurity in the color additive and not an additive itself, and thus not subject to the Delaney Clause and its elimination requirements.

The Environmental Defense Fund criticized the FDA’s thinking as setting a dangerous precedent. “Classifying these cancer-causing chemicals as ‘impurities’ does not eliminate their potential to harm people. FDA’s reasoning, if continued in future decisions, threatens to leave Americans exposed to cancer causing chemicals in their food,” the organization said in a statement released Nov. 10.

The FDA did not respond to a request for comment by publication time, though the agency did in part grant the petition from environmental advocacy groups by invoking the Delaney Clause to ban the use of methylene chloride to dilute inks used to mark fruits and vegetables. The Environmental Defense Fund called this “a significant step forward.”

The bans on the three solvents in food color additives and methylene chloride for marking produce will both go into effect on Jan. 11.

—Yaakov Zinberg, special to C&EN

US approves nuclear reactor construction at Dow plant

The US Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) has issued a construction permit for a project in which Dow will replace a natural gas boiler with a set of four small modular nuclear reactors (SMRs) made by X-Energy as the main power plant for Dow’s petrochemical facility in Seadrift, Texas. The firms say the reactors will provide both steam and electricity to the plant, cutting the site’s carbon dioxide emissions by 440,000 metric tons per year.

X-Energy is commercializing a new type of reactor that uses helium gas to transfer heat from the reactor core. Crucially, the design requires only a 400 m emergency perimeter around the reactor, much smaller than the 10 miles (about 16 km) mandated for conventional civilian reactors. That smaller distance makes it feasible for the reactor to provide heat directly to the plant via steam, increasing the practical energy yield compared to systems that send only electricity out from the reactor.

Though the firm has been working with the NRC since 2018, the agency completed its formal permit review in just 18 months under a newly streamlined process. The construction permit follows a safety approval the NRC issued at the end of last month. In an Oct. 30 press release, X-Energy says, “The NRC’s review establishes regulatory precedents for every Xe-100 project that follows, creating replicable pathways for increased efficiency in commercial nuclear licensing.”

—Craig Bettenhausen

FDA requires popular GLP-1 drugs to carry warnings of rare eye condition

The US Food and Drug Administration on Nov. 9 issued new requirements for glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist drugs, commonly known as GLP-1 drugs, to carry labels warning of a rare eye condition that can lead to blindness.

GLP-1 therapies such as Ozempic and Wegovy are a popular category of weight loss and diabetes-treatment drugs, now used by more than 1 in 10 US adults. There are 12 GLP-1 drugs currently approved by the FDA. But the drugs carry the risk of nonarteritic ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION), a condition where blood flow to the optic nerve drops, leading to sudden but painless vision loss in the affected eye. There is no treatment for the condition.

The FDA examined 126 randomized clinical studies of GLP-1 drugs and found 6.4 NAION cases per 100,000 person-years, compared to 3.8 NAION cases per 100,000 person-years for patients treated with placebos or other medications used to lower blood sugar levels, as GLP-1 drugs do.

“NAION cases have been reported for all currently marketed [GLP-1] products,” the FDA says in its announcement, while noting that the mechanism connecting GLP-1 drugs to vision loss remains unclear. European regulators also concluded last year that GLP-1 treatments can lead to NAION in rare instances.

Some physicians caution that the benefits of these drugs still far outweigh the risks for most patients.
