text:
Arena Energy will use a $480 million loan from the U.S. Department of Energy for its Project Elkhorn program, modernizing 22 offshore platforms off the coast of Louisiana.

The loan through DOE’s Office of Energy Dominance Financing (EDF) is aimed at increasing oil and natural gas production across the Gulf of Mexico shelf, according to a DOE announcement Nov. 12. At peak production, the project expected to add up to 38,600 bbls. of oil per day and up to 77 million cu. ft. of natural gas per day to U.S. energy production.

Enabled by the 2025 federal tax cuts, the loan “marks the Energy Department's first closed loan supporting domestic oil and natural gas production” according to the agency.

“The United States is the world’s largest producer and exporter of oil and natural gas, and thanks to President Trump, American energy production will continue to grow,” said Secretary of Energy Chris Wright.

“Project Elkhorn will increase oil production by up to 38,600 barrels per day and create thousands of jobs. By providing financing for projects like Project Elkhorn, the Energy Department is expanding domestic production and strengthening our energy security to power American prosperity for decades to come.”

Arena Energy currently produces about 30,000 bbls. offshore in the Gulf. Its Project Elkhorn will modernize existing offshore infrastructure and expand production capacity to add an estimated 125 million bbls. of oil and 250 billion cu. ft. of natural gas over the life of the project.

DOE and Arena officials estimate the project will create 2,400 construction-related jobs and 400 operations jobs in one of the nation's most important offshore energy corridors.

Arena was founded in 1999 “on the belief that the mature fields of the Gulf of America shelf still hold vast potential,” the company said in announcing the loan. “Today marks a significant milestone for Arena’s commitment to the shallow waters of the Gulf and for American energy production.”

Arena subsidiary Elkhorn Offshore will retool, refurbish, and repower offshore platforms in the Southern Eugene Island area off Louisiana.

“American energy dominance isn’t built only on new frontiers,” said Michael Minarovic, Arena’s CEO and founder, who started the company in 1999 “on the belief that the mature fields of the Gulf of America shelf still hold vast potential.”

“It’s built by putting proven American fields back to work. Starting today, that’s exactly what we’re doing in the Gulf of America. This financing from the Department of Energy lets us repower existing infrastructure, develop proved reserves, and keep producing some of the most reliable barrels in the world right here at home – with American workers, on American leases, for American refineries.”

text:
PRESIDENT TRUMP BLOCKED Massachusetts from unlocking new offshore wind from its own coasts, dealing a crucial blow to the state’s energy transition. So Gov. Maura Healey is testing the waters to the north instead.

The Healey administration is spearheading an effort alongside other New England states to tap into work underway in the Canadian province of Nova Scotia to advance offshore wind projects there, as it eyes potential energy supply and economic benefits here at home.

Massachusetts is issuing a formal request for information with Nova Scotia to test market interest and feasibility among energy developers, supply chain companies, port entities, organized labor, utilities, and the fishing industry. Maine, Connecticut, Vermont, and Rhode Island are also participating.

It’s just one procedural step on what would be a long road to achieving an ambitious vision of bringing energy generated by Canadian offshore wind into New England. But the move is a concrete signal of the state’s seriousness in collaborating with Nova Scotia to boost offshore wind and find a Plan B to the now-stalled domestic wind industry on which Massachusetts had been relying.

“We need more affordable, reliable energy, and that’s going to take working with our neighbors,” Healey said in a statement. “Massachusetts and Nova Scotia have a strong partnership, and we’re building on that relationship to explore new opportunities to bring offshore wind power to New England. This work has the potential to lower energy costs, strengthen our energy supply and create good-paying jobs in our port communities.”

Nova Scotia appeared ready to launch bids this winter to lease areas off its coast for wind development, though that timeline may be delayed.

Still, Massachusetts is looking to establish itself as a player in the province’s wind development well before any projects even get off the ground.

The 12-page RFI, issued Thursday, asks stakeholders to weigh in on how big potential Canadian offshore wind projects should be, what specific type of technology should be deployed, realistic timelines for project completion, and how existing US port capacity and supply-chain infrastructure could be leveraged to bring potential projects to life.

And the document starts to tackle what will be the pressing and likely messy question of transmission, pondering whether an undersea cable or a new power line is the best mode of actually getting the wind power into New England.

Stakeholders have until the end of the year to respond to the request.

Massachusetts is fresh off the completion just last month of Vineyard Wind, the country’s largest offshore wind project, and is finally seeing Revolution Wind to its south reach full-scale operations.

Now, the movement in Canada is another welcome sign as the state navigates soaring energy costs, rising power demand, and looming clean energy targets. And it’s part of Healey’s all-of-the-above approach to energy, in which she has also championed solar, adding more nuclear power, and expanding natural gas supply.

The opportunity in Nova Scotia for the Bay State could be twofold: Massachusetts and other states in the region could serve as customers for the wind power generated in Canada, and the state could see economic and jobs benefits given the role the state’s port in New Bedford has played in offshore wind construction in the Northeast.

Still, big questions remain about how much Canadian offshore wind can do to serve Massachusetts electric customers — much less provide a way out of the energy affordability crisis any time soon.

Even before Trump canceled permits and ground domestic offshore wind to a halt, cost overruns driven by record inflation and supply chain constraints roiled the industry, spooked developers, and stalled progress.

Plus, some recent energy projects built to deliver power from Canada into New England have left room for skepticism.

A 10-year process kickstarted by Massachusetts under Gov. Charlie Baker to build a hydropower transmission line from Quebec into the region, known as the New England Clean Energy Connect, finally came to an end when power started flowing through the project this past January.

Then came the problems.

Almost immediately after NECEC turned on, the region endured a stretch of frigid temperatures during what turned out to be the coldest winter in 20 years. Electricity didn’t flow into New England on the line for 12 days, arguably when the region needed it most to meet high demand — prompting a legal brawl between Massachusetts utility companies and Hydro Quebec that’s now winding its way through court.

The NECEC then inexplicably shut down during another two-week period this past May and June. The transmission line is estimated to supply one-fifth of the state’s energy demand.

The new joint effort with Nova Scotia is filled with hurdles that could make NECEC look simple, from financing the wind projects to clearing the extra regulatory steps needed to get them sited and carry that energy across international borders to the long distance that energy would need to travel to reach New England.

The RFI follows a memorandum of understanding that Healey and Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston signed earlier this year at the State House. Rebecca Tepper, secretary of energy and environmental affairs, told CommonWealth Beacon exclusively last year that she had visited Nova Scotia to meet with Canadian officials on offshore wind.

“If you’re going to start an energy infrastructure project,” she said at the MOU signing back in February, “the best time to do that is today.”

text:
Rep. Brian Mast, R-Fla., chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee who’s been pushing for stricter export control laws, said Thursday that Huang agreed to come in for a closed-door briefing before lawmakers break again for Thanksgiving on Nov. 20. Other Congress members have sent letters asking Huang to come and testify in Washington.

Meanwhile, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is under increasing pressure from members of Congress over how his office allowed Nvidia to sell its advanced chips to what reports allege to be a front for banned Chinese buyers. The Trump administration is made more vulnerable by Huang’s close relationship with Trump and its deference to the Nvidia CEO on chip policy matters.

“This incident raises significant concerns about the federal government’s ability to effectively enforce our export controls and protect our national security,” Sens. Chris Coons, D-Del., and Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., wrote in a letter to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and White House chief of staff Stephen Miller on Thursday, asking them to preserve documents related to Nvidia.

Reports suggest government officials “were aware of concerns about Nvidia, its relationship with Megaspeed, and the suspected Chinese intelligence operation, yet did not move to block the continued flow of advanced AI chips,” the senators said.

So far, Trump is standing by Lutnick. The president “maintains complete confidence in the secretary and his ability to carry out the position,” a White House official told Semafor.

Joon Kim has taken down mobsters, pursued a congressman, and investigated sexual harassment claims that toppled a New York governor. His latest assignment will decide the fate of a $4 trillion dollar company the global economy depends on.

The former acting US Attorney for the Southern District of New York was tapped to investigate whether Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was the target of a Chinese espionage campaign, following Huang’s bombshell admission Sunday that the chief executive had an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.

Kim, a 55-year-old prosecutor who joined Wachtell Lipton last month, will lead an internal probe overseen by a committee of independent directors, into whether Nvidia’s Huang compromised trade secrets — or, more pressingly, the US’ national security interests. The company has said it has confidence in its CEO and has “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.” A spokesperson for Wachtell declined to comment on the firm’s and Kim’s behalf.

Shares in Nvidia have dropped 10% since Huang’s admission, knocking $500 billion off the company’s market value and stoking worries about the future of a company that underpins an AI financing buildout that has ensnared most of the global financial system. It comes against a fraught national security backdrop in which US officials have been warning for months of foreign influence campaigns and corporate espionage.

A tangled web

Huang, a close confidant of US President Donald Trump, has pushed Nvidia to take stakes in hundreds of companies across the AI boom it supplies. The company has also entered into billions of dollars worth of financing deals up and down Wall Street.

Even Kim’s own employer, Wachtell Lipton, is not immune: OpenAI is one of Wachtell’s highest-profile clients, and the law firm’s M&A advisors are working on the company’s pending IPO, according to people familiar with the matter. Nvidia is a major OpenAI investor and the primary supplier of the chips that underpin the data centers (which Nvidia also finances) that power OpenAI’s models.

Corporate probes can range from window dressing to essentially prosecutorial in nature, and Nvidia has 4 trillion reasons to limit its damage. It’s unclear how far Nvidia’s board will let Kim roam, but the board has already drummed up corporate governance concerns: The unusually long-tenured board lacks the experience and stature typically found at companies as large as Nvidia’s and has let Huang run the company with no clear successor and more than 50 direct reports.

Mob bosses

Kim began his career at New York’s Southern District more than two decades ago, working in the organized crime unit before leaving for Cleary Gottlieb in 2006. The son of a South Korean diplomat, Kim traveled around the world, including in Jordan and the UK.

In his first stint as a federal prosecutor, Kim took on mob boss John “Junior” Gotti in a federal racketeering trial, trying him for the kidnapping of future New York mayoral candidate Curtis Sliwa. “His entire adult life, John Jr. has thought himself special, entitled to everything, accountable for nothing,” Kim said at the time.

His former colleagues describe Kim as dogged, citing his time at the Southern District in 2013, under Attorney Preet Bharara, where Kim pursued a successful case against disgraced former Congressman Anthony Weiner and briefly ran the Southern District after Trump fired Bharara.

Kim returned to Cleary in 2018, where he led a number of internal investigations into allegations of executive wrongdoing at large corporations, including Nissan Motors’ probe into former CEO Carlos Ghosn. But among his most defining cases was New York Attorney General Letitia James’ investigation into sexual harassment allegations against then-Governor Andrew Cuomo, which led to his 2021 resignation. Cuomo’s office was “rife with bullying, fear and intimidation,” Kim said when announcing his findings.

A sensitive assignment

Before Sunday, Huang and spokespeople for the company had publicly denied that the Nvidia CEO had an affair with Alice Huang. The company abruptly changed tack on Sunday, when Huang wrote a letter to employees admitting to the affair and announcing a plan to initiate an independent probe.

The company had assembled an independent committee to oversee the investigation and was on Sunday leaning toward tapping former Cooley CEO Stephen Neal, the Financial Times reported and Semafor can confirm. Some Nvidia directors also suggested tapping Cooley to run the independent probe, other people familiar with the matter said. Cooley is Nvidia’s longtime outside counsel and would have exposed the company to criticism that the probe wasn’t independent, especially since Cooley is best known for its tech and IP practices, and isn’t considered by white-shoe lawyers to have a top-tier white-collar investigations practice.

Nvidia declined to comment on either the nature of the independent committee or on whether directors considered tapping Cooley.

“Through our partnership with Massachusetts, we are exploring opportunities that could create jobs, attract investment, and help establish Nova Scotia as a clean energy leader.
Vermont is grateful to our partners for initiating this next step and proud to have also signed a Memorandum of Understanding with Nova Scotia to explore offshore wind development and delivery through Vermont.

text:
BOSTON — The Healey-Driscoll Administration today announced a major step in strengthening Massachusetts’ relationship with Canada to expand access to affordable, reliable clean energy across New England. Massachusetts and Nova Scotia have issued a Request for Information (RFI) to gather input and explore opportunities to develop offshore wind projects in Nova Scotia that would deliver energy to New England through existing and new transmission infrastructure.

Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston and Massachusetts Energy and Environmental Affairs Secretary Rebecca Tepper will speak at the New England-Canadian Business Council’s annual energy conference in Boston today to announce the partnership, building on the Memorandum of Understanding signed by Governor Maura Healey and Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston in February to strengthen regional cooperation on offshore wind development, transmission planning, workforce development and economic growth.

“We need more affordable, reliable energy, and that's going to take working with our neighbors,” said Governor Maura Healey. “Massachusetts and Nova Scotia have a strong partnership, and we're building on that relationship to explore new opportunities to bring offshore wind power to New England. This work has the potential to lower energy costs, strengthen our energy supply and create good-paying jobs in our port communities. We're excited to take this next step together.”

“Nova Scotia has some of the strongest offshore wind resources in the world and a long history of supplying energy beyond our borders,” said Premier Tim Houston. “Through our partnership with Massachusetts, we are exploring opportunities that could create jobs, attract investment, and help establish Nova Scotia as a clean energy leader. This request for information is an important step in understanding how we can work together to realize that potential.”

The RFI is an early, concrete step under the Memorandum of Understanding executed between Governor Healey and Premier Houston. The RFI, issued with participation from Maine, Connecticut, Rhode Island, and Vermont, recognizes the increasingly regional and interconnected nature of New England and Eastern Canada.

A wide range of stakeholders are invited to provide input, including developers, supply chain and port entities, utilities and system operators, labor organizations, academic and research institutions, environmental and fisheries stakeholders, and tribal and first nations groups. The RFI will help the region understand the market’s interest and capacity to develop offshore wind in Nova Scotia and the technical and commercial feasibility of transmission pathways to New England. In addition, the RFI will explore opportunities to strengthen the regional offshore wind economy through continued collaboration on supply chains, ports, and workforce development.

Statements of Support:

Frank Callahan, President, Massachusetts Building Trades Unions:

“We’ve worked hard to make sure clean energy is a union industry. We saw Vineyard Wind sustain thousands of good jobs along the South Coast. We need to continue to push this industry forward to support good union careers now and into the future. We look forward to continued partnership with the Healey-Driscoll Administration and Nova Scotia.”

Celina Cunningham, Acting Commissioner of the Maine Department of Energy Resources:

“Maine recognizes the value of regional coordination with our partners across New England and Canada. This RFI provides an opportunity to further explore the potential for responsible offshore wind in the region that supports energy affordability and economic growth. Maine’s leadership in offshore wind research combined with our marine-focused industries positions us well to advance the state’s interests as the region considers these opportunities.”

Emma Cimino, Acting Commissioner of the Connecticut Department of Energy and Environmental Protection:

“Connecticut is committed to working with our regional and Canadian partners to explore innovative approaches to advancing offshore wind and strengthening New England’s energy future. This RFI will help inform our continued, collective efforts to secure a more affordable, reliable, and increasingly clean power grid for our state and region.”

Chris Kearns, Acting Commissioner of the Rhode Island Office of Energy Resources:

“Rhode Island continues to work with our regional partners to explore opportunities that can strengthen and diversify New England’s energy supply and support our respective long-term energy goals. This request for information will help us better understand the potential for offshore wind development in Nova Scotia, including the infrastructure, costs and regulatory considerations associated with delivering that energy into New England. Regional energy coordination and collaboration are critical as we evaluate possible options to meet our future energy needs while maintaining reliability and affordability.”

Kerrick Johnson, Commissioner of the Vermont Department of Public Service, which serves as the state’s ratepayer advocate:

“Vermont must develop new options for clean, affordable power at scale to meet growing energy needs driven by our ongoing shift to electricity and away from fossil fuels. This RFI reflects a shared commitment of all involved to work together to tackle the toughest electric energy challenges our region faces. Vermont is grateful to our partners for initiating this next step and proud to have also signed a Memorandum of Understanding with Nova Scotia to explore offshore wind development and delivery through Vermont. Collaboration with our New England partners and Nova Scotia isn’t just beneficial – it is an essential path forward for our region’s energy future.”

Elizabeth Mahony, Commissioner of the Massachusetts Department of Energy Resources:

“Massachusetts has the ports, skilled workers, and policy know-how to get offshore wind built. Our partnership with Nova Scotia is poised to unlock real savings and economic development for the Atlantic Coast. We’re looking forward to digging in to the ideas and information that come from this RFI as we seek out the next major offshore wind and transmission opportunity.”

Ben Downing, CEO of the Mass Clean Energy Center:

“Massachusetts and Nova Scotia share deep ties across local communities and industries. Offshore wind offers our two regions an exciting opportunity to work together to lower costs, create good jobs, and generate cleaner, more reliable energy.”

text:
Triton manufactures the only UL 2200-listed Tier 4 Final generators above 200 kW, with certified models ranging from 50 kW to 1,250 kW for stationary standby, prime power, and microgrid applications nationwide.

-- Triton Power, a U.S.-based manufacturer of commercial and industrial generators, today announced that its Tier 4 Final generators, rated from 50 kW to 1,250 kW, are now UL 2200-listed and ready for any project requiring prime power and UL certification, from stationary standby to microgrids. This makes Triton the only manufacturer offering UL 2200-certified Tier 4 Final generators above 200 kW. Triton Power generators are built on engines designed from the ground up for Tier 4 Final by John Deere, Scania and Volvo.

Tier 4 Final UL Certification

Tier 4 Final is the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s most stringent emissions standard for diesel engines in the United States and is required nationwide for prime power, where a generator serves as the primary power source rather than an emergency backup. Tier 4 Final generators can run continuously, whereas stationary units are limited to emergency use.

UL 2200 is the safety standard for stationary engine generator assemblies. Certification confirms that a generator meets the standard's requirements for protection against electrical, fuel, and fire hazards.

The National Electrical Code requires permanently installed generators to be listed under UL 2200, and inspectors across most of the country enforce this requirement. As a result, Triton’s UL 2200-certified Tier 4 Final generators can be permanently installed at a facility and operated around the clock.

Increasing Demand

Triton has manufactured Tier 4 Final generators for over a decade. The newly UL 2200-certified lineup serves rapidly expanding markets. Jurisdictions in New York and California require Tier 4 Final engines for stationary standby generators and prime power, and U.S. government agencies increasingly specify them. The fastest-growing application is microgrids, where multiple Triton units are paralleled to power a town, military installation, or data center independently of the power grid, or to operate alongside a solar farm.

“Our certified models range from 50 kW to 1,250 kW and are powered by John Deere, Scania, and Volvo engines. All models are in stock and ready to ship,” said Eric Johnston, CEO of Triton Power. “This certification enables Triton Power dealers to bid on stationary standby and prime power projects nationwide that they couldn’t before. For larger prime power and microgrid projects, our Tier 4 Final line extends to 1,250 kW and can be paralleled to 37 megawatts. Our team is there to help dealers win business and support installation.”

Triton UL 2200-Listed Tier 4 Final Models

Triton Power’s UL 2200-certified Tier 4 Final generators are standard stationary units powered by engines from manufacturers well known to dealers and end-users:

John Deere: 50, 88, 110, 165, 200, 288, 400, and 500 kW

Scania: 300, 350 and 440 kW

Volvo: 550 to 1,250 kW

Triton’s broader Tier 4 Final line also includes Kubota-powered units from 13.5 kW to 30 kW, rental-grade mobile units from 15 kVA to 715 kVA, and Scania- and Volvo-powered twin-pack containerized units from 700 kW to 1,250 kW. These units are Tier 4 Final compliant but not UL 2200-listed.

All units feature non-proprietary Deep Sea digital controls, enabling any qualified generator technician to commission and service them. All UL-certified models are in stock at Triton Power’s Miami headquarters and ready to ship.

Available Exclusively from Triton Dealers

Triton sells generators exclusively through an experienced dealer network. Commercial and industrial inquiries are directed to the local Triton dealer. Approved Triton dealers receive factory-direct pricing, bid and spec support, and technical support in person, by video, and by phone. Generator dealers interested in adding the Tier 4 Final, UL 2200-certified lineup can apply at https://tritonpower.com/become-a-partner or contact the Triton dealer team at dealers@tritonpower.com or (305) 592-6300.

About Triton Power

For over 35 years, Triton Power has designed and manufactured commercial and industrial generators from 10 to 2,500 kW, running on diesel and natural gas, and built on John Deere, Volvo, Scania, Perkins, Cummins, and Kubota engines. The lineup includes standard, rental-grade mobile and containerized units, custom builds, and non-proprietary Deep Sea digital controls. Triton Power is one of the largest independent generator manufacturers in the Americas, and its expanding dealer network is driving its next stage of growth. More: https://tritonpower.com

description:

text:
The Progress Texas Daily Dispatch is delivered every weekday by Progress Texas Communications Director Chris Mosser. Rapid response on the breaking news stories Texas progressives need to know—all in less than 10 minutes!

Click below to listen! LINK TO MAIN PODCAST PAGE: https://progresstexas.org/progress-texas-podcast-network

High Voter Expectations On Data Centers

As recently as this time last year, approaching the 2025 holiday season, who would have thought that data centers and their impact upon both rural and urban Texas would turn out to be a central, catastrophic issue for the decades-long Republican lockdown on Texas politics? As the smoke clears on the humiliating defeat of those same Republicans, left only in control of the State Senate, as the 2027 legislative session draws near, AI and its infrastructure remain a central issue that’s developing in interesting directions.

Bipartisan Action Already Underway

A major political clash is inbound over the rapid expansion of the data center industry in Texas, exposing a growing conflict between what has become the state’s traditional pro-business economic development model under Republican rule, and the still-rising public concerns over who truly benefits from this particular strain of corporate growth.

For years, Texas has beckoned technology companies with generous tax breaks, inexpensive land, accessible energy, and minimal regulation, but the explosive rise of AI has fundamentally altered this dynamic. The outgoing GOP regime either ignored, or didn’t bother to ask about, the massive amounts of electricity and water these operations require—as you know, the crux of the matter for thousands of Texas voters: an unprecedented strain on public infrastructure and natural resources that everyday Texans now risk subsidizing, or losing altogether. With Democratic Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa preparing to take office and the 90th Texas Legislature set to convene in January, in the wake of a public revolt that spans political ideologies, lawmakers from both parties are now reevaluating the entire scenario.

Mateo Rosiles at USA Today says that as this begins, we have Senate Bill 293—authored by Republican Senator Joan Huffman and backed by 23 of the Texas Senate’s 31 current and incoming members. The bill proposes repealing the state’s sales tax exemption for data centers, which currently allows qualifying facilities to avoid paying sales taxes on electricity, servers, and cooling equipment for up to 20 years. And, Democratic Senator Judith Zaffirini has filed two additional bills: SB 33, which would require data centers to cover the transmission costs tied to their electricity consumption, and SB 36, which would place limits on data center companies’ access to state and local economic development incentives.

We spent a lot of time talking about bipartisanship in the 90th Legislature yesterday, and the data center dilemma, with its accompanying widespread public frustration, provides an example of a political lane where cooperation is particularly warranted. The June UT Austin/Texas Politics Project poll showed that 56% of registered voters oppose data center construction in their communities, period. Fears, reasonable or not, over water depletion, grid strain, and rising utility bills have driven local governments across the state to weigh temporary construction moratoriums (more on that coming up).

Outgoing Republican Governor Greg Abbott, long both a Big Tech champion and benefactor, tried desperately during the election to intervene in order to save his own political skin—placing a pause new facility construction to allow the auditing of proposed grid connections, directing energy regulators to prevent expansion costs from shifting onto consumers, and mandating stricter enforcement of water-use reporting—but as we’ve talked about, the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality has nonetheless continued to process new data center buildout applications, thus Abbott’s is an empty gesture that turned out too little too late for the governor anyway. The central debate now is no longer whether Texas wants data centers, but whether any resource-heavy corporate build should receive massive tax breaks and public subsidies without proving tangible and worthwhile public benefits.

SpaceX and Tesla: Full Steam Ahead

As all this plays out, Big Tech is by no means slowing their roll. Berenice Garcia at The Texas Tribune says that down in the Rio Grande Valley, Elon Musk’s SpaceX is planning a new $24 billion data center and an attached gas-fired power plant near the city of Brownsville, whose city leaders, at Musk’s request, recently removed the 444-acre project site from its city limits in exchange for $220 million dedicated to municipal water and wastewater infrastructure—a deal that’s drawn heavy scrutiny because at the same time, Brownsville was deploying a 90-day moratorium on new data center development. SpaceX urged rapid approval—warning that the $220 million offer would otherwise be withdrawn. Once de-annexed, the land was absorbed into the SpaceX company town of Starbase, placing the project outside Brownsville’s regulatory reach just as the city’s moratorium took effect.

Brownsville officials say all of this is about service logistics and critical infrastructure funding, but local residents and environmental groups are up in arms over the timing and the apparent subservience of the city—continuing to bend over backwards for corporate interests. The South Texas Environmental Justice Network is forming up protests, warning that the SpaceX gas-fired power plant is likely to worsen local air pollution while the proposed data center drains away already scarce regional water supplies—all, again, pointing back to Governor Abbott’s flimsy regulatory framework. Under the current rules, in generating its own electricity onsite, SpaceX will be able to bypass most oversight of their power generation apparatus—in other words, Elon Musk is way ahead of the state’s game, and it’s now up to the Lege to catch up.

Elon Musk’s New Texas Reality

For Musk, the Texas he fled California for is waking up to what’s happening, and evolving from an uncritical business haven into a more complex regulatory battleground. Reported by Benzinga, technology analyst Dan Ives said on the technology-based Pomp Podcast on Tuesday that if Musk wants to keep playing in our backyard, he’s gonna need to adopt a more diplomatic approach with state leaders who are no longer willing to rubber-stamp corporate expansion, and whose voters have come to view Musk and his ilk with intense disdain. Ives says Texas remains indispensable to Musk’s operations—he’s simply built too much here to just unplug and move to Florida. Ives also notes that all this sudden political uncertainty has contributed to a 20% to 25% discount in SpaceX’s valuation.

Beyond Starbase, Musk has that massive Terafab semiconductor venture with Tesla in Grimes County, which itself has sparked anxieties among the locals over water and power. Just like his hopes to flee all of this to Mars one day, Musk has dreams of putting data centers into orbit—but for now, his future is very much dug into Texas soil. Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has been leaning into the view that corporations doing business in Texas must prove their value to Texas: a big change from the old guard in protection of the public interest—at long last—displacing unconditional corporate accommodation.

Grassroots Resistance Rises In The Fort

Zeroing in on North Texas, Cecilia Lenzen at the Fort Worth Report says organized resident opposition is actively reshaping local policy on Big Tech development around Cowtown. Earlier this week during a public hearing, residents overwhelmingly urged the Fort Worth City Council to pass their own temporary moratorium on new data centers to allow time for stronger regulations to be enacted—the said moratorium is looking likely to take effect in February and continue through at least late May, dates coinciding directly with the 90th legislative session.

Community advocates in Fort Worth point to the November 3 election results in Tarrant County and across Texas as proof of a shifting political mandate that demands immediate, substantial action by the Legislature. Governor-elect Hinojosa’s campaign pledges of a statewide pause on data center approvals, restrictions on related nondisclosure agreements that hide projects from communities, union labor mandates, water protections, and more have inspired hope at the local level for salvation from this existential and self-inflicted dilemma.

Redefining The AI Agreement

Ultimately, Governor-elect Hinojosa faces a historic opportunity to fundamentally renegotiate Texas’s relationship with the tech sector, which in terms of jobs or benefits for the people of Texas, has essentially been let off the hook by the outgoing Republican regime. AI technologist Tal Feldman writes in an opinion piece for the Austin American-Statesman that under existing law, a $500 million data center can avoid state sales taxes for two decades while creating as few as 40 jobs. Under Governor Abbott, Texas has foregone roughly $1.3 billion in tax revenue from these exemptions in just last year alone, and state audits have already caught six of these facilities violating even these meager job-creation promises—many others remain unexamined and the expectation that they’ll also be audited, and soon, is high.

text:
Dive Brief:

The U.S. electric power sector will generate almost 4,390 billion kWh this year, up 2.7% from 2025 — a new production record driven by “rising demand from the commercial sector and increased cooling needs from warmer-than-average summer temperatures,” the U.S. Energy Information Administration said in its November Short-Term Energy Outlook published Tuesday.

Rising electricity demand “is met primarily by increasing generation from renewable energy sources,” EIA said. Although the rate of generation growth is expected to slow next year, the share of total U.S. generation supplied by utility-scale solar plants will rise from 7% in 2025 to 8% in 2026, reaching nearly 10% in 2027, according to the report. Wind generation’s share is expected to rise from 11% in 2025 to 12% by 2027.

EIA also expects the utility sector will install more than 25 GW of battery storage next year, reaching 91.7 GW of installed capacity by the end of 2027 — an increase of nearly 40% over expected 2026 totals.

Dive Insight:

Solar and wind generation are expected to add new capacity of about 72 GW and 20 GW, respectively, this year and next, EIA said.

“Generation from other energy sources is likely to remain relatively flat or decrease,” it added.

While commercial and industrial sector demand will continue to see robust growth next year, that could be “offset somewhat by lower residential electricity demand resulting from forecast milder summer weather next year,” EIA said.

The federal government’s energy data arm is forecasting U.S. gas generation’s share of the electric power generation mix to hold relatively steady at an average of about 40% in 2026 and 2027, and nuclear’s share to average 18%.

Coal’s share of generation will likely decline from 17% in 2025 to 15% by 2027 as 13 GW of capacity is scheduled to retire by the end of next year, EIA said.

“Although the share of generation from those fuels is falling, total generation from those fuels is relatively flat in the forecast, remaining in line with the combined generation from 2025,” according to the short-term outlook.

The electric power sector’s coal consumption has declined, relative to 2025, in eight of 10 months so far this year, EIA noted.

“The decreases have been driven by significant increases in wind and solar capacity as well as a 9% decline in the average natural gas price in the electric power sector during the second and third quarters of this year,” EIA said. “We expect coal consumption to decline an additional 5% in 2027, driven by a 19% decrease in natural gas prices for electric generating plants and further increases in wind and solar capacity.”

EIA’s report also forecasts significant battery storage growth. Capacity will rise from 28.9 GW in the first quarter of 2025 to 66 GW by the end of this year and 91.7 GW at the end of 2027, counting systems with a capacity of 1 MW or greater.

text:
India has prohibited the export of lithium-ion battery black mass in a move aimed at retaining valuable critical minerals within the country, strengthening domestic recycling capabilities and reducing dependence on imports, particularly from China.

The Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT), under the Ministry of Commerce, amended the export policy for lithium-ion battery black mass from 'Free' to 'Prohibited' with immediate effect through Notification No. 49/2026-27, dated 10 November 2026.

The government said the decision would ensure that battery waste generated in India is recycled and refined domestically rather than exported.

The move comes as India seeks to secure supplies of critical minerals such as lithium, cobalt, nickel and manganese, which are essential for electric vehicle (EV) batteries, renewable energy storage, electronics and advanced manufacturing.

What is lithium-ion battery black mass?

Black mass is a powder-like material recovered by shredding and processing discarded lithium-ion batteries and battery manufacturing waste. It contains valuable minerals, including lithium, cobalt, nickel and manganese, which can be extracted and reused in battery production.

Recycling black mass offers an alternative source of critical minerals, reducing the need for fresh mining and dependence on imported raw materials. It is particularly important for India, which has limited domestic reserves of several battery minerals.

Why has India banned black mass exports?

The government said domestic battery recyclers and critical mineral recovery units have been unable to utilise their full processing capacity because of inadequate availability of raw materials.

Despite the expansion of India's recycling infrastructure, black mass generated domestically has continued to flow overseas.

In some instances, Indian recyclers have also had to import the material to meet their requirements.

The export prohibition seeks to address this mismatch by ensuring that domestically generated black mass remains available to Indian recycling and refining companies.

How will the ban reduce India's dependence on China?

China has a dominant position in global critical mineral supply chains, particularly in processing and refining. It accounts for roughly 60% of rare earth mining, 70-90% of processing and separation, and around 94% of permanent magnet manufacturing.

Its influence also extends to the processing of minerals such as lithium, cobalt and graphite, which are essential for batteries, electric vehicles and clean-energy technologies.

India's dependence on imported critical minerals leaves its manufacturing industries vulnerable to supply disruptions and geopolitical tensions.

By retaining black mass within the country, India aims to recover lithium, cobalt, nickel and other valuable materials from discarded batteries and develop alternative domestic sources.

The ban will not immediately eliminate India's dependence on Chinese mineral supplies. However, developing domestic recycling and refining capabilities could gradually reduce this vulnerability.

How big is India's battery recycling capacity?

According to government data cited by The Indian Express, 57 lithium-ion battery recyclers are registered on the Central Pollution Control Board's (CPCB) Battery Waste Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) portal.

Together, they have an annual processing capacity of 5.17 lakh metric tonnes. However, their estimated input capacity specifically for processing lithium-ion battery black mass is around 75,500 metric tonnes annually, as per the report.

The government expects the export restrictions to improve feedstock availability and help domestic facilities operate more efficiently.

How does the ban fit into India's critical minerals strategy?

The measure complements the ₹1,500 crore Incentive Scheme for Critical Mineral Recycling, approved by the Union Cabinet in September 2025.

The scheme seeks to develop recycling capacity to recover critical minerals from secondary sources, including battery waste and electronic waste.

It also supports the National Critical Mineral Mission (NCMM), which aims to strengthen domestic mineral supply chains through exploration, processing and recycling.

Separately, the government has announced a ₹2,814 crore scheme providing capital expenditure support for developing domestic critical mineral processing capabilities, including lithium and nickel processing.

Why is battery recycling strategically important?

As demand for EVs, renewable energy storage and advanced electronics rises, securing battery mineral supplies has become an economic and strategic priority.

Recycling supports 'urban mining', which involves recovering valuable resources from discarded products and industrial waste instead of relying entirely on fresh mining.

For India, retaining black mass could help establish a circular economy in which minerals recovered from old batteries are reused to manufacture new ones.

It could also reduce dependence on overseas suppliers while supporting environmentally sound disposal and processing of hazardous battery waste.

The export ban is therefore not merely a waste-management measure.

It is part of India's broader effort to build strategic autonomy in critical minerals and reduce vulnerabilities in supply chains dominated by China.

title: GE Vernova validates hydrogen capability for LM2500XPRESS and LM6000 turbines
description:
GE Vernova has validated new hydrogen capabilities for two aeroderivative gas turbine platforms, advancing the technology needed to displace natural gas in power generation.
GE Vernova said its LM2500XPRESS can reach full power in five minutes or less while operating on hydrogen blends.
IEEFA estimated that supplying enough hydrogen to fuel the country’s 15 largest natural gas combined-cycle plants would require roughly doubling existing U.S. hydrogen production.

Hydrogen’s role in large-scale power generation also faces questions about cost and efficiency.
text:
GE Vernova has validated new hydrogen capabilities for two aeroderivative gas turbine platforms, advancing the technology needed to displace natural gas in power generation.

The company says that its LM2500XPRESS aeroderivative gas turbine package has been validated to operate on blends containing up to 50% hydrogen by volume using a dry low emissions (DLE) combustion system. GE Vernova said its LM2500XPRESS can reach full power in five minutes or less while operating on hydrogen blends.

It has also completed testing of its LM6000 platform using a single annular combustor (SAC), validating its capability to operate on 100% hydrogen.

Both milestones were achieved at GE Vernova’s new hydrogen testing facility in Greenville, South Carolina. The results demonstrate progress in addressing hydrogen’s combustion challenges.

The LM6000 testing demonstrated the platform’s ability to burn pure hydrogen, although the company did not disclose detailed NOx emissions results, efficiency data or operating costs.

The company said more than 120 of its gas turbines have operated on hydrogen or hydrogen blends, accumulating more than 11 million operating hours across its global fleet.

But expanding hydrogen combustion capability is only part of the equation. While turbine manufacturers continue demonstrating higher hydrogen concentrations, the industry’s biggest obstacles remain largely outside the combustor.

A report from the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA) identified inadequate hydrogen production and transportation infrastructure as major obstacles to commercial deployment.

The report found that the United States had about 1,600 miles of dedicated hydrogen pipelines, located primarily along the Gulf Coast, compared with roughly 305,000 miles of natural gas transmission pipelines.

Blending hydrogen into existing pipelines has been proposed as a possible alternative, but IEEFA said the latest research has raised more questions than answers about the technical and safety implications of introducing hydrogen into the system. In short, blending hydrogen into pipelines would weaken the steel, IEEFA said, potentially leading to cracks, leaks and complete failure.

Hydrogen supply presents another constraint.

IEEFA estimated that supplying enough hydrogen to fuel the country’s 15 largest natural gas combined-cycle plants would require roughly doubling existing U.S. hydrogen production.

And hydrogen blending delivers less carbon reduction than its volumetric concentration might suggest.

Because hydrogen contains approximately one-third the energy of natural gas per unit of volume, a 50% hydrogen blend supplies only about one-quarter of the fuel’s energy from hydrogen.

Hydrogen’s role in large-scale power generation also faces questions about cost and efficiency.

At POWERGEN 2025, Burns & McDonnell Technology Manager Megan Reusser highlighted the high costs of producing, transporting, and storing low-carbon hydrogen, along with energy losses associated with electrolysis.

Those constraints could make hydrogen more attractive for industrial applications, including refining, chemicals and steelmaking, than for widespread electricity generation.

Hydrogen could also find niche applications in backup power and facilities with access to dedicated fuel supplies.

title: We need to rethink climate action away from the Cop talks | Cop31 | The Guardian
description:

Ten years after the Paris treaty, are climate talks getting anywhere?, 7 November).
This could circumnavigate consensus-based negotiations and drive accelerated climate action.
Luckily, we’ve developed a roadmap for the US – the world’s top historical emitter – to take climate action while protecting the energy security of America’s workers.
Climate action does not have to be expensive for working America.
text:
As world leaders gathered in Turkey for the UN climate talks, Fiona Harvey was right to ask, “What’s the point?” (What’s the point? Ten years after the Paris treaty, are climate talks getting anywhere?, 7 November). She pointed to how over 10 years ago in Paris, countries came together for the 21st conference and signed an agreement that aimed to limit global heating to 1.5C above preindustrial levels. For the past two years, temperatures “have exceeded that threshold”.

I was at last year’s climate summit in Brazil, where it was obvious that the Cop process itself is a big part of the problem. The agreed text did not include “fossil fuels”, not to mention any reference to transition away from them. This is largely the result of how negotiations are conducted, as they rely on unanimous consent by all participating countries.

This has pushed a “coalition of the willing” to form outside the formal process that is attempting to drive a transition away from fossil fuels. This is welcome, but maybe it is time to rethink the process entirely?

Some – including Brazil and civil society organisations – have advocated for the creation of a UN climate council or Earth council. This could circumnavigate consensus-based negotiations and drive accelerated climate action. This would empower majorities, such as the 141-country strong coalition that voted in the UN general assembly in favour of the international court of justice’s advisory opinion on countries having an obligation to protect the environment from greenhouse gas emissions.

Other options include strengthening the role of the international court of justice itself to ensure countries implement their climate targets. Both could be achieved by adapting the UN’s founding document, the UN charter, an idea that is generating growing interest.

As Fiona’s article highlighted, the current talks have done their part in advancing the climate agenda. But as the effects of a changing climate become increasingly severe, we need to think about how we can tackle this crisis with far more determination, at much greater speed.

Olav Kjørven

Former UN assistant secretary general; senior adviser, Article 109

As your report notes, Cop31’s host wants “a tangible outcome … that people can see is real” (Cop31 must deliver climate progress that people can see is real, host says, 8 November). Here is what tangible could look like: receipts.

Two years ago in Baku, governments promised $300bn a year in climate finance. Since then the public has seen pledges, press releases and delivery plans without dates. Adão Soares Barbosa, the chair of the Least Developed Countries Group, a negotiating group of 44 nations, put it plainly: credibility will be measured “not by promises made, but by commitments fulfilled”.

So measure. Every country that signed the Baku goal should table a delivery plan in Antalya naming the amount, the instrument and the year. Grants counted separately from loans. Adaptation counted separately from mitigation. No double-counting private finance toward public promises.

The figures justify the scrutiny. Barely 0.2% of available climate finance reaches small island states for adaptation, for countries whose very existence is at stake. That is not a finance gap; it is an allocation choice.

Cop31 will deserve to be called a success if people can see the money moving. Publish the plans, with dates, and let the public check the receipts. Anything less is another communique.

Jackie Omotalade

Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, US

Even though the US government is noticeably absent from Cop31, the American people have voted for a new path that prioritises their economic wellbeing (Democrats to attend Cop31 climate talks boosted by midterms and eager to make up for Trump-era setbacks, 9 November). Luckily, we’ve developed a roadmap for the US – the world’s top historical emitter – to take climate action while protecting the energy security of America’s workers.

One proposal for Game Changers, a project of the Political Economy Research Institute at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, would make polluters pay into an extreme weather superfund by levying fees on large fossil fuel companies in proportion to their historical emissions. The fund would support state and local governments and federal agencies in disaster recovery and climate adaptation efforts.

Another game-changing proposal would phase down fossil fuels and provide energy security cashbacks for working families. These cashbacks would come from limiting emissions and compelling fossil-fuel producers to buy non-tradable permits at quarterly auctions. The proceeds would go directly to households to maintain their purchasing power and to community investments in resilience.

Climate action does not have to be expensive for working America. It can, in fact, be a source of economic revitalisation. Our newest crop of US leaders must make it a priority to reimagine economic and environmental policy to centre the wellbeing of people, not corporate profits.

James K Boyce

Amherst, Massachusetts, US

title: Is energy storage the missing piece of the renewables puzzle? | Abdul Latif Jameel®
description:
Responding to these effectively requires energy storage, not merely as an emergency backup, but as an essential element of day-to-day operations.
[26] With renewables forming 43% of Australia’s grid, battery storage is increasingly important to maintain resilience and balance supply with demand.
To meet the COP28 goal of tripling global renewable energy capacity by 2030 while maintaining energy security, energy storage needs to increase sixfold What’s the future for battery storage?
As Fady Jameel, Vice Chairman, International, Abdul Latif Jameel, says, “the need for better battery energy storage systems is intense.
They know that the rewards of success – for those involved and the wider world – will be considerable.” Five fast facts: the rise of battery storage Q: How fast is battery storage growing?
text:
Battery storage is becoming an indispensable component of power grids and energy plants, but can it be scaled up quickly enough to meet the world’s rapidly growing needs?

As electrification of the global economy continues at pace, attention is increasingly focusing on battery energy storage systems (BESS) that ensure a consistent supply of energy. So even if renewable generation itself fluctuates, our businesses, factories, and homes have a reliable, and continuing, source of power. With energy demand rising across the world, battery storage is becoming the Net Zero transition’s next big challenge.

How fast is the battery storage market growing?

The global battery storage market is expanding rapidly – and it shows no sign of slowing down. According to the latest data from the International Energy Agency (IEA), battery storage is the “fastest growing power technology today” with 108 GW of new capacity deployed worldwide in 2025, a 40% increase on 2024 figures. This equates to an eleven-fold increase in the past five years[1].

The same trend is evident in figures from BloombergNEF[2], which notes that global deployment has set new records every year since 2014. According to the data, it took only four years for annual battery storage additions to increase from 10 GW to more than 100 – far quicker than the time it took solar and wind energy to achieve the same progress (eight and fifteen years respectively). The research also found that in 2025:

China continued to lead the global battery storage market, responsible for 54% of additions

The US was the next biggest player, accounting for 16% of new storage

Deployment in Australia increased by almost six times since 2024

Saudia Arabia ‘leapfrogged’ some of its peers, working with Chinese suppliers

Statistics such as the increase of more than three quarters (75.5%) in global shipments of battery energy storage systems (BESS)[3] provide further indications of the sector’s current strong growth. And the trend is expected to continue over the next decade, with more than 300 GW of annual additions forecast for 2036[4].

What’s driving the growth of battery storage?

The total amount of battery storage capacity around the world is increasing for a number of reasons:

The rise of renewables:

The integration of renewable energy into power systems is increasingly driving the growth of battery storage. The output of renewable sources such as solar and wind varies depending on the weather and time of day. Having the ability to store energy in batteries and then release it later allows suppliers to deliver power on demand and stick to generation schedules. Businesses can also reduce costs, and the load on their systems, by storing excess energy and releasing it during times of high demand. This “energy shifting” has become the dominant application for battery projects, with its share of new projects increasing from around 40% in 2015 to more than 90% in 2025[5].

“As deployment pivots towards energy shifting and renewables integration, the duration of utility-scale batteries is increasing, with a rising share of projects offering four hours of storage or more,” states the IEA[6].

Having the ability to store energy in batteries and then release it later allows suppliers to deliver power on demand and stick to generation schedules

Artificial intelligence

AI is another important factor in the growing need for new battery storage. As well as requiring large amounts of power, AI creates rapidly changing, unpredictable loads. Responding to these effectively requires energy storage, not merely as an emergency backup, but as an essential element of day-to-day operations. In a 2025 survey, almost half of industry respondents (49%) named “AI dynamic power” as a factor driving changes they were considering to their energy storage technology[7].

Grid complexity

Booming sectors such as electric vehicles, AI and advanced manufacturing are creating a growing dependence on electric power globally. In turn, this is increasing the demands on, and complexity of, electrical grids. In many places, major improvement work is under way: in the European Union and the UK, for example, investment in grids is set to reach US$ 120 billion a year by 2030, according to McKinsey[8]. Alongside other technologies, battery storage can contribute to providing the flexibility needed to meet and manage energy demands efficiently. BESS also offers functions such as voltage and frequency regulation to help stabilize grids.

Booming sectors such as electric vehicles, AI and advanced manufacturing are creating a growing dependence on electric power globally

Falling costs

The cost of battery storage projects is falling rapidly amid increasing manufacturer competition, improved designs and lower pack prices. According to Bloomberg NEF data, in 2025 the global benchmark cost of a four-hour battery project dropped by 27% year-on-year to a record low (US$ 78 per MWh). This follows a decade of substantially decreasing prices, with installed costs falling around 20% a year on average between 2004 and 2014[9].

Policy

Government policies are a significant factor accelerating the growth of BESS, too. Net zero targets support widespread electrification, increasing demand on grids and driving the switch to renewables. Meanwhile, many governments have designed regulations or incentives specifically to support battery storage. In China, mandates to co-locate storage with renewable projects have underpinned much of the growth of BESS in recent years. These ended in 2025. In other countries (including Poland[10], Ireland[11] and Australia[12]) there are subsidies or effective requirements for battery storage.

How are key countries around the world using battery storage?

China is the world leader in battery storage, accounting for more than half of global BESS capacity by the end of 2025[13]. To a large extent, this capacity is a result of policies designed to reduce en1ergy waste. Curtailment of wind energy in the country – when production is deliberately reduced due to an oversupply – reached a high of 17% in 2016[14]. The following year,Chinese provinces began to bring in co-location mandates, which became national policy for power generation projects from 2021. This helped keep curtailment low, as well as driving rapid BESS growth.[15]

Much of this new storage capacity was underused, however, as although businesses had a strong incentive to build battery storage, they had far less motivation to use it effectively. In 2024, in the area served by China’s state grid corporation (80% of the country), the average system sat idle 91% of the time[16].

In this context, China is moving to a different phase. The emphasis is shifting from co-located BESS to more flexible standalone systems, which are not tied to a particular plant. This is driven by two policy changes:

In February 2025, ending the co-location mandate[17]

In January 2026, extending the policy of capacity remuneration (where power plants are paid for availability rather than just generation) to standalone BESS[18]

The results are striking: standalone storage has become the primary market driver, comprising 84.7% of new installed capacity between January and April 2026, with co-located systems accounting for only 8.4%[19].

Standalone systems can earn revenue in multiple ways, including energy arbitrage (storing energy at times of lower prices and selling it when prices rise) and leasing capacity. Policies such as moving to more flexible market-based pricing are helping increase China’s utilization of both standalone and co-located storage and there is still plenty of room for improvement. Analysts say optimizing the use of both co-located and standalone battery storage in 2025 could have shifted an amount of energy equivalent to powering Singapore’s whole economy for five months[20].

Analysts say optimizing the use of both co-located and standalone battery storage in 2025 could have shifted an amount of energy equivalent to powering Singapore’s whole economy for five months

“China has built the world’s largest battery storage fleet in record time, but having the batteries is not the same as using them. The next phase of China’s storage story will be defined not by how many gigawatts are added, but by how well they can support the new power system,” said Siming Liu, group strategy senior manager at Trina Solar[21].

The United States is the world’s second-biggest battery storage market, and the sector is rapidly growing here too. In the second quarter of 2026, 20.2 GWh of new capacity came online – enough to meet the daily requirements of 700,000 homes. Most of the recent growth came from huge, utility-scale systems, with seven installations with a capacity over 1 GwH coming online in Q2 alone, and the country is on course to see a 20% increase in battery capacity in 2026[22].

The two US states with the biggest battery capacity are Texas and California and their growth illustrates how there’s no single best way to develop the sector. In California, capacity has grown rapidly from less than 700 MW in 2019 to more than 21 GW today[23], allowing the grid to store the abundant solar energy generated during the day for use at night. It’s estimated that the state’s batteries could power about a quarter of its peak demand.

As well as falling prices and grid reliability concerns, this expansion has been driven by regulation, including the US’s first energy storage mandate in 2013. Underlying these policy drivers is the state’s target of 100% clean electricity by 2045.

Meanwhile, Texas has become the fastest-growing battery storage market in the country with little direct policy intervention. Instead, increased demand (through population growth and data centers), as well as economic opportunities through energy arbitrage, are among the most significant factors. Texas’ low-regulation business environment, including fast permitting processes, and large amounts of land are also thought to have contributed to the growth.

While California and Texas lead the field, other parts of the US are now making serious progress

While California and Texas lead the field, other parts of the US are now making serious progress, too. In Q2 2026, Arizona saw 6.2 GWh of new installations – the largest in the country, and the strongest quarter for any state on record[24]. The continuation of federal investment tax credits for energy storage projects, even as those for wind and solar are phased out, is contributing to the sector’s strong growth.

While the US and China are the front-runners in global battery deployment, other countries are making rapid advances.

Australia is now the world’s third-largest utility-scale battery market globally, with 4.3 GW of large-scale battery capacity reaching financial close in 2025[25]. In terms of capacity relative to population, the country already has a clear lead, with more than 1 GWh per million people, compared to less than 400 MWh per million people in China and the US.[26]

With renewables forming 43% of Australia’s grid, battery storage is increasingly important to maintain resilience and balance supply with demand. Across the country’s National Electricity Market, average battery discharge in the first quarter of 2026 reached 359 MW, more than three times the level a year previously[27].

Australia’s states and national government both provide strategic and financial support for BESS. The 500 MW Collie BESS, which went online in February, was the third BESS delivered by Western Australia’s state-owned energy company, Synergy, in three years[28], while in June, the government’s Capacity Investment Scheme (a revenue underwriting initiative) backed 15 new BESS projects with a combined capacity of 4.2 GW, expected to unlock US$ 4.2 billion in private investment [29].

“Our Capacity Investment Scheme is turning Australia’s pipeline of clean energy projects into jobs in regional communities and cheaper, more reliable power for millions of homes. We’ve got the best sun and wind in the world, and we’re using our sovereign renewables, stored in batteries, to shield our grid from global energy volatility and to bring down [people’s] energy bills,” says Chris Bowen, Australian minister for climate change and energy[30].

Australia is also a key market for Fotowatio Renewable Ventures (FRV), part of Jameel Energy and the Canadian infrastructure fund OMERS.

In February 2026, FRV Australia’s Armidale East BESS project in New South Wales was awarded a Long Duration Storage Long-Term Energy Service Agreement (LTESA). The LTESA framework is a key pillar of the state’s strategy to accelerate the deployment of long-duration storage solutions that support the security, resilience, and decarbonization of the electricity system.

Located around 16 km east of Armidale, the project will deliver a total capacity of 315 MW, of which 157.5 MW will feature an 8-hour duration system contracted under LTESA, making it one of the most significant long-duration energy storage systems currently under development in the country.

FRV Australia continues to grow its integrated portfolio of generation and storage projects to help build a more resilient and sustainable grid

Armidale East is expected to become FRV Australia’s third BESS project in the country, along with the Terang (see box) and Gnarwarre plants currently under construction in Victoria. With this milestone, FRV Australia continues to grow its integrated portfolio of generation and storage projects to help build a more resilient and sustainable grid. The company now operates nine PV facilities across Australia and New Zealand, surpassing 1 GW of capacity.

In focus: the Terang BESS

FRV Australia is contributing to the growth of Australia’s battery storage capacity through ambitious projects such as the Terang BESS in Victoria. Construction of the site began in August 2024 and is now nearing completion, with the facility already connected to the grid and energised[1]. It will have a discharge capacity of 100 MW and a storage capacity of 200 MWh.

The Terang facility is one of FRV’s many global BESS projects. Also in Victoria will be the 250 MW Gnawarre BESS, which reached financial close in 2025. The Australian sites join dozens of other ongoing FRV BESS projects[1] in countries including Spain, Italy, Germany and the UK.

What are the potential barriers to scaling up battery storage?

Battery storage is a proven, affordable, technology. So, what’s the catch? Many challenges concern the surrounding infrastructure and policy rather than BESS technology itself. Key factors that could hamper its growth include:

Connection delays

The growth of BESS is leaving grids scrambling to catch up. Bloomberg reports that in the US, for example, storage projects are “piling up in interconnection queues” as utilities struggle to make the necessary upgrades to support them. Across the country, the median wait time for connecting energy storage projects has risen from a year and a half in 2015 to five years in 2025[31].

Safety concerns

The safety risks of battery storage were dramatically highlighted last year by a major fire at one of the world’s largest BESS plants – Moss Landing, California – which lasted for days and destroyed 75% of the facility[32]. The 300 MW plant experienced a thermal runaway, a self-heating reaction resulting in extremely high temperatures and the emission of toxic gases, that is very difficult to put out.

The incident focused attention on the safety of lithium-ion batteries, the standard technology for BESS facilities. The US Environmental Protection Agency says many communities have raised legitimate safety concerns[33], while in the UK lawmakers say the risks present “unique challenges”.[34]

Planning & permission

In many parts of the world, safety worries and other local concerns are creating hurdles and delays for BESS projects. Some US towns have established moratoriums on BESS, and the UK planning system frequently blocks or delays projects[35].

Elsewhere in Europe, regulatory frameworks change frequently and can vary across different regions, creating uncertainty for developers. One law firm working in the sector says that in Germany, regulatory uncertainty “complicates planning, increases compliance risk and can delay investment decisions”.[36]

Supply chain challenges

China plays a major role in the global battery supply chain at every stage, from mining to processing and manufacturing. Chinese companies, for instance, control 25% of the world’s lithium mining capacity. The country processes 90% of the world’s graphite, and in 2023 accounted for 74% of global battery pack and component exports[37]. Similarly, Chinese system integrators, who produce complete BESS systems, hold a 76% share of the global market.[38]

The country’s dominance has contributed to falling prices, but in the long-term, it can create dependency and unpredictability for BESS projects. Dealing with developments such as Beijing’s recent pause on approvals for battery storage manufacturing plants[39], or the US government’s ban on the import of power equipment from certain countries, becomes more challenging when the supply chain lacks diversity.

To meet the COP28 goal of tripling global renewable energy capacity by 2030 while maintaining energy security, energy storage needs to increase sixfold

What’s the future for battery storage?

Battery storage capacity is expected to grow substantially in the coming years. To meet the COP28 goal of tripling global renewable energy capacity by 2030 while maintaining energy security, energy storage needs to increase sixfold, says the IEA, with battery storage accounting for 90% of the growth[40]. This would require an increase in deployment of 25% a year. McKinsey projects a higher increase in installed capacity: 50% a year between 2022 and 2030[41].

Achieving this level of growth will require a focused approach from industries and governments, with crucial considerations including:

Strategic policy. Overcoming bottlenecks in permission and connection requires clear regulation and strong leadership. The UK is one country that has recently reformed its connections pipeline to focus on “what’s needed, when it’s needed”, prioritizing “shovel-ready” projects[42]. US States such as California have measures to fast-track clean energy projects, replacing the need for various other permits.

Industry optimization. The best-performing BESS developers have capital expenditures that are 40% better than average, according to McKinsey, with much of this advantage explained by better approaches to contracting, engineering, procurement and construction. Optimizing system designs, training staff and enhancing sourcing arrangements are all examples of approaches that can help improve processes and drive down costs.

New technology. Future technological developments are likely to offer new ways to address challenges from safety risks to supply chain constraints. Sodium-ion batteries, for instance, have the potential to be a safer and cheaper alternative to current lithium-ion options. A Chinese company, CATL, recently unveiled the TENER sodium – claimed to be the world’s first real-world validated sodium-ion energy storage solution[43]. In the long term, such technology could reduce reliance on China due to sodium’s abundance.

As Fady Jameel, Vice Chairman, International, Abdul Latif Jameel, says, “the need for better battery energy storage systems is intense. Implementing BESS on the required scale will be a major challenge. But while this prospect is daunting, we can take heart from the imaginative, exciting ways that businesses and governments are responding. They know that the rewards of success – for those involved and the wider world – will be considerable.”

Five fast facts: the rise of battery storage

Q: How fast is battery storage growing?

A: Remarkably fast. The International Energy Agency (IEA) calls it the fastest-growing power technology today, with 108 GW added worldwide in 2025 – a 40% rise on the year before. Installed capacity has increased elevenfold in just five years.

Q: Why do we need so much of it?

A: Because the grid is changing. As solar and wind supply more of our power, storing energy for when the sun isn’t shining or the wind isn’t blowing becomes essential. Add surging demand from AI and electric vehicles, and storage becomes critical to keeping grids stable.

Q: Who’s leading the world in battery storage?

A: China, by a wide margin – it accounts for more than half of global capacity. The US is in second place, while Australia has become the third-largest utility-scale market and, per head of population, the global leader, with more than 1 GWh per million people.

Q: What’s holding back battery storage?

A: Many barriers are related to the systems and processes around implementation. In the US, the wait to connect a storage project has increased from 18 months in 2015 to five years today. Safety concerns are fueling local opposition and planning delays, and the supply chain is heavily concentrated in China, which creates uncertainty amid geopolitical tensions.

Q: Can the world build enough battery storage?

British Prime Minister Andy Burham said on Thursday that he was proud to support the summit’s focus on electrification.
Energy minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman told the leaders’ summit that emissions reduction is “what unites us”, “not necessarily the track to achieving it”.
Australia’s climate and energy minister Chris Bowen, whose country is co-leading the pledge with Türkiye, has defended its design.
