text:
More than a dozen countries, including Germany, South Korea, Pakistan and several small island states, have publicly backed the Turkish COP31 presidency’s flagship electrification pledge.

The voluntary pledge aims to raise electricity’s share of global final energy consumption to 35% by 2035, from 23% currently, but does not specify how that electricity should be generated.

The COP31 presidency is not expected to publish a full list of backers until next week, as it continues to rally support. But at least 14 countries have publicly endorsed the pledge, according to a Climate Home News analysis of speeches and official statements.

Alongside COP31 co-host Australia and COP32 host Ethiopia, they include Germany, Norway, Finland, South Korea, Pakistan, Zimbabwe, Eswatini, Togo and Liechtenstein, as well as the small island states of Palau, Seychelles and the Solomon Islands.

The European Union is widely expected to join the pledge this week, although member states still need to formally approve the decision, Politico reported. On Wednesday, President Ursula von der Leyen supported the pledge in her personal capacity and encouraged others to do the same.

Major economies still on the fence

Other major economies have welcomed COP31’s focus on electrification while stopping short of endorsing the pledge.

British Prime Minister Andy Burham said on Thursday that he was proud to support the summit’s focus on electrification. He said it matters for energy security, for creating good jobs in clean energy and manufacturing, and for lowering people’s bills.

Big fossil-fuel countries back Brazil-led transition roadmap

Some countries including Germany and the Netherlands call for the roadmaps to inform a key global review of climate progress in 2028

COP31 outcome needs to prioritise transition away from fossil fuels

Many countries are already working on parts of their transition, such as phasing out coal or ending fossil fuel subsidies, with more expected to follow soon

Brazil’s environment minister João Paulo Capobianco ssaid on Thursday that electrification was “an important front” in climate action, but warned it should not be pursued “for the sake of it”. It should instead serve as a means of improving efficiency and cutting emissions. He said Brazil would work with the Turkish proposal and suggest adjustments to allow “specific solutions” that reduce emissions, without giving details.

Saudi Arabia was more openly sceptical. Energy minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman told the leaders’ summit that emissions reduction is “what unites us”, “not necessarily the track to achieving it”. “The expansion of electrification does not necessarily mean cutting emissions, so long as we do not consider the sources of its production,” he said, adding that countries’ choices must be respected.

Clean power strings attached

Many of the nations formally backing the initiative have attached some strings to their support. At a high-level roundtable on Wednesday, the low-lying Pacific island nation of Palau said it would sign on to the pledge. But it added that electrification “must not become a substitute or a distraction” from the chief goal of transitioning away from fossil fuels.

Seychelles also endorsed the pledge but added that it must be connected with cleaner electricity. “Electrifying more activities while continuing to burn fossil fuels will not deliver the full economic or climate benefits,” the country’s representative told the roundtable.

Australia’s climate and energy minister Chris Bowen, whose country is co-leading the pledge with Türkiye, has defended its design. “Electrification is almost always a good thing,” he told the Outrage and Optimism podcast recently. He argued that switching to an electric car cuts emissions by 60% even on a coal-fired grid, and by 90% when powered by solar.

Doug Arent, senior fellow at the WRI Polsky Center for the Global Energy Transition, said the most important thing “is that there is significant support for the concept of electrification”. He expects more countries to “recognise their pathway to be behind the 35 by 35” in the coming years.

Calls for finance

Other developing countries backing the pledge have underlined the critical importance of access to finance. Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif showed off his country’s people-led boom in rooftop solar and growing rollout of electric vehicles. But he added that “momentum without finance cannot be sustained,” and said the burden of new technologies cannot fall on countries already in debt.

Zimbabwe backed the pledge but warned of the high capital costs and financial bottlenecks facing developing countries. Its representative proposed a global electrification investment facility that would provide first-loss guarantees for projects under Mission 300, an initiative to connect 300 million people in Sub-Saharan Africa to electricity by 2030.

The Solomon Islands, another supporter of the pledge, asked for a dedicated finance access window for small island nations and least developed countries (LDCs).

Tuesday saw the launch of a global finance coalition backed by COP31 host Türkiye and COP32 host Ethiopia aimed at supporting clean electrification in developing countries.

Closing the roundtable, Türkiye’s energy minister Alparslan Bayraktar, who chaired the session, claimed the 35x35 pledge had found broad support worldwide. He called for a “smart” energy transition that draws on all available technologies, including carbon capture, use and storage.

COP31 Bulletin Day 5: Cover decision wishlist issued as China bows out of COP33 hosting

Governments must start narrowing down what a political decision could look like in Antalya, while the conversation buzzes around who will host 2028’s important COP

Nepal’s climate suffering should pave the way for a safe and fair future

Young people in Nepal are seeking international solidarity from COP31 to help our nation tackle the worsening climate disasters knocking at all of our doors

We must strengthen trade cooperation to deliver on global climate goals

As governments turn to trade-related measures to deliver on their climate targets, cooperation is vital to reduce fragmentation, costs and build more resilient economies

Pacific leaves empty handed from COP31 “pledging event” for new fund

With developed countries only re-announcing old pledges, the facility remains $300 million away from meeting its 2026 target of $500m for resilience projects

Push for ocean roadmap that informs next global stocktake grows at COP31

A group of countries including African nations, European Union, and small island states wants COP31 to deliver an ocean roadmap towards 2028

Russia, Saudi Arabia and others are questioning the legitimacy of the Australian-Turkish push for an overarching COP31 agreement

Around 40 leaders, including Lula, Erdoğan and Albanese, addressed the summit in Antalya, where the UN chief proposed a “climate justice compact”

Türkiye pushes “zero waste” at COP31, but is it delivering at home?

Türkiye is hosting a Zero Waste Day at the UN climate summit, led by its First Lady, but its own waste generation keeps rising while plastic imports from Europe look set to boom

Big fossil-fuel countries back Brazil-led transition roadmap

Some countries including Germany and the Netherlands call for the roadmaps to inform a key global review of climate progress in 2028

Japan urged to ditch fossil fuel support to maximise clean-tech exports

Japan could be one of the big winners of Asia’s electrification push, but it must radically pivot its policies away from propping up fossil fuels, a new analysis says

text:
Nearly a decade after North Carolinians learned their drinking water had been contaminated with industrial chemicals for years, a new documentary is examining how it happened, the people affected and the ongoing fight to hold polluters accountable.

GENX: The Saga of Forever Chemicals, premiering Friday in Saxapahaw, traces the contamination of the Cape Fear River and the investigation that exposed a problem extending far beyond North Carolina.

For filmmaker Eli Yetter-Bowman, who grew up in Wilmington, the story also has a personal connection. He and his mother were exposed to contaminated drinking water, and both have autoimmune diseases. While it's unclear whether PFAS exposure contributed to their illnesses, their experience inspired Yetter-Bowman to investigate the broader health impacts of the contamination.

"What stood out to me most was the severity and the significance of the issue," Yetter-Bowman told WRAL. "The fact that back in 2017 when this really broke, that we were revealing something that had been happening for multiple generations was really devastating to me."

In 2017, the public learned that GenX, a chemical used in manufacturing nonstick coatings, had been detected in drinking water drawn from the Cape Fear River. The contamination was linked to industrial discharges from a chemical manufacturing facility near Fayetteville, now operated by Chemours.

GenX belongs to a larger group of synthetic chemicals known as PFAS, or per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances. Used in products ranging from stain-resistant fabrics to firefighting foam, many PFAS break down extremely slowly in the environment, earning them the nickname "forever chemicals."

Exposure to certain PFAS has been linked to increased risks of cancer, immune system effects and other health problems.

The discovery in the Cape Fear River sparked investigations, lawsuits and demands for stronger drinking water protections.

"The PFAS issue is completely unsolved," Yetter-Bowman said. "It has only grown, especially in terms of public awareness and our understanding of the extent of damage."

Telling the story beyond the science

Directed by Yetter-Bowman and Sammy Bauer of Ethereal Films, the documentary explores the history of PFAS contamination, its consequences for communities and the efforts to hold chemical manufacturers accountable.

The film features North Carolina Gov. Josh Stein, who served as attorney general during much of the investigation, environmental attorney Robert Bilott and actor and environmental activist Mark Ruffalo.

Bilott's legal battle involving DuPont inspired the 2019 film Dark Waters, in which Ruffalo portrayed the attorney.

Yetter-Bowman said conversations with those involved in the fight revealed a shared disbelief about how widespread contamination could occur.

"You just assume that this type of thing could never happen," he said.

The filmmakers also wanted to make the complicated science accessible while keeping the focus on people affected by contaminated water.

"When you go to somebody's house and realize like they can't take a shower, they can't wash their face, they can't cook their food, any of this in the same way that you and I could just at our house. It really changes your perspective," Yetter-Bowman said.

The film incorporates elaborate puppetry from Saxapahaw-based Paperhand Puppet Project to illustrate the history of contamination and explore what a cleaner future could look like.

Contamination remains a concern

WRAL has reported extensively on PFAS contamination in North Carolina for years, documenting its impact on families, drinking water systems and communities along the Cape Fear River.

That reporting includes the 2023 WRAL documentary Forever Chemicals: North Carolina's Toxic Tap Water, which examined decades of pollution and the families seeking answers about their health and access to clean drinking water.

More recent testing has revealed the nationwide extent of PFAS contamination.

An Environmental Working Group analysis of federal and state testing data found that nearly 197 million Americans are served by drinking water systems where PFAS have been detected, approximately 23 million more than previously identified.

The increase reflects expanded testing and does not necessarily mean contamination is worsening. Detection also does not necessarily mean a water system exceeds federal drinking water limits.

The Environmental Protection Agency established the first nationwide drinking water limits for several PFAS in 2024, including limits of 4 parts per trillion for PFOA and PFOS. The agency has since announced plans to reconsider some of those regulations.

In North Carolina, years of legal action, regulatory enforcement and investments in water treatment have led to efforts to reduce exposure.

Yetter-Bowman pointed to improvements in Wilmington's drinking water treatment as evidence of progress.

"I think it's always hardest when you first identify a problem, but it's like the first step in actually solving it," he said.

The documentary's premiere comes as Saxapahaw faces its own drinking water concerns. Testing conducted this summer found PFOA and PFOS above federal drinking water limits at all six tested locations in the community water system. The source of the contamination remains unknown.

A message of hope and accountability

Yetter-Bowman, who has also advocated for stronger action on PFAS contamination, said the documentary aims to show how community involvement has helped drive change.

"I want people to walk away understanding that this is an ongoing issue," he said. "This is an ongoing issue that affects them, and that they have a lot of agency to do something about it."

Despite the scope of the contamination, Yetter-Bowman said he hopes audiences leave with a sense of possibility rather than despair.

"This is a solvable issue. We'll do it together through collaboration," Yetter-Bowman said.

GENX: The Saga of Forever Chemicals premieres Friday, Nov. 13, at the Haw River Ballroom in Saxapahaw. Doors open at 6:30 p.m., with the screening beginning at 7 p.m.

A question-and-answer session with the filmmakers, Paperhand Puppet Project and environmental advocates will follow.

text:
Environmental Defense Fund and Atlas Public Policy today released a new report, The State of Clean Energy Manufacturing in Q3 2026, finding that the third quarter of this year saw the largest net investment gain in U.S. clean energy manufacturing since the start of 2024. However, a single major solar manufacturing project drove much of that growth, masking continued challenges for the broader sector as the Trump administration continues to pursue policies that impede the deployment of affordable clean energy.

Companies announced $11.9 billion in new investments and nearly 20,000 manufacturing jobs during the third quarter. After accounting for cancellations, the sector recorded a net gain of $11.6 billion in investment and 19,220 announced manufacturing jobs. However, nearly $7 billion of the quarter's investment growth came from an increase in the reported value of a proposed $10.1 billion solar manufacturing facility near Houston. Meanwhile, companies have canceled nearly $40 billion in planned investments and more than 54,000 announced jobs since January 2025.

"One major project can boost a quarter's numbers, but it doesn't signal a broader manufacturing recovery," said Grace Hauser, Technical Analyst, Clean Power at Environmental Defense Fund. "American manufacturing needs a steady pipeline of investments to create jobs and strengthen local economies. Nearly $40 billion in canceled projects and fewer new investments raise serious concerns about what's ahead. As a new Congress prepares to take office, lawmakers have an opportunity to support the long-term growth of this industry."

More than 70% of net clean energy manufacturing investment announced between 2000 and Q3 2026, totaling $187.8 billion and nearly 219,000 anticipated jobs, is concentrated in congressional districts represented by Republicans in the outgoing Congress. Georgia leads the nation in cumulative announced investment at $30.3 billion, followed by Texas at $24.7 billion, which jumped from fifth to second following Tesla's expanded investment announcement in the Houston-area solar project. Both states elected Democratic governors in November, while Democrats also regained control of both chambers of Congress. The new leadership will help shape federal and state energy policies that could affect the future of U.S. clean energy manufacturing.

Among the report's key findings:

One major project drove most of the quarter's investment growth. Companies announced $7.5 billion in solar manufacturing investments and $1.5 billion in transmission and grid equipment investments in Q3. Nearly $7 billion of the quarter's investment growth came from an upward revision to the reported value of the proposed Houston-area solar manufacturing project.

Large investments remain less frequent. Companies announced just eight clean energy manufacturing investments exceeding $1 billion since January 2025, compared with 24 during the preceding 18 months.

More factories are operating, but fewer investments are on the horizon. For the first time since tracking began, investment in operating clean energy factories exceeds the combined investment in those planned or under construction, raising concerns about future growth.

Cancellations continue to threaten jobs and local economies. Companies canceled $296 million in planned investments and 760 announced manufacturing jobs in Q3, bringing total cancellations since January 2025 to $39.9 billion in investment and 54,300 jobs. North Carolina has lost the most announced jobs, followed by Michigan, Ohio, and Illinois.

Battery manufacturers are shifting to new markets as EV investments slow. Facing weaker-than-expected EV demand and scaled-back projects, manufacturers are expanding into energy storage, defense and other applications.

Negative net job values appear in red. Data are from Q1 2022 through Q3 2026. Source: Clean Economy Tracker

The analysis uses data from Atlas Public Policy's Clean Economy Tracker to track publicly announced investments, cancellations and manufacturing jobs across the U.S. clean energy sector. text:
ARLINGTON, VA— ICYMI: For years, Americans for Prosperity (AFP) has made the case that fixing America’s broken permitting system is essential to lowering the cost of living, creating jobs, and unleashing American energy. This week, we’ve continued to urge Congress to pass BAAJA quickly.

Now, three of the country’s leading editorial boards are urging Congress to take the permitting reform deal on the table. All three focus on affordability. Here’s what they’re saying:

New York Times Editorial Board: “Democrats, Take the Deal”

November 12, 2026

The bill delivers on affordability. The board says the current system raises energy costs by keeping new projects, including cheap wind and solar, from coming online. In its words, “The status quo is expensive, dirty and unstable.”

Waiting is a bad bet. President Trump would almost certainly veto a Democratic rewrite next year, and time matters for climate goals.

Delay has real costs. Long-distance power lines typically take five to 13 years to build. The Quebec-to-New England line took about a decade and is projected to save consumers $50 million a year.

Data centers pay their own way. The bill requires data center operators to cover the full cost of the electricity they use, protecting everyday ratepayers.

A wide coalition. Backers include Senators Heinrich, Schatz and Whitehouse, plus Georgia’s Ossoff and Warnock, who voted to advance the bill.

Washington Post Editorial Board: “A major step toward historic permitting reform”

November 9, 2026

A broad, bipartisan vote. The Senate advanced the deal 73-25, including 22 members of the Democratic caucus, a strong sign it will pass the chamber. The board says it could be a “historic achievement” after decades of failed efforts.

Affordability is the argument. Democrats won the midterms promising to make life more affordable, and defending a bureaucracy that drives up energy prices clashes with that message.

The coalition keeps growing. Late amendments won over holdouts, including the Edison Electric Institute. Climate groups such as Evergreen Action, Citizens’ Climate Lobby and the Environmental Defense Fund, along with several trade unions, are backing the compromise.

Critics’ claims don’t hold up. The board says the bill expressly limits the executive branch from interfering with energy projects after they’re approved.

Bloomberg Opinion Editorial Board: “Democrats Should Take the Permitting Deal They Have”

November 11, 2026

A rare bipartisan win within reach. The board says Congress is on the cusp of a major victory, and that crossing the finish line will take “prudence, resolve and common sense.”

What the bill does. It streamlines environmental review, limits obstructive litigation, curtails capricious executive-branch actions, encourages green energy, expands transmission and gives companies and investors far more certainty.

Support is wide. Backers include industry, clean energy producers, many climate groups, business leaders, numerous unions, much of the Senate and the White House.

The benefits are striking. Citing Rhodium Group, the board says the bill could add up to 249 gigawatts of new clean energy capacity by 2040. One trade group estimates $4.2 billion a year in savings for manufacturers, another analysis projects more than 100,000 industrial jobs, and the board says power-sector costs could fall by $350 billion through 2050.

The backlog is enormous. About 2,060 gigawatts of generation and storage requests, roughly 1.5 times total existing capacity, are stuck in transmission bottlenecks. Even after recent reforms, fewer than half of environmental impact statements are finished within two years.

Relief for consumers. The board says red tape drags on growth, raises prices and costs jobs, mostly to the benefit of lawyers. It argues an electorate fed up with rising prices would welcome lower electricity bills.

Waiting won’t produce a better bill. The board says the bipartisan compromise may not survive future elections. It also notes Democrats failed to strike a deal in 2022 despite a governing trifecta.

Bottom line: Three editorial boards, three angles, one message. Permitting reform lowers costs, the deal is on the table, and Democrats shouldn’t wait for a better one that may never come.

title: 'It is much, much faster': could China's battery-swapping e-trucks be the answer to EV range anxiety?
description:
Battery swapping is not new in China, where more than 400,000 e-trucks (or over 90% of the global total) were sold last year.
When a truck approaches a battery-swapping station, the station’s cameras automatically identify the type of battery it uses by checking its number plate.
CATL, the world’s biggest battery manufacturer, is a key player in promoting battery swapping for heavy trucks in China.
In China, battery-swapping is still a minority charging method for its rapidly growing e-truck fleet.
Plus, battery swapping doesn’t necessarily mean drivers will save time, Xue says.
text:
Every day, Wang Bing drives his big electric lorry to send about five tonnes of goods between the cities of Haikou and Dongfang on Hainan, a tropical island in southern China. A round trip covers about 500 kilometres (310 miles). But refuelling is not something Wang worries about.

“When my battery runs low, I just drive my truck into a battery-swapping station to get a fully charged one,” says the 53-year-old, who shares the journey with a colleague in eight-hour shifts.

Wang has been a lorry driver for nearly three decades. In the first two of those, he drove conventional lorries fuelled by diesel. About five years ago, he began driving an electric model after the logistics company he worked for upgraded its fleet. In July this year, his old e-truck, which used conventional plug-in charging, was replaced by one with a swappable battery.

In the past, Wang had to spend an hour and half charging his battery each time, but with his new truck, it takes just five minutes or so to have a drained battery removed and a fresh one replaced. “I am very happy,” he says.

Battery swapping is not new in China, where more than 400,000 e-trucks (or over 90% of the global total) were sold last year. The Chinese carmaker Nio commercialised the technology nearly a decade ago for smaller electric vehicles (EVs). But in 2023, the Chinese battery behemoth CATL launched a battery-swapping system for electric lorries through a subsidiary brand called Qiji Energy.

To Wang, the biggest advantage of the technology is the time it saves. “It is much, much faster,” he says. “I don’t even need to leave my truck when the battery is being swapped.”

This swiftness builds on the cost advantage e-trucks already have over their fossil-fuelled peers when it comes to refuelling.

“Electricity is cheaper than oil,” Wang says. The per-kilometre fuelling cost for an e-truck works out about 1.1 yuan (12p) in Hainan, he says, significantly lower than that for a diesel truck, which exceeds 2 yuan (22p) a kilometre. “That means my e-truck can save more than 20,000 yuan (£2,200) per month,” Wang says.

When a truck approaches a battery-swapping station, the station’s cameras automatically identify the type of battery it uses by checking its number plate. “All the driver needs to do is to drive the truck into a designated area, and the battery will be swapped completely automatically,” says Wei Jiuchun, 46, a test driver at a Qiji Energy battery-swapping station in Suzhou, east China. Wei’s job is to help the station test its system for different models of heavy trucks and under different weather conditions.

It is not just time and fuel costs the technology saves but, in China, the initial lump sum a buyer has to put down to get an e-truck, says Mao Shiyue, a Beijing-based researcher at the International Council on Clean Transportation (ICCT).

The upfront purchase price for an e-truck is significantly higher than for a comparable diesel model, a major obstacle for those vehicles’ wider adoption in many parts of the world. In China, a customer opting for battery swapping typically buys an e-truck without a battery, and then rents the battery from a service provider. As the cost of a battery is about 40% of an e-truck’s price, the business model can make e-trucks a lot more affordable, Mao says.

The technology can also help minimise the pressure EV charging brings to the power grid, according to Mao, because swapping stations have more flexibility to spread out the charging time for the depleted batteries.

“If the grid sees a spike in electricity demand during peak hours, those stations can even act as an energy-storage station by returning the electricity stored in their batteries back to the grid to ease the strain,” he says.

CATL, the world’s biggest battery manufacturer, is a key player in promoting battery swapping for heavy trucks in China. The company’s support for the technology is critical for its large-scale rollout, says Phate Zhang, the founder of CnEVPost, a Shanghai-based outlet focusing on EVs.

CATL plans to put 900 battery-swapping stations into operation across China by the end of this year, expanding its current network twice more. By the end of 2027, it wants the number to reach 2,000.

The company has also teamed up with the London-based renewable energy supplier Octopus to bring the technology to Europe. It intends to open its first group of battery-swapping “mega hubs” in the UK next year, and a network of more than 30 hubs in Europe by 2035.

In China, battery-swapping is still a minority charging method for its rapidly growing e-truck fleet. In 2024, about one-third of the zero-emission trucks in the country featured this technology, while the rest largely had conventional plug-in charging, according to the latest available figures.

One downside is that drivers often need to stick to a particular service provider that caters to the specific type of swappable batteries their e-trucks use.

“For example, some batteries are swapped from the chassis, while others are swapped from the top of the truck,” says Xue Lulu, a senior associate at World Resources Institute China. “Even under the same technological route, batteries made by different companies often have different specifications.” This means drivers cannot drop into any random swapping station to get their trucks replenished, which could restrict the journeys they can make, she says.

Plus, battery swapping doesn’t necessarily mean drivers will save time, Xue says. During her field research in China, she found some lorry drivers would wait outside battery-swapping stations for one to two hours before going in because they wanted to avoid using the service during peak hours, to save money. “Logistics firms are extremely sensitive to costs,” she says.

The most suitable users are probably drivers who, like Wang, work on fixed routes served by battery-swapping stations. Mao says the charging method has been rolled out most successfully among companies that use heavy trucks in specific settings, such as those carrying goods in ports and factories, as well as within a city or between two nearby cities. “For unpredicted and long-haul routes, there are still challenges for rolling it out on a large scale,” he says.

title: DOGE cuts cost tribes $470M, gutting funding for climate projects - ABC News
authors: JOSEPH LEE/GRIST GRIST Associated Press, ABC News
description:
The funding, announced in 2024, was part of a larger $150 million allocation for tribal infrastructure in Alaska.
According to Brookings, despite historic investments flowing into Indian Country after the pandemic, a massive underinvestment in Indigenous communities continues.
The report authors are calling for policy changes that would ensure tribes receive funding, regardless of political winds.
That funding, which came under the Biden administration, included over $700 million in climate, energy, and infrastructure funding for tribes.
Maxim says that funding for Indigenous communities is a federal obligation based on treaties and other agreements with tribes and should be standard and irrevocable.
text:
Every year, Kotzebue, a small city in northwest Alaska, has a three-month window to receive all the diesel fuel it will use throughout the following year. It sits on a gravel spit that juts into Kotzebue Sound just north of the Arctic Circle, and is accessible only by air and sea. Ice keeps freight barges from reaching it for most of the year.

The community relies on diesel for 75 percent of its power, and residents put about 20 percent of their income toward buying it. That’s more than three times the average energy burden for low-income households nationwide.

“We’re pretty much at the mercy of world markets,” Chad Nordlum, who is the energy project manager for the Native Village of Kotzebue, told Grist. “Right now, with the Iran war going on, the diesel prices are very high and we’re locked in to much higher prices than we’ve had in the past. There’s really nothing the community can do about diesel prices, but what we can do is produce our own energy.”

That’s why Nordlum was so excited about a $20 million grant from the Environmental Protection Agency to support a wind energy project. The funding, announced in 2024, was part of a larger $150 million allocation for tribal infrastructure in Alaska. Nordlum says it would have lowered the community’s reliance on diesel to about 40 percent to 50 percent and given the tribe more control over energy and economic decisions.

But the Trump administration canceled the grant in May 2025. More than a year later, the project remains paused.

That cut was among hundreds of millions of dollars the Department of Government Efficiency pulled from Indian Country, and part of a broader pattern of funding rollbacks and underinvestment in Indigenous communities. Two new reports from the Brookings Institution show that the so-called One Big Beautiful Bill Act killed many of the funding streams established by the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act, while DOGE eliminated another $468 million, about half of which was allocated for environmental and natural resources. Another 11 percent targeted agriculture. Those projects include climate resiliency plans, renewable energy projects, and jobs programs.

According to Brookings, despite historic investments flowing into Indian Country after the pandemic, a massive underinvestment in Indigenous communities continues. Not only is that a violation of the federal government’s trust and treaty obligations to tribes, it is hindering Indigenous efforts to protect the environment and address climate change. The report authors are calling for policy changes that would ensure tribes receive funding, regardless of political winds.

Rob Maxim, who is Mashpee Wampanoag and a fellow at Brookings Metro, said climate and environmental funding is especially crucial for Indigenous communities because they are often the most severely impacted by climate change, especially after years of underinvestment.

“The actions that the Trump administration is taking are particularly significant, but it’s not totally out of trend with previous administrations,” he said. “And what we wanted to show was that actually this underinvestment is kind of the default for the U.S. rather than a blip.”

The true aberration was the unprecedented levels of funding after the pandemic. That funding, which came under the Biden administration, included over $700 million in climate, energy, and infrastructure funding for tribes. It covered projects like development of climate action plans, food systems analysis, and more. For example, the Hopi Tribe was to receive a $25 million grant to install solar panels for 600 homes. That grant, and the entire $7 billion Solar for All program, were cut.

Maxim says that funding for Indigenous communities is a federal obligation based on treaties and other agreements with tribes and should be standard and irrevocable. “The funding that was flowing to Indian Country was not being done on the basis of race or DEI, and it was absolutely not illegal,” he said. “It was aimed at the promotion of tribal sovereignty and the well-being of tribal citizens and tribal communities, and so that is, you know, an obligation that the U.S. government maintains.”

The White House did not respond to a request for comment. The EPA provided a comment several days after this story originally published Nov. 2.

“The Trump EPA is committed to ensuring taxpayer dollars are being used appropriately and has reviewed all funding activities with that lens. Through the agency’s General Assistance Program (GAP) and other granting programs, EPA has awarded more than $351 million in Tribal grants funding since the beginning of the second Trump administration,” the agency said in an email to Grist.

Glencora Haskins, a senior research associate and applied research manager at Brookings Metro, said that the administration had targeted funding to tribes, with “tribal” being the most frequently flagged term. “I think that there was a very surface-level view of what a lot of these programs were doing, rather than any deep interrogation of the types of systemic infrastructure deficits that programs were trying to fix,” Haskins said.

In Native communities throughout Alaska, and around the country, energy and infrastructure needs are especially acute because of increasingly frequent and destructive storms, wildfires, and other climate-driven disasters.

Haskins and Maxim recommend that Congress pass legislation that bars the cancellation of grants and contracts for tribes, and stipulates that all funding for Indigenous nations and communities is in service of trust and treaty obligations even if it is from a program with a different stated purpose. They also call for a statutory requirement that money should flow directly to tribes rather than having them seek reimbursement from the U.S. Treasury.

In Kotzebue, Chad Nordlum hopes the political tide will turn enough to get the funding for the wind project moving. In the meantime, he is working on a smaller solar project that he hopes will help alleviate the community’s energy challenges.

“Our main goals are energy security and economic development for the tribe, which is ultimately being able to invest in our own community, help make the lives of people here a little more sustainable,” Nordlum said. “We want our community to continue on into the future. We have to get a handle on our energy prices and availability.”

title: Data centers could lower your electricity bill. Will utilities let them? | Utility Dive
description:
On the one hand, many people blame data center companies for triggering new grid costs that others will pay.
As data center sales ramp up, the utility would see a windfall over the four years the new rates are in effect.
So why do utility rate proposals keep failing to account for data center load growth?
This creates a major windfall for utilities, at least temporarily, as data center load ramps up before rates can catch up.
Understanding these mechanics and the options for mitigating them will shape how regulators and stakeholders weigh the bill impacts of large load growth.
text:
Edward Burgess is a partner at Current Energy Group.

The debate over the impacts of new data centers on customers’ electricity bills is only intensifying.

On the one hand, many people blame data center companies for triggering new grid costs that others will pay. On the other, data centers hold great promise to lower customer bills.

For the latter, the theory is that, as high-utilization infrastructure users, data centers can absorb a large share of fixed costs that would otherwise be charged to existing customers.

To their credit, nearly 200 data center companies have signed the Ratepayer Protection Pledge, committing to pay their fair share of costs. However, achieving this commitment depends on cooperative action by local utilities to update their rates accordingly.

This raises an important question: Are investor-owned utilities willing to share the benefits of large-load growth with existing customers? Recent evidence suggests otherwise in some cases.

To fully understand this problem, let’s revisit the fundamentals of electricity ratemaking.

New rates are typically proposed by utilities but ultimately approved by state utility regulators. When utilities propose new rates, the core calculation is based on two key inputs: 1) utility costs in the numerator, and 2) utility sales in the denominator.

If the denominator increases more than the numerator (i.e., sales increase more than costs), then customer rates should decline on average.

But in the era of hyperscale load growth, the specifics of these inputs — how they are defined and when relative changes occur — matter a great deal. In several recent cases, utilities have simply neglected to increase kWh sales from new data center load in their rate proposals, while still including related cost increases.

For example, in North Carolina, Duke Energy recently proposed increasing customer rates by over 15% over the next two years.

However, this increase was based on a rate calculation that kept the denominator essentially frozen at 2024 levels — even though Duke had already contracted to add hundreds of MWs of new data centers in the coming years, and included costs triggered by this in its proposal.

Current Energy Group analyzed Duke’s proposal and presented expert testimony to the North Carolina Utilities Commission on behalf of the state’s Attorney General’s office. We found that 54% of the requested rate increase — approximately $1 billion annually — could be erased if kWh sales in the rate formula were simply corrected to reflect Duke’s own planning assumptions.

In fact, correcting just the kWh sales figure and one other key variable — return on equity — was enough to turn the proposed 15% rate increase into a 4% decrease, even with significant new grid investments.

A similar pattern emerged in Missouri, where Evergy Missouri Metro included costs for new gas generation to serve new data centers but did not account for the increased sales to those data centers in its rate calculation. As data center sales ramp up, the utility would see a windfall over the four years the new rates are in effect.

In Louisiana, increased sales from a new Meta data center could trigger an immediate customer refund over the next three years. Instead, Entergy proposed accounting methods to defer that benefit over a 20-year period.

This “one simple trick” of immediately updating kWh sales in the rate formula could save customers billions in the coming years. So why do utility rate proposals keep failing to account for data center load growth?

Some utility analysts might point to arcane explanations, such as the traditional practice of using a “historic test year.” There may be a grain of truth to that, but it is not a convincing argument given widespread concerns about affordability.

Duke, for instance, had the legal ability to propose a forward-looking Multi-Year Rate Plan but chose not to include any load growth in its rate proposal.

A more cynical view is that utilities are seeking to “lock in” higher rates before new data center load fully materializes and the denominator rises. This creates a major windfall for utilities, at least temporarily, as data center load ramps up before rates can catch up.

Traditionally, utilities have complained about “regulatory lag,” which arises when rates are not increased quickly enough to capture rising costs. Now, in the era of hyperscale load growth, we have the opposite problem — a “reverse regulatory lag.” Instead, rates are not being reduced quickly enough to capture rising revenue from large loads.

This problem is exacerbated by another challenge: As utilities slow-walk updates to the denominator (kWh sales), they speed-run updates to the numerator (costs recovered).

Many utilities, including Duke, use accelerated cost recovery mechanisms, such as Construction Work in Progress, to fund new infrastructure for load growth.

This further strains affordability. Infrastructure costs are front-loaded through near-term rate increases, while any rate relief from load growth won’t materialize for years.

Read More in Regulation & Policy

Under Duke’s original proposal, customers would pay for the construction of new gas-fired power plants four years before they start operating, and six years before data center load appears in the denominator.

As affordability concerns persist, what solutions should regulators consider?

Regulators should insist on up-to-date sales forecasts for any rate proposal and apply them immediately. If utilities rely on forecasts to plan and build generation, they should rely on those same forecasts to reduce rates by updating the billing determinants.

When revenue grows rapidly, regulators should ensure that utilities absorb more of the initial cost and risk involved rather than passing this on to consumers. For example, regulators should consider halting accelerated cost-recovery mechanisms. The regulatory lag problems those mechanisms sought to address are much less salient now.

For certain states, full revenue decoupling mechanisms can offer a solution. However, this might not be available in all cases or benefit all customer segments.

Whether hyperscale load growth raises or lowers bills depends on how and when the numerator and denominator are updated. Understanding these mechanics and the options for mitigating them will shape how regulators and stakeholders weigh the bill impacts of large load growth.

text:
LINCOLN, Neb. (DTN) -- A Ralston, Iowa, biodiesel plant that shut down two years and eight months ago is restarting production, Chevron U.S.A. Inc. announced Thursday.

In March 2024 Chevron Renewable Energy Group closed the 42-million-gallon Ralston plant as well as another biodiesel facility in Madison, Wisconsin, because of what the company described in a news release as "poor market conditions."

Chevron said the restart of the Ralston plant is supported by a commercial and operational agreement between Chevron and the farmer-owned Landus Cooperative.

It typically takes biodiesel plants two to six weeks to return to maximum production.

A Chevron spokesperson said the company does not have a definitive timeline for the plant's reopening but anticipates it will be mid-2027 before the plant comes back online.

"The decision follows improved biodiesel market conditions, and the neighboring Landus processing facility gives the plant an efficient feedstock supply chain," according to Chevron.

Chevron said the cooperative recently made updates to its Ralston processing facility.

"Ralston is well-positioned in the country's second largest state for soybean farming and the Landus facility processes more than 28 million bushels of soybeans a year, making it the largest mechanical crush facility in the U.S.," according to Chevron.

"Once fully operational, the Ralston facility will help increase the supply of biodiesel available to regional customers, support the broader diesel market and provide increased opportunities for soybeans raised by Iowa farmers. The restart is expected to create employment and contracting opportunities in the region, but timing and scope of workforce additions are still being assessed."

Chevron recently announced record crude throughput at its U.S. petroleum refineries, which operated at nearly 98% utilization in the third quarter, according to the company. It also achieved monthly renewable diesel and biodiesel production records in 2026, and the company has reinvested to bring more energy to a supply-constrained market.

"Restarting the Ralston facility reflects improved market conditions and Chevron's commitment to helping meet our customers' energy demands," said Andy Walz, Chevron president of downstream, midstream and chemicals.

"As global oil markets remain tight, Chevron is taking practical steps across our entire system to help strengthen fuel supply. Bringing Ralston back online will enable additional biodiesel production capacity while supporting the communities and customers we serve."

Chevron said the plant restart will be a "staged process" including staffing, maintenance, safety and operational-readiness activities prior to resuming production.

"The combination of soy processing and biodiesel production at the Ralston site has long represented a powerful partnership among our companies, communities and stakeholders," said Eric Heismeyer, Landus president and CEO.

"Landus is proud to collaborate with Chevron on this important step toward increased market access for our farmer owners and in doing so, contribute to Iowa's collective renewable fuel and agriculture leadership."

Monte Shaw, executive director of the Iowa Renewable Fuels Association, said restarting production at the Ralston plant is indicative of the effect of the latest Renewable Fuel Standard volumes.

"This may be the biggest sign yet of the powerful impact of the robust RFS blending levels finalized by the Trump EPA earlier this year," Shaw said in a statement.

"A major facility is coming back online, creating new demand for Iowa-grown soybeans and creating good-paying jobs in rural Iowa. IRFA strongly urges the Trump administration to maintain the RFS and to reject any actions that would reverse course. As the saying goes -- if it ain't broke, don't fix it."

text:
Andy Burnham has hailed a record investment in offshore wind, as the government tries to repair its green credentials after approving the controversial Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea.

On Wednesday the government announced a £12bn investment from the German energy company RWE and the US private equity firm KKR, as the prime minister prepares to travel to the Cop31 climate crisis summit in Turkey.

The investment package, which will go towards the creation of the Vanguard West and Vanguard East offshore windfarms off the Norfolk coast, is a “vote of confidence for building in Britain”, he said.

“It is great news for bill payers because every turbine we put up is power under British control, not at the mercy of events on the other side of the world.

“With coastal communities from Scotland to East Anglia powering Britain’s future, the places that host this energy benefit from the jobs and opportunities that it brings.”

The offshore wind projects will also receive £1bn in funding from the state-owned national wealth fund.

The windfarms are set to be providing power by 2030, with construction set to begin early next year. The wind investment is “believed to be the biggest of its kind in UK history”, the government said.

RWE said the Vanguard project represents one of the UK’s largest offshore wind developments, generating about 2.8 gigawatts, enough to supply 3m homes.

It estimated that the construction of the windfarms will create and support 2,300 jobs each year through its supply chain. The windfarms are expected to create a further 100 long-term permanent jobs when they are operational.

The energy company SSE also announced on Wednesday that the latest phase of its major offshore windfarm, Berwick Bank B off the east coast of Scotland, would “support” 2,600 existing jobs.

Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, said investment in offshore wind and clean power was “creating quality jobs and rebuilding industry, while delivering the clean power we need to lower bills and reach net zero”.

She added that Britain was “leading from the front as a renewable energy powerhouse”.

It comes as Burnham seeks to bolster his government’s under-fire green credentials at Cop31, where he is expected to give a speech on Thursday.

The prime minister has faced a backlash from Labour MPs and environmental campaigners over his government’s decision to approve the Jackdaw gasfield.

On Tuesday, ministers also rejected plans to build what would have been Britain’s biggest solar plant near the Blenheim Palace estate.

Fahnbulleh turned down the £800m Botley West project, which would have covered almost 3,500 acres of land. Developers said it would have provided enough electricity to power 330,000 homes.

Margaret Curran, in a letter on behalf of the energy secretary, wrote that the project would cause “substantial harm” to the green belt and the Blenheim Estate – home to Blenheim Palace, which is a world heritage site and the birthplace of Winston Churchill.

text:
The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) released A National Strategy for American Leadership in Batteries (the Strategy) in October 2026, organized around three objectives and six pillars aimed at rebuilding the domestic battery supply chain and accelerating commercialization of next-generation battery technologies. This Holland & Knight alert provides an overview of the Strategy and a look at where DOE's attention, and potentially its funding, may be headed next.

The National Strategy at a Glance

Objectives

Mine-to-Market: Establish a Continuous Domestic Value Chain by 2030

Discovery-to-Deployment: Achieve Technology and Manufacturing Leadership by 2035

Enable affordable, safe and reliable storage applications for the American public

Strategic Pillars

Target investments in the upstream and midstream supply chain steps

Accelerate commercial deployment of laboratory discoveries. Advance manufacturing innovation

Prioritize manufacturing process innovation

Mission-driven deployment for grid modernization

Coordinate national strategy with international partners

Invest in American talent

A Full-Aperture View of the Supply Chain

The Strategy takes a full view of the battery value chain. DOE acknowledges that recent investment has clustered in downstream cell and pack manufacturing, while upstream and midstream capacity still require significant investment. Under the Mine-to-Market objective, DOE calls for a continuous domestic value chain spanning upstream mining, midstream refining and engineered materials, and downstream cells, packs and end products, supported by domestic offtake of extracted resources, subcomponents and capital equipment. One of the Strategy's pillars commits DOE to prioritizing investment specifically in extraction, refining, recycling and equipment manufacturing. That explicit focus on extraction and refining is notable: It marks a departure from DOE's more traditional posture of funding downstream manufacturing and applied research, giving upstream and midstream players a clear signal of where DOE intends to direct resources.

Closing the "Valley of Death"

DOE identifies a long-standing funding gap between mid-stage research and near-mature commercial manufacturing, a persistent "valley of death" for new discoveries. The Strategy prioritizes funding for pilot, demonstration and validation facilities. To accelerate adoption, DOE is building manufacturability, scalability and market potential into how it evaluates early-stage applied research, considering cost and repeatability alongside scientific merit. DOE is also prioritizing investment in manufacturing process innovation itself, including continuous processing, super intelligence (SI)-enabled quality control and digital twins to boost factory yields. The Strategy's consistent message is that innovation in what gets made must be matched by innovation in how it gets made.

Supporting the Grid Through Reliable Storage

Finally, DOE responds to the surging energy demand now facing the grid, driven in large part by data centers and SI infrastructure. DOE commits to supporting the acceleration of affordable, safe and reliable storage technologies to help the grid absorb that growth, including a portfolio of fast-responding and long-duration storage assets that can add capacity faster than traditional infrastructure, strengthen resilience against extreme weather and other disruptions, and remain cybersecure as they scale.

The BattMan Accelerator: Putting the Strategy into Practice

Alongside the Strategy, DOE highlighted the BattMan Accelerator, which is led by Pacific Northwest National Laboratory with co-directors from Oak Ridge National Laboratory, the National Laboratory of the Rockies and Argonne National Laboratory.

BattMan provides end-to-end battery development capabilities, from advanced materials discovery and precursor development to pilot-scale materials processing, electrode manufacturing, cell prototyping and quality testing. It also supports workforce development through the University of Washington's I-BEAM certificate and master's degree programs.

Over time, BattMan aims to develop self-optimizing manufacturing systems that combine real-time process monitoring, SI, digital twins and closed-loop control to catch and correct manufacturing problems before they become costly scale-up failures. The consortium will also build industrial and academic partnerships to validate new manufacturing processes and accelerate deployment of commercially viable technologies.

What This Means for Funding and Engagement

Neither the Strategy nor the BattMan Accelerator comes with a corresponding notice of funding opportunity. Read together, however, the announcements make clear that battery technology, battery manufacturing and upstream material development are front of mind for DOE right now, and companies in those spaces should expect related funding opportunities to open over the next year, particularly around midstream supply chain gaps and manufacturing process innovation.

DOE has also been consistent in signaling that it wants industry and academic partners to use the national laboratories as a resource, including the technology and intellectual property the labs have developed as well as the labs themselves. Companies interested in future funding should strongly consider engaging with BattMan, the Critical Materials Innovation (CMI) Hub, Minerals to Materials Supply Chain Research Facility (METALLIC) or other national laboratory partnerships now, so those relationships are already in place when the next funding opportunity is announced.

Looking Ahead

DOE's Strategy and the BattMan Accelerator point to continued federal attention on battery supply chains and manufacturing. Companies operating anywhere along the value chain, from upstream mining and midstream materials to cell manufacturing and grid deployment, should begin conceptualizing projects now for the funding and partnership opportunities likely to follow.

“We’re pretty much at the mercy of world markets,” Chad Nordlum, who is the energy project manager for the Native Village of Kotzebue, told Grist. “Right now, with the Iran war going on, the diesel prices are very high and we’re locked in to much higher prices than we’ve had in the past. There’s really nothing the community can do about diesel prices, but what we can do is produce our own energy.”

That’s why Nordlum was so excited about a $20 million grant from the Environmental Protection Agency to support a wind energy project. The funding, announced in 2024, was part of a larger $150 million allocation for tribal infrastructure in Alaska. Nordlum says it would have lowered the community’s reliance on diesel to about 40 percent to 50 percent and given the tribe more control over energy and economic decisions.

But the Trump administration canceled the grant in May 2025. More than a year later, the project remains paused.

That cut was among hundreds of millions of dollars the Department of Government Efficiency pulled from Indian Country, and part of a broader pattern of funding rollbacks and underinvestment in Indigenous communities. Two new reports from the Brookings Institution show that the so-called One Big Beautiful Bill Act killed many of the funding streams established by the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act, while DOGE eliminated another $468 million, about half of which was allocated for environmental and natural resources. Another 11 percent targeted agriculture. Those projects include climate resiliency plans, renewable energy projects, and jobs programs.

According to Brookings, despite historic investments flowing into Indian Country after the pandemic, a massive underinvestment in Indigenous communities continues. Not only is that a violation of the federal government’s trust and treaty obligations to tribes, it is hindering Indigenous efforts to protect the environment and address climate change. The report authors are calling for policy changes that would ensure tribes receive funding, regardless of political winds.

Rob Maxim, who is Mashpee Wampanoag and a fellow at Brookings Metro, said climate and environmental funding is especially crucial for Indigenous communities because they are often the most severely impacted by climate change, especially after years of underinvestment.

“The actions that the Trump administration is taking are particularly significant, but it’s not totally out of trend with previous administrations,” he said. “And what we wanted to show was that actually this underinvestment is kind of the default for the U.S. rather than a blip.”

The true aberration was the unprecedented levels of funding after the pandemic. That funding, which came under the Biden administration, included over $700 million in climate, energy, and infrastructure funding for tribes. It covered projects like development of climate action plans, food systems analysis, and more. For example, the Hopi Tribe was to receive a $25 million grant to install solar panels for 600 homes. That grant, and the entire $7 billion Solar for All program, were cut.

Maxim says that funding for Indigenous communities is a federal obligation based on treaties and other agreements with tribes and should be standard and irrevocable. “The funding that was flowing to Indian Country was not being done on the basis of race or DEI, and it was absolutely not illegal,” he said. “It was aimed at the promotion of tribal sovereignty and the well-being of tribal citizens and tribal communities, and so that is, you know, an obligation that the U.S. government maintains.”

The White House did not respond to a request for comment. The EPA provided a comment several days after this story originally published Nov. 2.

“The Trump EPA is committed to ensuring taxpayer dollars are being used appropriately and has reviewed all funding activities with that lens. Through the agency’s General Assistance Program (GAP) and other granting programs, EPA has awarded more than $351 million in Tribal grants funding since the beginning of the second Trump administration,” the agency said in an email to Grist.

Glencora Haskins, a senior research associate and applied research manager at Brookings Metro, said that the administration had targeted funding to tribes, with “tribal” being the most frequently flagged term. “I think that there was a very surface-level view of what a lot of these programs were doing, rather than any deep interrogation of the types of systemic infrastructure deficits that programs were trying to fix,” Haskins said.

In Native communities throughout Alaska, and around the country, energy and infrastructure needs are especially acute because of increasingly frequent and destructive storms, wildfires, and other climate-driven disasters.

Haskins and Maxim recommend that Congress pass legislation that bars the cancellation of grants and contracts for tribes, and stipulates that all funding for Indigenous nations and communities is in service of trust and treaty obligations even if it is from a program with a different stated purpose. They also call for a statutory requirement that money should flow directly to tribes rather than having them seek reimbursement from the U.S. Treasury.

In Kotzebue, Chad Nordlum hopes the political tide will turn enough to get the funding for the wind project moving. In the meantime, he is working on a smaller solar project that he hopes will help alleviate the community’s energy challenges.

“Our main goals are energy security and economic development for the tribe, which is ultimately being able to invest in our own community, help make the lives of people here a little more sustainable,” Nordlum said. “We want our community to continue on into the future. We have to get a handle on our energy prices and availability.”

text:
Solar and energy storage developers face a changing landscape of federal policy on domestic manufacturing incentives, supply chain restrictions, and grid permitting as a newly elected Democratic congressional majority prepares to take office in January, according to Washington energy and tax analysts.

Speaking on the Norton Rose Fulbright Currents podcast hosted by partner Keith Martin, panelists Mike Catanzaro of CGCN Group, John Gimigliano of KPMG, J.C. Sandberg of the American Clean Power Association, Whitney Stanco of Compass Point Research and Trading, and Tom West of Capitol Tax Partners examined how divided government will shape federal support for utility-scale and distributed clean energy projects.

Domestic manufacturing incentives under Section 45X represent the most viable bipartisan opportunity for the solar and storage sector, said the panel. Under current law, Section 45X tax credits for U.S.-made solar modules, cells, wafers, inverters, and battery components begin phasing out after 2029.

Gimigliano and West indicated that lawmakers could extend the Section 45X timeline in a bipartisan tax package, provided Democrats agree to expand eligibility to technologies favored by Republicans.

Sandberg said extending Section 45X remains a top priority for the American Clean Power Association as a way “to continue the momentum the industry has had in reshoring” domestic supply chains.

Conversely, the panelists saw little near-term prospect of repealing Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC) supply chain restrictions or reviving the expired Section 25D residential solar tax credit.

West and Sandberg noted that while core prohibitions on Chinese equipment, intellectual property, and financing will remain intact, Congress could pass targeted technical corrections to clarify complex debt and equity compliance rules that have complicated solar and storage project financing.

“There are some things that could be fine-tuned to make it more workable in the marketplace that aren’t being soft on China but are being realistic about how these deals get transacted,” Sandberg said.

Tax equity investors and corporate tax credit buyers are also closely watching the Base Erosion and Anti-Abuse Tax (BEAT). Beginning in 2026, clean energy tax credits claimed by large corporations with foreign affiliates lost their 20% clawback cap and became exposed to a full clawback, threatening liquidity in the solar and storage tax credit transfer market.

Gimigliano suggested that Democrats plan to revisit international tax rules next year and could restore BEAT relief if framed as support for domestic clean energy deployment rather than a corporate tax cut.

“If you view it as relief for the renewable sector, it feels better, doesn’t it?” Gimigliano said. “I think it’s all about how it’s sold.”

Extending the July 4, 2026 construction-start deadline for utility-scale solar tax credits under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act faces steeper odds., said the panel.

While standalone battery storage retained its longer credit runway under the law, utility-scale solar projects that missed the July 4 threshold face a strict end-of-2027 placed-in-service cutoff. Senate and House Democratic leaders support extending the construction deadline, though Gimigliano noted that passing an extension before 2029 would likely require trading for White House priorities such as permanent tax exemptions on tips or Social Security.

In the near term, solar and storage projects stand to benefit from a 400-page bipartisan permitting reform bill currently before the Senate during the lame-duck session, which Stanco gave roughly 45% odds of passing both chambers before year-end. For solar and battery developers, the legislation streamlines National Environmental Policy Act and Clean Water Act reviews, strengthens federal backstop siting authority for interregional transmission, and includes dedicated provisions for distributed energy resources.

“The U.S. was always kind of seen as the place where, despite political winds and the topsy-turvy nature of it, if you had a permit, that permit was investable, and I think this package takes a big step toward that,” Sandberg said.

The permitting package also establishes “project certainty” guardrails prohibiting federal agencies from discriminating against specific energy technologies relative to a five-year historical baseline. Catanzaro and Sandberg noted that solar projects awaiting federal land approvals have lagged behind other technologies and require faster federal processing to meet rising power demand.

At the executive level, solar and storage developers are awaiting Department of Energy guidance on the August 26 Bulk Power System executive order, which restricts imports and use of grid equipment tied to foreign adversaries, a measure with direct implications for inverters, transformers, and battery energy storage systems. Ahead of a December 24 guidance deadline, industry groups are holding meetings with federal officials to advocate for targeted, risk-based boundaries and workable compliance transition periods.

State-level pushback against data center development could also reshape where and how solar-plus-storage projects are built in 2027. Catanzaro noted that 46 of 47 local ballot measures targeting data centers passed with restrictive outcomes, while newly elected Democratic governors in major growth markets like Texas, Ohio, and Georgia may pursue moratoriums or tighter siting guardrails.

At the same time, the federal permitting bill empowers states to establish less favorable utility rate classes for large computational loads, reinforcing the push for hyperscalers to pair data centers with dedicated behind-the-meter or co-located solar and storage generation.

“I still believe we’re going to build data centers in the United States, and it’s a slope that’s up and to the right,” Stanco said. “I just think that slope may be a little more gentle than what people were thinking at the beginning of this year, and that 2027 could be some time of regulatory friction.”

text:
Big Law firms are capitalizing on the demand for solar and battery projects, as developers look for new power sources to fuel artificial intelligence data centers.

Latham & Watkins’ Texas lawyers have handled about 40% more solar and battery storage deals this year than in the previous five years combined. To meet demand across the energy sector, it has added more than 50 lawyers statewide this year.

“We are in an unprecedented time in Texas with a simultaneous uptick in oil and gas, LNG and renewables, along with a wave of incremental work generated by the AI infrastructure buildout,” said Justin Stolte, a Houston partner and global chair of Latham’s energy and infrastructure group.

Houston-based Vinson & Elkins signed or closed 32 deals involving battery storage since October 2025, up 28% from 25 in the previous 12 months, the firm said. It has hired 19 lateral partners firmwide this year, most with traditional and renewable energy experience.

The boom is changing the business of Texas Big Law. The solar and battery projects are driving the need for billable hours at the development, financing and sales stages. Clients are also looking for lawyers who understand tax credits and construction contracts — and firms are staffing up to meet the demand.

“We never needed more construction, more capital improvements than we do right now,” said David Strickland, White & Case’s co-head of global project development and finance, referring to lawyers with those specialties. On Oct. 15, the firm named 47 partners globally effective Jan.1, including its largest US class since 2022. Among the promotions were Houston project finance lawyers Samer Mahjoub and Jack Moxon.

Latham this month hired five energy partners including Houston-based Chase Armbrust, who has worked on utility-scale and distributed solar projects, and Jessica Adkins, who works on renewable energy and electric power deals, the firm said.

Good Timing

Expiring federal tax credits for solar projects are helping to drive the Big Law demand.

Last year’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act strips federal credits from solar and wind projects that didn’t start construction by July 4, 2026, unless they produce power by Dec. 31, 2027. The deadlines have driven a surge in solar financings and sales, Stolte said.

In February and March, Latham helped Origis Energy raise about $885 million for a 413-megawatt solar project in West Texas. In February, Latham advised TPG on a majority stake in Sabre Industries, a supplier to utilities and data centers in Alvarado, Texas, in a deal valuing Sabre at about $3.5 billion.

A tax credit for standalone storage in the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act also prompted developers to start building project pipelines in late 2022 and 2023, said Josh Heideman, a Los Angeles Vinson & Elkins tax partner who has worked on many of the deals. Many of those projects are coming online now, as data centers flock to Texas.

The centers need power 99.99% of the time, and batteries store solar and wind energy until it’s needed, Heideman said. The batteries also supply power while a site waits years for a grid connection, then smooth out spikes in its use, he said.

“Battery storage and data centers turned out to be a natural fit,” he said. “The result is a lot of demand for storage and a lot of financing activity around it.”

Growing Demand

Matthew Falcone, a Vinson & Elkins M&A partner in Houston, said he expects four or five deals this year in which batteries make up a significant share of the value. In years past, the Texas portfolios his clients bought and sold were mostly solar and wind farms, he said.

Texas accounts for 53% of the 24 gigawatts of battery storage planned nationwide this year and should get about 40% of new US solar capacity, the Energy Information Administration reported.

Requests to connect data centers and other large power users to the Texas grid now exceed 460 gigawatts, about five times the grid’s record demand, according to Modo Energy, which tracks battery markets.

White & Case’s solar matters in the Americas jumped 105% from 2023 to 2026, and battery storage matters rose 69%. “This growth cycle has gone on longer and been more heated than everybody expected, and it just seems to be never ending,” Strickland said.

In July, a Kirkland & Ellis team led by Houston partners advised Blackstone-backed Aypa Power, which Kirkland calls North America’s largest standalone battery storage developer, on its roughly $7 billion sale to Brookfield. In May, Norton Rose Fulbright lawyers in Houston and Austin advised Bimergen Energy on transferring three planned Texas battery projects totaling 480 megawatt-hours to an affiliate of Frontier Power USA.

The politics may get harder. Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who won the Texas governor’s race on Nov. 3, campaigned on an immediate moratorium on data center development and accused developers of raising utility rates, Bloomberg News reported. She called Republican Gov. Greg Abbott’s moves to rein in data center operations “nothing more than an election year stunt.”

Strickland said he expects the result to shift timelines, not demand. “Some projects may move faster and others may take longer, but the underlying drivers of demand remain strong,” he said.

text:
The UK car industry is preparing to push for a two-year delay to Brexit tariffs on electric cars traded with the EU, after an initial European proposal suggested a shorter delay.

Tariffs are due to kick in on 1 January for the majority of electric cars traded between the EU and UK unless the two sides can come to an agreement to delay for a second time the implementation of “rules of origin” on batteries.

The Brexit deal, which was rushed through on Christmas Eve in 2020, included a clause that British and European electric cars would have to use batteries made in either the UK or the EU with local materials, or face 10% tariffs. The rules would not have existed had the UK remained in the EU.

The rules were initially meant to come into force on 1 January 2024, encouraging the industry to invest in local lithium-ion battery manufacturing rather than relying on the dominant Chinese battery industry. In 2020, the prospects seemed rosy, but three years later several prominent projects on both sides of the Channel had collapsed. The EU and UK agreed to extend the deadline in December 2023.

Other battery projects have since taken their place, but many are yet to produce at the scale required to meet European demand. Instead, carmakers are mainly reliant on imports from China, Japan and South Korea.

Carmakers in the UK and Europe are united in their calls for the introduction of the rules of origin to be delayed again. However, an agreement has yet to be reached, with the EU and UK also wrangling over whether Britain can be included in “Made in Europe” subsidies, and whether the UK should match EU tariffs on Chinese car imports. The topics are likely to form part of an EU-UK summit planned for next week.

The European Commission has shared proposals with the automotive industry to delay the start of the tariffs, although they have not yet been shared formally with the UK government. The proposals are understood to be highly technical, but essentially equate to delaying the start of the rules of origin by a year.

Some of the proposals are understood to include adjusting customs procedures and origin calculation methodologies, which could offer some temporary tariff flexibility.

However, some parts of the UK car industry believe more time is needed for the sector to adapt and for battery gigafactories to churn out enough units.

One executive in the UK said: “The industry will be really clear – two years minimum or we have the same discussion next year. Giga-industrialisation is happening in the EU and UK but it is not producing at the required volume yet.”

Another person said the negotiations would also focus on the technical details of the proposals, rather than simply aiming for a set time delay.

The European Automobile Manufacturers Association, an influential lobby group in Brussels, has argued that the tariffs are a serious concern for Europe’s automotive industry. It estimated that 82% of EU electric car and van exports to the UK would face the 10% customs duty in 2027 under the rules, adding costs of €1.47bn (£1.23bn) next year alone.

Mike Hawes, the chief executive of the UK lobby group SMMT, said: “The UK and EU must urgently agree pragmatic solutions to the challenges of Made in Europe and EV rules of origin, which if unresolved will cause severe damage to our deeply integrated industries.

“For the latter, any agreement must remove the massive tariff liability faced on electrified vehicles traded from 1 January, be workable for manufacturers on both sides and protect ongoing battery investment. Meaningful consultation with the UK industry is essential to ensure any solution delivers in practice.”
