text:
Why It Matters

Southwest Power Pool Inc. signed a new client registration on Nov. 5 with Williams & Jensen PLLC, putting Southwest Power Pool lobbying on the federal record under the Energy/Nuclear and Utilities issue areas. The filing lists one specific issue, "Southwest Power Pool's Market Initiative," and carries a $0 filing amount and no bills. ​

The registration lists three Williams & Jensen lobbyists: Chester Fields, George Baker and Dan Ziegler. It reports a registration date of Oct. 1. The filing lists Fields with experience in the office of Rep. Ron DeSantis (R-FL).

Broader Context

Recent federal energy activity involving Southwest Power Pool (SPP) bears on the registered issue areas, according to the sources below.

The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) accepted SPP's proposal for new study processes for High Impact Large Loads on Jan. 15.

SPP reported on March 13 that FERC approved its Consolidated Planning Process, which SPP said is intended to give developers more cost certainty.

SPP and the California Independent System Operator filed a joint report with FERC on Oct. 1 on near-term work on data exchange, model alignment and transmission constraints.

The U.S. Department of Energy issued orders on July 26 and Aug. 3 under Federal Power Act section 202(c) directing SPP to dispatch specified generation, according to the department.

Between The Lines

Rep. Lauren Boebert (R-CO) issued a press release on Oct. 6 praising a Department of Energy order directing Southwest Power Pool to keep the Craig Unit 1 coal plant available through Dec. 25. The release frames the order as necessary for grid reliability and baseload power.

At a July 22 Energy and Natural Resources Committee hearing, Judy Chang of FERC said the commission recently approved an SPP proposal that gives generators cost certainty on interconnection. Sen. John Barrasso (R-WY) asked what steps FERC will take to ensure states like Wyoming have a meaningful voice as SPP expands into the West.

Advertisement

Competitive Landscape

Two other organizations registered through other firms on both issue areas: Treaty Oak Clean Energy LLC signed with Continental Strategy LLC on Nov. 4, and PPC North America Corp. signed with Capitol Counsel LLC on Oct. 28. ON Energy Storage Inc. signed with Venn Strategies LLC on Nov. 5 on utilities.

The Bottom Line

The registration puts a three-person Williams & Jensen team on record for the grid operator's market initiative before federal offices. It names no bills.

text:
On Monday, the Senate voted 73-25 to advance permitting legislation, known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), that aims to expedite the approval of new energy projects, including for both fossil fuels and renewable energy. The legislation was authored by Senators Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Martin Heinrich (D-NM), Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV), and Mike Lee (R-UT).

Supporters of the legislation are framing it as a way to lower energy costs for Americans and reduce red tape. But critics of the legislation, including many environmental groups, argue that it would also weaken key environmental laws, undermine tribal protections, facilitate more data center construction, and depend on the Trump administration to implement it fairly.

The legislation provides the fossil fuel industry with some ironclad wins. For example, the legislation limits the ability for people to challenge projects under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) by requiring lawsuits to be filed within 150 days of the project’s approval. In order to sue, people would have also had to participate in the project’s public comment period. Furthermore, if a court finds a NEPA violation, it cannot cancel a permit, but can only send it back to the agency.

The legislation also weakens states’ abilities to block permitted projects that could impact water quality. State regulators would be required to “prove they would cause harm,” rather than “requiring pipeline companies and other developers to show their projects would protect water quality,” according to Inside Climate News. State regulators would have to provide “clear and convincing evidence” before denying certification.

While the legislation also contains provisions that could benefit renewable energy, many depend on implementation by the Trump administration. For example, the Trump administration would be responsible for making permitting available for renewables.

The legislation states that “all Federal agencies shall treat all applications for Federal authorizations or permits fairly and efficiently.” But the bill makes it difficult for those denied permits to prove wrongdoing. It requires filing a lawsuit that proves the project was “denied in bad faith as part of a pattern of disparate treatment by the Federal Government against the specific type of covered project at issue.” Critically, “[s]tatements, policies, Executive orders, or other guidance” that express support for or opposition to a type of project but are unrelated to permitting could not be considered evidence.

President Trump has championed the legislation, calling it “a BIG WIN for U.S. ENERGY INDEPENDENCE and DOMINANCE.” But Trump has already pledged that no wind projects will be approved. “I will not approve wind turbines because wind turbines are a major loser,” Trump told reporters.

Whitehouse has said that passage of the legislation relies on support for wind projects from the Trump administration. On Tuesday, Whitehouse dismissed Trump’s comments, stating that, “As long as the agencies continue to come through with the representations and promises that they have made — and we will see more of that in the next few days — then on we go, and we chalk that up to him being 80.” Counting on administration officials to disobey Trump is a dubious strategy.

The legislation was advanced without any public hearings. A rewritten version of the bill, which is 494 pages long, was released on Saturday, giving legislators little time to review before the vote on Monday. Republicans are in a rush to pass the legislation before the new Democrat-controlled Congress is sworn in.

If the legislation passes the Senate, it will then need to pass the House. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA) said that he expects the House to pass the bill. But with a razor-thin majority, it will likely require Democratic votes. A spokesperson for House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY) told Politico last week that the bill “falls short in several areas.”

Democrats could wait and hope to refine the legislation when they have control of Congress next session. But Whitehouse argued that it would be harder to pass next year, stating that “there’s no guarantee Congress would ever find another compromise that would be able to pass the Senate.”

Data centers pay more, but still come out on top

In last week’s midterm election, voters demonstrated strong opposition to data centers. There were 40 ballot measures across the country to ban or restrict data center construction and 38 of them passed. Exit polls showed that 76% of voters would oppose a new data center in their community and 56% of voters considered AI and data centers as a crucial or major factor in how they voted for Congress.

While voters made their opinion on data centers clear, the legislation’s approach to the issue is muddled.

The bill would require data centers to pay for the full cost of adding additional energy capacity, instead of passing the cost on to ratepayers and driving up utility bills. Studies have shown that this would raise costs for data centers by $35 billion over the next decade while household utility bills would decrease by up to $78 per year by 2040.

While the ratepayer protection provision is costly for data centers, critics of the bill say that it is an overall win for the data center industry. Allie Rosenbluth, the U.S. campaigns manager for Oil Change International, an environmental nonprofit, said the bill was a “massive giveaway“ for data centers that could increase fossil fuel usage.

Data centers require massive amounts of power, and in many cases, new data centers have been built alongside new gas power plants to fuel them. The legislation’s permitting changes will make it easier for data center owners to build these power sources and thus make it easier to build new data centers. The legislation’s environmental review and tribal consultation provisions could also expedite approval of proposals for data centers on public land, of which there are currently at least 17.

The legislation has been endorsed by the Corporate Energy Buyers Association and the Electricity Customer Alliance, two industry groups that represent major data center users like Google and Meta.

Who supports the permitting bill and who opposes it

A broad coalition of industry groups is hailing the legislation as a win.

The U.S. Chamber of Commerce issued a letter encouraging Congress to pass the legislation, calling it a “historic opportunity to modernize a system that too often delays progress and drives up costs.” Hundreds of local chambers of commerce and other industry groups signed onto the letter.

Darren Woods, chairman and CEO of ExxonMobil, said, “We support the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026. America cannot build the energy projects it needs if approvals take years and outcomes remain uncertain.” The American Petroleum Institute, with 137 other fossil fuel industry groups, signed onto a letter urging the passage of the bill.

Jason Grumet, CEO of the American Clean Power Association, said the bill would “substantially increase the deployment of clean resources.” A handful of environmental groups have backed the bill, including Evergreen Action.

Most environmental organizations, however, oppose the legislation. Hundreds of other environmental organizations have sent letters to congressional leaders expressing concerns with the bill. Sierra Club Executive Director Loren Blackford said, “As written, this bill achieves critical wins on transmission and potential emissions reduction. However, this does not justify abandoning Tribal consultation, clean water safeguards, and wildlife protections, nor further enabling a rogue president that is waging a war on clean energy.”

The bill has also been criticized by Native American organizations who argue that the bill does not go far enough to protect tribal sovereignty. A letter signed by 10 tribal organizations says the bill “disregards the sovereign rights of Tribal Nations.”

Democratic senators who voted against advancing the bill, including Ed Markey of Massachusetts and Ben Ray Luján of New Mexico, have expressed concern over the threat to tribal sovereignty posed by the bill. Additionally, Senator Catherine Cortez Masto (D-NV) voted to advance the bill this week, but said she would not support it in a final vote unless the provisions related to tribal sovereignty were changed. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY) also supported making changes to the bill during the amendment process.

text:
The Environmental Protection Agency has proposed a rollback of federal methane regulations but oil and gas sector analysts warned it could pose a significant threat to public health.Methane is considered both a “super pollutant” and a major cause of climate change, trapping 80 times as much heat in the atmosphere in the short term as carbon dioxide.Mary Sasso, attorney for the global science nonprofit Clean Air Task Force, said even states like Maine, which are far from oil and gas wells, would suffer from increased emissions tied to respiratory illnesses, birth defects and cancer.

“The language they seem incredibly preoccupied with – the profitability of oil and gas companies – so much so that the proposal almost completely ignores the health and welfare of communities and workers,” Sasso contended.

President Donald Trump called the Biden-era rules “unnecessary” and said their removal would help boost domestic energy production and lower consumer prices. Sasso noted while companies would save on compliance costs, methane leaks are a waste of natural gas which could otherwise be used to heat American homes.

Some large oil and gas companies have said they are committed to limiting methane emissions and have invested in technologies to reduce well and pipeline leaks but the EPA’s proposal focuses heavily on older, so-called “low-producing” wells, which, despite their name, account for roughly half of methane emissions in the oil and gas sector.

Sasso argued if the proposal is finalized, it would give states a pass on implementing their own plans to target methane and limit the ability of states like Maine to reach their ambitious climate goals.

“What that means for those of us who rely on natural gas to get through difficult heating seasons is that we are now being forced to use dirtier gas than we would have otherwise had access to,” Sasso asserted.

While some states, like Colorado, have moved to codify the Biden administration’s methane rules, Sasso pointed out others would see an opening to further deregulate industries. She added compressor stations, which maintain the flow of natural gas throughout New England, could also allow for greater emissions.

description:
Commenting on today’s speech by the Prime Minister Andy Burnham at COP31 in Turkey, RenewableUK’s Executive Director of Policy Ana Musat said: “The Prime Minister is right to highlight the fact that the shift to clean energy is the best route to lower bills and increase energy security, and the electrification of heat and transport is the best way to protect families and businesses from global fossil fuel price shocks.
“His commitment to the UK’s world-leading offshore wind industry is clear, as he noted that the major wind farms going ahead off the coast of East Anglia, RWE’s Vanguard East and West, will bring billions in private investment, power three million homes and support thousands of jobs.
“It’s great to see him announcing support for the Amplify programme which aims to secure £5 billion of new private finance for clean energy projects around the world.
He pointed out that the City of London is adept at galvanising investment and, with judicious support from the Government, the private sector is doing the heavy lifting when it comes to financing vital new clean energy infrastructure to keep Britain, and the world, powered up.
“We welcome the Prime Minister’s long-term pledge of a new era of British leadership on climate change action over the next decade, and we look forward to him setting out his Ten-Year Plan before the end of the year, in which renewables will undoubtedly play a central role in tackling the cost-of-living crisis and creating further jobs throughout the UK”.

title: Texas Democrats promised to rein in data centers. Now they have their chance - KUT
description:

text:
A year ago artificial intelligence and the large data center buildings they require to operate were a welcome fixture in Texas’ tech industry. In the midterms, they were a driving force for some residents to get out and vote blue.

Some Texans raised concerns about the facilities' enormous electricity demands, their potential impact on already strained water resources and the disruption that large-scale construction can bring to small towns.

Now that Democrats hold every top leadership position in the state and have control over the Texas House, what can they deliver to voters who want restrictions on the industry?

How Texas got here

In November 2025, Gov. Greg Abbott was calling Texas the epicenter of artificial intelligence development.

For roughly a decade, Abbott worked to make the state an attractive destination for new business. Tax breaks, business-friendly policies and a relatively permissive regulatory environment helped make Texas a desirable, and affordable, place for companies to build the massive facilities that power AI.

But as data centers have expanded across the state, public outcry began to get louder.

In the lead-up to the midterm elections, Abbott began changing his tone.

In July, he said it was time to start “pushing back against these AI data centers that are trying to build in our neighborhoods.”

Then, in September, he announced a pause on approvals for new data center permits until they participated in a new state audit. Before new facilities could connect to Texas' power grid, Abbott said developers would have to demonstrate they could manage their impact on power, water and infrastructure.

But critics were skeptical, saying Abbott's actions didn’t involve a clear timeline or enforcement policies and didn’t apply to most mid-size data center projects proposed in the state.

Gov. elect and then-candidate Gina Hinojosa said outright that she thought the audit was a political ploy.

“That only is an attempt to protect his election chances, not the people of Texas,” Hinojosa said in September.

Data centers were also a focus of her campaign. She pledged to freeze electricity rates and make corporations, including data center developers, pay their fair share.

What Hinojosa can do — and what will require lawmakers' buy-in

Hinojosa made three major promises related to data centers while campaigning. She said she would establish a moratorium on new development, end tax breaks for the industry and ensure local communities have a say in whether facilities are built.

At least one of those should be relatively easy to accomplish.

“I think that there's an expectation that the governor-elect will extend the moratorium and potentially strengthen it,” said John Hall, president and CEO of the Houston Advanced Research Center, an organization focused on environmental policy analysis.

Hall said extending the moratorium is largely within the governor's authority. In September, Abbott's pause on data center development began as part of an executive order.

The other promises will be more complicated.

Despite Democrats being in these top leadership positions and having the majority in the Texas House, Republicans will still control the state's Senate. The two chambers have struggled to find common ground in previous legislative sessions.

But data centers could be an exception.

“Data centers have brought together a bipartisan coalition of people,” Hall said.

Initiatives like ending tax incentives and giving communities more influence over development will likely require bipartisan support from the Texas Legislature.

Opposition appears to extend beyond party lines. In May, a Gallup News poll found that seven in 10 Americans disapproved of data centers being built in their communities.

“I have worked on water and environmental issues since 1983, and heretofore there has never been the level of bipartisan concern like exists on data centers,” Hall said.

That concern, he said, could create an opportunity for lawmakers to pursue new environmental regulations, including requiring data centers to meet the same air-quality standards as other industries, regulating carbon emissions and requiring greater transparency about their environmental impacts.

The role of state regulators

Even if lawmakers agree on new rules, the governor's ability to implement them will depend partly on the state agencies responsible for overseeing the industry; the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) and the Public Utilities Commission of Texas (PUC).

Sandra Haverlah, president of the Texas Consumer Association, said Abbott was able to get state agencies to comply with the audit he announced in September in part because their leadership had been appointed by him.

Members of both commissions serve six-year terms so, Hinojosa won't be able to appoint anyone to either board for some time. She might be able to appoint someone to the TCEQ board as soon as January, or her first appointment might not happen until September 2027.

In the meantime, Haverlah said, cooperation between the governor's office, state agencies and lawmakers will be important.

“Hopefully, what happens is that all the entities work together with the Legislature because appointees are still political people too,” she said.

Hinojosa has signaled she intends to facilitate that cooperation.

“We can have a strong economy, strong industry, and protections for the people of Texas. Those things are not mutually exclusive, and I'll make sure as governor I lead to ensure that that happens,” she said in an interview with CNN following the election.

Data center developers are preparing for a new political landscape

Leadership within the AI industry seem to hear the drumbeats of change too.

OpenAI Chief Financial Officer Sarah Friar said the company is focused on raising more money and strengthening relationships with existing data center operators during an interview with CNBC just days after the election.

“When I think about the midterms, I need to keep thinking about how do we keep investing to meet that customer demand,” Friar said. “But it also means we're gonna keep building out those relationships with communities.”

The election results reflect a broader shift in how communities across the country are approaching data center development.

Of 41 data center-focused ballot measures across 10 states, all but one succeeded in reining in the industry.

In a statement emailed to KUT News, the Data Center Coalition, a key industry lobbying group in the state, said it “looks forward to working with state leadership along with local officials, stakeholders, and Texas communities to continue building trust and supporting responsible data center growth.”

But energy policy experts say a change in state leadership is unlikely to stop projects that are already underway.

“Everything that's under development and construction right now will continue,” said Michael Webber, the former deputy director of the Energy Institute at the University of Texas at Austin. “It's really hard and expensive to stop projects that are partway through. But the process for new data centers might be a little different.”

Webber said efforts to reverse existing tax breaks and other financial incentives negotiated under Abbott could be unprecedented and potentially illegal.

The bigger question, he said, is what happens to the next wave of development.

Webber said the goal of new regulations shouldn't necessarily be to stop data center development altogether.

The facilities can bring economic benefits to communities, including jobs for skilled workers and additional funding through property taxes for public services such as libraries, parks, schools and courthouses.

“I think the goal for me … isn't to stop data centers because they offer a lot of economic upsides,” Webber said. “We just need to make sure it's operating with the lowest environmental impact possible.”

text:
Congressional Democrats have alerted more than 60 companies, individuals and agencies that they are potential targets of investigations into the Trump administration’s cuts to scientific research, rollback of environmental protections and pursuit of unorthodox business deals.

The letters reveal where Democrats, soon to be empowered with subpoena authority after their sweeping wins in last week’s elections, intend to focus as they examine some of the administration’s most unabashed deals and policy changes. The notices sent from top Democrats on two key House committees demand preservation of any documents that could be relevant to congressional oversight next year.

The attempt to dismantle one of the world’s leading climate and weather research institutions, a lucrative White House deal with a rare earths company and an organized campaign to delegitimize climate science ahead of a sweeping regulatory rollback are among the concerns related to letters sent by the House Science Committee Thursday morning and reviewed by The New York Times.

“This administration has engaged in an assault on the science enterprise in this country,” said Representative Zoe Lofgren, Democrat of California, who is expected to chair the House Science Committee next year. “There have been firings, coercing people to resign, impounding money and possible corruption.”

text:
New equipment is piling up at Tesla's lithium refinery near Robstown, Texas — and the latest aerial footage suggests the facility isn't done growing. Independent drone operator Joe Tegtmeyer captured the site on November 12, 2026, en route to Starbase for Starship Flight 15, continuing his regular tradition of overflying the plant. The images and video show hardware that wasn't present in prior passes, pointing to active construction or expansion work at a facility that only reached full operational capacity four months ago.

▶ Watch Video on X

Where the Plant Stands Today

To understand why new equipment matters here, it helps to know how far this facility has come in a short time. Tesla broke ground in May 2023 on a 1,200-plus-acre site outside Corpus Christi. Initial production began in December 2024, and the plant officially commenced operations in January 2026. By July 2026 — during an event Tesla called Lithium Day 2026 — the company announced the refinery had reached full integrated operational capacity.

That capacity is rated at approximately 20,000 metric tons of battery-grade lithium hydroxide monohydrate annually, according to verified reporting. Tesla says that's enough to support roughly 30 GWh of battery production, or somewhere between 500,000 and 1 million electric vehicles per year. The $1 billion-plus investment also introduced a proprietary acid-free alkaline leaching process that Tesla claims cuts greenhouse gas emissions by over 30% and reduces reagent costs by 60% versus conventional refining methods.

Already Feeding the Production Line

The plant isn't just operational in name. According to previous reporting, the first Cybertruck built with 4680 cells containing lithium from this Gulf Coast refinery rolled off the Giga Texas line on September 4, 2026. The first Cybercab produced using in-house manufactured cathode material from Giga Texas also draws on this lithium supply, as does the Tesla Semi. Battery materials move directly from the Robstown refinery to Giga Texas for 4680 cell production — a domestic supply chain loop that Tesla has been building toward since the plant was announced.

What the New Equipment Suggests

Tesla has never publicly announced a Phase 2 expansion for the Robstown plant, so the accumulating equipment Tegtmeyer documented doesn't have an official explanation yet. But the site's 1,200-plus-acre footprint was always conspicuously large for a single-phase 20,000-ton-per-year operation — a scale that strongly implied future expansion was planned from the start. New equipment arriving at an already-operational facility typically signals either capacity additions, process upgrades, or infrastructure for a new production line.

Given that Tesla's vehicle output is scaling with Cybercab ramp and continued Cybertruck production, demand on the 4680 supply chain — and by extension the lithium refinery — will only increase. The Robstown site's combination of available land, existing infrastructure, and direct logistics ties to Giga Texas makes it the logical place to expand domestic lithium processing if Tesla needs more throughput.

Tegtmeyer has been one of the most consistent aerial observers of this site since construction began, making his footage a useful baseline for tracking changes over time. Whether this latest equipment represents a modest capacity upgrade or the beginning of a larger expansion phase, the activity confirms the plant remains in active development — not simply running at steady state.

text:
The Wright brothers accomplished their famous first flight at Kitty Hawk, N.C., in 1903. With advanced air mobility (AAM) travel right around the corner, will 2026 be remembered as another watershed year for aviation, with Florida leading the way? Conditions look increasingly favorable for takeoff.

FLORIDA TREND Executive Editor Amy Keller recently wrote about her first-ever Waymo ride in Miami ["Tomorrowland," July 2026]. Waymo, for the uninitiated, is a ride-share service that uses autonomous, electric-powered vehicles to ferry passengers around a growing number of cities, mostly in the Sunbelt (including Orlando and Tampa). These driverless "robotaxis" are fitted with a suite of cameras, GPS receivers and light detection and ranging (lidar) sensors that help them navigate urban streets.

But what if those cars were fitted with small rotors and could fly, taking off vertically, a la The Jetsons? And what if you could hop into one for an airborne commute to work or school, to get to an important meeting, or to visit friends and family in a nearby city, all while avoiding congested streets and highways?

That future might be closer than you think. Airports and cities around Florida are studying ways to offer AAM service, which would include electric vertical takeoff and landing vehicles (eVTOLs) and facilities known as vertiports — air-taxi terminals, essentially.

"Florida will be the No. 1 state in the country for eVTOLs within a decade," declares former Republican state Sen. Jeff Brandes, a licensed pilot who's made AAM a priority of the Florida Policy Project, a St. Petersburg-based think tank he launched after leaving politics.

In fact, Florida could become the nation's first state to launch a commercial AAM network following the Florida Department of Transportation's selection for the federal government's three-year eVTOL Integration Pilot Program (eIPP) that launched in March. The eIPP, according to the FAA, will form public-private partnerships to safely regulate AAM operations — and competition is fierce.

"There are other places, like New York and Chicago and Los Angeles, that are vying for this as well," says Brett Fay, vice president of general aviation at Tampa International Airport, "but I think Florida makes a very good case and will certainly be one of the initial launch markets, depending on who the operator may be."

FDOT Secretary Jared Perdue is a fan of air taxis coming to Florida, referring to the state as "the target market for AAM (and) vertiport development." In fact, the agency has already mapped out "highways in the sky" — routes that roughly follow the state's interstate highway corridors.

FDOT envisions a multiphased approach to the creation of the state's aerial avenues, with AAM infrastructure first being built out along Interstate 4 between Tampa and Orlando. That would be followed by Port St. Lucie to Miami, Tampa to Naples, Miami to Key West and then Pensacola to Tallahassee. The second phase would see AAM routes developed from Daytona Beach to Jacksonville, Sebring to the east and west coasts, Orlando to Lake City, Tampa to Tallahassee and finally Jacksonville to Tallahassee.

"The state has been a real leader when it comes to this," says former St. Petersburg City Council member and U.S. Air Force pilot Ed Montanari, who chaired a local task force that put together a plan for AAM in the city. "We relied a lot upon state documents because we wanted to align what the state is doing and what the city of St. Petersburg is recommending." (See sidebar on page 90.)

Even as Florida accelerates its transition toward air taxi adoption, significant regulatory, infrastructure and public acceptance hurdles remain. Following is a closer look at some of the key challenges and recent developments shaping the industry across the Sunshine State.

From Highways to Skyways

The Florida Department of Transportation envisions a network of low-altitude flight corridors for air taxis, cargo drones and emergency vehicles that will be developed in several phases.

PHASE ONE

PHASE 1A: CENTRAL FLORIDA I-4 CORRIDOR

City Centers: Sarasota, St. Petersburg/Clearwater, Tampa, Lakeland, Auburndale, Sebring, Kissimmee, Orlando, Cocoa/Melbourne, Daytona Beach

Airports: Sarasota Bradenton International Airport, St. Pete-Clearwater International Airport, Tampa International Airport, Tampa Executive Airport, Lakeland Linder International Airport, SunTrax, Sebring Regional Airport, Kissimmee Gateway Airport, Orlando International Airport, Orlando Executive Airport, Orlando Sanford International Airport, Space Coast Regional Airport, Melbourne Orlando International Airport, Daytona Beach International Airport

PHASE 1B: PORT ST. LUCIE TO MIAMI

City Centers: Port St. Lucie, Stuart, West Palm Beach, Fort Lauderdale, Opa-locka, Miami

Airports: Treasure Coast International Airport, Witham Field Airport, Palm Beach International Airport, Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport, Miami-Opa locka Executive Airport, Miami International Airport, Miami Executive Airport

PHASE 1C: TAMPA TO NAPLES / MIAMI TO KEY WEST

City Centers: Fort Myers, Naples, Homestead, Marathon, Key West

Airports: Southwest Florida International Airport, Naples Municipal Airport, Homestead Air Reserve Base, Florida Keys Marathon International Airport, Key West International Airport

PHASE 1D: PENSACOLA TO TALLAHASSEE

City Centers: Pensacola, Tallahassee

Airports: Pensacola International Airport, Tallahassee International Airport

PHASE TWO

PHASE 2A: DAYTONA BEACH TO JACKSONVILLE

City Centers: St. Augustine, Jacksonville

Airports: Northeast Florida Regional Airport, Jacksonville International Airport

PHASE 2B: SEBRING OUT EAST AND WEST

PHASE 2C: ORLANDO TO LAKE CITY / TAMPA TO TALLAHASSEE

City Centers: Gainesville, Lake City, Inverness, Williston, Cross City, Perry

Airports: Gainesville Regional Airport, Lake City Gateway Airport, Inverness Airport, Williston Regional Airport, Cross City Airport, Perry-Foley Airport

PHASE 2D: JACKSONVILLE TO TALLAHASSEE

PROGRESS

Test Track

As Florida Trend's Mike Brassfield wrote in our previous look at the nascent AAM industry ["Sky-High Ambitions," May 2024], "It's not every day that the government has to deal with a whole new mode of transportation." It will take a village to raise eVTOLs, so the eIPP, according to the FAA, "will form public-private partnerships with state, local, tribal and territorial government entities and private companies to develop new frameworks and regulations for enabling safe AAM operations."

More than 30 proposals from across the country were submitted; the FAA chose eight. The initial batch of partners consists of departments of transportation in Florida, Louisiana, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Texas and Utah, along with the city of Albuquerque, N.M., and the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey.

The eIPP proposals requested by the FAA were required to include a plan to work with a private-sector maker of eVTOL aircraft. Some of the industry's leading manufacturers — including Archer Aviation, BETA Technologies, Electra, Eve Air Mobility and Joby Aviation — will supply test aircraft to FDOT, whose eIPP proposal includes development of cargo delivery, passenger transportation and medical response operations. The vehicles' performance will be observed and evaluated at SunTrax, FDOT's 775-acre test-track facility in Auburndale, northeast of Lakeland in Polk County. FDOT recently expanded SunTrax to include a 212-acre aviation campus — specifically for AAM purposes — that features six vertiports, a new 3,000-foot runway, high-speed charging pads, 20,000-sq.-ft. hangars and a four-story building for research, development and training. That building will also accommodate a passenger lounge for when commercial operations begin, according to FDOT.

"The memorandum of understanding we have with FDOT is based on maximizing the learnings as we bring this technology to the forefront," says Luis Perin, Eve Air Mobility's head of business development for the Americas. "It's all centered around SunTrax. It provides a very controlled environment to test these technologies."

"The memorandum of understanding we have with FDOT is based on maximizing the learnings as we bring this technology to the forefront. It's all centered around SunTrax. It provides a very controlled environment to test these technologies." — Luis Perin, an executive with Eve Air Mobility

Publicly traded Eve Air Mobility was spun off from Brazil-based Embraer, a global leader in aircraft manufacturing that has a production facility in Melbourne, home to Eve's U.S. headquarters. The company's Embraer pedigree gives it industry bona fides at time of intense competition for market share in the nascent AAM sector, which has already seen some notable failures, such as Lilium Aerospace. The German company went insolvent and wound down its operations in early 2025. The vultures circled, and Archer Aviation submitted a winning $21-million bid for its defunct rival's patents.

Prior to going out of business, Lilium had planned to develop a vertiport in Lake Nona, the masterplanned community that sits adjacent to Orlando International Airport (MCO). Tavistock Development Co. was also involved in the project, which would've created what Lake Nona called an "aerotropolis." MCO has since forged ahead with a vertiport project of its own, although it will be a small, bare-bones facility — more of a "vertistop," according to the airport — primarily used for testing eVTOLs.

However, many eVTOL makers, including Eve Air Mobility, await FAA certification of their aircraft before they can begin testing in earnest in the U.S. In the meantime, Perin says, Eve will conduct test flights in Brazil. He expects FAA certification to occur in 2028. "Up until that point, we will focus (on providing) our support to FDOT in the SunTrax facility, with our expertise around the infrastructure that is required for these aircraft," he says.

As it waits for FAA certification, Eve has already received about 2,700 letters of intent to buy its $5-million Eve 100 model (that would amount to a cool $13.5 billion in sales), an "industry-leading backlog," Perin says. The LOIs are "all backed up by some sort of financial commitment or deposit, and we've already started firming up those into binding purchase agreements."

SunTrax also struck a deal with eVTOL maker AIR, which announced in August that it will not only establish its U.S. headquarters at the Auburndale facility but also build an eVTOL production facility at the site — the first such company to do so. In a statement, AIR co-founder and CEO Rani Plut says the company already has "more than 300 customers" in Florida and that the state "simply makes sense" for the Israeli firm.

Public-Private Partnerships

AAM aircraft manufacturers have also collaborated directly with airports and their surrounding municipalities. Archer Aviation has partnered with Miami, West Palm Beach, Boca Raton and Fort Lauderdale to create a South Florida air taxi network. Privately owned properties such as Hard Rock Stadium and Apogee Golf Club are involved as well, with plans to integrate their existing helipad infrastructure into an air taxi network operated by Archer, which says it will be able to slash 60- to 90-minute commutes to 10 to 20 minutes via its four-passenger Midnight aircraft.

"Florida is a leader in AAM on all fronts," says David Pollard, director of aviation at Tallahassee International Airport, "and will certainly be among the first (states) to accommodate commercial AAM service."

Elsewhere around the state:

Tampa International Airport held eVTOL demonstrations as far back as 2023 — making it the first commercial airport in the country to do so — and it has continued to lay the groundwork for AAM, which has been "a focus of ours for probably five-plus years now," says Fay, adding that eVTOLs and vertiports feature prominently in the airport's 20-year master plan. "Aviation ... 20 years from now certainly will look very different than it does today," he says. In February 2025, Fay testified at a meeting of the Florida Senate's Transportation Committee, stating, "We have done more preparation and planning than probably most airports in the country."

Orlando International Airport (MCO) in May hosted a demonstration of Vermont-based BETA Technologies' ALIA, a fully electric conventional takeoff and landing (eCTOL) vehicle. Unlike an eVTOL, an eCTOL requires a runway for takeoff, although its smaller cousin, the electric short conventional takeoff and landing (eSTOL) vehicle, can become airborne on a shorter runway. Simon Newitt, BETA's head of sales and support, implied in a statement that Florida will be a focal point for the company. "BETA has flown more than 135,000 nautical miles in ALIA aircraft across the globe," he says. "That operational experience is what positions us to scale deliberately and efficiently for states like Florida, where near-term, short-haul cargo, medical and passenger demand is strongest." Also at MCO, a new takeoff and landing pad, dubbed a "vertistop," is under development and will give the airport the ability to test eVTOLs.

The Miami-Dade Aviation Department has partnered with Bell-Dancy Industries (BDI), a company that specializes in autonomous infrastructure for the aviation industry, to develop infrastructure required to support air-taxi operations, including a proprietary air-traffic management system. BDI's work will start with manned drone operations at Miami Executive Airport (TMB). As mentioned before, Archer Aviation also has been busy in Miami, laying the groundwork for a regional air-taxi network.

"There are other places, like New York and Chicago and Los Angeles, that are vying for this as well, but I think Florida makes a very good case and will certainly be one of the initial launch markets, depending on who the operator may be." — Brett Fay, vice president of general aviation at Tampa International Airport

Tallahassee International Airport (TLH) plans to develop up to four vertiports "to accommodate distinct use cases for corporate, commercial passenger, air cargo and other operations," says Pollard, its aviation director. TLH has already taken the first step toward AAM by installing an electric charging station for aircraft that's also capable of charging many of the city's electric fleet vehicles. Pollard says "dozens — if not hundreds — of new jobs" could result from the airport's investment in AAM infrastructure.

HURDLES

Soaring Costs

Who's paying for the creation of this brave new AAM world? How much will it cost? Will it be worth the investment? Will it be accessible to the general public or merely a novelty for wealthy people? FDOT has stated only that it expects significant public and private investment to foot the bill as the AAM market matures. The FAA will cover up to 100% of the cost of FDOT vertiport projects that do not already have federal support, and it will fund up to 80% of the cost of such projects that utilize federal funds.

"The infrastructure side is going to have to come from government," says Justin Urso, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Central Florida in Orlando who studies AAM, "because the return on investment doesn't make it viable for a private company to invest in significant infrastructure."

Consulting firm Deloitte, in a 2021 study, predicted that AAM could become a $115-billion industry and create more than 280,000 high-paying jobs by 2035. "This is equivalent to 30% of the U.S. commercial aerospace market and 0.5% of the country's GDP in 2019," the report states. But Deloitte's study concludes that the technology "must be secure, readily available and cost-effective" if it's going to be a game changer.

The push to integrate AAM into Florida's transportation network has drawn the ire of EV advocates who say the state hasn't done enough to build out the charging infrastructure for electric cars and has pivoted toward AAM at a time when some counties don't have any EV chargers. The Miami Herald obtained an FDOT document that refers to EV spending as a waste of taxpayer dollars. The Herald's report, published in late July, goes on to state that FDOT wants to divert nearly $200 million in federal funds that were earmarked by the Biden administration for EV chargers to the development of 32 vertiports around the state.

An FDOT spokesperson, in an email to the Tampa Bay Times, said the $198 million in Biden administration funds have not been diverted, and there's no "active proposal" to do so; however, some in the industry, such as TLH's Pollard, believe the state must make AAM infrastructure a priority.

"AAM aircraft certifications are right around the corner, and this industry is expected to flourish quickly," he says. "Clearly, AAM aircraft technology and development are outpacing infrastructure development across the country. Once these aircraft begin flying commercially, the infrastructure development will move quickly to catch up with aircraft operational needs."

Critics also take issue with eVTOLs themselves as a solution to Florida's traffic woes, saying there's no way the aircraft, which can transport only a few passengers at a time, will make a dent in the congestion. They also question whether air-taxi service will be affordable for everyday Floridians and believe the state should instead focus on mass transit initiatives.

"Advanced aviation, while a nice idea, is only going to benefit a few Floridians, particularly in the next decade or two," Bruce Edelston, a member of EV advocacy organization Drive Electric Florida, told the Tampa Bay Times.

Eve Air Mobility's Perin has a different take. "Ultimately, it's the goal of everybody in the industry to get economies of scale and reduce the cost to increase the total addressable market," he says, adding that he expects the eventual cost of commercial AAM to be on par with "premium ground alternatives" — presumably limousines and other high-end rides.

Power Demands

Electric air taxis will come with significant energy infrastructure needs. For an air taxi service to be a viable, stable business, aircraft will have to make multiple trips per day, and that means several charging sessions using quick-charge technology that demands much of the electric grid — anywhere from hundreds of kilowatts to a few megawatts.

"Any parking lot is effectively an eVTOL landing facility," says Brandes, the former state senator, "but what you really need is power. You're trying to put an incredible amount of power into these vehicles and take a ton of heat off of those vehicles in a short turnaround time."

Heat dispersion will be critical for safe, effective operation of eVTOLs and other electric aircraft. "You need a substantial charging capacity, but charging is limited by the amount of heat the battery can take," Brandes says, and there's a risk of battery explosion if heat isn't mitigated. "You've got to limit that heat."

Florida airports, Brandes says, will need to upgrade their power infrastructure to handle the increased loads required by next-gen aircraft. If they don't, brownouts become a risk. "Everything else is very solvable," Brandes says. "The energy problem is the story."

"You need a substantial charging capacity, but charging is limited by the amount of heat the battery can take. You've got to limit that heat." — Jeff Brandes, former state senator and licensed pilot

Eve Air Mobility's Perin concurs, saying, "We've talked to three [major] utility companies in Florida — Florida Power & Light, Duke and the Orlando Utilities Commission — and the generation of power upstream is not necessarily the issue. They're confident that they could get what's needed for eVTOLs to operate. Downstream, when you get to the charging infrastructure, there's investment that's necessary. Eve is not an infrastructure company, but we are providing the exact requirements for those investments to be made by infrastructure developers."

Noise, Safety and Public Acceptance

Vertiports and eVTOLs must also play nice with their neighbors if AAM is going to succeed, and that's where UCF's Urso and his research partner, Subith Vasu, a professor of aerospace engineering at UCF, enter the picture. They received a $750,000 grant from NASA to study how vertiport traffic would affect rural communities. They chose Ocala because Ocala International Airport (OCF) is viewed as a prime spot for a vertiport: It's close to the geographic center of the state, and the first generation of eVTOLs launched from there will be able to reach the state's major international airports in Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood, Miami, Orlando and Tampa.

Noise was also a factor in the researchers' choice. Airports are loud and vertiports will make them even louder — and noise pollution is more noticeable in rural areas. The sound generated by eVTOLs is more akin to a group of drones, but it still adds to the clamor.

"Airports generate a lot of noise," says Urso. At a vertiport, "you're going to be cycling in and out a lot of vehicles, so it's going to be a constant buzzing, potentially."

OCF does not offer regularly scheduled commercial routes, focusing instead on serving privately owned aircraft, charters and flight schools, so it's not as busy as larger airports. At the time of writing this article, OCF typically saw fewer than 10 arrivals and departures per day, and several of the takeoffs and landings were aviation school flights. The introduction of commercial AAM services would dramatically increase both air and ground traffic in Ocala, meaning additional investments in infrastructure around the airport would likely be needed. Urso and Vasu, as part of their NASA-funded study, are surveying Ocala residents to get a sense of how they feel about the changes AAM would bring to their community.

The duo's inquiries, though, raise a larger question about AAM: How will people respond to a revolutionary new way to move around?

"The infrastructure side is going to have to come from government, because the return on investment doesn't make it viable for a private company to invest in significant infrastructure." — Justin Urso, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Central Florida in Orlando who studies advanced air mobility

Urso compares the rush to develop AAM to "building the plane in the air." More than 200 companies around the world are racing to develop and build AAM aircraft at scale, he says, and they must be champing at the bit to see returns on their investments.

The eVTOL that Eve Air Mobility plans to bring to market first will be piloted by a human, which Perin, the company's head of business development for the Americas, believes will help people get more comfortable with AAM travel. "In the short term," he says, "we see the pilot being part of the equation. We see that autonomy is part of the roadmap for the future, but we don't know if people are ready to board an aircraft without a pilot."

As mentioned above, however, the AAM industry awaits FAA certification, which has been slow to come — but for good reason. Electric aircraft don't use conventional aircraft fuel, obviously, but they still pose risks to life, limb and environment.

"Thermal runway is a concern," Urso says. "Essentially, if the battery starts to overheat, what happens is it will continue to increase in temperature until it catches fire — and battery fires are notoriously hard to put out."

Vasu adds, "It's kind of like exponential growth." You wouldn't want to experience such a situation on the ground, in a car, let alone cruising along at an altitude of 3,000 feet.

AAM vehicle manufacturers, however, have come up with ways to minimize the risk of a battery fire spreading throughout their aircraft, Vasu says. Joby Aviation, for example, encases its batteries individually in titanium containers designed for thermal containment.

"The good thing," Vasu says, "is that these will be relatively short flights, so you won't be too far from a populated area and you can get to the ground fairly quickly."

text:
American commercial EV fleet charging specialist, Terawatt Infrastructure, has announced four new depot charging hubs across the US, located in San Francisco, Nashville, Miami, and Dallas. Altogether, the sites have a combined charging power of 22 megawatts, in theory enough to charge over 3,000 EVs per day.

Terawatt Infrastructure gives US depot charging a major boost

The four sites will help support selected and local fleets in their respective cities, with Terawatt overseeing the entire process – from development and construction, utility connections, and through to ongoing charger maintenance alongside its own charger management software and energy management tools.

The largest site, located close to DFW Airport in Texas, offers 7MW of power and will go live this quarter. A 6.6MW site in San Francisco serves one fleet’s Bay Area operations. A 4.5MW site near Nashville International Airport and a 3.5MW site in Miami’s Design District make up the rest, with the Miami site also opening this quarter.

The sites add to the almost 30 charging depots already in construction or development by Terawatt across the US, marking the rapidly increasing demand for fleet charging solutions across the country. While many EV-related incentives have been dropped by the current administration, it’s clear that some businesses are still seeing the clear benefits of an electric future, and focusing on the longer-term benefits of making the switch.

Neha Palmer, CEO and co-founder of Terawatt, commented:

“We are bringing to life the necessary infrastructure buildout for commercial electric fleets to operate reliably at scale. We’re excited to have new sites up and running across the country, with more on the way in 2027. Our vision of an electrified economy for a cleaner, safer planet is closer to reality than ever before.”

Pillar 2 - Scaling up electricity grid supply chains The Supply Chains Mission is developing practical international cooperation to address grid supply chain bottlenecks.
Pillar 3 - Advancing circularity in the wind sector The Supply Chains Mission is developing work to support greater circularity in onshore and offshore wind supply chains.
text:
Over the past year, the Supply Chains Mission has moved from agreeing a shared vision to advancing international cooperation across its four priority pillars, informed by engagement with partner countries, industry and international organisations. COP31 marks the next step in this shift towards delivery, with the Mission looking to turn this work into practical collaboration with partner countries, industry and international organisations in 2027.

This update builds on the shared vision set out at COP30 by Australia, Canada, Kenya, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom and Zambia, supported by the European Commission, highlighting progress to date and areas where the Mission is supporting greater international collaboration to tackle key challenges for clean energy supply chains.

We also welcome Oman to the Supply Chains Mission and look forward to working together to strengthen and diversify clean energy supply chains.

Pillar 1 - Unlocking better clean power supply chain data

The Supply Chains Mission has moved from identifying gaps in clean energy supply chain data to developing a practical plan for international cooperation.

Following publication of the International Energy Agency’s report on clean energy supply chain data, partners have agreed seven priority actions and developed a workplan. These include strengthening supply chain mapping, improving data sharing and interoperability, drawing on best practice from government, academia and industry, and exploring how international trade classifications can better reflect clean energy technologies.

The next phase will focus on implementing this workplan with partner countries and international organisations. This will include further technical collaboration and knowledge sharing between governments, industry and academia.

We are delighted UNIDO will be working with the Mission to help drive delivery of Pillar 1 through 2027.

Pillar 2 - Scaling up electricity grid supply chains

The Supply Chains Mission is developing practical international cooperation to address grid supply chain bottlenecks.

The Mission established an initial technical dialogue in May 2026 on grid supply chain bottlenecks and is focusing international cooperation on driving harmonised standards, demand aggregation and pooled procurement as key levers to address supply chain bottlenecks.

In June 2026, the Global Clean Power Alliance (GCPA) and Utilities for Net Zero Alliance (UNEZA) convened a senior government-industry roundtable at London Climate Action Week to test practical approaches in these areas, followed by a UNEZA member’s statement committing to greater demand visibility, harmonised equipment standards and coordinated procurement. Through the UNEZA partnership and emerging regional work, Pillar 2 is now developing practical routes to test these approaches and feed successful models into wider international cooperation, including through the UK G20 Presidency

Pillar 2 is bringing together a range of region-specific activities with the shared aim of promoting the diversification and resilience of grids supply chains. We are partnering with UNEZA to support their pooled procurement pilot in the Caribbean.

At COP31, the Mission also supported a discussion convened by UNEZA, bringing together utilities and manufacturers to agree practical action to strengthen supply chains, including greater standardisation, clearer long-term demand signals, and workforce development. The group committed to working towards a joint declaration committing to key actions, to be published at the IRENA Assembly in January. GCPA’s participation and endorsement provides a basis for continued collaboration with industry partners beyond COP31.

Pillar 3 - Advancing circularity in the wind sector

The Supply Chains Mission is developing work to support greater circularity in onshore and offshore wind supply chains.

We are engaging with Engineering X, founded by the Royal Academy of Engineering and Lloyd’s Register Foundation, the UK Offshore Renewable Energy Catapult and The Circularity Collective as potential technical partners, drawing on their expertise and existing work on the end-of-life management of wind energy assets.

The Mission is exploring practical international cooperation on decommissioning, reuse, refurbishment and recycling, as well as better forecasting of future turbine, component and material flows. It is also considering how greater consistency in terminology, methodologies, guidance and data could support countries as their wind sectors develop.

In 2027, interested countries and technical experts will help define priority activities and identify where international collaboration add value.

Pillar 4 – Unlocking clean power manufacturing opportunities in emerging markets

The Supply Chains Mission is developing its work to help emerging markets and developing economies capture greater economic value from the clean energy transition, including through manufacturing, investment, skills and capability development.

Work to date has explored investment opportunities in clean power supply chains, including the wind sector in Southeast Asia, and considered how skills and intellectual property partnerships could help build local capability.

The Mission is now engaging with partners to identify country priorities and initiatives that could form the basis for practical collaboration. This demand-led approach will help shape the next phase of work in 2027 and identify where international cooperation can support greater value-added manufacturing, skills development and supply chain diversification.

Looking ahead

COP31 provides a springboard for the Mission’s 2027 delivery programme. The focus will be on turning the technical work, partnerships and country engagement developed during 2026 into defined activities across the four pillars.

At COP31, the Mission hosted an event at the UK Pavilion, in partnership with SSE, bringing together governments, industry and international organisations to examine practical ways to unblock clean energy supply chain bottlenecks. The discussion will inform the Mission’s next phase of work, including opportunities for cooperation on grid supply chains, investment and manufacturing.

Through COP31 and beyond, the Mission will continue to provide a platform for countries to share expertise, develop practical solutions and identify opportunities for greater international cooperation to strengthen and diversify clean power supply chains.

title: The GOP lost its iron grip on Ohio. What's the outlook for clean energy? - Canary Media
description:
The main obstacle to utility-scale solar over the past five years has been a 2021 law, Senate Bill 52, that lets counties ban almost all such new projects within their territories.
Over a third of Ohio counties have now designated large swaths of land as off-limits to renewables under SB 52.
“It’s a brand-new day here,” said Neil Waggoner, Midwest manager for the Sierra Club’s Beyond Coal campaign, who’s based in central Ohio.
Very soon, Acton will choose leaders for various regulatory agencies, subject to confirmation by the Ohio Senate.
Senate Bill 294, which the Ohio Senate passed in June, may make building solar and wind even more difficult by specifying a minimum capacity factor of 50%.
text:
Democrats have finally managed to gain footing in Ohio’s halls of power — a shift that bodes well for clean energy in a state that’s become particularly hostile toward solar and wind.

Last week, voters ended Republicans’ 15-year-long trifecta in Ohio, picking Democrat Amy Acton to be their next governor (and the first woman elected to that office). While the GOP still controls the state House and Senate, Democrats won enough seats to break Republicans’ supermajority in the House, meaning the party can no longer unilaterally override the governor’s vetoes.

From 2011 until now, Republican control of all three branches of state government has increasingly favored the oil and gas industry while limiting the growth of renewable power and scaling back energy-efficiency standards.

Acton campaigned on a different vision. Her affordability plan pledged to promote ​“the lowest-cost and cleanest sources of energy readily available” and to reinstate energy efficiency measures, renewable portfolio standards, and demand response programs, which incentivize customers to reduce or shift their energy consumption when the grid is strained.

In a Substack post last month, Acton wrote, ​“Ohio politicians have made it nearly impossible to advance zero marginal cost generation such as wind and solar,” so most of the state’s electricity comes from higher-cost fossil-fuels. ​“I will reexamine these obstacles that, in the long run, hit Ohio families in their pocketbooks.”

The question is what Acton can actually do to move the needle.

The main obstacle to utility-scale solar over the past five years has been a 2021 law, Senate Bill 52, that lets counties ban almost all such new projects within their territories. Even without an outright ban, counties can block most projects before a developer can proceed with a permit application at the state level. SB 52 also applies to wind farms of 5 megawatts or more, though almost all proposals for large-scale wind projects stopped after a 2014 budget law more than doubled the distance that turbines must be from neighboring property lines.

Over a third of Ohio counties have now designated large swaths of land as off-limits to renewables under SB 52. Acton can’t change that law and others on her own, since doing so requires legislative action.

Still, clean energy advocates are optimistic that the new governor will be able to knock down some roadblocks.

“It’s a brand-new day here,” said Neil Waggoner, Midwest manager for the Sierra Club’s Beyond Coal campaign, who’s based in central Ohio.

Very soon, Acton will choose leaders for various regulatory agencies, subject to confirmation by the Ohio Senate. Those include the directors of the Ohio Environmental Protection Agency and the departments that deal with health, natural resources, agriculture, and development. The Ohio EPA handles permits for fossil-fuel plants and other polluting facilities, while the Ohio Department of Natural Resources decides matters dealing with hydraulic fracturing, injection wells, and coal mining.

Most notably for energy, those five agency directors will make up a majority of the voting members of the Ohio Power Siting Board, which issues permits for electric generation projections and other energy infrastructure. The board has seven standing voting members; the other two are the chair of the Public Utility Commission of Ohio and a member that represents the public.

Acton will eventually get to pick those last two members, too. The utility commission’s current chair, Jenifer French, can stay on as a regulator there until 2029, but the governor can at any time designate a different chair, who will then also head up the Power Siting Board. The term for the current public member ends in 2030.

Those personnel swaps could make Ohio friendlier to clean energy developers. In recent years, the siting board and its staff have mainly deferred to local governments on whether a solar or wind project is in the public interest. That has allowed the mere existence of local government opposition to derail projects, even when objections lack factual support or have been addressed by the developer.

Miranda Leppla, who heads the environmental law clinic at Case Western Reserve University School of Law, said she hopes the new board will take a genuinely broad view of the public interest, including a more critical examination of energy projects’ health and environmental impacts and the costs of climate change.

Acton will also appoint at least four of the Public Utilities Commission’s five members during her term, as their tenures come to an end. That agency is tasked with making sure Ohioans have reliable, affordable utility service. Leppla said new members could push utilities to embrace energy efficiency and demand response and pursue more equitable service across their territories.

At the legislature

While Acton cannot enact laws on her own, her election could force Republicans in the legislature to compromise more on energy policy.

“The majorities in the House and Senate are going to have to work with the governor,” Waggoner said. ​“That’s a good thing. That’s the way government is supposed to work.”

Democratic Rep. Tristan Rader, ranking minority member on the current House Energy Committee, said he expects there will be some cooperation and actual movement toward the ​“all-of-the-above strategy that at least Republicans have given lip service to these last couple of years.” Otherwise, nothing would get done.

Even if the legislature won’t abolish SB 52’s terms for letting counties ban solar and wind, Republicans will no longer be able to unilaterally override Acton if she vetoes bills to further restrict solar, wind, or energy efficiency.

“It would be fantastic to make sure we can’t go further down the path of promoting fossil fuels at the expense of different types of clean energy that could save Ohioans money and could do wonders for the impacts of climate change,” Leppla said.

However, there’s still the lame-duck session to get through.

One proposal, House Bill 1024, would shift authority for review of thousands of agency rules and processes from the governor to lawmakers — essentially letting them undo regulations without having to amend the law or risk Acton’s veto. Republican Rep. Jamie Callender introduced the bill last month, shortly before the election; he was also a primary sponsor of 2019’s House Bill 6, the coal and nuclear bailout law that gutted Ohio’s clean energy standards and is at the heart of the state’s ongoing utility-corruption saga.

Another gambit, House Joint Resolution 11, proposes making the governor’s veto power meaningless by letting simple majorities override it. Introduced days after Acton’s election, it would place the issue before voters as a constitutional amendment next year.

Meanwhile, lawmakers could try to ram through some energy bills before the new year. Senate Bill 294, which the Ohio Senate passed in June, may make building solar and wind even more difficult by specifying a minimum capacity factor of 50%. Capacity factor refers to the ratio between actual electricity production and maximum output if a source runs continuously. Federal data shows the average capacity factor is around 24% for U.S. solar farms and 34% for wind, meaning Ohio’s law could essentially force developers to add batteries — along with costs and complexity — to their projects to meet the 50% threshold

Another proposal, House Bill 862, would let utilities own nuclear plants — and possibly stick consumers with part of the costs. That would run counter to a 2025 law that generally bars regulated electric utilities from owning generation and passing costs on to customers in what is supposed to be a competitive market.

Other draft bill language circulated this week would also keep coal plants open, even if the owner has signed a contract agreeing to close a facility or convert it to natural gas. Most imminently, that could force a large unit at the Cardinal power plant in eastern Ohio to stay open, even though the group that runs it is bound to shutter the facility by 2028 under a 2015 settlement deal prior owner American Electric Power made with the Sierra Club.

Much then could depend not only on Acton’s plans for next year, but also on what happens between now and New Year’s Eve, when the legislative session ends. Nonetheless, Rader is optimistic that the election results will lead to more renewables coming online in Ohio.

Following the launch of Nigeria Industrial Policy February this year, a former Director General of UNIDO, has made a case for an energy policy if Nigeria is to achieve its industrialisation ambition, writes Dike Onwuamaeze

Former Director General of United Nations Industrial Development Organisation (UNIDO), Dr. Kandeh Kolleh Yamkella, was on a familiar turf on Tuesday, October 6, 2026. The occasion was the 6th Adeola Odutola Lecture, which was organised by the Manufacturers Association of Nigeria (MAN) as part of its 54th Annual General Meeting. The topic of his lecture was “Leveraging National Industrial Policy to Position Nigeria as Africa’s Industrial Hub.”

As he mounted the podium, his audience was expectant. One, the distinguished guest lecturer, Yamkella, has spent more than two decades, studying, analysing, promoting, packaging, delivering and advising government and businesses on industrial policies. Two, the federal government in February 2026 launched Nigeria Industrial Policy (NIP), the first in the country’s history.

The kernel of Yamkella’s message was clear and direct: the federal government should back its NIP with a clearly defined energy policy for the country, stating that energy policy must be part of an effective industrial policy.

He said: “Energy policy is industrial strategy. If we do not fix that, industry will die because no industrial strategy can succeed without reliable electricity.” This is already killing industries in Nigeria as energy cost is reported to constitute between 30 and 40 per cent of manufacturer’s production cost. And for some manufacturers, the energy cost is as high as 60 per cent.

“You know the story. It (energy) is killing your industry. Manufacturers spent an estimated N1.3 trillion on self-generated power in 2025, up from N781 billion in 2023, with energy now accounting for as much as 35 to 40 per cent of production costs. Here, some people even say 60 per cent of their operating costs. Whereas energy makes up roughly between 5.0 and 15 per cent manufacturing costs in countries such as India, Vietnam, Indonesia, Turkey, Mexico and South Africa.”

He remarked that the strategic point where Asia is beating Nigeria and most of Africa, is energy cost which it subsidies for its manufacturers. For Asia, energy and water is subsidised but in factories have to generate their own power and have their own boreholes. “So energy policy has to be part of industrial policy.”

Yamkella stated that countries do not industrialise simply by producing policy documents. According to him, industrial policy matters only when it becomes productive capacity, investment, technology, competitiveness, pushes value addition and creates jobs. Otherwise, it is as good as a piece of paper.

He, therefore, tasked government on practical, deliberate implementation of industrial policy. Policy, he said, is one side of the coin. And government deciding that it will drive industrialisation another.

That is how the Asians have done it. Because the risks and constraints are many even though Nigeria has the essential foundations for an industrial powerhouse. Yet, he reminded his audience that potential is not performance. Otherwise manufacturing contributions should not be between seven and eight per cent of the Gross Domestic Product (GDP) as it is currently in Nigeria. In addition, manufacturing exports generate only 3.0 per cent of the country’s export revenue, which, he said, is far below several other African peers.

He pointed out that Nigeria’s biggest economic paradox has been that the country has a large market and abundant resources, yet imports dominate everyday consumption.

“I am aware of the government’s effort to change this narrative through the Nigerian industrial policy launched on February 17 this year. Nigeria’s industrial challenge is therefore not a shortage of ambition or enterprise. It is the need to convert scale into productivity, competitiveness, and exports. So we must ask ourselves what it will take to make this ambition a reality at a time that the world is changing,” he said.

One of the ways to realise Nigeria’s industrial ambition is for the government to ensure that its newly launched industrial policy must become industrial action.

The former UNIDO chief said, “Policy is only the starting point. The true test of any industrial policy lies not in its design alone, but in the execution. So there are key parameters that government must monitor deliberately to check if the policy is working. These parameters are how many new factories are being established because of the new policy? How many existing factories are expanding? How much domestic value is created? How much investment is mobilised?

“I say this because in my career at UNIDO, over 75 countries I went to, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, the European countries, China, you name it, their governments are actually visiting factories to measures performance. If it is not going where they want it, the government will put public capital and change policy. The countries I know in Asia that made that break, like Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and others who are catching up, Vietnam, Cambodia, their governments measure how many new factories did we create?”

Yamkella said that rather than waiting for MAN to complain, governments in Nigeria should be asking MAN: how do we help your members grow? That’s how Indians grow.

He added, “That is why when the consultant came here to look at your textile sector, he looked at the cost of energy and water in Nigerian factories and said that even with cheap labour, you cannot compete because we find other ways to subsidise them by making electricity cheap. So government itself must want to measure and be a friend of MAN and the manufacturers on how to make them do better so that they can create jobs and wealth? It is deliberate policy. It is not just a paper. Government has to be deliberate. But there’s some hope.”

Apart from addressing the high cost energy, Yamkella said that Nigeria must think beyond its borders by become world’s dominant players in cement. fertiliser and electric car battery manufacturing. This, he stated, will require a new supply chain that will link the country with Togo and Congo.

“Now, fertilizer. Nigeria is producing urea. Togo has phosphate, and Congo has potash. Nigeria could be top five producer of fertilizer in five years. That is the aim, that is the dream. That is why Nigeria must think beyond its borders. You have the core already; your neighbours have the others. Morocco, Togo, Congo. It’s about you producing. But industrial policy should support that now to grow. How do we make that transform Nigeria into one of the leading fertilizer producers of the world? Because I tell you, from America to Europe, everybody’s struggling for fertilizer, ”he said.

Yamkella also believed that Nigeria can lead Africa in automobile manufacturing by using deliberate policy actions to drive production.

He said: “Nigeria’s industrial future cannot be defined by domestic market alone. Nigeria must manufacture for Nigeria, but also for West Africa, the rest of Africa, and in fact, the world. The opportunity before us is greater than the constraints. I know that, yes, Nigeria can be the powerhouse and the hub for West Africa, and in fact, for the rest of the continent as well.”

He recognised that Nigeria has one of Africa’s largest automotive markets and significant assembling capacity. But remarked that there is gap between license capacity and actual production that reminds us that license are not factories. According to him, “installed capacity is not production and assembly without local value chains is not industrial transformation.”

Nevertheless, the opportunity, however, is substantial in Nigeria to compete in electric motorcycles, battery swapping systems, buses, fleet vehicles, battery packs assembly, charging infrastructure, and other components for the automotive industry.

“But the biggest opportunity I see, and you are doing it already because your solid minerals policy on lithium that says if you want our lithium, you should process 30 per cent here,” he said, adding that Nigeria has “one policy already that is already attracting three, four companies to process your lithium. Put another policy to say now you make the batteries here.

“You become the battery hub for the region. That is industrial policy in action. But it has to be backed now by other policies,”he said.

Yamkella said that it is good that Nigeria has come back to embrace industrial policy after decades of deindustrialisation that was occasioned by wholesale embrace of the Washington Consensus that it is all about market liberalisation on the premise that industrial policy is not necessary anymore.
