text:
Companies combine complementary strengths in battery technology, software and systems integration to accelerate commercial and industrial energy storage deployment in the United States

GREENVILLE, S.C., Nov. 12, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- FENECON, one of Europe’s leading providers of energy storage systems and energy management software, and A123 Systems (A123), a global leader in advanced lithium-ion battery technology, have announced a strategic partnership in the United States to address growing demand for commercial and industrial battery energy storage systems.

The partnership pairs complementary strengths that are ideally suited for the U.S. storage market. FENECON provides systems integration capabilities; the world-class, open-source FENECON Energy Management System (FEMS); access to a U.S.-based distribution and sales network; and project experience from Europe. A123 brings advanced Lithium Iron Phosphate (LFP) battery technology, global manufacturing expertise, and deep cell-to-product and system know-how. Together, FENECON and A123 intend to expand their strategic collaboration in North America, leveraging their expertise to jointly develop and commercialize innovative, flexible, and intelligent energy storage solutions for commercial and industrial applications.

This strategic collaboration reflects FENECON's and A123's shared vision to expand their presence in the North American energy storage market. The companies intend to leverage their capabilities to explore opportunities that support the development and commercialization of energy storage solutions for commercial and industrial applications, which is closely aligned with FENECON’s plans to build and scale energy storage systems from its U.S. headquarters and manufacturing facility in Greenville, South Carolina.

While A123 contributes proven battery technology and international industrialization expertise, FENECON maintains its own system architecture for battery energy storage systems, a native software platform, and direct communication with customers. This creates a flexible foundation that can be adapted to different applications, technologies, and regional market requirements over time.

The collaboration is intended to support FENECON's expansion into commercial and industrial energy storage applications in the United States, drawing on A123's battery technology and FENECON's systems integration and energy management capabilities. Target applications include industrial and manufacturing sites, large retail and commercial facilities, and mobility and EV-charging locations. FENECON’s energy storage systems will support multiple applications across the U.S., including peak shaving, solar integration, EV charging, and backup power, all within one intelligent energy solution.

"The United States is a key growth market for FENECON, and our partnership with A123 Systems gives us an important foundation to accelerate market development while building out a localized supply chain,” said Thomas Goesswein, CEO of FENECON Inc. and FENECON International. "For C&I customers in the U.S., this partnership promises the combination of a dependable battery with our FEMS intelligent energy management, system integration, and multiple applications. This is where the strengths of A123 and FENECON are well matched.”

"By bringing together A123’s commercially fielded LFP battery technology and FENECON’s software-driven integration expertise, we are combining key competencies to strengthen the supply of innovative energy storage solutions tailored to the unique requirements of different markets and stakeholder needs. We believe this strategic collaboration brings together compatible strengths that can accelerate innovation, deliver greater value to our customers, and contribute to a more resilient and competitive energy storage industry,” said Dr. Jack Li, General Manager of A123 Systems LLC.

About FENECON

FENECON is a leading hardware and software specialist for energy storage solutions serving residential, commercial and industrial sectors worldwide. All storage systems are powered by FENECON’s internally developed energy management system, FEMS, which plays a central role in shaping OpenEMS, the open-source energy management platform. The company’s broad range of FEMS applications enables grid-supportive energy management and intelligent sector coupling that actively contribute to the energy transition.

Based on its proven energy storage and management expertise, the company ranks among the industry’s top innovators and is committed to a future powered entirely by renewable energy. Headquartered in Iggensbach, Bavaria, FENECON employs approximately 400 people and operates additional sites in Germany as well as a U.S. headquarters and manufacturing facility in Greenville, South Carolina, comprising approximately 35,000 square feet of production and office space.

FENECON’s performance, flexibility and innovation are reflected in numerous industry awards. The company was named "Innovator of the Year” in the TOP 100 competition for German SMEs in 2023, 2024 and 2025. Further recognition in 2025 includes The smarter E Award in the "Smart Integrated Energy” category for FEMS, the Top Innovation Award from EUPD Research, and the SolarProsumerAward 2024/2025 from EUPD Research in the HEMS and Storage categories. In 2024, FENECON also received the Bavarian SME Award and BAYERNS BEST 50.

A123 Systems LLC is a global leader in advanced lithium-ion battery technology, bringing over two decades of experience and innovation to the development and manufacturing of high-performance battery cells and smart battery systems. Specialized in and leading Lithium Iron Phosphate (LFP) technology, A123 serves a broad range of industries, including automotive, energy storage, and high-performance motorsport applications. text:
The U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE) Office of Energy Dominance Financing (EDF) announced the financial close of a $480 million loan for Arena Energy’s Project Elkhorn “to increase oil and natural gas production across the Gulf of America shelf”, a statement sent to Rigzone by the DOE recently noted.

According to the statement, the project will modernize 22 offshore platforms off the coast of Louisiana and, at peak production, is expected to add up to 38,600 barrels of oil per day and up to 77 million cubic feet of natural gas per day to U.S. energy production.

The statement highlighted that the announcement was “made possible” by U.S. President Donald Trump’s Working Families Tax Cut and marked the DOE’s first closed loan supporting domestic oil and natural gas production, “underscoring DOE’s commitment to advancing American energy dominance and delivering affordable, reliable, and secure energy for American families and businesses”.

In this statement, U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright said, “the United States is the world’s largest producer and exporter of oil and natural gas, and thanks to President Trump, American energy production will continue to grow”.

“Project Elkhorn will increase oil production by up to 38,600 barrels per day and create thousands of jobs. By providing financing for projects like Project Elkhorn, the Energy Department is expanding domestic production and strengthening our energy security to power American prosperity for decades to come,” he added.

EDF Director Gregory A. Beard said in the statement, “thanks to President Trump and Secretary Wright’s leadership, EDF is putting existing energy infrastructure back to work for the American people”.

“Project Elkhorn will expand domestic oil and natural gas production, create good-paying American jobs, and strengthen our energy security while generating substantial returns for American taxpayers,” he added.

Arena Energy currently produces approximately 30,000 barrels of oil per day offshore in the Gulf of America, the statement highlighted, adding that Project Elkhorn will modernize existing offshore infrastructure and expand production capacity - adding approximately 125 million barrels of oil and 250 billion cubic feet of natural gas to U.S. energy production over the life of the project.

“The project will create 2,400 construction-related jobs and 400 operations jobs in one of the nation's most important offshore energy corridors,” the statement noted.

“Under President Trump’s leadership, EDF is financing American energy infrastructure projects that increase domestic production, strengthen U.S. energy security, and lower costs for all Americans while responsibly managing taxpayer dollars,” it added.

In a statement sent to Rigzone late Wednesday, Arena Energy confirmed that its wholly owned subsidiary, Elkhorn Offshore, LLC, had reached financial close on a $480 million loan from the DOE’s Office of EDF supporting Project Elkhorn.

Arena said the financing will be used to retool, refurbish, repower, and expand capacity across offshore platforms in the Southern Eugene Island area off the coast of Louisiana, extending their use and enabling critical infrastructure upgrades.

“Project Elkhorn will return idled platforms to service and expand production and water-handling capacity at active facilities,” Arena highlighted.

“The project also includes the development of new natural gas pipeline infrastructure to connect future wells into existing pipelines, improving midstream connectivity across the field,” it added.

“Together, these investments are expected to add approximately 125 million barrels of additional oil and 250 billion cubic feet of natural gas production over the life of the project, helping ensure Americans have access to affordable, reliable, and secure energy while maintaining the highest standards of operational and environmental safety,” it continued.

“This increase in domestic production will lead to an estimated $1.6 billion in additional royalties collected by the federal government, a total return of more than three times for American taxpayers,” it went on to state.

Arena highlighted that the closing followed completion of the technical, legal, environmental, and financial due diligence required under DOE’s loan program.

“Arena was founded on the belief that the mature fields of the Gulf Shelf still hold vast potential, and Project Elkhorn is a critical part of that strategy,” Mike Minarovic, CEO and Founder of Arena Energy, LLC, said in the statement.

“The Southern Eugene Island area is one of the most prolific oil producing regions in American history, and its infrastructure still has decades of productive life ahead,” he added.

“What it needed was long-term capital to match the opportunity. This financing from the Department of Energy delivers that capital and lets us put existing infrastructure back to work, develop proved reserves, and keep producing some of the most reliable barrels in the world right here at home - with American workers, on American leases, for American refineries,” he continued.

“The Office of Energy Dominance Financing conducted a rigorous review of this project, and we are pleased to have earned its confidence,” Minarovic continued.

“Reinvesting in existing infrastructure is one of the most efficient ways to add American energy production, support skilled jobs, and generate value. Arena has paid more than $1.8 billion in royalties to the federal government since 1999, and Project Elkhorn will allow us to accelerate additional royalty income for American taxpayers for decades to come,” he went on to state.

The company confirmed that Project Elkhorn will support 2,800 jobs, including 400 operations roles and 2,400 construction jobs, “helping strengthen regional workforce opportunities in one of the nation’s most important offshore energy corridors”.

Arena Energy was founded in 1999 “on the belief that mature producing areas of the Gulf of America Shelf still held vast potential - and that with the right technology, talented oil and gas finders could unlock these drilling opportunities”, Arena Energy’s website states, adding that, “today, that vision has been realized many times over”.

“As an oil company in The Woodlands, Texas, Arena Energy focuses on pursuing the lower-risk exploration and production opportunities that remain in the Gulf after 50 years of drilling by larger oil companies,” the company’s site adds.

“Most of our projects are exploitation drilling prospects identified through detailed and technical field study,” it continues.

“As a result, our oil and gas reserve base has been created primarily through drilling wells rather than acquiring existing production. This approach sets us apart from nearly every other company operating in the Gulf today,” it goes on to state.

In its latest short term energy outlook (STEO), which was released on November 10, the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) showed that Federal Gulf of America oil production, including lease condensate, averaged 2.01 million barrels per day in the first quarter of this year, 2.04 million barrels per day in the second quarter, and 2.07 million barrels per day in the third quarter.

The EIA’s November STEO expects this output to average 1.94 million barrels per day in the fourth quarter and 2.02 million barrels per day overall in 2026. Federal Gulf of America production, including lease condensate, came in at 1.94 million barrels per day in 2025, the EIA’s latest STEO showed.

title: India bans black mass exports to retain critical minerals. Can domestic industry capture their value?
description:
On November 10, 2026, it prohibited the export of lithium-ion battery black mass, a move that could help retain an important source of secondary critical minerals within the country.
The government’s announcement explicitly identifies lithium-ion battery black mass as the material covered by the notification.
Black mass is more than battery waste The significance of the decision lies in what black mass represents.
A functioning battery recycling industry could build capabilities in secondary mineral recovery, advanced chemical processing and battery materials manufacturing.
Its 2023 assessment of EV battery material recycling made the case for treating recycling as part of India’s material security strategy.
text:
When an electric vehicle battery reaches the end of its life, the minerals inside it do not necessarily have to leave the economy with it. Lithium, cobalt, nickel and other valuable materials can be recovered and potentially used to manufacture new batteries. But until now, some of the black mass produced from discarded lithium-ion batteries in India has been finding its way to overseas markets, taking with it an opportunity to build domestic mineral recovery capabilities.

The Union government has now moved to address this. On November 10, 2026, it prohibited the export of lithium-ion battery black mass, a move that could help retain an important source of secondary critical minerals within the country. The decision is significant not simply because it restricts the export of waste, but because it raises a larger industrial policy question: can India turn the minerals recovered from discarded batteries into inputs for its own battery manufacturing industry?

The Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT) changed the export policy for the specified category of battery waste and scrap under ITC (HS) code 85491400 from “Free” to “Prohibited”, with immediate effect and until further orders. The provision covers specified unsorted battery waste and scrap that does not contain lead, cadmium or mercury. Transitional arrangements under the Foreign Trade Policy, 2023, will apply. The government’s announcement explicitly identifies lithium-ion battery black mass as the material covered by the notification.

Black mass is more than battery waste

The significance of the decision lies in what black mass represents. Produced by shredding end-of-life lithium-ion batteries and battery manufacturing scrap, it is a powder containing a mixture of recoverable metals, graphite and other residues. Depending on the chemistry of the original battery, it can contain lithium, cobalt, nickel and manganese. It is not, however, a finished material that can be used directly in new cells. It is an intermediate product that must undergo further processing to separate and recover its constituent materials.

For India, this distinction has strategic importance. The country remains substantially dependent on imports for several minerals and processed materials required for lithium-ion battery production. As domestic electric vehicle manufacturing and advanced chemistry cell production expand, access to these materials will increasingly influence the competitiveness and resilience of the manufacturing ecosystem.

Battery recycling offers an additional source of these materials, reducing dependence on newly mined resources or overseas supply chains. In effect, discarded batteries can become an urban mineral resource. The metals recovered from them could supplement supplies of primary minerals and reduce India’s exposure to disruptions in international markets.

An export ban closes the resource loop — but only partly

Until now, exporting black mass has meant that the opportunity to recover its constituent minerals could shift to processing facilities outside India. Countries importing the material could extract the metals, refine them and potentially integrate them into their own battery material supply chains. India, meanwhile, risked losing the downstream processing value.

The government has acknowledged this contradiction in its announcement, noting that domestic recycling and refining capacity has expanded but remains underutilised because of inadequate feedstock. It has also pointed to instances in which domestic recyclers have had to import black mass to meet their requirements even as material generated in India was being exported.

The export restriction addresses this mismatch by making domestically generated black mass available to Indian recycling and refining units. It also complements the ₹1,500-crore Incentive Scheme for Critical Mineral Recycling, approved by the Union Cabinet in September 2025 under the National Critical Mineral Mission. The scheme aims to build domestic capacity to separate and produce critical minerals from secondary sources, including battery waste and electronic waste. The Ministry of Mines has set out a six-year implementation period, running from 2025-26 to 2030-31.

This policy direction is consistent with concerns raised by the Centre for Science and Environment (CSE) about India’s battery-recycling framework. In its January 2026 report, “EV Battery Recycling and Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR): Reform the terms of action”, CSE identified black-mass exports as a drain on valuable domestic feedstock and an obstacle to building a circular battery economy. It also highlighted the problem of undervalued EPR certificates, arguing that inadequate financial incentives discourage investment in environmentally sound recycling and high-recovery technologies. CSE’s report called attention to the links between retaining recyclable material, improving the economics of domestic recycling and strengthening regulatory oversight.

The export prohibition addresses an important part of this problem. But keeping black mass within the country will not, by itself, ensure that India captures the full economic value of its minerals. That depends on its ability to process the material further.

The first constraint is likely to arise much earlier in the recycling chain: the collection of end-of-life batteries. Batteries are dispersed across electric vehicles, portable electronics and industrial applications. Their collection, safe transportation, testing and aggregation require organised systems. Fragmented supply chains and informal handling can result in material losses, safety risks and poor traceability.

The Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022, provide a framework through Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR), placing collection, recycling and refurbishment obligations on battery producers. They also prescribe minimum recovery targets for recyclers. For electric vehicle batteries, the minimum material recovery target reaches 90 per cent from 2026-27 onwards. The rules further require producers to use domestically recycled materials in new batteries from 2027-28, beginning at 5 per cent and rising to 20 per cent by 2030-31. The rules and subsequent amendments provide the regulatory framework for this transition.

These provisions can create demand for recovered materials, but only if compliance translates into actual recovery. EPR certificates must reflect genuine recycling and verifiable recovery, rather than simply the quantities of waste reported as processed. Traceability, from the battery collection through shredding and refining to final material recovery, will therefore be essential.

There is also an economic challenge. Advanced recycling requires investment in safe dismantling, pre-processing, chemical recovery, effluent treatment and quality control. Recovery yields, processing costs, scale and the market prices of recovered metals all influence commercial viability. LFP recycling, in particular, may require stronger producer responsibility mechanisms or other financial support to make recovery economically sustainable.

The export restriction could improve access to feedstock for domestic recyclers, but it does not guarantee sufficient volumes, predictable quality or viable processing margins. Nor does it create assured demand for the recovered materials. Domestic cathode and precursor manufacturing must develop alongside recycling if recovered minerals are to find a reliable market within India.

The next phase of policy action must therefore focus on building an integrated system: collection and aggregation networks, reliable battery chemistry and composition data, standards for black mass and recovered materials, transparent EPR accounting, and commercial arrangements linking recyclers with refiners and cell manufacturers. Customs and environmental authorities will also need to coordinate effectively to ensure that the restriction is applied in accordance with the material’s actual composition and classification.

The real prize lies beyond recycling

India’s opportunity extends beyond waste management. A functioning battery recycling industry could build capabilities in secondary mineral recovery, advanced chemical processing and battery materials manufacturing. CSE’s earlier work on battery material security, along with its research into developing batteries suited to Indian operating conditions, also underscore the importance of building domestic technological capabilities across the battery value chain. Its 2023 assessment of EV battery material recycling made the case for treating recycling as part of India’s material security strategy.

The export ban is therefore an important intervention, but its success will not be measured simply by how much black mass stays within India’s borders. It will depend on how much of that material is actually collected, processed and converted into battery-grade inputs.

title: New Utah gas utility settlement advances methane transparency and customer protections
description:

The settlement includes important commitments to improve transparency, reduce waste and help protect Utah gas customers.
This information will provide a much clearer picture of Wexpro’s methane emissions and help inform future methane reduction efforts.

text:
By: Logan Mitchell, Climate Scientist & Regulatory Manager, Utah Clean Energy and Veronica Ung-Kono, Attorney, U.S. Clean Energy, Environmental Defense Fund

When Utah Clean Energy learned about an expedited request before the Utah Public Service Commission to approve a new large-scale natural gas supply acquisition in Colorado, we had concerns and questions about how such an investment would impact energy affordability for Utah ratepayers, as well as climate change and air quality. To get answers, our team of experts moved swiftly to coordinate with other parties and intervene in the docket and ultimately negotiate a settlement with Enbridge Gas and Wexpro. This week, the PSC issued an order approving the settlement, detailed below, which we consider a positive first step in improving transparency and reducing risks and costs associated with natural gas.

Natural gas is a potent greenhouse gas and major contributor to air pollution in Utah and throughout the intermountain west.

Natural gas – used widely in Utah’s homes and commercial buildings for heat and cooking – is approximately 95% methane, a potent greenhouse gas that also contributes to Utah’s indoor and outdoor air pollution problems when combusted. In addition, methane leaks from gas production and distribution are pervasive throughout industry, posing a serious climate problem while also wasting valuable energy resources. Due to methane’s higher global warming potential (which is up to 87 times more potent than carbon dioxide over a 20-year time span), reducing leaks offers a critical opportunity to slow near-term warming.

To help address these challenges, Utah Clean Energy worked with Environmental Defense Fund and other regulatory stakeholders to negotiate a settlement with Enbridge Gas, Utah’s sole gas distribution utility, and Wexpro, a gas production company owned by Enbridge, regarding their proposed acquisition of a new gas production area in Colorado, Piceance III. The settlement includes important commitments to improve transparency, reduce waste and help protect Utah gas customers.

Wins for Utah ratepayers and the climate

One of the most significant achievements of the settlement is a requirement for new reporting on methane emissions and leak detection efforts from Wexpro’s gas production operations. Under the agreement, settlement parties along with Utah’s utility regulators will receive regular reports on methane emissions, leak detection and repair activities and well-level methane leakage intensity measurements. This information will provide a much clearer picture of Wexpro’s methane emissions and help inform future methane reduction efforts.

The settlement also requires Wexpro to conduct a first-of-its-kind economic analysis of its methane mitigation efforts. The study will examine methane emissions reductions, avoided gas losses, preserved revenues, mitigation costs and the financial payback of investments made since 2011. The findings will help quantify the economic value of reducing methane leaks and show how minimizing waste can benefit both customers and the environment.

In addition, Enbridge agreed to work with Utah Clean Energy, EDF and other stakeholders to explore gas demand forecasting, long-term system planning, and opportunities to reduce customer costs and risks. These processes are essential to help inform future decision-making around gas production and expansion efforts in Utah and the West. The settlement also establishes a process to explore improvements to Enbridge’s ThermWise gas efficiency and conservation programs that can help customers reduce gas consumption and lower their energy bills.

While no single settlement can address every challenge facing Utah’s energy system and climate emissions, this agreement is an important first step in improving transparency around large-scale gas utility investments. With additional data, information and analysis, Utah can make more informed decisions about the costs and risks to ratepayers and future generations who will ultimately be paying for these long-lived assets. The settlement lays the groundwork for a more affordable, resilient and climate-friendly energy future for Utah households and businesses.

title: Ask a Scientist: Who Has a Voice in Clean Air Protections? - The Equation
description:

During the Biden administration, the White House Office of Management and Budget (OMB) did a lot of work to assess and expand meaningful public participation in government decisions.
AAS: Why does this participation matter, and how did you end up focusing on the air pollution permitting process?
One specific environmental program where public participation is relevant is in Title V of the federal Clean Air Act (CAA), which covers operating permits for facilities that generate air pollution.
Some might have a lot of resources explaining how to participate in air permitting, but a confusing website.
text:
If developers and planners decide to site an industrial chemical plant next door to your home, you’d want the chance to speak up about it. Soliciting input from the communities and individuals affected by pollution is an essential part of how environmental and public health laws are enforced. Under the federal Clean Air Act, large polluting facilities like power plants, chemical manufacturers, and refineries need to have a building permit, and every permitting decision must go through a “notice and comment” process. Although this is a federal law, it’s largely implemented by state, regional, and local agencies. And as a new UCS analysis shows, how much influence people have on the air permitting process varies greatly depending on where they live.

Darya Minovi leads fair access research for the Center for Science and Democracy at UCS. She is the lead author of Community Access to Clean Air Decisionmaking: Analysis of State Engagement in Title V Permitting, a new report that looks state-by-state at how people can make their voices heard.

AAS: What inspired you to do this analysis?

Darya Minovi: Last year, our team did an analysis of how the Trump administration is limiting public input on regulations, and also developed a set of recommendations for how government agencies should ensure the public gets to participate. With the administration very clearly side-stepping or ignoring these public processes, we did not, to put it lightly, expect the federal government to be a willing recipient of our research and guidance.

During the Biden administration, the White House Office of Management and Budget (OMB) did a lot of work to assess and expand meaningful public participation in government decisions. That was essentially all thrown away when President Trump was inaugurated. After consulting with colleagues and partners, we wanted to know: in this vacuum where the federal government isn’t interested in making progress, could we work with states to advance the public’s ability to participate in environmental policies?

AAS: Why does this participation matter, and how did you end up focusing on the air pollution permitting process?

DM: When you look at the core principles of environmental justice, meaningful engagement is central. People have the right to understand what’s happening in their communities, and ideally be part of shaping those decisions. They need the opportunity to speak out and be respectfully listened to. People’s lived experience is expertise that can and should inform policy decisions. That’s democracy in action. At the federal level, environmental justice has been targeted and dismantled, but some states still value these principles.

One specific environmental program where public participation is relevant is in Title V of the federal Clean Air Act (CAA), which covers operating permits for facilities that generate air pollution. This includes power plants, refineries, trash incinerators, and factories that manufacture chemicals—under the law, these are often called “major sources,” and there are very specific legal requirements about public participation. It’s one of the main ways air pollution gets regulated. But even though CAA is a federal law, it’s largely state and local agencies that carry out this permit process.

When a facility owner or company wants to apply for a permit to operate, they must submit a permit application to the relevant state, regional or local agency. The agency writes a draft permit, which must be posted publicly in some way. The CAA requires agencies to accept public comments on the draft permit for at least 30 days and, if requested by the public, hold a hearing. Agencies also have a legal obligation to respond to substantive comments. These are very clear steps laid out in the law. It’s a high bar for participation, but we wanted to better understand how it works in practice.

What we found in our analysis is that the agencies with the authority to issue permits will approve Title V air permits unless there’s some clear problem with legal compliance. But the public can use that “notice and comment” process to slow down and influence what the facility will actually be permitted to do.

However, some agencies treat the public comment process as a set of boxes to check off. The law isn’t specific about meaningful engagement practices beyond public comment, so our analysis also looked at practices, programs, guidance, and laws at the state level, beyond what’s required by the federal government to enhance public participation in air permitting.

AAS: How did you do this analysis, and what did you find?

DM: We wanted to get the answers to three big questions.

How easy is it to find information about permitting and the process to provide input?

Are there any rules, practices or guidance the agency uses to enhance participation? Do the agencies have, for instance, formal advisory committees or laws that require enhanced public participation in permitting?

What’s the agency’s capacity to administer these processes? Do they have the personnel and the funding to give this the attention it needs?

We started with what I’ll call “desktop research”—reviewing agency websites and laws as though we were residents looking to navigate the process. All 50 states do have at least a website with some information. In general, agencies are posting draft permits and accepting public comments, as the CAA requires. But there are big differences in how that happens.

Public hearings aren’t very frequent and usually happen only if there’s a critical mass of people demanding them. We also reviewed nearly 90 permits from 35 different states—the public notices are often very technical, not easily readable by a layperson, and they’ll say things like “comments are due 30 days from posting date” instead of giving the actual dated deadline.

Very few states translate these notices into languages other than English. And we assessed whether the notices use “plain language” best practices—defining scientific terms, using white space and bullet points—and found that most states aren’t integrating these effectively. Minnesota and Michigan stand out as providing clear, readable information, and that’s largely the result of advocacy by local groups there.

We found that while 42 states had some resources describing how people can participate in permitting, the quality varied significantly. By and large permitting webpages and resources seem better designed for regulated industries, not the general public.

Ultimately, a public notice is only useful if you can find it, read it, and understand what it means and what you’re supposed to do to get involved!

We also wanted to know: do the comments make a difference? If they’re just going to get collected and sit on a shelf, that’s less meaningful than if agencies answer them or make actual changes to the permit in response. It’s very rare for agencies to deny a permit but there are ways for public comments to have an impact—correcting errors, adding monitoring requirements, strengthening enforcement.

AAS: You reached out to states to learn more. What did you find?

DM: Talking directly to these state agencies was an important part of our research. We built an 88-question survey, based on our September 2025 guidance, to ask agencies how they provide information, what they do to encourage participation, and what resources they have to carry the work out.

While we sent that survey to every state, only half the states responded in full, with 3 more responding partially. A few states said they intended to respond but didn’t, while others declined to participate or failed to respond entirely. That itself speaks to the capacity and, perhaps, interest these agencies have.

The states’ answers varied. Of the 28 states we heard back from, only 18 said they post responses to comments online, and only 13 could give us an example of when public comments resulted in a change to a permit.

At least 11 states have laws that go beyond what’s required in the CAA, and those laws often center environmental justice or cumulative impacts. States with these laws tended to have more readily available information on how to participate, as well as more resources and funding devoted to public outreach. Having these laws—or at least guidelines—in place does seem to create agency-wide changes to enhance public engagement.

Meaningful engagement takes time, money, and actual staff to manage the process. Only 20 of the agencies we spoke to provide training on public participation or environmental justice for staff, and only 16 have actual full-time staff dedicated to the process.

Unfortunately, the federal government is pushing in the opposite direction. Aaron Szabo, the (now former) director of the air-quality office at the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, issued a memo urging states to expedite the Title V permitting process and rapidly review permits—saying, explicitly, that agencies don’t get many comments, so they don’t really matter.

AAS: Which states were the standouts?

DM: I was surprised by how much variability there was between and even within states. Some might have a lot of resources explaining how to participate in air permitting, but a confusing website. Others might translate public notices in other languages, but have no other information about how to participate.

While there’s a lot of room for improvement, there are some instructive examples too. For example, North Dakota has explicit guidance on how to write an effective public comment, with examples of common mistakes to avoid. Connecticut and Wisconsin have specific “how to” webpages to help people make comments or request a hearing. South Carolina has a webpage specifically entitled “Air Quality Decisions” that lays out what decision was made and posts the comments made in response to the draft permit. Ohio was the only state that got an “A” grade for readability of a public notice, with most states falling in the B/C range.

Every state can do better, of course, and we have a set of recommendations for how these agencies can improve. Governors, state lawmakers, and agency heads have a role to play here—certainly with funding for agencies and laws, but also in how they direct their agencies to carry this process out. Using public health data, translating notices into culturally appropriate languages and presenting them in plain language, making sure there’s fulltime staff devoted to public participation—these are just some of the steps to make participating in the air permitting process more meaningful, so that people not only have their voices heard, but actually have influence on decisions that shape air quality in their communities.

Background

On October 27, 2026, EPA proposed broad revisions to the March 2024 New Source Performance Standards and Emission Guidelines for methane and volatile organic compound (VOC) emissions from the oil and natural gas sector under 40 CFR part 60, Subparts OOOOb and OOOOc (the 2024 Rule). 91 Fed. Reg. 68,234 (Oct. 29, 2026) (the October 2026 Proposal).

This is EPA’s latest step in reconsidering the 2024 Rule: in 2025, the agency extended several compliance deadlines and moved the super-emitter program and state plan deadlines to January 22, 2027. Then, in April 2026, EPA finalized narrower changes to temporary flaring and flare monitoring. The October 2026 Proposal goes much further, and EPA estimates it would save operators $45 billion.

Key Takeaways

Reduced requirements and more flexibility. The October 2026 Proposal would reduce requirements for marginal or conventional well sites, rescind the third-party super-emitter program, and allow 95% control as an alternative to routing associated gas to a sales line.

Broader than it looks. EPA is soliciting comment on more than 80 topics related to the proposed changes and comments on any other change to the 2024 Rule, so the final rule could reach further than the October 2026 Proposal.

Nothing changes yet. The 2024 Rule and its extended deadlines remain in effect, including initial annual reports due November 30, 2026.

Comments are due December 16, 2026. EPA will hold a virtual public hearing on November 16 at 10 a.m. ET.

What EPA Proposed

The October 2026 Proposal’s principal changes:

What EPA Is Asking About

Table 34 of the October 2026 Proposal lists more than 80 specific questions about which EPA is soliciting comments on related to the proposed changes. In addition to those questions, EPA is soliciting comments on any and all changes that could be made to the 2024 Rule, including changes that could, in EPA’s words, unleash U.S. energy dominance or would relieve operators of unnecessary regulatory burdens.

If a 2024 Rule requirement is imposing real cost, the door is open to ask EPA to revise it—even though EPA did not propose that change. Additionally, because the final rule could change provisions the October 2026 Proposal does not mention, nothing in the 2024 Rule should be treated as settled. Of the more than 80 solicited questions, those most likely to matter to operators include:

Process controllers and storage vessels. Whether to repeal the zero-emission standard for process controllers and allow routing to a control device, with added flexibility for sites without electricity; and whether to repeal or modify the 2024 “legally and practicably enforceable” criteria that determine when tanks and tank batteries are subject to the rule.

Marginal and conventional wells. Whether conventional wells should receive reduced requirements regardless of production, whether to split marginal wells into two tiers at six barrels of oil equivalent per day, and whether to reduce leak-monitoring requirements further.

Monitoring, recordkeeping, and reporting. Whether to repeal liquids unloading recordkeeping where operators can show no venting and, more broadly, whether inspection frequencies and documentation requirements cost more than they deliver.

The 2024 Rule’s foundations. Whether EPA’s best-system-of-emission-reduction determinations across the 2024 Rule underestimated costs or overestimated reductions, and whether any other 2024 requirement is technically achievable, cost-effective, or legally justified.

text:
NEW ORLEANS — When the North American Biochar Conference comes to the Ernest N. Morial Convention Center Nov. 16-18, New Jersey artist Abhijeet Shrivastava will showcase 12 works made with carbon-rich biochar, demonstrating how an emerging carbon-removal industry can connect environmental innovation with art, agriculture and commercial opportunities.

Shrivastava, a program manager at Microsoft with a background in climate consulting, architecture and urban design, began experimenting with charcoal and other carbon-based materials more than a decade ago. His first solo exhibition, “Black is Beautiful,” opened in Jabalpur, India, in 2012, and he has worked primarily in black ever since.

“I also work professionally in the climate and sustainability space, and I began using my art for climate storytelling,” Shrivastava said. “Along the way I discovered biochar and its benefits, experimented with it, and developed a customized material of my own.”

His work now combines artistic expression with carbon removal, using biochar, a carbon-rich material produced by heating organic matter in a low-oxygen environment, to create drawings that also serve as a form of long-term carbon storage.

“For me it is about more than making art,” he said. “The work should have a purpose, and that purpose is application on the ground, with certified environmental impact.”

Making Carbon Removal Visible

Biochar has attracted growing interest as a commercial product because of its potential to store carbon for extended periods while improving soil conditions. Shrivastava sees art as a way to help businesses, investors and the public understand an industry often discussed in technical or financial terms.

“A tonne of removal is abstract. A drawing made from the same material makes it visible and touchable,” he said. “When a visitor learns the black on the paper is carbon that will stay locked away for centuries, the market stops being a trading concept and becomes something they can see. That is the bridge the work is trying to build.”

Shrivastava also uses Certificates of Impact to document the environmental benefits associated with his artwork.

“Every finished piece carries a certificate that quantifies the carbon locked into it and traces its biochar to verified soil application on smallholder farms in Kenya and India, sourced through PlantVillage+ and Puro.earth and VCS verified projects,” he said.

“The farmers benefit because their crop waste becomes biochar that goes back into their soil, improving it, instead of being burned or left to rot,” he said.

Proceeds from his artwork also support farmers in India who use biochar to improve soil productivity and crop yields. According to his impact dashboard, the initiative has locked 125 kilograms of carbon dioxide and delivered more than 14 tons of biochar compost to participating farms in India and Kenya. The dashboard also reports an average crop productivity increase of approximately 15%.

“Each certificate quantifies the carbon in a single piece, and the impact is documented on the Impact page of my website for anyone to see,” he said.

From Art Galleries to Commercial Opportunities

Shrivastava’s work has reached audiences beyond the sustainability industry. His recent exhibitions include the 2026 MvVO ART AD ART SHOW at the Waldorf Astoria New York and a showing at the Oculus in Manhattan.

His work “Cities and Climate Change” was also selected in 2022 to illustrate Chapter 12 of the Fifth National Climate Assessment, which examines the built environment.

“The response has grown through awareness and campaigns,” he said. “The work is meant to heal as much as to depict, and that framing is reaching people.”

He now hopes to expand beyond individual artwork sales through partnerships with businesses and organizations interested in using art to communicate their sustainability initiatives.

“My vision now is to partner with companies and organizations, so the campaigns can make a larger impact than individual pieces can on their own.”

Beyond his own artwork, Shrivastava sees broader commercial opportunities for biochar.

“The opportunity is that biochar does two things at once. It stores carbon durably and it improves soil, so farmers, companies, and climate buyers all have a reason to care,” he said.

That commercial potential is also drawing investment in Louisiana. New Orleans-based Robinson Carbon recently announced plans for a $16.3 million biochar manufacturing facility in Alexandria, where wood manufacturing residuals will be converted into products for agricultural and environmental applications.

But expanding the market will require overcoming barriers related to awareness, verification and affordability. Shrivastava also sees opportunities to explore biochar’s use beyond agriculture and carbon storage.

“The challenge is trust and understanding. Most people have never seen biochar, verification has to be credible, and the cost has to work for the people growing the feedstock,” he said. “I am also trained as an Architect, and I want to experiment with biochar in building materials too.”

Bringing the Carbon Story to New Orleans

Shrivastava’s 12 works will be featured in the conference’s Product & Art Showcase, including pieces exploring forests, landscapes and cities, among them “The Carbon Forest.”

He will also participate in the conference’s “Importance of Storytelling” session Wednesday afternoon, Nov. 18, discussing how art can communicate the environmental and economic significance of biochar.

“The plan is to keep building through farm partnerships in Kenya and India, pairing sustainable agriculture with art campaigns, and through commissions that tell a sponsor’s story,” he said.

“What I hope attendees take away is simple. Their sustainability efforts, climate story, or farms have a story that art can tell.”

Electric vehicles are estimated to displace 1.9 million barrels per day of oil demand in 2026, yet create new dependencies on China, which dominates nearly all parts of the clean tech supply chain

ANTALYA, Türkiye , Nov. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- S&P Global (NYSE: SPGI) today releases a new report, Adopting Clean Technologies: The Energy Resilience Dividend. Released during COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, the report explores how clean technology adoption can strengthen countries' economic, energy and geostrategic resilience by reducing exposure to imported fossil fuels and global fossil fuel shocks, while also creating new external dependencies, particularly on China.

In the report, the S&P Global Institute brings together joint analysis from S&P Global Energy and S&P Global Ratings. The analysis covers nine advanced economies, plus case studies of Europe and China.

Key highlights:

Lower oil-import dependence is associated with greater economic resilience: Countries that rely less on oil imports reduce GDP impact of oil supply shocks by around 0.25 percentage points.

Europe's renewables expansion has helped reduce exposure to energy shocks: EU non-hydro renewable generation is up nearly 340 terawatt-hours (TWh) since 2021, 70% more than the 2016–2021 increase, and European clean tech investment in 2026 is expected to more than double 2021 levels.

Electric vehicles are reducing exposure to oil demand and price shocks: S&P Global Energy estimates battery electric and plug-in hybrid light vehicles (EVs) on the road globally will displace 1.9 million barrels per day of oil demand in 2026, nearly 2% of global oil demand.

China's EV scale is extending resilience beyond its domestic market: China exported nearly 2.5 million EVs in the first half of 2026, more than double the year-earlier period.

Clean technology creates new strategic dependencies: China dominates nearly all parts of the clean tech supply chain, from mining and processing of key metals and minerals to components and technologies, making supply chain diversification increasingly important to macroeconomic resilience.

"Our analysis suggests clean technology investment can deliver benefits that extend beyond climate objectives by strengthening countries' resilience to energy supply and price shocks," said Marion Amiot, Head of Climate Economics, S&P Global Ratings. "But the nature of energy security is also changing. As economies electrify, managing concentrated supply chains and new external dependencies will become an increasingly important part of the resilience equation."

"Energy, geopolitics, technology and capital flows can no longer be understood in silos, and this report shows why," said Alexandra Dimitrijevic, Head of the S&P Global Institute. "By bringing together expertise from across S&P Global, the Institute helps leaders see how these forces connect and plan with greater confidence."

text:
The free admission in celebration of Texas Recycles Day runs from Nov. 13 to 15

To celebrate Texas Recycles Day, H-E-B is giving Texans free admission to 20 nature centers across the state. From Nov. 13 to 15, each individual visitor should bring one recyclable plastic bottle or single-use plastic bag to one of the centers for free entry.

This effort is one of many that H-E-B supports throughout the year as a part of the retailer’s commitment to maximize recycling efforts throughout its business and the communities it serves.

H-E-B’s Our Texas, Our Future commitment also extends to the creation of new recycling opportunities throughout the state. H-E-B’s Recycling for Texans program helps fund municipal grants that support the creation and improvement of recycling programs for cities and counties across the state. In 2027, H-E-B will have donated $232,500 to Keep Texas Beautiful to support improving and expanding access to recycling in Bandera, Burleson and Real counties. The funds will not only better local recycling capabilities but will also divert valuable materials away from landfills. Since 2021, H-E-B has invested more than $1.2 million in recycling grants for more than 16 Texas communities that serve nearly 720,000 residents.

This year, the city of Columbus received a $36,000 grant through the Recycling for Texans program which strengthened the city’s recycling facility with new equipment and expanded recycling education and outreach efforts. H-E-B also helped support the opening of Port Arthur’s first-ever drop-off recycling center in August. Through a $109,000 grant in 2025 and an additional investment of $85,000 in 2026, the center provides residents a new and convenient recycling option. Within the center’s first two months of operation, nearly 6,000 pounds of cardboard was collected and diverted from Texas landfills.

As part of H-E-B’s Texas Recycles Day, the retailer also partnered with Austin ISD and San Antonio ISD during the Fall semester to foster recycling practices within local schools. Throughout the semester, district-wide recycling challenges encouraged students to collect recyclable materials and promote the practice across their campus. H-E-B awarded a combined $85,000 to participating schools, each of the top performing schools earned a donation between $1,000 to $10,000. The program resulted in a total of nearly 653,000 pounds of recyclable materials collected with more than 25,600 pounds from Austin ISD’s efforts and approximately 627,000 pounds of material collected by San Antonio ISD students. A special project will also recognize San Antonio ISD’s Bella Cameron Elementary with a revitalization of the school’s playground to enhance outdoor learning spaces and increase native landscaping.

Additionally, H-E-B expanded its Carrying Goodness partnership with Goodwill and food banks to extend the use of surplus reusable bags. The program is now active through Goodwill locations in Central Texas, San Antonio, Houston, and South Texas. Through the collaborative project, when donation-filled or empty reusable bags are dropped off at Goodwill locations in the regions listed above, Goodwill will give the bags to the food bank for use in food distributions. Nearly 85,000 bags have been donated since the program’s launch on Earth Day 2025. Every H-E-B store also has collection bins at the front entrance for customers to use to recycle plastic bags and other eligible plastic items, such as other retail shopping bags, produce bags, bread bags, dry cleaning bags, newspaper bags, and plastic overwrap for items like paper towels. Curbside customers also can bring eligible plastic items to be recycled when they pick up their orders.

Last year, H-E-B recycled 671 million pounds of material, including plastics, cardboard and paper. An additional 89.6 million pounds of food was recycled into compost or biofuel. H-E-B’s Hunger Relief program also donated 40.9 million pounds of excess food to feed Texas families. Since 2012, H-E-B has contributed approximately $30 million to over 500 environmental organizations in land and water conservation, habitat and coastal preservation, and community cleanups. To join H-E-B in its mission to reduce contamination in residential recycling, tips and best practices can be found on its Our Texas, Our Future website.

text:
Honda announced today that the 2028 CR-V, due out next year, will be powered exclusively by a new two-motor hybrid system, no gas-only option included. It's the biggest shift yet for one of America's best-selling SUV, and the first of several hybrid-only models Honda plans to roll out across North America by 2030.

The seventh-generation CR-V rides on an all-new platform and gets a fresh exterior design alongside the powertrain change. Honda says the move reflects where buyers already are: hybrid variants currently make up more than half of CR-V sales, and the automaker has posted back-to-back hybrid sales records in 2024 and 2025.

A New Platform And A More Efficient Hybrid System

The 2028 CR-V debuts the 5th generation of Honda's two-motor hybrid system, which the company says delivers better performance and efficiency than the version in today's CR-V. Honda is targeting a fuel economy improvement of more than 10% over the current hybrid, achieved partly by widening the range where the gas engine runs at its most efficient. A newly developed electric AWD unit is also part of the package, giving more precise and responsive control over how power gets to each axle, which should translate to steadier traction in slippery conditions.

The new platform underneath it all was built to balance rigidity and weight, with a modular design Honda says will carry across multiple models. Honda is framing it as a driving-experience upgrade as much as an efficiency one, describing the goal as a sportier, more engaging feel behind the wheel.

Why Honda Is Betting Everything On Hybrids Right Now

The timing lines up with demand. CR-V hybrid sales have grown nearly tenfold since the variant launched in 2020, and hybrids now account for roughly 30% of all Honda sales. The CR-V itself isn't slowing down either; it's on pace to top 400,000 units sold for the third year running, and remains the best-selling light-duty vehicle in the U.S. through October 2026, with more than 7.5 million units sold since it launched.

"With a 100% hybrid powertrain, the next-generation Honda CR-V will further expand the appeal of America's most popular SUV as demand for hybrid-electric vehicles reaches record levels," said Luis Guerra, assistant vice president of Honda National Auto Sales.

Built In Ohio, Assembled Across Three Plants

The new hybrid system will be produced at Honda's Transmission Plant in Ohio, which is being retooled to build hybrid systems for compact, midsize, and larger vehicles, with capacity set to grow by 250% in the coming years. Honda's Anna Engine Plant is adding a line for the next-generation 4-cylinder Atkinson-cycle engine that will power the CR-V and other future North American models.

Assembly stays spread across three North American plants, the East Liberty Auto Plant in Ohio, the Indiana Auto Plant, and Honda of Canada Mfg. Honda has built more than 7 million CR-Vs in North America since 2006. The announcement also comes as the CR-V approaches its 30th anniversary in 2027, and as Honda teased a separate large-size hybrid system last October in Japan built around a new V6 engine, hinting at where the electrification push goes next.
