name: EPA
title: 'Satisfactory Performer': How a Serial Polluter Keeps Thriving in Texas - Public Health Watch
authors: Shelby Jouppi, Jim Morris, Avi Paulson, Savanna Strott
description:
Highly flammable vinyl chloride is a known carcinogen that targets the liver, brain and other organs.
About 40% of them involved vinyl chloride.
Two years after the facility opened, the Texas Attorney General’s Office sued Formosa for 65 air violations involving excessive releases of vinyl chloride.
Just four days after the EDC unit opened in 1993, 2,000 gallons of EDC leaked out of a faulty joint, sending a worker to intensive care.
Formosa’s Vinyl Chloride Monomer, or VCM, unit, where it makes vinyl chloride, is especially feared and despised by workers.
text:
POINT COMFORT, Texas — For more than four decades, the Formosa Plastics plant here has been a picture of turmoil and indulgence. Situated in Calhoun County, on the Texas Gulf Coast, it has amassed a record of environmental contamination and workplace calamity that, in theory, should have subjected it to rigorous oversight and limited its ability to grow.

Instead, Texas regulators have given the Taiwan-based company permission to expand its Point Comfort plant 10 times in the past 16 years, allowed its managers to avoid spending money on pollution controls and slashed enormous fines the company was in line to receive.

The state’s stewardship of Formosa is crucial because the company’s foundational product — a resin that underpins production of a common form of plastic — requires the use of two chemicals so hazardous that the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency has short-listed them for possible restrictions or bans. Highly flammable vinyl chloride is a known carcinogen that targets the liver, brain and other organs. Ethylene dichloride, or EDC — an oily, smelly liquid used to make vinyl chloride — is a probable carcinogen that can quickly evaporate into a flammable, poisonous gas. Formosa has mismanaged both from its earliest days in Point Comfort.

Public Health Watch has spent the past 10 months examining Formosa’s environmental and worker-safety records and its relationship with the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality, or TCEQ. The TCEQ is the lead enforcer of federal anti-pollution laws in Texas, but our investigation shows that in Formosa’s case, the agency has behaved more like a sympathetic counselor than a flinty cop.

Among our findings:

The Point Comfort plant is among the nation’s top emitters of vinyl chloride, a carcinogen and a key ingredient in polyvinyl chloride, or PVC, a type of plastic used in pipes and other products. Most of Formosa’s emissions are allowed as part of its routine operations. But others are due to accidents, known as emissions events. While these incidents have generally declined at other large petrochemical facilities in Texas over the past two decades, they’ve increased at Formosa. About 40% of them involved vinyl chloride.

The TCEQ has cited Formosa for 587 environmental violations since 2010, but it has fined the company for only 71 of them, resulting in about $1.4 million in penalties. That amounts to less than three hours’ worth of sales last year for Formosa Plastics Corp. USA, the parent of Formosa operations in Texas and Louisiana. Formosa resolved 18 air pollution violations not by fixing the root causes but by obtaining permit amendments that allowed it to legally release more foul air. That’s like addressing chronic speeding on a stretch of highway not with an enhanced police presence but by raising the speed limit.

After a series of chemical releases, fires, explosions and 34 worker injuries at Formosa in the 2010s, the U.S. Department of Justice found that the company’s failure to follow operating instructions had left one of its units vulnerable to fire and explosion for close to two decades. In 2013, that unit ignited, injuring 14 workers, including two who had to be airlifted out of Point Comfort. The case was settled in 2021, with Formosa agreeing to pay $2.9 million in penalties.

Worker safety remains a pressing concern at the plant. At least 122 people were hurt there between 2020 and 2025 — more than at four other large Texas chemical facilities combined, according to a Public Health Watch analysis of self-reported federal injury data. In the first 10 months of this year, the Calhoun County Emergency Communications Division received 27 medical emergency calls from Formosa, according to 911 logs. That’s more than in all of 2014, the company’s recent peak. In August, a call came in for a worker who was severely burned on both legs and had to be airlifted.

For 18 years, Formosa stored some of its hazardous waste without a permit, a major infringement of federal law. When the TCEQ discovered the infraction in 2014, it could have penalized the company for each of the 6,534 days it was out of compliance, for a maximum fine of $51 million. Instead, Formosa was penalized for each year it was out of compliance. After additional discounts, its fine was just $103,000.

“This is like a list of red flags,” said Tom Mariani, who led the Justice Department’s environmental enforcement section during the first Trump administration and the Biden administration. “If the EPA came to me and said, ‘Well, here’s what we know about Company X,’ I’d say, ‘This entity deserves our attention.’”

Formosa’s environmental and worker-safety problems extend well beyond Texas.

In 1985, the company’s now-shuttered PVC plant in Delaware City, Delaware, was so rife with vinyl chloride leaks that the state revoked its operating permits and shut it down temporarily. Michael Castle, Delaware’s governor at the time, warned chemical manufacturers that “if we must make a choice between the interests of industry and the well-being of our constituents, invariably we will act in the interest of the public.”

In 2004, two years after Formosa took over a PVC plant in Illiopolis, Illinois, the facility exploded when a cloud of leaked vinyl chloride ignited, killing five workers and injuring three. Federal investigators found there had been a near-miss at the plant two months before the blast — and a similar close call a year earlier at a Formosa plant in Baton Rouge, Louisiana. The Illiopolis facility never reopened.

Formosa’s biggest environmental debacle, in 2016, made headlines around the globe. Wastewater spilled from the company’s steel mill on the coast of central Vietnam, leaving behind more than 100 tons of dead fish and sickening untold numbers of people. Formosa admitted responsibility and paid the Vietnamese government $500 million, but it is still being sued by victims of the disaster, who claim they haven’t recovered physically or economically.

These highly publicized episodes didn’t slow Formosa’s momentum in Texas.

Less than a year after the Vietnam spill, the TCEQ gave the company the go-ahead to build a third high-density polyethylene, or HDPE, unit — which makes the raw ingredients for milk jugs, trash bags and other consumer and industrial products — even though its two existing HDPE units had racked up major hazardous-waste violations and experienced two accidents that injured 19 workers. The project extended Formosa’s footprint north, into adjoining Jackson County, where it now owns 7,000 acres of undeveloped land — an expanse half the size of Manhattan.

In September 2023, shortly after TCEQ inspectors cited Formosa for its 43rd air-pollution violation that year, the agency gave the company permission to move deeper into Jackson County. The unit there will produce 1-Hexene, a flammable liquid that can irritate the eyes and respiratory tract and, in high concentrations, lead to unconsciousness or death. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, who was feted by Formosa executives during a 2024 trade mission to Taiwan, praised the project and announced that it qualified for a new state tax incentive program.

Fires, explosions and toxic discharges aside, the TCEQ classifies Formosa as a “satisfactory performer.” This designation shields it from the higher penalties, extra paperwork and slower permitting that can go with an “unsatisfactory” rating.

“Formosa is not an isolated case,” said Kathryn Guerra, a former TCEQ and EPA employee who now directs the TCEQ Watchdog Campaign for the advocacy group Public Citizen. “It’s what happens when the state favors corporate profit over public health. There’s nothing a polluter can do that would make the TCEQ not give it another permit.”

Public Health Watch sent a summary of our findings and a list of detailed questions to Formosa. The company did not answer the questions but sent an email saying it “takes its environmental and workplace safety responsibilities seriously. We work closely with the appropriate regulatory agencies, comply with applicable reporting requirements, and continually pursue improvements in our operations.”

We also sent summaries of our findings to the TCEQ, the EPA, the U.S. Occupational Safety and Health Administration, or OSHA, and state and federal elected officials.

The TCEQ declined to comment. Spokespeople for the EPA and OSHA did not respond to repeated requests for comment.

“Thank you for bringing this information to my attention,” State Sen. Lois W. Kolkhorst, a Republican whose district includes Calhoun County, said in a written statement. “I will take a closer look at these claims and consult with the TCEQ and other regulatory agencies about the sanctions or lack thereof. Safety of employees and meeting necessary and important environmental protections must be a top priority for the state.”

State Sen. Molly Cook, an emergency room nurse and a former volunteer environmental organizer, said the findings were “hard to hear. … This is just another example of how corporate entities are allowed to run wild in Texas at the expense of everyday Texans.” Cook, a Democrat from Houston, said that in the coming legislative session, she will be “laser-focused” on making sure TCEQ permits aren’t “rubber stamps” for companies that “soil our air and soil our water.”

A spokesperson for Abbott, a Republican who lost his bid for a fourth term last week, declined to comment. “I would have to refer you to TCEQ,” the spokesperson wrote in an email. A spokesperson for the governor-elect, Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa, did not respond to requests for comment. The governor appoints the three commissioners who oversee the TCEQ.

Fraught beginnings

When Formosa opened its plant on the eastern shore of Lavaca Bay in 1983, its primary product was PVC resin, a white powder that is mixed with chemicals, heated and shaped to make pipes, siding, packaging and other goods. Making the resin requires two extremely hazardous ingredients: vinyl chloride and ethylene dichloride, or EDC.

Formosa struggled to manage these chemicals from the start.

The plant was still under construction when EDC spilled onto the soil and seeped into the groundwater. Two years after the facility opened, the Texas Attorney General’s Office sued Formosa for 65 air violations involving excessive releases of vinyl chloride. In the late 1980s, the EPA found that Formosa had been storing and treating EDC-laced hazardous waste without a permit. The EPA later fined Formosa a then-record $3.4 million.

Despite more spills and air violations, in 1989 Texas and the EPA greenlit a $1.3 billion expansion that would enlarge the plant’s domain fivefold. The project included an EDC manufacturing unit that would give the company an in-house supply of the essential chemical.

Formosa said its investment would yield the “world’s safest and cleanest chemical complex.” News accounts told another story.

During the first year of construction, three laborers died and Formosa spilled about 500 gallons of EDC it was unloading from a barge. In 1991, a broken valve unleashed into the community a dense cloud of hydrochloric acid, which irritates the respiratory system and, in heavy concentrations, can cause a fatal buildup of fluid in the lungs. Nearby ranchers said it burned their eyes and throats and sent their cattle “bawling and running.” The following year, OSHA cited Formosa for dozens of workplace safety violations, including willfully failing to monitor for vinyl chloride when workers were being exposed above legal limits.

Just four days after the EDC unit opened in 1993, 2,000 gallons of EDC leaked out of a faulty joint, sending a worker to intensive care.

According to a class-action lawsuit residents filed against Formosa in 1994, the plant produced noxious “vapors, fumes, dust, smoke and odors. … There are also frequent explosions, powerful rumblings and vibrations from the Formosa facility which shake the ground of Plaintiffs’ property and rattle windows of Plaintiffs’ homes.”

Formosa ended up buying many of the homes and land at above-market prices, a lawyer for the plaintiffs said. Today, Formosa owns about a third of the residential properties in Point Comfort, and the town’s population is about a quarter of what it was when the company arrived.

In 1997, Formosa enlarged the EDC unit and boosted its shipping rate for the chemical. A string of tragedies followed. Just two months after regulators authorized the expansion, two workers were found dead in a tank of EDC. The following year, another EDC tank exploded, injuring 67 workers. News reports said the blast shook homes in Point Comfort, caused three schools to evacuate and sent an estimated 16,000 gallons of the chemical into the environment.

The company also fought to control releases of vinyl chloride it made and used on site. In 2009, Formosa signed a federal consent decree that included a $2.8 million fine and required it to spend an estimated $10 million to control leaks of vinyl chloride and other volatile organic compounds, or VOCs, and improve its handling of EDC- and vinyl chloride-contaminated waste at its Point Comfort and Baton Rouge plants.

The legally binding agreement remains in effect, and the company still hasn’t gained control of the two problematic chemicals, which wind up in the air, on the ground or on workers.

Formosa has reported 50 leaks of vinyl chloride to the U.S. Coast Guard’s National Response Center and the TCEQ since 2020. The gas escaped through misaligned or open valves, holes and cracks in piping, or broken equipment. On October 19 of this year, nearly 4,000 pounds of vinyl chloride was expelled from a ruptured pump, according to a report Formosa filed with the TCEQ. The leak lasted 17 hours.

Since 2020, Formosa has reported more than two dozen EDC spills and air releases, and at least four workers have been injured after coming into contact with the chemical, according to OSHA records. In one of those incidents, a worker cleaning out a tank of EDC suffered burns over 30% of his body and was hospitalized with kidney failure.

TCEQ records show the company is still cleaning up groundwater contamination caused by years of EDC and vinyl chloride spills. The agency and Formosa did not answer questions about the extent of the contamination or whether it poses a threat to the community.

The EPA recently concluded that EDC presents an “unreasonable risk” to industrial workers because it can damage the kidneys, respiratory tract and male reproductive system, and “over a lifetime can cause cancer.” The agency said it will deal with those risks by strengthening worker protections and monitoring and possibly restricting or prohibiting the production or use of the chemical.

Mariani, the former Justice Department lawyer, said his office handled many enforcement cases involving petrochemical companies. Those operations are extremely complex, he said, and it’s not uncommon for things to go wrong.

“OK, is anybody perfect? No. But it seems like this facility [Formosa] is pretty far away from perfect,” Mariani said. “The public record shows that the facility has had significant problems, which could well mean violation of law.”

‘Waiting for the big one’

Petrochemical plants are inherently dangerous places, where workers risk injury, illness or death every time they drive through the gates.

But Formosa workers face a higher risk of injury than those at other large petrochemical complexes in Texas, according to a Public Health Watch analysis of self-reported federal injury data. Between 2020 and 2025, more people were injured at Formosa than at four other facilities combined – ExxonMobil in Baytown, ExxonMobil in Beaumont, LyondellBasell in Channelview and Dow Chemical in Freeport.

Formosa’s Vinyl Chloride Monomer, or VCM, unit, where it makes vinyl chloride, is especially feared and despised by workers.

“It is the oldest unit at the plant and easily the scariest,” a former employee told Public Health Watch. He requested anonymity because he still works in the petrochemical industry. “They’ve done so little maintenance over time that the drainage ditches, canals, trenches are plugged.”

He described the unit as chaotic and replete with hazards.

“There was mud and dirt and crap that had never been cleaned up. There was hoses coiled up at the bottom of ladders where people were coming down off of towers. … There was pallets floating in or sunk in [standing water] out there for you to trip over. … It was a scene like I have never encountered in a plant in my life.”

A current worker, who asked not to be identified for fear of retaliation, said many of the VCM unit’s pipes are corroded. “Everything is either being shut down because stuff needs to be replaced or something’s busting,” he said. “It’s drama. There’s a lot going on.”

He said that until he was interviewed by Public Health Watch, no one had told him that vinyl chloride could cause cancer. The EPA is expected to decide next year whether the chemical presents an unreasonable risk to workers or the public and should be more strictly regulated.

About a third of Formosa’s emissions events in the past five years occurred at the VCM unit, according to TCEQ records. The unit battled a power surge, shutdowns, and bursting and leaking equipment that resulted in large releases of vinyl chloride, hydrochloric acid and EDC.

The former worker said his concerns extend beyond the VCM unit.

“The failure to follow safety rules was pretty profound,” he said. He frequently saw people bypass OSHA-mandated procedures, including lockout-tagout. That’s a potentially life-saving rule that requires shutting down and isolating equipment prior to maintenance, so workers aren’t exposed to electricity, chemicals or maiming hazards.

This lax safety culture, he fears, could lead to something cataclysmic.

“Formosa’s safety pyramid is chock full,” he said, referring to the theory holding that weak management, unsafe behavior and frequent small incidents build toward catastrophes. “They’re waiting for the big one at the top, and they’re adding to the bottom daily. It’s only a matter of time.”

Formosa itself has acknowledged the dangers that lurk in the facility. In a worst-case accident scenario it filed with the EPA, the company estimated that a 10-minute release from the VCM unit could uncork a ground-hugging cloud of hydrochloric acid that could travel 15 miles and put more than 20,000 people at risk of injury or death. According to TCEQ records, that unit has had five accidental releases of hydrochloric acid in the past five years.

Calhoun County’s Local Emergency Planning Committee coordinates with Formosa and other large chemical plants to prepare for accidents and natural disasters. The committee’s public information officer and the county’s emergency coordinator, Ladonna Thigpen, told Public Health Watch she was “not familiar” with Formosa’s worst-case scenario report. But she expressed confidence in the company.

“Accidents happen,” Thigpen said. “All you can do is prepare, and they do a good job at preparing and they have good teams out there.”

A different picture emerged when Public Health Watch reviewed lawsuits, 911 records and OSHA injury logs dating to 2017. We found similar workplace accidents occurring year after year.

On three occasions, workers were severely burned after falling into holes filled with hot liquid that had been left open or improperly covered with plywood or cardboard. A worker who fell into scalding condensate in the VCM unit wrote in a Formosa incident report, “When I took my sock [off] my skin came off.”

One worker’s lawsuit said she hadn’t been provided with fall protection and had plummeted two stories from a tower. Another worker died after falling 25 feet through a hole in the floor grating of an elevated platform, according to an OSHA inspection report.

At least 14 people were injured after coming into contact with EDC, caustic liquid, chlorine gas or other hazardous substances.

A worker’s lawsuit filed in August said he was installing a flange when acid poured out, penetrating his protective clothing and causing severe burns. Another lawsuit alleged that when a worker went to replace a valve that was supposed to be empty, she was hit in the face with a high-pressure blast of PVC powder and liquid latex. The blast knocked off her hard hat and safety goggles, she said, and sent her stumbling backward over a pallet someone had left on the floor.

In the past four years, OSHA has cited Formosa for nine serious violations. Seven were for endangering workers in the VCM unit by failing to follow lockout-tagout procedures and failing to inspect a vessel and piping, among other things. After negotiations with Formosa, the agency downgraded seven of the nine violations and deleted two, cutting the initial $134,400 in penalties almost in half to $71,300.

Public Health Watch asked Formosa about the recent workplace accidents, as well as conditions and safety practices in the VCM unit. The company did not answer the questions.

‘Putting out wildfires’

It’s OSHA’s job to protect people from workplace perils, but in Formosa’s case, the agency has mostly been missing in action. While OSHA has responded to injuries and worker complaints at Point Comfort, the agency’s last planned, comprehensive inspection of the facility took place a decade ago. Since then, at least 21 people have been severely injured there, agency data shows.

OSHA’s discontinuity is likely due to its traditionally sparse resources, which have become even leaner under the Trump administration. OSHA now has fewer inspectors than at any time in its 55-year history, the AFL-CIO reported this year. It would take the agency’s 70 inspectors in Texas 215 years to visit every workplace in the state.

Dean Wingo, a former OSHA area director in Fort Worth and assistant regional administrator in Dallas, led the agency’s investigation into one of Texas’s worst industrial disasters in recent decades: the 2005 explosion at BP’s Texas City refinery, which killed 15 workers and injured 180.

“I would say Formosa, from what I’ve looked at, is going to experience a catastrophic event if they don’t correct their behavior at some point,” Wingo told Public Health Watch. “That would be my prediction.”

The U.S. Chemical Safety and Hazard Investigation Board’s report on the Texas City accident pinned most of the blame on “serious deficiencies” in BP’s safety culture and the company’s failure to invest in preventive maintenance. “Warning signs of a possible disaster were present for several years, but company officials did not intervene effectively to prevent it,” the board said. BP paid a record $87 million in OSHA penalties for its role in the tragedy.

Wingo worries that Formosa could be heading down the same path, given its frequent chemical accidents, injuries and poor housekeeping practices.

“They’re not actively looking for hazards and fixing them,” he said. “They’re waiting until they become issues and then … the expression is ‘putting out wildfires.’ So, they don’t look at fire prevention; they just look at putting out the fires when they happen. Their safety program is reactive, not proactive.”

Overstretched regulators

If OSHA has done an imperfect job of protecting workers, the TCEQ has fallen short safeguarding everyone else. The agency says it prioritizes both public health and economic development. In fact, it often goes out of its way to accommodate the companies it oversees.

Formosa is a case in point.

Although the company has racked up hundreds of environmental violations in the past two decades, the resulting TCEQ fines average just $83,000 per year. For an enterprise that collected $4.4 billion in annual sales last year, that’s the equivalent of a typical American household losing $1.65 in the sofa cushions.

“When you’re talking about multibillion-dollar companies, the penalties have to be meaningful to their bottom line in order to deter them from further noncompliance,” said Guerra, of Public Citizen. “If you fine them the same amount that the CEO makes before lunchtime in a day, it’s not going to deter them.”

The Texas Legislature has increased maximum penalties for polluters twice in the past 15 years. But in 2011, the TCEQ undercut those penalty boosts: It stopped tripling or quadrupling fines for companies with especially bad records.

The TCEQ did, however, continue another practice: offering sizable discounts to companies that settle their cases quickly or show a “good-faith effort to comply” with the rules. Formosa received such discounts on 80% of the 29 enforcement orders Public Health Watch examined, even in cases where the company had been deemed a “repeat violator,” a designation that should, in theory, have qualified it for larger penalties.

The agency does have a cudgel at its disposal: It can fine companies for each day they commit a major violation of environmental laws. But in Formosa’s case, it’s rarely used.

Nine of the company’s violations over the past two decades qualified for this designation, including one that was outstanding for more than 18 years. If Formosa had been fined by the day, it could have drawn penalties ranging from hundreds of thousands to tens of millions of dollars. But the TCEQ wielded this hammer only twice during that period, both times on violations that lasted just a day or two.

Even if the TCEQ had a sudden urge to clamp down on big polluters, it would strain to make that happen. The size of the agency’s enforcement staff — 1,006 positions at last count — has remained stagnant, even as the number of permit holders has increased by about 111,000 over the past five years. Today, there is roughly one compliance employee for every 829 permittees — businesses as small as a laundromat or as large as the ExxonMobil complex in Baytown.

In its legislative budget request for 2028 and 2029, the TCEQ asked for an extra $16.1 million for enforcement and investigations. If the request isn’t granted, Guerra said, funding for these activities won’t increase enough to keep up with the rising number of regulated companies.

The TCEQ didn’t respond when Public Health Watch asked about the growing chasm between the regulators and the regulated. But the TCEQ commissioners — the political appointees who oversee the agency — got defensive when Guerra broached the topic at their regular March meeting.

Guerra fired off two performance metrics Public Citizen compiled using the agency’s own 2025 data: the fewest number of on-site inspections in eight years, including the COVID-19 pandemic, and a backlog of nearly 1,400 enforcement cases.

Commission Chairwoman Brooke Paup replied icily that she found Guerra’s presentation “incredibly offensive to the 3,300 TCEQ staff who work tirelessly to make sure that this environment is protected.” Another commissioner dismissed Public Citizen, which claims about 1 million members and supporters nationally, as “a group with a very small following.”

Luke Metzger, executive director of the advocacy group Environment Texas, said the TCEQ’s deferential treatment of Formosa and other polluters unmasks the state’s permissive approach to regulation.

“The TCEQ emphasizes that it focuses on [companies] getting to compliance, that enforcement is just one tool and we should look at the results, not just how much they’re being fined,” Metzger said. “Unfortunately, we see in this case, as we see in many others, that the company is not getting to compliance. It’s clearly not working.”

Still ‘satisfactory’

Today, the footprint of Formosa’s Point Comfort plant stands at 2,500 acres, an area three times the size of New York’s Central Park. Its network of tanks, pipes, stacks, office buildings and parking lots stretches for nearly 3 miles along Farm-to-Market Road 1593.

According to data compiled by Material Research L3C, a supply-chain information service, the facility makes more chemicals used in plastics production than any other in the country. Formosa Plastics Corporation USA — primarily composed of its Texas and Louisiana facilities — had $13.1 billion in total assets at the end of last year.

The company has spread some of its wealth throughout Calhoun County.

About 3,700 people now work at the Point Comfort site, making it an economic leviathan in a remote part of Texas. The pay is good enough to attract novices to the chemical industry, with new hires earning up to $27 an hour. To ensure a steady supply of homegrown talent, Formosa opened a training center in the old Point Comfort elementary school building, which it bought in 2014.

The company also contributes money and sweat equity to various projects and causes, sometimes voluntarily, sometimes to qualify for tax breaks. It has donated to dozens of religious institutions, and its employees participate in blood drives and beach cleanups. It hosts an annual golf tournament that generates hundreds of thousands of dollars for the United Way. In exchange for a tax abatement, it gave $2 million for a clinic at Memorial Medical Center in Port Lavaca, a city of 11,000 across Lavaca Bay from Point Comfort.

But its largesse has a hidden cost.

According to a study commissioned last year by the Texas Campaign for the Environment, Formosa has received $148 million in tax abatements from Calhoun County and its school district. About $39 million of that lost revenue could have been used to fund local needs like emergency services, law enforcement, roads and transportation, the study said.

Point Comfort itself has shrunk by more than half since Formosa began work on its first units, U.S. Census Bureau estimates show. The few hundred people who still live there are likely breathing more toxic air.

According to the state’s emissions inventory, Formosa’s releases of volatile organic compounds, or VOCs, have doubled since 2010, making it the sixth-largest source in Texas. VOCs can cause cancer, central nervous system damage and chronic respiratory impairment. But the state is not regularly monitoring the impact of these emissions on local air quality; its nearest VOC monitoring station is about 80 miles away.

Formosa’s only real reckoning in Texas has come not from any government agency but from a small band of locals indignant about the plant’s pernicious effects on the region’s bays and estuaries, which sustain commercial and recreational fishing and provide habitat for a rich array of wildlife, including endangered whooping cranes and sea turtles.

In 2017, an environmental group called the San Antonio Bay Estuarine Waterkeeper and fisherwoman-turned-activist Diane Wilson brought a citizen lawsuit under the Clean Water Act. It accused Formosa of dumping vast quantities of plastic pellets and PVC powder into Lavaca Bay, Matagorda Bay and Cox Creek. After a 2019 federal bench trial, the judge labeled Formosa a “serial offender.” The company signed a consent decree committing to pay $50 million into the Matagorda Bay Mitigation Trust and to obey a “zero discharge” mandate: No plastic waste should come from the plant’s wastewater or stormwater outfalls.

Formosa hasn’t kept that promise.

Since the lawsuit was settled, it has racked up more than 1,000 violations for spilling PVC powder primarily into Lavaca Bay and has paid an additional $44 million into the mitigation trust. The TCEQ recently closed an enforcement case involving hundreds of these releases and did not issue a penalty.

The agency’s willingness to stand up to Formosa will soon be tested again, because the wastewater permit that governs its discharges into Lavaca Bay is up for renewal. The permit, notably, is missing a “zero discharge” requirement.

Loretta Brown, who lives in Port Lavaca and runs cattle on a ranch in Calhoun County, attended a public meeting the TCEQ held about the permit last month. She wanted to know why the agency was “even considering another permit” given that Formosa has committed so many violations since the citizen suit was settled.

The TCEQ’s Michael Sunderlin, who is handling the permit renewal, replied that the agency had reviewed the company’s environmental record and rated it “satisfactory.”

“With 1,100 offenses since the last lawsuit — that comes back satisfactory?” Brown asked, incredulous.

***

Nine days after that meeting, the TCEQ faced a new Formosa-induced headache.

Just before 4 a.m. on October 28, silos of plastic pellets at the plant caught fire and detonated. Bursts of flames shot high into the sky. Homes trembled miles away. Anxious exchanges popped up in local Facebook groups. “Here we go again,” one user wrote.

Formosa assured the public there had been no injuries and told the state there had been no chemical releases significant enough to report.

After Wilson filed a complaint, the TCEQ said it would investigate.

Correction: An earlier version of this story incorrectly identified Ladonna Thigpen. Her correct title is reflected in the updated version.

text:
e.l.f. Beauty committed to sourcing 50% clean electricity across its brands' direct manufacturing suppliers by 2032, building on its existing commitment to 100% clean electricity for leased facilities.

The company launched a Supplier Clean Electricity Program and will purchase and retire one additional megawatt-hour of Energy Attribute Certificates for every megawatt-hour of clean electricity suppliers use to produce e.l.f. Beauty brands' products.

Clean electricity use among direct manufacturing suppliers grew from 2% in FY 2023 to 14% today; supplier electricity accounts for 11% of the company's total greenhouse gas emissions (Scope 3) in FY 2026.

e.l.f. Beauty today announced a commitment by its brands to source 50% clean electricity across their manufacturing suppliers by 2032, building on their ongoing commitment to source 100% clean electricity for their leased facilities.

Use of clean electricity across e.l.f. Beauty brands’ direct manufacturing suppliers has grown from 2% in fiscal year 2023 to 14% today, driven by supplier investments in on-site solar, green tariffs, physical Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs), and Energy Attribute Certificates. Building on that momentum, the company's new target further advances the clean electricity progress already underway.

To support this transition, e.l.f. Beauty is launching its Supplier Clean Electricity Program, encouraging its brands’ manufacturing suppliers to prioritize direct sources of clean electricity.

To amplify the program's impact, e.l.f. Beauty will purchase and retire one additional megawatt-hour of Energy Attribute Certificates for every one megawatt-hour of clean electricity suppliers use to produce e.l.f. Beauty brands’ products. This investment in clean electricity demonstrates a shared commitment between the e.l.f. Beauty brands and their suppliers.

Electricity consumption by direct manufacturing suppliers accounts for a meaningful portion of e.l.f. Beauty’s Scope 3 emissions, representing 11% of the company’s total greenhouse gas emissions in FY 2026.

“Clean electricity is one of our biggest levers to help cut Scope 3 emissions, and we've already seen what's possible — growing from 2% to 14% in just a few years. Our Supplier Clean Electricity Program pairs direct investment with hands-on collaboration, so clean electricity becomes an achievable reality for our manufacturing partners, not just an aspiration. As far as we know, e.l.f. Beauty is the first major beauty company to pair a supplier clean-electricity target with an annual clean-electricity commitment of its own” said Ellen Leung, VP of Transformation and Sustainability at e.l.f. Beauty.

text:
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), a massive bill over 400 pages, is designed to make it faster and easier to build energy projects as demand goes up and strain on the grid increases. Initially introduced at the end of September, the Senate voted on November 9 to invoke cloture, limiting the time that can be spent debating the bill as it moves forward.

Energy projects often span multiple states, and are governed by federal regulations, and use federal money. Because of this, permitting reform has been a longtime goal of lawmakers in Congress.

“(BAAJA) does some good things, like help(ing) to streamline the process for modernizing the grid, building new transmission lines, and investing in modernization of the grid,” said Chris Winter, an environmental attorney.

Winter is the director of the Getches-Wilkinson Center for Natural Resources, Energy, and the Environment at CU Boulder’s School of Law.

The bill alters the National Environmental Policy Act, or NEPA, the country’s “Magna Carta” of environmental law. It narrows what must be considered in environmental reviews for energy projects and excludes certain projects from environmental review altogether. It would also limit the types of federal actions that trigger environmental review.

Winter said BAAJA would also limit judicial review. For example, under new restrictions outlined in the bill, if someone sued the BLM over an oil and gas project, saying the environmental review was inadequate, “a federal judge… wouldn't be able to issue an injunction to prevent the drilling from happening,” Winter said.

“All the judge could do is send the document back to the agency for more work, but in the interim, the project would be allowed to move forward.”.

BAAJA also attempts to respond to recent disruptions in the world of energy development. Last year, President Trump took an aggressive stance on renewable energy, going so far as to pause the leases for large-scale offshore wind projects. In response, the bill tries to create some certainty for energy developers, by limiting the changes the federal government can make to permits after they’re issued, even if environmental regulations have changed since then.

“These two provisions operating together—no injunctions by a court and no ability to pull these permits back—would basically allow President Trump to have unfettered discretion to lock in a lot of extractive activity with very little or no meaningful public involvement on his way out the door between now and 2028,” Winter said.

The bill would also significantly alter the National Historic Preservation Act—specifically Section 106, which outlines the process of the federal government engaging Native American tribes as sovereign nations.

Wesley Furlong, staff attorney at the Native American Rights Fund, said BAAJA’s passage would be a huge blow to tribal sovereignty, and would undermine the government to government relationship between the U.S. and tribes.

He said BAAJA essentially does away with the process of tribal consultation on projects that may affect important sacred sites.

“The process very generally goes from this very robust stepwise consultative process to the agency just writing a report, giving it to the tribe and saying, ‘You have 45 days to comment and give us any information you have and then we're going to move on,’” he said.

“It is not consultation. It is almost like a notice and comment process.”

It would also remove the requirement for federal agencies to meaningfully consider tribal input, and gives agencies the discretion to say that an energy project is more important than protecting cultural resources.

Daniel Cordalis, another attorney with NARF, and a member of the Navajo Nation, said that in addition to the NHPA, tribes are also affected by changes to NEPA, the Clean Water Act, and the Endangered Species Act.

According to the bill summary, BAAJA “narrows the scope of review for water quality certifications, extends the term for permits issued under the National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System, and limits the time period for review of permits for discharges of dredged or fill materials.” It also seeks to expedite the review of federal permits, including by shortening the timeline for consultation and review on threatened or endangered species.

“The problem with this for tribes is we have legally protected rights—whether they're water and species and land protections—that demand a certain level of recognition and involvement in the processes,” Cordalis said. “They have to be accorded to certain levels of interest and protected under federal law. But those are pretty much reduced, and ignored throughout this bill.”

He said the bill is a solution in search of a problem.

“It's not like tribes are out there being obstructionists or using their authorities in ways that are extremely negative and harmful to project development,” he said. “Tribes are playing by the rules, they're being good permit partners. And so it makes no sense to be creating obstacles and making it harder for tribes to do the thing they’re already good at.”

“It's not just tribes that are getting cut out of this process,” added Furlong. “It is states, it is local governments, and it is also the public. And the bill specifically targets public engagement and prevents members of the public from engaging in this process.”

NARF is calling on Congress to hold the bill until the next Congress is sworn in, allowing for meaningful discussion with Indian Country on what permitting reform could look like. The National Association of Tribal Historic Preservation officers has also condemned BAAJA, along with attorneys general from Colorado and New Mexico, among other states.

Some environmental groups have expressed support for the bill, like the Citizens Climate Lobby and the Center for Climate and Energy Solutions. It’s also garnered a lot of support from members of the renewable energy industry.

In a letter to Congress, renewable energy trade groups wrote that the bill “represents substantial positive reforms to our permitting system, maintaining high environmental standards while providing clear rules for getting energy infrastructure built. BAAJA would help significantly increase clean energy deployment and expand our transmission network to deliver new, affordable, and reliable electricity to the homes and businesses that rely on it.”

BAAJA also has many supporters in the fossil fuels industry, like the American Petroleum Institute (including companies like Chevron, Exxon Mobil, and bp) and the National Mining Association.

Winter said that the process of advancing this bill has been highly unusual. It has not yet had a committee hearing, there’s no legislative history or Senate report. He and other legal scholars said they did not have much time to review manager’s amendments to the bill over the weekend before the Senate voted to invoke cloture on Monday.

“That we would fundamentally undermine all of these bedrock environmental laws that are important to maintaining our quality of life in rural economies… that that would all sail through Congress without any ability for the public to weigh in… it’s really difficult to accept,” he said.

Winter said the results of the recent midterm election changed the political dynamics surrounding BAAJA: voters sent a message that they want big money, corporate interests out of politics.

“And this bill would magnify that access and control for the largest corporate interest in America by a factor of ten, or 100, or 1000,” he said.

He said it’s likely that the Senate will try to pass this bill during its lame duck session before a new Congress is sworn in in January, though it would have to be approved by the House before becoming law.

title: Luxembourg supports cleaner production and vocational skills in Kosovo | LuxDev
description:
For manufacturing and processing businesses, energy costs and a reliable energy supply directly affect productivity and competitiveness.
Delivered through the Energy transition and climate mitigation in Kosovo project, the scheme translates Luxembourg’s support for the energy transition into practical investments within businesses.
The Dual Vocational Education and Training Grant Scheme supports 6 consortia, selected from 42 applications, bringing together businesses and vocational education providers.
This support forms part of the Skills for sustainable jobs in Kosovo project.
The Energy transition and climate mitigation in Kosovo project is funded by the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg and implemented by LuxDev, the Luxembourg Development Cooperation Agency.
text:
Thirty-nine enterprises and six consortia of businesses and vocational schools have been selected under two grant schemes supporting clean energy investments and dual vocational education in Kosovo. Financed by the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg and implemented in partnership with Kosovo institutions through LuxDev, the schemes address two closely connected needs: helping businesses modernise their production processes and developing the skills required for their growth.

The Clean Energy Grant Scheme supports 39 enterprises investing in renewable energy and energy efficiency. For manufacturing and processing businesses, energy costs and a reliable energy supply directly affect productivity and competitiveness. Investments such as solar energy systems and more efficient production equipment can help reduce energy consumption and operating costs, while supporting Kosovo’s transition towards cleaner energy.

The selected 39 companies will invest about EUR 656,000 in renewable energy and energy efficiency measures, supported by grants provided through the scheme. Delivered through the Energy transition and climate mitigation in Kosovo project, the scheme translates Luxembourg’s support for the energy transition into practical investments within businesses.

The Dual Vocational Education and Training Grant Scheme supports 6 consortia, selected from 42 applications, bringing together businesses and vocational education providers. All 6 selected partnerships operate in the wood sector, with each project expected to benefit at least 10 students. The selected projects represent approximately EUR 550,000 in grant support.

Through these partnerships, students will gain practical experience in real working environments, while businesses play an active role in developing their future workforce. Vocational education providers will also strengthen their links with industry, helping to align learning with employers’ needs.

This support forms part of the Skills for sustainable jobs in Kosovo project.

Together, the schemes reflect Luxembourg’s approach to supporting Kosovo’s economic development: connecting investment in businesses with investment in people. As enterprises adopt new technologies and improve their production processes, they need workers able to operate, maintain and adapt to them. Stronger cooperation between education and industry helps ensure that technological progress also creates opportunities for young people. The schemes bring together the institutions responsible for industry, energy and education to support more competitive enterprises, relevant vocational skills and sustainable employment.

The Skills for sustainable jobs in Kosovo project is funded by the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg and implemented by the Ministry of Education, Science, Technology and Innovation, and by LuxDev, the Luxembourg Development Cooperation Agency. The project aims to contribute to sustainable economic growth by supporting innovation, inclusiveness and social development in a greener Kosovo.

The Energy transition and climate mitigation in Kosovo project is funded by the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg and implemented by LuxDev, the Luxembourg Development Cooperation Agency. It is a comprehensive effort to address Kosovo’s energy challenges. The project’s primary goal is to facilitate the adoption of energy efficiency practices and renewable energy sources, thereby supporting Kosovo’s transition to clean energy. By optimising energy consumption and reducing carbon emissions, the project addresses critical challenges such as inefficient energy use and the low share of renewables in electricity generation. This transition is essential for both environmental and economic reasons, setting the stage for a more sustainable and resilient energy sector.

Definitive purchase agreements include meaningful prepayments and advances Oklo’s planned 1.2 GW Ohio campus with Meta; fuel deliveries beginning in 2029.

Secures fuel to power up to five Aurora powerhouses for multiple years, supporting initial Ohio deployments, future Aurora projects, and additional fuel for the Aurora-INL.

PIKE COUNTY, Ohio--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Oklo Inc. (NYSE: OKLO) (“Oklo”), an advanced nuclear technology company, today announced it has signed multiple definitive, multi-year contracts with Centrus Energy Corp. (NYSE: LEU) (“Centrus”), a uranium enrichment and nuclear fuel services provider, for high-assay low-enriched uranium (HALEU). Under the agreements, Oklo will make prepayments for future HALEU deliveries to support construction of new U.S. uranium enrichment capacity with Centrus. The agreements formalize the June 2026 letter of intent between Oklo and Centrus and include enough HALEU to support up to five Aurora powerhouses for multiple years, with fuel deliveries from Centrus’ American Centrifuge Plant in Pike County, Ohio, scheduled to begin in 2029.

The HALEU purchase is supported by Meta’s prepayment for future Oklo power production and secures fuel for the first phase of Oklo’s planned 1.2 GW power campus in Ohio. Meta’s previously announced agreement with Oklo linked prepayment for power with advancement of project development. With the funding, Oklo is able to advance fuel procurement with Centrus for the planned Ohio campus, which includes multiple Oklo Aurora powerhouses; expand Ohio’s clean energy workforce; and generate new local and state tax revenues through investment in energy infrastructure.

The fuel supply marks a major step toward scaling Oklo’s power business beyond its first reactor. Building on Oklo’s allocation of recovered Experimental Breeder Reactor II (EBR-II) fuel for its first Aurora powerhouse in Idaho, the Centrus agreements secure HALEU for the first phase of the Ohio power campus, future Aurora deployments, and later refueling of the Aurora-INL.

These agreements and its prepayments will further propel Centrus’ proven centrifuge manufacturing process that recently completed and began shipping its first new centrifuge as part of its domestic uranium enrichment expansion. Centrus has further de-risked its buildout by assembling a complete, unobligated supply chain to serve both the commercial and national security markets. Centrus has now secured $5.4 billion in customer contracts and commitments to purchase LEU and HALEU from the new capacity.

“Securing fuel is essential to scaling our power business beyond our first reactor in Idaho,” said Oklo CEO and co-founder Jacob DeWitte. “These agreements support our initial Ohio deployments and provide fuel for future Aurora powerhouses. Meta’s support helps advance fuel procurement for the Ohio campus and our work to deliver new, clean, reliable power to the grid.”

“These definitive agreements demonstrate that Centrus is ideally placed to meet and support the upcoming substantial commercial demand for HALEU,” said Amir Vexler, President and Chief Executive Officer of Centrus. “Oklo’s prepayments, which add to the others we have previously received, will help fund our buildout as we scale Centrus’ proven American Centrifuge technology and qualified manufacturing processes for commercial production. Together, we are accelerating the restoration of America’s uranium enrichment leadership.”

The agreements connect three Ohio-based efforts: Centrus’ enrichment expansion in Piketon, Oklo’s planned Aurora powerhouses, and Meta’s commitment to bring new electricity and jobs in support of its Ohio operations. With Meta’s committed demand for clean energy catalyzing both the power plant buildout and the domestic fuel purchase, the effort is expected to support thousands of direct and indirect jobs at full buildout and strengthen the fuel supply chain for advanced nuclear deployment across the United States.

About Oklo Inc.: Oklo Inc. is developing fast fission power plants to deliver clean, reliable, affordable energy at global scale; establishing a domestic supply chain for critical isotopes; and advancing nuclear fuel recycling to convert used nuclear fuel into clean energy. Oklo was the first to receive a site use permit from the U.S. Department of Energy for a commercial advanced fission plant, was awarded fuel from Idaho National Laboratory, and submitted the first custom combined license application for an advanced reactor to the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission. Oklo is also developing advanced fuel recycling technologies in collaboration with the U.S. Department of Energy and U.S. National Laboratories.

title: A Quebec town was once preparing for a big EV battery boost. Will it still come?
description:

The Nemaska plant is vital in Quebec’s plan to set up an EV battery manufacturing chain in the province.
But many in the Bécancour area say the setbacks are simply bumps in the road that leads to electrification.

text:
BECANCOUR, QUE.- Much of the heavy machinery at the Nemaska Lithium plant site in Quebec, is at a standstill after majority owner Rio Tinto issued dozens of layoff notices. Workers were not the only thing affected, construction on an EV battery chain that was nearly 80 per cent complete is now forced to pause.

This marks the latest sign for the town of Bécancour, located in a region known as “Battery Valley,” that plans for the area to become a hub of an EV manufacturing boom may not come to fruition.

“Decisions on further investment and project timing at Bécancour will depend on the outcome of the evaluation, project economics, market conditions, and customer needs,” Rio Tinto said in a statement.

The global metal and mining giant said it remains confident in the long-term outlook for lithium processing in Quebec and Canada, despite a decline in lithium prices as global demand for battery materials and electric vehicles has slowed.

The fallout could hit the town of Bécancour, which is nestled along the shores of the St. Lawrence River halfway between Montreal and Quebec City.

The Nemaska plant is vital in Quebec’s plan to set up an EV battery manufacturing chain in the province. In the same plan, the province promised to develop Bécancour into a hub.

Slow EV sales halt economic boost

As EV batteries and plants started to set up shop in the town’s industrial park in 202, Bécancour estimated it would see a boost of 1,500 direct and 5,000 indirect jobs, including in the restaurant industry and service sector.

The population grew slightly with the arrival of workers at construction sites. To accommodate them the city planned to expand schools, build housing and even purchase new ladder trucks for the local fire station.

However, when sales of EVs slowed, some projects were paused, while others were completely scrapped. In March, Nemaska announced it would scale down the pace of building its processing plant.

Though Quebec owns 46.1 per cent of Nemaska, the province’s new government said this week it would not spend a penny more on the project for the time being.

“Our sincere hope is that this is going to work, because I don’t want to be the guy to write off the $1.1 billion we invested,” said Quebec Minister of Economic Development, Innovation and Energy Stéphane Paquet.

But many in the Bécancour area say the setbacks are simply bumps in the road that leads to electrification.

“The battery file is here to stay,” said the prefect of the region Mario Lyonnais. “I am confident that the Nemaska plant will open. When it does, we will be ready and we will continue to prepare.”

Lyonnais says the battery boom was happening very quickly and that it was hard for the municipalities in the region to keep up with the pace of scaling up services.

He says the slowdown may allow the area more time to be fully ready for the grand opening of Nemaska and for a time when EV battery manufacturing delivers the region a boost.

title: Government bans export of lithium-ion battery black mass - Renewable Watch
description:
The Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT), under the Department of Commerce, has issued a notice prohibiting the export of lithium-ion battery black mass under ITC(HS) Code 85491400 with immediate effect.
The measure aims to ensure that black mass generated from end-of-life lithium-ion batteries and battery manufacturing waste is processed and recycled domestically.
Moreover, black mass contains recoverable critical minerals, including lithium, cobalt, nickel and manganese, which are essential for battery manufacturing, electric vehicles and energy storage systems.
The export ban is expected to improve feedstock availability and capacity utilisation for domestic recycling and refining units, while encouraging further investments and employment in the sector.
The measure complements the National Critical Mineral Mission and its Rs 15 billion incentive scheme for developing critical mineral recycling capacity from secondary sources.

Environmental advocates spoke out against cuts to Greensboro’s Office of Sustainability and Resilience at Tuesday's city council meeting.

Greensboro recently eliminated three positions from the office, including the Chief Sustainability Officer role.

It’s part of the city’s larger efforts to lower costs amid financial scrutiny from the state.

The office was created in part to help Greensboro transition to 100% renewable energy by 2040.

Elizabeth Chartrand, a member of the city's citizen-led Community Sustainability Council, asked officials to reinstate the employees.

Other speakers said the decision was at odds with council members' stated support for Greensboro’s environmental initiatives. City Manager Trey Davis stood behind the cuts, saying they were needed to “strengthen the city's fiscal position.”

title: Perovskite Solar Cells, Coming Soon To A Solar Module Near You - CleanTechnica
description:

The Great Permitting Battle Is Far From Over Perovskite solar cells represent just one key breakthrough area in the US solar industry.
text:
Support CleanTechnica's work through a Substack subscription, on Patreon, or on Stripe. Help us produce all of the high-quality, original content we publish week after week despite the challenges of content-scraping AI, antisocial media, inflation, and other hurdles.

Perovskite is a relatively inexpensive material that has attracted thousands of researchers since 2009, when a team of scientists in Japan first demonstrated its use in solar cells. They achieved a solar energy conversion efficiency of little more than 3%, but since science loves a challenge, that was just the beginning of the story. In the latest chapter, the US firms Heliene and Caeulux have just introduced a new perovskite-enabled solar module that hits the jackpot at up to 27% efficiency, and it is already in commercial production, no less.

Perovskite Solar Cells Meet Silicon

So far in the renewable energy transition, silicon has shouldered much of the heavy lifting due to its excellent solar conversion properties. Still, silicon is relatively expensive material that demands a complex manufacturing process. Perovskite is the reverse. Based on a naturally occurring mineral, synthetic perovskites can be lab-grown and applied to solar cell fabrication in a high volume, high throughput process similar to roll-to-roll manufacturing and other solution-based methods (see lots more perovskite background here).

There being no such thing as a free lunch, “raw” perovskite is challenged by natural conditions, namely, humidity. Tweaking the formula with other, more durable materials can resolve that problem. Researchers have also developed a tandem solution, in which a perovskite layer rests upon a silicon layer, providing an efficiency boost while minimizing the additional cost.

In the US solar market, the sticky wicket is the current state of federal energy, trade, and tax polices. Still, the red-hot demand for solar energy in the US has motivated solar stakeholders to steamroll over those obstacles, attracting overseas investors (here’s one example) as well as new domestic ventures.

On the domestic side, the Corning-backed manufacturer Heliene has been focusing on silicon while the startup Caelux has tackled the perovskite solar cell challenge with a glass substrate that can be layered onto other materials in a solar module. Now the two manufacturers have combined forces, with Caelux’s perovskite-doped glass boosting the conversion efficiency of Heliene’s N-type solar cells by up to 20%.

Caelux Meets Silicon

The Caelux-Heliene mashup comes at a time when Congress has finally put the wheels in motion to streamline the permitting process for energy projects. The two firms already have a running head start. On November 10, the two firms announced that commercial-scale production has already begun on their Hybrid-Tandem™ solar module

“Manufactured by Heliene in Minnesota, the perovskite plus silicon technology combines Caelux’s Energy Producing Glass with Heliene’s established silicon module platform to construct a solar module with two separate power generation layers that deliver higher power density,” Heliene explains.

“One of the advantages of Caelux’s technology is that we can integrate its Energy Producing Glass into our existing manufacturing lines without having to build an entirely new production setup,” added Martin Pochtaruk, Heliene CEO and Founder, in a press statement.

“With both companies manufacturing in the U.S., we’re bringing together two fully domestic supply chains to advance what’s possible with American-made solar,” Pochtaruk emphasized.

Stay tuned for the next development. The new modules are now in production at Heliene’s manufacturing facility Minnesota, with deliveries set for 2027. That’s just for starters. Caelux and Heliene have already targeted 29% efficiency and up for their next-generation modules.

More Solar Energy From Less Space

The conversion efficiency improvement is the gift that keeps on giving. In the rooftop solar sector, for example, high-efficiency solar cells enable developers to squeeze more electricity out of a given space, making a rooftop array more economical for smaller properties that are otherwise shut out of the market. The cost of a smaller, more effcient array can also ripple downwards in the form of savings on labor, hardware, and transportation expenses.

For rooftop solar in general, the boost in efficiency provides an opportunity to take full advantage of power sharing programs with local utilities, which enable solar owners to earn revenue and qualify for time-of-use discounts. The benefits can ripple into home energy storage systems and home EV charging as well.

On a larger scale, the space-saving angle can help alleviate land use conflicts that otherwise stymie solar development, particularly in the area of farm-to-solar conversion.

Although real estate development is by far the primary factor driving the loss of farmland in the US, solar opponents (looking at you, Brooke Rollins) have played the farm card to gin up resistance to solar development in rural communities. With efficiency improvements, the economic case improves for solar arrays on marginal lands and smaller parcels. That can be partcularly helpful in the community solar field, where solar arrays are typically smaller.

Additionally, the improved efficiency can help accelerate the uptake of agrivoltaic practices that balance energy-producing solar panels with grazing and croplands. These dual-use arrays can enable farmers to continue working their land while guaranteeing a revenue stream from the solar developer.

Furthermore, high-efficiency solar opens up new opportunities in the field of floating solar, where developers can make use of reservoirs and other human-engineered bodies of water instead of taking up space on land. By taking up less room on water for the same power generation capacity, floating solar can also squeeze into reservoirs where recreation and habitat conservation also compete for space.

The Great Permitting Battle Is Far From Over

Perovskite solar cells represent just one key breakthrough area in the US solar industry. Easing the federal energy permitting bottleneck is another. That can be a two-edged sword, enabling more fossil energy resources to flow through the pipeline. However, permitting reform could also prevent the fossil energy industry from running amok through federal energy policy.

Members of Congress are currently negotiating over the particulars of Senate Bill 5653, aka the “Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. If enacted as envisioned by the solar industry, the reforms will put a crimp in Trump’s “American Energy Dominance” policy, which has placed new and burdensome restrictions on both wind and solar activity in the US while aggressively supporting fossil fuels and nuclear, alongside other renewables including biomass, geothermal, hydropower. Even energy storage has come in for a share of love from the Trump administration, further underscoring the remarkable exclusion of wind and solar from federal energy policy.

The trade organization Solar Energy Industries Association, for one, is urging members on both sides of the aisle to ensure that permitting reform focuses on fairness, predictability, and certainty. In a letter to the House and Senate, SEIA emphasizes that solar and storage developers “cannot finance multi-year, capital-intensive projects without the predictability and certainty needed to build projects and connect them to the grid.”

“According to researchers at Wood Mackenzie, solar and storage represent 70% of the new capacity added to the grid thus far in 2026. Yet $120 billion in clean energy investment is caught up in current permitting delays, let alone the impact of permitting challenges to future deployment,” SEIA adds.

Of course, even if such a bill passes both Houses of Congress, US President Donald Trump could exercise his veto power, and he has already threatened to make copious use of it during his last two years in office. Nevertheless, US Presidents come and go, and this one is scheduled to go in January of 2029 — peacefully this time, one hopes.

text:
The Cuban-American congressman Carlos Giménez proposed to businessman Elon Musk to move Tesla's corporate headquarters from Texas to Florida, following the victories achieved by the Democratic Party in the first state during the midterm elections on November 3.

The Republican legislator believed that the new political landscape in Texas could make that state less attractive for the magnate's businesses and wants to seize the opportunity to attract investments to south Florida.

The proposal was announced this Wednesday through an official statement from Giménez's office, which confirmed the sending of a letter to Musk.

The letter, dated November 9, formally invites the electric vehicle manufacturer to consider relocating its headquarters and expanding its operations in Florida.

"I am writing to formally invite Tesla to consider relocating its corporate headquarters and expanding its operations from Texas to the free state of Florida," stated the representative of Florida's 28th District in the United States House of Representatives.

Giménez directly linked his proposal to the election results in Texas, where Democrats achieved historic victories after decades of Republican dominance.

"With the recent election of individuals who describe themselves as democratic socialists to positions of power in Texas, I share their concerns about excessive government interference, politically motivated investigations, and policies that punish success," wrote the congressman.

The legislator also stated that no company should face political retaliation for creating jobs, investing in American innovation, and contributing to the economic prosperity of the country.

In light of this situation, Giménez presented Florida as an alternative with lower taxes, less restrictive regulations, and a pro-private investment policy.

«While others seek to investigate and penalize success, Florida welcomes it», he stated in his letter, contrasting the business conditions of both states.

The congressman, who served as mayor of Miami-Dade from 2011 to 2020, particularly highlighted the advantages of South Florida for a potential expansion of Tesla.

He mentioned the regional infrastructure, the growth of the technology sector, the availability of specialized workers, and its strategic position to access the markets of Latin America and the Caribbean.

In statements gathered by The Washington Reporter, Giménez insisted that Florida is ready to welcome investments from the entrepreneur.

The legislator stated that his experience leading Miami-Dade County allows him to understand the region's potential to attract tech companies and create jobs, and he expressed his willingness to collaborate with Musk and state and local authorities to facilitate a potential Tesla installation.

The invitation comes after Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated Republican Governor Greg Abbott in Texas, ending decades of Republican control over the governorship.

The Democrats also secured the federal Senate seat contested between James Talarico and the Republican Ken Paxton, in addition to other victories in state positions.

The political change has sparked a debate about the relationship that the new authorities will have with Musk's companies, especially concerning public incentives, environmental permits, and the industrial and technological projects that the entrepreneur is developing in Texas.

The elected governor Hinojosa has proposed greater oversight of certain business activities, although she has also expressed her willingness to collaborate with the tycoon’s companies under conditions that protect the interests of the state's residents.

After the elections, Musk reacted with ironic messages to the Republican defeat, after having invested hundreds of millions of dollars in supporting conservative candidates, especially in Texas.

In a later post on November 7, the entrepreneur defended the conditions that had favored the growth of Tesla and SpaceX in that state, stating that both companies thrived there because they did not have to operate under a state government that they regarded as oppressive and extractive.

Tesla moved its corporate headquarters from California to Austin, Texas, in 2021, as part of the expansion of its industrial operations. The company operates its Gigafactory there, where it produces electric vehicles and develops new manufacturing lines.

The importance of Texas for his operations was recently highlighted in the plans announced by Musk to gradually reduce the production of the Cybertruck and expand the manufacturing of the Cybercab, his autonomous vehicle project, at those same facilities.

This is not the first time that Carlos Giménez has attempted to attract one of Musk's companies to South Florida. In December 2022, the congressman sent another letter proposing to move the headquarters of Twitter, now X, from San Francisco to Miami-Dade.

That invitation did not materialize. The headquarters of X ultimately moved to Texas, where Musk has also concentrated some of the operations of his other companies.

The US Senate voted 73-25 to take up a bipartisan bill speeding energy project permitting and requiring data centers to pay for their own power use.

The U.S. Senate voted 73-25 on Monday to take up a bipartisan bill that would speed federal permitting for large energy and infrastructure projects, from pipelines and power plants to clean energy and data centers. Backers, including the President and both clean energy and oil and gas trade groups, say it would ease grid delays and lower utility bills. For 12 years, Texas energy and environmental regulators have been influenced by Gov. Greg Abbott’s appointments to lead agencies. That includes the five-member Public Utility Commission, the three-member Texas Commission on Environmental Quality and, more indirectly, the board that oversees ERCOT.

On Jan. 19, that appointment power passes to Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa. But she won’t be able to reshape everything overnight. Some positions are immediately available for her appointments, but others are tied to expiring terms, and many require approval from the Republican-majority Texas Senate.

Public Utility Commission (PUC)

The Texas PUC is arguably Hinojosa’s most consequential appointment opportunity for influencing energy. The governor appoints all five members and designates the chair.

Day one: Hinojosa can name a new chair, replacing Thomas Gleeson. She can also move to replace Commissioner Courtney Hjaltman, whose term expired in 2025.

By late January: The Senate never confirmed Commissioners Patrick Rhode or Morgan Johnson. Hinojosa will need to resubmit their nominations or select replacements within the first 10 days of the legislative session, which begins Jan. 12.

Sept. 1: Terms expire for Commissioner Kathleen Jackson and Rhode, creating additional opportunities to change membership.

Hinojosa would have the opportunity to influence a majority of the five-member commission in her first year. If she also replaces Johnson in January and secures Senate approval, she could influence four of the five seats.
