name: Clean Energy
title: Meta's New Agreements Bring Clean Manufacturing to Data Center Supply Chains
description:
Through these commitments, we’re helping bring clean manufacturing to a commercial scale in the industries that build and supply our data centers.
These agreements build on a track record of testing, validating, and scaling lower carbon infrastructure solutions across our data center footprint.
Lower Carbon Cement and Concrete We’ve signed a multi-year agreement with Sublime Systems to support at least 180,000 tons of lower carbon cement production.
Both companies expect their early plants to add domestic capacity for lower carbon cement and create new American jobs.
That’s the outcome we are working toward: supply chains where lower carbon cement, steel, recycled plastics, and electric freight are standard options for any builder.
text:
Today, we’re sharing a new set of long-term purchase commitments spanning cement, steel, trucking, and recycled plastics. Through these commitments, we’re helping bring clean manufacturing to a commercial scale in the industries that build and supply our data centers.

Building the physical infrastructure that supports Meta technologies takes significant quantities of foundation materials: cement, steel, plastics, and the freight networks that move them.

Reducing the emissions associated with building infrastructure requires not only sourcing differently but bringing lower carbon materials and services into existence at commercial scale. Our multi-year commitments give suppliers the revenue certainty they need to build these solutions, and stepping in early helps demonstrate these technologies so the broader market can adopt them.

These agreements build on a track record of testing, validating, and scaling lower carbon infrastructure solutions across our data center footprint. That includes piloting mass timber architecture to replace traditional carbon-intensive materials, open-sourcing AI models to design faster-curing, lower carbon concrete formulations, and joining industry peers as a founding partner of the Data Center Innovation Initiative.

Lower Carbon Cement and Concrete

We’ve signed a multi-year agreement with Sublime Systems to support at least 180,000 tons of lower carbon cement production. Our support enables Sublime to build its first commercial-scale facility and gives us priority access to use Sublime Cement® in our data center construction pipeline.

We’ve also signed an agreement with lower carbon cement producer Fortera to support a new plant in Ste. Genevieve, Missouri. Both companies expect their early plants to add domestic capacity for lower carbon cement and create new American jobs.

These agreements build on earlier lower carbon concrete projects with partners like CarbonBuilt and CarbiCrete.

Clean Iron and Steel

Last year, we signed a multi-year agreement to support domestic clean iron from Electra’s first demonstration plant in Jefferson County, Colorado. We’re now taking that work from iron into steel: a new multi-year agreement with Sweden-based Stegra supports near-zero-emission primary steel, produced through a process that eliminates coal entirely from iron reduction.

Structural steel reaches our data centers through global supply chains. Supporting a first-of-its-kind facility through its production ramp helps validate technologies that can scale across the global steel industry.

Zero-Emission Freight Corridors

Building on initial zero-emission freight partnerships with NFI in Virginia and Nevoya (with the Center for Green Market Activation) in Texas, we’re expanding our work with Nevoya to now include a California and Arizona route along the I-10 interstate.

Electric trucks produce zero tailpipe emissions and run quieter than diesel. By supporting heavy-duty electric trucks and dedicated charging infrastructure along critical transport routes, we’re helping bring cleaner air and quieter streets along freight corridors in Virginia, Texas, California, and Arizona. The permanent, open access charging stations will support other commercial fleets along the corridor.

Recycled Plastics

Our long-term purchase agreement with MacroCycle Technologies is enabling the financing of their first commercial plant in the Southeastern US, which aims to divert hard-to-recycle plastic waste from landfills and local incinerators into 5,000 tons per year of high-value recycled PET.

Supporting American Industrial Leadership and Local Communities

Long-term commitments to future lower carbon production help build American industrial capacity. By focusing these efforts domestically, where we are actively expanding our data center footprint, we help anchor new projects where domestic supply of clean materials and services are limited today.

The benefits are tangible and local to the communities where our partners operate. Across planned and expanded US plants, this work is estimated to support hundreds of jobs across construction and long-term manufacturing.

How We Address Emissions in Our Value Chain

We use a range of tools to address emissions across our direct operations, energy footprint, and supply chain. Since 2020, we’ve matched 100% of our annual electricity use with clean and renewable energy, and we continuously work to reduce the emissions through efficient design, extending the life of hardware, reusing server equipment, and prioritizing recycled materials. While we work with our suppliers to use cleaner materials and services, we’re often limited by how deep into the supply chain our influence extends and what is available on the market.

These long-term purchase agreements are structured to deliver Environmental Attribute Certificates (EACs), which is one way we address emissions in the most challenging sectors. With an EAC, a supplier produces verified lower carbon materials or services, Meta pays for the environmental benefit, and the material or service is used in the local market. This enables us to support lower carbon production now, and where possible, secure priority access to use these materials directly in our future data centers as new factories come online and supply chains mature.

Building a Lower Carbon Ecosystem

These commitments do more than secure materials and services for Meta — deploying these technologies at commercial scale helps to make them available to the entire market. That’s the outcome we are working toward: supply chains where lower carbon cement, steel, recycled plastics, and electric freight are standard options for any builder.

ROCKVILLE, Md., Nov. 12, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- X-Energy, Inc. (Nasdaq: XE) (“X-energy” or the “Company”), a leading developer of advanced nuclear reactors and fuel technology, today announced third quarter 2026 financial results and operational highlights.

“Our third quarter results and recent project developments reflect meaningful progress in executing our strategy and advancing our technology toward commercial deployment. We are building momentum as we deepen relationships with leading energy and industrial companies and advance opportunities across our pipeline,” said J. Clay Sell, CEO of X-energy. “The NRC recently issued the construction permit for Dow’s Long Mott project in Texas and it was received over a month ahead of schedule. This marks the first construction permit issued by the NRC in the United States for an advanced nuclear project site designed to provide industrial process heat.”

“Furthermore, we are excited to collaborate with AEP, a major investor-owned utility with extensive experience and expertise developing and operating critical energy infrastructure. This project in Indiana represents our second announced commercial deployment opportunity supported by Amazon and gives us greater visibility into our path toward deployment. During the quarter, we also completed the vertical construction of our TX-1 fuel fabrication facility, and the next phase includes interior buildout and equipment installation. In addition, the acceptance of our Xe-100 reactor into the United Kingdom’s Generic Design Assessment process represents an important step toward advancing our opportunity in the U.K. with Centrica.”

“We are in a differentiated position of strength, supported by our strong balance sheet and significant funding. Our regulatory progress marks a major milestone for our technology, while our growing commercial momentum bolsters our pipeline of reactors and demand for TRISO-X fuel,” concluded Sell.

Operational Highlights

NRC Issues Construction Permit for Dow’s Long Mott Project: Dow and X-energy announced that the NRC has approved the Construction Permit Application (“CPA”) for the proposed Long Mott Generating Station in Seadrift, Texas ahead of schedule. The permit marks an important milestone in the regulatory review process for the proposed advanced nuclear project, which is being developed under the U.S. Department of Energy's Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program (“ARDP”). The project is intended to provide zero-carbon emissions electricity and high-temperature steam to Dow's Seadrift Operations site, replacing existing energy and steam assets near their end-of-life. The NRC's approval follows a comprehensive review of the proposed facility, site characteristics, construction plans, environmental considerations and safety-related information submitted as part of the CPA process. Issuance marks the first NRC CPA approval of a high-temperature gas-cooled reactor (“HTGR”) in nearly 60 years, the first-ever pebble-bed HTGR approval and the first-ever for an advanced nuclear industrial deployment.

Selects Fluor for Design and Engineering Services: For Energy Northwest’s Cascade Advanced Energy Facility near Richland, Washington, Fluor will provide engineering, design development, supply chain, estimating and project controls services for the areas of the plant containing the Xe-100 reactors and the systems that support them (the "nuclear island"). The agreement between X-energy and Fluor represents their second commercial contract for nuclear island engineering and design, building on Fluor's ongoing work for the Company’s first proposed Xe-100 project in Texas under the ARDP. This enables X-energy and Fluor to incorporate learnings from one project into the next, with the aim of targeting long-term cost and schedule reductions through standardization and highly repeatable project execution.

Executes First Order for Steam Generator Components: Announced the first procurement order of steam generator tubing from Alleima and Doosan Enerbility for the Company’s Xe-100 advanced SMR. This follows the signing of a strategic framework by the three companies earlier this year as the Company scales its supply chain to meet its growing commercial pipeline. Execution advances a safety-significant, long-lead component for the first deployment of the Xe-100. Alleima will leverage its expertise in high-temperature alloys to manufacture specialized steel tubing, which Doosan will bend into helical coils using its proprietary fabrication processes. These coils are a central component of the Xe-100 steam generator, safely removing heat to produce high-temperature steam at up to 565°C, and allowing a single Xe-100 to deliver both electricity and high-temperature process heat for industrial applications.

Partners with AEP and Amazon : Announced a JDA with AEP to advance feasibility work for a proposed 960 MW Xe-100 SMR project in Indiana. Amazon will provide certain project development funding for the effort, marking the second commercial deployment opportunity under X-energy and Amazon’s collaboration aimed to bring more than 5 GW of new nuclear capacity to the U.S. grid by 2039. X-energy and AEP will evaluate the development of a 12-unit Xe-100 plant in Sullivan County, Indiana. The proposed project would redevelop the AEP-owned brownfield site for advanced nuclear power, adding clean baseload capacity to help meet growing demand for safe, reliable energy.

U.K. Regulators Begin Design Review for Xe-100: The U.K. Government has directed regulators to accept the Xe-100 reactor for design review and advance X-energy’s and Centrica’s efforts to deploy up to 6 GW of new nuclear in the U.K. GDA acceptance formally triggers the process of assessing the design's acceptability for deployment and operation ahead of the technical and environmental evaluations required for site-specific licensing and permitting. The assessment is expected to take approximately three years and will be administered by the U.K. Office for Nuclear Regulation, the Environment Agency, and Natural Resources Wales. The submission builds on the Xe-100's U.S. licensing progress and is expected to benefit from expanded collaboration between the U.K. regulators and the U.S. NRC, enabling transfer of NRC-reviewed design documentation and safety analyses into U.K. design reviews.

TX-1 Vertical Construction Complete, Advances to Next Phase : Vertical construction for the shell of the Company's TX-1 fuel facility in Oak Ridge, Tennessee was completed on schedule in the third quarter. The project has advanced into its next phase of construction, which will include interior buildout, installation of fuel fabrication equipment and continued construction of supporting facilities. Once operational, TX-1 is expected to produce approximately 700,000 TRISO-X fuel pebbles annually, equivalent to 5 metric tons of uranium (“MTU”), with capacity to provide fuel for up to 11 Xe-100 reactors. The U.S. NRC granted TRISO-X a 40-year Special Nuclear Material License covering the facility earlier this year, the first-ever NRC Category 2 fuel fabrication license issued for the processing of high-assay low-enriched uranium. TX-1 is expected to be the first new commercial-scale advanced U.S. nuclear fuel fabrication facility built in more than 50 years.

“We’re focused on getting a permanent solution to the president’s desk through any viable legislative vehicle,” Skor added.

As the $2 billion South Carolina plant nears completion, Scout Motors has sold about 212,000 vehicle reservations. The count includes the Terra pickup truck and Traveler SUV, CEO Scott Keogh told CNBC. At the same time, the over $2 billion Blythewood Production Center is in its final stages of construction. Furthermore, the company expects full production to start next year.

The mix of the reservation is skewed toward combustion backup. Furthermore, about 87 percent of buyers chose extended-range electric vehicle models. Meanwhile, about 75 percent chose the Traveler SUV over the pickup. The company, which is backed by Volkswagen, will begin full production in 2028, with deliveries commencing then.

Other Projects

In other industrial news projects, Lee County has agreed to a tax incentive plan for Mesabi Metallics $15 billion Iowa steel plant. On Nov. 11, the Board of Supervisors unanimously approved the term sheet and a resolution in support of the term sheet. The vote is another milestone for the complex that leaders say will create thousands of jobs in southeast Iowa.

The framework sets three payments. During development and construction, Mesabi Metallics would pay up to $10.5 million to the host community. In addition, the company has to ensure that the assessed value of its property increases by at least $112 million before the tax rebate is received. Meanwhile, it would pay Lee County $50 million over 20 years in lieu of additional property taxes.

Scope of the Scout Motors South Carolina plant build

The plant outside Columbia is about 85 percent complete, per Keogh. But crews continue to lay the groundwork for supporting infrastructure and a $300 million supplier park around the main facility. Construction is in its final stages, Scout said Thursday.

Both powertrains are available in the product line-up. All-electric versions are offered in parallel with EREV variants, which include an engine as a backup generator for the electric motors and batteries. Hence, the company is going to introduce EREVs first and then EVs, based on the split in reservations. Scout will also begin with mid-range models, not the top-of-the-line trims, which is a conscious departure from the norm.

“The No.1 thing for me is I want to go get the best volume as soon as possible,” Keogh said. “In my mind, it’s how quick can you get to 100,000 units? It’s at 100,000 units where you can start to punch through.”

Outlook for the Scout reservation book

Keogh anticipates that the 212,000 count will double by the time customer production starts. Nevertheless, he repeatedly warned that reservations are not a guarantee of sales. Strong interest did not translate to conversions over the past 10 years of EV launches in the industry. Therefore, his goal is to have an order book of 12 to 18 months before production begins. I think we could easily be over 400,000 with reservations without doing too much work,” Keogh said. The key for us is how much of the initial production can we 100% presell?

The strategy also has a competitive background. Rivian was criticized earlier this year for releasing the most expensive versions of its R2 SUV first. Meanwhile, Scout’s volume-first strategy targets the same early-production window, but at lower price points. So, the completion of the plant and the delivery in 2028 are now the determining factors. The question is whether 212,000 reservations turn into the order book the CEO desires.

title: Weathering the storm: Tracking federal actions against offshore wind - Clean Air Task Force
description:
Cataloging the multi-pronged efforts to obstruct offshore wind development and implementation both emphasizes the uncertainty currently facing offshore wind and highlights the impact of federal actions on the industry.
Fifty percent tariffs on steel and aluminum, two key materials in offshore wind components, have substantially increased costs for offshore wind developers.
DOI then paused the leases of five offshore wind projects (including Empire Wind and Revolution Wind again) on December 22nd, 2025, citing undisclosed national security concerns.
The developers of all five projects—Empire Wind, Revolution Wind, Vineyard Wind 1, Sunrise Wind, and Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind—brought lawsuits in response, and courts granted either preliminary injunctions or stays in each case.
DOI made requests with similar rationales for Revolution Wind, for Maryland Offshore Wind, and for New England Wind.
text:
Offshore wind is a vital technology that can generate clean electricity and bolster grid resilience. At a time when volatile fossil fuel prices and projected increases for energy demand threaten energy security and inflate costs for ratepayers, offshore wind offers a high-capacity clean generation source for states looking to decarbonize and improve energy affordability. Since the start of 2025, however, the federal government has attempted to systematically dismantle the American offshore wind industry through actions such as presidential memoranda and executive orders, offshore wind lease buybacks, permitting freezes, stop work orders, and, to a lesser extent, legislation such as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA). In response to challenges brought by affected states, project developers, and trade organizations, courts have enjoined or struck down many of the administration’s actions. But the administration has appealed some of these decisions, and the status of many offshore wind projects remains threatened.

Information on the status of the industry today is not well documented or centralized. And yet, understanding the status of offshore wind is critical, given the importance of the industry to the United States’ long-term energy prospects and the often-limited decarbonization and generation options for coastal population centers. Cataloging the multi-pronged efforts to obstruct offshore wind development and implementation both emphasizes the uncertainty currently facing offshore wind and highlights the impact of federal actions on the industry.

Broader context for clean energy

Since the beginning of the second Trump administration, many actions by the Department of Energy (DOE) have created uncertainty for developers and investors across several clean energy industries. Cuts in federal funding for clean energy projects have had substantial impacts on many states, eliminating jobs and economic opportunities and threatening states’ abilities to meet clean energy goals. Government-wide staffing cuts, including an approximately 20% decline in staffing at DOE since January 2025, have slowed the permitting process for energy projects significantly.

Offshore wind has been implicated in this broader context of funding cuts for clean energy and changes to government staffing. For example, staffing cuts at the DOE Wind Energy Technologies Office and the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management (BOEM), which sits within the U.S. Department of the Interior (DOI) and is the lead agency on offshore wind permitting, have damaged agency capacity to permit and develop offshore wind. The administration also eliminated wind research and development and financial assistance programs at DOE, further obstructing offshore wind deployment.

Other administration actions, such as instituting tariffs, have increased project costs for several clean energy industries, including offshore wind. Fifty percent tariffs on steel and aluminum, two key materials in offshore wind components, have substantially increased costs for offshore wind developers. For example, in July 2026, the developer Dominion Energy increased its estimated total costs for the Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind Project by approximately $300 million dollars from its April 2026 cost estimate, citing tariffs to justify the increase.

In addition to the industry-wide challenges listed above, the administration has carried out a series of targeted actions to disrupt wind development, and in particular development of offshore wind. This blog documents the actions taken against the offshore wind industry since 2025 and identifies the implications these actions may have on efforts to build a reliable, decarbonized grid.

What has happened in the offshore wind industry?

Withdrawal of all areas of the Outer Continental Shelf (OCS) from offshore wind leasing

On the day of President Trump’s inauguration in 2025, the administration froze offshore wind permitting, withdrew all areas of the OCS from offshore wind leasing, and started a review of leasing and permitting practices through a presidential memorandum. In response to a lawsuit filed by states and a clean energy trade association (in which CATF and partners filed an amicus brief), the Federal District Court for Massachusetts vacated the lease freeze section of this memorandum in December 2025. However, federal agencies are still not permitting projects on the OCS.

Stop work orders and lease pauses

Next, BOEM began issuing stop work orders against fully permitted offshore wind projects. The first order, issued in April 2025, paused construction of the New York-based project Empire Wind and was ultimately lifted in May 2025. Even though BOEM eventually retracted the order, it reportedly cost Empire Wind’s developer approximately $200 million, or about $50 million per week while in effect. In August 2025, another stop work order targeted the Revolution Wind project off the coast of Rhode Island and Connecticut. Revolution Wind sued, and in September 2025, the Federal District Court for D.C. granted a preliminary injunction, allowing the project to proceed.

DOI then paused the leases of five offshore wind projects (including Empire Wind and Revolution Wind again) on December 22nd, 2025, citing undisclosed national security concerns. These projects were fully permitted and had already begun construction, with one project (Vineyard Wind 1 in Massachusetts) near completion and actively delivering power to the grid. The developers of all five projects—Empire Wind, Revolution Wind, Vineyard Wind 1, Sunrise Wind, and Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind—brought lawsuits in response, and courts granted either preliminary injunctions or stays in each case.

Shortly after the DOI lease suspensions, regional clean energy associations filed a lawsuit alleging that some federal agencies were arbitrarily “disfavoring” development of wind and solar compared to other energy sources through actions such as delaying or vacating permitting approvals. They received a preliminary injunction on April 21st, 2026, and the federal government is currently appealing.

Lease buybacks

Since March 2026, the administration has used lease buybacks and settlements to remove several offshore wind lease areas from future development, potentially constraining the industry’s long-term growth if the settlements withstand judicial scrutiny. In these settlements, DOI agreed to pay developers an amount equal to their initial wind lease purchase price in exchange for the return of the wind leases to the federal government, with the stipulation that the developer reinvests this money into fossil fuel or other infrastructure. There have been five buybacks of twelve different leases as of November 2026, with a total cost of approximately $4 billion.

However, these settlements are not a refund to developers. They are new expenditures of taxpayer dollars from the Judgment Fund, which exists to pay court judgments and settlements for lawsuits against the federal government. They are therefore the subject of five lawsuits from nine states to date, including complaints filed by coalitions of northeastern states and two others filed by California.

National security claims

As part of the previously routine permitting process for both onshore and offshore wind, DOD is required to issue determinations that verify that the turbines do not interfere with national security. In April 2026, however, DOD stopped processing these determinations entirely, freezing permitting for proposed wind projects on both private and federal land. A coalition of clean energy trade associations subsequently filed a lawsuit against DOD, and CATF and seven other environmental groups filed an amicus brief in support of that lawsuit in June. In August, the Federal District Court in Oregon granted a preliminary injunction requiring that DOD begin issuing routine determinations once more.

President Trump also issued a proclamation on October 22, 2026 that declared wind turbine product imports to be a threat to national security. The proclamation cites a report from the Secretary of Commerce that reportedly identified cybersecurity, grid, and radar interference concerns from relying on foreign imported products. The proclamation directs the Secretary of Commerce to pursue trade negotiations and agreements with foreign trade partners and monitor the imports of wind products, but it refrained from imposing new or additional tariffs.

Creation of the Marine Minerals Administration (MMA)

In July 2026, the Trump administration initiated a process to combine BOEM and the Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement (BSEE) into the MMA. The Obama administration had originally separated these two offices after the Deepwater Horizon oil spill in 2010 to create an organizational firewall between safety/environmental oversight functions and revenue collection functions, which had inherent conflicts of interest. The administration is recombining BOEM and BSEE, despite the conflicts of interest, in part to implement several executive orders that advance objectives related to fossil fuels and critical minerals. This includes Executive Order 14285, which focuses on developing additional capacity to assess and extract offshore critical mineral resources. Alongside staffing cuts at agencies like BOEM, the establishment of the MMA reduces and siloes BOEM’s role in permitting offshore wind, which requires substantial staffing and expertise. The organizational restructuring that would create the MMA is consistent with the administration’s other moves prioritizing offshore critical mineral extraction and fossil fuel development while deprioritizing offshore wind development. These actions constrain BOEM’s ability to exercise its authority to issue leases for renewable energy, despite Congress’s clear grant of authority to issue leases for that purpose under Section 8(p) of the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act (OCSLA).

Reexamining existing permits

In October 2026, the administration filed a series of motions in multiple legal challenges to offshore wind projects, agreeing with claims about BOEM’s construction and operations plans under OCSLA and seeking to have those approvals remanded to the agency. These motions are intended to allow DOI to reexamine permits for several projects that already cleared rigorous permitting processes, and, in the case of Revolution Wind, that are already fully built and in operation. DOI made requests with similar rationales for Revolution Wind, for Maryland Offshore Wind, and for New England Wind. This follows a court order from August 10, 2026 that granted a request from BOEM to reconsider its own approval of the Atlantic Shores Project, which was issued over the objection of the project developer.

Reduced tax incentives in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA)

In addition to the administration’s actions, Congress has reduced the tax incentives available for offshore wind development through the July 2025 passage of the OBBBA. The law accelerated the termination of the 45X (Advanced Manufacturing Production Credit) for manufacturing wind components, and limited eligibility for 45Y (Clean Electricity Production Tax Credit) and 48E (Clean Electricity Investment Tax Credit) for wind projects that begin construction after July 4, 2026. Under the Inflation Reduction Act, 45Y and 48E would have remained available until 2032 or the year the U.S. power sector achieved an emissions reduction target, while 45X was set to phase down in 2030 and expire in 2032. Following enactment of the OBBBA, wind projects “beginning construction” before July 4, 2026 remained eligible for 45Y and 48E. Developers could establish that construction had begun for the purpose of these credits by satisfying a 5% safe harbor provision, meaning they would need to demonstrate that they had spent 5% or more of the total cost of the project prior to July 4, 2026.

However, that same week in 2025, the administration issued an executive order that directed the Secretary of the Treasury to implement and enforce the OBBBA termination of clean energy tax credits. The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) subsequently released a notice that eliminated the 5% safe harbor methodology for wind tax credit eligibility. Several environmental groups challenged the IRS’s implementation of President Trump’s executive order, and on June 6th, 2026, the Federal District Court for D.C. vacated and remanded the notice.

What are the implications?

From the beginning of the second Trump administration, actions by the federal government have obstructed offshore wind development. Despite the administration’s nearly unbroken record of court losses related to wind energy, the lag between federal actions, lawsuits, and legal verdicts costs American ratepayers: any delay in offshore wind construction and permitting prevents necessary energy generation from getting online to meet continuing load growth projections. And, because of the specialized equipment needed to build offshore wind, delays often compound if the developer misses a construction window, racking up substantial additional costs. Upstream, the communities investing in developing a U.S. supply chain and manufacturing sector, such as specialized shipbuilders in Louisiana, are seeing their investments sit idle.

The uncertainty created by interfering with lawfully issued permits, halting permit processing for specific technologies, and interrupting construction of projects already in development also has long-term consequences for the energy sector and the American economy. Energy projects often require years of planning, development, and construction prior to initiating operations. Energy industry investors, faced with uncertainty due to arbitrary federal actions, may assess a riskier environment for all energy sector investment, and they will likely respond by reducing their exposure across all technologies. Investors need some degree of certainty that their long-term energy projects will be built even as power changes hands between political parties. The administration’s efforts to reexamine approvals of projects already permitted, under construction, and even in operation also emphasize the importance of ensuring that permits, once issued, remain durable through a project’s lifetime.

Offshore wind offers immense potential for domestic economic growth if given the opportunity for investment, as projections indicate that it could generate more than 186,000 jobs across its national supply chain and could demand $42 billion in US steel over the next two decades. The administration’s actions against offshore wind therefore threaten to cede a profitable and high potential U.S. industry to international competitors in China and the European Union, who are already leaders in offshore wind; as of 2025, China had deployed approximately 52 gigawatts (GW) of offshore wind, while the EU had deployed 21 GW, with both planning to install significantly more over the next few years. The offshore wind lease buybacks add to these geopolitical concerns, effectively removing a domestic and clean source of electricity in offshore wind and largely replacing it with infrastructure for export of liquified natural gas (LNG). Pursuing this course of action when the United States needs more domestic electricity generation to meet increasing energy demand weakens U.S. energy security and increases costs for ratepayers.

In addition, efforts to dismantle offshore wind impair many U.S. states’ abilities to meet projected load growth and decarbonization goals. The federal blockade forces many states to increase use of oil and gas peaker plants to meet high energy demand, generating more emissions and decreasing local air quality. Federal barriers to offshore wind also generate immense uncertainty for states working to proactively develop long-term energy and transmission plans.

Several of these states have also invested heavily in offshore wind workforce development (and continue to do so), with specialized training programs that are now in jeopardy. In addition to the training programs themselves, individuals who are already working in the offshore wind industry face severely constrained job prospects and risk their highly specialized training becoming a sunk cost.

In a separate post, CATF examines whether project certainty provisions in the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) would prevent near-term actions stopping clean energy projects and recommends changes to that bill to improve its efficacy.

The case for offshore wind remains strong despite continued uncertainty

The series of actions taken by the second Trump administration against offshore wind has been wide-ranging and disruptive, but offshore wind remains an important and viable technology that can assist states in addressing projected load growth, improving reliability, and meeting decarbonization goals. Projects that have been completed, such as Vineyard Wind 1 in Massachusetts, are offering critical value to the grid. Offshore wind has also significantly outperformed other energy resources and reduced electricity costs during severe weather events. Vineyard Wind 1, for example, had a much higher capacity factor—a measurement of how much electricity the project actually generated in a given time period compared to the maximum amount of electricity it could have generated— than natural gas plants during Winter Storm Fern. The capacity factor for South Fork Wind, an offshore wind project off the coast of Long Island, was essentially equivalent to the most efficient natural gas plants during the same winter storm, while also reducing power prices. Offshore wind makes a difference during heat waves as well, adding needed capacity to the grid when there is high electricity demand for cooling and lowering costs for ratepayers by reducing the need to turn on expensive peaker plants.

text:
The following blog is part of a series examining specific provisions in the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA). Clean Air Task Force is taking a close look at the bill to identify opportunities to strengthen its provisions, address potential gaps, and improve its effectiveness in meeting the country’s energy needs reliably and affordably.

In a separate post, Clean Air Task Force outlines the status of the administration’s efforts to prevent construction and operation of wind energy projects. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) includes a project certainty title motivated by a desire to prevent similar action against previously-permitted, unfairly denied, or unreasonably delayed projects in the future. We support preventing unjustified actions against clean energy projects, which are counterproductive to efforts to reduce electricity costs and power sector emissions. However, the provisions as currently drafted would be unlikely to do much to stem the administration’s ongoing efforts to stymie wind energy.

BAAJA’s project certainty title

Title IV of BAAJA, which covers project certainty, has three provisions.

Section 1401 is designed to prevent cancellation of or changes to federal authorizations or permits that have already been issued except under listed circumstances. If an agency takes one of these prohibited actions, the section provides for judicial review where the government bears the burden of demonstrating the listed exception applies. If the government does not carry that burden, the court may order reinstatement of the permit, injunctive relief prohibiting further actions to cancel or modify the permit or authorization, attorneys’ fees, costs associated with delay, and punitive damages.

Section 1402 is designed to prevent federal agencies from unfairly denying or delaying authorizations or permits for specific types of covered projects, which are listed. It creates a cause of action based on patterns of disparate treatment against a 10-year baseline. This section would also allow injunctive relief, attorneys’ fees, economic damages from denial or delay, and punitive damages.

Section 1403 is designed to prevent unreasonable delays for federal authorizations or permits by setting a deadline for decisions not subject to the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) of one year after an application is submitted, unless the federal government can prove a listed reason for failure to meet that deadline by clear and convincing evidence. This section allows courts to provide injunctive relief and retain jurisdiction to ensure compliance with the order, and it requires courts issue decisions as expeditiously as possible.

Part of Title IV’s logic is that there would be a deterrent effect from the threat of project developers bringing potentially costly lawsuits that would keep an administration from canceling, unfairly denying, or delaying projects. Following that logic, sections 1401 and 1402 would provide developers whose projects have been canceled, unfairly denied, or unreasonably delayed an avenue to seek judicial relief, not only in the form of permit reinstatements and injunctions but also including damages awarded from the Judgment Fund, a permanent, indefinite appropriation that is generally not affected by the annual appropriations process.

Although Title IV depends on payouts from the Judgment Fund as a deterrent, the Trump administration has already spent roughly $3.9 billion from this very account to prevent development of a dozen offshore wind leases. If the idea behind the damages awards is to create a disincentive for this or future administrations to cancel projects to avoid having to pay for those cancelations later, the efficacy of that mechanism is called into question because the current administration has already being willing to spend billions of dollars from the Judgment Fund to prevent wind projects from being built. If this administration is already willing to spend money from that fund voluntarily to prevent wind energy projects, why would it see being forced to spend from it as a reason to refrain from project cancelations or unfair denials in the future?

Other structural features of BAAJA’s permitting certainty title make wind energy projects less likely to take advantage of any benefits its legal process might provide. Most of the successful legal challenges to actions affecting wind projects have been brought by clean energy trade associations or states, with the notable exception of the five lawsuits challenging stop-work orders given to specific offshore wind projects, which were brought by the developers who would now be able to bring cases under section 1401(b)(4)(E) to challenge any further actions to prevent construction or operation with the same judge that issued injunctions. The permitting certainty title does not allow trade associations or states to bring cases under its provisions because they provide only for legal challenges brought by individual project sponsors or holders of federal authorizations (with Section 1402 even specifically prohibiting class actions).1 As a result, each project developer facing a cancellation or delay seeking to use BAAJA’s permitting certainty title to its advantage would have to file its case individually, which may be time consuming, cost intensive, and risky by creating exposure to political retaliation.

Additionally, offshore wind developers may be hesitant even to bring lawsuits for an unfair denial because of the requirement under section 1402(c)(3) that project developers either, absent a showing of impossibility caused in substantial part by the federal government, either complete the type of covered project or repay all remedies obtained under the section. This provision may create an unacceptable level of risk in an industry where factors unrelated to permitting, such as inflation, supply chain delays, and construction vessel availability, can all affect a project’s ability to complete construction. Another risk from this provision is that it does not give a time allowance for project completion or factors that the government must prove before it could seek repayment of remedies. For instance, without stating that the government cannot seek repayment while a project is making progress toward construction, there is a risk that an administration could unfairly seek recovery before a project even has enough time to come online.

The permitting certainty provisions also leave open certain tactics used by this administration. Section 1401, for instance, does not stop the government from seeking to remand already issued authorizations so long as someone has filed a legal challenge, even after manager’s amendment changes covered in a separate post. By contrast, provisions from the House-introduced the CERTAIN Act , not included in BAAJA, would prohibit the federal government from seeking to voluntarily remand or vacate an authorization without the consent of the permit holder. Incorporating this prohibition into BAAJA would prevent the type of filings we have seen in recent weeks, in which the administration has sought to reopen authorizations over developer objections in long-running challenges to offshore wind projects.

Importantly, the permitting certainty title also leaves the Trump administration’s go-to justification on the table: national security. Under section 1401(b)(1)(D), a project may be canceled without running afoul of any of those provisions if necessary to prevent immediate, specific, urgent, substantial, and proximate harm to national security. The manager’s amendment improved this section by restricting any allowable action taken due to national security information to be “narrowly tailored in scope, duration, and degree only so much as is necessary to remedy the specific issue the action is intended to address.” And regarding unreasonable delays, section 1403(d)(2) would allow otherwise prohibited delays in national emergencies where the only available response is to delay the permit.

Although the permitting title adds qualifier terms to the national security rationale, the administration could view these well-intentioned safety valves as continuing opportunities to invoke dubious national security justifications to attack wind energy. As covered in a separate CATF post, the administration has pointed to national security and emergencies as purported and pretextual justifications for its unlawful day one presidential memorandum on offshore wind, stop-work orders for offshore wind projects, the Department of Defense’s (DOD) wind freeze, offshore wind lease buybacks, and a recent Commerce Department determination on offshore wind. The administration may do little more to change its behavior if BAAJA were to pass than to add citations to these new provisions in an attempt to justify continued meddling.

How BAAJA’s NEPA changes eliminate alternate remedies for wind projects

Further complicating matters, BAAJA’s amendments to the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) would take away a valuable potential remedy that has been raised to stop the tide of attacks on wind energy projects. Section 1110 of BAAJA would make the only remedy available for violations of NEPA remand without vacatur, and courts would not be able to issue preliminary injunctions against the government for NEPA violations. These provisions would eliminate the ability of courts to give effective relief under NEPA, turning that law into a paper tiger.

Although the idea behind this provision is that minor violations or flyspecking errors would not stop a project from moving forward, in this context it would allow unlawful cancellations to remain in place despite NEPA violations. Several cases challenging the administration’s actions against wind energy have included NEPA claims. Among other allegations, state-led litigation challenging the series of offshore wind lease buybacks have brought claims that they violate NEPA. And although the district court that enjoined multiple Department of the Interior and U.S. Army Corps of Engineers policies that prevented wind and solar projects from being permitted ruled on other grounds, plaintiffs alleged violations of NEPA in their preliminary injunction motion in that case as well. In another example, in the successful challenges to the January 2025 presidential memorandum on offshore wind, plaintiffs alleged violations of NEPA, among other statutes. By preventing meaningful relief under NEPA, BAAJA would eliminate an option to successfully challenge cancelations and delays of clean energy projects in court.

BAAJA modeling likely overstates near-term benefits of project certainty title as drafted

Some current modeling of BAAJA’s effects on carbon emissions assumes that the permitting certainty provisions will ensure projects get built without considering the questions identified here about whether the permitting certainty title will put a halt to the administration’s actions against wind energy projects. One model of BAAJA’s effects shows 60 gigawatts more clean energy capacity by 2028—the remaining two years of this administration—after modeling an assumption that wind capacity additions would face no constraints, but compared to a baseline in the model without BAAJA that includes a 15-gigawatt limit through 2030. The modelers noted their methods reflected the stated intent of the permitting certainty provisions, rather than an analysis of whether they could have other consequences or looking at their efficacy. Other models did not incorporate permitting certainty , given questions about the title’s effects.

These modelers are transparent regarding assumptions they use to project BAAJA’s emissions effects, but the debate over the bill often decontextualizes the output numbers without relaying the modelers’ provided caveats about the limitations of modeling to capture these types of policy provisions. Given uncertainty about whether the permitting certainty title would protect near-term clean energy buildout, any emissions numbers relying on large increases in clean energy deployment over the next two years should be carefully scrutinized.

Changes may improve the efficacy of the permitting certainty title

Unfortunately, there is no easy legislative fix to stop this administration’s sustained obstruction of wind energy projects and other forms of clean energy, but an open amendment process would provides an opportunity for improvement. Consistent with the problems outlined above, if either the Senate or House proceeds with amending BAAJA, the Senate could address some of the issues raised above by:

Preventing federal agencies from petitioning a court for vacatur or voluntary remand of an authorization unless the project sponsor consents in writing to such a petition (as in section 2(d)(3) of the CERTAIN Act).

Eliminating section 1402’s prohibition on class actions and ensuring that trade associations have standing to bring suit collectively for affected member projects under sections 1401 and 1402.

Eliminate section 1402(c)(3), which is the requirement for completion of a project or repayment of remedies, given the possibility of factors outside the applicant’s control that may lead to project cancellation. The requirement in section 1402(c)(2)(B) in the manager’s amendment that applicants must demonstrate technical and financial ability to construct the project and any other projects for which the applicant has applied for federal approval should be sufficient to prevent frivolous suits.

To avoid open-ended use of national security justifications, require that the agency must promptly file its justification regarding new national security information or of a national emergency with the court within 30 days of a lawsuit being brought under section 1401 or 1403. (Any classified information would be filed under seal or in camera under section 1401(b)(4)(C)). Requiring the agency to file its national security or emergency justification promptly would allow an applicant who has faced a cancelation or unreasonable delay to timely seek a preliminary injunction, even faster than the 120 days for a decision set in section 1403(f).

Strike the proposed section 111(c)(5) of NEPA (in section 1110 of BAAJA). A possible substitute would be to require a court, before vacating an environmental document or authorization or issuing an injunction for a violation of NEPA, to consider (1) the seriousness of the order’s deficiencies and (2) the disruptive consequences of an interim change that may itself be changed. These factors come from a leading appellate court case, Allied-Signal, Inc. v. U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission,2 and they are regularly applied by district and appellate courts to determine if vacatur is the appropriate remedy in administrative law cases. By codifying and requiring this analysis, the concern that litigation over minor NEPA errors would prevent construction of projects would be addressed without making NEPA a paper tiger and preventing its use to counter unlawful project cancellations and delays. There is no need to restrict a court’s analysis for preliminary injunctions, which must already consider the balance of the equities and whether an injunction is in the public interest.3

Conclusion

Preventing the abuse of the federal energy permitting regime is a broadly shared goal, but it is not easy to achieve. BAAJA’s proposed permit certainty changes occur even as courts have already found the administration is failing to follow the law on permitting wind projects, and that it still refuses to do so. Recent filings in the challenge to the DOD’s wind freeze both allege the agency is continuing its review freeze using new mechanisms and also detail project-specific harms from those delays despite the court having entered an injunction. As plaintiffs in that case asked, if DOD “can quickly approve the projects with mitigation agreements awaiting countersignature in a deal on permitting reform legislation, it’s unclear why they can’t quickly approve the projects to comply with the Court’s order staying the freeze.” An assessment of the permitting certainty title’s immediate effects must consider the track record of the administration’s noncompliance with its existing legal obligations.

Even as the Senate voted on a motion to proceed on BAAJA, the President stated he would “not approve wind turbines because wind turbines are a major loser.” As others have noted, in an administration that does not mind losing in court or paying out of the Judgment Fund to stop clean energy, the permitting certainty title may have little deterrent effect. Members of Congress should carefully weigh the risks to achievement of the purported emissions benefits of the permitting certainty title when deciding whether to support the overall legislative package. They should use the amendment process to reduce the inadvertent risks the title presents, and, as outlined above, foreclose some of the clear barriers to protecting wind energy projects.

1 The manager’s amendment added a savings clause to section 1401 indicating that nothing in it limits or supersedes any equitable authority of courts to grant temporary or injunctive relief. That provision at least provides certainty that the creation of this new cause of action would not be exclusive, and the successful legal strategies that have already pushed back against delays and cancellations could continue, with the exception of claims based on violations of the National Environmental Policy Act due to separate provisions discussed later in this post.

2 988 F. F.2d 146, 151 (D.C. Cir. 1993)

3 See Winter v. United States, 555 U.S. 7, 20 (2008).

DALLAS, Nov. 12, 2026 /CNW/ — enCore Energy Corp. (NASDAQ: EU) (TSXV: EU) (the “Company” or “enCore“), America’s Clean Energy Company™, today announced its financial and operational results for the three and nine months ended September 30, 2026. Third quarter revenue increased 88% year over year to $16.7 million on higher uranium deliveries and a stronger average realized price, while the Company continued wellfield development at Alta Mesa and Upper Spring Creek ahead of final regulatory authorizations and took steps to reduce costs and align spending with permitting timelines.

“2026 has been a challenging year for enCore, and we have responded by reducing costs and focusing our capital where it matters most,” said Chief Executive Officer Rich Little. “We optimized operations to align spending with permitting timelines, while continuing to build the wellfields and infrastructure that underpin our next phase of extraction. The first phase of the Upper Spring Creek facility and wellfield and the Alta Mesa wellfield 3 Extension are complete and awaiting receipt of final TCEQ approvals. Key federal approvals are in hand at Dewey Burdock.”

Third Quarter and Nine-Month 2026 Highlights:

Revenue: Revenue of $16.7 million, compared with $8.9 million in the third quarter of 2025, reflecting delivery of 200,000 pounds of U₃O₈ compared with 130,000 pounds in the third quarter of 2025. Average realized sales price was approximately $83.46 per pound versus $68.28 per pound.

Cost of Sales: Cost of sales of $17.4 million, compared with $5.0 million in the third quarter of 2025; weighted average cost of uranium sold was $87.22 per pound versus $38.35 per pound, primarily reflecting a higher proportion of purchased uranium.

Gross Margin: Gross loss of $0.8 million versus gross profit of $3.9 million in the third quarter of 2025, primarily reflecting the higher cost of purchased uranium included in sales during the quarter.

Net Loss: Net loss attributable to enCore of $33.9 million, or $0.17 per basic and diluted share, versus $4.8 million, or $0.03 per share, in the third quarter of 2025. Results included a $17.0 million realized loss and $5.7 million unrealized gain on marketable securities.

Liquidity: As of September 30, 2026, unrestricted cash and cash equivalents were $5.1 million, marketable securities were $33.6 million, and inventory was $6.4 million. Working capital was $47.3 million. Marketable securities and inventory are not equivalent to unrestricted cash.

Nine-Month Revenue: Revenue increased to $50.7 million compared to $30.8 million in the nine months ended September 30, 2025. Uranium deliveries increased to 685,000 pounds compared to 480,000 pounds; average realized sales price was approximately $74.00 per pound versus $64.13 per pound for the same period.

Nine-Month Cost of Sales: Cost of sales increased to $54.1 million from $25.8 million, with weighted average cost per pound sold of $78.95 versus $53.71 for the nine months ended September 30, 2025. Of the 685,000 pounds sold in the nine months ended September 30, 2026, 560,000 pounds were purchased uranium, and 125,000 pounds were extracted uranium.

Operating Cash Flow: Net cash used in operating activities was $47.4 million for the nine months ended September 30, 2026, compared with $37.9 million in the corresponding prior-year period.

Nine-Month Net Loss: Net loss attributable to enCore was $70.0 million, or $0.36 per share, compared with $35.3 million, or $0.19 per share, in the prior-year period.

Operational Updates:

Alta Mesa – wellfield 3 Extension: The wellfield is ready for extraction, and the Company is awaiting final regulatory approval. enCore expects to begin extraction before the end of 2026.

Alta Mesa – wellfield 8: Development drilling continues, and the Company expects to begin extraction in early 2027.

Upper Spring Creek: The first phase of the satellite facility and wellfield development are complete. Operations are expected to commence before the end of 2026.

Alta Mesa East: Exploration drilling and preparation of permitting applications continue for an expansion into the adjacent project area.

Dewey Burdock: Key federal permitting milestones achieved to date include Environmental Protection Agency Class III and V underground injection control permits received in October 2025 and Bureau of Land Management approval of the Plan of Operations on June 15, 2026. Preliminary engineering is ongoing for the plant site and evaporation ponds, and the Company continues to advance state permitting.

Cost Discipline: In response to permitting delays in South Texas, which have reduced estimated 2026 extraction volumes, the Company executed a reduction in force in July 2026 that reduced overall headcount by approximately 20%. The Company also reduced rig activity to better align spending with permitting timelines and operational priorities.

During the third quarter, the Company distributed Verdera Energy Corp. shares to its shareholders. The shares distributed had a fair value of $8.4 million, and the Company recorded a $17.2 million realized loss on distribution. As a result of the distribution, the conversion rate on the Company’s 5.50% convertible senior notes due 2030 and the related capped-call strike and cap prices were adjusted, as described in the Company’s Quarterly Report on Form 10-Q for the quarter ended September 30, 2026.

Investor Information

enCore’s interim financial statements, including the accompanying Management’s Discussion and Analysis, are available in the Company’s Quarterly Report on Form 10-Q, which is being filed today with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (“SEC”) and with Canadian securities regulators on SEDAR+. It includes the Company’s consolidated financial statements for the nine months ended September 30, 2026, and the related notes and financial results. The report can be accessed at the SEC’s website at www.sec.gov, SEDAR+ at www.sedarplus.ca, and on enCore’s financials page at www.encoreuranium.com/investors/financial-statements/.

About enCore Energy Corp.

text:
European leaders are considering postponing a 10% tariff on electric vehicles built in Britain, according to a report.

The Financial Times claims that politicians in Brussels are consulting on delaying the levy in an effort to protect Europe’s auto industry from Chinese rivals.

The FT cited “several people close to the matter” and reported that the UK backed the plan.

Under post-Brexit rules of origin, from 1 January 2027, EVs exported from the UK to Europe will be subject to the 10% tariff unless at least 55% of their value originates in the UK or EU. Additionally, 70% of a vehicle’s entire battery must be from one side or other, and 65% of battery cells.

In June, the UK’s Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT) warned that the current Made in Europe stipulations would cost EV makers £1.4 billion in tariffs and, if implemented, the levy would damage both the UK and European car industries.

The rules of origin were developed to protect Europe’s auto industry from the growing threat of Chinese-made EVs. However, it is now feared that they could make Chinese models even more attractive in the UK, while British-built cars will become less competitive in Europe.

In September, the European Automobile Manufacturers Association (ACEA) warned that Europe’s battery manufacturing industry was not sufficiently developed to meet the requirements and 82% of the 520,000 EVs expected to be sold in 2027 would be subject to the levy.

According to the FT, sources close to the matter said that changes will be considered after a joint summit on 20 November. A compromise could include a one- or two-year deal that allows the offsetting of non-compliant exported vehicles against compliant domestic sales.

The UK and EU are each other’s biggest export markets, and earlier this month, a report from LSE Consulting called for joint action to protect the co-dependent industries from global competition. It said that cooperation and the inclusion of the UK in “Made in Europe” policies was in both parties’ interests.

Responding to the LSE report, Sigrid de Vries, ACEA director general, said: “The close ties between the EU and UK automotive industries are a strength we cannot afford to undermine.

“Both sides have a shared interest in building on this relationship to create the right conditions for investment, innovation and manufacturing. Closer cooperation and pragmatic policy choices will be key to ensuring Europe excels as a competitive place to build and sell vehicles.”

Mike Hawes, SMMT Chief Executive, added: “The UK and EU are bound by €80 billion in annual automotive trade and millions of jobs. At a time of intense global competition, this report makes clear the need for both sides to collaborate and remove barriers to trade.

“Our collective response must strengthen both sectors, with the UK included in ‘Made in Europe’ measures, a pragmatic solution to 2027 rules of origin, and stronger integrated supply chains.”

text:
India has prohibited exports of lithium-ion battery black mass with immediate effect, seeking to retain critical mineral-bearing battery waste within the country and strengthen domestic recycling and refining capacity.

The Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT), under the Department of Commerce, amended the export policy for lithium-ion battery black mass under ITC (HS) code 85491400 from ‘Free’ to ‘Prohibited’ through Notification No. 49/2026-27 dated November 10. The restriction will remain in force until further orders, with transitional arrangements under Para 1.05 of the Foreign Trade Policy 2023 applicable.

Black mass is the dark, powder-like material produced by shredding end-of-life lithium-ion batteries and battery manufacturing waste. It contains recoverable quantities of critical minerals, including lithium, cobalt, nickel and manganese, which are used in electric vehicle batteries, energy storage systems and other advanced applications.

The government said India's battery recycling and critical mineral refining capacity has expanded, but remains underutilised due to inadequate feedstock availability. Exports of domestically generated black mass have diverted valuable secondary raw materials to overseas markets, while some domestic recyclers have had to import material to meet their processing requirements.

The export prohibition aims to ensure that black mass generated in India is processed domestically, improving feedstock availability and capacity utilisation at recycling and refining facilities. The move is also expected to encourage investment and employment in the sector, increase domestic recovery of critical minerals and reduce reliance on imports and associated foreign exchange outgo.

The restriction complements the government's ₹1,500-crore Incentive Scheme for Promotion of Critical Mineral Recycling, approved by the Union Cabinet in September 2025 under the National Critical Mineral Mission. The scheme aims to develop domestic capacity to recover and produce critical minerals from secondary sources, including battery waste and electronic waste. Retaining black mass within the country is expected to provide feedstock to recycling facilities being developed under the scheme.

The policy also supports India's broader efforts to strengthen supply chains for battery manufacturing, electric mobility, energy storage and clean-energy technologies through domestic resource recovery and circular-economy initiatives.

The export prohibition could redirect Indian-origin black mass towards domestic recyclers, potentially tightening availability for overseas buyers. However, the extent of the benefit to domestic processors will depend on their ability to scale up downstream recovery of battery-grade lithium, cobalt and nickel, rather than merely collecting and shredding spent batteries.

title: Power Shift: State Election Wins Open Path for Climate Progress - Yale E360
description:
In Texas, which is facing a massive buildout of gas power, the incoming governor pledged a moratorium on new data centers.
While climate change was barely mentioned in these elections, many races were dominated by two closely related issues: data centers and utility regulation.
In the midterm elections, ballot measures to restrict data centers passed in 44 cities across the country and failed in only one.
In practice, that could mean laying more costs on data centers and utility shareholders and less on consumers.
Beyond hemming in data centers and utilities, several other election outcomes hold promise for the environment.
text:
After their sweeping victories in the midterm elections, Democrats will control both houses of Congress, meaning they will be able to shape the budget, conduct vigorous oversight and investigations, and refuse to confirm nominees for judgeships and other high positions — but their power will be constrained. Any ambitious new bill to tackle climate change, for example, will face President Trump’s veto pen.

But there are other ways for Democrats to make progress on climate, energy, and the environment — by wielding their newfound power in the states.

In the November 3 elections, Democrats flipped control of governors’ offices in Georgia, Iowa, Ohio, Nevada, and Texas, and are on track to win in Alaska, where votes are still being counted. They also attained trifectas — control of the governor’s office and both houses of the state legislature — in Arizona, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin.

This brings to 29 or 30 the number of states that will have Democratic governors in January, and to 22 the states in which Democrats have unified control of government. Meanwhile, Republican trifectas were broken in Georgia, Iowa, New Hampshire, Ohio, and Texas.

In Texas, which is facing a massive buildout of gas power, the incoming governor pledged a moratorium on new data centers.

While climate change was barely mentioned in these elections, many races were dominated by two closely related issues: data centers and utility regulation. Public outcry over the growth of data centers, which are driving ever more burning of natural gas, and the rising cost of electricity mean that Democrats have a mandate to advance energy reforms in the states they control.

By one estimate, tech companies are intent on spending more than $647 billion over the coming years to develop natural gas infrastructure in the U.S. to serve the voracious power demands of data centers. The planned expansions would grow the existing fleet of gas generators by roughly two-thirds. Natural gas is already the second largest source of greenhouse gas emissions in the U.S. (behind petroleum, but far greater than coal), and this investment would lock in its use for decades.

Against this backdrop, public opposition to data centers has rocketed. In the midterm elections, ballot measures to restrict data centers passed in 44 cities across the country and failed in only one. In her successful campaign for governor of Texas, which is facing the largest natural gas buildout in the nation, Gina Hinojosa pledged an immediate moratorium on new data centers. Many other winning candidates also promised more controls on data center construction.

Looking ahead, governors have the opportunity to appoint regulators who will further rein in data centers and the power utilities profiting from rising energy prices. Retail electricity rates are set by state public utility commissions, and in 38 states the commissioners are named by the governors. The newly elected Democratic governors of Ohio, Michigan, Wisconsin, Nevada, and Maine all campaigned on promises to appoint commissioners who would work to favor the interests of ratepayers over those of monopoly utilities.

In practice, that could mean laying more costs on data centers and utility shareholders and less on consumers. It could also mean encouraging more rooftop and community solar to help lower electric bills. Utilities have long campaigned against such projects, which cut into their profits.

In Georgia, where commissioners are elected, Democrats just won a majority of seats on the five-member commission, promising greater scrutiny of the utilities. In Pennsylvania, legislation to lower power bills by reducing utility profits recently stalled in the Republican-controlled state senate, but under the new Democratic trifecta, this legislation is expected to be signed into law. In Michigan, about 80 percent of voters approved a ballot measure that will block utilities from campaign spending (which the utilities are already challenging in court). And in Colorado, voters rejected a ballot measure, championed by gas utilities, that would have established a “right to natural gas” and blocked local moves to phase out gas appliances.

Most federal environmental laws set the floor, not the ceiling, for pollution standards. States may set stricter rules if they choose.

Beyond hemming in data centers and utilities, several other election outcomes hold promise for the environment. The Texas Railroad Commission, which regulates the state’s oil and gas industry, has long consisted of three Republican members. A Democrat won election to the body with a platform that included capping orphan wells and banning gas flaring — two important means of stemming emissions from drilling. He can now put these issues on the agenda. His election also makes it possible for Democrats to win control of the commission in 2028.

Democratic candidates for state attorney general triumphed over Republicans in Texas, Georgia, Iowa, Ohio, and Kansas. Republican attorneys general have been at the forefront of litigation aimed at weakening environmental regulations, and they have moved in concert to protect oil and gas companies from being held accountable for climate damages. These states are expected to reverse their positions in many cases, which might tilt the scales in some.

What else might Democrats do with all their new power?

Given the focus of almost all campaigns on affordability, not many states are likely to adopt measures that would transparently increase consumer costs, such as a tax on carbon. However, states have many other tools. Most federal environmental statutes, such as the Clean Air Act, set the floor, not the ceiling, for pollution standards. States may set stricter rules if they choose.

Of the 10 states that burn the most coal for power, Democrats will now control the governor’s office in seven: Texas, Kentucky, Illinois, Ohio, Wisconsin, Georgia, and Iowa. Governors in those states have considerable ability to shut coal plants down, for example, by setting air pollution standards that are too expensive for plants to meet.

If coal plants are to be shuttered and the use of natural gas slashed, the nation will need much more renewable energy, particularly wind and solar, to meet its growing electricity demand. One way to ramp up wind and solar is through renewable portfolio standards, which require utilities to acquire a certain percentage of their power from renewable sources. Today, 27 states have such standards, but many are so low that they have already been met. Democratic wins mean that more states can adopt renewable portfolio standards or strengthen and enforce those already on the books.

State leaders can also clear roadblocks for new renewable energy development. Over the last 30 years, more than 850 cities and counties have adopted restrictions on wind and solar, often spurred on by residents’ objections to large renewable installations proposed in their communities. In response, several states have adopted laws that centralize authority over such facilities, allowing them to override local bans. New York’s law has been especially successful at boosting wind and solar installations. Other states that now have Democratic trifectas could adopt similar laws.

States can encourage the uptake of electric vehicles by building more charging stations and providing rebates to EV buyers.

States may also encourage household solar by making it easier for homeowners to obtain approvals for rooftop arrays; enabling net metering; legalizing balcony solar; easing the siting of battery storage systems; and facilitating virtual power plants, which allow energy companies to link together and control home batteries, solar panels, thermostats, and other assets to balance the grid.

While states cannot require citizens to buy electric vehicles, they may encourage their uptake by building more charging stations, requiring new parking lots and garages to install fast chargers, and providing rebates to EV buyers to offset the recent loss of federal subsidies.

States can reduce emissions from the residential sector by incentivizing the installation of heat pumps, strengthening energy efficiency standards for buildings, and — though federal courts are split on whether this is permissible — barring new natural gas hookups.

These measures are only a fraction of what states can do. The Model Climate Laws Initiative, a joint project of the Sabin Center for Climate Change Law and Environmental Advocates NY, has posted more than 2,000 model and actual state and local laws, and it stands ready to draft many more. Thoughtful policies aimed at cutting power bills, curbing pollution, and advancing clean energy have been circulating for a long time. It is time to put those policies into action.
