text:
On a hillside north of Milford, Utah, the West’s energy future looks a lot like its past: 150 feet of latticed metal, centered around a drill.

Here, mud-soaked men in hardhats work above the rangeland scrub, stacking tube on tube, 90 feet at a time, into the unseen earth below. It’s rough work — two weeks on, two weeks off, all in service of punching a 9⅞-inch hole more than 10,000 feet into the tough granite basement of the Beaver Valley.

“What we’re doing here doesn’t look or feel much different from what you’d see in the Permian Basin,” said Sarah Jewett, chief operating officer of Fervo Energy, the Houston-based firm running the operation.

But at the place Fervo calls Cape Station, Jewett isn’t searching for gas or oil.

“What we’re looking for,” she said, “is heat.”

Three years ago, Fervo Energy broke ground on this patch of federal land in western Utah to pilot a new type of power plant — one that co-opts the hydraulic fracking techniques developed for the natural gas extraction to find a one-day replacement for fossil-fueled electricity: large-scale geothermal energy.

Last month, Fervo delivered its first watts of electricity generated at a Cape Station plant through transmission lines toward Delta, also in central Utah. There’s more on the way: Google has already purchased about 400 megawatts, with an option of upping that to a gigawatt by 2030, according to the firm. The timeline coincides with when the tech giant is considering opening a new data center nearby, drawing power straight from Fervo, Milford Mayor Nolan Davis told the Deseret News.

Estimates vary, but a single gigawatt can typically power between 700,000-750,000 homes. It’s a fraction of what Fervo CEO Tim Latimer projects for his Cape Station project. On Wednesday, Latimer said recent estimates determined Cape Station could produce up to eight gigawatts on its own — twice what the company originally projected. If true, the single site could make nearly enough to power all of Utah twice over on a hot summer day, according to Logan Mitchell, climate scientist and regulatory manager at Utah Clean Energy.

Nationwide, geothermal power plants generate about four gigawatts of power — 0.4% of the national output, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. Between Cape Station and Blanford, another site that Fervo is exploring in the same valley, Utah’s geothermal promise could revolutionize the West’s energy backbone — if companies like Fervo can scale it up at a cost palatable for everyday consumers, Mitchell said.

Those prospects are why important eyes are watching.

On Wednesday, U.S. Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum flew to Milford to tour the site, making it the first geothermal operation he’s visited as a cabinet member, according to a staffer.

“I would say this is a great example of President Trump’s energy dominance agenda, which really is about energy abundance,” Burgum said Wednesday. “It’s about reliable, affordable, secure energy. And the geothermal that’s being produced here is absolutely that.”

Geothermal has ‘crossed a tipping point’

Geothermal power isn’t new. Just up the hill from Cape Station, the PacifiCorp’s 34 MW Blundell power plant has been operating on a fault in the Mineral Mountains since 1984. But through geothermal’s history, Mitchell said, people have always had to harness it on the Earth’s terms. Blundell, for example, is fed by a nearby hot springs, with a boiling reservoir to turn the turbines that produce the power.

Cape Station manufactures those conditions. Crews drill parallel shafts that hook horizontally, and blast water down one. The water filters through intentional cracks, where the earth heats it to about 400 degrees Fahrenheit. The superheated water arrives on the return side and, under pressure, moves out of the ground, through a trunk pipe, and toward the power plants. Through a series of heat exchanges, the water then boils a different compound that does evaporate, expands, and turns the blades on one of dozens of massive turbines, producing electricity.

“Turn it on, run it for 30 years, and that’s your project,” Latimer said.

Unlike wind and solar, which spread across the landscape, Fervo’s “enhanced” geothermal is packed underground. On its Phase 2 drill site, eight wells are spaced 15 feet apart at varying depths. A separate operation’s turbines and solar arrays actually sit atop the tunnels. On a recent afternoon, so did antelope and sagebrush.

“More wells on less space means more energy,” said Roman Esqueda, who leads a drilling team at Cape Station. His team’s latest tunnel ran more than 18,600 feet, he said, but the above ground work took place on a pad about the size of a superstore parking lot.

And unlike Blundell, which exhausts steam, Fervo’s system is closed; both the water and the evaporative solution are reused, Latimer said. The state water board backs that claim: Fervo has been given a nonconsumptive use permit, pulling water from deeper than any farmer’s well and pushing it through the system over and over again.

“For a water-constrained state, that’s a really big deal,” said Emy Lesofski, director of the Utah Governor’s Office on Energy.

“For me,” she added, “This is an incredible advancement in technology, and it’s happening in Utah.”

That’s not an accident.

Nearby, the Department of Energy’s Utah FORGE, or Frontier Observatory for Research in Geothermal Energy, pioneered many modern geothermal methods, making data available to commercial outfits like Fervo. And, it mapped the underlying geology of the property Fervo now leases, “de-risking” a portion of the development, Lesofski said.

The data was “a look under the hood,” she said. And while it offered a head start, Fervo’s system could work almost anywhere, Mitchell said. Anywhere it is cheap enough, that is.

As it stands, geothermal energy is getting there, Mitchell said. PacifiCorp seems to agree: In a public input meeting for its 2027 Integrated Resource Plan, the parent company of Rocky Mountain Power found geothermal to be less expensive than natural gas. Solar and wind are cheaper, but they’re not considered a “firm, dispatchable resource,” Mitchell said. There’s too much down time.

“There’s a daily catastrophic failure on solar,” Burgum said. “It’s called sunset.”

Geothermal, though, can be up 24/7/365, Burgum said.

And now, according to Mitchell, its price “has crossed a tipping point.”

Critics have found reasons to be leery of Fervo’s technology — particularly its nonconsumptive water claims. Operational data will clear some of that up once the plant gets off the ground, Mitchell said. But barring any “showstoppers,” he said, the future of this new form of geothermal depends on price.

That’s something Jewett understands, too.

“Every decision we make out here is to drive the cost of geothermal down,” she said. “It shouldn’t be chosen because it’s a clean energy solution. It should be chosen because it’s affordable, and because it’s efficient.”

‘I never thought I’d see this happen in Milford’

Some five miles south, Milford Mayor Nolan Davis decorated his office in his town’s history: photos, flags, a slab of copper pulled from a local mine. In truth, he’s part of that history: between his time on the city council and the mayor’s desk, he’s been in public office more than 30 years. The mines, the railroad, the Smithfield hog farms — he’s seen Milford’s next-big-things all come and, ultimately, go, taking hundreds of jobs with them. Through it all, he’s seen his town of 1,600 dwindle to a pit stop on the way south to the booming hubs of Cedar City or St. George, and a generation leave on state Highway 257 with no reason to come back.

“We export our kids,” he told the Deseret News. “There’s nothing here for them.”

More recently, though, he’s added a camo Fervo hat to the decor — a nod to a different future. Soon, he may add the Google brand, too.

Davis says he fields five calls a week from data center developers. The energy coming from up-valley has put Milford back on the map.

To Davis, Fervo has been a “fantastic neighbor,” starting the day he met Jewett in the early days of development.

“The first thing she said was, ‘What can we do for you,’” he remembers. Since, Fervo employees have started going to football games, coaching Little League. They donated $15,000 to the town’s library, he said. The company’s subcontractors have worked to house employees and bolster city infrastructure, sparing Milford’s coffers.

Davis said he isn’t worried about Milford’s water supply or quality. And, he said he hasn’t felt any earthquakes commonly associated with fracking, though the U.S. Geological Survey reported several small tremors around the drill site Wednesday alone.

None of the power generated in the Beaver Valley has ever stayed local, he said. Producers “can sell it in California for a lot more than we pay in Utah,” he said. That’s OK, he said — if the new jobs it brings can help a few more businesses open back up on Main Street, or fill the empty desks at Milford High.

He doesn’t want his town to be Cedar City or St. George, he said. He wants to give the kids a reason to come back home. For the first time in a long time, he thinks it’s almost here.

“I never thought I’d see this happen in Milford,” Davis said. “I just thought we’d limp along. We’d be up, we’d be down, but we know how to survive. But in the past three months, it’s snowballed. Now, we really need to get down to work.”

Donald Trump is the “biggest loser we’ve seen in a long time” for scrapping action on the climate crisis and ceding the clean energy race to China, former US secretary of state John Kerry has said.

Kerry, speaking at the Cop31 climate summit in Turkey, criticized Trump for withdrawing the US from the international climate process and axing measures that reduced planet-heating emissions. Unlike almost all other countries in the world, the Trump administration has sent no delegation to the resort city of Antalya for the annual UN climate talks, which started on Monday.

The US president, who has previously called climate science a “hoax” and called for countries to drill for more oil and gas, again expressed his hostility towards clean energy on Monday. “I will not approve wind turbines because wind turbines are a major loser,” Trump, who has long-held animus towards wind farms, said about potential new legislation that would make it easier to build new energy projects.

Asked about his comments by the Guardian, Kerry said: “[The] first thing they should do is hold up a really big mirror so he can look at a loser, because he’s the biggest loser we’ve seen in a long time on all of these issues.”

“He’s missing the point,” Kerry, a former climate envoy for Joe Biden’s administration, added. “He’s missing the competitiveness with China. He’s missing the marketplace for goods that could be produced in the United States. We could be the supply chain for some of these.”

Under Biden, the US passed sweeping climate legislation that gave tax breaks for clean energy and electric vehicle manufacturing in a bid to compete with China, which has dominated clean tech.

Republicans eliminated most of this support, however, with Trump instead imposing tariffs on various goods and pouring public money into propping up struggling coal-fired power plants. Coal is the dirtiest of fossil fuels, causing much of the pollution that is dangerously overheating our planet.

“He declared he wanted to beat China, be number one in X, Y, or Z, and he walked away from the battlefield,” Kerry said of Trump. “He totally took America out of that sector. So honestly, if you want to be number one, you don’t do it by literally blackballing an entire sector of the economy.”

Kerry, who ran as the Democratic candidate for president in 2004, has repeatedly urged the US and the rest of the world to follow China’s lead on green energy. The overall rapid growth in renewables has helped prevent a significant amount of fossil fuel power going online, with global emissions edging down slightly last year.

Far larger and deeper cuts to emissions will be needed for the world to avoid catastrophic climate change, however, with countries gathering at Cop told by António Guterres, the UN secretary general, it was “long past time” to phase out fossil fuel use.

The dawdling progress in years of talks to even discuss fossil fuels, the central cause of the climate crisis, has provoked ire from advocates. “Cops have become greenwashed circuses,” said Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg, who arrived in Antalya on Tuesday. “That is the reality.”

Kerry acknowledged the ponderous progress and that politicians should talk differently about the climate crisis to engage the public. But he claimed that while it was not the central issue to the recent US midterm elections, concerns about global heating did overlap with alarm over rising energy costs and drove voters to the Democrats.

“I think we will have a number of candidates who will have this high on the agenda,” Kerry said of the victorious Democratic candidates. “And all of the analysis that I’ve seen, I mean real analysis, has said this was one of the issues that counted.”

text:
Electric Vehicles (EVs) have become increasingly popular, with the FBT exemption making them particularly attractive under salary packaging arrangements. The Federal Government has now introduced legislation to wind back the full exemption, with the proposed changes currently before Parliament.

What is proposed to change?

Subject to the legislation being enacted, the existing exemption will continue until 31 March 2027.

For new arrangements from 1 April 2027 to 31 March 2029:

EVs valued at $75,000 or less will retain the full FBT discount

EVs above $75,000 but below the applicable fuel-efficient luxury car tax threshold will generally receive a 25% discount on FBT payable

From 1 April 2029, eligible EVs under new arrangements will generally receive a 25% FBT discount.

What about existing arrangements?

The proposed transitional rules are intended to preserve the existing exemption for eligible EVs provided under a financially binding commitment entered into before 1 April 2027, while that commitment remains in place.

Employers and employees alike should exercise caution when existing arrangements are renewed or varied, e.g. refinancing a lease or changing employers, as changes may affect access to the transitional treatment.

What should businesses do?

While the legislation remains before Parliament, employers should start identifying existing EV arrangements and the dates of relevant binding commitments. Employers considering new or varied arrangements should also understand how the proposed rules may affect their FBT position.

For employees considering an EV, timing and vehicle value will become increasingly important when the legislation is eventually enacted.

This Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO) announces the availability of funds under the Diesel Emissions Reduction Act (DERA) Program and solicits applications from eligible entities to incentivize and accelerate the upgrade or retirement of the nation’s legacy diesel engine fleet. Eligible activities include the retrofit or replacement of existing diesel engines, vehicles, and equipment with the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and California Air Resources Board (CARB) certified or verified technologies.

There are several ways DERA recipients may implement projects and fund project partners, depending on the roles and responsibilities of each. If the applicant is the owner of the target vehicles, the applicant may directly implement the project. If the applicant is partnering with diesel fleet owners, the applicant may award subawards or participant support costs (e.g., rebates). Please refer to Section 9.B. for detailed guidance on funding partnerships.

After an extensive review of the program, the EPA revamped DERA requirements to ensure alignment with the Administration’s priorities, improve the quality of projects funded, expand the availability of technology choices, and respond to stakeholder requests for a simplified program structure. Consistent with agency grants direction, updates to 2 CFR §200.204 and DERA statutory requirements, this NOFO reflects these changes and inputs when compared to previous funding notice opportunities.

text:
Summary

The Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT) has prohibited the export of lithium-ion battery black mass under ITC(HS) Code 85491400 with immediate effect. The restriction, notified on 10 November 2026, aims to retain battery waste within India, improve feedstock availability for domestic recyclers and increase the recovery of critical minerals such as lithium, cobalt, nickel and manganese.

Article

DGFT changes export policy from ‘Free’ to ‘Prohibited’

The Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT), under the Department of Commerce, has prohibited the export of lithium-ion battery black mass through Notification No. 49/2026-27, dated 10 November 2026.

Under the notification, the export policy for the material covered by ITC(HS) Code 85491400 has been changed from ‘Free’ to ‘Prohibited’ with immediate effect and until further orders. The transitional arrangements under Para 1.05 of the Foreign Trade Policy (FTP), 2023, will apply.

The specified ITC(HS) code covers waste and scrap of primary cells, primary batteries and electric accumulators, including spent cells and batteries that are unsorted and do not contain lead, cadmium or mercury. The notification specifically identifies lithium-ion battery black mass under this classification.

Export restriction aims to secure domestic recycling feedstock

Black mass is the powder-like material produced by shredding end-of-life lithium-ion batteries and battery manufacturing waste. It contains recoverable critical minerals, including lithium, cobalt, nickel and manganese, which are used in battery manufacturing, electric mobility, energy storage, electronics and renewable energy technologies.

India relies significantly on imports for several of these minerals. Although the country’s battery recycling and critical mineral refining capacity has expanded, domestic facilities are not operating at their full potential due to insufficient feedstock availability.

The export of locally generated black mass has diverted recyclable material to overseas markets, while some Indian recyclers have had to import similar material to meet their processing requirements.

By restricting exports, the government intends to ensure that black mass generated in India is processed domestically. The move is expected to improve feedstock availability, increase capacity utilisation at recycling and refining facilities, and encourage investment and employment in the sector.

Policy targets higher recovery of critical minerals

Retaining black mass within the country is expected to increase the domestic recovery of lithium, cobalt, nickel and other critical minerals, potentially reducing India’s dependence on imports and the associated foreign exchange expenditure.

The measure is also intended to strengthen supply chains for battery manufacturing, electric vehicles, energy storage and clean-energy technologies. It supports the government’s Aatmanirbhar Bharat initiative by promoting domestic access to materials required for these industries.

In addition, domestic processing of black mass is expected to support the circular economy and the concept of urban mining, which involves recovering valuable materials from discarded products and waste. It could also reduce dependence on primary mineral extraction while enabling the environmentally sound treatment of hazardous battery waste under applicable regulations.

Export ban complements National Critical Mineral Mission

The restriction complements the government’s National Critical Mineral Mission (NCMM), which includes measures to expand domestic recycling and mineral recovery capacity.

In September 2025, the Union Cabinet approved a ₹1,500-crore incentive scheme to support the separation and production of critical minerals from secondary sources, including battery waste and electronic waste.

Ensuring domestic availability of black mass is expected to provide feedstock to recycling facilities being developed under the scheme and support the country’s efforts to establish a domestic critical mineral supply chain.

The policy also follows a broader approach adopted by several major economies to retain critical mineral-bearing battery waste and black mass for processing within their own borders.

FAQs

What has DGFT prohibited under Notification No. 49/2026-27?

DGFT has prohibited the export of lithium-ion battery black mass classified under ITC(HS) Code 85491400, changing its export status from ‘Free’ to ‘Prohibited’.

When did the export prohibition come into effect?

The restriction took effect immediately following the issuance of Notification No. 49/2026-27 on 10 November 2026 and will remain in force until further orders.

What is lithium-ion battery black mass?

Black mass is the powder-like material obtained by shredding end-of-life lithium-ion batteries and battery manufacturing waste. It contains recoverable minerals such as lithium, cobalt, nickel and manganese.

Why has India prohibited black mass exports?

The restriction aims to retain domestically generated black mass for processing in India, address feedstock shortages at recycling facilities, increase critical mineral recovery and reduce dependence on imported minerals.

How does the export ban support the National Critical Mineral Mission?

The measure is expected to improve domestic feedstock availability for recycling facilities supported by the ₹1,500-crore incentive scheme approved under the National Critical Mineral Mission in September 2025.

text:
On October 20, the two candidates running to represent Michigan in the U.S. Senate, Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers, took questions for an hour at the Detroit Economic Club. El-Sayed, the Democrat who had previously run for governor, made a name for himself years ago by connecting public health to the climate crisis. He published a fierce defense of the Green New Deal at the time, touting its economic, health, and planetary benefits. But last month at the Detroit Economic Club, El-Sayed didn’t mention the Green New Deal at all.

Instead, the only mentions of such a plan came from his opponent, who used it as an attack on El-Sayed and the Democratic party as a whole. “We need to make sure we don’t have the largest tax increase in the history of the country,” Rogers said, “which is, that’s what the other team is talking about doing.”

A vote for El-Sayed would ring in an era of “big government, government control, more rules, more regulation, another Green New Deal,” Rogers continued. It’s become a common refrain since President Donald Trump’s effort to rebrand the climate movement’s push for widescale public investment in renewable energy as a “Green New Scam.”

Two weeks later, El-Sayed handily won the race.

Even though many of the newly elected Democrats did not talk about the Green New Deal by name, the think tank Climate and Community Institute describes El-Sayed as belonging to a new class of green economic populists who are running for public office (and winning) by connecting the need for climate action to soaring utility bills and the hoarding of wealth by a handful of individuals and companies.

El-Sayed “clearly gets it,” said Patrick Bigger, research director at Climate and Community Institute, or CCI. The senator-elect’s platform, which proposes stricter regulations on data centers and energy companies, is “really exciting,” he said. These are promising climate agenda items — even if Democrats don’t explicitly call them that. For example, voters may oppose data centers in their backyard for any number of reasons, but some number of them are required for our digitalized reality and progressives now have an opportunity to take the companies behind them to task and get them to commit to reducing their strain on the local environment. Likewise, where voters came out in support of lowering utility bills, electeds now can talk further about investing in cheaper renewable energy systems like solar and wind power.

Bigger led a recent analysis that scored candidates in this year’s primary and midterm elections based on three questions: Is the candidate pushing for renewable energy or other climate actions? Do they name the rising cost of living as a voter issue, and have a plan to lower those costs? Do they articulate a populist vision by blaming wealthy corporations and powerful individuals for both the climate and affordability crises? CCI argues that candidates like El-Sayed who check all three boxes are the climate champions of the moment.

Other progressives named in the report include Will Lawrence, a co-founder of the Sunrise Movement, the climate group that first sounded the alarm for a Green New Deal in 2018. Lawrence, who will represent Michigan’s 7th District in the next Congress, points to his history of climate organizing on his website: “I will be among the most knowledgeable and dedicated members of Congress on water, climate and energy policy,” he writes. “I will fight for investment to secure the climate we depend on, adapt to the changes we can’t prevent, and finally drive our electric bills down.”

These “new folks headed to the House and the Senate who are really on board with a robust transformative approach to climate,” said Bigger, represent “a major shift.”

But not all climate progressives heading to Washington next year are so allergic to calling it the Green New Deal: Representatives-elect Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier in New York City name it specifically on their campaign websites and in the press. Still, this new wave of climate leaders may feel it’s time for the decarbonization agenda to get a refresh; Valdez and Avila Chevalier’s websites also include mentions of “a livable planet for all” and “a livable world for everyone,” respectively. In part, this diversity of messaging tactics reflects the fractured nature of the climate movement since Trump retook office with a checklist of Biden-era environmental regulations to roll back.

If progressive Democrats’ messaging on climate has shifted, said Aru Shiney-Ajay, executive director of the Sunrise Movement, it’s because the terrain they’re fighting in has changed, too. “I think, as the climate crisis gets worse and worse, it’s becoming increasingly clear that the strategy, policy-wise, needs to be incorporating climate change into every single aspect of what we’re doing,” she said. In other words, climate policy should not be framed as a separate issue from the economy, infrastructure improvements, or foreign policy. “It should be the defining framework within which we have to think about how we run our society,” said Shiney-Ajay.

In 2018, the Sunrise Movement burst onto the national stage by protesting outside House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi’s office — with the Green New Deal as their top priority. Just seven years later, members of the Sunrise Movement voted to reorganize around the priority of fighting authoritarianism and, in particular, the second Trump administration. Shiney-Ajay acknowledged that the climate movement has suffered in recent years.

But that doesn’t mean that the public has become disengaged from the climate crisis. In fact, voters across the political spectrum are more attuned to it than ever. “People are actually really hungry for something to do about climate change,” said Shiney-Ajay. “I think we will actually see a lot of momentum around stopping the climate crisis. And I certainly hope to build a movement that makes that possible.”

text:
The 12th World Green Infrastructure Congress , organised by the University of Lleida, saw 10 LIFE projects from 9 Member States and Ukraine shared practical, scalable solutions for greener cities, many of which feature in the new Greening cities with the LIFE Programme publication .

From European policy discussions to scientific research and real-world projects, the congress created a space where different perspectives could meet and move the conversation forward on how to make green infrastructure and nature-based solutions a core part of urban planning.

Opening the Congress, CINEA Director Paloma Aba Garrote said LIFE projects ‘turn policy ambition into practical action in their cities’. She emphasised that green infrastructure is vital to tackling heatwaves, flooding, biodiversity loss, air pollution, and resource pressure. She highlighted that that green infrastructure must be planned, financed and implemented as an essential part of our cities, noting that investing in urban green infrastructure means investing in healthier, more resilient, and more liveable cities.

How Barcelona and Lleida are putting green infrastructure in action

Star of the show was BIG4LIFE, which uses Building Integrated Greenery (BIG) systems including green roofs, living façades, rooftop gardens and vertical greenery to transform urban spaces and cooling down temperatures in our cities by using water and energy-saving techniques applied in architecture, building design and landscaping such as xeriscaping. Through monitoring 8 site buildings, the project’s innovative energy and irrigation management system has demonstrated that can reduce water consumption by up to 80% a major benefit for Mediterranean cities facing increasing water stress. The monitoring and participatory maintenance model involving residents and building owners is being replicated in Genoa and Athens, with further roll-out planned in Warsaw. Ms Aba Garrote toured two pilot buildings sites such as the Pérez-Iborra School in Barcelona. Its green roof garden combines, biodiversity features, a vegetable garden, rainwater harvesting, solar panels and monitoring equipment. The roof also functions as an outdoor classroom where students learn about sustainability and urban nature, while smart sensors feed continuous environmental impact data back to the University of Lleida.

Ms Aba Garrote had a discussion with the students who proudly explained how important the garden is in their environmental education, and how they contribute to providing science data. The University of Lleida is collecting data through a smart monitoring system installed on the green roof. These sensors continuously gather information about how the green garden is performing in cooling down temperatures and how it affects positively the local environment.

Nature-based solutions along the river Ebro

The LIFE Programme also builds climate resilience beyond urban centres. In Zaragoza, Ms. Aba Garrote visited LIFE Ebro Resilience , which uses nature-based solutions to restore the Ebro river basin while helping local communities adapt to flood risks. The project will benefit over 22 000 local residents, with plans for similar measures across 307 km of riverbed spanning 3 Spanish regions and 56 municipalities, reaching up to 1 million citizens. As project coordinator David Gargantilla noted, long-term success requires conservation along with ‘clear communication and cooperation with citizens, regions and municipalities, and economic actors, such as farmers throughout the basin’.

In addition to the LIFE Programme stand, LIFE also hosted a workshop — Greening European cities with LIFE: inspiring urban transformation in Europe — with the core message that LIFE projects serve as practical, actionable models for future urban development.

title: How the midterm results could affect Wisconsin's energy infrastructure, policy
description:
Governor-elect David Crowley ran on a campaign of both affordability and regulating data centers.
Other Democrats including Trevor Jung, who won in Senate District 21, called to repeal tax breaks for data centers.
More broadly, he has called for data centers to use up to 100% renewable energy.
Crowley said in a Scientist Network for Advancing Policy (SNAP) Q&A that he supports expanding nuclear energy in Wisconsin to meet clean energy goals.
“And just because clean energy has gotten so much better and so much cheaper, we actually have an opportunity to have both of those now.”
text:
Wisconsin's peak energy demand is predicted to rise by more than 40% by 2032, driven largely by data centers, according to state utility regulators. In January, Democrats will control both houses of the Wisconsin legislature and the governor's office for the first time since 2010, with the potential to redirect Wisconsin’s energy policy.

Governor-elect David Crowley ran on a campaign of both affordability and regulating data centers. Other Democrats including Trevor Jung, who won in Senate District 21, called to repeal tax breaks for data centers.

“There's a lot of low-hanging fruit because Wisconsin's really behind the rest of the country and the rest of the world on climate and clean energy,” Gregory Nemet, professor of energy analysis and policy at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, told The Daily Cardinal. “So we're in a position where we really need to catch up if we want to deal with climate change problems and deal with energy problems and affordability.”

Natural gas and coal generated 72% of Wisconsin’s in-state electricity generation in 2024. Wisconsin has no economically recoverable fossil fuel reserves, and therefore all coal and natural gas must be imported, according to Nemet. He said Wisconsin is a prime candidate for diversifying its energy resources.

Under Crowley’s proposal, any data center that receives state or local tax benefits must get at least 70% of its energy from renewable sources. More broadly, he has called for data centers to use up to 100% renewable energy.

“If we're just talking about data centers, yeah, they could be just 100% clean, and don't have to be renewable,” Nemet said.

Clean energy includes nuclear, which produces no carbon emissions but is not renewable.

Nemet also listed wind, solar, geothermal, batteries and nuclear power as other viable energy options for data centers that could contribute to the 100% clean energy goal.

Crowley said in a Scientist Network for Advancing Policy (SNAP) Q&A that he supports expanding nuclear energy in Wisconsin to meet clean energy goals.

“Reliable, carbon-free baseload power is essential to a grid that works for families and businesses,” Crowley told SNAP.

Affordability topped voters' concerns heading into the election. In an October Marquette poll, 48% of respondents ranked the cost of living and inflation as the most important issue, while only 4% ranked data centers as the most important issue.

State regulators recently approved We Energies' request for a 3.9% electric rate increase in 2027 and an additional 3.5% increase in 2028.

Enjoy what you're reading? Get content from The Daily Cardinal delivered to your inbox

“The promise of nuclear power is fantastic, and I do expect it'll play a role in the state,” Nemet said. “The biggest issue with nuclear by far is just how expensive it is to build nuclear and to run nuclear.”

While other lawmakers plan to delay retiring coal plants to offset the cost of nuclear expansion, as Tom Tiffany argued in a Congressional Letter, Crowley plans to look toward other renewable energy sources, such as solar.

Coal consumption in Wisconsin has declined between 2015 and 2024, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. However, this decline has plateaued in more recent years. We Energies has delayed retiring two coal units at its Oak Creek Power Plant for the third time, from the end of this year to the end of 2027.

Despite the slow rollback of coal, solar use is expanding in Wisconsin. About 12% of Wisconsin's in-state electricity net generation is provided by renewable resources. Solar resources were the largest contributors and provided about 41% of the state's renewable electricity generation, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. The largest solar project in Wisconsin history was approved in 2024: a 9,500-acre project in Portage County, expected to start construction this year.

“We're still a bit stuck in this mindset that there's a real trade-off between our public health and our environment and our economic growth, and that if we care about economic growth and jobs, we need fossil fuels, and if we care about the environment, we need clean energy,” Nemet said. “And just because clean energy has gotten so much better and so much cheaper, we actually have an opportunity to have both of those now.”

text:
ANTALYA, Turkey (AP) — Urgent action is needed to help countries hardest-hit by the effects of climate change, small island leaders said Thursday at the United Nations climate talks in Turkey, describing global warming as a life-or-death issue for their people.

“It is time to move past the talking,” said Alix Sebastien Pillay, vice president of Seychelles, who said the survival of his country, a 115-island archipelago in the Indian Ocean, is at stake. “For Seychelles, climate action is not simply an environmental priority.”

Pillay spoke on the second day of the leaders' summit at the U.N. climate conference, where governments are trying to reach consensus on how to address climate change and help countries at greatest risk. While the entire globe is threatened by souped-up storms, hotter heat waves, worsening droughts and bigger floods, island nations are among the hardest hit by climate change as they also have to deal with rising seas swallowing their land.

Pillay said Seychelles is experiencing millions of dollars of damage despite contributing little to global warming, and said a U.N. fund created for compensating vulnerable nations must be urgently strengthened.

“Climate recovery must not come at the expense of our development or push vulnerable nations further into unsustainable debt,” he said.

Report says world has failed to slow warming trends

A report released Thursday offered a grim assessment: Progress in slowing global warming has essentially stalled for the past five years because any steps forward were canceled out by inaction elsewhere.

The first five years after the 2015 Paris Agreement, the world did so much that it trimmed an entire degree Celsius (1.8 degrees Fahrenheit) from warming projections, but nothing has changed since, the independent Climate Action Tracker said in its report.

That means the world is now “headed toward an irrecoverable overshoot of 1.5 degrees Celsius” (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial temperatures, the threshold the world adopted during the Paris Agreement, according to the report.

Climate change is caused mainly by the release of greenhouse gases from the burning of fuels like gas, oil and coal. Confronting it means finding ways to drastically cut the amount of emissions put into the atmosphere each year. Countries establish plans to reduce emissions, with the speed of reductions and ways to achieve them differing by country.

But even if nations fulfill all their climate promises — which is a big if — the globe will end the century 2.6 degrees Celsius (4.7 degrees Fahrenheit) warmer than pre-industrial times, the report said.

The effects of inaction are already being felt, said Dalton Tagelagi, prime minister of the small Pacific Island of Niue. Climate change, coupled with this year’s extra-strong El Niño — a temporary warming in parts of the equatorial Pacific that increase extreme events such as heat waves, floods and droughts — are a warning of what could be in store.

“Sea temperatures in the central Pacific are more than three degrees above normal. It is a warning of what is coming if we do not cut emissions now,” Tagelagi said.

Vulnerable nations ask climate polluters to pay up

Leaders from countries ravaged by climate change said adequate financing must be made available to deal with climate disasters, such as the 2022 floods in Pakistan that submerged over a third of the country, resulting in thousands of deaths and over $30 billion in damage.

“The future we feared has become the present we are living,” said Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif. “Climate change knows no borders. No nation can face it alone.”

But how much can be accomplished at the summit is in question, as some of the top-polluting countries stayed away.

The United States — the world’s second-largest polluter after China and the largest historical polluter — was again absent after President Donald Trump withdrew the U.S. from climate negotiations. Still, a group of U.S. state and local leaders arrived in Antalya to show their commitment to combating climate change.

Speaking at an event on the sidelines of the talks, California Gov. Gavin Newsom said Trump’s “head is soaked with oil.”

“He’s a wholly owned subsidiary of Big Oil. And we have been on the receiving end of some of the most aggressive assaults on our climate leadership in a generation,” he said. “I don’t expect that his secretary of energy or secretary of interior are going to do anything but double down (on their current policies).”

In a side event with chanting and applauding activists, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, president of Brazil, which hosted last year's negotiations, said, "Nobody, no one from planet Earth, no country, no authority has more authority than Brazil when it comes to the climate, when it comes to the environmental issue.”

Lula challenged Trump, French President Emmanuel Macron by name and the governments of Germany and Portugal — “countries that used to dictate the rules to us” — to invest more in a fund to save tropical forestland, like Brazil has.

Climate activist Greta Thunberg chided those in power for failing to address the climate crisis.

“The planet is not dying, it is being killed,” Thunberg said at a news conference on the sidelines of the summit. “And we know by who. And it is being killed by the very same people often thought to come to our rescue. No one is coming to our rescue.”

The last time Thunberg attended a climate summit was the 2021 gathering in Glasgow, Scotland, where she dismissed world leaders’ promises as “blah, blah, blah.”

Britain announces appointment of first climate security risk envoy

The United Kingdom on Thursday announced the appointment of a special envoy to tackle security threats from climate change, one of the first such appointments anywhere in the world.

The appointment of Madeleine Alessandri follows a recent British government assessment warning that damage to ecosystems, driven partly by climate change, could disrupt food supplies and fuel conflict and migration since the island nation imports about 40% of its food.

“The climate crisis is not a distant threat. It is upon us all now, devastating lives and livelihoods everywhere,” British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said at the summit, adding that Britain would place climate resilience high on the agenda when it assumes the G20 presidency next year.

Climate activists said Burnham’s policies do not fully align with the sense of urgency he expressed in his speech.

“Burnham needs to start bridging the widening chasm between words and deeds on climate action,” said Ami McCarthy of Greenpeace UK.

___

Webber reported from Chicago, Borenstein from Kensington, Maryland, and Arasu from Bengaluru, India.

description:
“Kazakhstan’s methane satellite program sends a meaningful signal that leadership starts with action supported by transparency,” said James Turitto, Oil and Gas Methane Director at Clean Air Task Force.
“Kazakhstan is demonstrating what becomes possible when governments turn satellite methane data into action.
Working with UNEP, the country has already mitigated 10 major methane emissions events identified through the Methane Alert and Response System, addressing more than 31,000 tonnes of methane emissions.
Combined with locally owned capabilities, this approach could set a precedent for other methane-emitting countries and help accelerate methane emissions reductions globally.” said Vasily Yablokov, Product Director, AIRMO.
“Our work with government and industry partners in Kazakhstan over several years has shown the value of combining methane satellite data with practical action on the ground.
text:
ANTALYA – At COP31, during the Global Methane Pledge Ministerial meeting, the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources of Kazakhstan announced plans to develop a national satellite-based program to support regulations of methane emissions from the country’s oil and gas sector.

The program builds on the Memorandum of Understanding signed in September 2025 by the Ministry of Ecology, the Global Methane Hub, Carbon Mapper, and Clean Air Task Force (CATF). It will be developed with support from the Fossil Fuel Regulatory Programme (FFRP), a partnership of the Climate and Clean Air Coalition (CCAC) and CATF, with additional technical support from the International Energy Agency (IEA), the UN Environment Program’s (UNEP) International Methane Emissions Observatory (IMEO), Carbon Mapper, GHGSat, AIRMO, and Carbon Limits. It also draws on Kazakhstan’s established space industry and its experience in Earth observation.

“This initiative is part of implementing Kazakhstan’s Carbon Neutrality Strategy to 2060. As we strengthen our approach to methane in the oil and gas sector, independent satellite data will help make it evidence-based and effective,” said Alibek Kuantyrov, Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources of the Republic of Kazakhstan. “Reducing methane brings practical benefits for the climate, the economy and our international partnerships, and it helps keep us in step with evolving global expectations. As the world gathers in Antalya, we are taking a first concrete step that will evolve over time, and we hope it will strengthen cooperation on methane across Central Asia. At the national level, Kazakhstan is also developing its own space-based methane monitoring capabilities, with the aim of creating a domestic satellite solution.”

The program will be run by the regulatory agency and enable the use of satellite and aerial data to identify large methane releases at oil and gas facilities and connect that information directly to operators so that detection leads to verified repairs. It will complement Kazakhstan’s requirements on leak detection and repair, flaring, and venting.

“Kazakhstan’s methane satellite program sends a meaningful signal that leadership starts with action supported by transparency,” said James Turitto, Oil and Gas Methane Director at Clean Air Task Force. “While many methane reductions can and should be implemented immediately, high-quality emissions data is crucial to achieving deeper and more sustained reductions over time. The last few years have proven that advanced technologies play a vital role in comprehensive methane regulation and emissions reductions. At a time when some governments are seeking to delay methane accountability, this program shows how other producing countries can take proactive steps to build credibility, strengthen accountability, and accelerate methane reductions.”

Quotes from International Partners

“Methane super-emitters from the oil and gas sector offer the biggest near-term opportunities to mitigate this potent greenhouse gas. We applaud Kazakhstan’s leadership to address these events and look forward to working with the government and other partners to leverage data to empower targeted action, grow local capacity, and establish a successful model for others to follow,” said Riley Duren, CEO of Carbon Mapper.

Kazakhstan is showing how national leadership, strong regulations and international partnerships can turn methane commitments into concrete action. This initiative is an important step towards delivering measurable emissions reductions and offers a model for other oil and gas producing countries,” said Martina Otto, Head of the Climate and Clean Air Coalition Secretariat

“By connecting satellite detections to regulators and operators, Kazakhstan is demonstrating a commitment to action on mitigating methane emissions, one of the fastest and most cost-effective ways to slow warming. Kazakhstan is building a system where finding a leak leads to fixing it. We have better technology than ever to find and fix methane leaks in the oil and gas sector, and this is a model other producing countries can follow,” said Chris Konek, Lead Scientist, Global Methane Hub.

“Kazakhstan is demonstrating what becomes possible when governments turn satellite methane data into action. Working with UNEP, the country has already mitigated 10 major methane emissions events identified through the Methane Alert and Response System, addressing more than 31,000 tonnes of methane emissions. Its efforts to systematically integrate satellite monitoring into national regulation represent an important step forward, showing how cutting-edge data can drive tangible methane reductions.” said Giulia Ferrini, Head of UNEP’s International Methane Emissions Observatory.

“Kazakhstan has built a strong space industry and is now applying this expertise to methane monitoring through its own satellite programme and national monitoring platform. AIRMO is proud to support these efforts through our partnerships with Ghalam and Kazakhstan Gharysh Sapary, contributing our satellite technology, sensors and data processing algorithms. As a technology provider, we see the inclusion of satellite monitoring in national regulations as an important step towards faster detection and mitigation of major methane emissions. Combined with locally owned capabilities, this approach could set a precedent for other methane-emitting countries and help accelerate methane emissions reductions globally.” said Vasily Yablokov, Product Director, AIRMO.

“The IEA welcomes Kazakhstan’s leadership and concrete action on methane and is pleased to support the development of its satellite monitoring and response program. Effective use of satellite data can help address large emissions events, driving emissions reductions while supporting Kazakhstan’s energy security and climate goals. We look forward to continuing our collaboration on developing a robust methane regulatory framework informed by international best practices,” said Christophe McGlade, Head of the Energy Supply Unit, International Energy Agency.

“Our work with government and industry partners in Kazakhstan over several years has shown the value of combining methane satellite data with practical action on the ground. A national satellite-based program can strengthen this link, helping turn the detection of major emissions events into timely mitigation,” said Anastasia Isaenko, Principal Consultant, Carbon Limits.

“We look forward to supporting Kazakhstan’s satellite monitoring program. Having spent more than a decade detecting methane from individual facilities, we’ve seen firsthand how much progress is possible when government and industry align on a clear vision for action,” said Stéphane Germain, CEO, GHGSat.

Press Contact

Natalie Volk, Senior Communications Manager, Clean Air Task Force, nvolk@catf.us, +1-703-785-9580

About Clean Air Task Force

Clean Air Task Force (CATF) is a global climate organization working to advance the full range of solutions needed for a healthy climate and a thriving planet. Founded in 1996, CATF conducts research and analysis to identify promising solutions, then works across governments, industry, and partners in more than 40 countries to deliver them at scale. It takes no funding from governments or the industries it works to influence, so its analysis and advocacy follows the facts. Over 30 years, its work has helped shape major climate and energy policy around the world. CATF is consistently recognized as one of the most effective climate organizations in the world by independent evaluators including Giving Green and Founders Pledge. Learn more at cleanairtaskforce.org.

description:
The competition focused on sourcing and processing battery materials, recycling valuable materials, strengthening UK manufacturing and reducing reliance on overseas supply chains.
It aims to reduce the energy needed for recycling and keep valuable battery materials in the UK to support domestic manufacturing.
Investment in skills The Battery Innovation Programme has also awarded £3.6 million to three regional skills initiatives.
These will accelerate the development of the UK’s battery manufacturing workforce and strengthen national capability across the battery value chain.
University Centre Somerset will deliver Level 2 and 3 battery manufacturing training for the South West battery cluster.
text:
Delivered by Innovate UK on behalf of the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade, the competition is designed to support UK businesses and researchers to develop new battery technologies.

The competition focused on sourcing and processing battery materials, recycling valuable materials, strengthening UK manufacturing and reducing reliance on overseas supply chains.

Recycling batteries

Lithium Battery Recyclers Ltd has been awarded more than £1.2 million to lead project Reclaim, to develop a new UK process for recycling end-of-life electric vehicle batteries.

The process, developed by the University of Leicester, uses a tiny quantity of vegetable oil in water to separate valuable battery materials, including graphite, without acid leaching or hazardous chemicals.

The project will scale up the technology at a pilot facility in Widnes, Cheshire, and test the recovered materials for reuse in new batteries.

It aims to reduce the energy needed for recycling and keep valuable battery materials in the UK to support domestic manufacturing.

Reducing waste

Hyperbat, now part of Unipart Manufacturing Group, has received more than £2.4 million to lead a project.

This aims to reduce the number of electric vehicles written off because their batteries are damaged or no longer working as expected.

At present, it can be difficult to assess whether these batteries are safe to repair or reuse.

This can lead to unnecessary vehicle write-offs, higher insurance costs and valuable materials being lost.

The project will develop a clear process for checking each battery and deciding whether it can be repaired, reused , given a second life for energy storage or safely recycled.

The work could keep batteries in use for longer, reduce waste and create skilled jobs in the UK.

Feasibility studies

The competition has also awarded just over £6.2 million to 15 shorter feasibility studies exploring new ideas across the battery supply chain.

Running for between six and 12 months, these projects will test whether early-stage technologies could improve how batteries are made, used, reused and recycled.

This will help the most promising ideas move towards further development and commercial use.

Superdielectrics Group and Sytronix have been awarded almost £500,000 to test a new type of battery that could help data centres manage the rapid changes in electricity demand.

The water-based battery is designed to store and release power quickly, helping data centres run more AI servers without placing additional strain on local electricity networks.

The project will build on an existing battery pack and test how it responds to the changing power needs of AI systems.

If successful, the technology could help data centres make better use of their existing grid connections and expand without requiring immediate upgrades to local power supplies.

It could also provide a safer alternative to conventional lithium-ion batteries and reduce reliance on imported battery materials.

Investment in skills

The Battery Innovation Programme has also awarded £3.6 million to three regional skills initiatives.

These will accelerate the development of the UK’s battery manufacturing workforce and strengthen national capability across the battery value chain.

The investment will support the delivery of industry-focused nationally accredited training programmes across England.

These will equip learners with the skills needed to secure careers in one of the UK’s fastest-growing advanced manufacturing sectors, and help businesses access talent to meet increasing demand.

University Centre Somerset will deliver Level 2 and 3 battery manufacturing training for the South West battery cluster.

University College Birmingham, and Newcastle University with New College Durham in the North East, will expand their training to Levels 4 and 5.

Dr Valentina Gentili, Director of the Battery Innovation Programme, said:

As global demand for batteries continues to grow, it is increasingly important that the UK focuses on the areas where it can deliver the greatest impact and strategic value. The projects supported through this competition demonstrate the breadth of innovation taking place across the UK battery sector.

By investing in new technologies, strengthening supply chains and supporting business growth, we are helping to build the capabilities, expertise and partnerships that will further strengthen UK sovereign capability and position the UK as a leader in battery innovation.

Minister for Reindustrialisation Blair McDougall, said:

This funding will give Britain’s battery manufacturing industry the support they need to power the industries of the future and keep our country at the cutting edge of innovation.

Through our Modern Industrial Strategy we’re doubling down on Britain’s high-growth sectors like advanced manufacturing, and I want to congratulate all the winners on their success and their role in reinforcing Britain’s leadership in this fast-growing industry.

name: Clean Energy
title: Europe must stay the course on clean energy
description:
Europe can ill afford the twin costs of climate change and fossil-fuel dependence.
By mid-October, the war in the Middle East had added €106 billion to the energy import bill.
Consistency needed A more resilient and affordable energy system is within reach, but Europe needs to hold its nerve and follow through on the transformation it has begun.
Maintaining a credible Emissions Trading System would encourage greener production, and its revenues could help finance industrial modernization and clean power generation.
Outside the EU, many countries share its goals of limiting climate damage and securing clean energy and want to cooperate.
text:
Europe can ill afford the twin costs of climate change and fossil-fuel dependence. Last summer's heat is estimated to have caused more than 50,000 excess deaths.

The economic losses could reach around €180 billion, roughly 1% of the European Union's gross domestic product, comparable to its entire annual budget. By mid-October, the war in the Middle East had added €106 billion to the energy import bill.

With households struggling to make ends meet and bitter arguments over public spending and debt, these losses drain money the continent desperately needs.

Politicians who exploit anger over living costs still have to show they can bring them down, and ignoring climate damage and fossil-fuel dependence means ignoring two of the forces driving those costs up.

Clean electrification offers a way out: running transport, heating and industrial processes on homegrown, low-carbon power.

On the right path

The EU has already made substantial progress in electricity generation. Clean sources supplied 71% of it in 2025, with wind and solar together producing more than fossil fuels for the first time.

Gains remain uneven, as the contrast between Spain and Italy shows.

Spain's investment in renewables has reduced how often gas-fired plants set the wholesale electricity price. Since March's gas-price shock, this has helped keep prices far lower than in Italy, where gas still sets them much more frequently.

Italy's main business lobby, Confindustria, has called for faster deployment of renewables, warning that manufacturers could leave for countries with cheaper electricity. In turn, affordable power makes switching away from oil and gas more attractive.

Consistency needed

A more resilient and affordable energy system is within reach, but Europe needs to hold its nerve and follow through on the transformation it has begun.

China's strength in clean technology holds a lesson: the value of clear objectives backed by a comprehensive, stable policy framework.

Beijing has pursued this approach for more than 15 years, giving companies the backing to develop expertise and build extensive supplier networks. Matching those capabilities will also take time, and investors need confidence that European demand for these technologies will keep growing.

In 2027, MEPs face decisions, from the carbon market to the next seven-year budget, that will determine whether businesses can count on Brussels when making long-term investments.

Maintaining a credible Emissions Trading System would encourage greener production, and its revenues could help finance industrial modernization and clean power generation.

Connecting Spanish solar and North Sea wind would help meet demand as weather conditions change. This requires coordinated investment in grids, storage and interconnectors.

The European Parliament can make the EU budget work for energy independence by defending the proposed 35% climate and environmental spending target and ensuring the European Competitiveness Fund has the resources to help low-carbon industries expand. Regions also need funding to build infrastructure that brings jobs.

Outside the EU, many countries share its goals of limiting climate damage and securing clean energy and want to cooperate.

They want to cooperate on green manufacturing and diversifying supply chains. Working together on carbon pricing and the treatment of emissions in traded goods could reward cleaner production without simply shifting industry abroad.

Reports of the demise of the "Brussels effect" are exaggerated, at least on climate. Other governments still look to Europe's commitment when deciding how far and how fast to move.

Policymakers should not underestimate that influence, which makes the pressure from oil and gas companies to weaken Europe's methane rules all the more consequential.

Following through on the transition at home can help persuade others to act alongside the EU.

text:
real motors brings project: ARES closer to production

South Carolina-based Real Motors has brought its futuristic electric café racer, Project: ARES, onto the road, with new working prototypes and a limited production run planned for 2027. First introduced in 2024, the motorcycle attracted attention for its sculptural bodywork and sci-fi influences. Two years later, the company has opened preorders for its first 250 units, while a recent independent test ride offers a closer look at how the machine actually performs.

The latest prototypes retain the distinctive proportions of the original design, with broad body panels wrapping around the electric drivetrain and a sharply tapered seat extending over the rear wheel. In bright red, the 03 prototype takes on the appearance of a futuristic racing machine, complete with oversized white graphics and a rectangular headlight. Its front forks are concealed beneath prominent aerodynamic covers, giving the motorcycle a particularly solid presence from the front.

translucent bodywork reveals the machine beneath

Another prototype by Real Motors, numbered 04 and nicknamed ‘Ghost,’ explores the same design in black. Its dark, translucent bodywork allows glimpses of the mechanical components beneath the surface, including the electrical wiring running through the motorcycle. Without the familiar arrangement of a combustion engine and fuel tank, the design team has been able to reconsider the proportions of a traditional café racer, creating a continuous surface across much of the bike’s body.

Beneath this exterior, the electric powertrain has already demonstrated approximately 100 horsepower, with Real Motors reporting 1,000 Nm of torque at the rear wheel after gearing. The prototype carries an estimated weight of 485 pounds, giving it considerably more mass than its streamlined appearance might suggest. The low handlebars place the rider in the familiar forward-leaning café racer position, with the broad central body occupying much of the space between the knees.

an electric motorcycle with an analog feel

The riding experience is central to the project for Real Motors. The company describes its approach as ‘Electric Analogue,’ an attempt to preserve the physical connection between rider and machine even as the traditional engine gives way to an electric drivetrain. The controls remain familiar, while a small digital display provides essential riding information. The emphasis is on the sensation of operating the motorcycle and the immediate response of its electric motor.

During a recent test ride published by The Verge, journalist Tim Stevens found the Ghost prototype’s acceleration surprisingly smooth, with power delivered progressively across three riding modes. Its handling told a slightly different story. The motorcycle required more deliberate steering through corners than its racing-inspired silhouette might suggest, with the substantial battery weight contributing to its character on the road. The experience offers an early look at how Real Motors’ unconventional design translates into an actual riding machine.

the first 250 motorcycles are planned for 2027

Real Motors is now preparing Lot 01, a limited production run of 250 motorcycles worldwide. The currently listed production configuration uses a 65-kW electric motor paired with a 13.4-kWh battery, with an estimated top speed of 110 mph. These specifications differ from those of the higher-powered prototypes and Founder’s Edition. Prices for Lot 01 begin at $20,000, with North American deliveries currently anticipated in early 2027.

The company is also offering a selection of exterior liveries, allowing customers to choose how the sculptural bodywork will be finished. Its earlier Founder’s Edition is already sold out, while final specifications for Lot 01 are expected to be disclosed before manufacturing begins. The production timeline has shifted since the motorcycle’s initial announcement, but with working prototypes now on the street, Project: ARES is steadily approaching its first customer deliveries.

title: Hyundai's $1 billion Australian battery plant 'fell through' after government bungled talks

Hyundai Australia hasn't made any public comment on the proposed meeting and wouldn't comment on the matter when contacted by CarExpert.

text:
Hyundai Motor Group’s plans for a reported $1 billion electric vehicle battery factory in Australia allegedly fell through in 2024 after a ‘bungled’ meeting thwarted the project, according to text messages from a former trade commissioner for the NSW Government.

Appointed by Investment NSW, Mike Newman was senior trade and investment commissioner for North Asia, based in Japan and also covering South Korea, from 2021 to 2024.

In a news report on the former commissioner, Channel 7 said Mr Newman sent text messages in January 2024 regarding Hyundai’s plans to manufacture batteries in Australia.

The messages came as the then trade commissioner pushed for NSW Premier Chris Minns to meet with Hyundai regarding the project.

It’s believed Euisun Chung, the global head of Hyundai Motor Group, a massive manufacturing conglomerate which includes the Hyundai, Kia and Genesis auto brands as well as robotics and other technology businesses, was in Australia in early 2024 for a potential meeting.

Australia was seen as a prime location for battery manufacturing, given its critical mineral resources, and the Hyundai boss is believed to have sought a meeting either with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese or the premier of the nation's most populous state for initial talks.

“Hyundai execs got back to me and seem keen to invest north of $1bn [billion] in NSW including building a car plant. So seniority is a must. They invested $7bn in the US on a battery plant late last year… this is a massive opportunity,” Mr Newman is reported to have said in a text to the NSW Premier's chief of staff on January 17, 2024.

According to the Channel 7 report, Mr Newman’s messages revealed the NSW meeting “fell through” and was subsequently “bungled”, with the proposal moving to Victoria and Hyundai “ultimately" not investing.

Hyundai Australia hasn't made any public comment on the proposed meeting and wouldn't comment on the matter when contacted by CarExpert.

Mr Newman left the role in 2024 and is now the NSW leader of political party One Nation. His office was contacted by CarExpert for comment.

The prime minister’s office has also been contacted by CarExpert regarding the matter.

In April 2022, then opposition leader Mr Albanese visited Brisbane-based EV equipment maker Tritium in the leadup to the following month's federal election, which he won.

“The delay, prevarication and inaction from this government has meant that we’re missing out on opportunities,” he told media during the Tritium visit.

“There’s such a thing as first-mover advantage. Now, we’ve lost that. But what we need to do is embrace the action that is there from action on climate change, which will actually be good for our economy and good for jobs.”

The plans for a meeting between Hyundai and the government were mentioned in a NSW Parliament budget estimates hearing on September 2024.

This saw Anoulack Chanthivong, who remains the NSW Minister for Industry and Trade, questioned by Deputy Leader of the Opposition in the Legislative Council Sarah Mitchell on the project.

“Hyundai… Their global chair, CEO and COO, I’m told, requested to meet with both you and the premier in January this year to discuss a billion-dollar battery manufacturing opportunity,” Ms Mitchell said, according to the transcript.

The transcript recorded Mr Chanthivong telling Ms Mitchell he couldn't recall every meeting request, suggesting he may have been on personal leave in January 2024.

“I'm not begrudging you personal leave, but my issue is that you had a billion-dollar opportunity with a major global company for this state, who then went and met with Victoria because they couldn't get a meeting with you.

“That is not, I think, what the taxpayers of New South Wales would be expecting from you as trade minister, with respect,” Ms Mitchell said.

A 2022 report prepared for the Future Battery Industries Cooperative Research Centre estimated that diversified battery industries could contribute around $7.4 billion annually to Australia’s economy and support more than 34,000 jobs by 2030.

“The NSW Government did not receive any formal proposal from Hyundai to establish a vehicle manufacturing plant in NSW,” Mr Chanthivong’s office told CarExpert.

“Governments regularly engage with a wide range of companies regarding potential investment opportunities, but we do not comment on hypothetical scenarios about potential future investment decisions by individual companies.

“The NSW Government remains focused on attracting investment, supporting advanced manufacturing and creating jobs across the state.”

Hyundai established a battery plant in West Java, Indonesia, in July 2024, when President Joko Widodo attended the ceremonial opening of the country’s first EV battery factory.

In August 2026, the NSW Critical Minerals Processing and Advanced Materials Innovation Program was announced, with a goal to establish “a pipeline of locally developed technologies ready for up-scaling, investment and market adoption”.

“From clean energy to advanced manufacturing, critical minerals will underpin the technologies that power the future,” Mr Chanthivong said in a press release at the time.

Australian company Clutch Industries recently secured funding to build a scalable battery manufacturing line in Coburg North, Victoria.

The near-$20 million project includes $6.77 million in funding from the Australian Renewable Energy Agency (ARENA).

text:
Reports related to this article:

Written by Daniel Graeber for IIR News Intelligence (Sugar Land, Texas)

Summary

Democrats said they want to do more with renewable energy when they take power over the U.S. Congress in January. The wind energy market is on pace for a 5% expansion and already ranks second in the world, behind China. Europe, meanwhile, will serve as a benchmark for wind futures.

Democrats to Prioritize Clean Energy

A change in power in the halls of the U.S. Congress may see a stronger push for renewables, with wind energy in the U.S. market already on pace to increase by nearly 5% from 2026 levels.

The federal U.S. government expects total wind energy to account for 498.1 billion kilowatt-hours this year, expanding some 5% by next year even as U.S. President Donald Trump continues to throw his support behind fossil fuels.

Industrial Info is tracking dozens of grassroots projects in the U.S. market. Xcel Energy and the Public Service Company of Colorado are planning to launch the Singing Grass Wind Farm by 2027. If built as planned, the plant would provide more than 600 megawatts (MW) of power to the state grid by August.

In Texas, which has the largest wind-energy footprint in the nation, Canadian energy company Enbridge is planning to provide 152 MW of power from its Easter Wind Farm by March. Texas leads the way in U.S. wind energy, with about a quarter of the nation's total.

Democrats may try to do more in January when they take control of both chambers of Congress. However, President Trump still holds veto power over Congress and he is considered highly unlikely to sign legislation supporting wind energy.

"We will advance policies that lower costs, expand access to quality and affordable health care, protect consumers and the environment, prioritize clean energy, and rein in Big Tech," said Rep. Frank Pallone, Jr., the current ranking member of the House Energy and Commerce Committee.

Democrats could prioritize clean energy programs by working to reinstate clean-energy tax credits that were phased out by the Republican led or dust-off other incentives. Still, the United States ranks second in the world, behind China, in terms of wind energy. Germany ranks third.

Europe Gets Its Own Lift

Germany got a lift on Monday when GE Vernova said it would deliver three onshore wind turbines that could account for 5.5 MW each to German energy company Stadtwerke Heidenheim AG for its Schlotberg-Jüchsen wind farm.

"Our continued investment in Salzbergen reinforces our dedication to a robust, local supply chain, aiming to help ensure that Germany's energy goals are supported by reliable, industrialized 'Made in Germany' technology," said Marcas Breatnach, the regional sales leader for GE Vernova.

Elsewhere, the company expects to spend $9 billion to acquire German energy Trench Group GmbH from private equity firm Triton Partners. GE Vernova's wind-energy business contributed $72 million to companywide earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA), marking a return to profitability during the third quarter.

The company cited improved services margins for onshore wind-energy projects and lower costs associated with offshore projects.

Also in the European market, pricing agency Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) announced plans to launch wind energy futures based on output from Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Spain and the United Kingdom. Those countries account for more than 70% of the installed wind energy capacity in Europe.

"Wind volume is now a significant part of the power sector, and customers want a way to manage it alongside what they already trade with us," said Gordon Bennett, the managing director for utility markets at ICE.

Wind volume is in pace to increase. The International Energy Agency said in a report published last week that onshore wind is on pace to increase 1.7-fold by 2031. Permitting reforms are expected to incentivize the wind energy sector in Europe, but growth looks sluggish elsewhere.

"Growth is declining in the United States due to the phaseout of tax incentives, while rising curtailment in markets such as Brazil and Chile is adversely affecting project economics and

slowing expansion in Latin America," the report read.

The Trump administration has thwarted offshore wind energy development, forking over billions of dollars in some cases to convince companies to forfeit their leases.

Key Takeaways

Despite political rhetoric, U.S. wind energy is expanding

The IEA expects those trends to develop globally.

By the Numbers

5% increase in power from U.S. wind sources by 2027

Microsoft Corp. aims to find ways to power its data centers without relying on government subsidies or driving up costs for other electricity consumers.

“We don’t want other customers to be paying for our growth,” Noelle Walsh, Microsoft’s president of cloud operations and innovation, said at a BloombergNEF conference in Houston. “We will pay our own way.”

The tech giant plans to build $117 billion of computing capacity this year for artificial intelligence and cloud services as data centers emerge as a key concern across the US, including in this month’s midterm elections that gave Democrats control of Congress.

Microsoft, the longtime backer of ChatGPT maker OpenAI, maintains that its “community first” approach to data centers means voters should benefit from their construction rather than suffer from negative effects.

Microsoft is working with Chevron Corp. and Joulent LLC — a company founded by investment firm Engine No. 1 — on a giant behind-the-meter data and power project in West Texas that has been held up by Texas Governor Greg Abbott’s moratorium on new data-center approvals. Abbott was defeated by Democrat Gina Hinojosa in the recent election, with his opponent pledging to take a potentially tougher stance on permitting.

Even so, Chevron is still aiming to get the development, named Project Kilby, up and running by 2028 and fully operational by 2031.

Any project that doesn’t provide a net benefit to its communities is “doomed to fail,” said Jeff Gustavson, Chevron’s president of new energies. Kilby will provide jobs and stable tax revenues to West Texas, he said.
