text:
Global electric vehicle (EV) sales rose 8% year-on-year to 2.09 million units in October, driven by surging European demand and North America’s first annual increase of the year, according to Benchmark Mineral Intelligence on Thursday.

However, worldwide sales dipped 3% month-on-month from September’s record high.

Cumulative deliveries for the first 10 months of this year reached 17.5 million units, marking a 5% increase compared with the same period last year.

In Europe, EV deliveries jumped 36% from a year ago to 510,000 units, led by a 49% surge in battery electric vehicles.

Germany recorded its highest EV penetration rate since December 2022, as electric models accounted for over 45% of the new car market, while UK sales grew 30% annually.

North American EV sales rose 24% annually to 130,000 units, marking the region’s first annual growth this year, largely due to a lower comparison base following the expiration of US federal tax credits in late 2025.

Meanwhile, China’s domestic EV market contracted 12% year-on-year to 1.14 million units amid subdued local demand.

Despite domestic headwinds, Chinese automakers pushed passenger new energy vehicle exports to a monthly record of nearly 600,000 units in October.

Sales across the rest of the world surged 85% year-on-year to 300,000 units, fueled by sharp expansion in markets such as Australia and Brazil.

text:
Chief Executive Chatrapon Sripratum outlines growth targets, operational expansion, and domestic manufacturing advantages during Ban Pho facility tour.

Energy Absolute Public Company Limited (EA) is sharpening its strategic focus on commercial electric vehicles (EVs), positioning its manufacturing arm, Absolute Assembly Company Limited (AAB), to capture expanding domestic market opportunities and projected 2027 growth.

Speaking during a media briefing and facility tour at AAB’s assembly plant in Ban Pho, Chachoengsao Province, on Wednesday (November 11), Chief Executive Officer and Executive Committee Chairman Chatrapon Sripratum outlined the group’s forward-looking operational readiness, commercial vehicle strategy, and structural cost advantages under evolving tax frameworks.

The strategy centres on leveraging EA's integrated ecosystem—which spans vehicle assembly at AAB, battery manufacturing, charging infrastructure via EA Anywhere, and carbon credit management—to capture growing demand across commercial transport segments.

"Our strategy is built on offering a complete, integrated solution rather than operating merely as a vehicle reseller," Chatrapon said. "By combining domestic assembly, local charging network installation, competitive electricity rates, and carbon credit structured solutions, we significantly reduce total cost of ownership for commercial fleet operators."

Production Readiness and Fleet Delivery Timeline

The Ban Pho assembly plant, operating in a designated Free Zone, has achieved commercial readiness across its key production stages: frame welding, Electro Disposition Painting (EDP) anti-corrosion dipping, vehicle assembly, and dynamic track testing.

The plant currently holds an annual assembly capacity of approximately 3,000 units under standard operating shifts, with potential expansion up to 9,000 units under maximum output.

A central focus of AAB’s current production schedule is the supply of 1,520 air-conditioned electric buses for the Bangkok Mass Transit Authority (BMTA) project, conducted in partnership with Nakhonchai Air and Nex Point Public Company Limited (NEX).

More than 200 units have already completed assembly, with daily output running at 7 to 10 vehicles. Vehicle deliveries to the BMTA are scheduled to begin towards the end of the first quarter of 2027 and run through the second quarter, aligning with the expected timeline for financial revenue recognition.

Revenue contribution from the BMTA contract alone is projected to reach approximately 6.0 to 7.0 billion baht.

"People rely on buses every day to get to work, go to school, and return home," Chatrapon stated. "Our responsibility begins while each bus is still in the factory. The expertise gained by our local workforce, from structural welding through to system testing, establishes a permanent domestic capability for public transport manufacturing."

Regulatory Tailwinds and Domestic Value

EA's commercial strategy is positioned to capitalise on impending regulatory and fiscal policy adjustments in Thailand. With excise taxes on imported commercial vehicles expected to rise from 10 per cent to 35 per cent, locally assembled vehicles meeting statutory local content thresholds stand to gain a competitive pricing margin over direct imports.

AAB’s production lines achieve a local content ratio of 40 per cent in labour and domestic components, exempting its output from import duties within the Free Zone environment.

"Import tariffs on completed commercial vehicles from foreign markets can range between 20 and 40 per cent," Chatrapon noted. "Operating a full-scale assembly line within a Free Zone that satisfies domestic content requirements creates a distinct structural cost advantage. As fiscal policies increasingly favor domestic manufacturing, our setup ensures long-term pricing competitiveness."

Beyond the BMTA fleet, EA is targeting three core commercial segments:

● Intercity Coaches and Transit Buses: Supported by annual nationwide registration replacement demand of approximately 2,500 units.

● Logistics Prime Movers (Head Trucks): A market with annual registration demand of 3,000 to 4,000 units, where electric models have achieved initial purchase price parity with Euro 5 diesel equivalents.

● Commercial Trucks and Vans: Covering light, medium, and heavy-duty trucks (15,000 to 17,000 units annually), as well as commercial passenger and cargo vans.

Carbon Offset Integration and Market Expansion

A key differentiator within EA’s business model is its active carbon credit management framework.

Under an ongoing bilateral agreement aligned with Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, EA has transferred ITMOs (Internationally Transferred Mitigation Outcomes) carbon credits generated from electric bus operations in Bangkok to Switzerland, with an export quota of up to 500,000 tonnes through 2030.

The group is currently expanding this carbon offset mechanism to cover its commercial logistics and prime mover fleets.

Looking ahead, EA is evaluating additional public sector tenders, including an anticipated 800-bus BMTA fleet procurement expected early next year, alongside potential export opportunities for right-hand-drive electric buses within Southeast Asian markets.

"We have demonstrated our capability across more than 2,000 electric buses currently operating in municipal transport," Chatrapon said. "With our ecosystem established, our primary goal is to drive operational execution, fulfil order backlogs, and maintain disciplined growth across the commercial EV sector."

text:
BECANCOUR, QUE.- Much of the heavy machinery at the Nemaska Lithium plant site in Quebec, is at a standstill after majority owner Rio Tinto issued dozens of layoff notices. Workers were not the only thing affected, construction on an EV battery chain that was nearly 80 per cent complete is now forced to pause.

This marks the latest sign for the town of Bécancour, located in a region known as “Battery Valley,” that plans for the area to become a hub of an EV manufacturing boom may not come to fruition.

“Decisions on further investment and project timing at Bécancour will depend on the outcome of the evaluation, project economics, market conditions, and customer needs,” Rio Tinto said in a statement.

The global metal and mining giant said it remains confident in the long-term outlook for lithium processing in Quebec and Canada, despite a decline in lithium prices as global demand for battery materials and electric vehicles has slowed.

The fallout could hit the town of Bécancour, which is nestled along the shores of the St. Lawrence River halfway between Montreal and Quebec City.

The Nemaska plant is vital in Quebec’s plan to set up an EV battery manufacturing chain in the province. In the same plan, the province promised to develop Bécancour into a hub.

Slow EV sales halt economic boost

As EV batteries and plants started to set up shop in the town’s industrial park in 202, Bécancour estimated it would see a boost of 1,500 direct and 5,000 indirect jobs, including in the restaurant industry and service sector.

The population grew slightly with the arrival of workers at construction sites. To accommodate them the city planned to expand schools, build housing and even purchase new ladder trucks for the local fire station.

However, when sales of EVs slowed, some projects were paused, while others were completely scrapped. In March, Nemaska announced it would scale down the pace of building its processing plant.

Though Quebec owns 46.1 per cent of Nemaska, the province’s new government said this week it would not spend a penny more on the project for the time being.

“Our sincere hope is that this is going to work, because I don’t want to be the guy to write off the $1.1 billion we invested,” said Quebec Minister of Economic Development, Innovation and Energy Stéphane Paquet.

But many in the Bécancour area say the setbacks are simply bumps in the road that leads to electrification.

“The battery file is here to stay,” said the prefect of the region Mario Lyonnais. “I am confident that the Nemaska plant will open. When it does, we will be ready and we will continue to prepare.”

Lyonnais says the battery boom was happening very quickly and that it was hard for the municipalities in the region to keep up with the pace of scaling up services.

He says the slowdown may allow the area more time to be fully ready for the grand opening of Nemaska and for a time when EV battery manufacturing delivers the region a boost.

Divert Inc., West Concord, Massachusetts, has announced the opening of its new Integrated Diversion & Energy Facility in Lexington, North Carolina, in the central part of that state.

The firm says the new facility converts unsold food that can no longer be donated into renewable natural gas (RNG) to and fertilizer to support the regional agriculture sector. “The facility also recovers food-bound water to run its own operations and captures data to help customers prevent future waste,” states Divert.

The Lexington facility is expected to serve more than 2,500 retail grocery locations and 20 retail distribution centers in the region by the end of this year.

Additionally, the company says it will responsibly process unsold food, food byproducts and residuals from food manufacturers and other businesses in the southeastern United States.

“The success of Divert’s circularity platform is driven by our employees and rooted in our customer base,” says Ryan Begin, CEO and co-founder of Divert. “The strong customer relationships we have built over the past 20 years are what allow us to invest in regional infrastructure, including our new facility here in Lexington.”

Grocery chain Harris Teeter is among the anchor customers served by Divert’s Lexington Integrated Diversion & Energy Facility, along with fellow retailer Publix and wholesaler UNFI.

“When food can no longer be donated, our partnership with Divert helps us find a productive use for it, reducing waste and protecting the value of food across the communities we serve,” says Danna Robinson, director of corporate affairs and customer relations at Harris Teeter.

At full capacity, the Lexington facility will be capable of processing up to 120,000 tons of unsold, non-donatable food annually from food retailers, distribution centers, warehouses, and manufacturing locations annually, according to Divert.

RNG that can be injected directly into local pipeline infrastructure already is being produced at the Divert facility from unsold food in the area, adds the firm.

“This facility will reduce food waste and create RNG, helping our state power its future,” says North Carolina Governor Josh Stein. “North Carolina is a leader in innovation and the clean energy economy, and I am pleased to welcome Divert Inc. to be part of our thriving business and energy ecosystem.”

“North Carolina represents the fourth largest food and beverage industry in the United States and ranks eighth nationally in agricultural production,” says Begin. “This makes Lexington an ideal location for advancing circularity in our food system, and this facility will allow us to serve more businesses, keep more food out of landfills and recover valuable resources that can be put back to productive use.”

text:
Solar will make up more than 80% of the new renewable capacity sub-Saharan Africa installs to 2031 under the IEA’s Renewables 2026 forecast, which puts distributed systems at 42GW and expects South Africa and Nigeria to account for almost half of the region’s additions.

Rooftop and off-grid solar bought by households and businesses is behind the upgrade to the International Energy Agency’s sub-Saharan Africa renewables forecast, which Renewables 2026, published on 6 November, raises by 54% on the agency’s previous assessment. The IEA lifted its solar PV outlook for the region by nearly 36GW even as it cut its expectations for utility-scale solar by nearly 7GW, and it now expects distributed systems to add 42GW between 2026 and 2031, with solar making up more than 80% of all new renewable capacity installed over that period.

On the agency’s numbers, solar’s share of electricity generation in sub-Saharan Africa climbs from about 3% today to 11% by 2031, with wind reaching 7%. Hydropower still supplies nearly a third of the region’s electricity at the end of the forecast, and South Africa and Nigeria are expected to account for almost half of the new renewable capacity added across the region in those six years.

The IEA attributes the turn towards distributed systems to unreliable grid power and persistent electricity shortages, which are pushing households and businesses to generate their own supply, and it points to limited access to finance and insufficient grid infrastructure as the constraints holding back larger utility-scale projects.

Africa added a record 11.3GW of renewable capacity in 2025, according to IRENA, lifting the continent’s installed renewable base by 15.9% to 82,397MW. Across the world, the IEA expects almost 4,800GW of renewable capacity to be added between 2026 and 2031, about 60% more than in the previous six-year period, and for the first time it sees Africa and Asia leading growth outside China. Additions across sub-Saharan Africa, the Middle East, North Africa and South-east Asia are forecast to almost triple compared with the six years before.

Fatih Birol, the IEA’s Executive Director, said “today, it’s mainly energy security that is driving renewables’ expansion”, adding that “the new chapter of the renewables growth story is a truly global one.”

text:
New Delhi: The Indian government has enforced a ban on export of lithium-ion battery recycled materials, in order to ensure that critical minerals found in battery waste remain accessible for domestic processing.

The Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT) has issued a notification amending the export policy for lithium-ion battery black mass from “free” to “prohibited’ with immediate effect. The notification is dated November 10.

“The export prohibition is intended to ensure that Black Mass generated in India is recycled and refined within the country,” the Ministry of Commerce and Industry said in a statement.

The measure is expected to assure feedstock availability for domestic recycling and refining units, improve their capacity utilisation and encourage further investment and employment in the sector, it said.

Black mass is the dark powder left after used lithium-ion batteries or battery manufacturing scrap are shredded and larger pieces of metal and plastic are removed. Depending on the battery chemistry, refiners can recover lithium, nickel, cobalt and graphite from the powder.

The ministry claimed that the move will “increase domestic recovery of lithium, cobalt, nickel and other critical minerals, thereby reducing import dependence and the associated foreign exchange outgo.”

“It will also strengthen supply chains for battery manufacturing, electric vehicles, energy storage and clean-energy technologies,” it said.

India has more capacity to process black mass than it generates, leaving refiners short of raw material. Recovering more of these materials at home could reduce battery makers’ reliance on imports, said Ajay Srivastava, founder, Global Trade Research Institute (GTRI).

Critical minerals are essential inputs for electric mobility, advanced chemistry cell batteries, energy storage, electronics and renewable energy. India depends substantially on imports for several of these minerals.

As per the DGFT notification, the ban covers all items under ITC (HS) code 85491400. Materials under this export code include waste and scrap of primary cells, primary batteries and electric accumulators, as well as spent cells, batteries and accumulators, which are unsorted and do not contain lead, cadmium or mercury.

title: Planning, permits and interconnection carry $266 billion of Brattle's $614 billion DER estimate
description:
The report was prepared for The Pew Charitable Trusts and is titled The National Case for a More Distributed Power Grid.
On April 28, Pew released a DER policy playbook, Distributed Energy Can Unleash the Resilient, Affordable Grid of the Future, with six recommendations.
Brattle's analysis finds that addressing three of them could deliver $266 billion in avoided power system costs through 2050.
By Brattle's own numbers, three process reforms carry $266 billion of the $614 billion, a bit more than two-fifths, so a large share of the value sits in utility planning rooms and local permit offices.
Distributed capacity, on this evidence, is one line in a large buyer's portfolio rather than a replacement for utility-scale supply.
text:
US DER capacity could more than quadruple if key policy barriers to deployment are removed, according to a Brattle Group report cited by T&D World. That would add more than 400 GW by 2050, roughly a third of the country's current generation fleet, and the report estimates the shift could avoid $614 billion in US power system costs through 2050. The report was prepared for The Pew Charitable Trusts and is titled The National Case for a More Distributed Power Grid. It counts distributed solar, battery storage, managed EV charging and flexible heating and cooling across residential, commercial and industrial customers.

The big number gets the headlines. The smaller one is more useful. On April 28, Pew released a DER policy playbook, Distributed Energy Can Unleash the Resilient, Affordable Grid of the Future, with six recommendations. Brattle's analysis finds that addressing three of them could deliver $266 billion in avoided power system costs through 2050. The three are incorporating distributed resources into distribution system planning, reducing permitting costs and reforming interconnection processes. That suggests a large share of the savings could come from process changes rather than new technology.

By Brattle's own numbers, three process reforms carry $266 billion of the $614 billion, a bit more than two-fifths, so a large share of the value sits in utility planning rooms and local permit offices. For a distribution planner deciding whether a customer battery fleet belongs in the next load forecast, that matters more than any national headline figure. It matters too for the energy lead at a company with a big new load waiting in the interconnection queue.

What the model counts, and what it displaces

Brattle's report page says the study combines long-term power system modeling with an assessment of where local distribution upgrades could be deferred. It covers 25 US regions and looks at both the bulk power system and the distribution system. That second piece carries a lot of the case. Customer-sited storage and flexible load compete most directly with feeder and substation spending, so a model that only looked at the bulk system would likely understate their value.

Ryan Hledik, a Brattle principal and report coauthor, said many homes and businesses already own technologies able to help the grid handle rising demand, and that uptake of those technologies will keep growing. In his view, utilities should count them as resources in their planning instead of leaving what they can do untapped. He wrote the report with Kate Peters, Sophie Edelman, Prisha Tiwari, Carly McAdam and Akhilesh Ramakrishnan.

Maureen Quinlan, who leads Pew's work to decarbonize the grid, pointed to historic demand driven by data centers, new manufacturing and electrification. She said DERs could deliver a significant amount of new energy supply if the barriers to adopting them are removed, and called the report evidence that pragmatic policy changes enabling the technology can save billions and cut emissions.

A separate scenario tests a harder target. Pew's release says that if the generation fleet must be carbon-free by 2050, expanded DERs would offset about 175 GW of utility-scale capacity. In that case, annual generation costs in 2050 would come down by $45 billion. That equals nearly 20% of the added cost of moving the power supply to zero carbon. The repeated 175 is a coincidence worth flagging: one is gigawatts of capacity in the carbon-free case, the other is a count of gas plants in the status quo comparison.

The storage result needs a careful citation. Expanded DERs would move utility-scale storage capacity toward distributed storage and other flexibility close to customers, but Pew's release and the PR Newswire version put that shift at about 105 GW, while Brattle's own report page says about 116 GW. Anyone quoting the figure in a filing or a board deck would do well to take it from the full report rather than a press summary.

A cheaper bet on uncertain demand

For a utility weighing a wave of data center interconnection requests, the overbuild scenario may be the most practical finding in the report. Suppose anticipated load growth falls short. Relying more heavily on distributed resources would then trim what is spent on overbuilt energy infrastructure from 2030 through 2040 by $33 billion, which works out to a cut of roughly 40%. Brattle frames this as flexibility for utilities planning around uncertain demand from data centers, manufacturing and electrification.

The PJM numbers show how big that uncertainty is. Energy-Storage.news, in reporting by April Bonner, cited an October 2025 US Energy Storage Coalition study finding that PJM's summer peak would rise 16 GW by 2028 and a further 30 GW by 2032. That projection assumes all the demand in PJM's 2025 load forecast materializes. The "if" is the whole planning problem. A utility that builds conventional capacity for load that never shows up spreads the cost of the extra plant and wire across every ratepayer.

The pressure is already political. The outlet reported that the projected load increase and interconnection queue backlogs have drawn calls for reform from local leaders and the federal government, and that PJM is considering multiple reform paths.

Forecasting method is part of the problem. The Energy Systems Integration Group's Long-Term Load and DER Forecasting report, covered by T&D World in August 2025, found that forecasts have historically scaled annual energy use or peak demand, an approach that often misses localized adoption of new technologies. It recommends hourly, high-resolution forecasts and scenario-based methods that account for drivers such as policy changes and market signals.

Julieta Giraldez of Electric Power Engineers, who chaired the task force behind it, stressed aligning forecasts across entities to reconcile system-level data with local grid needs. That gap matters for the Brattle case. Battery and flexible-load value lands feeder by feeder, which suggests a planner relying on a system-wide peak forecast could miss much of the deferral value the report's distribution assessment is built to find.

PJM is already paying for distributed capacity

PJM is the country's largest Regional Transmission Organisation, covering parts of 13 US states and the District of Columbia, and is the location of Virginia's "Data Centre Alley," the world's biggest cluster of data centres, according to Energy-Storage.news. A deal there offers a small real-world counterpart to the national model. On June 2, Google and Voltus announced a three-year agreement under which Voltus will aggregate up to 100 MW of distributed resources each year from local businesses and homes into a Google-funded virtual power plant, the outlet reported.

Voltus will then pay customers who participate, "turning Google's capacity demand into real economic benefits for PJM customers," in the companies' words. They describe it as a bring-your-own-capacity deal, a structure the US government has encouraged through steps such as the White House's "Ratepayer Protection Pledge," which Energy-Storage.news called largely symbolic and which Google and other major tech companies signed.

That payment flow mirrors one of the report's mechanisms. Brattle and Pew say DERs let customers, rather than large-scale power developers, earn compensation for services they provide to the grid, with net savings large enough to benefit all customers through lower rates. In the Voltus structure, a data center's capacity need becomes a check to a local homeowner or business.

Set against 400 GW, 100 MW a year is a rounding error. What it shows is a large buyer paying for distributed capacity as part of how it gets power, which is the kind of transaction Brattle's numbers assume will become routine. For data center developers in congested regions, the Google-Voltus structure is a working precedent that procurement teams can point to.

It also sits beside much bigger, more conventional deals by the same buyer. In March, Google announced plans with DTE Energy for a Michigan data center including 1,600 MW of solar paired with 450 MW of storage, which Google will fund and DTE will operate over a 20-year contract. In February, Xcel Energy said it would install 30 GWh of Form Energy's iron-air batteries at a Google-owned data center in Pine Island, Minnesota. Distributed capacity, on this evidence, is one line in a large buyer's portfolio rather than a replacement for utility-scale supply.

What the reforms look like at project level

On April 16, Lightshift Energy, which both develops and operates projects, announced a portfolio of five battery storage projects in Virginia, all built at distribution scale. Transmission-scale projects of 200 MW to 500 MW require years of PJM interconnection studies and tens of millions of dollars in upgrade costs, the outlet reported. Lightshift is avoiding that route and installing smaller batteries, typically 20 MW or less, at distribution substations that already exist, aiming to reduce the impact on regular energy consumers.

Lightshift's design choice shows the interconnection problem from the developer's side: sizing projects to existing substations is a way to stay out of the slowest part of the queue. Reform of the kind Brattle priced would matter most for developers who cannot shrink their projects to fit.

Pat Wood III, co-chair at Pew Charitable Trusts, discussed the nonprofit's DER Policy Playbook with Energy-Storage.news Premium. The playbook outlined ways to incentivize DERs in the US. To make entry easier, Pew recommends automated permitting for residential installations and simpler interconnection processes for commercial providers. The goal of these administrative changes is to lower costs and shorten the delays that slow deployment. On implementation, the report emphasized the importance of aggregating DERs into virtual power plants.

Those two administrative fixes line up with two of the three reforms behind the $266 billion, and the aggregation point describes what Voltus is doing for Google. Read together, the PJM deals look like early, small-scale versions of the playbook's process changes.

The household number, read carefully

By 2050, Brattle estimates, the average household could pay $122 a year less for electricity in current dollars than it would under the status quo. That saving would cover about half of the projected bill increase above the inflation rate the study assumes. The number is real, but it takes a long time to arrive. It describes where things stand in 2050, so a regulator can't count on it in the next rate case.

The strongest objection to the headline figure is that it depends on policy. Most of the levers belong to state regulators and local permitting offices, and only the $266 billion is tied to named reforms. The rest of the headline figure could depend on other barriers coming down as well. For planners, the safest reading treats the $266 billion as the part with a clear to-do list attached.

The first real-world check

Brattle has published the full report and a technical appendix, so utility planning teams can test its assumptions against their own territories. The closer signal is in PJM. The Google-Voltus contract runs three years with a 100 MW annual target, and whether Voltus fills that each year will show more about how fast distributed capacity can be recruited than any 2050 projection can.

text:
TII KAMAG has delivered 25 ePrecisionMover (ePM) electric swap body movers to Deutsche Post DHL Group, for use at yard logistics operations at parcel centers in Germany. The new vehicles will be introduced gradually at parcel centers where high throughput, short turnaround times and operational availability are critical.

In 1995, DHL became the first customer to receive a KAMAG swap body mover. At DHL’s parcel centers, swap body movers handle internal transport. The KAMAG ePM is designed to enable precise maneuvering of swap bodies among loading gates, ramps and staging areas.

The KAMAG ePM produces no local emissions, making it suitable for urban logistics sites. Compared with diesel-powered alternatives, operators also benefit from improved energy efficiency, reduced noise levels and lower maintenance requirements.

The KAMAG ePM is designed for round-the-clock, multishift operations. Its battery supports typical shift cycles, and the vehicle can be integrated into existing workflows with suitable charging infrastructure. Opportunity charging can also be used when needed without interrupting operations.

“The demands placed on parcel networks continue to grow, both in terms of handling performance and sustainability,” said TII KAMAG Head of Yard Logistics Sales Godehard Eidenhammer. “With the KAMAG ePM, we offer a solution that combines both dimensions and integrates seamlessly into existing and scalable logistics processes.”

Deutsche Post DHL Group representative Dane Becker said, “The electrification of our yard logistics is a key element of our sustainability strategy. With the KAMAG ePM, we are investing in a high-performance, emission-free solution that meets our operational requirements for parcel handling while contributing to the reduction of our CO₂ emissions.”

A surface transportation bill moving through Congress would require electric vehicle owners to pay an annual federal fee beginning at $130.

The fee could then increase by $5 each year, with a maximum of $150, according to the proposed legislation.

Owners of plug-in hybrids would have to pay $35.

Current funding for surface transportation is set to expire next month. The electric vehicle fees could take effect as soon as December if approved by Congress.

The government uses money it collects from gasoline taxes to help pay for road projects. Electric vehicles do not require gasoline, so those drivers do not pay that tax.

title: 5 years of fighting climate change haven't done much and stronger targets are needed, report says
authors: Suzan Fraser, Seth Borenstein, Sibi Arasu And Tammy Webber, Associated Press, Suzan Fraser, Seth Borenstein
description:
“Aggregated climate action has now essentially stalled for five consecutive years with positive and negative actions canceling each other out,” the independent Climate Action Tracker said in its report.
Climate change is caused mainly by the release of greenhouse gases, which happens when fuels like gas, oil and coal are burned.
Confronting climate change means finding ways to drastically cut the amount of emissions put into the atmosphere each year.
"Countries really do need to strengthen their targets.” That's the message island leaders gave the rest of the world Wednesday.
Even more leaders of island nations were expected Thursday to reinforce what to their people is a life-or-death message.
text:
ANTALYA – The world has failed to slow or stop global warming trends in the past five years because plans weren’t realized and efforts that would have helped were canceled out, a report said Thursday.

The grim assessment came during a U.N. climate meeting in Antalya, Turkey, where more government leaders were due to speak Thursday about the state of a warming world and what they hope to do about it.

“Aggregated climate action has now essentially stalled for five consecutive years with positive and negative actions canceling each other out,” the independent Climate Action Tracker said in its report. The first five years after the 2015 Paris Agreement, the world did so much that it trimmed an entire degree Celsius (1.8 degrees Fahrenheit) from warming projections, but nothing has changed since, the report said.

Climate change is caused mainly by the release of greenhouse gases, which happens when fuels like gas, oil and coal are burned. Confronting climate change means finding ways to drastically cut the amount of emissions put into the atmosphere each year. Countries establish plans to reduce emissions, called nationally determined contributions. The speed of reductions and ways to achieve them are different by country.

Because collective efforts of countries haven't significantly reduced global emissions, the world is now “headed toward an irrecoverable overshoot of 1.5 degrees Celsius” (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial temperatures, which is the warming threshold the world adopted during the Paris Agreement, according to the report.

The report said if the nations of the world fulfill all their climate promises — which is a big if — the globe will end the century 2.6 degrees Celsius (4.7 degrees Fahrenheit) warmer than preindustrial times. That's the same pace the globe was on in 2024 and 2025, showing the new set of promises made last year have “failed to the move the needle” of projected warming, said report lead author Sarah Heck, a climate policy analyst at Climate Analytics.

“This is still not enough,” Heck said. "Countries really do need to strengthen their targets.”

That's the message island leaders gave the rest of the world Wednesday. Even more leaders of island nations were expected Thursday to reinforce what to their people is a life-or-death message. While all the globe is threatened by climate change's souped-up storms, hotter heat waves, worsening droughts and floods, island nations also have to watch rising seas shrink swallow up their land.

“Every new oil well drilled, every piece of coal extracted is a threat to my country’s future. The discovery of new fossil fuel resources is not something to celebrate, but something to fear,” Marshall Islands President Hilda Heine said Wednesday as her colleagues from Tuvalu, Bahamas, Antigua and Barbuda, Niue and other islands are expected to make similar pleas Thursday. “No one has the right to pollute their neighbors.”

“It is time to wake up,” said Heine, who recalled coral that she watched go from “bright and lush” to white with bleaching this year. She said the response of the world to the inevitability of passing the 1.5 warming limit target “must be overwhelming or the world we know is over.”

To fight climate changes, the rich world needs to not just promise more, but also deliver more money to poor nations to help them recover from climate damage and adapt to a warmer world, Barbados Prime Minister Mia Mottley said Wednesday.

“Pledges are not payments. But even the promised pledges are now 70% below previous levels,” Mottley told her fellow leaders. “So the applause in this room, let us be clear, has never rebuilt a single home in any country.”

text:
BECANCOUR, QUE.- Much of the heavy machinery at the Nemaska Lithium plant site in Quebec, is at a standstill after majority owner Rio Tinto issued dozens of layoff notices. Workers were not the only thing affected, construction on an EV battery chain that was nearly 80 per cent complete is now forced to pause.

This marks the latest sign for the town of Bécancour, located in a region known as “Battery Valley,” that plans for the area to become a hub of an EV manufacturing boom may not come to fruition.

“Decisions on further investment and project timing at Bécancour will depend on the outcome of the evaluation, project economics, market conditions, and customer needs,” Rio Tinto said in a statement.

The global metal and mining giant said it remains confident in the long-term outlook for lithium processing in Quebec and Canada, despite a decline in lithium prices as global demand for battery materials and electric vehicles has slowed.

The fallout could hit the town of Bécancour, which is nestled along the shores of the St. Lawrence River halfway between Montreal and Quebec City.

The Nemaska plant is vital in Quebec’s plan to set up an EV battery manufacturing chain in the province. In the same plan, the province promised to develop Bécancour into a hub.

Slow EV sales halt economic boost

As EV batteries and plants started to set up shop in the town’s industrial park in 202, Bécancour estimated it would see a boost of 1,500 direct and 5,000 indirect jobs, including in the restaurant industry and service sector.

The population grew slightly with the arrival of workers at construction sites. To accommodate them the city planned to expand schools, build housing and even purchase new ladder trucks for the local fire station.

However, when sales of EVs slowed, some projects were paused, while others were completely scrapped. In March, Nemaska announced it would scale down the pace of building its processing plant.

Though Quebec owns 46.1 per cent of Nemaska, the province’s new government said this week it would not spend a penny more on the project for the time being.

“Our sincere hope is that this is going to work, because I don’t want to be the guy to write off the $1.1 billion we invested,” said Quebec Minister of Economic Development, Innovation and Energy Stéphane Paquet.

But many in the Bécancour area say the setbacks are simply bumps in the road that leads to electrification.

“The battery file is here to stay,” said the prefect of the region Mario Lyonnais. “I am confident that the Nemaska plant will open. When it does, we will be ready and we will continue to prepare.”

Lyonnais says the battery boom was happening very quickly and that it was hard for the municipalities in the region to keep up with the pace of scaling up services.

He says the slowdown may allow the area more time to be fully ready for the grand opening of Nemaska and for a time when EV battery manufacturing delivers the region a boost.

text:
In October, research company Norstat surveyed Estonian residents to find out their main concerns regarding offshore wind farms, which organizations they trust to assess potential impacts, and how they would like to be involved in the planning of offshore wind developments. The findings also provide valuable background information for the preparation of ELWIND, a joint offshore wind energy project between Estonia and Latvia. The Estonian findings form part of a broader survey conducted across the three Baltic States.

When it comes to assessing the potential impacts of offshore wind farms, Estonians place the greatest trust in universities and research institutes, named by 53% of respondents. Local communities were considered the most trustworthy source by 7% of respondents, while 6% placed their trust in environmental organizations.

Potential impacts on the marine environment and biodiversity were identified as a concern by 44% of respondents. Nearly one-third expressed concern about the potential effects on birds and bats (29%) and local quality of life (28%). The same proportion of respondents (28%) highlighted uncertainty surrounding electricity prices. Potential impacts on fish populations and fisheries were mentioned by 27% of respondents.

In addition, people are concerned about whether the economic benefits generated by offshore wind farms will reach local residents and to what extent decision-making processes related to these developments can be trusted.

The most common expectation is to receive regular, easy-to-understand information about the progress of developments and their potential impacts. This was highlighted by 44% of respondents. The opportunity to express their views was considered important by 40%, while 33% emphasized the need for independent impact assessments.

Nearly one-third of respondents (32%) would like offshore wind farms to generate direct benefits for local communities. Public discussions and meetings were considered important by 26% of respondents.

The survey also reveals differences between demographic groups. For example, 52% of respondents aged 18–29 would like to receive regular and clear information, compared with 37% of those aged 60–74. Respondents of Russian ethnicity expressed greater concern than ethnic Estonians about uncertainty surrounding electricity prices and the transparency and reliability of decision-making processes.

The findings suggest that communication and engagement activities should take into account the expectations of different target groups. In addition to environmental impacts, it is also important to explain the potential economic implications of offshore wind developments.

ELWIND is a joint pre-development offshore wind energy project between Estonia and Latvia. As part of the project, a marine area west of Saaremaa is being studied to determine whether, and under what conditions, it could be suitable for offshore wind energy production. The project involves environmental and technical studies, the results of which will provide a basis for assessing potential impacts and making further decisions. In Estonia, the project is led by the Environmental Investment Centre (KIK).

According to Aivi Allikmets, ELWIND Project Manager at KIK, the survey findings help provide a better understanding of the issues surrounding offshore wind farms that matter most to people.

“When planning an offshore wind farm, the first step is to understand the natural state of the marine area and how potential development could affect it. That is why it is essential that decisions are based on comprehensive research rather than assumptions. It is equally important to understand the questions and concerns of local communities. The Norstat survey provides us with additional insight into the issues that matter most to people and the areas where greater clarity is needed,” said Allikmets.

The Norstat online survey was conducted from October 14–22, 2026 and involved 1,001 Estonian residents aged 18–74. The survey explored concerns related to offshore wind farms, levels of trust in different stakeholders, and expectations regarding public engagement. Respondents could select more than one answer to several questions; therefore, the percentages may add up to more than 100%. The survey was commissioned by the Investment and Development Agency of Latvia (LIAA).

text:
Conceptual render of a proposed V-NOMAD™ technology platform

Australian Vanadium Limited (AVL), the parent company of Smart Energy Council member VSUN Energy, has signed a funding agreement with the Western Australian Government for up to $15 million to support a proposed vanadium electrolyte manufacturing facility.

The funding will support the design, construction and commissioning of the facility, which is intended to supply electrolyte onsite for future vanadium flow battery projects, including long-duration energy storage projects pursued by VSUN Energy.

Under the agreement, the WA Government will contribute up to 50% of eligible project costs, capped at $15 million, with AVL responsible for funding the balance. Payments are subject to the agreement’s conditions, including applicable project milestones.

The funding has been awarded through the Investment Attraction Fund’s New Energies Industries Funding Stream Round 2.

AVL Chief Executive Officer Graham Arvidson said the grant would support the company’s plans to connect Western Australian vanadium production, electrolyte manufacturing and utility-scale battery deployment, including opportunities pursued by VSUN Energy.

VSUN Energy is AVL’s wholly owned renewable energy and energy storage subsidiary, focused on developing the Australian market for vanadium flow batteries.

Australian innovation and manufacturing

The vanadium flow battery was invented in Australia by Professor Maria Skyllas-Kazacos and her team at UNSW.

For The Smart Energy Council, this Australian invention illustrates what a Future Made in Australia can and should look like: Australian innovation and technologies helping to secure sovereign supply chains and build our manufacturing base.

We congratulate our member VSUN Energy and its parent company AVL on this funding milestone, and wish the VSUN team well on their journey.

name: Texas American Energy
title: Finding My Way Home: ﻿ ﻿A Veterans Day Story | American Ag Network
description:
One day you’re in a war zone, where every decision matters and the consequences can be life or death.
Our CEO, Geoff Cooper, an Army veteran himself, has never once made my continued military service an issue.
According to the Department of Energy’s 2026 U.S. Energy and Employment Report, 16 percent of America’s corn ethanol workforce is made up of military veterans.
Through Veterans for Renewable Fuels, we’re working to share those stories, connect veterans, and recognize the remarkable contributions they continue to make.
One of the things I appreciate most about working at RFA is that I’m surrounded by people who understand military service from different perspectives.
text:
A few days before I was back home in Council Bluffs, Iowa, I was still in combat in Afghanistan.

Think about that for a moment. One day you’re in a war zone, where every decision matters and the consequences can be life or death. A few days later, you’re back home, where life has been moving along pretty much as usual.

There’s no switch you can flip to turn that off. At least, I couldn’t find one.

My military journey began in 2000, when I enlisted at 17 years old, still in high school. This was before September 11, before Afghanistan and Iraq, and certainly before I had any idea what the next 25-plus years would bring.

I first deployed to Afghanistan in 2004–2005 while attending college. I eventually earned my commission as an Army officer, graduated from the University of Iowa, and found my way back to Council Bluffs, taking a job at Southwest Iowa Renewable Energy (SIRE) in 2009.

Then Uncle Sam came calling again.

In 2010, I was back on active-duty orders, preparing for another deployment to Afghanistan. This time, I was an infantry officer serving as the executive officer of a heavy weapons company.

It was a highly kinetic deployment. We experienced real, sustained combat. We lost a soldier in our battalion, others were wounded, and there were plenty of days I won’t soon forget. Some of those experiences are stories for another day.

What matters here is that just days after leaving that environment, I was home.

And I struggled. Badly.

I was dealing with post-traumatic stress disorder, although I became pretty darn good at hiding it. I’d spent months operating at full throttle, constantly looking over my shoulder, responsible for soldiers and making decisions under pressure. Suddenly, everything slowed down.

I didn’t know how to slow down with it.

Fortunately, I worked for some pretty remarkable people.

SIRE’s plant manager, Dan Wych, whose father was a Vietnam veteran, just seemed to understand. Our CEO, Brian Cahill, gave me a long leash, trusted me, and somehow always knew the right time to check in.

They gave me space when I needed it. But perhaps more importantly, they gave me purpose and responsibility. I eventually became SIRE’s regulatory manager, a position they allowed me to help shape. Their support meant so much that I nominated SIRE for recognition through Employer Support of the Guard and Reserve (ESGR), which the company received.

Fast-forward to today, and I’ve found that same support at the Renewable Fuels Association.

Our CEO, Geoff Cooper, an Army veteran himself, has never once made my continued military service an issue. Drill weekends, annual training, teaching future Army leaders? He gets it. I even had the privilege of surprising him with an ESGR Patriot Award during an RFA board meeting. His reaction was priceless.

My direct supervisor, Tad Hepner, whose wife served in the Army National Guard, is cut from that same cloth. He’s always had my back, given me the flexibility I need, and been a sounding board when I needed one.

Today, I’m developing skills over decades in the Army and putting them to work at RFA, including through our new Operation Safe Plant OSHA training initiative.

According to the Department of Energy’s 2026 U.S. Energy and Employment Report, 16 percent of America’s corn ethanol workforce is made up of military veterans. One in six.

I’m proud to be one of them.

Through Veterans for Renewable Fuels, we’re working to share those stories, connect veterans, and recognize the remarkable contributions they continue to make.

One of the things I appreciate most about working at RFA is that I’m surrounded by people who understand military service from different perspectives. My colleague Robert White is also an Army veteran, having served in Korea and parts of Eastern Europe. While our military experiences were different, there’s a certain camaraderie among veterans that doesn’t require much explanation. It’s part of what makes our Veterans for Renewable Fuels initiative so meaningful to me. We’re not just recognizing veterans across the industry; we’re bringing together people who share a commitment to service, even if their paths to the ethanol industry looked very different.

Dan Wych, Brian Cahill, Geoff Cooper, and Tad Hepner have all demonstrated that to me.

I left Afghanistan carrying experiences that will stay with me for the rest of my life. Coming home wasn’t nearly as easy as I thought it would be.

The Army got me home. The people in this industry helped me find my footing once I got there.

One in six. I’m proud to be one of them.

name: Detroit American Energy
title: Incoming US Lawmakers Pledge Major Shifts on Data Centers, Infrastructure and More - ENR
authors: Bryan Gottlieb, Richard Korman, Pam McFarland, Debra K. Rubin, focusing on federal environmental, black holes, trends in global engineering, corporate business, legal news, selects ENR's commentary
description:
Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinajosa (D) has called for a data center moratorium and legislation to require large load users to pay for power and infrastructure.
All 21 restrictive data center measures in Ohio passed, including one in the town of Trenton banning data centers exceeding 25 MW that is set to impact a planned Amazon Web Services project.
New Democratic Governor-elect Amy Acton is expected to seek a statewide data center construction pause.
“it is going to be more difficult to get data center projects approved," ABC Chief Economist Anirban Basu told the Wall Street Journal.
WSP Global CEO Alex L'Heureux said only "a small part" of its transmission and substation work is directly related to data center infrastructure.
text:
At the state level, many will be watching energy sector changes in Texas with the extent of its political shift. U.S. Senate newcomer James Talarico (D) campaigned on an “all-of-the-above” energy platform that supports renewable energy while still protecting the state’s oil and gas sector, although it does not specifically mention nuclear energy.

Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinajosa (D) has called for a data center moratorium and legislation to require large load users to pay for power and infrastructure. She supports grid upgrades to add more "clean and affordable energy,” but warned that developers not "trample on the rights of property owners to build ... transmission lines in record time because high-load users demand it."

Iowa’s new Democratic leaders are split on planned restart of the 615-MW Duane Arnold nuclear plant. Sen.-elect Josh Turek (D) is opposed to the action, stating that most of its power is intended for use by Google, but Gov.-elect Rob Sand (D) supports it as long as data centers pay “their full freight.” Kansas Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton has called for Congress to create a federal agency to regulate AI, similar to what the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission does for nuclear power.

At least two new Democratic governors have fathers who were craftworkers—David Crowley in Wisconsin, son of a union electrician, and California's Xavier Becerra, son of a union laborer. “Gov. Becerra knows what a union construction paycheck means to a family," said Emily Cohen, CEO of state union construction group United Contractors. "Now he must turn that understanding into real leadership—replacing declining gas-tax revenue, delivering water infrastructure across California and moving high speed rail forward. None of this will be easy. We plan to work closely with his administration."

Permit Reform: First Step on an Uncertain Journey

The U.S. Senate cleared a key procedural step on Nov. 9 for new legislation on permitting reforms for energy infrastructure and data centers, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, which given current circumstances may be one of the few bills congressional lawmakers hope to pass in the lame duck session before a new Democratic-led Congress is sworn in Jan. 3.

New blue majorities in the Senate and the House of Representatives may challenge that effort however, saying the bill does not go far enough to reign in data center development or scrutinize new energy infrastructure. The incoming Congress is also expected to seek greater oversight and accountability of Trump administration officials and improve affordability of energy for voters who showed up in record numbers to reject current federal government policies.

House passage of the permitting reform bill remains a toss-up before year-end despite its bipartisan support, said Holt Edwards, a principal at public affairs firm Bracewell, on a Nov. 4 post-election webinar. Democrats now “will likely walk back and reassess whether [permit reform] should be ... handled in the upcoming Congress when they hold a much stronger bargaining position,” he said.

For the rest of 2026, beyond must-pass legislation—which includes federal government and military funding beyond Dec. 11 to avoid a shutdown—significant action on key construction issues is unlikely, according to multiple sources that spoke with ENR.

Also likely to be held up until the new term is reauthorization of federal surface transportation funding—beyond an anticipated short-term extension to keep most transportation programs financed, said Ben Brubeck, CEO of Government Affairs Solutions LLC, an industry consulting and advocacy firm.

The American Road and Transportation Builders of America and Associated General Contractors of America are seeking a new, five-year authorization bill rather than short-term or annual extensions. “AGC’s priority remains a robust, multiyear reauthorization that provides predictable funding, prioritizes core formula programs and gives states flexibility to address their infrastructure needs,” said Alex Etchen, vice president of government relations.

The House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee approved the BUILD America 250 Act in May but it has not advanced to a full vote and there is no companion bill yet introduced in the Senate. When the Democratic majority begins to address transportation funding, it will likely want resumed investment for low-carbon infrastructure such as public transit, rail, electric vehicle charging stations and pedestrian and bicycle lanes, Etchen and others added.

Renewed Focus on Data Centers

New data center restrictions approved by voters in 40 of 41 local ballot measures on Nov. 3 capped a year of other government-imposed curbs that is already having an impact on the market, with S&P Global tracking 182 delayed or canceled U.S projects, about 77% tied to local opposition.

But the small town of Harwood, N.D., (est. pop. 818) rejected a local anti-data center ballot measure, allowing work to continue on an estimated $3-billion, 1.8-million-sq-ft complex on 900 acres north of Fargo set to complete next year with Oracle as its end user. Fargo-based Century Builders is executing the structural shell, civil utilities and site coordination. The measure, pushed by local residents to require independent reviews and public hearings, was defeated as proponents successfully lobbied to site the megaproject for its economic benefits.

All 21 restrictive data center measures in Ohio passed, including one in the town of Trenton banning data centers exceeding 25 MW that is set to impact a planned Amazon Web Services project. New Democratic Governor-elect Amy Acton is expected to seek a statewide data center construction pause.

“We are particularly concerned that some measures presented as responses to data centers reach well beyond them," said Dan Edwards, CEO of two Ohio Associated General Contractors chapters, noting that under at least one measure, new requirements now could also affect construction of schools, hospitals, residential and commercial developments. "Voters need to understand that broader reach. A measure prompted by concern about one type of development can impose lasting restrictions on investments the community needs and wants.” He said the state utility regulator "already has tools to address costs and protect customers through rates and cost allocation. We support responsible development that addresses legitimate concerns … and preserves Ohio’s ability to attract investment and create good jobs.”

Incoming Democratic governors Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia, Jocelyn Benson in Michigan and Deb Haaland in New Mexico also campaigned on enacting temporary pauses on data center construction.

New congressional progressives also may support a call from Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) for a national data center moratorium, but if legislation advances at the federal level, it is likely to be more modest, with increased community and environmental protections, consultant Brubeck told ENR.

The blue wave also will likely change energy decision-making approaches by state public utility regulators, with Georgia’s Democratic sweep give its commission a 3–2 majority for the first time in decades. Texas also added a Democrat to its all-Republican Railroad Commission, which oversees the state’s oil and gas industry.

The country's anti-data center public sentiment brought promises soon after the election from major artificial intelligence companies for changes in their development practices. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman announced on Nov. 5 a pledge to pay for its own grid upgrades, create localized water plans and abandon controversial non-disclosure agreements that have kept early-stage projects secret from local residents.

Tech giants Google, Meta, Microsoft, Oracle, Amazon, Nvidia and Anthropic also formed a new alliance with environmental advocacy groups including the Natural Resources Defense Council and Sierra Club to co-develop strict national guidelines to directly address community concern over grid strain, water depletion, economic benefit and and infrastructure transparency.

Speaking at a post-election Wall Street Journal event, Meta President Dina Powell McCormick said the tech giant is weighing its data center infrastructure expansion strategy, looking to add to existing campuses with local agreements in place. Other hyperscalers could seek non-U.S. locations to expand, market observers said.

The trend caused some post-midterms anxiety on Wall Street, with shares falling on Nov. 5 for data center suppliers such as Caterpillar, Cummins, GE Vernova, Johnson Controls and Carrier. “it is going to be more difficult to get data center projects approved," ABC Chief Economist Anirban Basu told the Wall Street Journal. In the group's Nov. 10 economic update, he noted a sharp backlog decline in October "largely due to worsening prospects for the 88% of contractors not under contract to work on data centers."

Justin Hauke, Baird Equities senior research analyst for construction and industrial sectors, said In a Nov. 5 market assessment, “it’s hard to not view [the data center political trends] as a negative over the intermediate term, especially for bookings/timing, but we fail to see this as a fundamental derailing of a generational investment cycle."

Fluor Corp. CEO Jim Breuer told investors "there is a little bit of growing concern around the data center ecosystem, but we feel pretty good that our diversity is working as we are not overly exposed to some concerns that are out there." WSP Global CEO Alex L'Heureux said only "a small part" of its transmission and substation work is directly related to data center infrastructure. Utility capital plans are being driven by load growth from multiple sources."

Data centers comprise 47% of Turner Construction's backlog, and none have been cancelled or postponed yet, said spokesman Chris McFadden, but the firm will likely expand its presence in stadiums and their related entertainment districts, as well as health care and aviation. "That sentiment expressed Tuesday at ballot boxes, we have been adjusting to for over a year," he said. The view was echoed by Juan Santamaria, CEO of Turner parent Hochtief in a Nov. 5 investor call. "Short-term regulatory-driven impacts will impact primarily location shift and timing dynamic, but it's not a structural demand issue,” he said.

Congress Set to Expand Oversight of Trump Administration

Democratic congressional leaders will move to restore funding to traditionally well-financed infrastructure programs that have seen their funds rescinded or significantly reduced by the Trump Administration, Senate Appropriations Committee Vice-Chair Patty Murray (D-Wash.) said in floor remarks Nov. 10.

“A Democratic Congress means building infrastructure for all Americans—instead of letting [President Donald] Trump build monuments to himself," she said. "Republicans have voted to cut off vital investments to create great jobs and rebuild America’s infrastructure … that people use every day.”

One area the Democrats plan to look at is the administration's push to take equity stakes in companies or construction projects that receive federal funding, with incoming chairs planning hearings, subpoenas and Government Accountability Office probes on how officials picked investment recipients. Since the start of the second Trump term, the government has announced 43 deals involving stock ownership totaling around $30 billion, according to the Council on Foreign Relations. While the U.S. Commerce Dept. said stakes will "enhance the return for the U.S. taxpayer," Jonathan Hillman, council senior fellow, said “there are many dealmakers and no chief investment officer for Washington’s growing portfolio.”

Passage of a new water resources bill, production tax credits for sustainable buildings and infrastructure as well as an end to tariffs that have caused supply chain issues and hiked materials costs all are on the table in the next session, said Steve Hall, executive vice president of the American Council of Engineering Cos. But the upcoming 2028 presidential election will increasingly impact the agenda and any dialogue between parties in both chambers, he said.

However, infrastructure legislation—such as transportation, water resources and permitting —might be one area where lawmakers can agree. “I think we have to be practical in terms of our expectations of what we can get through Congress,” Hall noted.

Democratic and Republican caucuses now are choosing new leaders. A number of Senate Democrats, particularly progressives and some newly elected, seek a new direction from current minority leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.). No successor has yet been formally nominated, but Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland is a possibility and has expressed interest, Sen. Sanders said.

In the House, current Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) is expected to be elected Speaker by his peers during a vote next week.

Among congressional Republicans, John Thune (R-S.D.) was re-elected Nov. 10 as his party’s Senate leader. “We remain united in our commitment to advancing conservative priorities, working with President Trump and our colleagues in the House, and holding the line against Democrats’ efforts to enact their far-left, liberal agenda.” In the House, conservative Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) defeated Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) to serve as Republican leader. Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) will reprise his role as party whip.

description:
A law that eliminated North Carolina’s interim climate target increased Duke Energy earnings per share 17% in 2026, according to Duke’s most recent earnings report.
This is the first earnings report showing how much more Duke shareholders earned as a result of the 2025 law.
Duke Energy spokesperson Gillian Moore provided some context behind the footnotes.
When Duke Energy buys and transports fuel, it passes those costs directly onto ratepayers.

text:
A law that eliminated North Carolina’s interim climate target increased Duke Energy earnings per share 17% in 2026, according to Duke’s most recent earnings report. But Duke says the difference comes from a different part of the law — and that the effect on earnings will be “neutral” in the long run.

In 2025, the North Carolina General Assembly passed a law that eliminated the state’s 2030 climate goal. That goal had required Duke to reduce planet-warming emissions by 70% from 2005 levels. Sue Sturgis, research and communications manager for the Energy and Policy Institute, said Senate Bill 266 was “a really big deal.”

“It was really the bill this session that was the ‘Duke bill,’” Sturgis said, referring to last year’s legislative session.

The law also changed how Duke Energy recovers the cost from customers for building new power plants, making it less risky for the utility to invest in energy sources like natural gas-fired generators and nuclear reactors. Ratepayer advocates say this also shifts the risk onto the people who buy that electricity, while clean energy advocates worry that this makes cheaper solar farms less appealing to the utility.

Sturgis said the Energy and Policy Institute was curious to see how soon these and other changes would affect Duke’s bottom line. This is the first earnings report showing how much more Duke shareholders earned as a result of the 2025 law. The reference to SB266 appears as two footnotes in the nearly 40-page report.

The report shows the difference between earnings now and this time last year.

In the report, Duke says it earned 32 cents more per share this year due to “riders and other retail margin.” Of that, the company attributed 9 cents per share to SB266. In total, Sturgis calculated that the law earned Duke shareholders between at least $66 million to $74 million in 2026, though it didn’t detail how.

“We don’t even know which section of the law is producing this result,” Sturgis said.

Duke Energy spokesperson Gillian Moore provided some context behind the footnotes.

“The North Carolina Power Bill Reduction Act (SB266) did not increase costs to customers but simply changed the method by which purchased power costs are recovered,” Moore said in a written response to WFAE.

When Duke Energy buys and transports fuel, it passes those costs directly onto ratepayers. The utility doesn’t make or lose money on fuel for its power plants. That didn’t change after lawmakers passed SB266. Duke sets rates to recover those fuel costs during the base rate case and adjusts them through annual fuel riders.

Duke Energy also buys power from other grids and third-party power plants, often to ensure reliability during extreme weather, and those costs are eventually passed on to customers.

All of those costs have always been paid for by customers. Before SB266, Duke recovered some of those costs through annual fuel riders and some through the base rates it charges for electricity. Now, it recovers all of them through a fuel rider, aligning North Carolina with recovery in most other states – but the total amount recovered is the same over time. The legislation also prevents Duke from over- or under-recovering what it paid for fuel or power.

Moore said the timing of this change in recovery method under SB266 led to the extra 9 cents per share in third-quarter earnings.

“It is a timing issue and expected to reverse in coming quarters and will therefore be neutral,” Moore wrote.

text:
Tesla says Chicago’s first 50 Semi trucks are on their way for delivery, putting a number behind the electric truck’s arrival in the region just a day after the company announced a new local charging site.

“Hello Windy City,” the Tesla Semi account wrote on X on November 11. “Chicago’s first 50 Semis en route for delivery.”

The update follows Tesla’s announcement of six Semi Megacharger stalls in Hodgkins, Illinois, southwest of Chicago. Together, the two announcements put trucks and charging infrastructure in the same region as Tesla expands its commercial vehicle business.

Tesla’s accompanying photo shows four silver Semis parked side by side at sunset. The company describes the 50 trucks as en route, so this is a delivery update rather than confirmation that all 50 have been handed over or put to work.

There is already a sizeable Chicago-area order in the background. In September, HMD Trucking owner Henry Malukas told MotorTrend he was buying 50 Tesla Semis for roughly $15 million. His business operates nearly 700 diesel big rigs across Illinois and Indiana.

Malukas pointed to lower maintenance requirements as a major reason for the purchase and said his company was installing its own chargers in Chicago. However, Tesla’s new post does not name the customer or customers receiving these trucks, so it does not establish that this shipment is HMD’s order.

Recent Semi deliveries

The Semi’s customer rollout began with PepsiCo in December 2022, years before the current production ramp. DHL Supply Chain confirmed its first Semi delivery on December 4, 2025, saying the truck was already operating in Central California after a successful pilot.

By March 2026, Hight Logistics was showcasing its new Semi while delivering a customer container to the TPM logistics conference. More recently, IMC Logistics said in a LinkedIn update that its Semi had arrived and was “already hitting the road.” Those are examples of trucks reaching customer operations, while Chicago’s latest batch is still described as en route.

The manufacturing backdrop has changed too. Tesla announced high-volume Semi production in Nevada in September. Its third-quarter update subsequently confirmed that volume production had begun and listed installed annual Semi capacity at 25,000 trucks. That is factory capacity, not a delivery total or the current production rate.

In that update, Tesla rated the top Semi variant for 500 miles of range at a full 82,000-pound gross combination weight, with energy use of 1.7 kWh per mile.

The nearby Megacharger addition is relevant beyond this first batch. Tesla says its truck chargers can deliver up to 1.2 megawatts and recover up to 60% of a Semi’s range in 30 minutes, depending on charging conditions. Access to that network can give fleets more options than relying entirely on charging at their own depots.

For Chicago operators considering electric trucks, the next practical test will be how the Semis fit daily routes, charging stops and maintenance schedules once they enter service.

Which Chicago-area fleet would you like to see put Tesla Semis to work next?

text:
By Satoshi Sugiyama TOKYO, Nov 12 (Reuters) - The dollar hel…

LONDON, Nov 12 (Reuters) - British property surveyors were t…



A drone view shows Tesla electric vehicles (EVs) waiting to be loaded onto a ship at a car export terminal in the port of Shanghai, China November 10, 2026. China Daily via REUTERS

By Mathias de Rozario

Nov 12 (Reuters) - Global demand for electrified cars returned to growth in October, reflecting a very low US comparison base coupled with continued growth in Europe, data from UK-based research firm Benchmark Mineral Intelligence showed on Thursday.

"Even though the Chinese market is down domestically, that has then in turn resulted in a lot of OEMs pushing the exports and contributing significantly to the rest of the world," Benchmark data manager Charles Lester told Reuters.

• Global sales of new battery-electric and plug-in hybrid electric vehicles climbed 8% from a year ago to 2.09 million vehicles in October, while year-to-date volumes were up 5% at 17.5 million units

• “China’s year-on-year decline narrowed to 12% as manufacturers continued to lean on exports, with passenger car NEV (new energy vehicle) exports reaching almost 600,000 units, another monthly record,” Lester said

• European sales grew 36%, helped by subsidies, rising fuel prices, EU emissions legislation and a rising number of models

text:
As the market for Chinese electric vehicles intensifies in South Korea, efforts to enhance the competitiveness of domestically produced electric vehicles through tax incentives are lagging. A bill proposing tax benefits for domestic production has been introduced in the National Assembly, but the scope of support remains undecided, and there is a possibility that export volumes could be excluded. Concerns are rising within the automotive industry that the tax incentives may end up being ineffective.
On November 11, the National Assembly's Finance and Economy Committee held a meeting to review the proposed tax law amendments. The automotive industry is particularly focused on whether tax credits for domestically produced electric vehicles will be implemented and what the extent of those benefits will be. With major countries like the United States and China actively promoting their electric vehicle industries, tax support for domestic production facilities remains a legislative challenge.
The proposed bills in the National Assembly differ in terms of eligibility and calculation methods for tax credits. The government’s proposal includes the establishment of a domestic production tax credit based on the income tax or corporate tax proportional to the sales of eligible items produced and sold domestically. In contrast, a revised bill introduced by Democratic Party lawmaker Lee Un-ju includes provisions to extend tax credits to vehicles produced domestically and exported.
If tax benefits are only provided for vehicles sold domestically, electric vehicles intended for export would be excluded from support. Hyundai Motor Group has set a goal to increase its annual domestic electric vehicle production to 1.51 million units by 2030, with 61% of that total, or 920,000 units, earmarked for export. Analysts warn that if tax credits are limited to domestic sales, the support's effectiveness for export-oriented production facilities could be significantly restricted.
Additionally, industry representatives are calling for the introduction of direct refund systems that would allow companies to benefit even if they do not generate sufficient taxable income, alongside tax support linked to production performance. They argue that given the ongoing large-scale investments in facilities for electric vehicle transition, relying solely on corporate tax reductions may limit the effectiveness of the support.
An industry official stated, "Since domestically produced electric vehicles are supplied not only to the domestic market but also to overseas markets, excluding export volumes will inevitably limit the effectiveness of tax support. To enhance the competitiveness of domestic factories, support that considers overall production performance is necessary."
