October 1, 2026: IPS Group, a developer of smart parking and mobility technology serving municipalities, universities, transportation agencies, and commercial parking operators, was acquired by Nayax (TAE: NYAX) for $350 million. The acquisition brings together complementary capabilities in unattended commerce, combining Nayax’s payments infrastructure and global distribution network with IPS Group’s smart parking hardware and software solutions. IPS Group develops single-space parking meters, parking management software, mobile payment platforms, sensor-enabled monitoring systems, and electric vehicle charging infrastructure, enabling customers to manage parking operations, process payments, and collect real-time utilization data.

The acquisition establishes Hypercharge’s first US-based operating platform and advances its strategy of consolidating electric vehicle charging businesses with recurring revenue, long-term contracted customers, and opportunities for operational synergies across North America. Refuel Electric Vehicle Solutions provides turnkey EV charging deployment, infrastructure financing, incentive filing support, station commissioning, and billing services, enabling property owners to offer charging access without upfront costs or operational burden.

Sustainable Energy & Infrastructure Litigation Updates — November 2026

By Jacob Hupart

Court Decisions. On October 8, 2026, an earlier state court decision dismissing New York City’s lawsuit against major fossil fuel companies under New York’s consumer protection laws for alleged greenwashing (i.e., holding out certain products as more environmentally friendly than advertised) was affirmed on appeal. This decision demonstrates the significant hurdles that governments and private plaintiffs will encounter when trying to impose greenwashing liability on fossil fuel companies, as “the general public . . . is now well aware of the fact that the use of fossil fuels results in greenhouse-gas emissions and is the primary driver of climate change.” In other words, the general level of knowledge concerning climate-related issues has now made it more difficult to impose liability on those involved with fossil fuels because it is hard to prove the fossil fuel companies engaged in deceptive practices when the public is already aware of and has taken into account the nature of their business.

State Regulatory Action. On October 23, 2026, Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier filed a lawsuit against First Street Technology, Inc. in connection with allegedly faulty climate risk factors published by First Street for real estate properties. (First Street provides climate risk scores for individual homes and other real estate listed for sale, including through popular homebuying websites.) Specifically, the Florida AG asserts claims under Florida’s consumer protection laws, focusing on alleged flaws in First Street’s methodology, the resultant climate risk scores, and First Street’s failure to publicly disclose all aspects of its methodology. This action effectively seeks to apply the legal playbook developed by state attorneys general in greenwashing litigation targeting ostensibly green consumer products to climate and sustainability data providers.

First Solar and CubicPV Enter Patent Licensing Agreement for Perovskite Solar Technology

First Solar and CubicPV entered into a nonexclusive US patent licensing agreement related to perovskite solar technology. The transaction gives First Solar access to CubicPV’s issued and pending US patents as First Solar continues work toward developing perovskite photovoltaic products across multiple US solar market segments. Perovskite solar technology uses a class of semiconductor materials that absorb light and convert it into electricity, offering potential applications in next-generation, high-performance solar cells and modules.

title: LNG at a Legal Crossroads: Export Growth, Regulation and the Gulf Coast
description:
The Gulf Coast LNG (liquid natural gas) industry is entering another period of significant development and evolution.
The Gulf Coast has become central to the U.S. LNG industry, and that position is unlikely to change.
The Gulf Coast LNG Landscape The scale of current LNG development illustrates the stakes and volume of energy development.
The result is a multifaceted Gulf Coast development environment in which a project’s legal exposure can extend well beyond the LNG terminal itself.
What Texas Energy Lawyers Should Be Watching The Gulf Coast LNG industry is entering a period in which growth and legal complexity are advancing simultaneously.
text:
The Gulf Coast LNG (liquid natural gas) industry is entering another period of significant development and evolution. For Texas energy companies and relevant counsel, the future will likely require navigating overlapping federal authorizations, environmental review, pipeline infrastructure, and a changing energy policy landscape.

The Gulf Coast has become central to the U.S. LNG industry, and that position is unlikely to change. Developers are increasingly pursuing new modes of transport (like trains) and expanding existing facilities and related pipeline infrastructure from South Texas to the Texas-Louisiana border. But LNG development is not simply a question of whether a project can be built. The more consequential legal questions arise at the intersections between:

Federal and state jurisdiction

Export authorization and facility permitting

Environmental review and project schedules

Infrastructure and commercial commitments

Regulatory approval and litigation risk

Use of legacy assets in newer projects and successor liability issues

For personal injury attorneys handling energy-related injury and wrongful death claims, these intersections can be critical to understanding the operational circumstances behind an incident. They can be instrumental in identifying potentially responsible parties and evaluating the regulatory framework that may inform litigation.

The Gulf Coast LNG Landscape

The scale of current LNG development illustrates the stakes and volume of energy development. In September 2026, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) issued a draft environmental impact statement for the proposed Corpus Christi Liquefaction Stage 4 and Corpus Christi Pipeline Expansion projects. The proposed expansion would add four liquefaction trains with a maximum capacity of approximately 1,200 billion cubic feet per year, two 220,000-gallon LNG storage tanks, additional marine facilities and related pipeline infrastructure.

At the other end of the Texas Gulf Coast, Rio Grande LNG continues to move through federal regulatory processes in their attempt to secure long-term authorization for exports from a proposed six-train facility in Cameron County. The FERC has separately been conducting environmental review of a proposed Train 6 expansion.

Port Arthur presents another example. Department of Energy (DOE) records reflect ongoing federal authorization activity involving Port Arthur LNG Phase II, including proposed additional liquefaction trains. A September 2026 filing sought authorization for some re-exports from the terminal under that is currently under construction in Jefferson County.

The result is a multifaceted Gulf Coast development environment in which a project’s legal exposure can extend well beyond the LNG terminal itself.

Who Regulates LNG and Why Jurisdiction Matters

One of the first questions counsel should ask is deceptively simple: Which agency has jurisdiction over which part of the project?

For onshore and near-shore LNG export facilities, FERC generally has authority under Section 3 of the Natural Gas Act to authorize siting and construction. FERC also has authority under Section 7 over certain interstate natural gas pipeline facilities. FERC conducts the applicable environmental review under the National Environmental Policy Act for projects within its jurisdiction.

The DOE has a separate role concerning the export of the LNG commodity itself. Under Section 3 of the Natural Gas Act, exports to countries with qualifying free-trade agreements are treated differently from exports to non-FTA countries. The DOE conducts a public-interest review for non-FTA exports, considering factors such as domestic supply, energy security, economic impacts, etc.

Other agencies can enter the picture, depending on the issues at hand. The Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) establishes and enforces federal safety standards for LNG facilities under 49 C.F.R. Part 193. The U.S. Coast Guard also has responsibilities involving LNG vessels and marine transfer areas.

Closer to home, state agencies, including the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality and the Railroad Commission of Texas, may have authority over particular environmental, pipeline or other legal issues.

Pipeline and Infrastructure Dependencies

An LNG terminal cannot operate without the infrastructure that feeds it. Natural gas must be directed to the liquefaction facility. This process requires interstate pipelines, expansions, compression facilities, and interconnections. Additionally, marine infrastructure must be able to accommodate LNG carriers. There are also issues of storage, power, water, roads, and other supporting infrastructure that require separate permits and contractual considerations.

FERC’s current pipeline docket illustrates the scale of that relationship and how the industry is expanding in the Gulf Coast region. One example is the Sabine Crossing Pipeline Project. The project proposal includes a 55.6-mile pipeline spanning Texas and Louisiana with a capacity of 2.7 billion cubic feet per day. There are many other pending projects, but the Sabine Pass project illustrates the extensive reach these projects have.

Litigation and Regulatory Challenges on the Horizon

The next wave of LNG disputes may not resemble traditional environmental litigation. Potential disputes could involve complex and emerging issues:

Permitting and emissions issues

Challenges to federal environmental reviews or project authorizations

Pipeline routing, land-use and property disputes

Ownership and control changes

Marine and navigation concerns

Construction delays

Contractor disputes

Supply and offtake agreements

Force-majeure and change-in-law provisions

Financing and project-development obligations

Safety and operational incidents after projects enter service

Legal exposure in this industry can also evolve over the life of a project, making a lifecycle perspective potentially important. For example, a developer may initially focus on obtaining authorization and financing. But during construction, their attention shifts toward contractor performance, schedule risk and land issues. Then, focus shifts again once operational and regulatory compliance, safety, environmental obligations and commercial performance become more prominent.

That lifecycle perspective may be particularly important for counsel representing companies with multiple projects or long-term infrastructure portfolios.

What Texas Energy Lawyers Should Be Watching

The Gulf Coast LNG industry is entering a period in which growth and legal complexity are advancing simultaneously. For Texas energy lawyers, several issues deserve particular attention.

First – Jurisdictional mapping should occur early. Understanding which agency controls each aspect of a project helps identify where approvals may overlap.

Second – Regulatory assumptions should be stress-tested. Federal energy policy changes. Long-term projects need to account for the possibility that regulatory priorities or agency interpretations will evolve during the project lifecycle.

Third – Infrastructure dependencies deserve the same scrutiny as the LNG facility itself. Pipeline capacity, interconnections, marine facilities and supporting infrastructure can determine whether a project functions as planned and within appropriate safety guidelines.

Finally – Commercial documents should anticipate regulatory uncertainty. Long-term agreements negotiated years before may not apply today when companies encounter circumstances that were difficult to predict. Change-in-law, force-majeure, delay, termination and dispute-resolution provisions can therefore become critical components of project risk allocation.

Major LNG Expansion Means More Awareness of Changing Laws

The Gulf Coast’s LNG expansion presents substantial opportunities for Texas and the broader U.S. energy market. But as the expansion moves forward, important legal questions may arise not from any single regulation or agency, but from the interaction of regulation, infrastructure, contracts and changing energy policy.

For counsel, developers and investors, that is where the legal crossroads begin.

title: Leading small modular nuclear reactor will be late and over budget - Canary Media
description:
North America’s first small modular reactor project is running into two familiar challenges for the nuclear industry: timing and cost.
The Darlington project, located east of Toronto, is the first new nuclear build in Canada in more than three decades.
It’s also the first test of a small modular reactor design that is being pursued by developers in the U.S. and beyond.
The Tennessee Valley Authority received a construction permit for a BWRX-300 from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission in September.
Timeline and cost overruns have plagued North American nuclear projects and help explain why reactor construction has been anemic in recent decades.
text:
North America’s first small modular reactor project is running into two familiar challenges for the nuclear industry: timing and cost.

Ontario Power Generation said in a Tuesday earnings release that the first BWRX-300 unit at its Darlington site will not come online by its October 2030 target and will blow past its budget of $7.7 billion Canadian ($5.4 billion U.S.). The utility didn’t share new targets — it’s working on a revised assessment of cost and schedule that it expects ​“to be substantially completed by mid-2027.” It is the project’s second slip: When Ontario Power announced the design in late 2021, it said the reactor could be completed as early as 2028.

The Darlington project, located east of Toronto, is the first new nuclear build in Canada in more than three decades. It’s also the first test of a small modular reactor design that is being pursued by developers in the U.S. and beyond. The Tennessee Valley Authority received a construction permit for a BWRX-300 from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission in September. Developer Blue Energy has also started the NRC application process to build a BWRX-300 in Texas.

Unlike other next-gen nuclear designs recently greenlit for construction in the U.S., GE Vernova Hitachi’s BWRX-300 uses the same light-water technology that undergirds most of the world’s existing nuclear fleet today. It’s designed to produce 300 megawatts of carbon-free electricity — a substantial amount, but far less than a conventional large-scale reactor.

Timeline and cost overruns have plagued North American nuclear projects and help explain why reactor construction has been anemic in recent decades. Just look at the latest nuclear power plants to be completed in the U.S.: Georgia Power’s Vogtle units 3 and 4, both large-scale AP-1000 reactors that came online in 2023 and 2024, took an extra seven years and $17 billion to wrap up.

Nevertheless, nuclear energy is seeing resurgent financial and policy support in North America and elsewhere as demand for electricity — especially carbon-free electricity — rises.

The Darlington project is part of that wave. In total, Ontario Power Generation plans to build four units at a cost of $20.9 billion Canadian, and federal and provincial investment funds have since committed up to $3 billion Canadian for minority stakes in the project. In the U.S., the Biden administration backed nuclear power as an anchor for an emissions-free grid, and both Trump administrations have embraced it under the banner of ​“energy dominance.”

Proponents of SMRs argue that smaller, repeatable designs like the BWRX will be cheaper and faster to build than large-scale reactors. The idea is that mass manufacturing and construction of these reactors will create a sort of learning-curve effect, so even if the first unit is expensive to make, the 100th unit will be far cheaper. But right now, this is only a hypothesis. Just two SMR plants are operating commercially worldwide, in Russia and China, and some in the nuclear industry argue that it’s more economical to stick with big reactors.

Given that the Darlington project is the first attempt at building a BWRX-300, some budget and timeline overruns aren’t surprising. Ontario Power Generation itself said that the update ​“reflects GE Vernova Hitachi (GEVH) Nuclear Energy’s ongoing engineering for its first-of-a-kind SMR, which has impacts on construction execution and supply chain performance.”

“GE Vernova Hitachi is committed to working closely with Ontario Power Generation (OPG) and our partners to deliver the Western world’s first commercial SMR,” a GE Vernova Hitachi spokesperson told Canary Media in an emailed statement. ​“While engineering and design maturity are important considerations, as OPG’s update recognizes, there are multiple interconnected contributions across engineering, procurement and construction, as well as evolving market conditions, including inflation and geopolitical risks.”

While overruns are expected for a first-of-its-kind project, their scale matters. If costs or timelines balloon by too much, it could have a chilling effect on the other efforts to develop BWRX-300 reactors. Vogtle offers a cautionary precedent. Even though its second new reactor was 30% cheaper to build than its first, what’s remembered is the project’s enormous overall price tag.

title: Whose Voices Shape Pollution Policy? | News - McCormick School of Engineering

text:
When it comes to regulating pollution from heavy-duty trucks, economic concerns may carry more weight than climate and public health benefits, according to a Northwestern Engineering study.

In new research, researchers used AI and other computational tools to analyze nearly 5 million words from public comments submitted to the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) during the development of emissions standards for heavy-duty vehicles.

Their analysis revealed a striking pattern. The EPA was more likely to acknowledge comments about costs and implementation timelines as well as comments from the trucking industry than concerns around public health and climate change.

These findings raise questions about whether the regulatory process itself could slow progress toward cleaner transportation. The study also provides a powerful example of how emerging AI tools can help researchers better understand the complex processes that shape government policy.

The study was published Nov. 1 in the journal Sustainable Cities and Society.

“Heavy-duty trucks make up 5 percent of vehicles on the road, but they produce 28 percent of greenhouse gas emissions,” said Northwestern’s Amanda Stathopoulos, the study’s senior author. “Because heavy-duty vehicles make a disproportionate impact, we’ve been trying to understand why the transition from diesel to electric isn’t happening. We decided to look into how the EPA weighs opinions from many different stakeholders.

“We found the EPA gives more attention to stakeholders from the heavy-duty vehicle industry regardless of how substantive their public comments were. And, ultimately, the EPA finalized requirements that were softer than originally proposed.”

Stathopoulos is the William Patterson Junior Professor and associate professor of civil and environmental engineering at the McCormick School of Engineering, where she leads the Mobility and Behavior Lab. Deirdre Edward, a former PhD student in Stathopoulos’ research group, is the study’s first author.

Competing comments

Before finalizing major environmental regulations, federal agencies solicit public comments from manufacturers, industry leaders, environmental organizations, public health advocates, and other stakeholders.

“The barrier to entry to submit a comment is basically zero,” Stathopoulos said. “The process is open to essentially anyone who wants to weigh in on proposed regulations. The idea is the EPA will look at those comments to see if they made an error or missed anything. Based on that feedback, they might revise their plans and make a final ruling that becomes official.”

Although diverse opinions help the regulatory process, these groups often have competing priorities. Some emphasize the environmental and health benefits of stricter standards, while others raise concerns about costs, technological feasibility, and whether manufacturers have enough time to comply. Understanding how agencies respond to thousands of pages of feedback is a massive challenge.

Analyzing millions of words

To understand the impact of these comments, the Northwestern team examined the EPA’s Phase 3 greenhouse gas emissions standards for heavy-duty vehicles. Proposed in April 2023 and finalized in March 2024, the Biden-era regulations sought to establish increasingly stringent emissions limits for new trucks and other heavy-duty vehicles. Although the EPA repealed the standards in February 2026, under the Trump administration, the public comments and regulatory responses still provided a valuable case study for how competing interests shape environmental policy.

With thousands of pages of public feedback, the researchers had plenty of material to examine. Stathopoulos’ team analyzed 1,171 unique public comments containing approximately 4.74 million words, along with the EPA’s official written responses.

“The EPA acknowledges some of the comments with written responses,” Stathopoulos said. “But responses are only legally required if the comment is substantive. Otherwise, they are not obligated to answer.”

Rather than manually sorting through the enormous collection of comments and responses, the team developed a computational framework that combined AI with traditional text-analysis techniques.

“If you were to read all of these words, it would take you months,” Stathopoulos said. “We really needed a computational approach to make sense of all the text.”

Mapping different themes

First, the researchers used computational methods to identify recurring themes in the comments, such as environmental benefits, economic costs and implementation challenges. Then, they used an AI language model to analyze the sentiment expressed in the comments. They also used generative AI to evaluate the substantiveness of each comment, distinguishing between general statements and more detailed arguments.

The team then categorized commenters by stakeholder type and compared their submissions with the EPA’s official responses. By examining both sides of the exchange—what stakeholders said and how regulators responded—the researchers were able to identify patterns.

“We could map out the breakdown of different themes,” Stathopoulos said. “That allowed us to visually plot out the discourse and pinpoint agreement or disagreement.”

Not all arguments receive equal attention

The Northwestern team’s analysis revealed significant differences in the issues raised by different stakeholder groups as well as how the EPA addressed those issues. Most notably, the EPA acknowledged comments focused on costs and implementation timelines more frequently than those advocating for climate and public health.

“This pattern persisted even after we accounted for the substance of the comments,” Stathopoulos said. “We could see really strong trends there. Basically, it didn’t matter what heavy-duty vehicle stakeholders talked about. They always got a response.”

Stathopoulos emphasized that this doesn’t necessarily mean that the EPA agreed with those arguments or changed its policies in response. Instead, the findings reveal differences in regulatory attention, raising questions about how agencies balance competing priorities. And those differences could have implications for cities working to reduce freight-related pollution.

“One explanation is that regulators are particularly attentive to stakeholders with greater legal resources, who may be more likely to challenge a regulation if their concerns aren’t addressed,” Stathopoulos said. “Smaller nonprofits and individual citizens don’t necessarily have the same expertise to frame legal arguments. Our approach could help agencies recognize meaningful concerns that otherwise might get overlooked simply because they weren’t expressed with the right legal language.”

title: COP31: Electrification Is Necessary - But Not Sufficient - to End Fossil Fuel Dependence
description:

text:
As governments consider a global electrification target at COP31, they must ensure it supports commitments to renewable energy and transitioning away from fossil fuels – and does not open the door to more fossil gas expansion.

In short:

Electrification is essential and the proposed COP31 target deserves support. Electrifying 35% of energy consumption by 2035 can help cut emissions, lower energy costs, expand energy access, and reduce dependence on volatile fossil fuels – but these benefits risk being too little, too late unless it’s done right.

Electrification alone is not enough. IEA research shows that achieving the 35% target under current energy policies would deliver some emissions reductions, but risks driving new fossil gas investment and falls far short of what is needed to course correct towards limiting warming to 1.5°C.

Strong fossil fuel guardrails are therefore critical. The target must be explicitly linked to renewable energy expansion and plans to transition away from fossil fuel production and use, so growing electricity demand does not become another justification for fossil gas expansion. It also must be backed by public finance for the target to be met.

Does electrification alone end fossil fuel dependence?

Electrification is an important tool to tackle the climate crisis. Replacing fossil fuel-powered cars, heating systems, and industrial processes with electricity can meaningfully reduce emissions, improve energy efficiency, and help build a cleaner, more affordable energy system.

According to the International Energy Agency’s (IEA) special report on electrification, accelerated electrification could save fuel-importing countries more than $400 billion annually by 2035 compared with 2025 levels, while significantly reducing global oil consumption.

That’s why the proposed global target to increase electrification to 35% by 2035 at COP31 is a welcome and important step. But electrification is necessary, not sufficient, to deliver the transition away from fossil fuels. To deliver on its climate promise, governments at COP31 must ensure any commitments on electrification go hand in hand with three essential conditions: rapidly expanding renewable energy, accelerating the transition away from fossil fuels, and public finance supporting implementation and fair accessibility.

What does the International Energy Agency’s research say about electrification?

The IEA’s analysis shows that more rapid electrification to 2035 can deliver emissions reductions, even with an electricity mix based on business-as-usual policies. But it also reveals an important distinction between electrification that reduces emissions and electrification that delivers the scale of reductions needed to meet the Paris Agreement’s goals.

Sources: IEA Electrification special report; IEA World Energy Outlook 2025

According to the IEA:

Meeting the 35% electrification target with the electricity mix implied by current or stated government policies will reduce energy sector carbon-dioxide (CO2) emissions by 20-25% by 2035. In this case, the world would fail to meet the emissions reductions objectives of the 2023 Global Stocktake and the Paris Agreement, and significantly breach 1.5ºC or even 2ºC.

In the IEA’s Net Zero Emissions (NZE) scenario that supports a 1.5ºC aligned pathway, energy-related emissions need to fall by almost 55% by 2035 – with renewable and efficiency solutions scaling up much faster to replace fossil fuels, eliminating the need for any new oil, gas, and coal production beyond existing fields and mines.

Electrification only gets the world close to a long-term 1.5ºC pathway if renewable energy ramps up to both: 1) fully meet added electricity demand and 2) rapidly displace existing gas – and coal-fired electricity supply.

Does more electricity mean more fossil gas?

Unless it is explicitly renewables-based, a high electrification target risks leaving the door open to further fossil gas expansion that is incompatible with climate goals. Under a scenario where the world reaches the 35% electrification target but electricity generation follows the mix implied by current policies, fossil gas use in the power sector could increase by approximately 430 billion cubic meters (bcm) by 2035, rising 30% above today’s levels.

That’s a very different trajectory from the steep decline in fossil gas use required to meet global climate goals. Under the NZE scenario, fossil gas use in the power sector must decline significantly – by 60% (900 bcm) – by 2035, with fossil fuels nearly phased out of the power sector in advanced economies.

Source: IEA Electrification special report

How do we get the COP31 electrification target right?

Securing a clear recognition at COP31 that a 35% electrification target must be powered by renewable energy and accompanied by robust and immediate measures to phase out fossil fuel supply is not just a question of diplomatic language: it is about ensuring the target has integrity, and is not weaponized by the fossil fuel industry to justify expanding fossil gas supply and infrastructure. The point of COP decisions is to send global signals to governments and markets about the collective direction of travel. Let this signal be clear: the future is in renewables powering an electrified global economy, not in fossil gas.

Wealthy countries must lead in transitioning away from fossil fuels and deliver public finance on fair terms so countries across the Global South can expand affordable renewable energy access, strengthen their electricity systems, and support workers and communities through a just transition.

Electrification is a critical part of building a cleaner, more affordable, and more secure energy future. The proposed COP31 target can help accelerate that shift, but it must be done in a way that is fair and supports fossil fuel phaseout.

text:
Climate mandates collide with economic reality in Britain.

This week it seems that another Net Zero domino will fall. The Government is reported to be on the point of announcing that the Zero Emission Vehicle (ZEV) mandate, which lays down targets for the sale of new cars, will be watered down. This follows a consultation launched in August. At present, manufacturers are under an obligation to ensure that a rising percentage of their vehicles are pure electric or else face punitive fines of up to £12,000 for every petrol and diesel vehicle they sell over the limit. The required proportion rises from 33% in 2026 to 80% in 2030 and thereafter to 100% by 2035, at which point even hybrids will be banned. The UK car industry is falling well short of the targets, in spite of offering large incentives on electric vehicles. 26.6% of new cars sold in Britain so far this year have been pure electric. The industry also fell short of the 22% and 28% targets in 2024 and 2025 but largely avoided fines because of get-out clauses which made some allowance for increased hybrid sales.

Actually, the situation for UK manufacturers is more dire than the above figures suggest. A growing share of electric vehicle sales are coming from Chinese manufacturers who are able to undercut European ones, thanks in part to China’s dominance in battery manufacturing. Jaecoo accounted for 1.2% of the UK market in 2025 and 3.4% so far in 2026. BYD increased its market share from 2.3% to 3.9% over the same period. In other words, European manufacturers are falling shorter of the ZEV target than the overall figures suggest. It is becoming painfully clear that a continuation of the ZEV mandate on its current trajectory is going to cause further serious damage, if not deliver a fatal blow to UK car manufacturing. Some ministers, including Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds, are said to favour reducing the 2030 target to 50%.

Unsurprisingly, Labour’s Net Zero fundamentalists such as Ed Miliband are reported to be against reducing the target. But the issue is complicated by Andy Burnham’s negotiations for a reset of Britain’s relations with the EU. Electric vehicles represent one area in which UK regulation, post-Brexit, has been more stringent than EU regulation. EU rules already allow for a small proportion of cars manufactured after 2035 to have internal combustion engines. The European Parliament’s Environment Committee last week voted for a further relaxation. If Burnham signs up for a deal which forces Britain into “dynamic alignment” with EU regulations, it will almost certainly mean us having to adopt the same EV targets as the EU. Labour ministers who are both Europhile and Net Zero fundamentalists are going to have to choose what is most important to them.

But there is something even more significant to be drawn from the revision of ZEV targets. Virtually every interim target on the way to the Government’s overall, legally binding 2050 Net Zero target is being abandoned, or relaxed, as it flies headlong into reality. New oil-fired boilers were due to be banned from 2026, gas-fired boilers by 2035. There were going to be 600,000 heat pump installations a year by 2028.

All these targets have gone, once it became clear that they could not be met. Moreover, the electricity grid was going to be fully decarbonised by 2030; that target has already been subtly downgraded to 95% carbon-free and is coming under constant pressure. Another target soon to go will likely be the one requiring 10% of jet fuel used by airlines to be Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) by 2030. The Government confirmed this target last month, but as with ZEV, the use of SAF is running well behind track.

Yet at the same time the Government continues to insist that it remains committed to its overall Net Zero target of 2050. But how does it expect to be able to achieve that when it is on a trajectory well short of what it used to think was necessary to achieve this? The year 2050, perhaps, still lies such a distance into the future that the current generation of ministers and MPs feel they don’t need to worry about it too much. At some point, though, the 2050 Net Zero target is going to reach a crunch point at which it has to be relaxed, if not abandoned altogether. I doubt the current Government will want to make the call, but I will give the 2050 Net Zero target until 2030 at the latest.

text:
BMW Group has contracted Samsung SDI to supply European-made cells and LG Energy Solution to supply US-made cells for its Gen6 high-voltage batteries from the late 2020s. In Europe, they join CATL and EVE Energy. Cells feed five new BMW battery assembly plants in Germany, Hungary, China, the US and Mexico.

The BMW Group has contracted Samsung SDI and LG Energy Solution as additional battery cell suppliers for its sixth-generation (Gen6) high-voltage batteries. Samsung SDI will supply cells produced in Europe, and LG Energy Solution will supply cells produced in the US.

According to the Munich, Germany-based automaker, both suppliers will deliver from their existing plants in those regions from the late 2020s onwards. BMW has not disclosed contract volumes, values or which supplier plants are involved.

With the latest nominations, BMW will source European-produced cells from CATL, EVE Energy and Samsung SDI. LG Energy Solution joins the company’s cell supply base in the US.

The contracts fall under BMW’s “local for local” purchasing approach, in which the company buys components close to its vehicle production wherever possible to shorten transport distances and improve supply security across Europe, Asia and North America.

“Diversifying procurement is an integral part of the BMW Group’s purchasing strategy. We aim to ensure our products’ global competitiveness and to be successful in different markets. To achieve this, we operate as locally as possible in our value chains, leveraging the potential of our global procurement markets. Through our battery cell partnerships, we are actively strengthening value creation in Europe and the US,” says Nicolai Martin, member of the board of management of BMW AG responsible for purchasing and supplier network.

The same approach applies to Gen6 battery assembly, which takes place at five new facilities BMW has built close to its vehicle plants: Irlbach-Straßkirchen in Lower Bavaria, Germany; Debrecen, Hungary; Shenyang, China; Woodruff, South Carolina; and San Luis Potosí, Mexico.

“Our global partner network with leading cell manufacturers ensures that we have a resilient, flexible and competitive battery cell supply,” says Hendrik Lang, head of purchasing and quality of high-voltage batteries at BMW AG.

BMW says localizing cell production requires significant investment, supply chains developed with technology partners, and those partners’ willingness to set up local operations. The company aims to build regional battery ecosystems over the long term, which it says depends on attractive local conditions and workable political regulation during industrialization periods.

Alongside its supplier network, BMW runs three cell competence centers in Bavaria. The Battery Cell Competence Center (BCCC) in Munich researches new cell technologies for future batteries. The Cell Manufacturing Competence Center (CMCC) in Parsdorf studies how to produce cells at high quality and resource efficiency, and builds and tests near-series cells. At the new Cell Recycling Competence Center (CRCC) in Salching, raw materials are recovered using a direct recycling process developed by BMW and returned to production. Encory GmbH will build and operate the CRCC, while BMW owns the intellectual property for the recycling method.

“Our competence centers enable us to actively shape technological developments and meet our partners on an equal footing,” explains Lang.

text:
Calls are growing for a redesign of the tax credit system to respond to the spread of protectionism and changes in industrial structure. There are also arguments that, just as support for domestic production is being expanded, a new tax incentive framework is needed for information security investments in the financial sector.

According to relevant government ministries on the 11th, the Ministry of Economy and Finance is reviewing whether to add electric vehicles to the domestic production tax credit to be introduced next year. The domestic production tax credit, referred to as a “Korean version of the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA),” is a system that provides income tax and corporate tax credits based on production volume for items produced domestically.

In its tax reform proposal released in August, the Ministry of Economy and Finance selected six sectors for support under the domestic production tax credit: solar power generation, wind power generation, secondary batteries, semiconductors, core materials, and AI (artificial intelligence) robot components. Electric vehicles, a long-standing wish of the automotive industry, were not included in the supported sectors of the domestic production tax credit.

The Ministry of Economy and Finance did not directly include electric vehicles as support targets on the grounds that secondary batteries, a core component of electric vehicles, are already included. However, with growing concerns over a crisis in the electric vehicle industry, arguments have emerged that they should be included as direct support targets. The Ministry of Economy and Finance has not completely ruled out the possibility of support.

The limitations of existing tax credits lie behind the introduction of the new system. The Integrated Investment Tax Credit focuses on supporting initial equipment investment, which limits its ability to alleviate cost burdens at the production stage. The Korea Institute for Tax Administration also pointed out in a preliminary feasibility assessment of the domestic production tax credit that “existing investment-centric tax support alone has limitations in responding.”

Information security investments in the financial sector are also cited as an area where tax support should be expanded. Financial regulators have ordered financial institutions to expand security investments in response to successive hacking and data breach incidents. However, the current Integrated Investment Tax Credit is designed primarily around tangible assets such as machinery and equipment, limiting support for intangible assets such as security software and AI (artificial intelligence)-based security systems.

Just as the domestic production tax credit was newly established to encourage domestic production, there are calls to reform the tax support system in the information security sector to reflect the changing investment environment and policy importance. To this end, proposals have been made to expand the scope of the Integrated Investment Tax Credit to include intangible assets related to information security. A bill with a similar purpose is also pending before the National Assembly.

text:
On Monday night, November 9th, at an intense, impassioned rezoning hearing in Davidson County, NC, Duke Energy revealed a stunning bit of information it had previously held close. Duke, via its subsidiary Piedmont Natural Gas, was seeking the rezoning of 1,616 acres of forested and farmed land along the last undeveloped part of the Yadkin River for a massive “enhanced” liquefied natural gas (ELNG) facility. The ELNG facility would liquefy and store gas from a major pipeline in huge, 20-story-high tanks, and then regasify it and relay it to be burned in 2,730 MW of proposed combined cycle power plants (CCs) on the Davie County side of the river.

Late in the evening, after a record-size crowd begged the Commission to deny the rezoning, a Commissioner asked what seemed like a simple question: how long could the ELNG facility provide gas to the proposed gas power plants without help from the pipeline?

A representative from Duke subsidiary Piedmont Natural Gas replied: 26 days. In other words, if the Transco methane gas pipeline that runs through Duke’s property cannot provide any gas at all to the combined cycles for 26 straight days, the plants can still run full blast — “peak burn” — on just the gas stored at the ELNG facility for almost a month.

Sounds reasonable? Comforting? Here’s the thing: if there ever comes a day when Duke Energy cannot access capacity on the Transco pipeline for 26 straight days, we have much bigger problems. The Transco pipeline runs the length of the East Coast – from the Gulf of Mexico up to New York City, and it supplies gas to electric and gas utilities all along the way.

In all likelihood, if Duke can’t access any gas capacity at all on Transco for these two plants for almost four weeks, then there are bigger gas supply issues all along the pipeline, and we might actually be in an Eastern Interconnection blackout (the grid from the Rockies to the Atlantic).

And if the entire grid is down, the 2,730 MW of combined cycles cannot run either. No one has power. This begs the question of why Duke wants to build the largest utility ELNG plant in the US under the guise of “fuel security,” sized it for a never-before-seen situation — but if it actually happens, the ELNG will completely fail to provide fuel security due to the larger implications of a 26-day outage on Transco.

Here’s the thing: Duke kept this information completely secret during the Carbon Plan Integrated Resource Plan (CPIRP) process this past summer. In the CPIRP, Duke is asking the NC Utilities Commission (NCUC) to approve a plan that includes the ELNG and the two dependent CCs.

Both the size of the ELNG tanks and the duration of the ELNG without pipeline access were classified as “Attorneys Only” and were not accessible to intervenors, including SACE, even under our non-disclosure agreement. We could not offer our East Coast interstate gas pipeline expertise to help guide our own attorneys’ questions or Public Staff’s and Commissioner’s questions on the planned size and worst-case scenario operations.

Because SACE works across the Southeast, we have unique knowledge of the entirety of the pipeline systems that serve our region and beyond. But that expertise was kept out of the process at the NCUC that will determine whether Duke should be allowed to pursue the ELNG facility and ultimately whether ratepayers should have to pay for it.

Ratepayers should not have to pay for it. It is ridiculously large and ultimately does not provide the extreme fuel security that Duke has touted. It doesn’t even provide security for Piedmont Natural Gas’ customers because it isn’t on the PNG system. It is in an isolated location on Transco. The entire project is a boondoggle that Duke has desperately tried to keep hidden from real scrutiny because Duke is poised to make huge profits if the project gets approved.

Duke succeeded in getting the parcel rezoned, paving the way for a project that will ruin that section of the river forever. While the Davidson County Commissioner who raised the question did vote with the 4-3 majority on Monday to rezone the property from Rural-Agricultural to Heavy Industrial, we are grateful that he did ask that one important question right before the vote that shines a spotlight on Duke’s dirty tricks.

We are still awaiting the NCUC’s order on the CPIRP, which is expected by the end of the year. If Duke succeeds in gaining zoning control of the Davie County side of the project, Duke is expected to file for the Commission’s approval of the two CCs in Davie County and the ELNG project in Davidson in February. SACE will be there to help the Commission scrutinize this boondoggle before construction begins and before Duke can ruin the last wild section of the Yadkin River, pollute the air and water, and further increase all Duke customers’ bills.

text:
BILLINGS, Mont. – President Donald Trump's administration wants to sell public lands to states, tribes and local governments as part of an effort to “decrease the size of the federal estate," according to a new five-year plan presented by the Interior Department.

Agency officials said the sale of federal property would allow the government to focus resources on “nationally significant" lands. They offered no details on what lands could be sold, nor the scope or location of potential sales.

The proposal drew quick objections from some lawmakers, including Republican Rep. Ryan Zinke of Montana, who was Interior Secretary in Trump's first term.

The plan also calls for strategic land transfers and exchanges to support greater energy production, a centerpiece of the administration's pro-fossil fuel policies. It reflects the Trump administration’s view of most public lands as assets to be used, rather than to be set aside for preservation.

The Interior Department oversees more than 750,000 square miles (1.9 million square kilometers) of land — an area greater than Texas and California combined — along with vast underground mineral reserves. That puts the agency at the center of a contentious, decades-long debate over whether the government controls too much land.

The Associated Press sent emails to Interior officials Wednesday requesting comment and further details.

Most public lands are in Western states. In some, the government controls the vast majority of land, protecting it from potential exploitation but also hindering growth. Nevada, for example, is almost 80% under federal control.

Interior officials said that under the plan a portion of any land sale proceeds would go back to the buyer for conservation purposes elsewhere.

Yet it’s uncertain if Interior Secretary Doug Burgum can achieve the administration’s goals without cooperation from Congress.

Zinke’s office said in a statement that he “remains firmly opposed to the sale or transfer of public lands." He will vote against any legislation on the issue if it happens before the lawmaker leaves Congress at the end of this term, the statement said.

The ranking member of the Senate Natural Resources Committee also pledged to fight any federal land sales or privatization efforts.

“These lands belong to the American people, not private interests looking to cash in. Public lands belong in public hands,” said Sen. Martin Heinrich, a New Mexico Democrat.

Some Western lawmakers last year sought to sell vast tracts of land in Utah and Nevada, saying that could generate revenue and ease growth pressures in booming cities. Among the proposals, Utah Republican Sen. Mike Lee suggested selling more than 2 million acres (8,000 square kilometers) to states or other entities.

Those efforts failed amid bipartisan opposition.

The plan sets out a road map for the Interior Department's priorities and actions between 2026 and 2030. Future administrations would not be bound by it.

The department regulates mining, drilling, grazing, recreation and other activities that many state and local officials want greater control over. Interior includes the Bureau of Land Management, National Park Service, Fish and Wildlife Service and Bureau of Indian Affairs.

The agency's strategic plan was last updated four years ago under former Democratic President Joe Biden.

title: The Wildfire Emissions Protection Act May Have Unintended Consequences
description:
Differentiating Pollution from Prescribed Burns and Wildfire But prescribed burns themselves generate air pollution.
Moreover, as human-caused events, prescribed burns appear to fall outside the statutory definition of exceptional events.
In other words, the bill makes explicit that prescribed burns qualify as exceptional events, even though they are human caused.
Emerging empirical research indicates that prescribed fires reduce expected net emissions exposure by reducing the risk of larger fires.
This change may be intended to address the fact that prescribed burns are small and attributing pollution to them is difficult, or that prescribed burns are planned and permitted in advance, before any clear causal relationship can be established.
text:
In addition to devastating local effects, wildfires produce vast amounts of particulates and other air pollutants that can seriously harm human health, sometimes hundreds or thousands of miles away from the fire itself. One of the best tools for mitigating wildfire spread and reducing wildfire intensity is prescribed burning—the use of controlled fire to consume fuel that otherwise could feed an uncontrolled fire. But how clean air laws should deal with prescribed burns turns out to be a tough problem—one that the US Congress is attempting to address with the Wildfire Emissions Prevention Act (WEPA), which passed the Senate unanimously in September and may be considered by the House of Representatives in the post-midterm lame duck session.

WEPA aims to reduce barriers to prescribed burns in the Western United States, where catastrophic wildfires have become frequent and prescribed fire remains underused. If WEPA passes without further revision, then the policy could encourage increased use of prescribed fire in the West—and ultimately reduce associated air pollution—but it could have unintended consequences for air quality elsewhere, especially in the Southeast and Great Plains.

Differentiating Pollution from Prescribed Burns and Wildfire

But prescribed burns themselves generate air pollution. Moreover, as human-caused events, prescribed burns appear to fall outside the statutory definition of exceptional events. But for some time, EPA has engaged in legal contortions to allow prescribed fires to be treated as exceptional events. This process carries legal risk, and some Western policymakers have argued that EPA approval processes are sufficiently onerous to discourage prescribed burns. In short, the Clean Air Act as implemented may be discouraging a valuable tool to prevent wildfires, while treating even preventable fires as if they had no emissions impact.

WEPA, if it passes, would partially address this inconsistency by defining prescribed burns as exceptional events and, therefore, excluded from air-pollution regulation. In other words, the bill makes explicit that prescribed burns qualify as exceptional events, even though they are human caused. States would still have to apply to EPA to exempt individual air-quality days due to prescribed burns, but the path to exemption is smoothed in three ways: the standard of proof for attributing low air quality to prescribed burns is relaxed, applications are automatically approved after a year if EPA fails to act, and EPA is required to write new regulations that will (presumably) lead to a more streamlined application process. The bill also allows the agency to make grants for wildfire prevention and wildfire smoke-mitigation programs, though it does not provide any new funding to do so.

One issue with the bill as currently written is that WEPA does only a small part of the larger job we recommended in our 2025 paper to make clean-air law a meaningful tool for reducing wildfire pollution. Removing barriers to prescribed burns is good, but even better would be to encourage burns and other wildfire-prevention strategies by requiring states to use those strategies to get exceptional-events designations for wildfires. This bill offers a carrot, but it should wave a stick, too.

Second, we think more consideration should be given to the implications of the bill for forest practices in different areas of the country. Prescribed burns are underutilized in the West; however, the practice is common in the South, where for a variety of reasons related to culture, topography, and land ownership, prescribed fire is widely used in forest management. According to the National Association of State Foresters’ most recent report on prescribed-fire use, 63 percent of acres burned in prescribed fires in the United States in 2020 were in the Southeast. In that region, approximately 20 percent of exposure to particulate pollution results from prescribed fires, and in some areas, smoke from prescribed fire raises PM2.5 (particulate matter smaller than 2.5 micrometers in diameter) by more than 3.5 micrograms per cubic meter—10 percent of EPA’s daily allowable amount—on upward of 50 days per year. Prescribed fires are also common in the Great Plains, where they are frequently used for range management, not for wildfire risk reduction; in the National Association of State Foresters’ survey, Kansas ranked among the top states in terms of acres burned using prescribed fire, with more than 1 million acres burned in both 2018 and 2019.

Emerging empirical research indicates that prescribed fires reduce expected net emissions exposure by reducing the risk of larger fires. However, the research to date mainly centers on California. It is hard to know the extent to which this research, which supports greater permissiveness toward smoke from prescribed burns in the West, is also applicable to the South or the Great Plains.

Meanwhile, the existing prevalence of prescribed-fire use in the South, combined with the proposed relaxation of the standard of causation and the one-year default to approving exceptional events, raises concerns about consequences for air quality in the region.

WEPA would relax the burden of proof for excluding poor-air-quality days due to prescribed burns from the regulatory record; the state would have only to show that a causal relationship is “reasonably expected to exist” between air pollution and burns, whereas for wildfires, a clear causal relationship must exist for a bad-air-quality day to be excluded from the record.

This change may be intended to address the fact that prescribed burns are small and attributing pollution to them is difficult, or that prescribed burns are planned and permitted in advance, before any clear causal relationship can be established. Either way, given the widespread use of prescribed fire in the South, changing the burden of proof might enable states to use prescribed fire to strike a large number of days from the record, including days on which the air quality is poor mainly for reasons unrelated to prescribed fire. This problem could be avoided—while still maintaining the bill’s goal of reducing barriers to burns—by allowing air-quality data on days affected by prescribed fire to be adjusted based on a simplified state or regional adjustment rule, but not dropped altogether.

As for one-year automatic approval, while we appreciate the desire to not let administrative bottlenecks slow down the pace of prescribed burns, such a default could end up granting approvals that wouldn’t have passed muster if review had occurred. A better approach would be to create conditions that enable timely review, even for the potentially large number of exceptional-event demonstrations that might be submitted for prescribed burns. The bill’s lower standard of causation already is a step in this direction. Combined with other measures, like an expedited review process for prescribed burns and an increase in EPA review capacity, timely review could be achievable without automatic approval. And if air-quality data on days affected by smoke from prescribed fire were adjusted rather than dropped, an expedited review process would carry relatively few risks, since no approval could strike a poor-air-quality day from the record entirely.

In the case of prescribed burns for range management, though, it is not clear that exceptional-event status should be granted at all. WEPA’s premise is that prescribed burns, though human caused and avoidable, should nevertheless be allowed to be treated as exceptional events due to their potential to reduce wildfire hazard and, ultimately, smoke. But WEPA’s definition of prescribed fires appears to include range-management fires, despite the fact that these intentional fires are not primarily intended to reduce wildfire hazard and may provide no net air-quality benefits. WEPA could avoid giving these activities undue protection from air-quality regulation by more carefully defining which prescribed fires are eligible for exceptional event status.

Finally, clarity is needed on § 319(b)(4), which requires EPA to “lead” exceptional-event demonstrations when states, local authorities, or Tribes request it. Some have argued that the strain placed on state resources by linking poor air quality to exceptional events could be reduced by allowing states to cooperate and apply for regional exceptional-event status. EPA-led demonstrations could ease the burden on states, but this provision could give EPA a degree of control over the exceptional-events process that many states may not want, and that both environmental and forestry groups might oppose depending on who is in charge of the agency.

Seeing the Forest for the Trees

title: A 44-acre nuclear dump in Pennsylvania where a fuel plant buried its waste in 10 trenches ...
description:
Someone digs it up, it goes in a truck, the truck leaves, and no one on the street gives it a second look.
Between 1960 and 1970, the Nuclear Materials and Equipment Corporation (usually just called NUMEC) buried low-level radioactive waste there in 10 trenches.
According to the Corps, that waste came out of work done under Atomic Energy Commission contracts, mostly turning out fuel for the Navy’s nuclear submarines and for power plants.
According to the Tribune-Review, Corps officials have pointed to old mines under the site, which could cave in and let the waste shift.
Since April 7, the contractor’s dug out close to 1,560 cubic yards of waste, plus 115 drums of the 55-gallon kind.
text:
Hauling dirt off a job site is about as dull as heavy work gets. Someone digs it up, it goes in a truck, the truck leaves, and no one on the street gives it a second look.

So it’s a little unusual for the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers to put out a press release about one truck. On October 27, the first load of contaminated soil left the Shallow Land Disposal Area in Parks Township, Pennsylvania, headed for a licensed disposal site out of state. The Corps announced it the next day.

That truck’s been a long time coming. Congress told the Corps to clean this place up more than two decades ago, and the dirt it’s carrying has been in the ground since the 1960s.

The site covers 44 acres along the Kiskiminetas River, near Apollo and Vandergrift, about 23 miles outside Pittsburgh to the east-northeast. Between 1960 and 1970, the Nuclear Materials and Equipment Corporation (usually just called NUMEC) buried low-level radioactive waste there in 10 trenches. According to the Corps, that waste came out of work done under Atomic Energy Commission contracts, mostly turning out fuel for the Navy’s nuclear submarines and for power plants. BWX Technologies still owns the land.

The cleanup runs through something called FUSRAP, the Formerly Utilized Sites Remedial Action Program. Basically, it’s the federal program for places that got contaminated during the early days of America’s atomic energy work, and the Corps is the agency that shows up with the excavators. Parks Township got on that list through Section 8143 of Public Law 107-117, which Congress passed in 2002, and it’s been a FUSRAP site ever since.

This is the Corps’ second try

The Corps has actually been here before. It started digging in 2011 and stopped that same year after finding safety violations by the contractor it had on site at the time. Trenches 2 and 3 got partway done, down to about 8 feet, and the other eight trenches stayed as they were found.

The second attempt hasn’t been quick either. Over the years, the start date slid from 2023 to 2024, then to spring 2025, then summer, then fall, then winter, which is about as many times as I’ve promised to clean out my garage. Digging finally started on April 7, beginning with the topsoil over Trench 8.

In fairness, this isn’t a garage. Col. Nicholas Melin, then commander of the Corps’ Pittsburgh District, called it “one of the most complex and specialized construction projects” in the Corps’ whole portfolio in a Corps news story last fall, and I’m inclined to cut them a bit of slack on the schedule.

Old mines are why it’s coming out

So why not just leave it buried?

It’s a fair question when the waste’s been sitting there for decades. According to the Tribune-Review, Corps officials have pointed to old mines under the site, which could cave in and let the waste shift. “It was determined it was an unacceptable risk to leave it long-term,” project manager Steve Vriesen told residents at a public meeting last year.

You’ll notice the Corps has put a lot of effort into keeping the neighbors in the loop. It says a serious accident on site is unlikely, and it’s held tabletop exercises with local first responders and run a joint drill with them too. Pennsylvania’s Department of Environmental Protection was also set to run its own air monitors around the site, so the Corps isn’t the only one checking its homework. That’s a pretty sensible setup, if you ask me.

So how do you move radioactive dirt?

Slowly, and in small bites. Crews remove material in batches of roughly half a cubic yard, according to the Tribune-Review, and trenches under a roof sit inside buildings with their own air filtration. Trench 8 is in one of those buildings, which covers trenches 4 through 8. A second building covers Trench 1, while the Corps plans to dig trenches 2, 3 and 9 in the open, since it expects to get through them in one season. Trench 10 comes last.

Every scoop goes into a soil bag, and every bag goes through an X-ray machine. Depending on what the X-ray shows, a bag can get more scans, sampling and lab tests, and the Corps keeps going until it knows exactly what’s in there. Then the sealed bags get packed into what the Corps calls intermodal shipping containers. If you haven’t heard the term, an intermodal container is a shipping box built to move between trucks and trains without being unpacked, and these are heavy-duty steel. Trucks haul them about 60 miles northwest to Wampum, Pennsylvania, where they go onto rail cars bound for Utah, and the Tribune-Review has reported the final stop as a disposal site in Clive.

“The waste is transported in accordance with the Department of Transportation regulations,” Vriesen said in the Corps’ announcement, adding that there are safety checkpoints at every step. It’s arguably the least exciting way anyone could move this stuff, and frankly, that’s the idea.

We’ve seen old nuclear material come out of storage before, like the uranium-233 canisters being cut apart inside a glovebox, and it’s rarely fast. And if you caught our piece on the Moab cleanup train, you’ve already seen radioactive leftovers riding the rails in Utah.

It’s a long way from done

The Corps hasn’t said how much went out on that first truck. Its release doesn’t give a weight or a container count for the shipment, which is a bit of a shame if you like your milestones with a number attached. It does give a running total, though. Since April 7, the contractor’s dug out close to 1,560 cubic yards of waste, plus 115 drums of the 55-gallon kind.

For scale, the Tribune-Review has put the total buried in the 10 trenches at about 33,000 cubic yards, and the Corps’ project page says roughly 30,000 tons of material has to be dug up and processed. By July, the Corps’ own progress chart had Trench 8 at 57% complete, with 728 cubic yards excavated and nothing disposed of yet.

When the Corps first laid out the trucking plan, the Tribune-Review reported it as up to 12 shipments a week, with three trucks running two days a week. The Corps estimated last November that the whole job would run about six years at a cost of roughly $500 million, and it’s said the timeline depends on how long the trickier material takes to remove. I’d expect that six-year figure to move at least once more.

If you live nearby and want to ask how much was on that first truck yourself, the Corps has scheduled its next public information session for December 2.

title: Turning battery waste into strategic mineral wealth - The Hindu
description:

A resource closer to home The Government of India is pursuing international partnerships and domestic exploration to secure critical mineral supplies.
Recycling can also help build India’s critical minerals processing capability, which the country currently lacks, while China has a stranglehold over critical mineral processing.
Second, industry and research labs should intensify research and development in mineral recycling technologies.
The opportunity is significant, but battery recycling is not an immediate windfall for businesses.
text:
In his concluding remarks at the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi on September 13, 2026, Prime Minister Narendra Modi warned against the “weaponisation of technology and critical minerals”. His remarks assume significance amid rising global demand for critical minerals such as lithium, nickel and cobalt. As transport and other energy-intensive sectors increasingly shift towards electrification, the demand for electricity, lithium-ion batteries and electrical conductors is also growing.

Their ores are either scarce or their supply chains geographically concentrated, leaving these critical minerals vulnerable to geopolitical tensions, resource nationalism, trade restrictions and other disruptions. China currently dominates critical mineral processing. For India, which is heavily dependent on imports, securing reliable supplies has therefore become a strategic priority.

A resource closer to home

The Government of India is pursuing international partnerships and domestic exploration to secure critical mineral supplies. It must also tap a growing resource available in its backyard: minerals recovered through recycling. End-of-life (EoL) lithium-ion batteries, which contain economically valuable minerals, can be treated either as waste or as a “waste-to-wealth” resource. The opportunity is considerable if a proper recycling system is put in place.

India already uses lithium-ion batteries extensively in mobile phones and other electronic devices. Yet, when these products reach EoL, their batteries often end up in landfills or informal recycling channels run by kabadiwalas. While the informal sector plays an important role in waste management, its manual methods are often inefficient and unsafe. Material recovery rates are reportedly just 10%-20%, compared with over 90% in formal recycling facilities. Consequently, significant quantities of critical-mineral-bearing e-waste continue to flow through informal channels. As India shifts towards electric vehicles (EVs), can it afford to lose the economic value locked in these waste streams?

With more than 8.7 million EVs running on Indian roads by FY 2025-26, the volume of spent batteries is expected to rise as numbers grow. This should be viewed as a waste-management challenge and resource security opportunity.

Analysis shows recycling could meet about 10% to 12% of India’s lithium demand for EV battery manufacturing. While this will not make India self-sufficient in minerals, recycled materials can serve as a strategic secondary source alongside mining and overseas sourcing. Recycling can also help build India’s critical minerals processing capability, which the country currently lacks, while China has a stranglehold over critical mineral processing.

India’s Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022, provide an important foundation through extended producer responsibility, but the ecosystem needs to mature. The current low volume of EoL batteries should not create complacency. “Just in time” investment in recycling facilities and logistics may not be realistic; capacity needs to be planned ahead of the expected surge in spent batteries. This creates a business risk, as plants may operate below optimal utilisation initially and face uncertainty in generating enough revenue to cover financing costs.

The strategy to adopt

India therefore needs a holistic strategy. First, recycled critical minerals should be incorporated into strategic resource planning. The proposed national critical mineral stockpile should include a mandated share of recycled minerals, creating predictable demand for domestic secondary resources and encouraging recyclers to recover minerals rather than produce only the intermediate product known as black mass.

Second, industry and research labs should intensify research and development in mineral recycling technologies. Diverse battery chemistries make recovery challenging and recycling economics can be unattractive. Technologies delivering higher mineral recovery and purity with no environmental impact will be critical.

Third, India needs standards for battery characterisation, recycled mineral quality and second-life applications, supported by testing infrastructure and a “design for repurposing and recycling” approach at the manufacturing stage.

Fourth, retired-battery collection must become easier for EV users. EV manufacturers and their dealer and service networks should offer remunerating take-back or buy-back options. Without active aam aadmi participation, scaling a circular economy will be difficult.

Finally, battery recyclers need patient capital to establish facilities with long gestation periods. The opportunity is significant, but battery recycling is not an immediate windfall for businesses.

Preparing for the battery surge

India should not wait for millions of retired EV batteries to accumulate before deciding what to do with them. The country is still early enough in its EV transition to build circularity into the system. Done well, battery recycling can turn an EoL liability into a domestic resource, create a new industrial ecosystem and provide a modest but meaningful buffer against critical mineral supply shocks. The EV revolution should not end when a battery leaves a vehicle. That is where India’s circular-economy opportunity begins.

Shyamasis Das is Fellow at the Centre for Social and Economic Progress. The views expressed are personal

text:
Germany is well positioned to benefit from a growing global market of climate technologies like EVs, renewables and energy-efficient construction, said state-owned development bank KfW, citing a report produced with consultancy Deloitte.

“Climate technologies are a dynamic growth market offering major opportunities for Germany and Europe,” said KfW CEO Stefan Wintels, presenting the report at a press conference on the sidelines of the UN climate change conference COP31 in Antalya, Turkey. He added it would bring a twofold benefit of furthering emissions reduction and boosting Germany’s economic competitiveness, but warned that competition is fierce and supply chains vulnerable. While Germany was in a good position, it had to become better at turning its pioneering research and development into growth, Wintels said.

The report showed that China dominated the green tech market with 26 percent of global export value of emissions reduction goods in 2025, while Germany ranked second (10%). However, Deloitte’s head of global sustainable finance Hans-Jürgen Walter emphasised that the country could “not win the price war around standardised basic components.” Instead, the country’s strength lies in the export of high-quality system solutions. He warned that the high concentration of global production in a few countries, for example for battery cells and solar components, leaves supply chains vulnerable to shocks and geopolitical pressure, arguing against putting a lot of effort into building up domestic production capacity. “We should therefore only build up our own production capacities where real bottlenecks and dependencies are a threat,” Walter said.

With an average annual growth of 6.3 percent between 2017 and 2025, trade in climate tech is growing faster than trade in goods as a whole (4.7% average), said the report, with emissions reduction technologies growing fastest (8%). Investments in clean energy and electrification are expected to reach 2.2 trillion US dollars globally this year, almost twice the level of investments in oil, gas and coal (USD 1.2 trillion), said KfW.

German industry association BDI has said in the past that the country’s industrial success in the future depends on businesses doing well on green technologies such as modern power grids, wind energy, green hydrogen production, electric mobility, and heat pumps. While the government has introduced many policies that could support these sectors, the recent decision to weaken heating transition rules or efforts to reverse the de-facto combustion engine car ban at EU level risk putting up additional hurdles to clean tech expansion.

Asked in Antalya about the apparent discrepancy when it comes to EV regulation, German environment ministry state secretary Heike Henn countered that “current consumer behaviour is helping the technology to achieve a breakthrough, regardless of what the final rules at European level look like.”

text:
An approximately $400 million wind farm is operational in Carroll County. The 183-megawatt wind farm is the largest in Arkansas and, according to a news release, provides electricity to Microsoft.

Boulder, Colo.-based Scout Clean Energy said Thursday (Nov. 5) that its Nimbus Wind Farm is operating after two years of construction. The company developed Nimbus, worked with more than 50 participating landowners, and conducted geotechnical studies to place the project’s 30 turbines on ridgetops in Northwest Arkansas, according to the release.

The wind farm generates enough electricity to power more than 40,000 homes annually. Of its 30 turbines, 26 have tip heights of 644 feet, and four have tip heights of 590 feet. The project has a life expectancy of about 30 years.

The release shows the project will contribute about $31 million in property taxes to Carroll County over its operating life.

“Nimbus is a project close to our heart,” said Michael Rucker, CEO and founder of Scout Clean Energy, a Brookfield portfolio company. “Nimbus was one of the original projects Scout was developing when we founded the company, and we are so proud of the many years of support from project landowners, local officials, construction and offtake partners, and members of the Carroll County community that made this project possible.”

Coral Gables, Fla.-based MasTec was the general contractor, and more than 280 people worked on the project during construction, which started in late 2024.

Scout Clean Energy has signed a power purchase agreement with Microsoft for the project’s output, according to the release. Scout operates the project, has on-site operations staff, and monitors its performance from its 24/7 Remote Operations Center in Boulder. Scout has two full-time workers on site. The total number of full-time workers will reach up to seven in the coming months.

Scout is developing more than 22,000 megawatts of wind, solar and storage projects across 23 states. It has developed approximately 2,000 megawatts of operating and under-construction renewable energy assets in the United States, 1,200 megawatts of which the company owns and operates.

description:

“This is an historic moment for my country,” Albanese said, adding Australia was “proud to be a leader on climate action”.
