As a major fossil fuel exporter, he said a “responsible leader” would have talked about developing a pathway out of fossil fuels.
text:
Anthony Albanese has said governments have a “solemn responsibility” to act on climate change in a historic speech to the UN’s climate summit, but he failed to mention the fossil fuels driving the crisis.

The Australian prime minister landed in the Mediterranean resort city of Antalya on Wednesday morning where the Cop31 talks are being presided over by his climate change minister, Chris Bowen, but hosted by Turkey.

Only moments before Albanese spoke on the same stage, the UN secretary general, António Guterres, said unambiguously that keeping the 1.5C temperature goal alive “means no new coal”.

In a packed conference room, Turkey put on an opening ceremony of whirling traditional dancers, booming music and a film shot around the world with characters saying “We need to talk”.

“This is an historic moment for my country,” Albanese said, adding Australia was “proud to be a leader on climate action”.

“Proud to be a renewable energy leader, creating the clean industries, businesses and jobs of the future. And proud to be here fighting for the interests of our Pacific family,” he said.

Australia had pushed for a role at the climate summit, he said, “because we wanted to speak for the people of the world who need urgent action, including those from our Pacific family”.

Australia is the world’s second-largest exporter of coal for burning in power stations and the largest exporter of coal for steel making. A fifth of the world’s exported LNG comes from Australia.

Albanese pointed to “significant successes” for the country on climate change, including doubling renewable energy generation in six years that accounted for half of the country’s electricity, and building one of the world’s biggest rooftop solar and battery markets.

Guterres and several countries are pushing for the talks to progress a proposal from last year’s Cop hosts, Brazil, for countries to develop detailed plans to move away from fossil fuels.

Guterres told the conference: “Leaders – and in particular those from developed countries – cannot keep expanding fossil fuel production while claiming to be committed to 1.5C.”

He said to keep the globally agreed goal of limiting global heating to 1.5C within reach, coal power had to fall by at least 75% by 2035.

Unabated coal power – that is, coal generated without safely capturing the carbon dioxide emissions – “must be all but phased out” by 2040, and oil and gas use cut by a third, he said.

“Every government must align its policies, investments and infrastructure plans accordingly. That starts with credible national roadmaps to transition away from fossil fuels – protecting workers and communities.

“That means no new coal. No new oil and gas infrastructure that puts 1.5C further out of reach.”

Guterres has consistently called out fossil fuel production and lobbying and the lack of action on climate change as temperatures and weather extremes have worsened.

Adam Bandt, the former Greens leader and now chief executive of the Australian Conservation Foundation, said Albanese had “bluntly ignored” the secretary general’s message.

“The prime minister’s speech wasn’t just a missed opportunity, but by refusing to rein in coal and gas expansion or even mention it once, it was a snub to the secretary general’s call to tell the truth,” he said.

“At this summit, Australia is getting repeatedly called out for opening new coal and gas mines and the government can’t dodge it for ever.”

Bill Hare, the Australian chief executive of Climate Analytics and a veteran of Cop meetings, said it was “disturbing” that Albanese had failed to mention fossil fuels.

As a major fossil fuel exporter, he said a “responsible leader” would have talked about developing a pathway out of fossil fuels.

“It still seems to be a dirty word. It’s the elephant in the room,” he said, pointing to 38 fossil projects approved by the Albanese government since it was elected in 2022.

Australia and Turkey are seeking support for a global goal to see 35% of final-use energy coming from electricity by 2035 – up from about a fifth today.

Speaking during a roll-call of heads of state and world leaders, Bowen said the world was asking if multilateralism could rise to meet a “polycrisis” of climate change, energy security, conflict and the power demands of artificial intelligence.

“Is international cooperation still a way forward? This fortnight we can answer those legitimate concerns and questions with a simple answer: Yes,” he said.

name: EPA
title: Democrats are at Cop31 to show that the US has not abandoned the fight against climate change
description:
But will this shift translate into meaningful changes in US climate change policy?
As the US has a decisive role to play in global climate policy, sending a non-official coalition signals that many Americans are still working to combat climate change.
Trump has repeatedly stated that climate change is a hoax and refused to attend the Cop31 climate talks being held in Turkey.
On the international front, Trump was equally determined to undermine global efforts to fight climate change.
But the Democrats’ seismic midterm win may be a sign of optimism for those fighting to address climate change.
text:
The results of the US midterms on November 3 delivered a resounding victory for the Democrats, and a major loss for US president Donald Trump and the Republican party.

Gaining control of the Senate and the House of Representatives has emboldened the Democrats, giving them a renewed sense of political legitimacy and a mandate to pursue their agenda. But will this shift translate into meaningful changes in US climate change policy?

The Democratic sweep will change the political dynamics around US climate policy and how the country cooperates with the international community on this issue. Although there was no official US presence at the 2025 Cop conference, held in Brazil, a coalition of 100 local US leaders, including governors, mayors and other top city and state officials, attended as part of the US Climate Alliance. Former US vice-president Al Gore, and former US secretary of state John Kerry are part of an unofficial US group at the 2026 gathering.

Kerry said in a speech there: “Americans are committed to taking back their future, and we will build and rebuild our partnerships as we do that.”

Being on the ground at Cop is important. As the US has a decisive role to play in global climate policy, sending a non-official coalition signals that many Americans are still working to combat climate change.

Trump has repeatedly stated that climate change is a hoax and refused to attend the Cop31 climate talks being held in Turkey. But 20 Democratic members of Congress will be attending, although they have been denied official state department funding for the trip.

During the first and second Trump administrations, the US has been an outlier among wealthy countries when it comes to fighting climate change. Trump has actively backed the use of fossil fuels, undermining clean energy projects, and rolled back legislation that stipulated emission standards for vehicles.

Trump also weakened greenhouse gas reporting requirements and methane regulation. Then in February 2026, the Trump administration rescinded the Environmental Protection Agency’s 2009 finding that greenhouse gases threaten the health and welfare of the public, which had regulated the emissions from new cars and other vehicles. This had provided the legal foundation for regulation under the Clean Air Act.

On the international front, Trump was equally determined to undermine global efforts to fight climate change. Famously, he withdrew from the Paris agreement, part of a global initiative to address climate change, and refused to attend Cop summits. But the Democrats’ seismic midterm win may be a sign of optimism for those fighting to address climate change.

Data centres are big issue

The biggest issues of the midterms were affordability, corruption and the Iran war, but issues related to fighting climate change were also on voters’ list. There is growing concern about data centres. As many as 56% of US voters felt that data centres and AI were either a major or even crucial factor in influencing who they voted for, with only 13% saying it was not a factor at all.

Data centres require millions of gallons of water for cooling systems, and this is expected to rise to 73 billion litres of water a year by 2028. Over half of planned AI facilities in the US will be situated in areas that have significant water shortages or drought conditions.

After the midterms, Zoe Lofgren, a Democrat, is likely to become the chair of the House of Representatives’ committee on science, space and technology once the new session starts in January. She wants to tackle the administration’s “climate denialism”.

Lofgren’s leadership, along with new Democratic members of the committee, may offer it more power to reverse some of the Trump administration’s changes to science policy.

However, the Democrat midterm wins will not mean that the US is automatically back at the negotiating table at Cop nor that the US will be able to rejoin the Paris Accords while Trump is president. Trump still has the power to make these decisions and can continue to keep the US out of international climate initiatives, regardless of who controls Congress. The US Constitution says nothing about withdrawing from treaties, which creates uncertainty for what the Senate’s role might be.

The election, however, does signal that there is considerable domestic opposition to his approach. And while Congress has not passed follow-up legislation prohibiting presidential withdrawal from the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), it has continued to fund several UNFCCC initiatives. During the Biden administration, the US significantly increased climate finance from US$1.5 billion (£1.1 billion) a year in 2021 to US$9.5 billion in 2023.

Democrats could also push back on Trump’s current policies, using their power to hold hearings, investigate the administration’s dismantling of climate programmes and challenge cuts to scientific research. The Democrats can also use the power of Congress’s control of spending to protect or restore funding to some of these environmental initiatives.

They could also try to introduce legislation that reinstates some of the clean energy initiatives that had been implemented in past administrations to strengthen emissions standards and support clean energy. The big issue, however, is that Trump has made it clear that he is going to be very active in using his veto power, and without a two-thirds majority in Congress, the Democrats will not be able to override this.

What does this mean globally?

What this all means is that the world cannot expect the US to be a reliable and constructive partner at Cop with Trump still in power. Trump will probably continue to forge ahead with expanding fossil fuel production, while weakening international climate cooperation, even if the electorate disapproves of these policies.

Ironically, Trump’s greatest contribution to the fight against climate change was his initiation of the war with Iran, which helped to cut global fossil fuel carbon dioxide emissions by 0.4% due the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. But climate scientists note this is not a long-term solution.

While the Democrats’ electoral victory offers a glimmer of hope for renewed climate action, both domestically and internationally, restoring US climate leadership will take time, especially while Trump remains in power.

description:
Developers building data centers for the AI boom need power faster than the US grid can deliver it, so more of them are planning their own gas plants.
My latest story looks at a new BloombergNEF report that digs into what that means for emissions: • About 181 GW of gas-fired generation has been proposed alongside data centers, with more than 90% of it in the US • If all announced on-site gas for US data centers is built, it would emit about 345 million metric tons of CO2e a year • That’s 152 million tons more than if those data centers ran on average grid power, equal to about 10% of US power-sector emissions in 2025 Many of these plants are meant as stopgaps until a grid connection comes through.
But BNEF warns that once they’re running, the economics may keep them going, locking in fossil fuels for the long term.
“The grid performs well on reliability and cost and sustainability, but it has a major weakness: It fails on speed, and that’s the one thing we care about today,” BNEF’s Musfika Mishi said at the BNEF Summit in Houston today.

Wind manufacturing’s downfall: A few years ago, offshore wind manufacturing seemed destined to rise in the U.S., accelerated by Inflation Reduction Act incentives and a growing number of proposed projects. But the Trump administration disrupted that boom, jeopardizing manufacturing facilities in Louisiana and along the Atlantic Coast. (Canary Media)

Record-breaking batteries: Georgia Power cut the ribbon on the state’s largest battery storage project, a 530-MW system in Cherokee County. The array of Tesla batteries will temper power prices by charging up via the grid when demand is low and releasing that electricity when energy needs rise. (CBC News)

Pairing a docile breed of cattle with higher panels could serve as a model for other developers looking to take solar grazing beyond sheep. (Canary Media)

Lightning strikes: A coalition of Louisiana landowners has sued the Public Service Commission over a new rule they say violates the state’s constitution. The Lightning Directive gives utilities a fast track to power plant approvals without the need for much public disclosure, and Entergy Louisiana plans to use it to build seven gas plants and transmission lines to serve a Meta data center. (WWNO)

Megamerger update: Virginia State Corporation Commission hearings on the merger of NextEra Energy and Dominion Energy continued this past week, gathering protestors who say the mega-company would jeopardize power affordability and reliability. (Virginia Mercury)

Budding nuclear plans: In Virginia’s Campbell County, utility Appalachian Power Co. is seeking state permission to charge customers to fund a small modular nuclear reactor project. The development is still in very early stages, as are talks of a microreactor in Wise County. (Cardinal News, Cardinal News)

Sunrise in South Carolina: Silfab Solar has resumed production at its South Carolina solar cell and module manufacturing facility after chemical leaks shut down the factory for eight months. (PV Magazine)

The American Soybean Association (ASA) and Growth Energy, the national largest biofuels trade association, say otherwise.

text:
What do Alabama, Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi and Texas have in common?

They’re all states with large oil interests — and they all want a pass from the Environmental Protection Agency to give their refineries an exemption from the Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS).

Under RFS, the EPA sets the number of gallons of biofuels that the nation’s oil refiners must blend into the nation’s fuel supply each year. Five governors are petitioning EPA to waive all 2027 RFS compliance requirements for petroleum refiners in their states, arguing that it would lower fuel prices.

The American Soybean Association (ASA) and Growth Energy, the national largest biofuels trade association, say otherwise.

“These requests, if acted on, would strike a major blow to domestic U.S. soybean markets and rural economies more broadly,” ASA wrote in a statement blasting the waiver requests.

The group warns that at least one petition falsely claimed that a waiver would support agriculture and poultry producers — despite the economic benefits that strong renewable fuel demand provides to both industries and rural communities.

“Like all Americans, farmers are feeling the impact of the price at the pump and having to make difficult choices to remain in business,” ASA added. “But make no mistake: undercutting the RFS by waiving compliance would result in a giveaway to refineries that are making record profits while U.S. agriculture would be left holding the bag.”

ASA pointed out that U.S. oil and gas companies have made a record $160 billion in profits since April, which is an increase of over 175% compared to last year. The group also cited current RFS blending volume obligations that have boosted domestic demand for U.S. soybeans, driving billion of dollars in investments from soybean processors.

“This growth in domestic soybean processing creates jobs, improves local on-farm basis for farmers, and lowers the cost of soybean meal used by livestock producers as demand for soybean oil increases availability,” ASA added.

Since RFS was put in place in 2005, American biorefineries have produced more than 250 billion gallons of ethanol, while also purchasing nearly 93 billion bushels of corn.

That equates to $425 billion in revenue to American farmers.

Growth Energy said EPA would be undoing the historic work of the Trump administration, which set record-high blending volumes for 2026-27, if it gave in to the governors’ waiver requests.

“If EPA were to grant these states the special treatment they’re asking for, it would increase fuel prices — not lower them — by reducing the amount of ethanol being blended into America’s fuel supply,” said Growth Energy CEO Emily Skor.

text:
PRESS RELEASE: Utility-scale solar developers are increasingly co-locating battery storage with new solar photovoltaic capacity. As of September 2026, over 16% of new utility-scale solar capacity added this year is co-located with operable battery storage, compared with 2% in 2017, according to data reported to EIA by operators.

Reported plans for solar additions scheduled to come online in the last three months of this year show that the share with co-located battery storage could increase to 19% this year. Longer-term plans indicate that this trend will continue, with the portion increasing to more than 30% in plans submitted for 2027 and 2028.

When operators co-locate battery storage with solar, they can direct solar electricity output to the grid or to the battery, depending on the wholesale prices. Wholesale prices in regions with large solar participation tend to fall when solar contributions are high and rise as they decrease. Plants with both solar and battery storage can manage the combined output of their generating resources to maximize their value in a changing wholesale price environment.

Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, EIA-860M, Monthly Update to the Annual Electric Generator Report

We publish unit-level generator inventory data based on our annual and monthly data collections, including information on design attributes for all utility-scale plants. Although battery storage and solar units at the same plant often enter commercial service at different times, the EIA-860 and EIA-860M data collection program tracks these developments and provides a monthly summary that can be used to identify co-located technologies.

Southwest states have higher-than-average solar capacity shares relative to their total generating capacity and also have higher levels of co-located utility-scale solar and battery capacity. As of September, 13% of the total U.S. utility-scale generating capacity is solar photovoltaic, and 18% of that is co-located with battery storage. The share of solar generation co-located with battery capacity in California, Arizona, New Mexico, and Nevada is more than double the national average.

Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, EIA-860M, Monthly Update to the Annual Electric Generator Report

Dive Brief:

BMW Group has announced a supply agreement with Samsung SDI and LG Energy Solution for cells used for its sixth-generation high-voltage batteries, the automaker announced in a press release.

LG Energy Solution will supply battery cells for BMW electric vehicles in the North America region, while Samsung SDI will supply cells for EVs manufactured in Europe, beginning in the late 2020s.

“Our global partner network with leading cell manufacturers ensures that we have a resilient, flexible and competitive battery cell supply,” Hendrik Lang, head of purchasing and quality of high-voltage batteries at BMW, said in a statement.

Dive Insight:

BMW’s goal to localize its supply chains, with cell production in close proximity to the five high-voltage battery manufacturing facilities recently built near to its vehicle plants, including sites in Irlbach-Straßkirchen in Lower Bavaria; Debrecen, Hungary; Shenyang, China; Woodruff, South Carolina; and San Luis Potosí, Mexico.

Having regional infrastructure to produce batteries near its existing facilities helps secure jobs according to Lang, while reducing the geographical distances between suppliers, batteries manufacturing facilities and vehicle assembly plants boosts the automaker’s competitiveness.

In Europe, in addition to BMW’s supply deal with Samsung SDI the automaker previously secured two additional supply agreements — with China-based battery makers CATL and EVE Energy.

“Diversifying procurement is an integral part of the BMW Group’s purchasing strategy. We aim to ensure our products’ global competitiveness and to be successful in different markets,” Nicolai Martin, member of the board of management of BMW responsible for purchasing and supplier network, said in a statement. “To achieve this, we operate as locally as possible in our value chains, leveraging the potential of our global procurement markets.”

BMW also sees the timing of these supply partnerships as key success factors. The automaker said that establishing a localized battery supply chain demands significant investment and is dependent on the willingness of global technology companies to establish local operations near its global manufacturing facilities. Having a favorable regulatory climate is also necessary, per the release.

Along with strengthening its global battery cell supply chain, the automaker has also established in-house expertise in the development, production and recycling of batteries across three EU facilities.

BMW operates a Battery Cell Competence Center in Munich where it is exploring future battery cell technologies. A second site, the Cell Manufacturing Competence Center in Parsdorf in Upper Bavaria, is studying how future cells can be produced with higher quality and maximum efficiency, per the release. The third location, the new Cell Recycling Competence Center in Salching, Germany, is recovering raw materials using a recycling concept developed by BMW, which will be used to produce new batteries.

“Our competence centers enable us to actively shape technological developments and meet our partners on an equal footing,” said Lang.

Along with establishing a localized battery cell supply chain with Samsung SDI and LG Energy Solution, BMW has completed recent investments to ramp up EV production in both the U.S. and Europe.

In February, the company announced it was investing roughly 650 million euros ($760 million) on facility upgrades at Plant Munich to produce electric vehicles built on its updated Neue Klasse platform. Internal combustion engine vehicle production is due to end at the plant by late 2027, after which BMW says the factory will only build EVs.

Over the summer, BMW completed a $1.7 billion investment project at its Plant Spartanburg in South Carolina to expand the factory and fund the construction of the Woodruff EV battery plant to support expanded electric vehicle production in the U.S.

title: The permitting bill will let the Trump administration ignore NEPA - Earthjustice
description:
But there’s also been discussion of a law BAAJA doesn’t change: the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).
So, its new NEPA analysis can’t lead to a change in the permit.
Without meaningful judicial remedies, NEPA will be virtually impossible to enforce, especially against bad faith actors like the Trump administration.
And that’s how people enforce NEPA.
Which is all to say that there are no “NEPA lawsuits.” There are only “APA lawsuits to enforce NEPA.” The limits on judicial remedies in BAAJA apply to APA lawsuits to enforce NEPA.
text:
Most people who are trying to understand the Senate’s permitting bill, the Bipartisan Affordability and American Jobs Act (BAAJA), have heard of the (many) laws it amends: things like the Federal Power Act, the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act and the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). Earthjustice posted our full analysis of those changes here.

But there’s also been discussion of a law BAAJA doesn’t change: the Administrative Procedure Act (APA). Specifically, some of the bill’s proponents are saying Senate Democrat negotiators pulled a fast one on their Republican counterparts by giving away the right to seek injunctions for NEPA violations while secretly preserving it via the APA.

I’ve litigated NEPA cases from both sides; as a defense lawyer in DOJ’s Environment and Natural Resources Division, and from my plaintiff-side perch at Earthjustice. So let me explain why the BAAJA believers are wrong:

Section 1110 of BAAJA says that “the only remedy the court may order to redress [a NEPA] violation is to remand, without vacatur or issuance of an injunction, the applicable order to the agency.” That means if an agency does a shoddy NEPA analysis while issuing a permit, the only thing a court can do is send the NEPA analysis back to the agency to do it again. The permit stands in the meantime, and the project can continue.

But wait, there’s more: Section 1401 of BAAJA says that the agency can’t revoke or modify a permit after it has been issued except under very limited exceptions. So, its new NEPA analysis can’t lead to a change in the permit. And Section 1106 exposes the agency to serious liability if it doesn’t hit tight deadlines for issuing NEPA analyses, forcing the agency to rush and eliminate any real consequences for a screwup. That’s why eliminating people’s ability to stop or improve a project really matters.

Without meaningful judicial remedies, NEPA will be virtually impossible to enforce, especially against bad faith actors like the Trump administration. And not just for wind towers or transmission lines. For coal mines, gas pipelines, clear cuts, and mining projects too. The Trump administration has already shown its willingness to blow past the law to permit these, and it will exploit BAAJA to launch an epic permitting campaign on behalf of its fossil fuel patrons.

Here’s where the BAAJA believers start throwing screwballs. First, they say that even though Section 1110 forecloses injunctive relief under NEPA, injunctive relief will remain available under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA). Courts will almost certainly reject the argument. Here’s why:

This argument starts from the premise that there is a distinction between suing under the APA and suing under NEPA. There isn’t, because you can’t sue under NEPA. Plaintiffs sue under another law: the Administrative Procedure Act. That law is the operating system for government agencies. It tells them how they have to regulate (with public input, transparency, and sound factfinding), and it requires them to follow the law. If they don’t, the APA gives people the right to sue. And that’s how people enforce NEPA.

Which is all to say that there are no “NEPA lawsuits.” There are only “APA lawsuits to enforce NEPA.”

The limits on judicial remedies in BAAJA apply to APA lawsuits to enforce NEPA. How do I know? Because Section 1110 of the bill states that its NEPA provisions apply to any claim that “seeks judicial review under any provision of Federal law” for a NEPA violation. “Any provision” includes the APA.

It’s highly unlikely that a court would get creative with its reading. The Supreme Court has consistently said that courts should give effect, if possible, to every clause and word of a statute. Therefore, judges are not going to be eager to read the bill’s sweeping limits on judicial review to apply to non-existent “NEPA lawsuits.” They’re going to recognize that Congress was eliminating vacatur and injunctive relief in APA suits to enforce NEPA.

Finally, the Trump administration is right now arguing before the Supreme Court that, even without BAAJA, the APA doesn’t allow courts to vacate anything—permits, regulations, whatever.

As someone who has personally practiced in this area of law and who works with hundreds of litigators who do so daily, I hope I’ve set the record straight.

description:

text:
Labour MPs are urging the government not to weaken its electric vehicle targets as divided cabinet ministers prepare for a crunch meeting on Thursday to thrash out a compromise.

Members of the climate and nature crisis caucus (CNCC) say ministers must not water down a legal requirement for carmakers to ensure that 80% of the vehicles they sell in 2030 are electric, saying doing so would be a backward step and “shortsighted”.

The intervention comes as Louise Haigh, the de facto deputy prime minister, prepares to meet the energy, business and transport secretaries to decide whether to change the target. A meeting planned for Wednesday has been pushed back to Thursday, according to government sources.

Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, wants to slash the target to 50%, while Heidi Alexander, the transport secretary, wants to cut it to about 60%. Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, is pushing for it to remain as close to 80% as possible.

Sources say Haigh, who is standing in for Andy Burnham after the prime minister recused himself over a potential conflict of interest, is likely to support a middle route and agree a new target of between 60% and 65%.

With a final announcement likely this month, Labour MPs are making a final push for ministers not to reduce the target, which many see as emblematic of the government’s approach to the green agenda.

Chris Hinchliff, the chair of the CCNC, wrote to Alexander on Tuesday saying that a decision to cut the 2030 target would be a “step backwards”.

“This would undermine the government’s wider net zero ambitions and our credibility as a climate leader on the world stage,” he added.

Arguing that reducing the target would undermine Burnham’s push to reindustrialise Britain, he said: “Diluting the mandate would be a backward-looking distraction from the urgent need for a coordinated industrial strategy.”

The Department for Transport has been contacted for comment.

Hinchliff is being backed by several other Labour members of the caucus. Clive Lewis, the MP for Norwich South, said: “We need more ambitious targets, not less ambitious ones. What this will say to the country is that we set these targets and then drop [them]. We need to show some consistency and ambition.”

Nadia Whittome, the MP for Nottingham East, said: “This is the government’s biggest decarbonisation policy. Watering it down would carry serious environmental consequences and it wouldn’t help the cost of living.”

Some Labour MPs from industrial areas are backing cuts to the target. Antonia Bance, the MP for Tipton and Wednesbury, said: “A 50% ZEV target by 2030 would give manufacturers a more realistic pathway while still keeping us on track for net zero.

“We can cut emissions and create the cars of the future – but we also need to protect good jobs, investment and supply chains here in the UK.”

Others in the party, however, are concerned that decisions such as weakening the EV policy and approving the Jackdaw gasfield are undermining the government’s green credentials and could risk boosting the Green party.

“Climate is not something that seems to be close to Andy [Burnham]’s heart,” said one MP. “Decisions like the EV mandate and Jackdaw develop a sense, which the public pick up, that we are not very progressive.”

BMW Group has announced a supply agreement with Samsung SDI and LG Energy Solution for cells used for its sixth-generation high-voltage batteries, the automaker announced in a press release.

“Our global partner network with leading cell manufacturers ensures that we have a resilient, flexible and competitive battery cell supply,” Hendrik Lang, head of purchasing and quality of high-voltage batteries at BMW, said in a statement.

Dive Insight:

BMW’s goal to localize its supply chains, with cell production in close proximity to the five high-voltage battery manufacturing facilities recently built near to its vehicle plants, including sites in Irlbach-Straßkirchen in Lower Bavaria; Debrecen, Hungary; Shenyang, China; Woodruff, South Carolina; and San Luis Potosí, Mexico.

Having regional infrastructure to produce batteries near its existing facilities helps secure jobs according to Lang, while reducing the geographical distances between suppliers, batteries manufacturing facilities and vehicle assembly plants boosts the automaker’s competitiveness.

In Europe, in addition to BMW’s supply deal with Samsung SDI the automaker previously secured two additional supply agreements — with China-based battery makers CATL and EVE Energy.

“Diversifying procurement is an integral part of the BMW Group’s purchasing strategy. We aim to ensure our products’ global competitiveness and to be successful in different markets,” Nicolai Martin, member of the board of management of BMW responsible for purchasing and supplier network, said in a statement. “To achieve this, we operate as locally as possible in our value chains, leveraging the potential of our global procurement markets.”

BMW also sees the timing of these supply partnerships as key success factors. The automaker said that establishing a localized battery supply chain demands significant investment and is dependent on the willingness of global technology companies to establish local operations near its global manufacturing facilities. Having a favorable regulatory climate is also necessary, per the release.

Along with strengthening its global battery cell supply chain, the automaker has also established in-house expertise in the development, production and recycling of batteries across three EU facilities.

BMW operates a Battery Cell Competence Center in Munich where it is exploring future battery cell technologies. A second site, the Cell Manufacturing Competence Center in Parsdorf in Upper Bavaria, is studying how future cells can be produced with higher quality and maximum efficiency, per the release. The third location, the new Cell Recycling Competence Center in Salching, Germany, is recovering raw materials using a recycling concept developed by BMW, which will be used to produce new batteries.

“Our competence centers enable us to actively shape technological developments and meet our partners on an equal footing,” said Lang.

Along with establishing a localized battery cell supply chain with Samsung SDI and LG Energy Solution, BMW has completed recent investments to ramp up EV production in both the U.S. and Europe.

In February, the company announced it was investing roughly 650 million euros ($760 million) on facility upgrades at Plant Munich to produce electric vehicles built on its updated Neue Klasse platform. Internal combustion engine vehicle production is due to end at the plant by late 2027, after which BMW says the factory will only build EVs.

Over the summer, BMW completed a $1.7 billion investment project at its Plant Spartanburg in South Carolina to expand the factory and fund the construction of the Woodruff EV battery plant to support expanded electric vehicle production in the U.S.

text:
Earlier this year, two rPlus Energies plants achieved commercial operation: the Green River Energy Center in Utah and Pleasant Valley Solar 2 in Idaho. By early November, both were helping secure a new loan.

PV Tech's Shreeyashi Ojha reported on November 4 that rPlus has closed a revolving credit facility of up to $450 million. It runs for three years and offers both cash borrowing and letters of credit. The money goes to developing and building the company's near-term solar and storage projects across the American West, and it is backed by cash flows from nearly 1GW of operating assets, with those two plants named first.

Seen from outside, this is one more financing headline in a busy week for solar finance. For a utility procurement lead or a data center energy buyer weighing an independent power producer as a counterparty, it shows something more useful. It shows the order in which a developer turns finished plants into the money for its next ones, and how short that cycle can be.

Construction debt first, then the revolver

Green River combines 400MW of solar with a 400MW/1,600MWh battery system, enough for four hours of storage at full output. In 2024 rPlus raised more than $1 billion in construction debt for the project. Wells Fargo Securities, Truist Securities, MUFG Bank, KeyBanc Capital Markets and Crédit Agricole Corporate and Investment Bank led that financing. PacifiCorp buys the plant's power under a power purchase agreement signed in October 2022. Pleasant Valley Solar 2 received a separate $179 million construction loan in December 2024. Groundbreaking and construction mobilisation for each project commenced in April 2025.

Both plants achieved commercial operation and completed term financing earlier this year. Construction loans are tied to one plant and carry its build risk. Once a plant is running and its debt has been moved to long-term terms, it produces cash that lenders can see. The revolver suggests that, for rPlus, that cash was enough to support borrowing at the company level within months of the plants coming online.

The lender list deserves a close look. CIBC's New York Branch served as lead left arranger and administrative agent. It syndicated the facility to six banks: Zions Capital Markets, MUFG, Wells Fargo, KeyBank, Truist Bank and National Bank of Canada. A syndicate this size suggests lenders are comfortable lending against plants that are already producing. Kirkland & Ellis advised rPlus, and Milbank advised the lenders.

Plants that reached full commercial operation on July 21 were, by early November, part of the security behind up to $450 million for rPlus Energies' next round of building. CFO Natalie Jackson called the facility evidence of the team's progress and of lenders' confidence in the company's long-term plans.

Utah, Idaho and a three-party contract

Sandbrook Capital backs rPlus, which operates as an independent power producer: it develops projects and then keeps ownership of them. Utah and Idaho are the focus of its portfolio, which totals more than 12GW of output. In Idaho, its acquisition of the Blacks Creek and Bluebird solar projects from Qcells and Mission Clean Energy took its solar and storage pipeline in the state beyond 1GW. The company is also developing three pumped hydro projects, one each in Wyoming, Nevada and Utah.

Company president Luigi Resta has described the strategy in interviews with PV Tech's sister site Energy-Storage.news. rPlus builds in rural areas that have seen little clean energy development and whose economies have long relied on coal and gas. Speaking about the pumped hydro pipeline in September 2024, he highlighted its ability to provide grid inertia as coal-fired power plants retire. He added that rPlus plans to contract project output through tolling agreements with utilities.

Pleasant Valley is the part large power buyers should study. When PV Tech's Will Norman covered the deal in May 2023, the 200MW Pleasant Valley Solar project had signed a long-term PPA with Idaho Power. Meta had arranged it through an Energy Services Agreement so it could get renewable power from the same grid that serves its new data center in Kuna, Idaho. At the time, rPlus said it was the largest solar project contracted to the Idaho Power system. The structure suggests a large buyer can secure local renewable supply by working through its utility, not only by contracting with a developer directly.

For data center operators that want new local supply in a regulated utility territory, that sequence is a real reference point. A buyer-brokered utility contract led to a plant that is now running and now financeable. And that plant is helping fund the developer's next projects in the same region.

Sizing $450 million against one Utah plant

The figure should not be overread. Green River alone took more than $1 billion in construction debt, more than twice the revolver's ceiling, so this facility will not finance a project of that size by itself. Given its three-year term and letter-of-credit capacity, it most likely covers development spending, credit support and early construction costs on near-term projects. Each large build would probably still get its own project loan. rPlus has not described the split, so that reading stays a conditional one.

A project loan looks very different, and PV Tech's Joseph Loe reported one in October. In Minya, Egypt, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) announced US$265 million in lending for a new 1.2GW solar PV plant that will sit alongside a 600MWh battery energy storage system. The EBRD itself is putting in US$160 million of that total. Bank of Jordan is providing US$75 million, and the Climate Investment Fund is adding up to US$30 million on concessional terms. The borrower is a single special purpose vehicle, Nefer Menya for Renewable Energy, and the Egyptian Electricity Transmission Company will buy the plant's power under a 25-year PPA. That loan is tied to one plant and one buyer. The rPlus revolver is tied to a group of plants and a pipeline.

What buyers in rPlus territory can ask

For utilities and large buyers in Utah and Idaho, where most of the rPlus pipeline sits, the facility gives a few concrete things to ask any developer, not only this one:

Does the developer have a company-level facility backed by plants already running, or is every project financed alone?

Does that facility include letters of credit, and does its three-year term cover the contract milestones being negotiated?

Which operating assets back it, and how long have they been running?

These are editorial suggestions, not requirements reported in the coverage. Still, they come straight from how this deal is built. A developer that can borrow against operating cash flow is in a different position from one still waiting on its first plant to come online.

The next sign to watch is where the borrowing goes. If Blacks Creek and Bluebird reach construction during the facility's term, or a pumped hydro project signs a utility tolling agreement, that will show which projects the operating plants are funding.

text:
US energy storage manufacturer SolarBridge Technology has introduced the Golden Gate STC-P135, a 135 kW bidirectional power conversion system (PCS) designed for commercial and industrial energy storage applications.

The Delaware-incorporated company, founded in 2025 and headquartered in Dallas, will showcase the modular unit at RE+ 2026 in Las Vegas ahead of planned commercial production at its Texas assembly facility in early 2027.

Power conversion systems play a critical role in battery storage by managing electricity flow between battery enclosures, host facilities, and the grid. However, evolving federal trade regulations have elevated equipment sourcing into a primary compliance hurdle for project developers. Under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, storage installations that incorporate components from a Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC) risk losing eligibility for the 30% federal Investment Tax Credit. Additionally, recent Federal Communications Commission rules restrict the import of foreign-made inverters and power conversion systems lacking pre-existing FCC equipment authorization.

Meeting FEOC and FCC requirements is the reason SolarBridge exists, stated Kemp Qiu, Chief Executive Officer of SolarBridge. Integrators need equipment that keeps their projects eligible for federal incentives, and SolarBridge is building that hardware in Dallas, Qiu said.

Modular architecture

The 135 kW unit aims to address supply constraints in the commercial and industrial sector, where power conversion equipment manufacturers have historically focused on multi-megawatt central architectures. System integrators can scale the modular units up to approximately 1 MW to match site-specific load requirements. SolarBridge also offers an Integrated AC Cabin housing up to four units to deliver 540 kW of aggregated capacity.

The Golden Gate STC-P135 features a rated AC power output of 135 kW, a maximum AC apparent power of 148.5 kVA, and a maximum efficiency of 98.7%. The unit supports a maximum DC voltage of 1500 V and a maximum DC current of 206 A. When the DC bus voltage is between 720 Vdc and 820 Vdc, the power conversion system operates in a three-phase, three-wire grid-connected configuration at 480 Vac.

The system supports both grid-tied and off-grid operations and maintains full power output at ambient temperatures up to 45°C. Its modular design allows individual unit swaps during maintenance without requiring a complete site shutdown.

Customers can pair the hardware with SolarBridge’s proprietary, AI-powered energy management system, which stores customer data on domestic servers to execute demand charge management, time-of-use arbitrage, solar self-consumption, and backup power protocols. The company plans to have its non-FEOC supply chain independently certified by a third-party law firm by early 2027 while completing FCC equipment authorization.

Dallas facility

Manufacturing equipment is scheduled for installation at the company’s Dallas facility in November 2026, with local assembly, functional testing, and software loading commencing in the first quarter of 2027. The facility is expected to employ approximately 50 workers during its initial phase, with a targeted monthly output of 1,000 to 1,500 units, representing up to 2.5 GW of annual production capacity.

Every unit leaving the facility will undergo full-power operational testing prior to shipment to engineering, procurement, and construction firms and system integrators. Select energy storage companies are scheduled to receive sample units for field testing in December 2026.

SolarBridge plans to expand its product lineup in the second quarter of 2027 with the introduction of the STU-P450, a liquid-cooled 450 kW string power conversion system. The higher-capacity model is designed to anchor turnkey utility-scale block stations up to 7.2 MW, which will coincide with a Phase II manufacturing expansion near Dallas.

text:
(Washington, D.C.) – Today, House Science, Space, and Technology Committee Chairman Brian Babin and Ranking Member Zoe Lofgren praised the Senate’s passage of the Weather Research and Forecasting Innovation Reauthorization Act of 2026 (S. 3923), introduced by Senator Ted Cruz and a bipartisan group of Senate colleagues.

Chairman Babin and Ranking Member Lofgren issued the following statements:

"Reliable weather forecasts and timely warnings are essential to protecting American lives and property," said Chairman Brian Babin. "Last year's devastating floods in Texas served as a tragic reminder of the need to better predict severe weather and communicate critical information to communities in harm's way. The Weather Act Reauthorization represents an opportunity to modernize our nation's forecasting capabilities and strengthen emergency preparedness. Building on the legislation the House Science, Space, and Technology Committee advanced last September, the Senate-passed bill reflects a bipartisan, bicameral compromise and a shared commitment to protecting American communities. I thank Chairman Cruz, Ranking Member Lofgren, Rep. Lucas, and our colleagues in both chambers for their hard work in reaching this agreement. I look forward to continuing our efforts to get this legislation across the finish line."

"This is a long time coming," said Ranking Member Zoe Lofgren. "The Weather Act Reauthorization will give NOAA the support it needs to carry out its critical mission. I want to thank Chairman Babin, my former Committee partner, Mr. Lucas, and the dedicated staff on both sides of the aisle for getting this to the finish line. The World Meteorological Organization just released its State of the Climate update, emphasizing that the supersized El Niño we are experiencing is expected to bring record heat, flooding, and drought conditions for the next year. Now more than ever, more observations and data are needed to bolster our nation's forecasting capabilities to protect lives, property, the economy, and national security. We have to ensure that NOAA has the tools, staffing, and infrastructure to help support communities prepare for and respond to disasters. This bill will help us do that. I hope the president will see the importance of this legislation and sign it into law soon."

Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee Chairman Ted Cruz and Ranking Member Maria Cantwell also emphasized the importance of the legislation following its passage:

"Today, the Senate took a pivotal step toward ensuring Americans are prepared for severe weather," said Chairman Ted Cruz. "Texans know all too well the devastation storms can bring. The lives lost in the July 4, 2025, Texas floods are a heartbreaking reminder of what is at stake. The Weather Act brings together over a dozen bipartisan bills to modernize radar systems, deliver more accurate and timely forecasts, and improve warnings so families and first responders have more time to act, no matter where they are and no matter the time of day. These improvements will help protect property and, more importantly, save lives in Texas and across the country."

"Americans are facing increasingly dangerous and costly weather disasters, and better forecasts give communities more time to prepare and get out of harm’s way," said Ranking Member Maria Cantwell. "The Weather Act will advance next-generation weather radar, modernize lifesaving warning systems, and improve forecasts for atmospheric rivers and wildfires, like the devastating fires that forced thousands to evacuate in Spokane last month. Today’s Senate passage brings us one step closer to giving forecasters, emergency managers, and communities the tools they need to save lives and protect property."

The Senate-passed legislation builds on the bipartisan Weather Act reauthorization bill advanced by the House Science, Space, and Technology Committee in September 2025. The agreement also incorporates priorities championed by House Republicans, including efforts to modernize NOAA Weather Radio, improve fog forecasting, and address gaps in weather radar coverage.

text:
A solar or wind farm in ERCOT can watch wholesale prices fall below zero, which makes a project hard to finance. Ever.green sells companies 5- to 10-year contracts for a project’s renewable energy certificates (RECs, credits for megawatt-hours of clean power), giving developers revenue they can take to the bank.

A pending greenhouse gas protocol change would phase in hourly matching, counting clean power only in the hour and on the grid where a company uses it. Backers say that cuts double counting. Ever.green Chief Executive Cris Eugster says it would steer buyers away from long-term contracts on dirtier grids. We recorded an interview with him in October.

On this week’s Energy Capital Podcast, Joshua Rhodes talks with Eugster, Ever.green’s co-founder and a former chief operating officer of CPS Energy, about how long-term contracts get clean projects built.

The rest of the conversation:

Solar for schools: REC contracts at $25 to $35 each, against $2 to $3 on the spot market, lower the power bill for 15 Wayne County, W.V., schools enough to free up money for teachers.

How the deals work: Ever.green signs as the developer’s one counterparty and splits a project’s RECs among several companies, so no developer negotiates with five sets of corporate lawyers. “Contracted revenue is like gold,” Eugster says.

Keeping an old wind farm running: how REC revenue supports the repowered Ocotillo wind farm in Big Spring, Texas, while the owners sells power at merchant prices.

Proving the money mattered: Eugster says no one can prove a project wouldn’t have been built anyway, so Ever.green asks developers to attest its contract is material.

Gamers as buyers: how the platform SuperPower pooled player subscriptions behind the 110 MW Three W solar farm in Hill County, and Eugster’s hint that other industries will follow next year.

Who carries price risk: why Eugster says a fixed REC price lets corporate buyers back new projects without taking on the price swings of power purchase agreement.

Plus: the data center race and its emissions, CPS Energy’s 771 MW Save for Tomorrow Energy Plan efficiency program, ERCOT’s batch zero study, Eugster’s path from MIT and McKinsey to Houston City Hall, and nuclear.

How are rates not gonna go up? How are resources not gonna be used, whether it’s water or environment? I think are super big questions, and you’re trying to solve these questions in a environment where there’s just a race to build more and faster. If you’re slow, you’re gonna lose a seat at the table. And so I would hope that there would be an interest, whether it’s a requirement or just self-interest, to basically build these data centers in a way that minimizes impacts to our environment and our communities. And Michael Webber and I have talked about this. There’s so much money that they should be able to do this the right way. You know? And I’d love to get your take on it. The challenge is the velocity and the competitiveness and the race, that makes it really hard to kind of be thoughtful in how do you do this thing the right way.

Joshua Rhodes: Yeah, no, for sure. I mean, I think that bleeds into like, you know, even community pushback and things on data centers. A lot of it is just this velocity, right? Like I model the electricity grid all the time, and I often make the joke, I’ll model it out as far into the future as you believe the price of natural gas will be. And historically, it’s like 2 percent load growth, and supply chains were built around, you know, supporting 2 percent load growth, at least at ERCOT. Other places a little bit flatter. But yeah, I mean, this is like, you know, 5x the grid in five years. It took us 100 years to get to 91 GW, and you wanna get to 500 GW in five years. Like just ain’t gonna happen, right? You just can’t get that much steel in the ground. Even if we, you know, cloned you a few times, we’re still not gonna get that much steel in the ground. I think it is some of that velocity, right? This whole Batch Zero process is trying to inject some discipline into that. Some of the pauses and the audits and things like that are trying to like, you know, inject sanity into that space, and so hopefully we can know what’s real so that we can actually build the infrastructure around, and the policy around, you know, what is real versus, like, these numbers that nobody believes. But we don’t know what the right number is. And you said earlier, it’s like, you know, business would rather have bad policy than uncertain policy, right? It’s just like at least know where your goalposts are. Even if they’re 200 yards that way, you’ll figure out how to kick the ball through it. But like, you know, if they’re just moving all the time, that’s a tougher one.

Cris Eugster: Yeah. I feel like if we could solve the velocity problem, I think we could figure out the power issue. I think if we don’t solve the velocity issue... And like you said, you know, there are some pretty good movements, and again, led by Texas on some of the Batch Zero and, you know, the slowing things down a bit to get things right. I think if we had more time, the technology’s there to do this thing the right way. And even some of the simple stuff like, “Let’s just do a combined cycle behind the meter.” Like, these data center, they’re gonna value the chips, not the combined cycles. If those chips are saying, “I gotta back off power,” like, you know, in a microsecond, that turbine’s gonna have it— Like, there are fundamental issues on even straightforward designs that I don’t think people have fully thought through, again, because of velocity. They’re just trying to get stuff done.

Joshua Rhodes: I think a lot of like conceptual behind the meter projects have run into the physical limitations of steel and the ability to move, right? It’s just like software’s one thing, steel’s another, right? In terms of being able to move, and it’s like, you know, getting those... If you want five nines of reliability, a single power plant’s not gonna give you that. I don’t care how new it is or how good it is, like, you’re not getting that. That’s why we have a grid, right? It’s like to share that risk around, give you that space. You know, it’s probably a lot easier to do this in a growth environment than like a declining environment, right? Like trying out new structures and projects, it sounds like y’all are doing, like it’s probably easier to try that out in a sector that’s growing versus one that’s stagnating, wouldn’t you say?

Cris Eugster: Yeah, 100 percent. You know, you see some of the, you know, these PPAs from the nuclear side. Like nuclear’s always been a very interesting kind of zero emission resource, but how do you put capital that perceives it as risky? How do you get the regulations to be more efficient? I think because this is a growth environment, I think nuclear’s back in play, which I think is exciting.

Joshua Rhodes: Yeah. No, I mean, I feel like, I think almost anything’s in play right now that is able to make a megawatt hour of electricity, is a really interesting space.

Cris Eugster: I think being in a growth environment is really good, and I think we can be thoughtful and we can do a lot of good things, try a lot of good things. I think the challenge is if we’re running too fast and lose our kind of foresight and strategy and perspective, I think that’s where we get into trouble.

Joshua Rhodes: Yeah. Absolutely. Well, Cris Eugster, thank you for coming on the Energy Capital Podcast.

name: EPA
title: EPA Oil and Gas Enforcement Drops in New Mexico Under Trump - Capital & Main
description:
Capital & Main examined 170 entries tied to oil and gas companies filed on the EPA’s enforcement and compliance webpage for New Mexico.
“EPA enforcement has not declined,” he said.
Recent studies linked oil and gas operations to radioactive airborne plumes and other air pollution in the Permian Basin, the nation’s largest oil field.
While oil and gas enforcement numbers have dropped, the EPA has not been idle in other areas in New Mexico.
Since then, outside watchdogs have called the numbers misleading — primarily because the EPA under Trump is taking credit for work done during the Biden administration.
text:
A review of an Environmental Protection Agency database of enforcement and compliance documents for New Mexico shows a drop in cases dealing with oil and gas operations since the start of the second administration of President Donald Trump.

Capital & Main examined 170 entries tied to oil and gas companies filed on the EPA’s enforcement and compliance webpage for New Mexico. Those entries include inspection reports, information requests and enforcement documents dating back to 2012.

Oil and gas-related enforcement entries bounced around in the single digits before peaking in the first two years of the administration of President Joe Biden: 26 entries for 2021 and 24 for 2022. Ten entries were listed for 2025, most in the opening months of the Trump administration before the agency announced a 23% reduction in its workforce. Eight were recorded in 2026 through Nov. 4.

Cliff Villa, a professor of law at the University of New Mexico School of Law, said he’s noticed a change at the agency.

“EPA has lost a lot of people, including a lot of institutional knowledge,” Villa said. “That’s not easy to replace.” Before joining the university, Villa worked for more than 20 years as an EPA attorney under both Democratic and Republican administrations.

Oil and gas revenues have swelled New Mexico’s coffers to record levels in recent years. At the same time, such operations have directly and indirectly generated record amounts of hard-to-dispose-of oilfield wastewater, raised the specter of $1.6 billion in cleanup costs for abandoned wells and fouled the air in the oilfields. That last issue — cleaning New Mexico’s air — has been the EPA’s main goal in New Mexico in recent years, and the need for help is reflected in how oilfield pollution cases can tie up state resources for years.

Capital & Main sent questions about the declining numbers of enforcement and compliance documents to the EPA’s regional office in Dallas, which oversees New Mexico operations. They were answered by Michael Bastasch, deputy director for regional media and programs in the EPA’s Washington headquarters. He called questions about declining numbers “a baseless narrative.

“EPA enforcement has not declined,” he said.

“EPA has lost a lot of people, including a lot of institutional knowledge.”

~ Cliff Villa, professor of law at University of New Mexico.

Bastasch put the responsibility for policing the oil and gas industry on New Mexico: “New Mexico has delegated authority under the Clean Air Act, which means they take the lead on air quality enforcement within their borders.”

Historically, air quality issues have been the primary cause for EPA oil and gas investigations in New Mexico, and the New Mexico Environment Department does have an agreement — known as a State Implementation Plan — that allows it to take the lead on federal Clean Air Act investigations. Those investigations are generally conducted in partnership with the EPA, not in lieu of the EPA.

James Kenney, the New Mexico Environment Department secretary, worked for years at the EPA before beginning his state job under Democratic Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham. In a 2022 interview with Capital & Main, Kenney said the EPA wasn’t allowed in New Mexico under the previous governor, Republican Susana Martinez, and “the first thing we did is invite EPA in.”

The working relationship has changed since then.

“Notably, [the Environment Department] has seen a decrease in joint enforcement actions,” said Drew Goretzka, director of communications at the New Mexico Environment Department. He said that past work took the form of joint inspections, flyovers using optical gas imaging and complicated enforcement actions — areas in which the EPA is able to bring its much larger workforce and money to bear.

For example, in 2019 and 2020, the EPA conducted airborne inspections of New Mexico’s oilfields on behalf of the state. The flights uncovered dozens of leaking facilities, though it resulted in only slow-rolling enforcement actions against a few of the polluting companies.

Asked if flights might return in the future, Bastasch said, “EPA does not comment on whether inspections and compliance monitoring activities will occur.”

Kyle Tisdel, senior attorney and climate and energy program director at the Western Environmental Law Center, said the fallout of decreasing EPA enforcement further burdens state agencies “both in identifying the wells and operators chronically violating emissions standards, and then prosecuting those violations and holding individual operators responsible.”

Goretzka also said that the EPA’s “retreat” adds further compliance and enforcement costs to the state.

“EPA’s lack of enforcement in the Permian Basin makes it more difficult to protect New Mexicans’ air quality.”

~ Drew Goretzka, director of communications at the New Mexico Environment Department.

“EPA’s lack of enforcement in the Permian Basin makes it more difficult to protect New Mexicans’ air quality,” he said.

Recent studies linked oil and gas operations to radioactive airborne plumes and other air pollution in the Permian Basin, the nation’s largest oil field. Asked about the findings, Bastasch dismissed work that was “based on studies performed on data from the Biden Administration that purport to show that air pollution in New Mexico comes from New Mexico.”

Bastasch’s responses exhibited a recurring anti-Biden administration theme, with answers that regularly name-checked the former president.

When asked if the reductions reflect the Trump administration’s plan to “unleash American energy,” he said, “Enforcement will be consistent with the law and the rule of law, unlike during the Biden Administration.”

Bastasch did not respond when asked how or when the Biden administration’s actions were inconsistent with the law.

While oil and gas enforcement numbers have dropped, the EPA has not been idle in other areas in New Mexico. In May, the agency issued around 60 warnings to small water co-ops across the state for failing to file paperwork identifying the kinds of pipes in their systems, a requirement under the Safe Water Drinking Act.

Bastasch said that the EPA concluded more than 2,300 civil enforcement cases between Jan. 20, 2025, and Jan. 19, 2026, “a ten year high — over 400 cases more than in the final year of the Biden Administration.” But those are national figures and not specific to New Mexico.

The EPA began promoting the numbers in March. Since then, outside watchdogs have called the numbers misleading — primarily because the EPA under Trump is taking credit for work done during the Biden administration.

For example, in early September, the EPA issued Compliance Agreements and Final Orders against two of New Mexico’s top-10 oil and gas producers: Chevron USA Inc. for $440,341 and Permian Resources Operating LLC for $691,253. The cases reflect violations found during on-site inspections in 2024 during the Biden administration.

“These fines are not surprising, nor is the fact that the violations were identified by the Biden administration,” said Tisdel, the Western Environmental Law Center lawyer.

He added that state and federal agencies rely on self-reporting by oil and gas companies for day-to-day monitoring. But, “as these fines indicate, there can be substantial gaps between what is reported by industry and the emission violations found here,” he said.

The EPA has worked in New Mexico this year, too. The agency entered into expedited settlement agreements with Occidental Permian Ltd. at its North Hobbs Plant and with Enterprise Products Partners LP at its Dark Horse Treating Facility for not filing required risk management plans on time. Those plans, updated every five years, are used to alert first responders and nearby residents to possible environmental threats.

Settlement agreements are a quick way for companies to resolve violations by paying a fine and promising to fix the underlying problem. According to the agreement documents, Occidental Permian filed its plan a week late in May and paid a $1,600 fine. Enterprise Products Partners filed roughly three weeks late in June and paid a $2,000 fine.

What comes next for the EPA and New Mexico is an open question.

“It will be great again,” predicted Villa, the University of New Mexico professor. “In the meantime, there are many other opportunities for enforcement, including states and tribes and local governments and non-governmental organizations.”

“But my sense is that out of the ruins of this moment, there will be opportunity.”

~ Kyle Tisdel, climate and energy program director at the Western Environmental Law Center.

Villa also highlighted provisions in federal statutes allowing citizen lawsuits where people and organizations can sue companies or the federal government for violating air and water regulations.

In 2022, the conservation group WildEarth Guardians sued OXY USA and OXY USA WTP LP — both subsidiaries of Occidental Petroleum Corp. — over violations of the Clean Air Act. The group said the suit resulted in millions of dollars’ worth of facility upgrades, a $500,000 civil penalty and another $500,000 penalty “to support air quality and public health improvement projects in southeast New Mexico” that eventually resulted in a new mobile air monitoring station for the New Mexico Environment Department.

The dramatic changes at the EPA “won’t simply be reversed by a future administration,” Tisdel cautioned. “But my sense is that out of the ruins of this moment, there will be opportunity … to imagine a future and regulatory and enforcement framework that is commensurate to the mounting crises we face.”

“It does create opportunities, though, for students who are in school today, including my own students,” Villa said. “They will have opportunities to be a part of a rebuilding of the federal government. And I see my job right now as a teacher as helping prepare them for that rebuilding.”

title: BMW Group localises battery cell supply chains in Europe and US - Automotive Logistics
description:
Combining regional supply chains with a globally diversified supplier network, BMW Group has announced new contracts with two additional cell suppliers to localise battery production in both Europe and the US.
According to BMW Group, these additional manufacturers will supply the group from their established plants in the respective regions from the late 2020s onwards.
"Through our battery cell partnerships, we are actively strengthening value creation in Europe and the US."
Local battery assembly BMW's "local for local" approach extends beyond battery sourcing to battery assembly too.
For example, at BMW's Battery Cell Competence Center (BCCC) in Munich, experts are exploring new cell technologies for future high-voltage batteries.
text:
As demand for battery electric vehicles (BEVs) continues to grow and BMW Group transitions towards production of more electric vehicles, the automaker is taking a "local for local" approach to sourcing the sixth-generation (Gen6) high-voltage batteries used in its Neue Klasse vehicles.

Combining regional supply chains with a globally diversified supplier network, BMW Group has announced new contracts with two additional cell suppliers to localise battery production in both Europe and the US.

Read more: How nearshoring and battery localisation are reshaping Europe’s EV supply chain amid shifting demand, Chinese competition, and policy shifts

With battery investments in flux, Europe’s OEMs push for local supply chains amid geopolitical shifts and Chinese EV competition.

Samsung SDI will be added to the list of manufacturers supplying BMW Group with Gen6 batteries in Europe, as well as existing suppliers CATL and EVE Energy. Meanwhile in the US, a new contract will see these batteries also supplied by LG Energy Solution. According to BMW Group, these additional manufacturers will supply the group from their established plants in the respective regions from the late 2020s onwards.

"Our global partner network with leading cell manufacturers ensures that we have a resilient, flexible and competitive battery cell supply,” commented Hendrik Lang, head of purchasing and quality of high-voltage batteries at BMW.

In addition, Nicolai Martin, member of the board of management of BMW responsible for purchasing and supplier network, noted that diversifying procurement is an integral part of the group's purchasing strategy. He emphasised that being successful in different markets around the world and ensuring the global competitiveness of its products are top priorities from BMW Group.

"To achieve this, we operate as locally as possible in our value chains, leveraging the potential of our global procurement markets," said Martin. "Through our battery cell partnerships, we are actively strengthening value creation in Europe and the US."

Local battery assembly

BMW's "local for local" approach extends beyond battery sourcing to battery assembly too. Currently, production of BMW's Gen6 high-voltage batteries takes place at five recently built production facilities strategically located near its vehicle plants in regions around the world.

By locating these battery assembly facilities in close proximity to existing plants, BMW Group has said it is able to strengthen regional infrastructure and existing facilities, while helping to secure jobs.

The group also noted that this strategy allows it to reduce the distances between its suppliers, its battery facilities and its vehicle plants. In doing so, BMW Group can keep down transport costs, avoid carbon emissions from long-distance shipments and limit the group's exposure to transport-related disruptions.

Upskilling for the whole battery life cycle

Alongside the diversification of suppliers and its investment in building regional battery ecosystems, BMW Group has also focused on building comprehensive in-house expertise in the development, production and recycling of battery cells.

As part of this effort, the group has established a range of competence centres across the Germany state of Bavaria, each exploring different parts of the battery life cycle. For example, at BMW's Battery Cell Competence Center (BCCC) in Munich, experts are exploring new cell technologies for future high-voltage batteries.

And at the group's Cell Manufacturing Competence Center (CMCC) in Parsdorf, research is focused on methods of producing the highest-quality battery cells with the most efficient use of resources.

BMW Group is also working with its partner Encory to build and operate a new Cell Recycling Competence Center (CRCC) in Salching. Here, valuable raw materials will be recovered and reintegrated into the group's production process, using an "innovative direct recycling concept" that BMW Group has developed.

Ford Motor Co. leaders want the world to know that the automaker's electric vehicle batteries last a really long time.
