text:
Concerns about EV battery longevity and replacement cost remain a significant hurdle for many potential buyers.

Ford's data was inspired by a customer who drove over 400,000 miles on the original Mach-E battery.

Industry experts note that this level of battery durability is impressive but standard across most modern electric vehicles.

Ford Motor Co. leaders want the world to know that the automaker's electric vehicle batteries last a really long time.

But that fact doesn't necessarily make Ford a standout in the car industry where battery technology has advanced across the board where most automakers can assure consumers that, if you buy an EV, you won't need to replace its battery for hundreds of thousands of miles, industry experts said.

"Pretty much all EVs are connected and (automakers) collect telemetry data on things like battery state of health and charging patterns in addition to capturing the data when cars come in for service. So they all have a pretty good idea of how batteries are holding up," Sam Abuelsamid, vice president of market research at Telemetry, told the Detroit Free Press. "They typically have 8-10 year/100,000 mile warranties on the battery, so everyone wants to make sure they'll actually last that long."

So on Nov. 9, Ford decided to share its tests publicly to show that its batteries do last that long.

The Dearborn-based automaker issued a media release and published a blog titled: "Five years in, Mustang Mach-E battery data shows what real world electric vehicle durability looks like." The blog points to customer David Blenkle, a Santa Cruz, Californian who runs a small private car service, for inspiring Ford's battery study. Blenkle has driven a whopping 400,000-plus miles in his 2022 Mustang Mach-E on the original battery.

"His battery health has remained strong through unusually high-mileage use," Kevin Vander Laan, Ford's technical leader of high-voltage battery cells and systems, wrote in the blog of Blenke. "His experience gave our team a chance to compare one exceptional ownership case with what we are seeing across the broader fleet. The bigger question was if David’s experience reflected a broader pattern. So, we decided to look back at the Mustang Mach-E owners who started it all: the Class of 2021."

Ford said it found that Blenkle was not an outlier. Other Mach-E owners who clocked high mileage over five years of ownership also retained significant battery strength. Ford said as of August this year, across its full 36,000 2021 Mach-E lineup in the U.S. and Canada, its EV batteries maintain an average of 90% health at 100,000 miles. That means the high-voltage battery pack has lost 10% of its original energy storage capacity, but can still hold and deliver 90% of the range it had when the car was new.

It's impressive, but it is also industry standard, experts said.

"While I haven't seen much third-party data on Mach-E battery durability, other sources have published lots of data on how batteries are holding up, notably recurrentauto.com," Abuelsamid said. "Except for early Nissan Leafs that had air-cooled batteries and a lot of early degradation, most EVs have somewhere between 90% and 95% capacity at 100,000 miles. So Ford's numbers are right in the ballpark."

Expert: Ford's results are likely legit

In fact, Abuelsamid said the Mach-E uses basically the same LG batteries found in a lot of other vehicles. He noted that outside of "some fires triggered by manufacturing flaws," such as the Chevrolet Bolt and Porsche Taycan, "the (batteries) are pretty durable."

While having a manufacturer rate its own products is not the best measure of quality, it's a starting point for reassuring consumers that EVs are durable, Sam Fiorani, vice president of global vehicle forecasting at AutoForecast Solutions, told the Detroit Free Press.

"Among the biggest issues for consumers contemplating an EV purchase is the cost and longevity of the battery," Fiorani said. "The fear that a battery will have a catastrophic problem requiring a fix potentially costing over $10,000 is holding many people back from making the plunge. With so many EVs on the road today, proof of how they are holding up can now be measured and the results used to calm the fears of buyers."

Fiorani said increasingly there are independent companies conducting similar battery testing and comparing the results across brands. Therefore, Ford releasing its data publicly means that "if these outside companies provide results dramatically different than that of the manufacturer, like Ford, it can result in loss of consumer trust. But, in this case, it’s unlikely that Ford is putting its thumb on the scale."

Fiorani added that studies from AVILOO in Europe — an Australian technology company specializing in battery diagnostics — and Standford University in the United States have provided similar industry-wide results, proving that modern EV batteries do not degrade as quickly as the industry initially expected.

"Degradation of about 2% per year falls in line with Ford’s results," Fiorani said.

Mach-E drivers nearly made it to Neptune

Ford spokesman Jake Bley told the Detroit Free Press that the automaker validated its battery health data internally with its high-voltage battery engineering team and then had it "reviewed by peers and confirmed for public release."

Ford said its 36,000 Mach-E's have driven a collective total of about two billion all-electric miles across the United States and Canada in the past five years — that is almost enough miles to reach the planet Neptune.

Bley said Ford's data showed that more than 2,000 of its Mach-Es on the road today have passed 100,000 miles, averaging better than 91% battery health, and more than 30 have passed 200,000 miles while averaging 88%.

Most of the vehicles fall between 87% to 97% battery health, the average being 92%, indicating to Ford engineers that there is a consistent and positive pattern across Ford's real-world fleet.

Ford's Vander Laan said this data matters to Ford primarily because "long-term battery health remains one of the biggest questions for many people considering an electric vehicle, and real-world data like this helps make that conversation more concrete."

In the meantime, Ford uses field data such as this to inform current and future electric vehicle programs. Ford is preparing to launch its new Universal Electric Vehicle platform at its Louisville Assembly Plant in Kentucky. The first EV off that new architecture will be the all-electric midsize pickup, Fathom. It will be followed by a family of more EVs, and they will use a different battery than the LG in the Mach-E, Abuelsamid said.

"Mach-E uses LG pouch cells with NMC cathode chemistry," Abuelsamid said. "UEV is using prismatic cells with LFP cathode. LFP should last five to 10 times as long."

Until then, Ford's Vander Laan offered a few habits that help support long-term battery health. First is charging on Level 2 at home for daily driving and saving DC fast charging for the days you need it. Also, help manage temperature extremes when you can such as parking in the shade in the summer. Finally, follow the charge-level recommendations in the Ford App for your specific vehicle. The recommendations are designed for that car's battery system.

name: Clean Energy
title: Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband's speech at the Clean Energy Transition & Electrification ...
description:
And the question for all countries is: do we learn the lessons of this age, or do we stick our heads in the sand?
And it’s right to say it’s only possible because of the extraordinary transformation we’ve seen over the last two decades in the price of clean energy.
But we also recognise that it’s in our self-interest as a country for all countries to invest in electrification.
And I just want to say one very simple thing: as a Foreign Minister, this is a national security issue.
And it’s time that all Foreign Ministers, Prime Ministers, saw it as a national security issue, because whether it’s food security, infrastructure security, population displacement, these have profound national security implications.
text:
It is right to start with what our populations are seeing, which is more conflict across the world than at any time since World War II, climate breakdown affecting so many countries, and the cost-of-living crisis in food and fuel prices.

And the question for all countries is: do we learn the lessons of this age, or do we stick our heads in the sand?

And we need to learn the lessons.

The first and most profound lesson, and we’ve seen it with the Iran war, with Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, is there can’t be security while you are dependent on fossil fuels, because you are subject to the fossil-fuel rollercoaster that you don’t control from geopolitical conflict.

For Britain, half of our recessions since the 1970s have been caused by fossil-fuel crises, and obviously people are being hit very hard.

Even the world’s largest fossil-fuel producer, the United States, is not immune. Vice President Vance has said the Iran war has had real effects on voters.

And what’s true for the US is even more true for fossil-fuel importers, representing 75% of the world’s population.

So, lesson one: don’t believe that fossil-fuel reliance can give us security, because the facts show otherwise.

Second, unlike in the past, there is an alternative to fossil fuels: clean-energy electrification.

I applaud the Turkish Presidency for their vision in putting this idea at the centre of COP31. And it’s right to say it’s only possible because of the extraordinary transformation we’ve seen over the last two decades in the price of clean energy.

And that’s thanks to many people around the room, public and private sectors working together. Costs are plummeting.

The UK is determined to lead by example.

We have a mission for clean power by 2030, new petrol and diesel cars phased out by 2030, and a Warm Homes Plan to electrify heating.

But we also recognise that it’s in our self-interest as a country for all countries to invest in electrification.

So we are announcing an investment of £200 million over the next four years through the Private Infrastructure Development Group, PIDG, which will help to mobilise an estimated $1 billion per year in private capital to support climate-resilient infrastructure in emerging economies across Africa and Asia.

My third and final point is the other part of the perfect storm, which is climate breakdown.

And I just want to say one very simple thing: as a Foreign Minister, this is a national security issue.

And it’s time that all Foreign Ministers, Prime Ministers, saw it as a national security issue, because whether it’s food security, infrastructure security, population displacement, these have profound national security implications.

And resilience will be very much part of our chairmanship of the G20 next year.

The final thing I’ll say: it’s very inspiring to see all of the people in this room and at this COP. Not just because it’s old friends, but because it is a sign of multilateralism: countries working together in their own interests.

And we owe it to the citizens of our countries to do this, to learn the right lessons, and to understand that electrification is the future.

We must make the era of clean-energy electrification come of age.

Thank you so much.

text:
A California company’s plans for a medical radiopharmaceuticals plant in the central Indiana LEAP District is facing questions over whether it could possibly open the door for a nuclear power generation site.

A contract between the Indiana Economic Development Corp. and a subsidiary of Oklo Inc. for land purchases lists several possible uses for the site near Lebanon, including “nuclear power generation, radioisotope production, research and development.”

Democratic legislators challenged an IEDC official during a State Budget Committee meeting Tuesday over the company’s intentions during discussion of the agency’s request for $20 million toward expanding the LEAP District by 185 acres for the project.

Mark Wasky, the IEDC’s senior vice president, told the committee that discussions with Oklo had “focused on radioisotopes,” which are medications that contain a small amount of a radioactive substance.

That did not satisfy Democratic legislators about the future options for the company that describes itself on its website as an “advanced nuclear technology company developing fast fission power plants” along with “building a domestic supply chain for critical isotopes and advanced nuclear fuel recycling capabilities.”

“Can you look us in the eye and say that you’re not going to come back over here and tell us that there will be nuclear generation discussion by that project that could feed into data centers into the LEAP project?” asked Sen. Fady Qaddoura, D-Indianapolis.

Wasky replied that nuclear power plants had not been discussed with the IEDC.

“I can’t say today whether or not those conversations may occur in the future, but we have not had any conversations about building power to serve the data center within the LEAP District,” Wasky said.

A few LEAP District opponents protested outside Tuesday’s committee meeting. The district aimed at attracting high-tech businesses now spans some 6,700 acres and has faced persistent public criticism as the state has poured about $1 billion into its development.

Wasky said Oklo’s project would still need to gain approval from Lebanon city and zoning officials before proceeding with construction.

But Rep. Ed DeLaney, D-Indianapolis, criticized what he described as insufficient public disclosure about the development proposal, which was listed on the Budget Committee’s agenda as “Project Phoenix.”

“This is not what people would call a confidence building method and that’s a real problem,” DeLaney told Wasky. “We need confidence in the IEDC.”

Santa Clara, California-based Oklo told the Capital Chronicle that it is considering the LEAP District for a potential “isotope production and processing facility focused initially on producing materials used in targeted cancer treatments.”

“We’re still evaluating the project and engaging with the local community, and no final commitment to build in Indiana has been made,” Oklo spokeswoman Bonita Chester said in an email.

Chester did not address a question about the possibility of electricity generation at the site.

The Budget Committee voted 4-1 to approve the IEDC’s request, with support coming from Sens. Ryan Misher, R-Mishawaka, and David Niezgodski, D-South Bend; Rep. Jeff Thompson, R-Lizton, and State Budget Director Chad Ranney.

Rep. Greg Porter, D-Indianapolis, voted against approval, joining the objections from Qaddoura and DeLaney, who are non-voting members of the committee.

Porter said he saw no harm in waiting until the committee’s next meeting in December to take action for greater transparency.

“I’m asking that we stop this or slow it down,” Porter said. “They can come back and look at it again.”

This story has been updated with comment from Oklo Inc.

text:
The old saying, “Waste not, want not,” rings especially true in America's Battery Belt.

Today, roughly 10% of the material used to make an electric-vehicle battery ends up as manufacturing scrap. But a proposed $110 million project aims to turn that scrap back into material for producing new batteries right here in the U.S. — and do so in as little as seven days.

Behind the effort are two NJIT alumni at Princeton NuEnergy (PNE): co-founder and CEO Chao Yan (M.S. '13, Ph.D. '17) and founding partner and chief operating officer Peng Zhao (M.S. '13).

Since its startup beginnings in 2019, PNE has grown into a pioneer in direct battery recycling — reusing valuable cathode material from scrap instead of breaking it down to recover its metals — just as U.S. battery manufacturing has taken off.

The company has now been selected to negotiate for $50 million in U.S. Department of Energy grant support for a planned facility capable of rejuvenating 3,000 metric tons of cathode material annually.

“No one has moved direct recycling to this scale yet,” Zhao said. “We're bringing this technology to the commercial world with this first-of-its-kind facility. The goal is to build a true domestic closed loop — keeping these critical battery materials in the U.S. and bringing down their cost.”

Cathode material in manufacturing scrap can be essentially brand new, Zhao says, but conventional recycling shreds it into “black mass” to recover metals such as lithium, nickel and cobalt.

Zhao estimates U.S. manufacturing scrap and end-of-life batteries generate roughly 100,000 metric tons of battery waste annually, much of it requiring further processing overseas.

PNE's patented Cathode-to-Cathode® process instead uses low-temperature plasma to clean and restore cathode material for reuse.

“Think about it like you have a dirty spoon,” Zhao explained. “The traditional recycling process is like taking that spoon, melting it down and extracting the metals one by one, then sending them overseas to make a new spoon and importing it back so you can use it. What we do is more like simply putting the spoon in a dishwasher. The cathode material is still good — it just has impurities. We use plasma to clean the surface, remove those impurities, polish it and use it again right away.”

Building the Closed Loop

Above: Engineers oversee battery recycling operations at Princeton NuEnergy's facility in Chester, South Carolina. Credit: Princeton NuEnergy.

PNE plans to save U.S. battery scrap from that globe-spanning journey. Construction of the proposed facility is targeted for early 2027, with the roughly 30-month project expected to begin operating in 2029.

“Battery factories produce manufacturing scrap every day,” Zhao said. “We take that scrap, rejuvenate the cathode material and give it back to our customer to make a new battery. This closed loop is within the United States.”

A DOE-backed study with Argonne National Laboratory found PNE's rejuvenated cathode material could cost about 45% less than comparable virgin material.

“It’s also a national security issue,” Zhao said. “If you fully rely on foreign countries for critical battery materials and something happens geopolitically, how can you build your EV? How can you build your data center? How can you build your defense applications?”

“A lot of direct recycling is still at the lab scale,” Zhao said. “Some approaches use organic solvents that become difficult to handle safely at this scale; others are very expensive. We use low-temperature plasma to remove impurities from cathode active materials, reducing costs and minimizing waste.”

Yan said scaling the technology comes down in part to how PNE builds its facilities. More than 90% of the equipment is commercially available, while the company's proprietary components are designed in modules that can be replicated as production needs grow.

“Depending on the capacity required, we replicate these modules and deploy them in parallel to meet each facility’s production needs,” Yan said. “This modular design allows us to deploy the technology quickly at different scales to meet customers’ varying capacity needs.”

PNE's next Cathode-to-Cathode® facility would also allow other battery manufacturers to validate the company's process before potentially bringing it to their own sites.

For Yan, reaching 3,000 metric tons annually would mark a significant step toward bringing direct recycling into widespread industrial use.

“This facility has the potential to redefine how critical battery materials are recovered and reintroduced into the U.S. supply chain,” Yan said. “More importantly, it establishes a commercially viable model we can replicate across the country.”

PNE plans as many as 10 production lines around the country over the next decade, totaling 30,000 metric tons of annual capacity.

“This is a seed,” Zhao said. “We need to let the seed grow, then go to 10 branches.”

It's a scale far beyond what Zhao envisioned when Yan, whom he knew from their days sharing a dorm at NJIT, began working on his plasma-based purification technology under chemistry professor Lev Krasnoperov nearly a decade ago.

Zhao had taken a different path. An NJIT career fair internship with Panasonic North America became a 10-year career, eventually taking him to a senior manager role in technology commercialization at the Panasonic Innovation Center in Harrison, New Jersey.

When Yan approached him around 2018 about using plasma to recycle batteries, Zhao saw its potential but wasn't convinced the market was ready.

By 2020, the market was catching up. Major automakers were accelerating their electric-vehicle plans and U.S. battery manufacturing was expanding. Zhao left Panasonic the following year to join PNE full time.

Since then, PNE has built toward commercial scale — from early pilot work to its direct recycling line in Texas and a commercial-scale black mass production facility in South Carolina. Zhao said the company has also raised $38 million in equity financing and received or been selected for more than $73 million in federal grant support, including the $50 million DOE funding still under negotiation.

The $110 million facility would be its biggest step yet.

“I always believe we want to do the right thing at the right time with the right people,” Zhao said. “Right now, I feel we have all three.”

title: Prime Minister hails major investment in UK renewables - GOV.UK
description:
Alongside making an important contribution to domestic energy security, clean, homegrown power will protect the UK from global energy shocks raising energy prices and bring down bills for good.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: This major investment in UK renewables is a vote of confidence for building in Britain.
Because for me, a clean energy future is one that brings down bills.
Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said: This is another vote of confidence in British homegrown, clean energy.
Investment in offshore wind and clean power is creating quality jobs and rebuilding industry, while delivering the clean power we need to lower bills and reach net zero.
text:
Thousands of jobs will be supported as two major offshore wind projects mark progress towards delivering clean homegrown energy for millions of homes, ahead of the Prime Minister’s travel to the COP31 Leaders’ Summit in Türkiye.

Energy company RWE, together with global investment firm KKR, have announced a total investment of £12 billion, believed to be the biggest of its kind in UK history to date. It will give the green light to its Vanguard West and Vanguard East offshore wind farms, set to be operational by 2030 and delivering clean, secure, homegrown power to homes and businesses that will protect families from global fossil fuel price shocks.

The investment comes as the Prime Minister heads to the COP31 summit, underlining how Britain’s action on climate change and clean energy is bringing good, skilled jobs and new opportunities for local people in industrial and coastal communities across the country.

On top of bolstering the UK’s green energy future, the investment will support more than 2,400 jobs during construction and operation, and once operational, the wind farms will have the capacity to supply the equivalent of around three million UK homes. Alongside making an important contribution to domestic energy security, clean, homegrown power will protect the UK from global energy shocks raising energy prices and bring down bills for good.

The decision marks a major milestone for the project, with the developers now making their final investment commitment to deliver the projects. Onshore works are already well advanced, with construction offshore set to begin in early 2027.

The financing for these projects includes a £1 billion investment from the UK’s National Wealth Fund - the UK’s publicly-owned policy bank that aims to drive more than £100 billion of finance into the UK economy. This investment, the National Wealth Fund’s largest in offshore wind to date, demonstrates how the right use of public money can help unlock private investment and generate a return for the taxpayer, as well as powering homes with clean homegrown power Britain controls.

The government recently announced a new, additional Energy Wealth Fund to take this mission further. The fund will be linked to the Government’s future revenues from the North Sea, investing in renewable and low carbon energy projects and support the net zero transition – starting with a £2 billion injection of funding.

On top of this, Scottish-headquartered SSE has announced that the latest phase of its major offshore wind farm, Berwick Bank B, will back 2,677 skilled jobs in manufacturing, engineering and project delivery across the north of England and Scotland, with the company contracting Siemens Energy for the manufacturing of wind turbines and substation platforms. This includes the creation of 130 new project delivery roles in Glasgow and Montrose.

At its full capacity, Berwick Bank, off the East coast of Scotland, could become the world’s largest offshore wind farm, capable of meeting more than 6% of current UK electricity demand. Its delivery would strengthen long-term energy security and help deliver the homegrown, affordable energy the country needs.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said:

This major investment in UK renewables is a vote of confidence for building in Britain. And it is great news for billpayers because every turbine we put up is power under British control, not at the mercy of events on the other side of the world.

With coastal communities from Scotland to East Anglia powering Britain’s future, the places that host this energy benefit from the jobs and opportunities that it brings.

Our National Wealth Fund means that public investment is working alongside private capital to build homegrown energy and bring a return for the taxpayer. Because for me, a clean energy future is one that brings down bills.

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said:

This is another vote of confidence in British homegrown, clean energy.

Investment in offshore wind and clean power is creating quality jobs and rebuilding industry, while delivering the clean power we need to lower bills and reach net zero.

As the world gathers at COP31, Britain is leading from the front as a renewable energy powerhouse, turning the fight against climate change into a brighter future for British companies, industrial communities, and future generations.

CEO of RWE AG Markus Krebber said:

Together with KKR, we are delivering two of the UK’s largest offshore wind projects, strengthening domestic electricity generation and making an important contribution to the country’s long-term energy security.

Co-Head of European Infrastructure at KKR, Vincent Policard, continued:

Our work with RWE demonstrates how private capital can help turn the UK’s energy ambitions into reality, supporting economic growth and delivering critical infrastructure capable of powering around three million UK homes.

SSE Chief Executive Martin Pibworth said:

This is public-private partnership in action. Clear political direction, matched by businesses prepared to invest, is translating into real-world investment in British jobs, skills and manufacturing. From Hull, Newcastle and Manchester to Glasgow and Montrose, you can see what that means for communities across the country.

Berwick Bank B is a huge opportunity for the UK and, working with Siemens Energy, we’re backing those industrial capabilities while building the infrastructure needed for a more affordable and secure energy system.

And it’s a powerful and timely example as world leaders gather at COP31. There is already a clear acknowledgement that clean electrification is the route to decarbonisation, greater energy security and sustainably lower bills. We hope to see the ambition needed to turn that recognition into more investment like this.

The announcement is part of the government’s efforts towards a more affordable, clean energy system, with stronger consumer protections, greater public control and communities sharing in the benefits of renewable and low carbon power.

Last week saw the introduction of the Energy Independence Bill, a down payment on reforms that will put affordability at the heart of the energy system and unlock barriers to delivering clean power.

Measures include bringing rogue operators under greater public oversight, strengthening protections for households and businesses, and giving local people more control over and a greater stake in the clean energy projects built around them.

The government is protecting households from rising costs through removing standing charges and giving households £100 to help them pay their bills this winter, and putting Britain in control of its energy future, through a fair transition to green energy and seizing on the opportunities presented by renewables.

title: MAN electric truck feeds 350 kW back to the grid in SPIRIT-E bidirectional charging project
description:
Led by the Technical University of Munich (TUM), the project tested bidirectional charging at freight forwarder Spedition Schmid’s depot in Regensburg, Germany, from August 2023 to October 2026.
Bidirectional charging functions were developed and tested on the MAN eTGX electric truck and on mobile and stationary charging systems from project partner SBRS.
Using the Equigy platform, the project also demonstrated how electric trucks can help grid operators ease bottlenecks in the electricity network.
The partners say bidirectional charging is particularly attractive for trucks with regular depot dwell times and annual mileage below 100,000 km.
“Through SPIRIT-E, the MAN eTGX has demonstrated that it can serve as a bidirectional energy storage system,” said Georg Grüneißl, Head of Product Strategy at MAN Truck & Bus.
text:
The SPIRIT-E research project, which includes MAN Truck & Bus and Traton R&D, has shown that electric trucks can store energy and feed it back into local and public power grids.

Led by the Technical University of Munich (TUM), the project tested bidirectional charging at freight forwarder Spedition Schmid’s depot in Regensburg, Germany, from August 2023 to October 2026.

Bidirectional charging functions were developed and tested on the MAN eTGX electric truck and on mobile and stationary charging systems from project partner SBRS. The partners coordinated the interfaces between the vehicle, charging station, charging operator control software, site energy management system, electricity trader and grid operator.

The project implemented ISO 15118-20, the standard for communication between vehicles and charging infrastructure during charging and discharging. An eTGX with 480 kWh of usable energy fed electricity through a bidirectional DC charging station at up to 350 kW into the depot’s energy network (vehicle-to-site, or V2S) and the public grid (V2G). The truck also charged other vehicles from its battery (V2V).

In a test environment from software company PowerBot, the partners simulated an electric truck buying electricity when prices are low and selling it when they are high. Using the Equigy platform, the project also demonstrated how electric trucks can help grid operators ease bottlenecks in the electricity network.

Whether bidirectional charging pays off depends on factors including operating profiles, annual mileage, dwell times, battery size, electricity prices, grid charges, on-site power generation and grid connection capacity. The partners say bidirectional charging is particularly attractive for trucks with regular depot dwell times and annual mileage below 100,000 km. According to project calculations, average energy-cost savings are around 10%, and up to 20% under optimal conditions.

“Through SPIRIT-E, the MAN eTGX has demonstrated that it can serve as a bidirectional energy storage system,” said Georg Grüneißl, Head of Product Strategy at MAN Truck & Bus. “We are now working to bring this feature into series production. At the same time, we are developing a consulting concept for our customers that will help them unlock the full potential of this rolling power bank.”

text:
ANTALYA, Turkey — It's time to act decisively and urgently to curb global warming, which is wreaking havoc with deadly floods,heat waves and other disasters, the United Nations chief told world leaders Wednesday as formal talks began at the U.N. climate conference in Turkey.

"We know the truth. Now we must act on it because climate action is more than a fight over a number or a thermometer," U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres said in an opening speech. "We are in the fight for our lives and our children's future."

But top leaders of the world's three biggest polluting nations — China, the United States and India, together responsible for more than half of the world's carbon dioxide emissions — skipped the summit, known as COP31.

Their absence left a handful of national leaders and U.N. officials to press for action as a new report warned of a widening gap between countries' climate pledges and actual emissions cuts.

Scientists say global warming is likely to exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above preindustrial levels. Limiting warming to that threshold was a goal of the 2015 Paris Agreement and remains a focus of international negotiations.

Guterres outlined a framework for climate negotiations, saying they must prioritize ending fossil fuel reliance, adapting to a warmer world, increasing financial support for poorer countries bearing the brunt of climate change, and promoting cooperation over conflict.

"We do not need countries to agree on everything. But we do need them to cooperate on the things no country can solve alone," he said.

But addressing climate change has been overshadowed by wars, inflation and geopolitical conflicts, Brazil's President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva said. He pledged to protect the Amazon, the world's largest rainforest, and urged world leaders to work together for a just, sustainable future.

"Brazil is back to defend the continuity of a healthy planet," he said.

More than 70 world leaders and senior government officials are speaking at the summit, though what can be accomplished remains uncertain in the absence of leaders from key nations.

"It really is a disgrace that just one of the seven G7 heads of state and only a handful of G20 leaders are attending this summit," said Mohamed Adow, director of Power Shift Africa, a climate and energy think tank. "The world's biggest economies should be leading the response to the climate crisis, not leaving it to others."

The United States, the world's second-largest polluter after China, is absent from the talks for the second consecutive year. President Donald Trump, who has called climate change a hoax, has targeted offshore wind projects and removed rules limiting power plant emissions.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen attended, but many leaders of European countries stayed away.

"More than half of the top leaders of the EU countries are not showing up at the leaders' summit," Climate Action Network Europe Director Chiara Martinelli told The Associated Press. "If Europe wants to help steer the global transition, it needs to show up and be part of it."

The gap between nations' climate plans and action on the ground is widening, according to an annual climate change performance index published Wednesday by Germanwatch and the New Climate Institute.

"Overall, current collective efforts are not enough to prevent catastrophic climate change. But we see clear potential for improvement," said Jan Burck of Germanwatch.

Ranking among the worst performers in limiting emissions were COP31 host Turkey and Australia, which is leading the negotiations.

The talks come as the war in Iran has driven up global prices for oil, gasoline and products such as fertilizers and pesticides. Those increases have prompted governments to rethink energy policies and investment in renewable sources such as wind and solar.

Past talks have been criticized for producing promises that later went unfulfilled.

Delegates at the 2023 conference in Dubai agreed to transition away from fossil fuels such as coal, oil and gas, the main drivers of climate change. But subsequent conferences in Azerbaijan and Brazil yielded little agreement on how to reduce their use. Last year's conference in Brazil produced a compromise deal pledging more money to help vulnerable nations adapt to climate change.

text:
November 2026

Now read the report in full

Executive summary

The UK and EU face a shared energy security challenge: how to build a clean, affordable, and resilient energy system in a world of growing geopolitical uncertainty, supply chain vulnerabilities and climate-related risks. Meeting this challenge will depend increasingly on cooperation, interconnected infrastructure and access to diverse sources of energy.

Current arrangements for trading electricity between Great Britain (GB) and continental Europe are inefficient and increasingly costly. The separation of UK and EU electricity markets following Brexit has cost British and European consumers over €500m.[1] As renewable generation and the North Sea take on a more strategic role in Europe’s electricity system these costs are likely to grow. Without closer cooperation, barriers to cross-border trading and developing shared infrastructure will constrain the efficient use of Europe’s energy resources.

This is particularly important in the North Sea, where the nine countries involved in the North Sea Energy Cooperation (NSEC), including the UK, have committed to 120GW of offshore wind by 2030 and 300GW by 2050. GB alone could account for more than 40% of North Sea offshore wind capacity by 2030. Realising this potential will require countries to plan and deliver infrastructure together, supported by electricity markets that enable power to flow efficiently across borders.

This paper identifies three priorities that should form part of a single strategic agenda: aligning carbon pricing arrangements, reintegrating UK and EU electricity markets, and coordinating the development of the North Sea. Together, these measures would strengthen energy security, unlock investment and help deliver a more affordable and resilient European energy system.

First, carbon pricing arrangements must support continued trade in low-carbon electricity between the UK and the EU. As discussions on linking emissions trading systems progress, it will be important to agree how GB electricity should be treated under the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), including a pathway towards exemption. Without this, analysis suggests that imports of clean GB electricity could fall by more than 50%, EU consumer costs could increase by up to €4.6 billion annually and carbon emissions could rise by up to 2.4MtCO₂ per year.[2]

Second, closer integration of UK and EU electricity markets would deliver significant benefits for consumers and the wider energy system. Recoupling markets reduces the costs of inefficient cross-border trading, strengthens the investment case for hybrid interconnectors such as Nautilus and LionLink, and creates opportunities for GB participation in European balancing platforms, capacity mechanisms and cross-border power purchase agreements.

Third, closer coordination on the North Sea on infrastructure, spatial planning and supply chains will be essential to realising the region’s full potential. This means ensuring that national plans are developed in a coordinated way, maximising opportunities for shared infrastructure and hybrid projects, and securing full UK membership in the NSEC and in the Industrial Accelerator Act’s Union origin framework from the outset.

The decisions taken today will shape Europe’s energy system for decades. Closer cooperation offers both the UK and EU an opportunity to strengthen energy security, unlock investment and reduce costs. The prize of integration is significant, and the cost of fragmentation is one neither side can afford.

The strategic case for energy interdependence

From energy independence to interconnected resilience

A decade on from the UK’s referendum on EU membership, political arrangements have changed, but geography, physics and economics remain the same. The UK and EU remain linked by electricity interconnectors, shared offshore energy resources, critical supply chains, and similar climate ambitions. In an era defined by geopolitical uncertainty and growing energy security concerns, effective cooperation is more important than ever.

Recent shocks have reinforced this reality. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine exposed Europe’s vulnerability to international fossil fuel markets, while recent conflict in the Middle East has highlighted the continued risk associated with dependence on internationally traded fuels. As a result, both the UK and the EU are increasingly pursuing electrification and low-carbon energy not only as a route to decarbonisation but also as a means of strengthening economic and energy security.

This is reshaping the nature of energy security. Historically, security centred on ensuring access to the fuels needed to generate electricity and meet demand. As the UK and Europe transition towards increasingly electrified, low-carbon energy systems, resilience will depend not only on reliable generation, but also on access to diverse energy sources, flexible resources and interconnected infrastructure. This allows countries to draw on one another’s resources when domestic supply is constrained, making the wider system more resilient to disruption. In this context, trusted international partnerships and closer UK-EU energy cooperation are becoming strategically essential.

Interconnectors as Europe’s shared source of flexibility and resilience

Interconnection between European markets, particularly across the North Sea nations, is increasingly important to managing the variability of renewable generation and strengthening system resilience. Interconnectors act as ‘shock absorbers’, allowing electricity to flow from areas of surplus to areas of scarcity and giving countries access to a wider pool of generation. For example, combining wind generation in GB with nuclear generation in France can smooth fluctuations in output and reduce short-term variability in generation by up to 30%.[3]

The value of interconnection was also illustrated by the April 2025 Iberian blackout, where links with France and Morocco were critical to supporting the restoration of the electricity system. Cross-border flows provided access to essential system support, including black start capability, voltage, frequency and inertia control. As European electricity systems become more variable and decentralised, and risks to critical energy infrastructure grow, this contribution to system stability and security of supply will be paramount.

The economic case for greater interconnection is equally compelling. Cross-border electricity trades in the day-ahead market already account for 39.5% of EU and Norwegian electricity demand.[4] Analysis of the EU’s Ten-Year Network Development Plan (TYNDP 2024) estimates that by 2040, every €1 invested in expanding cross-border transmission capacity will reduce needed generation costs by more than €2 through access to increased flexibility.[5]

Europe’s growing interconnection gap

Delivering a resilient and integrated European power system by 2040 will require 318GW of cross-border capacity, almost double the 167GW projected by 2030. This means a further 151GW must be delivered during the 2030s at an estimated cost of at least €150 billion.[6] However, the current project pipeline falls significantly short of this ambition. Given the long lead times associated with planning, consenting and constructing major infrastructure, the window for making the investment decisions needed by 2035-40 is already closing.

The shortfall is also unevenly distributed, with eleven countries collectively representing almost 80% of EU electricity generation, projected to miss the EU’s 2030 interconnection target.[7] Crucially, some of the largest gaps are concentrated in key European electricity markets, including Germany, the Netherlands, France and the Republic of Ireland, which together represent almost 50% of EU GDP. [8] This risks leaving some of Europe’s most economically significant markets without the cross-border capacity needed to realise the full benefits of an integrated electricity system.

The challenge also includes the underutilisation of existing capacity. The Agency for the Cooperation of Energy Regulators’ (ACER) 2025 Monitoring Report found that EU TSOs spent €4.3 billion managing 60TWh of grid congestion in 2024, equivalent to Austria’s entire annual electricity consumption.[9] Much of this congestion reflects insufficient cross-border and zonal electricity capacity. Despite the EU’s Clean Energy Package requirement for TSOs to make at least 70% of physical transmission capacity available for cross-zonal trade, core region TSOs made just 54% of physical transmission capacity available on the most congested lines in 2024, meaning Europe captured only 40% of the €580 million in potential welfare gains.

A strategic partner for Europe

The UK has a critical role to play in addressing Europe’s growing interconnection gap and strengthening the resilience of its energy system. As a major player in offshore wind development, with significant potential to support the deployment of hybrid assets and integrated offshore infrastructure in the North Sea, the UK is central to realising the benefits of greater regional cooperation. The following sections examine the choices on carbon pricing, electricity market arrangements, infrastructure and supply chains that will determine whether the UK and EU can turn this shared opportunity into reality.

The North Sea: Europe’s shared energy future

The North Sea as a strategic asset in Europe’s future energy system

The North Sea is becoming the strategic centre of Europe’s future energy security, providing the clean power and cross-border flexibility that electrified economies will depend on. The nine NSEC countries, including the UK, have committed to reaching 120GW of offshore wind capacity by 2030 and at least 300GW by 2050, 100GW of which will be made up of joint projects like offshore hybrid assets.[10] These targets represent the backbone of Western Europe’s future decarbonised electricity system, underpinning the energy needs of more than 260 million people and industries that account for roughly 60% of Europe’s GDP.[11]

As part of the Hamburg Declaration, TSOs have committed to identifying 20GW of economically viable cross-border projects, including hybrid interconnectors by 2027. This represents almost one-sixth of the additional interconnection capacity needed to deliver an optimised European electricity system during the 2030s.[12]

The UK’s role in powering Europe’s energy transition

The UK is already a leading player in the expansion of the North Sea energy system. Five new interconnector projects have been approved, including GB’s first two hybrid projects, Nautilus (1.4GW to Belgium) and LionLink (1.8GW to the Netherlands). Together, these will increase GB’s interconnector capacity with continental Europe by more than 6GW.

Despite rising costs, supply chain constraints and wider market pressures slowing offshore wind deployment in the EU, the UK remains Europe’s leading offshore wind market. Following the successful CfD Allocation Round 7 (AR7) in 2026, a record 8.4GW of capacity was secured, strengthening an already substantial project pipeline. The UK could therefore account for more than 40% of North Sea offshore wind capacity by 2030, supported by its national target of 43-50GW, the largest national target in the region.[13] Yet greater cooperation to unlock investment is essential: current projections suggest the North Sea will reach only 87GW by 2030 and 257GW by 2050, falling short of the NSEC targets.[14]

GB is currently a net importer of electricity from the EU. In the year to September 2025, interconnectors enabled imports of around 43TWh, equivalent to 13% of total supply, while 12TWh was exported.[15] However, this relationship is set to change, with GB set to become a net exporter by 2030, supplying European markets with low-cost, low-carbon electricity.[16] This gives the UK an increasingly important role in Europe’s efforts to secure affordable clean energy, strengthen energy security and support reindustrialisation.

The opportunity is significant for both sides. For GB, interconnection will allow surplus North Sea wind to reach European consumers, generating export revenues rather than being curtailed. Hybrid interconnectors offer potential to link multiple markets through an integrated North Sea network, improving resilience, flexibility and access to affordable energy. For the EU, GB’s growing renewable surplus can provide a source of clean power, displacing more expensive gas generation when continental supply is constrained. The North Sea is more than a location for offshore wind development: it is the infrastructure through which a more secure, affordable and interconnected European energy system can be built.

Planning for one interconnected energy system

Realising the North Sea’s potential will require countries to plan infrastructure together rather than develop national strategies in isolation. The Hamburg Declaration recognises this, with a commitment to coordinate planning and permitting, strengthen supply chains and develop the workforce needed to deliver the region’s offshore ambitions.

The UK’s Strategic Spatial Energy Plan (SSEP) will therefore need to be developed in active dialogue with the national network plans of other North Sea countries and NSEC’s work on a coordinated offshore energy infrastructure plan. It is not yet clear how effectively these processes will align. The UK should ensure that its SSEP interfaces with the emerging regional planning framework from the outset, rather than seeking to reconcile national and regional plans at a later stage.

The cost of fragmentation

Inefficient electricity trading leaves value on the table

The benefits of interconnection are well established, but current trading arrangements between GB and continental Europe do not make the most efficient use of available capacity. Under explicit trading, electricity and interconnector capacity are bought and sold separately, based on forecasts of market prices. This means electricity does not always flow in the direction that market prices would indicate. Implicit trading, by contrast, allocates electricity and interconnector capacity together, allowing power to flow automatically towards markets where it is most valuable. This was the arrangement in GB before 2021 and remains standard across much of Europe. Energy UK analysis suggests that explicit trading creates inefficiencies up to 25% of the time.[17]

Scenario A: Consider a winter day when wind generation in GB is exceptionally weak and electricity demand is high. Gas generation must increase to meet demand, with the final units of generation often disproportionately increasing wholesale prices which regularly exceed £100/MWh. Efficient interconnection can help reduce these costs by allowing GB to access cheaper electricity from neighbouring markets, displacing the most expensive gas generation. As Figure 1 illustrates, during periods of high gas generation in recent years, increased imports have coincided with lower wholesale prices. More efficient trading could therefore help to narrow the £100/MWh gap between spot prices of £200/MWh and £300/MWh during these kinds of events, reducing volatility.

Figure 1: Gas and import proportions and spot price at maximum periods of gas generation on tight winter days[18]

Figure 2 shows a day of extremely low wind. Gas generation was high throughout, but the relationship between import levels and the wholesale price is evident. Increased imports displace the most expensive gas generation, reducing price pressures. On 20th January 2025, the evening spike in demand alongside reduced imports caused a huge spike in spot prices, where implicit trading may well have dampened the price spikes.

Figure 2: GB imports and spot price on 20/01/2025[19]

Scenario B: Consider the summer of 2022, when the French nuclear fleet was blighted by extended maintenance shutdowns,[20] and Norwegian hydro generation fell to the lowest level in a decade. This contributed to increased scarcity across continental markets connected to GB. As shown below, in Figure 3, Britain was able to increase its power generation and export much more, switching from a net importer to a net exporter of power for eight consecutive months.

Figure 3: Monthly data for Norwegian hydropower generation, French nuclear generation, and GB net imports[21]

The value of interconnection during periods of scarcity

In general, the correlation of stress events between GB and the interconnected continent is low. Looking at periods where prices in Belgium, Denmark, France, or the Netherlands exceeded €200/MWh since 2024, the price in GB was below €200/MWh 74% of the time.[22] With this in mind, efficient interconnection serves both sides. GB’s power system diverges enough from its interconnected neighbours to make it a real asset to be coupled with, acting as a buffer to high prices.

Furthermore, GB has different weather patterns and a different profile of electricity generation to interconnected nations on the continent. This diversity is a strength to all those who can tap into it. Figure 4 demonstrates how GB’s power system would contribute to this diversity. For example, GB greatly bolsters dispatchable capacity, increasing gas by 84% and biomass and waste by 118%. As Britain accelerates towards its Clean Power 2030 goal, the benefits to both sides only get stronger.

Figure 4: Capacity of power generation technologies in Belgium, Denmark, France, the Netherlands (Connected EU), with GB added[23]

The growing economic cost of market fragmentation

The costs of fragmented trading are not limited to periods of system stress. Analysis has shown that consumers in GB and the EU lost an estimated €500m in the first three years following decoupling.[24] Interconnector operators also stand to lose more than €1bn in congestion income, weakening the commercial case for future investment.

Offshore Hybrid Assets (also known as multipurpose interconnectors) are interconnectors that connect offshore wind farms to multiple countries. Through combining generation and transmission assets, these projects are cheaper than conventionally building them separately. However, developers have stated that without market coupling they cannot be operated effectively.[25] Future projects will likely be delayed, not connect to GB, or not go ahead at all as a result, increasing the cost of meeting the Ostend Declaration target of 300GW of offshore wind by 2050 by £13bn.[26]

The scenarios above illustrate the cost of fragmentation during periods of system stress. However, the cost is not confined to periods of crises, and market fragmentation is imposing a daily economic penalty and weakening the investment case for the cross-border infrastructure Europe needs to secure its energy future.

The operational and commercial costs of exclusion

Beyond more efficient cross-border trading, closer market integration could enable greater coordination of balancing services, allowing GB and EU operators to share flexibility and access a wider pool of reserves. It would also provide a stronger basis for coordinating cross-border capacity and adequacy. As electricity systems become more interconnected and the challenge of managing volatility grows. these arrangements are increasingly important. Yet GB’s exclusion from the IEM makes coordination more complex. GB assets could make a greater contribution to European adequacy and system management, but this requires closer alignment of market arrangements and operational frameworks. In particular, regulators on both sides currently lack a common framework for coordinating restrictions on cross-border flow during periods of system stress.

Closer market integration could also create new commercial opportunities including cross-border power purchase agreements (PPAs) between GB generators and EU industrial consumers seeking long-term access to clean electricity and greater price certainty, which remain limited between GB and EU markets. Without market coupling, day-ahead prices are determined through separate auctions, while cross-border capacity is not allocated through a single, integrated process. This creates additional uncertainty for generators and buyers seeking to manage price and delivery risks, constraining the development of cross-border contracts at scale. Market coupling could help to address these barriers alongside greater regulatory alignment on Guarantees of Origin (GOOs), Renewable Energy Guarantees of Origin (REGOs), balancing arrangements and relevant contractual arrangements.

Building a more integrated carbon market

Why ETS linkage and CBAM alignment must go hand in hand

The cost of market fragmentation extends beyond electricity trading. Differences in carbon pricing arrangements, and how these are recognised at the border, risk creating a further barrier to cross-border trade just as the UK and EU seek to deepen their energy relationship. The evidence points to a clear risk that CBAM could make cross-border electricity trade more expensive, reduce flows of clean electricity from GB and weaken the investment case for future interconnection. The consequences would extend beyond the immediate cost to consumers, undermining the wider benefits of an integrated North Sea energy system.

Afry’s 2024 impact study highlights the scale of the potential costs.[27] Its modelling projects that EU electricity imports from GB could fall by more than 50% once CBAM costs take effect in 2027, rising to over 85% by 2040. This would represent a loss of 53TWh of clean electricity annually, equivalent to Denmark’s entire electricity demand. EU consumers could also face annual wholesale electricity cost increases of €2.3 to €4.6 billion, including €740 million in Germany, €524 million in France and €344 million in the Netherlands. The impact on future investment could be equally significant. Annual congestion rents, an important source of revenue underpinning the business case for interconnectors and hybrid assets, could fall by 50% to 90% across all GB-connected borders. Afry estimates this could undermine the business case for future interconnector projects by €75 million and €170 million per GW in a single year.

The consequences would extend beyond electricity costs and investment. A study by the London School of Economics suggests that applying CBAM to electricity imports from GB risks reducing UK renewable electricity exports to the EU by up to 164 GWh in a single year.[28] Conversely, avoiding CBAM charges on electricity from GB could prevent the EU from needing to import an additional €2bn in gas imports annually, as increased fossil fuel generation would otherwise compensate for reduced renewable imports from the UK.[29]

The climate consequences are equally counterproductive. The studies project that total carbon emissions across the EU and GB increase by 1.5 to 2.4 MtCO₂ annually in the initial years following CBAM implementation, equivalent to the annual emissions of up to 8.3 million cars. This reflects increased curtailment of GB renewable generation, alongside greater gas and coal generation in the EU to compensate for reduced imports.

There is an opportunity for the UK and EU to address this as part of an agreement on ETS linkage. Recognising the equivalent carbon costs already faced by GB electricity generators would help avoid additional charges on electricity traded across the Channel, protecting consumers and industry on both sides. The two parties should ensure that the benefits of ETS linkage are reflected in the treatment of electricity under CBAM from the outset, rather than leaving cross-border trade exposed to unnecessary costs during implementation. This would be a practical near-term win for both sides, supporting clean electricity flows, reducing costs and preserving the investment case for the interconnectors and offshore infrastructure needed to strengthen Europe’s energy security.

Strengthening Europe’s industrial competitiveness

Building a competitive and coordinated North Sea supply chain

A competitive European energy system will also depend on the strength of the industrial capabilities and supply chains that underpin it. Offshore wind already supports tens of thousands of jobs, with the Hamburg Declaration providing a platform for further growth across manufacturing, ports, engineering and specialist supply chains. The UK’s Clean Energy Industries Sector Plan, the subsequent Electricity Network Sector Growth Plan and Great British Energy’s £300 million Supply Chain Fund collectively demonstrate a growing commitment to strengthening domestic supply chains, coordinating infrastructure investment and addressing critical manufacturing bottlenecks. Importantly, the Sector Plan also recognises the value of alignment with EU processes. [30]

But these supply chains are European and the same manufacturers, installation vessels and specialist engineering firms serve projects across the North Sea. National procurement frameworks, such as Ofgem’s Advanced Procurement Mechanism and emerging EU initiatives should therefore be designed to support coordination and interoperability across borders.[31] Exploring joint procurement of critical, supply-constrained components through the North Sea Energy Cooperation (NSEC) should be a practical near-term priority. Better coordination of demand would help secure manufacturing capacity, achieve economies of scale and reduce the risk of countries competing against one another for limited supplies, driving up costs and delaying delivery.

Protecting UK-EU supply chain integration under the Industrial Accelerator Act

A more immediate risk to this integrated supply chain comes from the EU’s proposed Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), currently progressing through the EU legislative process. Its Union origin framework, which determines which manufactured components qualify for EU support schemes and public procurement, has become increasingly restrictive through successive drafts. The European Parliament’s draft report proposes that Union origin requirements for low-carbon technology support schemes should apply by default only to EU27 manufacturers, with the inclusion of third countries subject to a delegated act and seven conditionality criteria.

The UK’s status under the IAA has been left to be resolved during the remaining legislative negotiations. For the UK’s offshore wind sector, which is an important part of the wider North Sea supply chain, this creates material uncertainty. Under the proposals as currently drafted, UK-manufactured components could be excluded from EU support schemes, including Contracts for Difference (CfDs), unless the UK secures qualifying third-country status. This risks the creation of barriers within supply chains that are already deeply integrated across the region.

The Commission would have powers under the current proposal to extend the list of eligible countries, and the UK is understood to be well placed to secure inclusion. However, providing clarity from the outset would offer greater certainty for manufacturers and investors on both sides of the Channel. The UK and EU should therefore work towards an agreed arrangement that recognises UK-manufactured components in the Union origin from the Act’s entry into force. This would reflect the deeply integrated nature of their clean energy supply chains, support investment in manufacturing capacity across the region and give practical effect to their shared commitments under the Hamburg Declaration.

Conclusion

The UK and EU have a shared interest in building a more integrated, resilient and secure energy system. But realising this opportunity requires progress on several interconnected fronts: closer participation in the Internal Electricity Market, linkage of the Emissions Trading Systems, and an agreement on mutual recognition and CBAM treatment. These are not separate policy issues, but essential components of a wider strategic partnership.

The consequences of delay are increasingly tangible. Uncertainty over market arrangements and Offshore Bidding Zones continues to complicate the investment case for major projects in the North Sea, while creating risks for the integration of GB into planned European energy islands. Meanwhile, investment decisions that will shape the North Sea energy system of the 2030s and 2040s are being made now.

The window to act is short, and the frameworks being designed today will either enable closer UK-EU integration or make it structurally harder to achieve. The choice is between a coordinated North Sea energy system that delivers greater resilience, security and shared prosperity, and continued fragmentation that leaves both sides more exposed to future shocks. The question is no longer whether cooperation makes sense, but whether the political will exists to deliver it before the opportunity passes.

Policy recommendations

Agree on mutual recognition of carbon prices paid by GB electricity exporters as a step towards full ETS linkage. As part of a potential agreement on ETS linkage at the next EU-UK Summit, both sides should agree a provisional CBAM exemption arrangement for electricity trade. This would prevent the perverse suppression of clean energy flows that would otherwise cost EU consumers up to €4.6 billion annually and increase aggregate EU and GB carbon emissions by up to 2.4MtCO₂ per year.

Recouple the GB-EU electricity markets as the key to unlock investment and effective cross-border flexibility and capacity. This is the prerequisite for all subsequent integration measures that will not only save consumers money on both sides but also unlock the potential of the North Sea for cross-border capacity and flexibility arrangements, turning the region into a ‘shared battery’, shielding nations in the region from market volatility and increasing system resilience for all.

Formally reintegrate the UK into the North Sea Energy Cooperation framework. Full UK membership would strengthen cooperation on supply chains and strategic planning, including securing UK inclusion in the IAA Union origin framework. It would also enable closer alignment of national offshore energy plans, ensuring a coordinated approach to spatial planning, and ensure harmonised national plans and a lowered overall cost of North Sea development.

text:
Toyota's KEI-01 is just over 11 feet long, has a 660cc three-cylinder engine and will be assembled in Indiana, but the figure that shapes everything else about it is the 25 mph top speed in Toyota's own release. That number puts the truck in the federal low-speed vehicle class, where the rules on what a vehicle must survive are not the ones a Tacoma has to meet.

Toyota Motor North America announced the truck and a revived Scion by Toyota brand on Nov. 10 from Plano, Texas, a day after reveal events in Ypsilanti Township, Michigan, and Frisco, Texas. The KEI-01 reaches the U.S. in the second half of 2027 with a continuously variable transmission, standard selectable four-wheel drive, a bed rated for up to 600 pounds and a right-hand-drive cab under 5 feet wide. Toyota did not give horsepower, fuel economy, a towing rating or a price.

The company calls the truck intentionally low-volume and niche. It will go first to fleets through Scion by Toyota dealers chosen from the existing Toyota network, and Toyota says only that it "may consider" limited retail sales later.

Why a 25 mph cap is how a truck this small gets built here

Toyota says the KEI-01 is designed to comply with Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard No. 500. NHTSA's definition of a low-speed vehicle, effective June 5, 2006, is a four-wheeled vehicle that can reach more than 20 mph but no more than 25 mph, with a gross vehicle weight rating under 3,000 pounds.

The test procedure NHTSA uses for the standard is a checklist: headlamps, turn signals, taillamps, stop lamps, reflectors, mirrors, a parking brake, a DOT-marked windshield, a 17-character VIN and lap or lap-and-shoulder belts at every seat. The procedure covers equipment, loading and a speed run. It contains no crash test.

NHTSA did not hide the trade-off. When it raised the weight limit in 2005, the agency wrote in a Federal Register notice that a low-speed vehicle lacks the occupant protection of other four-wheeled vehicles, and that such vehicles could not meet standards written for larger ones, such as the 30 mph barrier crash standards. The same notice warned of greater risk of injury or death on roads with a posted limit of 35 mph and encouraged states to be careful about allowing low-speed vehicles on public roads.

Toyota has not said why it chose this category. My read is that the cap buys a vehicle that can be built in small numbers without a full crash-structure program, and that the price is paid in where the truck can go. The federal standard defines the vehicle; states decide where it may run. A KEI-01 will be a farm, campus, resort or municipal tool long before it is anyone's commuter.

What Washington has said about tiny cars

A Jan. 13 White House release listed the authorization of production of affordable, efficient "tiny cars" among the administration's regulatory changes. Toyota's release mentions no president or administration, and nothing in the documents I reviewed connects the KEI-01 to that line.

The Transportation Department's Sept. 28 announcement of the final fuel economy rule, published in the Federal Register on Sept. 30 (Vol. 91, No. 188, docket NHTSA-2025-0491), does not mention kei cars or microcars. It does say existing rules discourage hatchbacks, wagons and smaller-footprint vehicles, and that reclassifying small crossovers could add lower-cost options. Beginning with model year 2030, vehicles would be classed by intended use, and the department projects the fleet moving from about 70% light trucks to about 70% passenger cars.

That rule sets standards for passenger cars and light trucks for model years 2022 to 2031. The KEI-01 is designed for a different standard and Toyota gives no fuel economy number. Rules still steer what lands on a truck, as the 2027 F-150 V8 showed this fall, but nothing published so far shows this policy producing this truck.

Fifty jobs and a pilot-sized plan in Princeton

Toyota is putting $34 million into Toyota Motor Manufacturing Indiana for the KEI-01, which it says adds about 50 jobs and upgrades production and logistics infrastructure. That works out to $680,000 per job, The Auto Wire's arithmetic, though the money covers equipment and logistics, not wages. The Princeton plant builds the Grand Highlander, Highlander, Lexus TX and Sienna Hybrid, and Toyota lists 427,844 vehicles built there in 2025 by more than 7,380 employees. Fitting a niche model into a plant running that volume is a familiar squeeze; Honda found a flexible Ohio line still ran out of room.

Toyota's own kei experience comes from Japan, where it sells commercial vehicles it sources from Daihatsu. A Feb. 2 Toyota Global release describes the battery-electric Pixis Van as an OEM vehicle based on the Daihatsu Hijet Cargo, built at Daihatsu's Oita (Nakatsu) plant, and says kei commercial vehicles make up about 60% of Japan's commercial vehicle fleet. The U.S. release does not say where the KEI-01's platform or engine comes from, which matters to anyone who will have to buy parts for a right-hand-drive 660cc three-cylinder. Japan's kei class was built around Japanese rules that the U.S. does not share.

What to watch before 2027

Four details will settle what this truck is. Price comes first, since Toyota has promised more information only "as plans are finalized." Next is the gross vehicle weight rating, which has to stay under 3,000 pounds and decides how much of the 600-pound bed is usable with two people in the cab. Third is which states let a 25 mph four-wheel-drive truck onto which roads. Last is whether the retail option ever opens, because fleet-only sales through hand-picked dealers mean most buyers will never see one.

If you could have an 11-foot, 25 mph, four-wheel-drive truck for your farm, shop or campus, would you take it, or does a truck that can't keep up with traffic fall short of the small, cheap pickup the "tiny cars" talk suggested?

We can build a future of clean energy independence – or lock in another generation of fossil fuel dependence.
text:
The following is a transcript of remarks delivered by UN Secretary-General at the COP31 High-Level Dialogue on Clean Energy Transition and Electrification at COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, on 11 November 2026.

Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen,

I welcome the ambition of the 35-by-35 Global Electrification Pledge.

Now we must make it real – and make it clean.

The crisis in the Middle East has once again exposed the price of fossil fuel dependence.

Three out of four people live in countries that are net importers of fossil fuels.

A shock thousands of kilometres away is driving up the cost of transport, running a business or putting food on the table.

Real energy security means breaking this dependence.

Clean electricity can do that.

Cutting import bills. Cleaning the air. Creating decent jobs. And slashing emissions.

I urge action on three fronts.

First, accelerate clean electrification and the transition away from fossil fuels.

And I praise the International Energy Agency for its constant advocacy.

That means more electric buses, cars and trucks.

More efficient electric heating and cooling.

More industries powered by clean electricity.

And delivering the global goals to triple renewable capacity and double energy efficiency improvements by 2030.

New oil and gas projects and import terminals risk locking countries into high costs and stranded assets for decades.

Second, build the grids and storage to power the clean energy age.

Around 3,000 gigawatts of renewable and storage projects are well advanced, but waiting for grid connections.

That is four times the wind and solar capacity the world connected last year.

And the queue grew by 60 per cent in a single year.

We must modernize grids. Build storage. Speed up connections.

And link power systems across borders.

Through the Global Grids Accelerator launched at our Climate Summit in September, the United Nations is bringing governments, development banks and investors together to get projects moving, starting in Africa and Southeast Asia.

I urge governments to bring forward priority projects. And I urge financing partners to back them.

Third, make clean electricity affordable and available to all.

Fossil fuels have failed to deliver on universal energy access.

Hundreds of millions of people still live without electricity.

They cannot be left behind by the clean energy revolution.

The geography of the energy transition is shifting.

Emerging and developing economies will drive an increasing share of new demand and new capacity.

But finance is not keeping pace.

Emerging and developing economies outside China receive only around one dollar in five invested in clean energy.

And many face borrowing costs two to three times those of advanced economies.

That must change.

I urge shareholders of multilateral development banks to give those banks the resources and the room to take more risk.

Guarantees and concessional finance must grow.

And developing countries must be supported to turn plans into investable projects.

Investment must reach communities waiting for their first connection.

Use it to lower bills for households. Build clean industries.

And ensure workers have the skills and social protection they need through the transition.

Excellencies,

Let us resolve to take the next steps from Antalya focused on clear commitments: what countries will electrify, how they will power cleanly, and how they will finance it.

The future of energy is being built now.

We can build a future of clean energy independence – or lock in another generation of fossil fuel dependence.

We have the technology.

We have the economic case.

Now we need the political will to deliver.

Thank you.
