description:
In Short : West Bengal has announced an attractive investment assistance framework offering incentives of up to 120% for eligible semiconductor, electric vehicle and battery manufacturing projects.
In Detail : West Bengal is stepping up efforts to attract investments in advanced manufacturing by offering investment assistance of up to 120% for eligible projects in the semiconductor, electric vehicle and battery sectors.
Establishing battery manufacturing facilities within West Bengal could support domestic production of battery cells, modules, packs and associated components.
Semiconductor, EV and battery manufacturing projects require specialised industrial land, reliable electricity, water supply, logistics facilities, skilled manpower and technology partnerships.
Overall, West Bengal’s proposed 120% investment assistance for semiconductor, electric vehicle and battery projects represents an ambitious attempt to strengthen its position in India’s next-generation manufacturing landscape.
text:
In Short : West Bengal has announced an attractive investment assistance framework offering incentives of up to 120% for eligible semiconductor, electric vehicle and battery manufacturing projects. The initiative aims to attract large-scale industrial investments, strengthen advanced manufacturing capabilities and position the state as an emerging destination for strategic technology industries. The policy support is expected to encourage domestic and international investors, promote employment generation, develop local supply chains and accelerate the state’s participation in India’s expanding semiconductor, electric mobility and energy storage ecosystems.

In Detail : West Bengal is stepping up efforts to attract investments in advanced manufacturing by offering investment assistance of up to 120% for eligible projects in the semiconductor, electric vehicle and battery sectors. The incentive framework reflects the state’s ambition to establish itself as a competitive industrial destination and participate more actively in India’s rapidly expanding electronics, clean mobility and energy storage markets. The initiative is also expected to strengthen investor confidence and encourage the establishment of technology-intensive manufacturing facilities.

The proposed investment assistance is designed to improve the financial attractiveness of setting up industrial projects in the state. By providing substantial policy support, West Bengal aims to reduce the initial investment burden on companies entering capital-intensive sectors. Semiconductor fabrication, electronics manufacturing, battery production and electric vehicle facilities generally require significant upfront expenditure, advanced machinery, specialised infrastructure and long-term technology commitments. Targeted incentives could therefore play an important role in encouraging companies to consider the state for their manufacturing expansion plans.

The semiconductor sector represents a particularly strategic opportunity for West Bengal. Global demand for semiconductor chips is increasing across automobiles, consumer electronics, telecommunications, artificial intelligence, industrial automation and defence applications. India is making significant efforts to establish domestic semiconductor manufacturing capabilities and reduce dependence on international supply chains. West Bengal’s proposed incentives could help attract investments in semiconductor-related manufacturing, assembly, testing, packaging and supporting electronics industries.

Electric vehicle manufacturing is another important focus of the investment initiative. India’s transition towards electric mobility is creating opportunities across automobile manufacturing, electric motors, power electronics, charging infrastructure and associated components. West Bengal could seek to attract investments in electric two-wheelers, passenger vehicles, commercial vehicles and their supporting supply chains. Developing a local EV manufacturing ecosystem would also help create employment opportunities, encourage technological innovation and support the country’s broader clean transportation objectives.

Battery manufacturing and energy storage represent another critical area of potential investment. Rising demand for electric vehicles and renewable energy integration is increasing the need for advanced battery technologies and large-scale energy storage systems. Establishing battery manufacturing facilities within West Bengal could support domestic production of battery cells, modules, packs and associated components. Such investments could also strengthen the supply chain for stationary storage applications, which are becoming increasingly important for ensuring reliable electricity supply from solar and wind power projects.

The investment assistance framework could generate wider economic benefits through the development of industrial clusters and supporting infrastructure. Semiconductor, EV and battery manufacturing projects require specialised industrial land, reliable electricity, water supply, logistics facilities, skilled manpower and technology partnerships. Coordinated infrastructure development and a supportive regulatory environment will therefore be important for translating investment proposals into operational manufacturing facilities. Strong linkages with universities, technical institutions and research organisations could further strengthen the state’s industrial capabilities.

The initiative also reflects increasing competition among Indian states to attract strategic manufacturing investments. Several states are introducing sector-specific policies, capital subsidies, tax incentives and infrastructure support to secure projects in semiconductors, electronics, electric mobility and advanced materials. West Bengal’s offer of up to 120% investment assistance could provide a distinctive advantage in attracting investors, although the actual benefits will depend on eligibility conditions, project size, investment categories and the detailed implementation guidelines.

Successful implementation will require more than financial incentives. Investors will also evaluate policy stability, ease of doing business, infrastructure readiness, access to skilled workers, supply-chain availability and the speed of regulatory approvals. Establishing strong industrial ecosystems and ensuring effective coordination between government agencies and private companies will be essential for attracting long-term investments. The state will also need to build specialised training and research capabilities to meet the technical requirements of advanced manufacturing industries.

Overall, West Bengal’s proposed 120% investment assistance for semiconductor, electric vehicle and battery projects represents an ambitious attempt to strengthen its position in India’s next-generation manufacturing landscape. By targeting strategically important sectors linked to digital technology, clean mobility and energy storage, the state aims to attract capital, generate skilled employment and develop competitive industrial supply chains. If supported by effective implementation, infrastructure development and sustained investor engagement, the initiative could help West Bengal emerge as an important contributor to India’s advanced manufacturing and clean energy ambitions.

text:
Electric cars and energy storage setups are changing quickly, and battery makers are adapting just as fast. South Korean suppliers POSCO Future M and LG Energy Solution are partnering to ensure that shift has an ample supply of materials.

POSCO Future M signed a Future Cooperation MOU (Memorandum of Understanding) with LG Energy Solution. Under the deal, POSCO Future M expects to supply 720,000 tons of cathode and anode materials to LG Energy Solution over seven years, running from 2027 through 2033. Both sides plan to settle product roadmaps and sign a formal contract before the end of the year.

Shifting Gears to Meet Demand

A large part of the plan centers on lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cathode materials. Demand for LFP is climbing fast, thanks to cheaper electric cars and power-hungry AI data centers.

To keep up, POSCO Future M plans to convert high-nickel production lines at its Pohang plant into LFP lines, aiming to start full-scale supply to LG Energy Solution early next year. Later on, they want to cut costs even further by tapping into POSCO Group’s lithium resources from salt lakes in Argentina.

The deal also covers synthetic graphite anode materials, produced in Korea and Vietnam. These help batteries charge faster and hold up better over time, making them a great fit for modern electric vehicles. For existing nickel-cobalt-manganese materials, the teams plan to recycle metals from spent batteries to keep production costs down.

Building for the Long Haul

Both teams agreed to collaborate on advanced tech, including materials for sodium-ion batteries, ultra-high-nickel cathodes, and silicon anode materials.

The two companies also plan to navigate shifting global trade rules as a team. That includes keeping an eye on prohibited foreign entity requirements in the U.S. and Europe’s Industrial Accelerator Act.

This move matches POSCO Group’s broader plan to become a national supplier of critical resources. With its own lithium reserves and graphite mines, POSCO Future M is setting up a steady, practical supply chain to keep electric cars and hardware moving forward.

text:
NEW YORK, Nov 10 (Reuters) – will rise to record highs in 2026 and 2027 due to power-hungry and electrification, the US said in its Short-Term Energy Outlook (STEO) on Tuesday.

The projected that will rise from a record 4,216 billion kilowatt-hours (kWh) in 2025 to 4,306 billion kWh in 2026 and 4,370 billion kWh in 2027. If correct, 2026 would be the third year in a row of record demand.

Demand is surging largely due to data centers dedicated to artificial intelligence. Homes and businesses have also been relying more on electricity and less on fossil fuels for heat and transportation.

The EIA forecast that power sales in 2026 will rise to 1,546 billion kWh for residential consumers, 1,557 billion kWh for commercial customers and 1,061 billion kWh for industrial customers.

The all-time highs stand at 1,519 billion kWh for residential consumers and 1,503 billion kWh for commercial customers in 2025 and 1,064 billion kWh for industrial customers in 2000.

As renewable output rises, the EIA said the share of power generation from coal will slide from 17% in 2025 to 15% in 2026 and 2027, while the share of in 2026 will hold steady from 2025 at 40%, then ease to 39% in 2027.

The percentage of will rise from around 24% in 2025 to 25% in 2026 and 28% in 2027, while nuclear power’s share will hold at 18% in 2026 and 2027, the same as in 2025, according to the outlook.

The EIA projected that gas sales in 2026 would slide to 12.2 billion cubic feet per day (bcfd) for residential consumers and 9.4 bcfd for commercial customers, but rise to 23.8 bcfd for industrial customers and 37.4 bcfd for power generation.

Those figures compare with all-time highs of 14.3 bcfd in 1996 for residential consumers, 9.9 bcfd in 2025 for commercial customers, 23.8 bcfd in 1973 for industrial customers, and 36.8 bcfd in 2024 for power generation.

(Reporting by Scott DiSavino; Editing by David Gregorio)

text:
China exported about 927,000 passenger vehicles last month, up 62.3% from a year earlier, the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers said Wednesday. Demand for electric vehicles and hybrids drove the growth.

However, domestic demand continued to be weak, with passenger vehicle sales declining 27.4%, to about 1.7 million units, compared with October 2025.

From January to October, China exported more than 8 million passenger vehicles, compared with 4.8 million in the same period in 2025, according to the association. Domestic passenger car sales fell to 14.5 million from 19.4 million in the same period last year.

Domestic car sales have fallen for months as cuts to some government subsidies for buyers and growing economic uncertainty have dampened demand. A fierce price war, intense competition and excess supply have also prompted automakers to step up their overseas push.

China’s domestic retail car sales could total about 18.5 million vehicles in 2026, the lowest level in years, according to Cui Dongshu, of the China Passenger Car Association.

But car exports could exceed 10 million, according to Cui and other auto analysts. Markets including Europe, Latin America, the Middle East and Southeast Asia are among those where Chinese carmakers are expanding.

“Exports are becoming a central growth driver for some Chinese automakers as domestic demand remains weak,” said Chris Liu, a Shanghai-based senior analyst at the technology research and advisory group Omdia.

Chinese automakers, however, face growing export challenges, including protectionist measures. The European Union, under mounting pressure to reduce its huge trade deficit with China, recently reached a deal with Beijing to curb Chinese hybrid vehicle exports over the next few years.

China’s planned reduction in export tax rebates starting next April is also likely to raise some export costs and squeeze automakers’ profits.

To reduce risks, Chinese automakers have been expanding production overseas to replace some direct exports, including by setting up plants in Brazil and Hungary. S&P analysts say that shift could also weigh on China’s auto export figures in the months ahead.

text:
Archrock, an energy infrastructure company listed on the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE), has agreed to acquire HiVolt Energy in an all-cash transaction valued at up to $450m.

Based in Texas, HiVolt Energy is a provider of electrical infrastructure solutions.

Archrock, which is also a Texas-based company, provides natural gas compression services to the energy industry.

The agreement includes an upfront payment of $415m at closing, along with earn-out incentives of up to $35m linked to the achievement of certain commercial milestones.

The transaction aims to expand Archrock’s range of energy infrastructure services by combining its existing natural gas compression capabilities with HiVolt’s prime power microgrid platform.

Archrock president and CEO Brad Childers said: “Combining HiVolt’s proven prime power microgrid platform with Archrock’s natural gas compression offerings will transform our company into a broader provider of energy infrastructure.

“HiVolt has built a proven, differentiated platform in the energy microgrid market that complements our core compression business and will enable us to provide additional essential services to customers across the energy value chain, particularly in power-constrained geographies.

“The transaction also offers upside from future industrial markets. We are confident that this transaction will advance our strategic priorities and drive long-term growth and value creation for Archrock shareholders.”

HiVolt currently has over 80MW of contracted prime power capacity supported by long-term power purchase agreements, typically lasting five to eight years.

The company has also secured access to more than 500MW of near-term generation equipment.

Archrock stated that the acquisition is expected to be immediately accretive to its earnings per share and cash available for dividend per share.

The company expects to fund the $415m cash portion of the purchase price using its available credit facility.

The transaction, including the earn-out component, reflects a multiple of approximately 6.1 times the midpoint of HiVolt’s projected 2028 adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortisation (EBITDA) range of $70m to $75m. Around 70% of this EBITDA is supported by contracted and awarded opportunities.

The board of directors of Archrock has approved the deal, which is anticipated to close in early 2027, subject to regulatory approvals and standard closing conditions.

Following completion, HiVolt will operate as a separate business segment within Archrock and will continue to be led by its current CEO, Josh Evans.

Archrock plans to maintain HiVolt’s operations and personnel, including its presence in Midland, Texas, while working to extend its reach across the US.

text:
On-site gas contracts can run 15 to 20 years with fixed charges or minimum purchases, so a slower plant can cut output faster than it cuts the gas bill.

Air Products' fiscal fourth-quarter volume growth in the Americas came partly from an asset sale tied to a customer contract that ended early. In its Nov. 5 earnings release, the company said Americas sales rose 27% on 26% higher volumes, "including a significant asset sale associated with an early contract termination in the Americas." It did not name the customer, the plant or the terms that ended the agreement.

The release does not say whether the customer's production fell short or whether a minimum-purchase clause played a part. It does put a recent, concrete case behind a question manufacturers face whenever output slips. Industrial gas contracts for on-site supply can commit a plant to fixed monthly charges or minimum purchases for well over a decade, while production forecasts change every quarter. How much of the gas bill falls when a line slows depends on how the contract was written.

What an On-Site Gas Contract Commits a Plant To

Air Products' on-site and pipeline supply, which generates about half of the company's sales, is generally governed by contracts of 15 to 20 years, or 10 to 15 years for smaller on-site plants. Those contracts commonly include "fixed monthly charges and/or minimum purchase requirements," along with price escalation tied to external indexes. Electricity and natural gas costs are passed through by formula, surcharge or tolling arrangement.

Linde's 2025 annual report describes similar terms. Its on-site agreements are generally total requirement contracts running 10 to 20 years, with minimum purchase requirements and price escalation. Linde estimated about $62 billion in future revenue from minimum purchase requirements and engineering plant sales as of Dec. 31, 2025. That figure excludes on-site sales above the contractual minimums, and Linde expects about half of the minimum-purchase revenue within six years.

Bulk deliveries work differently. Air Products says its liquid bulk and packaged gas sales do not include minimum purchase requirements, and those contracts generally run five years or less. Linde's merchant agreements usually run three to seven years. The storage containers at the customer's site are usually owned and maintained by Linde and leased to the customer, so a change of supplier can also mean a change of tanks.

How Much of the Gas Bill Moves When Output Falls

Consider an on-site agreement with a fixed facility charge of $30,000 a month, a gas price of $0.50 per unit and a monthly minimum of 80,000 units. At a planned 100,000 units, the plant pays $80,000, or $0.80 per unit. If production drops and the plant takes 65,000 units, it still pays the fixed charge plus the 80,000-unit minimum, for $70,000. Volume fell 35%. The bill fell 12.5%, and the effective cost rose to about $1.08 per unit consumed.

Nothing in that example touched the quoted price of $0.50. The higher cost per unit came from the part of the bill that does not track consumption. A procurement team comparing two offers on price alone would miss that difference. So would a finance team that budgets gas as a variable cost per ton of output. Energy pass-through adds another layer, since a formula tied to contracted volume behaves differently from one tied to metered flow when the plant runs slow.

Suppliers are committing capital on the other side of these deals. Air Products expects $3.0 billion to $3.5 billion in capital spending for fiscal 2027. Some of that capacity is built for specific customers. Air Liquide's three new U.S. gas plants include an Indiana facility built to supply SK hynix's first U.S. semiconductor fab. A buyer asking for a volume band or a scheduled review is asking the supplier to carry part of the demand uncertainty on equipment built for one site.

Electronics Gains Diverge From Weaker Industrial Demand

One contract template may not suit every plant, and the suppliers' own outlooks show why. Air Products expect "limited growth globally" in manufacturing and "continued pressure in Europe due to higher costs and weak macroeconomic environment." The same slides cite pressure from imports on European metals and continued weakness in European chemicals. Electronics points the other way. Air Products booked more than $2.0 billion in new electronics wins, has a new asset ramping in Taiwan and is assessing a pipeline of more than $4.0 billion, largely in electronics and space.

Linde's results on Oct. 29 also leaned on electronics. In its third-quarter release, sales rose 9% to $9.4 billion, with volume growth led by electronics, chemicals and energy, and manufacturing. The release said customer proposal activity "remains robust, particularly across electronics," and put Linde's contractual sale-of-gas project backlog at $7.9 billion.

title: Three Indian Americans in TIME's 2026 climate leaders list
description:

Sridhar was recognized in the Titans category for his work developing fuel-cell technology through Bloom Energy.
She serves as executive director of Climate Reserve at the Aspen Global Change Institute.
Dasgupta was named in the Defenders category for his leadership of WRI, an international research organization working on climate change, forests, oceans, sustainable cities and sustainable development.
TIME introduced the TIME100 Climate list in 2023 to recognize influential figures driving climate action through business and other initiatives.
text:
Three Indian Americans have been included in TIME magazine’s 2026 TIME100 Climate list, which recognizes 100 individuals influencing the global response to climate change.

K.R. Sridhar, founder and CEO of Bloom Energy; Aparna Shrivastava, executive director of Climate Reserve at the Aspen Global Change Institute; and Ani Dasgupta, president and CEO of the World Resources Institute (WRI), were recognized in the Titans and Defenders categories.

Their contributions cover different areas of climate action, including electricity generation, the preservation of scientific research and the expansion of clean-energy initiatives.

Sridhar was recognized in the Titans category for his work developing fuel-cell technology through Bloom Energy. The company’s systems generate electricity on-site and can operate using different fuels, including natural gas, biogas and hydrogen. The technology offers an alternative to conventional power generation, although its environmental impact depends on the fuel used.

Bloom Energy’s partnership with Oracle has brought its technology into the growing market for data center power. In April 2026, Oracle and BorderPlex Digital Assets announced that Bloom fuel cells would power Project Jupiter, an artificial intelligence data center campus in Doña Ana County, New Mexico.

The project is expected to use up to 2.45 gigawatts of installed fuel-cell capacity. The announcement said the fuel-cell system would replace previously planned gas turbines and diesel generators.

Read: Two Indian American biomedical engineers named 2027 Siebel Scholars (October 16, 2026)

Before founding Bloom Energy, Sridhar was a professor of aerospace and mechanical engineering at the University of Arizona, where he also directed the Space Technologies Laboratory. He advised NASA on space technology and research related to Mars exploration.

Sridhar earned a bachelor’s degree in mechanical engineering from the National Institute of Technology Tiruchirappalli in 1982. He subsequently completed a master’s degree in nuclear engineering in 1984 and a PhD in mechanical engineering in 1990 at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. He is also a member of the National Academy of Engineering.

Shrivastava was recognized in the Defenders category for her work supporting climate scientists and preserving research capacity amid changes to federal science programs in the United States.

She serves as executive director of Climate Reserve at the Aspen Global Change Institute. The initiative works to connect climate experts with organizations and funding partners, helping them continue research and related work. Shrivastava joined the institute after more than 14 years working at the intersection of climate, development and finance.

Her previous position was leading the climate office at the U.S. International Development Finance Corp., where she oversaw climate investments across clean energy, resilient infrastructure, agriculture and the circular economy.

Climate Reserve was established to help retain scientific expertise and provide opportunities for researchers whose work has been affected by changes in federal funding and staffing. TIME reported that the initiative had placed at least 50 experts at 25 host institutions and mobilized more than $4.5 million in support.

Dasgupta was named in the Defenders category for his leadership of WRI, an international research organization working on climate change, forests, oceans, sustainable cities and sustainable development.

Read: Indian American professor Rita Mitra earns 2026 teaching award (October 23, 2026)

One initiative highlighted in connection with his work is the Latin America Clean Energy Coalition, launched by WRI and partner organizations in November 2025 at the COP30 climate conference in Brazil. The coalition aims to accelerate corporate clean-energy adoption, support the decarbonization of key industries and expand clean-energy investment across Latin America.

WRI also served as the secretariat for the 2026 Our Ocean Conference, held in Mombasa, Kenya. The conference concluded on June 18 with 320 commitments valued at $6.4 billion from governments, businesses and civil society organizations for ocean conservation, sustainable fisheries, climate resilience and the blue economy.

The recognition also comes amid WRI’s work on transport electrification in Ethiopia. The organization has supported the country’s efforts to develop an electric mobility strategy.

Ethiopia’s national five-year e-mobility strategy sets a target of increasing the share of electric vehicles among newly registered vehicles from 40% to 80%. It also includes plans to expand charging infrastructure and encourage local vehicle production.

In his interview with TIME, Dasgupta described climate action as an economic transition rather than solely an effort to reduce carbon emissions. He also identified India and Brazil among the middle-income countries with an important role in developing the clean economy.

TIME introduced the TIME100 Climate list in 2023 to recognize influential figures driving climate action through business and other initiatives. The 2026 edition is the fourth annual selection.

text:
With the growth of the US population, expansion of many new industries and rising costs of traditional energy, there is a need for both more and cleaner power in the US.

Over the next eight years, peak electricity demand is projected to increase by 33%, with annual electricity usage up 47%. This demand is driven by factors such as population growth, expanded electric vehicle (EV) charging, increased electrification of homes and businesses, heavy industry and manufacturing, the retirement of thermal generation, and the rise of data centres to meet artificial intelligence (AI) computing demand. By 2030, data centres could account for nearly 12% of total US electricity demand.

The ageing American power grid cannot support this major surge in demand. Modernising the energy grid and incorporating new technologies are essential to addressing supply and demand challenges.

Historically, storing electricity generated during off-peak hours has been impossible outside of specific areas suitable for pumped hydropower. Not every location has these preconditions for pumped hydro – namely elevation and water. For example, Texas is not known for its elevation, nor is Arizona for its abundance of water.

Fortunately, batteries have emerged as a practical solution to historical energy capture challenges.

Overcoming energy challenges with BESS

Batteries can enable the modern grid by storing and releasing energy from both traditional (i.e. natural gas, coal) and renewable (wind and solar) electricity generation to deliver power to customers when they most need it. In addition to supporting residential, industrial, and data centre demand for electricity, battery-powered energy storage systems (BESS) can also insulate the grid from large, fluctuating loads.

BESS are helping to bring more power online faster than ever because these projects can be designed, commissioned, and connected to the grid more quickly and efficiently than any other grid technology. In many cases, it can take years for the conventional grid to expand, but new ESS can be deployed to bolster the existing grid in a matter of weeks. BESS are mass-produced, containerised, and scalable from a few dozen to 1000 MWh or more.

In short, BESS help the grid manage the large new loads coming online by making better use of existing resources and avoiding unnecessary infrastructure buildout, while also improving reliability during periods of peak demand.

Batteries and AI

Within the specific context of AI data centres, BESS can smooth out the power quality issues they experience as a result of their unique and volatile load patterns. BESS can also add flexibility for more capacity at AI data centres, helping projects get up and running more quickly and reducing CAPEX costs through the storage of electricity during off-peak hours to be used at times of peak operation. BESS can also help AI data centres be more responsible utility customers by smoothing out potential load changes and therefore reducing the burden on the local grid, preventing possible power surges, and keeping energy costs stable.

In fact, the U.S. Federal Energy Regulatory Commission began requiring data centre operators to invest in their own generation and transmission infrastructure starting in June 2026. These behind-the-meter (BTM) solutions can help offset the risk of grid bottlenecks to overall US electricity generation and represent a growing opportunity for BESS.

Batteries have more uses in AI data centres beyond their central role in ESS. In the event of failures, battery-based uninterruptible power supply (UPS) systems can help data centres get back online nearly instantaneously, unlike diesel generators, which are slow to power up. BESS can also be used in concert with diesel generators to ensure seamless operation of these centres.

The wider effects

In addition to helping the grid expand, working more efficiently, better incorporating renewables for a cleaner grid, and offsetting the energy demands of AI data centres, BESS could also potentially help make electricity more affordable.

According to The New York Times, electricity is the second biggest energy expense most people pay after vehicle fuel. Residential electricity prices have soared by 30% since 2020.3

This affordability crisis is driven by:

Transmission and distribution costs.

Rising fuel costs – much of the electricity in the US is generated by burning natural gas, the price of which has been rising since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and further compounded by the situation in Iran.

Supply and demand – the amount of electricity currently being generated is not matching demand.

The costs of fixing, rebuilding, and operating an increasingly antiquated power grid.

The impact of natural disasters including wildfires in California, storms in the Southeast, etc.

BESS can mitigate these issues by:

Curbing the unnecessary buildout of new transmission lines and power generation just to satisfy peak demand.

Enabling more incorporation of renewables like wind and solar into the electricity sourcing while still being compatible with traditionally created energy.

Creating electricity at off-peak hours and storing it for when it is needed to compensate for fluctuations in sourcing and demand.

Helping modernise the grid.

Helping offset the impact of wildfires, storms, and other natural events that threaten grid stability.

While ESS is currently the primary focus in the US for battery manufacturers like LG Energy Solution, it is important to remember that the large-format battery business was built on the back of the EV market. The EV market has not taken off as expected, but LG Energy Solution has responded by:

Expanding overall capacity by converting existing EV lines at many of its North American plants to ESS lines.

Scaling up its ability to build larger pack and link systems, also in the US LG Energy Solution does not just build battery cells, but complete energy storage systems – 20-ft-long ESS enclosures capable of 5.11 MWh of storage, which are grouped together at energy storage sites and operated with advanced software to create gigawatt-hour scale deployments across the US.

Strengthening its overall product competitiveness by adding technologies like lithium-iron phosphate prismatic batteries to its mass-production portfolio.

Working toward commercialising additional long-duration ESS technology like sodium-ion batteries.

Powering the future

With their ability to create jobs at all levels, enable essential electricity growth, and modernisation while powering key industries, batteries should be seen as a critical component of American infrastructure and a critical way to ensure affordable, consistent, and plentiful energy to meet growing societal demands.

title: India Bans Lithium-Ion Battery Black Mass Exports - Deccan Chronicle
description:
Chennai: The government has prohibited exports of the waste, scrap or spent lithium-ion battery.
The Directorate General of Foreign Trade prohibited exports of waste, and scrap of primary cells, primary batteries and electric accumulators, spent primary cells, spent batteries and spent electric accumulators, unsorted and not containing lead, cadmium and mercury.
This includes Lithium-ion battery black mass.
Black mass is the dark powder left after used lithium-ion batteries or battery manufacturing scrap are shredded and larger pieces of metal and plastic are removed.
Depending on the battery chemistry, refiners can recover lithium, nickel, cobalt and graphite from the powder.
text:
Chennai: The government has prohibited exports of the waste, scrap or spent lithium-ion battery. This will help recovery of lithium, nickel, cobalt and graphite from the scrap.

The Directorate General of Foreign Trade prohibited exports of waste, and scrap of primary cells, primary batteries and electric accumulators, spent primary cells, spent batteries and spent electric accumulators, unsorted and not containing lead, cadmium and mercury. This includes Lithium-ion battery black mass.

The order will come into effect immediately.

India recorded zero exports of these items in FY2026. According to GTRI, the government would have acted to prevent future shipments and keep the material available to domestic refiners. India has low resources of these materials and most of supply is met through imports.

Black mass is the dark powder left after used lithium-ion batteries or battery manufacturing scrap are shredded and larger pieces of metal and plastic are removed. Depending on the battery chemistry, refiners can recover lithium, nickel, cobalt and graphite from the powder.

Recovering more of these materials at home could reduce battery makers’ reliance on imports.

However, black mass can also contain toxic electrolyte residues and heavy metals that require further treatment. Hazardous-waste rules require prior permission for such shipments, but exporters can evade scrutiny by declaring the material as cobalt powder, a nickel intermediate or another industrial product.

“Effective enforcement will depend on Customs checking how the material was produced as well as how it was declared since a different name or tariff code can conceal the same waste,” GTRI said.

name: Clean Energy
title: Clean and secure: India–EU–UK cooperation is key to building diversified cleantech supply chains
description:
The message is clear: India, the EU and UK are well positioned for deeper cleantech cooperation.
Deeper India–EU–UK clean energy dependencies would therefore mean benefits for both industrial competitiveness and energy security for all partners.
India, EU and UK offer complementary strengths for building cleantech value chains India can build on its trade agreement discussions with the EU and UK to cooperate on developing cleantech value chains, with benefits for all partners.
An India–EU–UK green transition accelerator platform could bring together governments, business, and investors to turn priority cleantech opportunities into commercially viable partnerships.
Cooperation has benefits beyond India, the EU and the UK India–EU–UK cooperation can build competitive clean tech industries, diversify supply chains and widen access to affordable clean technologies across the Global South.
text:
The week before COP31, the Bharat Renewable Energy Summit (BRES) in Delhi demonstrated India’s ambition and action on clean energy, and the opportunities for partners such as the EU and UK. The message is clear: India, the EU and UK are well positioned for deeper cleantech cooperation. Brand new trade agreements offer a foundation for discussions about how market access can be turned into investible projects. The partners have complementary strengths across five key cleantech value chains, where collaboration can build domestic manufacturing capacity in India and diversify sourcing and markets for the EU and UK. Deeper India–EU–UK clean energy dependencies would therefore mean benefits for both industrial competitiveness and energy security for all partners.

With disruptions in West Asia again exposing the cost of relying on concentrated and vulnerable fossil fuel supplies, securing reliable, affordable renewable energy is increasingly inseparable from economic resilience and industrial competitiveness for India, the EU and the UK alike. Recent comments from Indian Prime Minister Modi reflected this shift, when he stated that: “Energy security is directly linked to economic security. And we all know that the future of energy security lies in clean energy. If we continue to remain excessively dependent on fossil fuels, the global economy will continue to face repeated disruptions.”

This is not just rhetoric. The IEA estimates that renewables avoided more than $100 billion in coal and gas import costs for India between 2011 and 2025, with cumulative savings projected to more than double by 2030. India has now surpassed 300 gigawatts (GW) of renewable capacity, reached over 50% non-fossil installed capacity five years ahead of the target in its 2030 climate action plan (NDC), and become the world’s second-largest solar module manufacturer. The direction of travel is even more ambitious, with a vision of achieving around 2000 GW of renewable energy capacity by 2047.

India, EU and UK offer complementary strengths for building cleantech value chains

India can build on its trade agreement discussions with the EU and UK to cooperate on developing cleantech value chains, with benefits for all partners. There is considerable untapped potential; in 2024, bilateral trade between India and the EU accounted for just 1% of their respective imports of solar PV modules, wind generators and lithium-ion batteries.

This cooperation should focus on specific value chains where combining the partners’ respective capabilities can improve competitiveness and supply chain resilience. Discussion at a recent roundtable convened by the International Solar Alliance (ISA), Dalberg and E3G identified opportunities across five cleantech value chains that are particularly critical to delivering a clean, resilient power system (see table below).

India’s expanding manufacturing base, engineering capabilities, competitive costs and a large growing domestic market complement EU and UK strengths in research, innovation, industrial expertise and investment. For India, these partnerships can strengthen domestic manufacturing and improve access to advanced technology. For the EU and UK, deeper partnerships with India offer opportunities to diversify sourcing and expand markets for technology, equipment and investment.

SectorComplementary strengthsPartnership opportunitiesSolarIndia: Expanding module production

EU & UK: Upstream technology and equipmentJoint ventures (JVs) in cells, wafers, glass and equipment

Co-develop perovskite and tandem cellsEnergy storageIndia: Scaling lithium iron phosphate (LFP) and new chemistries

EU & UK: Scaling nickel manganese cobalt (NMC); materials and equipment expertiseJVs in battery materials, cells and equipment

Align standards, traceability and certificationGreen hydrogenIndia: Growing alkaline electrolyser production

EU & UK: Alkaline and proton exchange membrane (PEM) expertiseCo-develop electrolysers and balance-of-plant systems.

Partner on derivatives production and offtake, and align certification for trade.WindIndia: Competitive onshore components

EU & UK: Advanced and offshore componentsJointly manufacture advanced and offshore components

Enable market access through testing and certificationGridsIndia: Transformers and conductors

EU & UK: High voltage direct current (HVDC), stability systems and advanced cablesExpand equipment trade and ease supplier qualification

Jointly develop advanced grid system

Practical steps to turn trade agreements into investment

The timing is right, with new trade agreements to build on. The India–UK Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA) has been in force since July 2026; the India–EU Free Trade Agreement (FTA) is expected to be signed in December 2026 and enter into force in early 2027.

Turning market access into investible projects however requires immediate practical action. The discussion at our roundtable identified key priorities for how to advance delivery:

Set a target to increase cleantech trade for the next three years and translate market access into predictable two-way demand. Give manufacturers the confidence to invest and scale through long-term purchasing commitments from industrial buyers and utilities, and public procurement opportunities wherever eligible. Investment protection and intellectual property safeguards could support joint ventures and technology sharing.

Build on existing partnerships to address specific supply chain gaps. The EU–India Trade and Technology Council (TTC); Clean Energy and Climate Partnership (CECP), Horizon Europe, India–UK Energy Dialogue and India’s bilateral cooperation with EU member states can help advance concrete opportunities across priority value chains. Initiatives such as the Indo-German collaboration on next-generation solar cells, and the India–UK Offshore Wind Taskforce, can connect industrial partners, support cooperation and project development.

Make it easier for suppliers to serve both markets. Align standards and explore mutual recognition of testing and certification to widen sourcing options for European buyers and market access for Indian manufacturers.

Bring buyers and financiers in early. Develop a small portfolio of industry-led manufacturing projects in priority cleantech sectors with agreed production requirements and credible demand. EU and UK development finance institutions and export credit agencies could work with Indian financial institutions to reduce financing costs and improve bankability, complemented by joint investment in R&D and industrial skills.

Create a platform to deliver. An India–EU–UK green transition accelerator platform could bring together governments, business, and investors to turn priority cleantech opportunities into commercially viable partnerships. Building on existing partnerships and institutional mechanisms, such a platform would help channel technical support and finance into project preparation, standards and certification cooperation, skills development, and technology demonstrations and pilots. Directing part of the proposed €500 million in EU support under the FTA towards such a platform could help relevant activities, helping to build a credible project pipeline that attracts wider public and private finance.

Cooperation has benefits beyond India, the EU and the UK

India–EU–UK cooperation can build competitive clean tech industries, diversify supply chains and widen access to affordable clean technologies across the Global South.

Clean electrification offers a shared agenda connecting energy security, industrial competitiveness, and emissions reduction. Existing partnerships, including through the International Solar Alliance (ISA), provide routes for delivery while engagements with diplomatic initiatives such as the Global Energy Transition Forum, and the Global Clean Power Alliance could open further opportunities. The challenge now is to turn shared interests and trade frameworks into commercially viable partnerships at pace and scale delivering investment, competitive manufacturing, skilled jobs and reliable clean energy across all three economies and beyond.

name: Texas Environment
title: As Texas embraces carbon storage, a Black community questions the risks
description:
Carbon injection wells proposed in Texas Companies in Texas are working on 13 different projects to inject and store carbon dioxide underground.
The volume of carbon dioxide injected underground through those agreements will equal emissions from 2 million cars.
Carbon dioxide leaking into water could increase its acidity and cause metals to contaminate it, according to advocacy groups and experts.
Christian has argued carbon dioxide is good for plants, rather than acknowledge the robust science that shows people burning fossil fuels has caused carbon dioxide concentrations in the atmosphere to rise, driving up global temperatures.
(Cheek community leaders have a list of wants too, including improved roads, a community center and an emergency warning system.)
text:
CHEEK — On a rural road outside Beaumont, a Texas energy giant is preparing to pump carbon dioxide underground to permanently store it and keep the gas from contributing to global warming. The project could be the first of its kind to start operating in the state.

It’s a long-awaited milestone for the oil and gas industry, which has touted carbon capture and storage as an important tool for cleaning up industry emissions. Texas lawmakers threw their support behind the technology, while state regulators spent years seeking permitting authority from the federal government to try to clear projects faster.

The Texas Railroad Commission, which oversees the oil and gas industry, won that authority late last year and approved this ExxonMobil project in September. But the nearby community of Cheek has asked commissioners to reconsider the permit decision.

The area close to the project is predominantly Black, and many residents are working class or elderly. People there don’t trust the company’s assurances that it will keep residents and their groundwater safe.

Only a small number of carbon storage wells have been permitted so far across the United States, and some CO2-related accidents have already happened. Experts and community advocates have warned of the risk for pipeline accidents and potential underground leaks. Leaders in Cheek are concerned the injected carbon dioxide could contaminate groundwater or get into the air and suffocate them. They worry emergency responders won’t be equipped to rescue them.

Carbon injection wells proposed in Texas

Companies in Texas are working on 13 different projects to inject and store carbon dioxide underground. Most are concentrated near existing pipelines and have multiple wells.

“We’re just shocked that they would want to do this so close to homes,” said Douglas Cormier, the 67-year-old president of the Cheek Texas Community Association, who grew up in the rural town and lives there with his wife near his daughters and grandkids.

Residents explained they don’t want to be the test subjects for the technology, and some experts argue it’s more distracting than effective in fighting climate change. Harvard University History of Science Professor Naomi Oreskes, who studies disinformation and climate change, has called carbon capture and storage “mostly a dangerous distraction.”

A recent investigation by Drilled and ProPublica showed it would take more resources than feasible for carbon capture and storage to reduce emissions enough to avoid extreme warming. Companies have canceled or paused nearly a third of 19 proposed carbon storage projects in Texas so far.

But carbon capture supporters argue that storing emissions is an important part of an “all of the above” approach to fighting climate change. Federal tax credits support carbon capture projects. Locally, East Texas remains attractive because of its existing carbon dioxide pipeline network (owned by ExxonMobil), its geology and nearby industrial facilities that might pay for their carbon to be stored.

ExxonMobil has seven agreements with companies to store the greenhouse gas. The volume of carbon dioxide injected underground through those agreements will equal emissions from 2 million cars.

“The community’s concerns around safety of any sort of an injection project are valid and real and need to be taken seriously,” said Nichole Saunders, senior director and lead counsel for energy transition with the Environmental Defense Fund. “At the same time, the need for more carbon management infrastructure to get to where we want to go on climate is also real.”

So far, the case has raised questions about whether companies and the Railroad Commission are doing enough to address community concerns as a backlog of projects awaits approval.

Agency watchdogs say the commission has a history of failing to keep communities safe from industry risks. It’s also facing pressure from state Rep. Drew Darby, leader of the House’s energy resources committee, who told the agency at a September hearing that carbon-capture projects needed to be moving at “utmost pace while protecting the public.”

In a statement to the Tribune, Railroad Commission spokesperson Bryce Dubee said the organization has a record of protecting drinking water while regulating injection wells. Winning the authority to regulate carbon storage “speaks volumes to this expertise,” Dubee said.

ExxonMobil held early meetings with community members in Cheek. The company’s permit requires it to install automatic shut-off systems for the injection wells, monitor the underground carbon dioxide plume and post a phone number where the operators can be reached around the clock.

The permitting program requires coordination with local emergency officials, according to the commission. ExxonMobil sponsors emergency training programs through the Texas A&M Engineering Extension Service in College Station.

“We want community members to know they can count on us to operate responsibly, communicate openly, and put safety first every day,” Senior Vice President Dominic Genetti wrote in a blog post.

But the day following Darby’s comments, after hearing ExxonMobil hadn’t talked with the community since the residents hired lawyers, Railroad Commission Chair Christi Craddick scolded ExxonMobil for not supporting residents enough. Some people from Cheek had taken a bus to be there to voice their concern.

“Give them information,” she said. “Be there for their safety. Give ‘em a fire truck if that’s what they want.”

Then Craddick voted for the permit.

Community distrust

Photos and posters about the area’s decades-long history hosting local rodeos hang in 81-year-old Preston Frank’s self-made museum in Cheek. Like many who live here, Frank, an upholsterer, inherited the land from his family. He considers it an important way to build generational wealth.

“That’s the reason why we’ve been fighting ExxonMobil,” he said. “We don’t want them coming in here and diminishing the value of the land.”

Just west of Beaumont off Interstate 10, the unincorporated community of Cheek is split by the highway and railroad, with many homes sitting on large tracts of land dotted with cattle and horses. People wave to each other. On the north side, there’s a Catholic and a Baptist church. Once a year, residents gather for a community picnic at the park.

ExxonMobil plans to compress carbon dioxide into an “almost liquid state,” pump it thousands of feet deep into the Earth and let it flow into little spaces in the rock, where scientists expect some to dissolve into salty water in those spaces or get stuck like a drink spilled in sand. Residents from the start had concerns.

How does ExxonMobil know where the molecules will go? What if they don’t behave as expected? What if the project gets abandoned?

Carbon dioxide leaking into water could increase its acidity and cause metals to contaminate it, according to advocacy groups and experts. If it leaks back into the air or a pipeline ruptures and people are caught in a big enough plume, they won’t be able to breathe or run gas-powered cars to escape.

“Contamination of drinking water with CO2, or with metals or chemicals leaching out of rock due to CO2 acidification of the water, could be very costly if the affected aquifer is used by a lot of people,” Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory researchers wrote in a 2007 paper. “[O]nce any aquifer is contaminated, it will remain so.”

The Cheek Texas Community Association signed on in July 2025 with attorneys at the nonprofit Earthjustice, which charges no cost. They fought the permit approval all the way to a state administrative hearing in March this year where they argued ExxonMobil hadn’t done enough to adequately ensure water and public safety would be protected and wasn’t monitoring a large enough area underground.

“It’s the first one in an area so close to a community, and that’s why the water issues and the safety issues are so paramount here,” said Jen Powis, who leads Earthjustice’s Gulf regional office.

The project also raised familiar concerns over environmental justice, a term used by researchers who have shown communities of color suffer a greater proportion of environmental harm than whiter, wealthier areas. Residents feared ExxonMobil saw in their homes a place where the company could more easily and cheaply push a project through.

The company already built three unassuming injection wells at the edge of the community. Only some residents in Cheek signed so-called pore space agreements with ExxonMobil for use of the small pockets in underground rock where the carbon dioxide will be stored and that property owners control under current case law.

“I’m just thinking they found an area where they can do it and not expect a lot of resistance,” said James Strambler, 70, a former IBM technician who moved there around 2017.

After the March hearing, a technical examiner and administrative law judge recommended moving the permit forward to the commission for a vote.

State gains power

Texas’ work to win the authority to permit carbon storage wells dates back more than a decade.

In 2009, Texas lawmakers passed a law authorizing the railroad commission to design a framework for how the state would regulate these projects in a way that upheld federal law. In 2022, the state formally applied to the Environmental Protection Agency for that authority.

At a virtual July 2025 hearing held by the EPA, the Texas Oil and Gas Association, a trade group representing 90% of the state’s fossil fuel production, said approving carbon capture and injection would be an economic boom for the state.

Gaining permitting power for carbon storage wells was “essential for our state’s economic future and energy leadership,” said Todd Staples, the group’s president, following the hearing.

Supporters of the technology are quick to point out that carbon dioxide makes sodas fizzy and creates the tunnels of fog that Texas football teams run through. They cite a study done by Texas A&M researchers that found the danger of leaks presents “a low probability of occurrence” — a risk that can be monitored and managed.

Advocates also point to the state’s decades-long history of injecting carbon dioxide into wells under a different type of permit as a way to draw more oil out of the ground and also store some of the greenhouse gas, a process known as enhanced oil recovery, which ExxonMobil has pursued for decades.

“This has been put in place now for over 50 years,” said Scott Castleman, spokesman for the Gulf Coast Carbon Capture and Storage Alliance, which represents Calpine, Chevron and ExxonMobil. “Certainly, there is more discussion and opportunity for this industry to scale, and so that’s where you’re starting to see projects and interest in areas that may not have seen this before.”

Establishing community trust will “make or break” projects as the industry grows, said Sophia Cunningham, executive director of the Houston Energy Transition Initiative at the Greater Houston Partnership. Best practices include engaging the community early and providing different, meaningful ways for people to give input and discuss possible benefits.

“It’s a technology that can reduce emissions associated with our industrial activities, and so that is a good pursuit and it’s important to support that,” Cunningham said. “But it’s also reasonable to expect that not everybody in a community is going to want that.”

Residents near projects should be asking whether there would be a helpline to call for any issues, or whether truck drivers would observe weight limits for roads and bridges, said Susan Hovorka, a research professor at the University of Texas at Austin’s Bureau of Economic Geology. In Hovorka’s mind, research and experience have already proven the technology to be safe.

“It’s not utterly without peril, and so people are not foolish to ask,” Hovorka said, “But … their anxiety is sometimes maybe higher than is practical and realistic.”

But there have been serious incidents in other parts of the U.S.

In Mississippi, a carbon dioxide pipeline ruptured in 2020 after heavy rain caused a landslide, releasing a vapor cloud of CO2. A government investigation found that first responders had not been notified about the safety risks and “had to guess” what they were. Dozens of people went to the hospital.

Injected fluid at another facility in Illinois leaked into “unauthorized zones” underground, which most residents learned about in a news article.

Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry paused the state’s review of new applications to ensure any permit issued would be in compliance with state regulations, citing a need for a review process that considers “the safety of our citizens and environment and that streamlines the process for greater efficiency.” Louisiana has permitted three carbon dioxide wells to be constructed so far but not to begin operating.

In other states with permitting authority as of mid-October, Arizona hasn’t permitted any carbon injection wells. North Dakota has approved eight active injection wells across three projects, and Wyoming has approved five wells in one project.

“The benefit isn’t there,” said Naomi Yoder, an environmental researcher who opposed Texas’ bid to regulate the technology and raised concerns about potential harm to the environment and communities. “So it doesn’t make any risk worth it, and there is risk involved. You can’t possibly sequester enough carbon dioxide to make it worth it.”

Can Texas improve?

In the Texas state hearing in September, the day before ExxonMobil’s Cheek permit won initial approval, Darby reiterated the importance of supporting the industry. Virginia Palacios, executive director of the agency watchdog group Commission Shift, told him they should also ensure companies pay for equipment and training for emergency responders.

Meanwhile, Railroad Commissioner Wayne Christian has vehemently opposed these projects. Christian has argued carbon dioxide is good for plants, rather than acknowledge the robust science that shows people burning fossil fuels has caused carbon dioxide concentrations in the atmosphere to rise, driving up global temperatures.

He voted against ExxonMobil’s permit, saying he didn’t think it was safe.

Newly elected Railroad Commissioner Jon Rosenthal, who will join Craddick and Christian on the three-person commission, told Inside Climate News he supported the state taking over regulation of the wells.

Some projects have meanwhile stalled. Oxy said in its latest earnings call in August that its carbon storage project — the first and only other one approved in the state so far — was coming online “as we look forward.”

Other projects are moving forward, including ExxonMobil’s second project near a community not far from Cheek, called Nome. The commission is collecting public comment on that project this week at hearings on Monday and Tuesday. ExxonMobil named this one “Sunflower,” fitting with the Cheek project called “Rose.”

In late October, environmental and community advocates knocked on residents’ doors to invite them to a meeting about how to advocate for themselves. Only one person from the project’s area attended. Several arrived from Cheek, lending advice on what they’d learned while attendees ate pasta and salad.

The meeting hosts characterized the technology as a financial boon to industry and the Railroad Commission while putting drinking water at risk. The colorless, odorless gas can also cause suffocation, presenter Alexis Iwasiw warned the group.

“At high concentrations … it can lead to serious injury or death,” she said.

The next night, ExxonMobil held an open house in the small Nome City Hall. They served boudin balls and shrimp and offered colorful pamphlets about the company’s safety record, how to respond in an emergency and how drinking water would be protected. They displayed a poster of other pipelines in the area.

As the sun went down, the group of several dozen made its way outside, where the ExxonMobil presenters enthusiastically launched into explaining how CO2 is safe at certain levels. With a call of “let it rip, tater chip,” they released the gas from a demonstration pipeline, where it puffed out visibly like white smoke.

Mike Doguet, a 72-year-old rice and turf farmer turned real estate developer, looked on. He believed the company did a much better job communicating with residents in advance here than in Cheek. The company is paying for new firefighting equipment, he said, among other community support. (Cheek community leaders have a list of wants too, including improved roads, a community center and an emergency warning system.)

One of the Sunflower project’s injection wells sits across the street from Doguet’s home in Nome, making neighbors wonder if there was oil. Doguet’s daughter lives next door and his son isn’t far. He wasn’t worried about safety.

“In my mind, it’s going to encourage new industry. It’s going to be good for the environment. It’s all positive to me,” Doguet said. “I don’t see the negatives.”

As the presentation went on, a resident from Cheek peppered the ExxonMobil employees with questions. One of the ExxonMobil presenters snapped back, telling her they were in the business of keeping substances in pipelines and would always err on the side of safety.

A former ExxonMobil employee and Nome resident in the crowd, 77-year-old Lawrence Riley, piped up to say that in his decades of experience, he’d never had a pipeline emergency: “They are very, very safe, I am telling you,” he said.

Wearing an ExxonMobil hat, 71-year-old Mayor Kerry Abney at one point walked through the CO2 cloud. He thought the project was great: Workers were shopping at Big D’s in town, contributing to sales tax, he said. People had a chance to make money in a place where agriculture is tough.

As Abney put it in an interview: “Santa Claus came.”

The Cheek resident watching the plume crossed her arms, looking skeptical.

Carlos Nogueras Ramos and Zach Leggio contributed reporting.

Transcript:

Last December, the Army’s first battery-electric locomotive went into service at Fort Hood in Texas. And it’s benefiting both the climate and national security.

The rail industry has long relied on diesel engines that emit climate-warming carbon dioxide and pollution that’s dangerous to breathe.

Ira Dorfman of Innovative Rail Technologies says his company’s zero-emissions design reduces those harmful impacts without trade-offs to the train’s power or performance.

Dorfman: “It’s important that we can do everything that a traditional diesel locomotive can do, and we’ve proven that …we can pull as many Abrams tanks as that diesel locomotive can pull.”

The locomotive they built for the Army comes with another advantage, too. It has a bidirectional charging system that allows electricity to flow both ways, so its batteries can provide a source of power to Fort Hood during severe weather or other emergencies.

Dorfman acknowledges that purchasing a new electric train is expensive.

Dorfman: “Most of the locomotives that are running today were built between the 1950s and the 1970s.”

And they’re typically rehabilitated instead of fully replaced.

But for the Army, investing in an electric locomotive is also an investment in resiliency.

title: America's Republican Defeat Offers Only a Glimmer of Hope for Global Climate Policy Change
description:
The distance between electoral promises, congressional powers and actual reductions in greenhouse gas emissions remains considerable.
But it offers an opportunity to reverse some of the damage inflicted on American climate policy over the preceding two years.
Whether this translates into even a marginal shift in global climate policy remains uncertain.
Even a substantial American reduction would not, by itself, change the trajectory of global warming dramatically.
A turning point, but not yet a transformation The Republican defeat has opened the door by just a crack to create space for rebuilding climate policy and contesting fossil-fuel expansion and environmental deregulation.
text:
The Democratic victory in the November 2026 US midterm elections offers little hope for international climate action. The distance between electoral promises, congressional powers and actual reductions in greenhouse gas emissions remains considerable.

The Democratic Party’s sweeping victory in the November 3 American midterm elections, securing control of both the Senate and House of Representatives, is a political setback for President Donald Trump’s fossil-fuel-centred agenda. But it offers an opportunity to reverse some of the damage inflicted on American climate policy over the preceding two years. Whether this translates into even a marginal shift in global climate policy remains uncertain.

The US accounts for ~13% of global fossil-fuel and industrial CO₂ emissions and is historically the largest contributor to atmospheric greenhouse gas accumulation. Its withdrawal from the Paris Agreement, dismantling of environmental regulations and promotion of oil, gas and coal have weakened an already struggling international climate cooperation. Other governments have consequently found it easier to justify delaying their own commitments.

The Democratic victory challenges this direction, but it is important to examine what the new Congress has actually promised.

What have the Democrats promised?

There are some encouraging indications in the statements made by Democratic leaders before and after the election. In March 2026, Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer announced a five-point energy affordability agenda. Its principal commitments were to expand clean energy, restore renewable energy tax credits under the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA), accelerate electricity transmission and storage infrastructure, protect consumers from rising electricity prices and ensure that data centres bear the costs of their enormous energy requirements. Schumer promised that restoring IRA clean-energy tax credits would be among his first priorities upon securing a Senate majority. He also advocated investment in geothermal and nuclear energy alongside solar and wind.

The significance of these commitments lies in the connection they make between climate action and employment, energy affordability and economic competitiveness, rather than presenting them exclusively as environmental obligations.

The House Democrats have also developed a policy blueprint through their Sustainable Energy and Environment Coalition. Its proposals include building retrofits, energy efficiency, expanded transmission infrastructure, greater transparency regarding data-centre energy and water consumption, and protection against arbitrary cancellation of clean-energy funding. Representative Kathy Castor, associated with this initiative, described it as a vision of a clean and prosperous economy benefiting everyone.

Texas Senator-elect James Talarico and Ohio Senator-elect Sherrod Brown campaigned on energy affordability, the economic consequences of expanding data centres and consumer interests. These positions suggest that a new political constituency is emerging around the economics of the energy transition.

Nevertheless, climate change itself was not a central theme of the Democratic election campaign. This is an important limitation. The party has demonstrated greater willingness to support clean energy, but has not yet presented a unified commitment to phasing out fossil fuels.

How much can American emissions actually decline?

A quantitative assessment helps distinguish political expectations from realistic possibilities.

The Climate Action Tracker’s 2026 assessment projects that, under the Trump administration’s current policies, American greenhouse gas emissions (GHG) could reach 5.7–6.0 billion tonnes of CO₂-equivalent annually in 2030. This represents a reduction of only 20–25% below 2005 levels.

More significantly, these emissions are projected to be approximately 14–15% higher in 2030 than under the Biden-era policy trajectory assessed in 2024.

The difference indicates the potential scale of the climate-policy reversal. Restoring the IRA incentives, protecting renewable energy projects and reinstating vehicle and power-sector emissions regulations could recover part of this lost reduction.

For comparison, the US Environmental Protection Agency’s modelling of the original IRA projected economy-wide CO₂ emissions reductions of 35–43% below 2005 levels by 2030. These were projections under the original legislation, not forecasts of what the new Congress can achieve.

It would therefore be misleading to assume that the Democrats can immediately deliver a 35–43% reduction. Their more realistic initial objective would be to prevent further deterioration and recover some of the emissions reductions lost through the Trump administration’s policies.

There are also institutional constraints. President Trump retains executive authority and can veto legislation. Although Democrats control both chambers, they do not automatically possess the votes required to overcome a presidential veto. Restoring tax credits and reversing executive deregulation will therefore require either bipartisan agreements or a subsequent change in presidential administration.

The immediate impact of the Democrats’ victory is more likely to be congressional oversight, resistance to further deregulation, protection of existing clean-energy investments and renewed state-level climate initiatives.

What does this mean for global warming?

Even a substantial American reduction would not, by itself, change the trajectory of global warming dramatically. Global greenhouse gas emissions reached approximately 54.1 billion tonnes of CO₂-equivalent in 2025. Even if American policies were restored sufficiently to recover the emissions gap with the earlier Biden-era trajectory, the reduction could amount to only 1–2% of current global annual greenhouse gas emissions. The direct contribution to slowing global temperature rise would consequently be small. The greater significance of an American policy shift would lie in encouraging other major emitters to strengthen their GHG reduction commitments.

The UNEP Emissions Gap Report 2025 estimated that existing national commitments, if fully implemented, would still lead to ~2.3–2.5°C of warming this century. Under current policies, the projection was ~2.8°C. The world needs much deeper reductions, not merely a return to pre-Trump policies.

A turning point, but not yet a transformation

The Republican defeat has opened the door by just a crack to create space for rebuilding climate policy and contesting fossil-fuel expansion and environmental deregulation. If the Democrats succeed in using this opportunity to garner greater US support for adaptation, renewable energy, and climate resilience programmes for climate-vulnerable countries, there is a glimmer of hope for the Global South to renegotiate international climate finance and technology cooperation that benefits them.

But the Democrats have yet to demonstrate that they are prepared to confront the structural dependence of the American economy on fossil fuels and ever-expanding energy and material consumption. The election offers a very guarded hope, not a climate victory. Its ultimate significance will depend on whether the Democrats translate their promises into measurable emissions reductions, restore international climate cooperation and recognise that the climate crisis is fundamentally a question of ecological limits and global economic and climate justice.

text:
The Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT), under the Department of Commerce, has prohibited the export of lithium-ion battery black mass to strengthen domestic recycling capacity and ensure greater recovery of critical minerals.

The DGFT amended the export policy for the item, classified under ITC (HS) Code 85491400, from ‘Free’ to ‘Prohibited’ with immediate effect and until further orders. The transitional arrangements under Para 1.05 of the Foreign Trade Policy (FTP), 2023, will apply.

ITC (HS) Code 85491400 covers waste and scrap of primary cells, primary batteries and electric accumulators, including spent cells, batteries and accumulators that are unsorted and do not contain lead, cadmium or mercury. The notification specifically identifies lithium-ion battery black mass under this classification.

Black mass is a powder-like material generated by shredding end-of-life lithium-ion batteries and battery manufacturing waste. It contains recoverable quantities of critical minerals, including lithium, cobalt, nickel and manganese.

These minerals are essential for electric mobility, advanced chemistry cell batteries, energy storage systems, electronics and renewable energy technologies. India remains substantially dependent on imports for several of these critical resources, making domestic recycling an important avenue for strengthening supply security.

According to the government, although India’s capacity to recycle battery waste and recover critical minerals has expanded significantly, it remains underutilised due to inadequate availability of feedstock. The export of domestically generated black mass diverts valuable secondary resources overseas, while some domestic recyclers have had to import the material to meet their requirements.

The export prohibition aims to ensure that black mass generated in India is processed and refined within the country. It is expected to improve feedstock availability for domestic recycling and refining facilities, enhance capacity utilisation and encourage fresh investments and employment in the sector.

The measure is also expected to increase the domestic recovery of lithium, cobalt, nickel and other critical minerals, reduce import dependence and lower the associated foreign exchange outgo.

By retaining these resources within the country, the government aims to strengthen supply chains for battery manufacturing, electric vehicles, energy storage and clean-energy technologies, in line with the vision of Aatmanirbhar Bharat.

The move is also expected to promote the circular economy and ‘urban mining’ by recovering valuable minerals from discarded batteries, reducing dependence on primary mining and supporting environmentally sound recycling of hazardous battery waste in accordance with applicable environmental regulations.

The decision complements the government’s initiatives under the National Critical Mineral Mission (NCMM), including the Rs 1,500-crore incentive scheme approved by the Union Cabinet in September 2025 to develop recycling capacity for the separation and production of critical minerals from secondary sources such as battery waste and electronic waste.

Retaining black mass within India is expected to ensure adequate domestic feedstock for recycling facilities being developed under the scheme.

The measure is also in line with steps taken by several major economies to retain critical mineral-bearing battery waste and black mass for domestic processing and resource recovery.

-PIB
