text:
A bipartisan federal permitting reform package championed by U.S. Sen. Shelley Moore Capito cleared a key procedural hurdle in the Senate Monday, advancing debate on legislation supporters say could accelerate energy and infrastructure projects and reduce costs for American consumers.

The Senate voted 73-25 to invoke cloture on a motion to proceed to the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, a measure Capito helped develop as chairwoman of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee.

The vote does not represent final passage of the legislation. It allows the Senate to move forward with consideration of the bill.

Capito spoke on the Senate floor ahead of Monday's vote, arguing that lengthy federal permitting and environmental review processes have delayed investments, prevented job creation and increased costs for businesses and consumers.

"Businesses large and small, looking to invest meaningfully in our country, lack the certainty they need to make decisions," Capito said.

She cited National Association of Manufacturers data estimating permitting delays cost manufacturers $12.1 billion annually, including $87 million in additional costs in West Virginia. She also referenced McKinsey data estimating $1.8 trillion in investments are tied up in the federal permitting system, including $22.3 billion in West Virginia.

The legislation was developed by Capito and Republican Sen. Mike Lee of Utah, along with Democratic Sens. Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island and Martin Heinrich of New Mexico.

The proposal would revise federal environmental review and permitting requirements under several laws, including the National Environmental Policy Act, Clean Water Act and Endangered Species Act. It also includes changes involving the National Historic Preservation Act and Federal Power Act.

Among its provisions is the Ratepayer Protection Act, which Capito said would require potential data center developers to pay their own infrastructure costs rather than shifting increased electricity expenses to other utility customers.

The bill has drawn support from the Electric Power Supply Association, which represents competitive power suppliers and formally endorsed the legislation Oct. 7.

"BAAJA will bolster electric grid reliability, lead to more affordable power, and continue to ensure critical environmental protections," said Todd Snitchler, EPSA president and CEO, following Monday's vote.

The organization said faster permitting for energy infrastructure would help competitive power generators deliver electricity to the grid. In competitive power markets, private investors, rather than utility ratepayers, assume the financial risk of building new generation capacity, according to EPSA.

Capito said the legislation is intended to benefit a broad range of projects, including coal mines, wind energy developments, natural gas pipelines, solar farms and steel mills. She also emphasized provisions intended to provide greater certainty for projects that have received permits and reduce delays associated with litigation.

Capito said her office had received letters of support from more than 1,000 stakeholder organizations, including energy producers, renewable energy groups, labor unions and business associations.

She also cited a White House Council of Economic Advisers analysis estimating the legislation could generate between $82 billion and $164 billion in additional economic output annually.

Capito said the proposed reforms could increase real wages, reduce electricity bills and lower everyday expenses for American households.

"The environmental permitting and review processes should be tools for informed decision-making, not reasons that decisions can't be made," Capito said.

The legislation still must clear additional Senate consideration and receive approval from the House before it can reach President Donald Trump.

text:
(CBS NEWS) — With data centers cropping up around the United States, the cost of the energy infrastructure on which they rely, and who pays for it, are among the country’s most debated economic and political questions.

A new study finds that in 2025, the rising energy costs associated with AI data centers landed hardest on lower-income, rural households, which bore disproportionate shares of the financial burdens compared with the data centers themselves.

Authored by Cornell University researchers and published this week in the journal Nature Energy, the study analyzed growth in both energy demand and infrastructure projects along four major U.S. power grids between 2020 and 2025.

It also looked at data from 4,000 existing and proposed data centers across the U.S. Its results showed that the AI boom, and the buildout of data centers used to support it, hike up energy costs in ways that place the greatest economic strain on people who benefit least from the technology.

The study found that data centers unevenly raised wholesale power prices.

Those costs are determined through an open marketplace where electricity is bought and sold in bulk between power generators and utilities before reaching transmission lines, and, eventually, consumers. Power grids that were already stretched saw the greatest price increases, researchers said.

In California’s southern Bay Area, data centers were estimated to raise wholesale energy prices by almost 20% last year.

In Texas’ Dallas-Fort Worth area, the increase in 2025 approached 17%, according to their estimates.

Both regions have seen influxes of data centers in recent years.

Places like New York, where data centers are less prevalent, didn’t experience significant changes in wholesale energy prices, according to the study.

Higher wholesale prices had a downstream effect on energy consumers, the researchers said, as residential customers paid huge fractions of the spending on transmission built for data centers.

The study found that spending across the four power grids jumped from $2 billion in 2020 to $34.2 billion in 2025, with data centers responsible for $8.25 billion of energy infrastructure costs last year.

Residential users were responsible for just under $3.5 billion, but they were billed more than $16 billion while data centers were billed about $3 billion.

Researchers said that antiquated formulas used to allocate energy costs along a power grid have historically divided those costs based on previous energy consumption, rather than new growth. That means households take on much of the costs for developing new power infrastructure.

Residents of rural and lower-income areas saw their bills skyrocket, and in some cases faced increases in energy costs that were 76% larger than residents of urban communities, according to the study.

The researchers said that despite the concentration of data centers near metropolitan hubs, the financial loads they trigger often seep into surrounding suburban and rural areas because of policies that govern how energy costs are shared across regions.

They argued that such policies warrant review.

Researchers also pointed to what they called a “paradoxical mismatch”: According to the study, states that faced the largest cost increases, like West Virginia and Ohio, also reported the lowest uses of generative AI compared with other states around the country.

The study also found instances where states saw price increases linked to AI data centers located geographically far from them, essentially paying for infrastructure “they neither contribute to nor benefit from,” researchers said.

Residents in New Jersey and Pennsylvania helped pay for power grid updates tied to data center growth in Virginia, for example.

One unnamed senior House Democrat reported receiving over 500 calls in two days. A Democratic chief of staff, also unnamed, said their office had received around 300 calls, many urging support for Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), who has shown no public interest in running for speaker.

"Democrats in both chambers can't go back to business-as-usual politics," said Ezra Levin, the leader of Indivisible—a progressive advocacy group—that has called for Democrats to choose a new speaker. "People want leadership that's ready to join the rest of us in this new era of politics."

In the Senate, Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) is considering a challenge to Chuck Schumer (D-NY) for majority leader. Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) has said he would back Van Hollen if he runs, and several other incoming Democrats have declined to endorse Schumer.

Opponents of Schumer argue that his fealty to the Democratic donor class has led to limp opposition to President Donald Trump and resistance to positions that large majorities of Democrats support, like Medicare for All, ending military aid to Israel, and bringing a swift end to the president’s war in Iran.

The grievances against Jeffries are largely the same. As Joseph Geevarghese, executive director of the progressive advocacy group Our Revolution, summed up in August, “Jeffries’ instinct is to negotiate with the Trump power structure rather than draw lines and fight it.”

Roughly 40 Democrats would need to vote for someone else in order to prevent Jeffries from taking the gavel. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY), a potential 2028 presidential contender who is popular with the Democratic base, told Drop Site that organizing the votes to challenge Jeffries—as Republican holdouts did when they delayed Kevin McCarthy’s election as speaker in January 2023—“should be absolutely part of the conversation” among progressive Democrats.

"But you have to remember, during that time, there was a very small margin that allowed for that kind of thing to happen,” she said.

Ocasio-Cortez said that without a clear alternative, there’s “no material scenario” in which Democrats could block Jeffries from becoming speaker. She added that “in a contested race [it’s] a different situation.”

In October, RedBox Research, the polling arm of the super political action committee (PAC) A Fight Worth Having, surveyed likely voters in 31 races across 11 states. In the pooled results, only 19% wanted Jeffries as speaker, while 48% wanted “someone else.” Among Democratic respondents, 39% wanted Jeffries and 38% wanted someone else.

Writing about plans for another round of polling, Corbin Trent, a co-founder of Justice Democrats who helped conduct the October surveys, noted Tuesday in an op-ed published in Common Dreams that “support for Jeffries and Schumer is still nearly non-existent, especially where seats flipped.”

“To keep the promises these candidates made, we’ll have to take on the Democratic establishment, corporate greed, and powerful institutions," he added. "People with power and money don’t want to give it up. Unless we pull it from their death grip, we won’t get this country back on the right path.”

Palantir has also received hundreds of millions of dollars in federal contracts as it has developed a "mega-database" full of Americans' private taxpayer information.

As NextGov reported, Trump could be forced to renominate LoSapio after the new legislative session begins on January 3, if Congress is unable to confirm the nominee before the end of the current session, during which lawmakers will be busy debating a continuation of government funding and defense spending.

text:
EnviPath’s AI models predict whether new chemicals will degrade into substances which pose risks to human health or ecosystems and how long they will persist in the environment.

That’s important information for makers of fertilisers, pesticides, cosmetics and pharmaceuticals, and for environmental regulators, especially in the European Union where rules are strict.

As chemicals enter the environment, bacteria munch away on them. A harmless chemical can degrade into something toxic, while the opposite can also occur, with toxic chemicals becoming harmless.

EnviPath addresses a critical and well recognised gap in environmental risk assessment: while the hazards of parent chemicals are often well characterised, their transformation products are frequently unknown, despite often being more persistent, mobile, or toxic.

“These models can come up with answers in seconds or minutes,” says Jörg, who’s a senior lecturer in the School of Computer Science. “A company planning a new product can identify problems right at the start instead of years into the development process.”

UniServices, the University of Auckland company which supports the commercialisation of University research, funded Jörg to get the company off the ground in late 2024. Jörg is CEO and his former student Tim Lorsbach is co founder and chief technology officer, based in Germany. The company is likely to seek capital for expansion in 2027.

“I’ve worked on this project and its antecedents for my whole academic life, so you can imagine how keen I am for it to succeed,” says Jörg. “It’s not just the commercial opportunity, it’s doing something for the environment.”

EnviPath licenses companies to use its technology and access the data. It’s free for academic users, who number in their thousands. “There’s only one other commercial company in this area and we believe we’re providing a superior service,” says Jörg.

The company’s openly disclosed methods and scientific papers published by Jörg and his colleagues in peer-reviewed journals have established enviPath’s credibility with manufacturers and regulators.

The latter include the European Food Safety Authority, the Helsinki-based European Chemicals Agency (a regulatory arm of the European Union), and the Environmental Protection Agency in the US.

In the European Union, a strict regulation called REACH (Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation and Restriction of Chemicals) has applied to chemical substances since 2006.

EnviPath is promoted at scientific conferences and via a regular booth at SETAC Europe, one of the largest international conferences in environmental toxicology and chemistry. Regulators are kept informed via direct discussions, technical exchanges, and formal presentations.

Andy Shenk, former CEO of UniServices, is an adviser to enviPath. “From the perspective of university commercialisation and technology translation, enviPath represents a strong example of research with genuine market relevance,” he says.

“The platform combines scientific credibility with a clear value proposition for regulators and industry, which is essential for successful commercial development.”

NRC clears Long Mott

The U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission issued a construction permit on Nov. 9 for the Long Mott Generating Station, a four-reactor Xe-100 project planned for Dow's Seadrift Operations in Calhoun County, Texas.

Long Mott Energy, a wholly owned Dow subsidiary, will build four Xe-100 units that together would deliver 320 megawatts of electricity and 800 megawatts of thermal output, with each module designed for roughly 80 megawatts of electric capacity and 200 megawatts of heat.

X-energy said the project is configured around the energy needs of a chemical plant, with high-temperature steam for manufacturing processes and surplus electricity exported to the grid.

NRC Chairman Ho K. Nieh said, "Today, the new NRC is issuing America's first construction permit for a high-temperature gas-cooled reactor in more than half a century," as the agency described the approval as a series of firsts.

The NRC’s review moved on an 18-month schedule set when the application was formally accepted in June 2025, after Dow filed in March of that year, and the agency completed its environmental assessment and a finding of no significant impact in May and wrapped up its safety evaluation on Oct. 30.

Reporting for this sectionBigGo FinanceInteresting Engineering

Safety dispute and timeline

The Union of Concerned Scientists questioned both the safety claims and the pace of the review, and Edwin Lyman said, "The NRC only accomplished this feat by pushing consideration of critical safety questions to a later date—issues the NRC should've fully resolved before green lighting construction." X-energy said the Xe-100 uses helium to carry heat away from graphite pebbles containing tri-structural isotropic, or TRISO, fuel particles, and the design avoids the shutdowns conventional plants need for refueling. The NRC permit does not allow fuel loading or operation, and a separate operating license is required before the plant can begin generating power.

Dow said the approval is not a final investment decision, and the company expects to weigh a preliminary investment decision in 2027 with full construction starting only after a final decision. TechCrunch said X-energy’s approval gave the company a "small jolt" while its shares were trading at less than half their initial offering price.

Reporting for this sectionTechCrunchBigGo Finance

Industrial heat and next steps

The Long Mott project is being developed with support from the Department of Energy's Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program, and X-energy said the department has signaled it intends to raise its support to a total of $2.15 billion. X-energy said the architecture supports siting close to industrial facilities and envisions an emergency planning zone of 400 meters, while the figure reflects the company's design assumptions rather than a blanket rule for future advanced reactors. The project’s four Xe-100 units are expected to start supply in the early 2030s, and X-energy said first supply is targeted for the early 2030s.

Amazon’s Climate Pledge Fund led a $500 million Series C-1 round for X-energy, and Amazon committed to buying 5 gigawatts of capacity from the startup. Erik Funkhouser, executive director of the nonprofit Good Energy Collective, said, "It is significant that there is an industrial customer involved who, specifically, plans to procure large-scale industrial heat," linking the project to validation of cogeneration of heat and electricity using advanced nuclear technology.

text:
The U.S. Senate voted this week to move ahead with debate of the permitting reform Act promoted by Oklahoma U.S. Sen. Alan Armstrong who hailed the vote as a “major step forward.”

In a statement following the Monday night vote of 73-25 to begin debate on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA), the Senator said, “I applaud my colleagues on both sides of the aisle for coming together to advance meaningful permitting reforms that will make it easier to build the critical infrastructure our economy needs and help keep energy affordable in America.”

He went on to state that the vote shows Congress can still tackle long-term, complex challenges.

“This is an incredibly important moment for our country. Now it’s time to finish the job and pass this bill.”

Armstrong emphasized permitting reform almost from day one when he was appointed by Oklahoma Gov. Kevin Stitt last spring to succeed Markwayne Mullin following his appointment as Homeland Security Secretary.

Sen. Armstrong was joined by Oklahoma Sen. James Lankford in supporting the sweeping bipartisan energy and infrastructure permitting reform package. Of the 25 Nay votes, some came from oil and natural gas producing states.

They included Sen. Michael Bennet, D-Colorado who explained why he voted against it.

“Our electric grid is under significant strain and faces growing demand. We need to build new transmission, bring more energy, especially clean energy, onto the grid, and keep electricity affordable. We should make it easier to build new infrastructure, and I strongly support efforts to make this a reality. However, permitting reform is complex, and the details matter. I am concerned that not all perspectives were sufficiently heard during the drafting of this far-reaching piece of legislation.”

He contended the bill does not do enough to ensure sovereign Tribal governments can protect their cultural resources and ancestral homelands.

Democrat Ben Ray Lujan, a U.S. Senator from New Mexico where the Permian Basin oil production is a strong economic factor, voted against the act and cited similar reasons.

“I share the serious concerns raised by New Mexicans across the state, particularly our Pueblo and environmental leaders, and believe they must be addressed. After spending the last month listening to these concerns, I cannot support advancing the bill in its current form.”

Another Republican who voted ‘no’ was South Dakota Sen. Mike Rounds. His office did not include a statement following the vote. He was the only Republican who voted against advancing the act.

However, he previously had stated on X and via his Official Facebook Page the legislation transfers contested transmission line cases to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) if they are not resolved within 12 months, which he argues gives a weighted advantage to developers over local input.

Montana U.S. Sen. Tim Sheehy did not vote.

Chief Engineer Don Federico explained how the vehicle has continued to evolve: "Through our own testing, and by gathering feedback from professional drivers, including our own Master Driver, Akio Toyoda, we have continued to refine the concept in the spirit of Akio's call to drive, break, fix, and learn."

As Federico described it, the development team focused on two key principles from the outset: "exhilarating confidence."

About a month and a half ago, Akio Toyoda was inducted into the Automotive Hall of Fame in the United States. During his speech, he mentioned being involved in an incident just days before while driving an off-road vehicle. As it turns out, the vehicle in question was the Side-by-Side Concept.

This shows how relentlessly the team continued refining the vehicle right up to the final stages of development.

The Side-by-Side Concept uses the hybrid Tacoma powertrain, delivering what Federico called the kind of immediate, powerful response expected from a serious off-road machine.

To ensure that capability goes beyond specs, the concept features:

26 inches (660 mm) of suspension travel

35-inch (889 mm) tires

17 inches (432 mm) of ground clearance

All are class-leading figures, designed with a simple goal: making sure the capability is real.

The vehicle is intended to tackle everything from high-speed desert racing and demanding trail runs to technical rock-crawling sections. Yet one of its most intriguing features is something only an electrified vehicle can offer: Silent Mode.

"It allows the vehicle to navigate trails on battery power alone. which creates a new way to engage with nature. One that is quieter, and more immersive. It's a great example of how electrified technology can expand the experience of adventure."

As a concept vehicle, Toyota intends to continue learning from it while exploring what the future of off-road mobility might look like. The lessons gained here are also expected to influence future truck development.

Federico described its origin as a response to a very practical question: "How to make short-distance mobility easier, more useful, and more seamlessly integrated into everyday life."

The lightweight vehicle was developed over several years by a small team of chassis and electrical engineers who continually refined the design based on real-world testing and customer feedback.

The current version can be folded in approximately 30 seconds and is so compact that it can fit in the trunk of a GR86 sports car.

Electric bikes may already be familiar to Toyota fans. Chairman Toyoda drew attention on social media when he used a similar mobility device around the 2025 Japan Mobility Show venue. The BKE Concept, however, takes portability and practicality even further.

The bike can be charged using the 110V AC outlets already available on many Toyota vehicles, making it convenient for camping, errands, last-mile transportation, or even serving as a pit bike alongside a GR86.

Beyond convenience, the concept reflects Toyota's broader sustainability ambitions.

"For short trips it offers a practical alternative to larger vehicles, helping reduce carbon emissions by matching the vehicle to the journey."

Federico linked it directly to Toyota's long-standing goal: "To think beyond the conventional automobile and define mobility in a broader way."

One particularly Toyota-like detail emerged during development. Federico recalled that feedback from Toyoda, who frequently rides prototype versions, led engineers to enlarge the rear fender after he noted that the original design allowed water to splash onto riders when going through puddles. A small improvement, perhaps, but a fitting example of Toyota's spirit of continuous improvement, or kaizen.

Though vastly different from the Side-by-Side Concept, Federico emphasized that both vehicles share the same purpose: "To expand the meaning of mobility."

Together they offer an early glimpse of how Scion by Toyota can approach mobility from multiple directions while remaining rooted in Toyota's core strengths.

It will be assembled at Toyota's Indiana plant, supported by a $34 million investment and approximately 50 new jobs.

While kei trucks have long been valued in Japan for their maneuverability and practicality, they are still relatively uncommon in the United States, where full-sized pickup trucks dominate the landscape.

David Christ, Group Vice President and General Manager of the Toyota Division introduced the vehicle this way: "Let's talk about a small truck with some big possibilities."

Pointing to rising interest in kei trucks, he explained: "The love for Kei trucks has really taken off and it got us thinking... what could our take on this segment look like?"

Toyota hopes owners will use the vehicle as a foundation for their own ideas and applications, much as the original Scion customers once customized their vehicles to fit their individuality.

Although compact, KEI-01offers surprising functionality. Toyota sees applications ranging from light-duty hauling and agricultural work to facility maintenance and short-distance commercial transport. An enclosed cabin with both heating and air conditioning further broadens its usefulness.

According to Christ, these qualities could prove particularly attractive to:

Small business owners

Ranch operators

Customers who need to operate well in limited spaces

All this, while benefiting from low operating costs and easy ownership.

KEI-01 will start sales in the U.S. under a pilot program beginning in the second half of 2027 for fleet customers. Toyota will evaluate opportunities to expand availability following the pilot program and might consider limited retail sales in the future depending on market conditions and customer demand.

As a Low-Speed Vehicle, KEI-01 complies with U.S. regulations that limit maximum speed to 25 mph.

Closing the event, Christ returned to the broader mission behind the brand. He described Scion by Toyota as a place for exploring new mobility possibilities while opening doors to fresh ideas and new directions.

"As we shape the brand, we'll keep asking what could mobility make possible for people? How could it fit into their lives and help them do what they love, or inspire them to try something new?"

He then left the audience with a preview of what lies ahead: "Today is just the beginning, and we can't wait to share what's next."

And finally, perhaps the clearest expression yet of what Scion by Toyota hopes to become: "Imagining what's possible and opening the door to new ways to move. That's what Scion by Toyota is all about."

For Toyota, Scion is no longer simply a brand aimed at younger buyers. It is becoming a platform for experimentation, a home for unconventional ideas, and a place where the definition of mobility itself can continue to evolve. What comes next remains unwritten, but the first chapter has begun.

In a future article, Toyota Times plans to explore the development story behind KEI-01, including perspectives from the Indiana-based team and the evolving role of kei trucks in North America.

text:
A multidisciplinary coalition led by the University of Utah’s Energy & Geoscience Institute (EGI) and John and Marcia Price College of Engineering has been awarded a major grant from the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) National Energy Technology Laboratory (NETL) to establish The Uinta-Piceance Basin Carbon Management and Community Engagement Partnership (Award DE-FE0032575).

Civil and Environmental Engineering research assistant professor Dr. Nathan Moodie is principal investigator of the Uinta-Piceance Basin Carbon Management and Community Engagement Partnership, which began Oct. 1, 2026. Dr. Ting Xiao, who led the original proposal at the Energy and Geoscience Institute (EGI) and is now an assistant professor at Texas State University, serves as co-principal investigator and project manager.

Spanning eastern Utah and western Colorado, the partnership brings together key academic institutions, state geological surveys, technical colleges, and local stakeholders to accelerate the equitable, safe, and environmentally responsible deployment of storage-based carbon management (CM) infrastructure.

As the Uinta-Piceance Basin transitions toward a low-carbon energy economy, this regional initiative addresses key technical, regulatory, environmental, and logistical challenges. The team will assess underground storage capacity, optimize carbon transport routes, mitigate regional air quality challenges, and empower local communities and energy workers through specialized educational programs.

Mapping the subsurface for safe, large-scale carbon storage

Evaluating deep geological formations is fundamental to permanent carbon dioxide (CO2) storage. The technical team will aggregate petrophysical, geophysical, and geological datasets to build comprehensive basin-wide structural models.

Using state-of-the-art simulation tools, the project will:

Identify reservoir and sealing formations: Characterize suitable deep storage target zones while protecting Underground Sources of Drinking Water (USDW).

Evaluate injectivity and plume dynamics: Model CO2 movement, pressure front expansion, and long-term storage integrity.

Determine areas of review (AoR): Evaluate pressure interference across potential stacked storage zones, existing hydrocarbon wells, and saltwater disposal operations to support Underground Injection Control (UIC) Class VI permitting.

Addressing regional air quality and harnessing cross-cutting innovations

The project extends beyond subsurface geology to assess broader energy systems and environmental interactions across the basin:

Air quality modeling and permitting support: Portions of the Uinta Basin are designated as winter ozone nonattainment areas by the EPA. Led by Dr. Seth Lyman at Utah State University’s Bingham Research Center, researchers will construct a basin-specific air quality modeling framework. This effort will model baseline emissions and evaluate how carbon capture deployment, including NOx reduction and expanded CO2-enhanced oil recovery (CO2-EOR), can lower permitting risks and support environmental compliance.

Critical minerals & rare earth elements (REE): Dr. Michael Free (University of Utah) will analyze produced waters from regional oil and gas fields to evaluate the technical and economic feasibility of extracting domestic critical minerals and REEs essential for clean energy technology.

Solar energy & grid integration: Dr. Mingxi Liu and Dr. Milind Deo (University of Utah) will examine integration strategies for combining abundant regional solar energy and energy storage with the power loads required for CO2 compression, transport, and injection.

Transportation & infrastructure planning: Under the leadership of Dr. Erin Middleton (Carbon Solutions), the team will map optimal CO2 transport corridors (pipelines and rail) to connect regional industrial emitters with storage hubs while minimizing safety hazards and population exposure.

Empowering local communities, tribal nations, and the energy workforce

A central priority of the partnership is ensuring that local communities, Tribal Nations, and traditional energy workers directly benefit from the emerging carbon management sector.

Mobile learning laboratory: Dr. Javier Tellez Rodriguez at Colorado Mesa University (CMU) will deploy an advanced hands-on mobile laboratory to deliver mobile vocational training in high-demand fields like welding and mechatronics directly to rural communities and Tribal Nations across western Colorado and eastern Utah.

Workforce reskilling & curriculum development: In collaboration with Uintah Basin Technical College (UBTech), CMU, and regional universities, the project team will map skill sets from traditional energy jobs into carbon management careers, creating new certifications and technical curricula.

Geologic field education: Led by the Utah Geological Survey (Dr. Gabriela St Pierre) and the Colorado Geological Survey (Dr. Nathan Rogers), interactive field trips to regional geological sites and operational facilities will provide students, local leaders, and Tribal Nations with firsthand insights into carbon storage mechanics.

Transparent data sharing and technical stakeholder support

To foster public trust and support regional industry development, the project team will launch the Uinta-Piceance Basin Carbon Management Explorer Database and public web portal. Connected directly to DOE’s Energy Data eXchange (EDX), the platform will host open-access geospatial, environmental, and geological data.

Furthermore, the partnership will offer direct technical assistance to regional operators, regulators, and community members, providing guidance on Monitoring, Reporting, and Verification (MRV) plan development (EPA Class VI and 45Q tax credit compliance), pore space management, and regulatory risk reduction.

title: Beyond the Automobile: Scion by Toyota Opens the Door to New Mobility Ideas

text:
As the automotive industry undergoes what is often described as a once-in-a-century transformation, what is this new brand setting out to achieve? And how does it connect to the original Scion, which attracted younger customers in North America before transitioning into Toyota in 2016?

Simon Humphries, Chief Branding Officer of Toyota Motor Corporation, explains the thinking behind Scion by Toyota, while three vehicles unveiled at the event offer a glimpse of the brand's vision for mobility.

The Scion brand was launched by Toyota in North America in 2003, targeting Generation Y customers. Its lineup included the xA, xB, tC, and the affordable sports coupe FR-S. It also pioneered new approaches to marketing and sales, including online retail initiatives and extensive customization options.

Over time, however, customer expectations evolved. Younger buyers increasingly sought practicality alongside style and driving enjoyment, while many of the lessons learned through Scion had already been incorporated into Toyota-brand vehicles. In 2016, Toyota announced that the Scion brand would transition into Toyota.

More than one million Scion vehicles were sold, with roughly 70 percent of buyers new to Toyota–about half were under the age of 35. This helped Toyota attract an entirely new customer base in North America.

Simon Humphries, Chief Branding Officer at Toyota, reflected on what Scion by Toyota carries forward from the original Scion brand in the United States.

"Good evening, everyone. It's good to be back in Texas, a place that's never been afraid to think big."

"At Toyota, we have always been driven by product. But product itself is driven by people. That may sound obvious. But it is fundamental to the way we think about our brands. Because we don't design for an average. We design for someone. We try to see the world through their eyes. Where they live. What they need. What excites them. We create something with character exactly for them."

That thinking can be seen in vehicles across Toyota's global portfolio, from the adventure-ready Tacoma in the United States, to the boldly expressive Crown Sport in Japan, and the endlessly adaptable Hilux Champ in Thailand.

Humphries emphasized that the vehicles may be very different and the people who drive them may also be different. "Very different vehicles. Very different people. But all unmistakably Toyota."

At the same time, some experiences can only exist when a brand creates a world entirely its own.

Since its launch, Lexus has challenged conventional assumptions about what a premium automotive brand could be, not only through its vehicles, but also through the experiences it creates for customers, the services it provides, and the relationships it builds. That pursuit produced vehicles such as the LFA, a car that became a symbol of Lexus's willingness to push beyond expectations.

As change accelerates around the world, Lexus continues evolving as well, pursuing a future of luxury centered ever more closely on the individual needs and aspirations of each customer.

Yet for some people, moving forward means something entirely different. Sometimes, it means going faster.

That spirit led Humphries to talk about the next brand in Toyota's portfolio: GR. Built around Toyota Chairman and Master Driver Akio Toyoda's conviction that roads build cars and that motorsports develops both cars and people, GR exists to challenge and improve through competition.

"GR exists because some people find freedom in the pursuit of speed. It is forged on the track and lives through community."

Drivers, engineers, mechanics, and enthusiasts all play a role in that process, pushing one another to continuously improve.

Humphries then highlighted another brand with an equally distinctive identity: “Century. A very different understanding of what ultimate luxury can mean.”

Each of these brands offers a unique perspective and a unique experience.

Century. Lexus. GR. Toyota. Daihatsu.

Humphries summarized the philosophy simply: "Different brands for different people."

Taken together, these brands cover an extraordinarily broad spectrum of the automotive world.

Humphries wanted the audience to consider the meaning of “the automotive world.” He explained: "People, their desire for mobility doesn't begin and end with the car. There is so much more beyond it."

And that is where Scion by Toyota comes in.

Those familiar with Scion may remember its original mission. More than twenty years ago, the brand gave a new generation access to something the automotive mainstream didn’t.

"You didn't simply buy a Scion, you made it your own. And in its time, that was quite rebellious."

While Humphries emphasized that the original Scion existed within the boundaries of the automobile, " … this time, we're setting out to do something different. To go beyond those boundaries and redefine them."

"This is not a reboot of Scion."

Humphries explained the inspiration behind the project by recalling a conversation with Toyoda, who said: "Why not bring these new ideas for new mobility solutions together under the Scion name... to take that same experimental spirit and point it somewhere new."

Visitors to last year's SEMA (Specialty Equipment Market Association) Show may already have seen the first signs of this direction through the Scion 01 concept. Humphries said: "It was a glimpse, but also a statement of intent."

“As human beings, we have always been wired to be curious. To have this innate desire to push a little further. To ask, what else is possible? To want to know, what’s beyond?”

That idea is reflected in the brand's slogan: "With Scion by Toyota... Beyond Starts Here."

Beyond Roads. Beyond Boundaries. Beyond Measure.

Scion by Toyota, Humphries said, gives Toyota the freedom to expand the horizon of mobility itself.

He explained this horizon as Freedom Lab: "A place to experiment what's next. Beyond Challenge. Beyond Convention. Beyond Blueprints. A place where new ideas can evolve into something meaningful. Something our customers can make their own."

Humphries stressed that Scion by Toyota provides only the starting point. "But Beyond finishes with you.”

“Use it in a way we hadn't imagined. Put your mark on it."

Perhaps Scion by Toyota is something like an unwritten book.

As Humphries put it: "We know the first few pages. We know why it needs to exist. We may not know every chapter. But we know where to start."

What that beginning looks like will vary from one region of the world to another.

Take America. A vast country of wide-open spaces, where nearly 70 percent of the land lies beyond paved roads. “That’s quite an invitation to explore, isn’t it? Especially from behind the wheel of our adventure-ready Side by Side Concept. So why not start there.”

The next idea takes that thinking one step further: “We've also been exploring how our BKE Concept could extend your adventure when the road can take you no further.”

Yet going beyond convention does not always mean thinking bigger. “Sometimes, it's about making more possible with something smaller.”

That idea is embodied by the KEI-01 (“kay zero one”), a compact vehicle designed to do far more than its dimensions might suggest.

“Of course, we've been thinking in all shapes and sizes. Some of what we've created may feel familiar. Some of it, perhaps, less so. Each one starts in a different place. But each one takes us somewhere beyond the expected.”

Humphries then invited the audience to see what that future could look like: “And now, perhaps it’s time to see ‘beyond’ take shape. Because imagining the possibilities is one thing. Actually building them? That's where the fun begins.”

And with that, he handed the stage to the person who helped turn those ideas into reality.

"So, let's take a look at what 'Beyond' looks like in practice. And there's no one better to introduce these concepts than the person who helped bring them to life. Don, over to you."

text:
Calibrant Energy, a leading provider of on-site energy solutions, on November 10 announced the close of a $145-million debt facility led by Investec for solar and battery storage projects across multiple U.S. power markets. The portfolio includes a 120-MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) serving a hyperscale data center customer in the PJM territory. Citi, Liberty Bank, and Siemens Financial Services also participated in the facility.

Data center operators are looking for ways to get online faster as PJM and federal regulators work through how large power users connect to the grid. Calibrant’s engineered BESS solutions give energy-intensive facilities greater control over how and when they draw power. This flexibility supports faster interconnection timelines and reduces the need for costly grid infrastructure upgrades that would otherwise be passed on to other ratepayers.

“Data center operators are choosing on-site energy storage because it is a fast, reliable, and effective way to get online and operate as responsible grid citizens,” said Phil Martin, CEO of Calibrant Energy. “With this financial close and site mobilization for a hyperscale data center, Calibrant continues to demonstrate that large-load flexibility is not just possible but a commercial reality today.”

Calibrant’s turnkey, zero-capex solutions unlock the path to reliable power that the world’s largest power users need to grow their businesses. “Investec is proud to support Calibrant and Macquarie on this transaction,” said Fred Petit, co-head of Energy & Infrastructure North America at Investec. “We value the opportunity to partner with experienced investors and operators, and to provide financing that advances the energy transition and the critical infrastructure needed to meet growing power demand across the U.S.”

Calibrant Energy now has more than 5.9 GWh of battery storage capacity in operation, in construction, or under exclusive development agreements, including additional sites with the same hyperscale customer. This growth reflects rising demand from large power users for on-site energy solutions that accelerate speed to power while easing strain on the grid. It also reflects customers’ preference for a trusted, experienced partner that can develop, own, and operate these solutions and deliver the power outcomes their business plans depend on.

The U.S power sector is going through profound change. The new administration slowed the pace of regulatory initiatives, courts placed key rules on hold, and multiple environmental standards affecting generation and transmission entered periods of reconsideration. text:
Key Takeaways

The Senate voted 73-25 to invoke cloture on the motion to proceed to the permitting reform bill, clearing the way for floor debate and amendments.

A revised manager’s amendment exempts certain vertically integrated utilities from new planning requirements, preserves utility rights of first refusal and requires developers to seek state approval for one year before pursuing federal siting.

The amendment clarifies that agencies may modify or revoke permits in response to court orders and removes several contested historic preservation changes, though some tribal organizations still oppose the bill.

If the Senate passes the bill, it moves to the House, where its prospects depend on securing enough bipartisan support.

After Senate negotiators released an amendment intended to address concerns raised by lawmakers, utilities, environmental organizations and tribal governments, the Senate voted 73-25 on Nov. 9, 2026, to invoke cloture on the motion to proceed to the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) of 2026. The vote cleared a significant procedural hurdle to bring the legislation closer to Senate consideration. The vote paves the way for the Senate to formally take up the bill, debate its provisions and consider potential amendments. Senate action is expected to continue throughout the week, with additional procedural votes and negotiations over amendments likely as lawmakers work toward final passage in the Senate and consideration by the House of Representatives.

Notable changes include:

Transmission Planning and Utilities: The amendment maintains the bill’s core transmission reforms while addressing concerns raised by Republican regulators and southeastern utilities. It exempts certain vertically integrated utilities from new coordinated generation and transmission planning requirements, preserves existing utility rights to build transmission infrastructure (right of first refusal), and requires developers to pursue state approval for one year before seeking federal intervention instead of going through state and federal approvals simultaneously. In exchange, the amendment expands federal siting authority to cover state-owned land and certain advanced transmission technologies and gives developers greater flexibility in financing new transmission projects by allowing developers to use the cost allocation formula even when projects receive approval entirely through state processes.

Environmental Protections and Permitting Certainty: In response to concerns from environmental organizations and legal advocates on project certainty, the amendment clarifies that federal agencies may modify or revoke permits in response to court orders, addressing criticism that the original language could shield unlawfully issued permits. It also expands protections against discriminatory federal permitting practices and requires court approval of certain legal settlements.

Tribal Consultation and Historic Preservation: Following objections from tribal governments and organizations, the amendment removes several controversial changes to the National Historic Preservation Act, including provisions affecting culturally significant properties and tribal historic preservation authority. However, several tribal organizations continue to oppose the legislation and call for the removal of the remaining historic preservation reforms.

Data Centers and Ratepayer Protections: Responding to growing concerns about data center development and electricity costs, the amendment establishes a new Department of Energy technical assistance program to help state, local and tribal governments evaluate proposed data center projects. It builds on existing provisions allowing states and utilities to require data centers to cover infrastructure costs associated with their operations. To close a potential loophole that would have disadvantaged larger behind-the-meter natural gas generation at data centers, the amendment limits the provision to resources under 5 megawatts (MW).

Transmission Oversight and Consumer Costs: The amendment preserves provisions allowing state regulators and the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) to scrutinize certain local transmission investments that could increase electricity costs. It also expands oversight to include replacement infrastructure, addressing concerns raised by consumer and utility watchdog organizations.

Next Steps

With cloture invoked on the motion to proceed, the Senate must complete the remaining procedural steps before formally taking up the bill. Senators may then consider the substitute amendment, additional amendments and eventual final passage. If approved by the Senate, the legislation would move to the House for consideration, where its prospects will depend on securing sufficient bipartisan support.

McGuireWoods and McGuireWoods Consulting continue to monitor Senate floor activity and any further amendments and will provide updates as the legislation advances. For more information, contact the authors or a member of McGuireWoods Consulting or McGuireWoods’ Energy Enforcement & Regulatory Counseling Practice Group.

text:
On November 9, 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit issued a published opinion in United States of America Chamber of Commerce v. Sanchez, No. 25-5327 (9th Cir. Nov. 9, 2026), resolving an appeal from the denial of a preliminary injunction against California’s corporate climate-disclosure laws, the Climate Corporate Data Accountability Act (SB 253) and the Climate-Related Financial Risk Act (SB 261). The Court declined to block SB 253’s Scope 1 and Scope 2 disclosure requirements, but concluded that SB 253’s Scope 3 disclosure requirement and SB 261 in its entirety likely violate the First Amendment. For companies preparing initial SB 253 reports, the ruling does not alter the November 10, 2026 deadline for Scope 1 and Scope 2 reporting.

The most consequential open question now sits with the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California (the trial court), which must decide on remand whether the Scope 3 disclosure requirement can be severed from the rest of SB 253.

Companies Covered by SB 253 and SB 261

According to the Court, SB 253 applies to any entity doing business in California with more than US$1 billion in annual revenue, a group that a recent report cited by the Court estimated at approximately 1,971 companies. SB 261 applies to companies doing business in California with more than US$500 million in annual revenue, which the Court said covers approximately 2,675 companies. As we reported on August 4, 2026, when the California Air Resources Board (CARB) released its 15-day modifications, coverage turns on entity-level revenue and “doing business in California” tests.

In a facial challenge, several chambers of commerce and business associations (the Chambers) argued that both laws are unconstitutional as written, rather than only as applied to a particular company. That framing raised the Chambers’ burden: the Court explained that a facial challenge succeeds only if a law’s unconstitutional applications substantially outweigh its constitutional ones.

The Ninth Circuit’s Decision

At issue on appeal was the trial court’s refusal to issue a preliminary injunction, an early court order that blocks a law while the lawsuit proceeds. To obtain one, a party must show that it is likely to succeed on the merits, that it is likely to suffer irreparable harm, that the balance of equities tips in its favor, and that an injunction is in the public interest. The trial court had treated both laws as regulating commercial speech, applying the deferential standard of Zauderer v. Off. of Disciplinary Couns., 471 U.S. 626 (1985), to SB 253 and intermediate scrutiny to SB 261. In an opinion by Judge Jacqueline H. Nguyen, the Ninth Circuit affirmed that decision in part and reversed it in part.

Scope 1 and Scope 2 Disclosure Requirements Not Blocked: Scope 1 covers emissions from sources a company owns or directly controls, and Scope 2 covers emissions from purchased electricity, steam, heating, or cooling. Drawing on its recent decision in Pharm. Rsch. & Mfrs. of Am. v. Stolfi, 153 F.4th 795 (9th Cir. 2025), which treated an Oregon drug-pricing reporting law as a regulation of commercial speech, the Court held that these disclosures regulate commercial speech because they compel factual information about emissions from a company’s own operations that investors, insurers, and other capital-market participants use to decide whether and on what terms to transact with the company. The Court reasoned that “emissions disclosures function like product warnings in capital markets.”

Commercial speech generally receives intermediate scrutiny, under which California (the State) must show that the law directly advances a substantial interest through means not more extensive than necessary. The Court concluded that the Scope 1 and Scope 2 disclosure requirements likely satisfy intermediate scrutiny because they directly advance the State’s substantial interests in mitigating information asymmetries for investors and in reducing emissions. The Court did not decide whether the more deferential Zauderer standard applies.

Throughout its analysis, the Court emphasized that these disclosures consist of factual emissions data reported using standardized measurement protocols the industry has long employed and that SB 253 does not require any reporting entity to attribute culpability, to assign moral significance to its emissions, or to endorse the State’s climate-policy positions. Companies remain free to contextualize their disclosures, to dispute their significance, or to provide explanatory commentary. The Court also concluded that the State’s third asserted interest, preventing misleading “greenwashing” claims, is not sufficiently supported by the record. Turning to the remaining injunction factors, the Court found that the Chambers had not shown irreparable harm from the Scope 1 and Scope 2 disclosure requirements.

Scope 3 Disclosure Requirement Likely Unconstitutional: Because Scope 3 disclosures concern what the Court called “diffuse third-party conduct in the value chain,” the Court held that they are insufficiently tethered to a company’s own operations and capital transactions to qualify as commercial speech. That conclusion triggered strict scrutiny, a demanding standard that requires the State to show that the law furthers a compelling interest and is narrowly tailored to achieve it, and to use a less restrictive alternative where one would serve. Even assuming the State’s interests are compelling, the Court concluded that the State had not shown that the Scope 3 disclosure requirement is narrowly tailored. The Court found that companies do not possess Scope 3 data the way they possess Scope 1 and Scope 2 data, and that data collected from value-chain participants may be difficult to verify and prone to error. The Court also found that nothing in the record indicated that estimates based on industry averages or proxy data are more reliable than estimates the State or the public could generate, that the connection between Scope 3 emissions and a reporting company’s risk exposure or profitability is too remote, and that no study in the record examined mandatory Scope 3 reporting.

SB 261 Likely Unconstitutional: The Court held that SB 261 compels noncommercial speech because the climate-risk framework it incorporates requires companies to make predictive and normative judgments about how climate change should shape their future operations, a subject the Court described as “politically fraught,” within a State-prescribed framework. The Court found that a company’s option to state that it faces no climate-related risks does not change the noncommercial nature of the required speech. The Court also noted that the State “all but concedes it cannot satisfy” strict scrutiny. Even assuming the State’s interests are compelling, the Court found that SB 261 is not narrowly tailored because less restrictive means were available, such as disseminating existing voluntary climate-related financial risk disclosures to the public, incentivizing voluntary disclosure, or directly regulating emissions.

Severability Question Remanded: SB 253 contains a severability clause, Cal. Health & Safety Code § 38532(i), which addresses whether the rest of a law can stand if a court strikes down one part. The Court remanded for the trial court to decide, in the first instance, whether the Scope 3 disclosure requirement is severable.

Further Proceedings and the 2027 Legislative Session

On remand, the severability question matters beyond Scope 3. The Court found that, absent severance, the Scope 3 defect would exist in “every application” of SB 253, and that the Chambers had shown that enforcement of the statute as written would cause irreparable injury. The trial court’s answer therefore bears on whether the Scope 1 and Scope 2 disclosure requirements can be enforced on their own.

Importantly, the ruling is not a final decision on whether the laws are constitutional. The Court evaluated only whether the Chambers are likely to succeed for purposes of preliminary relief, and the litigation will continue in the trial court. The Court’s commercial-speech analysis also rests heavily on Stolfi, in which a petition for certiorari was filed in the U.S. Supreme Court in February 2026.

Separately, the California Legislature resumes in January 2027, and the authors of SB 253 and SB 261 could revisit these topics and propose new legislation aimed at obtaining this type of information.

Takeaways and Next Steps

Putting aside the severability question, the ruling leaves the near-term SB 253 obligations described in our August 4 post intact while unsettling the Scope 3 and SB 261 work that was to follow. The Court’s opinion reflects as much: it treats factual emissions data from a company’s own operations as commercial speech, and it treats disclosures that depend on third-party conduct or require value-laden judgments on a politically fraught subject as noncommercial speech subject to strict scrutiny.

text:
Abstract

Transport decarbonization in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) requires approaches that reflect differences in vehicle use, electricity systems, financing, industrial priorities and institutional capacity. This Structured Policy and Practice Review synthesizes research and policy/practice evidence on alternative vehicle pathways and infrastructure readiness through four purposively selected country cases: Rwanda, Kenya, South Africa and Nigeria. It considers electric two- and three-wheelers, electric buses and minibuses, passenger electric vehicles, battery-as-a-service (BaaS), charging and battery swapping, renewable energy integrated charging, compressed natural gas (CNG), and emerging hydrogen applications. Across the cases, adoption is shaped by upfront costs, foreign exchange exposure, electricity access and reliability, local distribution network capacity, charging and refueling availability, battery lifecycle management, and the design and implementation of policy. The evidence suggests that high-utilization commercial fleets may offer early electrification opportunities where duty cycles, financing and charging arrangements are suitable; this is not a universal conclusion, and passenger electric vehicles, public transport electrification and alternative fuels may be relevant in other contexts. Solar plus storage, managed charging, time-of-use tariffs and vehicle-to-grid services should be evaluated against local grid conditions, cost, reliability, lifecycle emissions and regulatory readiness rather than presumed to be preferable. The four cases are illustrative, not statistically representative, and available evidence is insufficient for a defensible cross-country ranking of overall readiness or effectiveness. The review recommends targeted and evaluated incentives, grid-aware infrastructure planning, safe battery reuse and recycling systems, inclusive engagement with informal transport operators, and transparent monitoring of costs and real-world outcomes. It identifies priorities for better comparable fleet data, tropical battery performance evidence, and implementation and end-of-life reporting.

1 Introduction

Decarbonizing transport across Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) is linked to climate commitments, urban air quality, energy security and economic development ( Adun et al., 2024). However, the potential contribution of transport technologies to these goals depends on national circumstances, including transport demand, electricity generation, infrastructure availability, fiscal capacity and vehicle market characteristics. Research on electric mobility in African cities demonstrates that the effects of vehicle electrification on electricity systems can differ by vehicle type and charging behavior ( Lukuyu et al., 2024). National transport systems, fiscal capacity, electricity supply and vehicle markets differ substantially. These differences caution against treating any single technology or policy package as suitable for the entire region. Electric vehicles, gaseous fuels and, in selected heavy-duty applications, hydrogen may play different roles depending on local demand, infrastructure and lifecycle emissions ( Lah, 2017; Cunanan et al., 2021; Ude et al., 2019). Because emissions outcomes depend on both vehicle technology and the energy used to power it, technology comparisons should consider lifecycle impacts rather than tailpipe emissions alone ( Faria et al., 2013). Transport decarbonization can contribute to air quality improvement, reduced petroleum dependence and industrial development, but the magnitude and distribution of these benefits depend on how vehicles are produced, powered, financed and used ( Caetano and Merven, 2017; Doorga et al., 2022).

Charging infrastructure must therefore be planned alongside electricity system development, transport demand and local distribution network constraints. Modeling for Nairobi shows increased electric vehicle adoption can place pressure on distribution transformers under some charging scenarios, while smart charging can help manage peak demand ( Lukuyu et al., 2024). Distributed solar and battery storage may be useful in particular locations, but should be evaluated against grid-connected alternatives on cost, reliability, emissions and maintainability rather than assumed to be universally preferable ( Hermanus and Cirolia, 2024). Evidence from South African minibus taxis also indicates that solar-supported charging is a potential option for some high-utilization paratransit operations, although its suitability depends on vehicle energy requirements and charging opportunities ( Abraham et al., 2021).

Many African cities rely on a mix of formal public transport, informal paratransit and commercial two- and three-wheelers. These modes are important to mobility systems but differ in their operating patterns, ownership arrangements and infrastructure needs. Research on electric two-wheeler taxis in Kenya, for example, evaluates adoption feasibility using trip characteristics, relative fuel and electricity costs, and the capacity of the electricity system ( Pawlak et al., 2023). These services create potential opportunities for electrification because some vehicles have intensive duty cycles and predictable operating routes. Nevertheless, affordability, vehicle availability, maintenance capacity and the distribution of benefits require explicit assessment; evidence that a technology reduces local air pollution does not by itself demonstrate poverty reduction or improved livelihoods. The transition also has institutional implications; operators, transport associations, savings and credit cooperative organizations (SACCOs), mechanics and passengers can influence vehicle selection, financing, maintenance and service delivery. Their involvement is therefore relevant to implementation planning, particularly where informal operators play a substantial role in passenger transport ( Evans et al., 2018; Cirolia and Harber, 2021; Gałuszka et al., 2021).

A second structural consideration is the prevalence of imported secondhand internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles, which can reduce acquisition costs while extending the use of older vehicle technologies. The United Nations Environmental Program's global assessment of used vehicle trade identifies the large flow of used vehicles into developing markets, including African countries, and documents regulatory gaps affecting vehicle quality and environmental performance [ United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), 2020]. Policy responses such as vehicle standards, inspection regimes and fleet renewal incentives should account for affordability and access to mobility, particularly for lower-income households and operators. This requires balancing the environmental and safety benefits of cleaner fleets against the role of lower-cost used vehicles in providing access to transport. A third consideration is exposure to fuel price changes, currency depreciation and unreliable electricity supply. These factors can affect vehicle acquisition costs, imported spare parts prices and the relative operating costs of electric and combustion technologies. Their effects should be assessed using country-specific cost and infrastructure evidence rather than assumed to be uniform across SSA. CNG may be relevant in some gas-producing markets, but its role should be assessed against methane leakage, fuel availability, refueling access and the risk of locking in fossil fuel infrastructure. Research on Nigeria's CNG transport-fuel sector identifies barriers to adoption and highlights the importance of coordinated institutional and policy responses ( Ogunlowo et al., 2017). In addition, lifecycle emissions research shows that the climate performance of natural gas vehicles depends on factors including fuel chain methane leakage and vehicle efficiency, reinforcing the need for context-specific assessment ( Alvarez et al., 2018).

Research on African electric mobility has documented a growing set of national policies and demonstration projects, but important gaps remain in consistent data on adoption, implementation and outcomes. An Africa-wide assessment of electric-mobility policies reviewed documents from all 54 African countries and found that availability and coverage vary, with gaps across several non-fiscal, administrative and regulatory measures ( Nnene et al., 2026). This review contributes a structured comparison of selected country contexts and links the evidence to practical policy questions concerning vehicle segments, energy infrastructure, finance and governance. It distinguishes policy announcements and stated ambitions from evidence of implementation and observed outcomes, where such evidence is available.

The review does not assume that SSA will reject passenger electric vehicles or follow one alternative pathway. Rather, it examines the proposition that high-utilization commercial vehicles may be a practical entry point in some settings because operating patterns, charging needs and financing can be organized around fleet use. This is a proposition to assess, not a conclusion assumed in advance: the feasibility of commercial vehicle electrification depends on vehicle duty cycles, charging access, financing arrangements, electricity system capacity and the costs borne by operators. Evidence from Kenya and South Africa illustrates why these factors need to be examined at the level of particular vehicle segments and operating contexts ( Pawlak et al., 2023; Abraham et al., 2021). This proposition must be considered alongside national strategies that support passenger EVs, local assembly, public transport electrification and alternative fuels. The appropriate pathway is therefore context-dependent, and recommendations should follow evidence on cost, infrastructure, emissions and implementation outcomes.

The review has four objectives: (1) to compare the potential roles and constraints of passenger electric vehicles, electric two- and three-wheelers, electric buses and minibuses, CNG, flex-fuel systems, and green hydrogen; (2) to examine enabling conditions and barriers involving electricity supply, charging and refueling, tariffs, capital and foreign exchange risk; (3) to compare policy approaches and available implementation evidence in Rwanda, Kenya, South Africa, and Nigeria; and (4) to derive evidence-linked policy options for governments, utilities, investors and transport sector stakeholders. The four countries were purposively selected to represent contrasting policy and market contexts relevant to the review questions. They are illustrative cases rather than a statistically representative sample of SSA, and the findings are interpreted in light of differences between countries rather than generalized automatically to the whole region.

2 Review methodology

2.1 Review design and rationale

This article adopts a Structured Policy and Practice Review framework to synthesize peer-reviewed research and documented policy and practical evidence on alternative-vehicle technologies, electricity and charging infrastructure, battery lifecycle management, financing, regulation, and market implementation in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). It is neither a protocol-driven systematic review nor a meta-analysis and does not estimate pooled effect sizes. Structured policy and practice reviews are particularly advantageous for evaluating complex, rapidly evolving socio-technical transitions in developing contexts where gray literature, regulatory mandates, and empirical research intersect ( Gicha et al., 2024; Nnene et al., 2026). Unlike systematic reviews that often exclude gray literature and policy documents, this framework integrates scholarly literature with real-world policy instruments and project-level implementations to bridge the gap between academic theory and practical governance. This approach accommodates diverse technologies, national contexts, and evidence types, supporting interpretive and comparative conclusions rather than statistical generalization across SSA.

2.2 Search source and search concepts

The initial literature search was conducted in July 2026 using Web of Science as the sole bibliographic database. The search was restricted to publications published from 2000 through 2026. Three thematic areas guided the search: (1) alternative vehicle technologies, commercial adoption, and country-level implementation in Sub-Saharan Africa; (2) vehicle-to-grid (V2G) integration and decentralized or renewable-powered charging systems; and (3) battery circularity, second-life applications, regulation, and recycling. In the search strings, “TS” denotes the Web of Science Topic field, which searches titles, abstracts, author keywords, and Keywords Plus. The following search strings were used:

Search 1 - Alternative vehicle technologies, commercial adoption, and country-level implementation in Sub-Saharan Africa: TS = (((“alternative vehicle* ” OR “electric vehicle* ” OR EV OR E2W OR E3W OR “electric bus* ” OR “compressed natural gas” OR CNG OR “flex-fuel” OR “green hydrogen” OR “hydrogen fuel cell* ”) AND (“commercial adoption* ” OR adopt* OR deploy* OR implementation OR transition) AND (“Sub-Saharan Africa” OR Africa OR Rwanda OR Kenya OR South Africa OR Nigeria))).

Search 2 - V2G, decentralized grids, storage, and system performance: TS = ((“vehicle-to-grid” OR “vehicle to grid” OR V2G) AND (microgrid* OR “micro grid* ” OR “mini-grid* ” OR “mini grid* ” OR “decentralized grid* ” OR “distributed grid* ” OR (solar AND BESS) OR “battery energy storage”) AND (optim* OR “techno-economic” OR “techno economic” OR model* OR performance) AND (integrat* OR adopt* )).

Search 3 - Battery circularity, second-life use, policy, and recycling: TS = ((“battery circularity” OR “second life” OR “second-life” OR repurpos* OR reus* ) AND (batter* OR “electric vehicle” OR EV) AND (regulator* OR policy* OR framework* ) AND (“solar storage” OR “stationary storage” OR “energy storage”) AND (recycl* OR “recycling infrastructure”)).

2.3 Eligibility and evidence selection

Sources were eligible if they addressed at least one review objective and provided relevant evidence on alternative-vehicle technologies or adoption, electricity supply and distribution, charging or battery swapping, refueling, battery lifecycle management, policy instruments, finance, emissions, or implementation in SSA. Peer-reviewed studies and attributable government, regulatory, utility, and program documents were prioritized for country-specific claims. Studies from outside SSA informed general technical concepts but were not treated as direct evidence of conditions in the four selected countries. Claims were strictly limited to the geographical scope, methods, publication date, and findings of the supporting sources.

The Web of Science search retrieved 1,432 records. Database filters covering the 2000-2026 publication period, English-language publications, peer-reviewed status, and duplicate removal excluded 721 records before screening, leaving 711 records for title and abstract screening. Of these, 345 records were excluded at the title and abstract stage, leaving 366 full-text peer-reviewed papers to be assessed for eligibility. Following full-text assessment, 301 reports were excluded, leaving 65 peer-reviewed sources for the qualitative synthesis. An additional 14 government, regulatory, utility, or program documents were identified through Google web searches and used as supplementary evidence outside the Web of Science screening process.

2.4 Case selection and comparative framework

Rwanda, Kenya, South Africa, and Nigeria were purposively selected to compare contrasting policy, market, and infrastructure conditions rather than to represent SSA statistically. Rwanda provides a case for examining national e-mobility policy in a comparatively small market; Kenya offers evidence on commercial electric two-wheelers, battery swapping, and renewable-energy integration; South Africa illustrates passenger-EV policy, automotive manufacturing ambitions, and electricity-system constraints; and Nigeria provides a case for examining CNG policy, fuel-market changes, and electricity-access constraints. These profiles serve as analytical lenses, rather than claims that the identified characteristics are exclusive to any single country. Ethiopia, Uganda, and Ghana are acknowledged as relevant regional comparators but are not examined as full comparative case studies.

2.5 Data extraction, synthesis and limitations

Evidence was synthesized qualitatively across five interlinked dimensions: (1) vehicle segments and documented deployment; (2) electricity access, reliability, and distribution-network capacity; (3) charging, battery swapping, renewable integration, and refueling infrastructure; (4) policy design, legal status, and implementation outcomes; and (5) finance, operator economics, and inclusion. For each source, the synthesis considered source type, publication date, geographical scope, methodology, and implementation status, distinguishing proposals and enacted instruments from funded programs, pilots, and measured outcomes. Where comparable data were unavailable, including fleet registrations, infrastructure coverage, electricity reliability, operating costs, battery performance, and policy outcomes, the review identifies evidence gaps rather than assigning unsupported readiness scores or rankings. The principal limitations of this review are reliance on a single bibliographic database, uneven reporting across countries, and the potential omission of relevant studies not captured by the search strategy. The four purposively selected cases support contextual comparison but not statistical generalization, causal attribution, or pooled-effect estimation. Finally, the synthesis informs the recommendations in Section 7 by linking proposed actions to constraints and evidence gaps identified in the technology and country analyses. 3 Technological pathways

Transport decarbonization requires matching vehicle technologies to duty cycles, operator economics, infrastructure and the emissions profile of the energy source. The pathways reviewed here are not mutually exclusive and should not be treated as a single ranked list. Figure 1 provides a quantitative contextual indicator for the four case-study countries' population access to electricity (access is not a measure of reliability or distribution capacity), while the country comparison and subsequent sections distinguish access from reliability, distribution capacity and charging infrastructure. A key analytical constraint across the literature is the scarcity and inconsistency of quantitative data regarding consistently dated EV fleet numbers, functioning charging and swapping infrastructure points, and power system reliability metrics across SSA markets; where comparable empirical datasets are unavailable, this review explicitly highlights data gaps rather than relying on unverified estimations or speculative projections.
