text:
The following blog is part of a series examining specific provisions in the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA). Clean Air Task Force is taking a close look at the bill to identify opportunities to strengthen its provisions, address potential gaps, and improve its effectiveness in meeting the country’s energy needs reliably and affordably.

The country needs to build more efficient, cost-effective regional and interregional electric transmission lines to achieve broadly shared economic and emissions reductions goals. We appreciate the bipartisan efforts of the architects of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) to bring much-needed attention to transmission reform.

BAAJA enters a policy space shaped most recently by Order 1920, FERC’s landmark long-term transmission planning rule, and must be considered in light of that Order.1 Order 1920 is premised on the theory that, absent clear and specific mandates requiring regional transmission planning that unlocks competition and meets all foreseeable system-wide needs as efficiently as possible, transmission owners—who generally earn guaranteed profits on whatever they build in their own territories—default to short-term, piecemeal, inefficient transmission buildout that maximizes their profits. The pre-Order 1920 status quo failed to deliver high-voltage interstate transmission needed to drive economic growth, failed to achieve emissions reductions, and thwarted competition needed to deliver cost savings to consumers. Because prior FERC rulemakings left too much room for utilities to avoid or minimize compliance, Order 1920 set clear and specific requirements for conducting long-term regional transmission planning, built around common-sense planning principles described further below.

As with BAAJA’s provision on a Coordinated Planning Process (which we evaluated in our recent blog post), BAAJA’s transmission provisions seek to improve a broken status quo. The bipartisan drafters’ aim is to achieve more efficient and cost-effective regional and interregional transmission planning and buildout across the country—a goal we share. We believe certain modifications are needed to realize those aims. This blog examines the language in BAAJA section 2103, which covers regional and interregional transmission planning, and suggests modest, targeted revisions designed to ensure proper implementation and withstand judicial review in a legal landscape reshaped by recent Supreme Court decisions limiting agency independence and discretion.

1. BAAJA’s Transmission Planning Requirements

BAAJA’s Section 2103 would amend the Federal Power Act (FPA) to include regional and interregional transmission planning requirements captured in a new section 225. In the amended draft passed by the Senate on November 9, subsection (c) of this provision requires that within 180 days of enactment, FERC shall, “by rule:

require each transmission planning region to establish a process for planning for regional transmission facilities in accordance with this section;

require neighboring transmission planning regions to jointly establish a process for planning interregional transmission facilities in accordance with this section;

require each transmission planning region to submit to the Commission for approval (A) a regional transmission planning process; and (B) a joint interregional transmission planning process with each of its neighboring transmission planning regions…; and

establish rate treatments for regional and interregional cost allocation.”

Operative planning requirements for both regional and interregional planning are found in subsection (d), which requires both processes to “contain the following core elements:”

“A common set of input assumptions and models, on a consistent timeline, that: (A) allow for” the identification and selection of specific transmission facilities, for construction or modification, including through the use of advanced transmission conductors; (B) “consider, to the extent reasonable and economical,” modifications that maximize existing transmission infrastructure or rights-of-way; and (C) “consider interactions with” existing transmission plans and planning processes, including BAAJA’s new consolidated planning process;

“A common set of transmission benefits for planning and cost allocation,” including 6 listed benefits; and

“Selection criteria” governing project selection that provide improved reliability, protect or benefit consumers, and are consistent with the public interest.

Under subsection (e), planning must start within one year of BAAJA’s effective date and be conducted on four-year cycles; transmission plans complying with the rule must be filed within two years of enactment.

2. Regional Transmission Concerns

Our question in evaluating new FPA section 225 is how its planning requirements compare to the status quo requirements under existing FERC regulations, primarily those of Order 1920, the implementation of which is just now under way. Our primary concern with new section 225’s requirements is that they are considerably less comprehensive and more permissive than those of Order 1920. And while the drafters may have intended to require FERC to base its new rule on Order 1920, the language as drafted does not ensure this. But a simple fix would address both concerns.

Order 1920: Measure Thrice, Build Once

Because transmission is an expensive and long-lived asset, it should be planned not just for today’s demands but should be sized and placed to meet foreseeable long-term needs. This ensures that the multi-billion-dollar transmission line meant to last for 50-70 years isn’t already undersized the moment it is built, requiring ratepayers to overpay repeatedly to rebuild the same line or multiple lines, when good planning would have consolidated those needs into one larger, cheaper project. But prior FERC planning requirements under Order 1000 served largely as voluntary guidelines that allowed transmission owners to evade efficient planning.

To correct this, Order 1920 requires planning to be conducted as follows: First, to identify the scope of future system-wide needs, Order 1920 requires a holistic assessment of all expected changes in demand and supply across the entire transmission system over the next 20 years. Transmission providers must model the impact of seven specific factors that drive supply and demand—including state energy laws, technology trends, planned retirements, interconnection requests, new large loads, and extreme weather. Setting mandatory factors are necessary not just to keep the grid reliable but to ensure that transmission owners can’t favor affiliated generating resources by ignoring transmission needs such as state clean energy requirements. Second, they must forecast needed transmission across a minimum of three different future scenarios. Having multiple possible forecasts is essential to building a resilient energy system prepared not just for next summer’s hottest day but for events that may have low probabilities but carry high risks for the grid, such as extreme weather or cyberattacks. Third, to pick the most efficient solutions, transmission providers must assess and compare the full value of potential transmission projects meeting identified needs over that same 20-year horizon, using a minimum of seven mandatory benefit metrics. And as part of project assessment, planners must assess four different alternative transmission technologies. These requirements are needed to force transmission providers to identify more cost-effective solutions for ratepayers both by squeezing more out of existing assets for very low costs, as well as accurately assessing the value of large regional lines, whose multiple benefits take longer to exceed build costs, but then continue to run for decades. Fourth, planners must identify facilities that efficiently address long-term transmission needs, and project selection must be made using pre-determined, transparent criteria that aim to maximize benefits accounting for costs over time, without overbuilding facilities. Selected facilities go through a cost allocation process that allows state input on the proposed projects and requires assignment of costs roughly commensurate with benefits, as required under the cost causation principle.

BAAJA Steps Back

Despite the existence of Order 1920, BAAJA directs FERC to promulgate a regional transmission rule within 6 months of enactment. But the statutory elements of the required BAAJA regional transmission rule are generally less comprehensive than the overarching requirements of Order 1920, and more akin to the permissive structure of Order 1000. For example, unlike Order 1920, BAAJA does not require that planning be system-wide, holistic, scenario-based, or use a 20-year horizon. No specific factors driving transmission must be assessed, such as state laws, integrated resource plans, or trends in fuels costs and technology. This would allow a return to siloed planning processes that examine only one type of transmission need at a time (e.g., reliability, economic, or policy-driven needs), using single and often inaccurate forecasts, on timeframes too short to accurately reflect the true benefits of regional transmission—as was the case with prior, unsuccessful planning orders.

While BAAJA generally has fewer requirements than Order 1920, some of them also differ in substance, as detailed further below. Because of these substantive differences, FERC may issue some kind of new rule, which could cause confusion for FERC and transmission planners about whether to move forward with Order 1920 planning or wait for a new rule. While speeding the build-out of transmission to unlock cheaper, cleaner power is a stated goal of BAAJA’s drafters, adding confusion and potential delay to the Order 1920 process that is still getting under way could unwittingly undermine that goal. While FERC could fulfil some of its duties under BAAJA by issuing a rule incorporating Orders 1920, 1920-A, and 1920-B, this provision does not require it to do so, and this or a future FERC could instead issue a new rule that hews more closely to less-robust elements spelled out in new FPA section 225(d).

Subsection 225(h) does not codify Order 1920 into law

CATF supports clearly codifying Order 1920’s more comprehensive and stringent mandates into law, which we understand to be the intent of the drafters. But drafter intentions bind neither FERC nor the Courts, especially in light of the Supreme Court’s 2024 Loper Bright decision limiting agency discretion to go beyond the statutory text.2 If new FPA section 225 is meant to codify Order 1920 as a mandatory requirement, it needs modification on top of the changes made in the manager’s amendment. We break down the problem and propose textual fixes.

As further explained below, proposed subsection 225(h) does not codify mandatory compliance with Order 1920 because it neither limits the scope of compliance to Order 1920 nor prevents FERC from making compliance with Order 1920 optional. Additionally, its limitations to compliance with existing rules conflicts with statutory requirements that differ from those existing rules.

In the draft released in early November 2026 with the manager’s amendment, new FPA subsection 225(h) reads:

“(h) Compliance With This Section—A Commission order or rulemaking regarding transmission planning that is effective as of the date of enactment of this section, including orders published in the Federal Register on April 28, 2025, December 6, 2024, and June 11, 2024, shall constitute compliance with the regional transmission planning and cost allocation requirements of this section and relieves the Commission of the requirements under subsection (c)(1).

A careful review of the text is necessary to determine how FERC commissioners could pursue a rulemaking, and how reviewing courts might interpret this subsection. There are two issues with the structure that are likely to present problems with its enforcement.

First, the scope of subsection (h) is unbounded, unclear, and does not explicitly reference or limit compliance to Order 1920. Rather, it states: “A Commission order or rulemaking regarding transmission planning that is effective as of the date of enactment of this section, including orders published in the Federal Register on April 28, 2025, December 6, 2024, and June 11, 2024, shall constitute compliance … and relieves the Commission of the requirements under subsection (c)(1).” While these dates correspond to the publication of Orders 1920, 1920-A and 1920-B in the Federal Register, the provision neither specifically mentions the relevant orders, nor limits compliance with BAAJA planning requirements to Order 1920. Under this language, FERC or transmission planners could plausibly point to compliance with prior orders already deemed to be ineffective, such as Order 1000. And while subsection (h) states that compliance with existing orders “relieves the Commission” of its drafting requirements under subsection (c)(1), it does not prohibit FERC from issuing a new rule that allows transmission owners to choose to comply with regional transmission planning via less stringent orders.

The key word to guide interpretation of this subsection is “including.” This word creates inclusive rather than exclusive language. In other words, compliance with Order 1920 counts, but it is not the only way for FERC or transmission owners to comply. The Supreme Court, in conducting statutory interpretation, has said of the term, “including” or “includes”: “the verb ‘includes’ instead of ‘means…’ is significant because it makes clear that the examples enumerated in the text are intended to be illustrative, not exhaustive.” Christopher v. SmithKline Beecham Corp., 567 U.S. 142, 162 (2012) (emphasis added). In writing statutes post Loper Bright, when federal courts will not defer to reasonable agency interpretations of statutes, likely court interpretations of statutory text hold more importance.

Thus, the inclusive list of dates in the statute illustrates a set of orders that could be used by FERC or transmission owners to comply with the requirements of new FPA section 225. As a result, this rule does not prohibit FERC from issuing a rule now or in the future that effectively makes the more stringent requirements of Order 1920 optional instead of mandatory—especially since the proposed statutory requirements are themselves highly flexible.

Second, subsection (h) ties compliance with its statutory requirements to existing rules, which presents additional problems.

While BAAJA directs FERC to promulgate a regional transmission rule that differs from Order 1920 in many respects (as explained above), BAAJA also requires FERC to incorporate into the new planning rule certain elements that are not currently part of Order 1920 (or other potentially qualifying existing orders). For example, new section 225: (1) directs FERC to apply its transmission planning and cost allocation rules to Power Marketing Administrations such as Bonneville Power Administration;3 (2) has a different set of required benefits such that FERC may need to clarify or expand Order 1920’s benefits list;4 (3) adds an element not explicitly required by Order 1920, requiring transmission providers to consider modifications that maximize existing infrastructure to the extent reasonable and economical; (4) shortens the planning cycle from five years to four;5 and requires consideration of the new consolidated planning process set forth in section 2106 of BAAJA.6 These new requirements, not present in previous planning rules, mean that FERC may issue a new rule to comply with these statutory directives. However, section 225(h) then states that compliance with any existing order (which do not include such requirements) constitutes compliance with the statute, an outcome that creates nonsensical results.

At the point where we are asking these questions, it means the statute is not clear, and this likely leaves the meaning in the hands of the courts, creating a risk that the Court will view this as a mistake that Congress would have to fix. See Lamie v. U.S. Tr., 540 U.S. 526, 542 (2004) (cleaned up) (“If Congress enacted into law something different from what it intended, then it should amend the statute to conform it to its intent. It is beyond our province to rescue Congress from its drafting errors, and to provide for what we might think … is the preferred result.”)

In sum, if FERC fills in gaps as its drafters intend, the planning provisions of BAAJA may ultimately reaffirm Order 1920. But the statute as written provides textual escape hatches for FERC and transmission providers to avoid the most critical elements of sound transmission planning and too much uncertainty about how reviewing courts will interpret its requirements. Congress should not leave sound regional transmission planning up to the interpretive discretion of other branches: it needs to speak clearly.

There are easy fixes

The most direct way to achieve the economic, affordability, and emissions reduction benefits of improved transmission planning is not to require a separate, new FERC regional transmission rulemaking. Instead, BAAJA could directly require all subject transmission providers to conduct regional transmission planning and cost allocation in compliance with Order 1920. This would clearly codify Order 1920, bypassing the need for FERC to do anything and limiting the ability of future administrations or courts to weaken its requirements. Like BAAJA’s proposed structure, however, it would lock in compliance to an existing rule.

Alternatively, FERC’s rulemaking authority under new FPA section 225 could be written to unambiguously require Order 1920 as a floor and not a ceiling, which could be achieved through simple language in either subsection (c) or (h) such as:

“The regional transmission planning and cost allocation rulemaking under Sections (c)(1), (c)(3)(A), and (c)(4) shall incorporate, at a minimum, the requirements of Orders 1920, 1920-A, and 1920-B as set forth in 89 Fed. Reg. 49,280 (June 11, 2024), 89 Fed. Reg. 97,174 (Dec. 6, 2024), and 90 Fed. Reg. 17,692 (Apr. 28, 2025).”

Such language would allow FERC to address BAAJA’s new requirements and continue to strengthen Order 1920, while preventing any future rollback of its core requirements.

3. Interregional transmission

Alongside a new regional planning rule, new FPA section 225 also directs FERC to issue an interregional planning rule. A strong interregional planning rule is much needed. But the permissive language of section 225’s interregional transmission planning requirements do not do enough to expand beyond the existing requirements of Order 1000 and Order 1920. Incumbent transmission providers have strong economic incentives to avoid efficient interregional buildout and have a long history of successfully taking advantage of permissive, non-mandatory language. And unlike regional planning requirements, FERC doesn’t have a better existing rule to reference, so the agency may be more likely to stick to statutory requirements, especially in light of the tight implementation deadline. BAAJA should be amended to address these concerns and strengthen the interregional planning requirements.

Many of section 225’s interregional planning elements are already required under Order 1000, part of the status quo that has failed to deliver the system of high-voltage interregional transmission required for the growing U.S. economy. For example, Order 1000 requires “the development and implementation of procedures for neighboring public utility transmission providers to identify and jointly evaluate transmission facilities that are proposed to be located in both regions.”7 That is, Order 1000 requires transmission providers to develop procedures for interregional planning. And these procedures must “identify possible interregional transmission facilities that may more efficiently or cost-effectively address the individual needs identified in their respective local and regional transmission planning processes.”8 But Order 1000 does not: have firm requirements on what any of these procedures must entail, require interregionally-focused transmission planning, or require selection of interregional projects identified in the coordination process. In practice, this has meant that interregional planning rarely occurs, and even when interregional needs are identified, planning regions fail to address them.

Order 1920 included improvements to Order 1000’s interregional coordination requirements that, once implemented (compliance plans are just now being filed), are in many ways comparable to BAAJA’s interregional planning provisions. Under Order 1920’s revised interregional transmission coordination procedures, transmission providers must share information generated as part of their regional transmission planning process with neighboring regions, including identified transmission needs and potential facilities to meet those needs, as well as the identification and joint evaluation of interregional transmission facilities that may be more efficient or cost-effective in meeting such needs.9 By requiring neighboring regions to share transmission needs and potential projects developed under the same core minimum requirements for holistic, scenario-based planning, Order 1920 puts regions on more common ground to identify transmission needs that may be more efficiently addressed through interregional projects.

As with regional transmission, BAAJA’s interregional provisions should be assessed within the context of these existing requirements.

What does new FPA section 225 say about interregional transmission?

The operative requirement of subsection 225(c) is for FERC to require transmission providers to “establish a process for planning interregional transmission.” But it does not explain how any planning must be conducted, nor does BAAJA require that any interregional facilities be built if planning determines such lines to be efficient and cost-effective.

Recall that Order 1000 already requires transmission providers to develop and implement procedures for interregional planning. It is not clear how BAAJA’s requirements have more teeth than Order 1000: requiring a “process for planning interregional transmission” (BAAJA’s plain text) is synonymous with requiring “procedures for neighboring public utility transmission providers to identify and jointly evaluate transmission facilities that are proposed to be located in both regions” (Order 1000’s plain text). Without clearer requirements governing the planning process, there is little assurance that BAAJA’s interregional planning provision would produce better outcomes than similar requirements under Order 1000.

In particular, the “elements” BAAJA requires in these processes are too permissive to ensure needed change given transmission owners’ continued economic incentives to avoid building interregional transmission that would reduce costs for ratepayers. For example, BAAJA requires “a common set of input assumptions and models on a consistent timeline that … allow for joint identification and selection of specific interregional transmission facilities.” BAAJA does not specify what those inputs must entail or how they must be studied. As any common inputs can allow for joint identification and selection of transmission projects, BAAJA’s text does not exceed the requirements of existing Orders 1000 and 1920. The same provision states that joint identification and selection can be “including through the use of advanced transmission conductors.” While this provision allows for advanced transmission technologies to be identified and selected, Order 1920 found that, absent a specific mandate to assess advanced transmission technologies as part of the planning process, such projects (which are often cheap and easier to build) will be ignored.10

And while BAAJA does require that there be a common set of minimum benefits, it does not say how they must be applied. Moreover, as mentioned above, BAAJA’s planning provisions lack critical requirements for identifying holistic transmission needs and efficient solutions: a minimum 20-year planning horizon, consideration of reasonably foreseeable factors driving transmission needs across the entire system, such as state energy laws or large load demands; and evaluation of solutions against all transmission needs at once, instead of in separate silos. Clear mandates using the same core planning framework of Order 1920 are critical to achieve BAAJA’s goal of building interregional transmission.

Congress can modify this provision to ensure cost-effective interregional planning happens

First and foremost, while the Manager’s Amendment now requires that interregional planning be conducted, new FPA section 225 should include essential requirements for how to conduct that planning, without which the resulting plans are unlikely to meet long-term future needs or identify efficient, cost-effective solutions. Specifically, planning must:

Be based on a minimum 20-year outlook;

Identify systemic transmission needs by conducting scenario-based analyses across multiple future scenarios that each incorporates the seven mandatory factors of Order 1920 along with relevant factors specific to interregional needs;

Evaluate potential transmission projects addressing the identified needs holistically (i.e., projects that would meet reliability, economic, and policy needs at once) and determine efficient and cost-effective solutions by assessing all foreseeable benefits proposed projects could provide (including a mandatory minimum set of benefits);

Require assessment of low-cost solutions such as alternative transmission technologies and improved joint operating agreements;

Use project selection criteria that are transparent, not unduly discriminatory, and aim to maximize cost-effectiveness; and

Include input from relevant state entities and other key stakeholders on scenario planning, project selection, and cost allocation.

In addition to these factors, because interregional transmission is such a critical asset for the nation’s grid––not just for maintaining reliability during extreme weather, but also in meeting new demand from large loads, increasing access to cheap power, and helping maximize stability across a diverse array of resources—Congress should strongly consider requiring FERC to set minimum levels of interregional transfer capacity between regions that reflect meeting holistic transmission needs. Such a mandate would ensure not only that good projects get planned but that they get built. Together, these requirements would build on the positive aspects of Order 1920 and Order 1000 and bring interregional planning closer to the modern, efficient system that our economy requires.

* * * *

Order 1000 taught us that words matter. Transmission providers have economic incentives to build inefficient, piecemeal, costly transmission—and that patchwork has burdened the American economy and cost American ratepayers for decades. BAAJA’s drafters seek to move beyond the outdated planning modalities that have constrained transmission in the past. To do that successfully, BAAJA must place firm, clear, prescriptive requirements on transmission providers—or risk a repeat of past failed attempts at transmission reform. We commend the BAAJA transmission provisions for tackling this issue proactively and productively. But we suggest drafters further strengthen the transmission provisions, through less permissive and more comprehensive terms that clearly mandate planning practices that will actually identify and select the most efficient and cost-effective projects. Doing so will increase reliability while lowering electricity costs across the country.

title: Oversight Edge: Preparing for Congressional Scrutiny in the New Congress | JD Supra
description:

Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Ranking Member Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) is in line to chair the Senate Banking Committee.

text:
And we are off to the races! Two days after the election, Senator Richard Blumenthal, the incoming Chairman of the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, sent 58 oversight letters to all the company CEOs, foundations, and individuals who donated to the White House ballroom, threatening alternative measures to obtain documents if they are not submitted by January 4th.

Unless you have been directly involved in congressional oversight, it is hard to appreciate the breadth, scope, and potential impact on companies. The legal, political, and reputational consequences are often not fully realized until it is too late. For example, the way the big three automakers traveled to a Congressional hearing in 2008 damaged their reputation.

This update is the first of many future insights from Holland & Hart's Congressional Oversight and Investigations team we’re calling Oversight Edge. The team consists of professionals who have led oversight efforts for Congress, federal agencies, and private companies, and who bring that first-hand experience to clients facing congressional scrutiny.

Key Takeaways

Federal money invites document requests. Loans, grants, contracts, equity stakes, and tariff relief are the common thread across committees. Know who made the decisions and what the board knew.

Proximity to the administration is an exposure. Dealings with the president’s family, contracts with agencies under scrutiny, and even donations can draw a letter with no allegation of wrongdoing.

Affordability drives the agenda. Companies in fuel, food, housing, health care, and consumer finance should expect questions about prices, margins, and “record profits.”

Your regulator contacts are fair game. Permitting wins, rule rollbacks, and communications with EPA, Interior, and the Pentagon will be requested.

CEOs will be called to testify. Incoming chairs have promised witnesses under oath. The first response to a letter matters more than hearing prep.

What is Congressional Oversight?

As a co-equal branch of government, Congress has broad authority to examine how federal agencies develop and implement policy, spend federal funds, and carry out their responsibilities.

That authority does not stop at the federal agencies. Congressional oversight can also reach private companies and organizations, whether or not they have dealt directly with the federal government.

Congressional investigations take many forms, and they can escalate. A committee may:

Request documents or communications

Seek a transcribed interview with committee staff

Call a witness to testify at a public hearing

Issue a subpoena

In some circumstances, refer a matter to the U.S. Department of Justice

Likely targets for oversight

The oversight agenda of Democrats will be organized committee-by-committee—each with its own jurisdiction, staff, and investigative priorities—and the committee asking the questions largely determines the issues in play, the tools available, and the pace of escalation. The committees below are the ones most likely to drive scrutiny of companies in the new Congress.

House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform

The House Oversight and Government Reform Committee (Oversight Committee) has the broadest investigative reach in the House, and incoming Chairman Robert Garcia (D-CA) issued a two-word statement on election night: “Lawyer up.” The next day, Ranking Member Garcia commented, “The Trump crime family is the top of our investigative priorities,” and said the Oversight Committee will be “focused like a laser” on four investigations:

(1) the president's family members;

(2) immigration enforcement by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE);

(3) corporate corruption; and

(4) the handling of the Jeffrey Epstein files.

Two of these probes could reach well beyond the White House. Garcia has framed the corporate corruption probe around the claim that CEOs and corporations are making “record profits” while everyday Americans are struggling. That echoes the affordability message Democrats across the ideological spectrum campaigned on. One Democratic senator described the priority as “any kind of corruption with the administration that has raised costs.”

The probe of President Trump’s family could also reach companies doing business with the government. Democrats have questioned contracts awarded to companies “associated with the president's son.” Ranking Member Garcia has also named pay-to-play contracting at the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) as a target.

Critical minerals are already part of the oversight picture. In August of this year, Ranking Member Garcia and House Natural Resources Ranking Member Jared Huffman (D-CA) requested records about a large federal loan to a minerals company with reported ties to the president's family. Investigations like this focus on who influenced the selection, how the government's support was structured, and whether private relationships affected public decisions.

Requests by Ranking Members Garcia and Huffman show how oversight can work between committees. Garcia and House Judiciary Ranking Member Jamie Raskin (D-MD) have also discussed running joint investigations. Ranking Member Garcia has said administration officials would likely receive subpoenas on the first day of a Democratic majority. Companies with significant business before the federal government, including those that have received federal loans, contracts, or other support, should plan now for document requests, which means knowing who made key decisions and what senior management or the board knew.

House Committee on Energy and Commerce

The House Energy and Commerce Committee has one of the widest jurisdictions in Congress, covering energy, health care, pharmaceuticals, telecommunications, consumer protection, and environmental matters. Ranking Member Frank Pallone (D-NJ) has already announced that he will seek to retake the Committee gavel as he has served as the top Democrat on the committee since 2015—and developed an extensive oversight record during the first Trump Administration. Democrats on the Energy and Commerce Committee’s Oversight and Investigations Subcommittee have a long history of company-focused inquiries, and Democratic leaders have already signaled that oversight of the administration will dominate the next two years.

“Affordability” is another key theme that underpinned the Democrats’ election wins and will undoubtedly shape the Energy and Commerce Committee’s oversight. That means a focus on fuel and electricity prices and grid reliability, especially as it relates to the data center boom and spike in gas and diesel prices during the Iran War. Other likely priorities—based on numerous inquiries Energy and Commerce Democrats sent to agencies throughout the 119th Congress—include the rescission of Biden-era environmental and public health rules, drug pricing and health care costs, data privacy and artificial intelligence, and product safety.

House Committee on Natural Resources

The House Natural Resources Committee oversees the Department of the Interior and its agencies, making it a central venue for Democrats' oversight plans. Ranking Member Huffman has formally announced that he will seek the gavel and is in line to chair the committee now that Democrats have won the House. Ranking Member Huffman has made his intentions crystal clear: “We're going to be making up for two years of zero oversight by this feckless MAGA Congress.” To do this, he promised at the committee’s last markup before the election that Democrats would “follow the evidence” and “put witnesses under oath.”

Expect early scrutiny of the Trump family's role in critical minerals deals, along with permitting procedures, offshore wind settlements, and implementation of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Natural Resources Democrats have also investigated corporate sponsors of the 250th anniversary celebrations and questioned plans to open federal lands to data center development. As part of their interest in permitting reform, expect Democrat scrutiny over Department of the Interior permitting decisions.

House Committee on Armed Services

The House Armed Services Committee oversees the Department of War (DOW) and writes the annual National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), giving it a growing role in energy and natural resources policy. House Armed Services Ranking Member Adam Smith (D-WA) is expected to assume the gavel and has already indicated that he will pursue “vigorous oversight” of the defense community in a November 4th letter to colleagues announcing his bid for the chair. Ranking Member Smith also called in his letter for reestablishing the committee's oversight and investigations panel.

In addition to the Iran War and boat strikes in the Caribbean Sea and Pacific Ocean, renewed interest in energy permitting will result in oversight of DOW’s Siting Clearinghouse, which reviews proposed energy projects and transmission lines for potential interference with military radar, training routes, and testing ranges. Over 100 on- and offshore wind projects have been held up over the last two years with DOW citing “national security” concerns; the committee has pledged to examine this issue.

Expect Ranking Member Smith to pair that review with his call for probes into Pentagon investments in defense companies, which could extend to DOW’s growing energy supply chain portfolio, such as the Office of Strategic Capital’s $250 million conditional loan commitment to scale domestic battery cathode production in Tennessee.

House Committee on Agriculture

The House Agriculture Committee will be under new leadership as both Congresswoman Shontel Brown (D-OH) and Congressman Jim Costa (D-CA) launched bids to lead the committee. Generally, the Agriculture Committee addresses the challenges facing farm country through an update to the Farm Bill, which is traditionally passed every five years. However, the last Farm Bill was enacted in 2018 and farm programs have been operating under continual extensions of the 2018 Farm Bill since it expired in 2023.

While the Agriculture Committee typically conducts oversight of the Department of Agriculture (USDA), in 2022 it took testimony under oath from the meatpacking industry in a hearing titled: “An Examination of Price Discrepancies, Transparency, and Alleged Unfair Practices in Cattle Markets.” This hearing was in response to high beef prices, low producer profits, and concerns with industry concentration. Because many midterm campaigns were won on a theme of affordability, the Agriculture Committee may seek to use this type of oversight again.

House Committee on Financial Services

Ranking Member Maxine Waters (D-CA), who chaired the House Financial Services Committee in the last Democrat Majority, is the favorite to lead it again. If she does, expect the committee to set aside the current effort to pass crypto market-structure legislation and turn instead to oversight of the industry, including the Trump family’s crypto ventures. Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) enforcement, the banks, and the independence of the prudential regulators are also likely targets.

Ranking Member Waters has announced her plans: “We must methodically investigate President Trump’s crypto corruption, financial conflicts of interest, and his concerted efforts to kill investigations and prosecutions against businesses owned by his friends and allies.”

On the consumer side, look for attention to scams involving peer-to-peer payment apps and to housing costs. Ranking Member Waters brought the heads of the largest U.S. banks before the committee during her last tenure, and most observers expect a repeat. Congressman Sean Casten (D-IL) is also running for the top Democratic seat on the committee and has made similar promises to dig into the President’s crypto business and potential conflicts.

Congressman Emanuel Cleaver (D-MO) led the Housing Subcommittee previously and will probably do so again. His stated priorities include how the Trump Administration is carrying out the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, passed earlier this year; HUD’s shifting approach to fair housing enforcement and homelessness programs; how the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) manages and funds affordable housing; and the conduct of Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) Director Bill Pulte.

House Committee on Ways and Means

Ranking Member Richard Neal (D-MA), who chaired the House Ways and Means Committee in the 116th and 117th Congresses, has said he will seek the chairmanship again now that Democrats have won the House. On the oversight front, his list is long:

Corruption allegations involving the administration and the Trump family

President Trump’s $10 billion suit against the Internal Revenue Service (IRS)

How the wealthy are taxed

Renewable energy credits

Reports that the IRS gave taxpayer data to DHS, Frank Bisignano’s role as IRS CEO, and the effects of last year’s IRS staffing cuts.

On trade, we expect Ranking Member Neal to look hard at companies that won tariff relief through trade deals and to support efforts to unwind tariffs on particular industries.

Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs

Ranking Member Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) is in line to chair the Senate Banking Committee. Her focus will likely be Wall Street, crypto, and claims that President Trump has used his office to enrich himself. The largest banks are already bracing for their CEOs to be summoned to testify, as has typically happened when Democrats run the committee. Ranking Member Warren’s interests also go beyond the banks. Earlier this year she and her Democratic colleagues on the committee asked for a public hearing on prediction markets, and she has previously pushed for Nvidia’s CEO, Jensen Huang, to appear before the panel.

Senate Committee on Finance

Senator Ron Wyden (D-OR), the Ranking Member and former Chairman of the committee, is expected to take the gavel back. He has said he plans to go after tax cheats and investigate health insurers, banks, and drug companies. “Trump and Republicans have been running a smash-and-grab job on the American people,” Senator Wyden said. “Under my leadership, the top priorities of the Finance Committee will be affordability for us, accountability for them.” He also plans to look at the role that large banks played in financing Jeffrey Epstein.

Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources

Senator Martin Heinrich (D-NM) is expected to take the Senate Energy and Natural Resources (ENR) Committee gavel, after serving as its Ranking Member. He has expressed interest in pursuing oversight of government equity deals in critical mineral and rare earth projects, specifically how agencies select mining and processing companies for equity stakes and other financial deals. He has also flagged concerns over ownership by foreign adversaries of mining companies operating in the U.S. Finally, Senator Heinrich plans to investigate the Trump Administration’s decision to consolidate the Department of the Interior’s Bureau of Ocean Energy Management and the Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement.

Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works

The Senate Environment and Public Works (EPW) Committee is likely to see one of the sharpest changes in tone of any Senate panel. Senator Jeff Merkley (D-OR) is the likely Chairman in the Democrat-controlled Senate and is expected to scrutinize oil and natural gas projects.

Recently, as the Chemical Safety Subcommittee Ranking Member, he sent requests to the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) regarding the hiring of former chemical industry staff in key positions overseeing the industry. As Chairman, he is expected to broaden his oversight across all the EPA's political staff. He is particularly interested in industry influence over regulatory decisions and is expected to probe corporate communications with the EPA.

Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry

Like the House Agriculture Committee, the Senate Agriculture Committee is traditionally known for a more genteel approach to oversight of USDA in place of extensive oversight of private industry. The election of new Midwest and Southern Senators from farm states who ran on affordability may push the committee to address affordability through the Farm Bill or build a thorough record to determine if there are industry practices driving up food prices.

It is likely that Senator Michael Bennet (D-CO) will lead the committee in the 120th Congress. Senator Bennet has indicated that his goals would be to address agricultural trade, conservation, and farm labor issues. The committee has limited jurisdiction over trade and farm labor, meaning that those issues could be brought into the oversight orbit of the Senate Judiciary and Finance committees, respectively.

Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs

The Homeland Security Committee will have new Democratic leadership with the retirement of current Ranking Member, Senator Gary Peters (D-MI) and Senator Margaret Hassan (D-NH) will become the new Chairman. While it is expected that she will focus her efforts on the DHS and the various ICE, border, and immigration issues that the Democratic Party has focused on for the last two years, the committee has the broadest oversight portfolio in the Senate.

As noted above, the Chair of the Subcommittee on Investigations, Senator Blumenthal, has already launched an investigation into the White House ballroom. Senator Hassan has also expressed interest in conducting cost-of-living oversight, which could include multiple issues including energy, food, and housing.

Senate Armed Services Committee

Senator Jack Reed (D-RI) is expected to retake the gavel of the Senate Armed Services Committee. Ranking Member Reed is interested in oversight of the DOW’s Siting Clearinghouse, especially considering his effort to include a provision in this year’s NDAA that requires the Siting Clearinghouse to decide on pending projects in 180 days.

His agenda is also likely to feature DOW’s critical minerals deals. At a February hearing, Ranking Member Reed questioned the department’s $400 million, 15 percent equity stake in MP Materials, stating, “I have questions about the legal basis, financial terms and strategic rationale for these transactions. The legal basis appears questionable.”

He also raised concerns about potential Antideficiency Act exposure from multiyear funding commitments. Those questions will carry more weight with the gavel: the One Big Beautiful Bill Act gave the Office of Strategic Capital authority to subsidize up to $100 billion in critical minerals loans and guarantees, and the office has since announced conditional commitments including $500 million for Phoenix Tailings’ rare earth separation facility and $400 million for Sunrise Energy Metals’ scandium operations in Australia.

Expect Ranking Member Reed to push for clearer statutory guardrails on equity stakes, a conversation that he and current Chairman Roger Wicker (R-MS) have said is already underway with their House counterparts.

Senate Judiciary Committee

Current EPW Ranking Member Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI) is expected to chair the Senate Judiciary Committee. He is expected to conduct vigorous oversight of the Department of Justice, especially what he deems lawfare, and he is also expected to continue some of his past environmental oversight targets. He has been investigating the fossil fuel industry by reviewing the campaign contributions, corporate earnings, and investor communications of dozens of companies, signaling out the industry for what he calls “dark money” campaigns against climate change.

Looking Ahead

Oversight in the 120th Congress will begin on day one, and the first response to a committee letter sets the course for everything that follows. Companies with federal funding, business before agencies under scrutiny, or pricing power in a consumer-facing market should take stock now: know where your federal touchpoints are, who made the key decisions, and what records exist.

text:
The Senate is fast tracking legislation that would reduce permitting times for energy projects, but possibly to the detriment of longstanding policies protecting the environment.

The Associated Press reported that the Senate voted 73-25 to advance the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA). The bill was drafted in response to growing electricity costs from sources like grid-connected hyperscale data centers. By reducing permitting times, energy projects, like solar energy or onshore oil drilling, could address rising energy costs.

However, environmental groups consider BAAJA a reckless response to an immediate need for more power. The bill would amend sections of the Natural Environmental Policy Act, Clean Water Act and Endangered Species Act of 1973 to shorten review periods for new projects, and reduce which projects actually require reviews under these acts.

“We shouldn’t and don’t need to endanger our wildlife just to save a few dollars on gas. We shouldn’t and don’t need to weaken the rules that protect our water from pollution in order to build more clean energy. We shouldn’t facilitate more global-warming air pollution. And we definitely shouldn’t be taking away the public’s right to weigh in on projects that can ruin their environment, make them sick and lessen their quality of life,” said Lisa Frank, executive director of Environment America.

Despite the bill’s threat to environmental measures, the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) has voiced its support for BAAJA, as have hundreds of companies in the solar and energy storage industry. More than 300 groups co-signed a letter addressed to Congress yesterday imploring the House pass this bill.

“Americans urgently need lower energy costs, a better electric grid and more nergy made in the U.S.A. This bipartisan legislation delivers all three,” said Tim Pawlenty, CEO of SEIA.

SEIA conducted an analysis that claims passing BAAJA could spur 167 GW of new solar energy on the grid between 2028 and 2035, while curbing the country’s CO2 emissions by 20%.

“Updating and expediting transmission and clean energy permitting is essential to delivering lower costs, reduced air, water and climate pollution, protecting communities and expanding the grid for the American people,” said Loren Blackford, executive director of Sierra Club, in a press statement on Sunday. “But rushing legislation that erodes Tribal sovereignty and people’s right to have a say in what is built in their communities, abandons clean water safeguards and wildlife protections, while further enabling a rogue president that is waging a war on clean energy and our public lands is not an acceptable outcome.”

title: World leaders begin talks at UN climate conference amid concerns that actions are inadequate, slow
description:
ANTALYA, Turkey (AP) — World leaders began to arrive Wednesday to start formal discussions at the United Nations climate change conference in Turkey, hoping to agree on concrete actions to curb global warming after a year of deadly floods, heat waves and other climate-related disasters.
But what can and will be accomplished at the Conference of the Parties, called COP31, remains to be seen.
Last year's Brazil conference produced a compromise agreement pledging additional money to help vulnerable nations adapt to climate change.
Access was expected to become increasingly difficult as security measures increase and key conference areas are temporarily blocked with the arrival of world leaders.
U.S. President Donald Trump, who has called climate change a hoax, has targeted offshore wind projects and removed rules limiting power plant emissions.
text:
ANTALYA, Turkey (AP) — World leaders began to arrive Wednesday to start formal discussions at the United Nations climate change conference in Turkey, hoping to agree on concrete actions to curb global warming after a year of deadly floods, heat waves and other climate-related disasters.

But what can and will be accomplished at the Conference of the Parties, called COP31, remains to be seen. Past talks have been criticized for making promises that later fell flat.

While delegates at the 2023 conference in Dubai agreed to transition away from fossil fuels such as coal, oil and gas — the leading contributor to climate change — subsequent conferences in Azerbaijan and Brazil ended with little agreement on reductions. Last year's Brazil conference produced a compromise agreement pledging additional money to help vulnerable nations adapt to climate change.

This year's conference officially kicked off Monday with Turkey hosting and Australia leading negotiations at a time of fears that the world is not moving quickly enough.

Many participants, who struggled with overcrowded transport links and traffic congestion, set out for the summit venue before sunrise to avoid lengthy delays. Access was expected to become increasingly difficult as security measures increase and key conference areas are temporarily blocked with the arrival of world leaders.

Scientists say global warming is likely to exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above preindustrial levels of the early 1800s. Limiting temperature rise to that threshold was a goal set during the 2015 Paris Agreement and has been a focus of international negotiations.

The talks also come as the war in Iran has increased global prices of gasoline, oil and products made with them, such as fertilizers and pesticides. That has pushed governments to rethink energy policies and investment in renewable energy sources like wind and solar.

“We don’t need more promises, we need plans,” said John Kerry, former U.S. secretary of state and former presidential climate envoy, though the U.S. itself, the world’s second-largest polluter after China, is noticeably absent for the second year in a row.

U.S. President Donald Trump, who has called climate change a hoax, has targeted offshore wind projects and removed rules limiting power plant emissions.

___

Milko reported from Islamabad and Webber reported from Chicago.

U.S. President Donald Trump, who has called climate change a hoax, has targeted offshore wind projects and removed rules limiting power plant emissions.

___

Milko reported from Islamabad and Webber reported from Chicago.

text:
More than 300 solar and energy storage companies sent a letter to congressional leadership urging the immediate passage of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (S. 5653), framing federal permitting reform as an urgent necessity to lower power bills and accelerate clean energy deployment.

Organized by the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA), the coalition sent the letter to House Speaker Mike Johnson, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer. The signers, representing companies that collectively employ 280,000 Americans, argued that outdated federal permitting processes remain one of the primary obstacles to connecting lower-cost renewable energy to the electric grid.

Solar and storage technology represent the fastest and most affordable new electricity resources to deploy, the coalition stated in its letter to congressional leaders. However, the current system of permitting limits the speedy deployment of clean, lower-cost solar and storage, creating delays that ultimately cost American families in higher utility bills, the group said.

According to market research from Wood Mackenzie cited in the letter, solar and energy storage projects account for 70% of all new utility-scale generation capacity added to the U.S. grid so far in 2026. Despite that market dominance, an estimated $120 billion in clean energy capital investment currently remains stalled in federal permitting queues and regulatory reviews.

Streamlining federal project reviews

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act proposes several key policy adjustments to streamline federal oversight and accelerate project development schedules. First, the legislation requires federal reviews, interagency consultations, and access to federal lands to treat all energy technologies neutrally without discrimination. The bill also guarantees permit certainty by preventing lawfully issued federal permits from being paused, revoked, or slow-walked for political reasons.

Additionally, the measure establishes predictable deadlines for federal reviews under the Endangered Species Act and U.S. Army Corps of Engineers programs, alongside reasonable timelines for judicial reviews. The proposal further modernizes regional transmission planning to ensure new generation resources can reliably reach high-demand customer centers. Finally, the policy provides distributed energy generation resources direct access to participate in wholesale energy markets.

Solar and storage developers cannot finance multi-year, capital-intensive projects without the predictability and certainty needed to build projects and connect them to the grid, SEIA noted in the letter.

The coalition urged lawmakers to pass S. 5653 swiftly to meet surging national electricity demand, alleviate inflationary pressure on consumer power bills, and maintain domestic supply chain momentum.

name: Clean Energy
title: A bipartisan permitting bill could unleash energy development with major caveats
authors: Tosin Akintola, Eric Boehm, Josh Pauzé, C.J. Ciaramella, Jacob Sullum
description:
The federal permitting process has stifled development in America's energy, housing, and transportation industries for decades.
Under the bill, modifications to energy infrastructure along existing routes and projects already evaluated by another agency would also be exempt from NEPA review.
A state or tribal environmental review could also serve as NEPA compliance.
BAAJA removes permit requirements for onshore oil and gas drilling on nonfederal land, and expedites approval for renewable energy, geothermal, hydropower, or offshore energy projects.
Despite its goal of narrowing federal involvement in large infrastructure projects, BAAJA gives some regulators greater authority over the energy sector.
text:
On Monday evening, the Senate moved one step closer to passing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) with a 73–25 procedural vote to bring the bill to the floor for the full chamber to consider.

Sponsored by Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R–W.Va.), chairwoman of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, the 494-page bill would modify the federal permitting process by limiting the scope of environmental reviews and expediting the timeline for project approval.

The federal permitting process has stifled development in America's energy, housing, and transportation industries for decades. The average timeline to complete an environmental impact statement—the most stringent review under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA)—is over two years, according to a 2025 report by the White House Council on Environmental Quality.

The bill would address this challenge by expanding categorical exclusions—projects that don't require NEPA review—including for transmission and interstate natural gas pipeline repairs, upgrades, and expansions. Under the bill, modifications to energy infrastructure along existing routes and projects already evaluated by another agency would also be exempt from NEPA review. A state or tribal environmental review could also serve as NEPA compliance.

BAAJA removes permit requirements for onshore oil and gas drilling on nonfederal land, and expedites approval for renewable energy, geothermal, hydropower, or offshore energy projects. For projects in the energy and critical minerals industries, the bill sets a deadline for issuing permits that don't require environmental reviews—a year from the date of the last complete application submitted—and creates a path to petition the courts for relief if an agency fails to meet it. It also sets deadlines for federal agencies to issue permits once an environmental review is complete and limits the onerous review process under the Clean Water Act, National Historic Preservation Act, and Endangered Species Act, which are often used to stymie projects.

Critically, BAAJA addresses one of the biggest NEPA hurdles: litigation. The bill limits who can file a NEPA-related lawsuit and shrinks the statute of limitations to 150 days. Despite its goal of narrowing federal involvement in large infrastructure projects, BAAJA gives some regulators greater authority over the energy sector.

Drawing on public displeasure with data centers, the bill tasks the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) with ensuring that data centers or cryptocurrency mining facilities "incur the full cost of the transmission service they require." It requires utilities to "provide financial assurances or contributions sufficient to cover the cost of the facility or upgrade" before making any improvements to facilities if those improvements serve data centers. A manager's amendment added to the bill last week would also expand FERC's authority by allowing the agency to issue permits for project sites on state-owned land and broaden its oversight of regional power grid operators.

With a bill this dense, plenty of groups across the political spectrum have something to applaud—in fact, BAAJA has received support from industry trade groups and the environmental lobby. At the same time, enough controversial portions could keep it from passing.

The transmission portions—which give the federal government a larger role in modernizing and expanding the nation's electric grid (a task federal regulators have proven ill suited to perform)—could prompt some conservative groups or lawmakers to withdraw support. That has sunk comprehensive permitting reform in the past. Meanwhile, a coalition of tribal nations stands opposed to the bill, arguing it usurps their authority over tribal lands and "undermines" their "ability to protect history and culture." Even prominent advocacy groups like the Sierra Club and Natural Resources Defense Council—which oppose the bill because of its environmental provisions—concede it would increase the number of clean energy projects built in the country.

President Donald Trump is also a wildcard. On Sunday, he described it as a "BIG WIN for U.S. ENERGY INDEPENDENCE and DOMINANCE," although he's stopped short of endorsing every provision. One such provision includes prohibiting federal agencies from revoking or rescinding fully permitted projects—a tactic the administration has used to stymie offshore wind projects. On Monday, Trump told reporters the bill "hasn't been fully negotiated," and that he wouldn't "approve wind turbines" as part of a deal to pass the bill "because wind turbines are a major loser."

The procedural vote is just the first step in a long legislative process to pass the bill before a new, Democratically controlled Congress begins in January. There was little pushback on the Republican side, with every party member except for Sen. Mike Rounds (R–S.D.) voting yes. Democrats have been harder to gauge, with 23 senators voting no, including Sens. Jeff Merkley (D–Ore.), Ed Markey (D–Mass.), and Bernie Sanders (I–Vt.). Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D–N.Y.), who voted yes on the measure, said he had "outstanding concerns" with the bill and that he'll "fight to address" them during the amendment process, Axios reported Tuesday.

text:
Price trends

According to the commodity market analysis system of SunSirs, the spot price of lithium carbonate experienced a brief rebound mid-week during the period from November 2 to November 6, 2026. On November 6, the benchmark price for battery-grade lithium carbonate, as tracked by SunSirs, reached 94,500 RMB/ton—a 4.4% increase from the previous day—before subsequently falling back. As of November 10, the benchmark price stood at 90,000 RMB/ton, representing a 25.6% decline compared to the same period last month. This recent uptick was driven by market sentiment rather than a fundamental shift in supply and demand.

Nature of the Rebound: Fluctuations in Macro Expectations

Following the Democratic Party's gains in the U.S. midterm elections, there is renewed potential for the restoration of clean energy tax credits under the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA), alongside anticipated increases in investment for energy storage and power grids. Market expectations suggest a push for policies favoring clean energy and electric vehicles, which has brightened the global demand outlook for new energy. Consequently, the market's outlook for lithium carbonate—as a key energy metal—has improved, triggering a brief shift in sentiment; however, the underlying supply-demand fundamentals remain essentially unchanged.

Real-world side: Downward shift in cost support

Quotes from the upstream mining sector have weakened, causing the cost curve to shift downward in line with the pricing anchor. The landed price of SC6 spodumene concentrate has continued to decline, falling by more than 10% week-on-week.

Anticipated Downward Pressure: The Dual Burden of Weakening Demand and Resuming Production

Both domestic sales of new energy vehicles (NEVs) and new energy storage installations have fallen short of expectations.

Total scheduled production for lithium batteries in November reached 323 GWh—a 5.0% month-on-month decline, marking the first such monthly drop this year.

The latest data from the China Passenger Car Association (CPCA) shows that sales of broad-sense passenger vehicles in October reached 1.653 million units—a year-on-year decline of 27.3%, but a month-on-month increase of 1.4%. Sales of new energy vehicles (NEVs) in October totaled 1.109 million units, down 13.7% year-on-year and up 2.3% month-on-month.

On November 9, a meeting was held regarding the resumption of production at the Jianxiawo lithium mine, owned by CATL. The objective is to complete the restart within November; once operating at full capacity, the mine is expected to produce approximately 10,000 tons of lithium carbonate per month—an amount equivalent to 12.5% of the total monthly domestic production.

Production capacity at overseas mines continues to ramp up. Between November 2 and November 8, 86,000 tonnes of lithium concentrate were shipped from Australia to China—an average of 71,000 tonnes per week. Meanwhile, lithium concentrate production is coming online in several African nations, including Zimbabwe, Mali, and Ghana. On November 9, the fifth shipment of lithium concentrate from the Bougouni lithium mine—totaling 17,400 tonnes—arrived at Yangpu Port. This brings the cumulative volume shipped in 2026 to 93,300 tonnes, with an additional 30,000 tonnes scheduled for December, pushing the annual total beyond 120,000 tonnes. Industry estimates place the landed cost in China within the range of 80,000 to 100,000 RMB/ton.

The market may be shifting from destocking to restocking. With supply remaining tight in the near term but easing further out, prices are fluctuating in response to these competing dynamics.

Overall, this rebound is driven by macroeconomic sentiment rather than an improvement in supply and demand fundamentals. With the resumption of production acting as a constraint, prices are more likely to fall than rise; the actual evolution of market supply and demand remains the key factor to watch.

description:

The waiver request applies only to 2027 RVOs, not 2026 RVOs.
Refiners have repeatedly shown that if they are not required to blend lower-cost renewable fuels into the gasoline supply, they won’t.
The Iowa Renewable Fuels Association said weaking the RFS would undermine farmers, renewable fuel producers, and rural economies while leading to higher prices.
Ethanol lowers fuels prices because it is less expensive than gasoline and adds gallons to the market.
text:
Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey and Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry on Nov. 9 submitted a petition to U.S. EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin seeking a partial waiver of the compliance year 2027 Renewable Fuel Standard renewable volume obligations (RVOs).

In the petition, Ivey and Landry cite “near-record diesel prices driven by global supply disruptions arising from the conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine” as one reason for the waiver request, along with high renewable identification number (RIN) prices and other factors.

The waiver request applies only to 2027 RVOs, not 2026 RVOs. “Because the 2026 compliance year is nearly complete, the petitioning states seek relief only for 2027, where a waiver can provide meaningful, prospective relief without disturbing compliance obligations that obligated parties and renewable fuel producers have already planned around for 2026,” the governors wrote. “We believe waiving the obligations will allow for the economic use of renewable fuel without burdening our citizens with the high prices this program imposes.”

Representatives of the biofuels industry are speaking out against the claims made in the petition and calling on the EPA to reject the request.

“Any suggestion that ethanol blending compelled by the RFS is somehow raising gas prices is abjectly absurd and demonstrably false,” said Geoff Cooper, president and CEO of the Renewable Fuels Association. “Wholesale ethanol prices are $1 per gallon lower than wholesale gasoline prices today, and DOE recently reported that E15 prices are 40 cents per gallon lower, on average, than standard E10 gasoline prices. Refiners have repeatedly shown that if they are not required to blend lower-cost renewable fuels into the gasoline supply, they won’t. Far from delivering ‘relief’ at the pump, a waiver of the 2027 RFS requirements would remove a dependable source of lower-cost, lower-carbon fuel from the marketplace and cause higher gas prices. It would also harm struggling corn and soybean farmers in Alabama, Louisiana, and across the country by undermining demand for their crops. EPA should swiftly and soundly reject these waiver requests.”

Growth Energy also cautioned the governors’ request would increase fuel costs and hurt farmers. “The request asks EPA to undo the historic work the Trump Administration has done to drive growth in American biofuels and rural communities across the U.S.,” said Emily Skor, CEO of Growth Energy. “If EPA were to grant these states the special treatment they’re asking for, it would increase fuel prices—not lower them—by reducing the amount of ethanol being blended into America’s fuel supply. As any driver can see when they drive past a station that offers E15 or E85, the more ethanol in a fuel, the more affordable it is.”

“The President should not grant this request and should not break the promises he’s made to rural America in order to further line the pockets of refiners that are already reporting record profits, made off the backs of American consumers and farmers,” Skor added.

The Iowa Renewable Fuels Association said weaking the RFS would undermine farmers, renewable fuel producers, and rural economies while leading to higher prices.

“With all due respect to the governors, during this time of high fuel prices, the last thing you want to do is reduce supply,” said Monte Shaw, executive director of the IRFA. “The real solution is to unleash additional U.S. supply, which Congress can do by removing barriers to year-round E15 sales. Ethanol lowers fuels prices because it is less expensive than gasoline and adds gallons to the market. Expanding the use of low-cost ethanol, made right here in America, would lower prices at the pump. Consumers need real solutions, not ineffective political potshots.”

“It is absurd to claim that implementing the RFS in 2027 is causing severe economic harm – the year hasn’t even started yet,” Shaw continued. “Just look at the price of gasoline without ethanol – it’s way more expensive. Further, renewable fuels production is expanding, not contracting. Renewable fuels do not rely on imported feedstocks or the Strait of Hormuz. President Trump knows we need more, not less, domestic fuel supply. That’s why he set robust RFS blending levels for 2026-2027 in the first place. Now would be the worst time to reverse course. IRFA urges President Trump to swiftly reject this misguided petition and ensure certainty for the marketplace.”

text:
From July 25th through July 31st, the Climate Jobs Institute (CJI) hosted an international educational delegation to London, England, bringing together state legislators and labor leaders from across New York State. This was CJI’s fourth educational delegation designed to equip leaders with global insights on the clean energy transition and highlight how other nations are implementing innovative policies, strategies, and technologies to meet current and future energy demands while creating good union jobs. The delegation's agenda included visits to a nuclear power station currently under construction and meetings with local labor unions, industry leaders, and elected officials.

The delegation kicked off Monday morning with a visit to the British Parliament with CJI partners at Climate Jobs UK (CJUK), for a presentation by the Labour Climate and Environment Forum (LCEF) and the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR), giving an overview of the United Kingdom’s clean energy transition, labor market, and key drivers of this work in both the public and private sectors. Following this presentation, the delegates met with union leaders from CJUK, Mike Clancy, General Secretary of Prospect Union, Gary Smith, General Secretary of GMB, and Dave Douglas, Chair of Climate Jobs UK, to dig deeper into labor’s role in the UK’s energy transition and the biggest opportunities and challenges facing workers. Lastly, delegates heard from a panel of rank-and-file workers who spoke about the training and opportunities available to them, the challenges the transition may pose to their work, and how their communities are receiving the changes that come with it.

The next day, the delegation traveled west to visit the Hinkley Point C nuclear power station, where two new nuclear reactors are under construction. This visit gave the delegates an important opportunity to learn firsthand about the construction process, opportunities for workers and local communities, and the impact on the UK’s energy goals. Workers from Hinkley joined the delegation for lunch on site for candid discussions about their training and how locals welcomed the work. Lastly, a guided tour of the construction site highlighted the project's complexity and size, and how developers approached safety and security. The tour also prompted a discussion of supply-chain opportunities ahead of possible growth in the industry in New York, and the ways that a nuclear plant can provide jobs beyond construction and operations.

Wednesday’s programming focused on renewable energy and grid infrastructure. Delegates started the day with a conversation with RenewableUK, an organization representing nearly 500 companies spanning the full supply chain that develop, operate and maintain the UK's wind, tidal, and storage infrastructure. With the delegates and CJUK, RenewableUK discussed what industrial policies could help the UK build out offshore wind in a way that would create union jobs. Calling in from Scotland, Michael Shanks, Minister of State in the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, spoke with the group on the government’s approach to reaching net zero emissions and how this intersects with other priorities, such as jobs and national security. The last meeting of the day was with National Grid, a major grid operator that also operates in New York and throughout the United States.

On the final day, delegates focused on transit. The morning began with a meeting with The National Union of Rail, Maritime and Transport Workers representatives to learn how UK transit operates, how funding sources differ from New York, and the history of the union’s impact on public transit. The day ended with a meeting with Mete Coban MBE, the Deputy Mayor of London for Environment and Energy. Delegates discussed London’s borough-by-borough approach to tackling the environmental crisis and the challenges each neighborhood faces in building critical transit infrastructure, like electric vehicle charging stations.

Over the week, the Climate Jobs Institute’s delegation gave New York legislators and labor leaders a close look at how the UK is pursuing its clean energy transition while building good union jobs. As New York moves forward with its own clean energy goals, the delegation offered lessons on training, supply chains, and local job creation that can help shape policy at home.

text:
WeaveGrid has launched EVConnectNC, a managed charging program for North Carolina's Electric Cooperatives. The program is already operating at Roanoke Electric Cooperative and South River EMC.

Why it matters

The program is designed to help cooperatives monitor charging patterns and shift electricity use to lower-cost periods as electric vehicle demand grows. It also reflects an effort to align consumption with available grid capacity.

The program offers up to $120 per year to enrolled members who charge at least 90% of the time during off-peak hours and use a minimum of 200 kilowatt-hours per month. North Carolina's Electric Cooperatives supports 26 community-based cooperatives, though the source does not report how many have enrolled.

The players

WeaveGrid

WeaveGrid is a grid orchestration software provider for electric utilities that offers its DISCO platform for asset-level visibility and device-level control of EVs, batteries and flexible loads.

North Carolina's Electric Cooperatives

North Carolina's Electric Cooperatives is an organization that supports the state's 26 community-based electric cooperatives and their member utilities in operating the program.

The details

EVConnectNC allows members of participating cooperatives to earn incentives by charging electric vehicles during off-peak hours. WeaveGrid's software uses connected vehicle and charger data to monitor charging patterns, and the program works with certain EV models from Dodge, Jeep, Lexus, Tesla and Toyota, as well as home chargers from ChargePoint, Emporia and Wallbox.

November 10, 2026: EVConnectNC program launch announced

text:
Ford has hired former General Motors executive Marissa West as its new vice president of vehicle programs.

West will lead vehicle program and program operations teams as Ford plans to refresh most of its global vehicle portfolio.

She previously spent 21 years at General Motors, holding several leadership positions including president of GM Canada.
